title: A closure returned from a closure that captures one of the outer closure's own non-`Copy` captures passes `karac check` but the MIR build refuses it: `let base = vec![1, 2, 3]; let make = |n: i64| |x: i64| x + n + base.len(); let f = make(1);` gives `cannot move a non-Copy value out of a borrowed place` (§3.7)
detail: MEASURED on a release build of the B-2026-10-24-9 fix (eede6bfd40): `fn main() { let base = vec![1, 2, 3]; let make = |n: i64| |x: i64| x + n + base.len(); let f = make(1); println(f"{f(0)}"); }` prints `All checks passed.` from `karac check`, while `karac __mir-run` gives `error[mir]: build: 3:25: cannot move a non-Copy value out of a borrowed place: take a copy with .clone(), ... (core semantics §3.7)`. The inner closure is returned, so it escapes and captures `base` by move (core semantics §9.3); the outer closure, whose body therefore moves `base` out of its environment, still captures `base` by `ref` (EnvMode::Ref), so the inner closure's capture is a move out of `(*env).base`. Per §9.1 the outer closure's body moves the place, so the outer capture should be by move too, making `make` a `OnceFn` (§9.4). EXPECTED by that reading, not measured: one call compiles and prints 4, a second call is E0500. Check and the MIR build disagree on the same program, so one of them is wrong; the spec reading above says the build's capture inference is. Not seen when the inner closure captures a `Copy` place, a reference, or the outer closure's parameter (those pass on both, pinned in tests/mir_closure_results.rs). Owner: Thread B (MIR builder capture inference), unverified ownership.
fix: a5ec3ea61c handles closures that return closures in the builder. When a closure's body returns a closure literal (found through the walk note_returned_closures already uses, now `returned_closures_of` in src/mir/lower.rs), each non-`Copy`, non-handle, non-reference place of the outer closure's that the returned closure uses joins the outer closure's moved captures. So the outer closure captures that place by move (§9.1) and its environment is consumed per call (§9.4), and the escaping inner closure's by-move capture (§9.3) no longer moves out of a borrowed environment. A `shared` handle is still counted from the outer environment, which keeps borrowing it. The row's program prints 4 on the interpreter, compiled and ASan. Pinned by tests/mir_closure_returns_closure.rs (a Vec capture; a handle plus a Vec through a block tail with an early `return`), on all three lanes. Control on main: 0 of 2 pass. The checker still accepts a second call or a later use of the moved place, and the build then refuses it with an internal move-check error; that is B-2026-10-26-9 (Thread A).

title: Writing a `mut` field of a captured `shared` handle makes a closure `MutFn` (E0518 at an `Fn` slot), though the capture itself is unchanged and a borrowed-`self` method doing the same write is callable from an `Fn` closure
fix: 0c3f03df1f. The capture is the handle, and a write into the object behind it leaves the handle as it was: any handle may write a `mut` field (core semantics §6.2), as the borrowed-`self` method already could from an `Fn` closure. src/typechecker/core_ref_write.rs (`writes_through_a_handle`) now skips the capture-write mark for a place that projects a field out of a `shared` handle, directly (`cache.stream = ..`, `cache.items.push(..)`) or through a struct field holding one (`b.h.n = ..`). Writing a field of an owned capture, or assigning the handle itself (`cache = C { .. }`), still makes the closure `MutFn`. §9.6 now says so in one sentence. The row's program checks and prints `4` and `3` on `__mir-run`, `__mir-llvm-run` and ASan (clean). Pinned by corpus/core/ok_closure_writes_through_a_captured_handle and tests/core_strict_check.rs `a_closure_writing_through_a_captured_handle_is_fn` (control at 43776f0cec: 0 passed, 1 failed). Corpus check sweep and the 9-package compare unchanged.

title: `karac check` treats a closure that returns a closure as an `Fn` that borrows its captures, when the returned closure escapes and moves a non-`Copy` capture out (§9.3), which makes the outer closure move that place in and an `OnceFn` (§9.1, §9.4): a second call, or a use of the place after the outer closure is made, passes check and the MIR build refuses it with an internal move-check error
detail:
Split from B-2026-10-26-8, whose builder half is fixed. With `let base = vec![1, 2, 3]; let make = |n: i64| |x: i64| x + n + base.len();`:
- `let f = make(1); let g = make(2);` passes `karac check`, and `karac __mir-run` now says `error[mir]: move check main: bb3[term]: use of _4, which may have been moved or never initialized`. §9.6 says a second call of an `OnceFn` is E0500.
- `let f = make(1); println(f"{f(0)} {base.len()}");` passes check, and the build says `move check main: bb4[0]: use of _1 ...`. §9.3 says using the moved place afterwards is E0500, fixed by cloning before the closure.

Both should be E0500 from check, naming `base` and the returned closure. The checker's closure kind (node type `Fn { once }`) and capture modes for the outer closure need the returned inner closure's by-move captures, as the builder now does (src/mir/lower.rs, `returned_closures_of` in closure lowering). Owner: Thread A (check), unverified.
fix: 016b5608ec, with ca82f0ac13. A closure literal returned from another closure (its body's tail, through blocks, `if`, `match`, `return`, tuples, arrays and struct literals) escapes by core-semantics §9.3, so it captures by move, and the outer closure that hands it back moves the capture each call: the outer closure is `OnceFn` when the capture is not `Copy`. src/core_escape.rs walks a closure body as an escaping position ("returned from a closure"), for closure literals only; src/typechecker/closures.rs counts a capture of a returned closure as a consume (`returned_closure_spans`, `capture_walk_by_move`). The row's program runs to `4` with one call; a second call is refused as "an OnceFn is called once", and a use of the capture after is "value 'base' was moved into an escaping closure". ca82f0ac13: such a closure copies a `ref` it captures and MIR keeps that borrow where the result lives (B-2026-10-24-9), so the B-2026-10-25-20 borrow-capture refusal now counts only closures that escape further (core_escape's `closure_result_only`); tests/mir_closure_results.rs passes again. Pinned by tests/core_strict_check.rs `a_closure_returning_a_capturing_closure_is_once` (control 0 passed, 1 failed). Corpus check sweep and the 9-package compare unchanged. Known gap: a closure returned through a call is not followed.

title: `karac check` accepts an escaping closure created inside a loop that captures an outer non-`Copy` binding, which moves it on every iteration; `karac run` stops at an internal MIR move-check error instead of a diagnostic
fix: 647464dbbb. An escaping closure moves its captures in when it is created (core semantics §9.3), so a loop around the creation moves an outer non-`Copy` capture again each iteration (§3.3). Since B-2026-10-25-14 the loop-of-consume rule (src/rc_predicate.rs) skipped a consume inside a capture's closure body, which is right for a loop inside the body but lost the loop around the creation. src/cfg.rs now records each closure literal's creation block (`Cfg::closure_creations`), and the rule checks the loops around it, as it checks a container store's call site, with the same loop-local `let` and rebind exemptions. The row's program is refused as "value 'prog' was moved into an escaping closure ...", with the clone fix, in a `for` and in a `while`, also when the body reads the capture in a loop of its own; MIR's move check refuses the same programs. A clone made inside the loop, a non-escaping closure and a borrowing task closure check and run. Pinned by corpus/core/err_escaping_capture_in_loop and tests/core_strict_check.rs `an_escaping_closure_made_in_a_loop_moves_its_capture_each_time` (control at aec61f30b3: 0 passed, 1 failed). Corpus check sweep and the 9-package compare unchanged.

title: `karac check` counts a capture of an ESCAPING closure as moved when a nested closure in its body reads it (`is.iter().map(|i| look(p, *i)).sum()`, with `p: ref Prog` in `look`): a later read of `p`, or a read in another `match` arm, is 'moved into an escaping closure, used again here', while both MIR backends run it and the same body in a plain function checks
fix: 6f363a1aa2. The capture-scope rule from B-2026-10-25-14 keyed a read inside a nested closure to the innermost enclosing closure, so a non-escaping closure nested in an escaping one (`is.iter().map(|i| xs[i])` inside a closure returned or stored) saw the escaping closure's by-move capture as a move at the read, and a later read in the same escaping body as a use after move. src/use_classifier.rs now tracks which closures on the stack escape (`escaping_closure_flags`) and keys the capture scope to the OUTERMOST closure that takes the name by move, so every read inside its body, nested or not, reads the one captured copy. The apps thread's program runs to `61 21`. Pinned by tests/core_strict_check.rs `a_nested_closure_reads_an_escaping_closures_capture` (control 0 passed, 1 failed). Corpus check sweep and the 9-package compare unchanged.

title: A `shared` handle crosses a task boundary inside a function value: a closure capturing a `shared` struct, erased to `Fn` and captured by a `TaskGroup.spawn` closure, passes `karac check` (E_NOT_CROSS_TASK does not look through `Fn`), and under `KARAC_THREADS=4` its non-atomic count double-frees
fix: 6cfb8ff699. Ruled (review thread, core-semantics §6.3 in e2302c538a): a function value is CrossTask only when everything its environment reaches is, through nested closures and erased `Fn` / `MutFn` / `OnceFn` values. src/typechecker/fn_env_cross_task.rs computes what each function value's environment reaches (closure literals, bindings of them, closures nested in closures, function-typed parameters), and refuses with E_NOT_CROSS_TASK: a TaskGroup.spawn closure holding such a value (the row's program), a function value passed to a parameter that some callee spawns (a fixpoint over calls), and a handler passed to `Server.serve` / `serve_tls` / `serve_ws` / `serve_ws_tls`. The message names the capture and its type; the help points at a `sync` type with `Mutex[T]` or `Atomic[T]` for its `mut` fields. A `sync` store reached through an `Fn`, and a plain capture, still check and run. Thread C moved todo-api and the shortener to a `sync` store first (8d7144c1d8, kara-katas 10b8e29b); the pre-migration versions of both are refused, and b061b33e01 refreshes the corpus shortener copy, which still held the `shared` store. Corpus check sweep otherwise unchanged; 9-package compare unchanged. Pinned by corpus/core/err_fn_value_shared_crosses_task and tests/core_strict_check.rs `a_function_value_reaching_a_shared_handle_does_not_cross_a_task` (six programs; control at b5230d6642: 0 passed, 1 failed).

title: Two `par` branches that walk one `frozen` graph of a `shared struct` race on its reference counts on the pool (KARAC_THREADS=4): ThreadSanitizer reports the count write in the traversal (`kara.sum`, `kara.main.c0`) against `drop.shared Node` on another worker, where core-semantics §6 says a `frozen` handle is never counted and §11.3 lets frozen handles into tasks
detail:
MEASURED with the M4 item 11 lane (`run.py --backend mir-llvm-tsan`, f5689254b4) on a debug llvm karac at f5689254b4 and a TSan runtime archive built with std instrumented (-Zbuild-std=std,panic_abort, RUSTFLAGS=-Zsanitizer=thread; CLAUDE.md § Runtime archives). Six runs each, KARAC_HASH_SEED=1, KARAC_THREADS=4, `karac __mir-llvm-tsan source.kara`, exit 86 counted:
- corpus/fixtures/memory_sanitizer/concurrency/asan_frozen_vec_worklist_traversal_across_par_branches_no_leak: 4/6
- .../asan_kata133_clone_graph_bfs_across_par_branches_no_leak: 3/6
- .../asan_frozen_alias_traversal_across_par_branches_no_leak: 1/6 (and fixtures/par_codegen/frozen_alias_traversal_computes_correctly_across_par_branches reported once)
Shape of the report (frozen_alias): `Write of size 8 ... by main thread: kara.sum <- kara.driver.c1`; `Previous write of size 8 ... by thread T1: drop.shared Node <- kara.sum`; location a 72-byte heap block (a Node). vec_worklist: writes in kara.main.c0 / kara.main.c1 (the two branches) against drop.shared Node. So reading a handle out of a frozen value (`let k = n.kids[i]`, `worka.push(g)`, `for ka in na.kids`) counts it and drops it with the non-atomic `shared` count, on two workers at once: a lost update can free a live node.
Not this row: the other reports of the first TSan run (borrow-flag table, stdout buffer, channel queue, all `program_state!` behind a std Mutex) were the archive's precompiled std hiding the lock from TSan; 15 of 17 re-run went quiet with an instrumented std. Outputs are right today (the plain lanes pass), so this shows only under TSan or as a rare crash.
Owner: drop schedule (counting in MIR lowering/drop elaboration for frozen places). Spec: a frozen handle is never counted (core-semantics §6, Gowtham 2026-10-10), so the fix is to not count, not an atomic count. The CI `tsan` leg fails on these until fixed; the pool goes default-on only once it is green (M4 plan item 11).
fix:
dfce639b14. The ownership check's frozen walk already handed over which `let`s are aliases of a frozen place and which `Vec` locals are frozen worklists (OwnershipCheckResult.frozen_alias_bindings / frozen_element_containers, keyed by initializer span), but only the legacy codegen read them; v2 lowering ignored them, so `let k = n.kids[i]` and `q.push(g)` took a non-atomic count. Lowering now carries them (`FrozenHints`) and records each body's frozen locals; `mir::frozen::uncount`, run after the borrow flags, rewrites an alias `x = retain(p)` to `x = &p` (its drops become gotos, a whole use takes its own `retain((*x))`), and a worklist's pushes of `t = retain(q)` to `Vec[T].__push_frozen(&mut c, &q)` (an uncounted copy of the handle) with `Vec[T].__forget_items(&mut c)` before each drop, so the drop frees the buffer and releases nothing (natives in interp.rs and backend/mir/call.rs). A local whose MIR is not that shape keeps its counts: correct, only not count-free.
MEASURED: the 37 corpus programs with `frozen`/`freeze`, `karac __mir-llvm-tsan`, KARAC_THREADS=4, KARAC_HASH_SEED=1, three rounds, instrumented-std TSan archive. Before (at 3232cb4c25): 6 reported every round (the three rows' fixtures, fixtures/par_codegen/frozen_alias_traversal_computes_correctly_across_par_branches, kata 133 clone_bfs_par, fixtures/mir_tasks/mir_tasks_par_branches_each_copy_a_frozen_handle). After: none, except mir_tasks_par_branches_each_copy_a_frozen_handle, which `karac check` refuses (expect = "error:E0512", freeze of a temporary) and which the direct `karac __mir-llvm-tsan` run executes without the ownership check; a lane that honours `expect` judges it as refused. Corpus at 4 workers on mir-interp, mir-llvm and mir-llvm-asan (apps, core, par, mir_*, concurrency, par_codegen): no new failure (clone_bfs_par's ASan leak is the cyclic clones', red since gate113).
Pinned by tests/mir_frozen_uncounted.rs (the MIR shape, all three backends on one and four workers, TSan five runs each), run in CI's tsan job.

title: E_CHAR_AS_NARROW_INT on an ASCII char LITERAL (`'#' as u8`) carries no edit and its help does not name the byte literal `b'#'`, so `karac fix` leaves each one for the author, though the literal fits and the rewrite is exact (23 hand edits in mini_markdown)

For a char literal that is ASCII, cast to `u8`, the typechecker's `Cast` arm (src/typechecker/exprs.rs) now reports E_CHAR_AS_NARROW_INT with "'#' is ASCII, so write the byte literal `b'#'`" and a machine-applicable edit replacing the whole cast. `byte_literal` spells the bytes that need an escape as `b'\''`, `b'\\'`, `b'\n'`, `b'\t'`, `b'\r'`, `b'\0'`, or `b'\xHH'` for any other control byte. detail:

- 4 workers (m4b-speedup-9030678cd-t4.md, 9 runs; rerun9030a/ and rerun9030b/, 21 runs each): hotel_audit 0.886 / 0.852 / 0.897, 18..24 ms runs with 2 loops, 3 statement groups and 2 reductions as tasks, par cpu/wall 1.14; freight_audit 0.859 / 0.897 / 0.910. RE-TIMED, three more 21-run timings on 4 workers at 9030678cd0 (rerun9030c/, d/, e/), with sensor_merge (no task site) as the noise control: hotel_audit 0.970 / 0.976 / 0.921; freight_audit 0.857 / 1.031 / 0.911; milk_collect 0.868 / 0.734 / 1.186; risk_batch 0.875 / 1.071 / 0.884; sensor_merge 1.237 / 1.008 / 1.002. On these 5..24 ms programs one 21-run median swings by 0.15..0.45, so the 4-worker half of this row is noise at this resolution; a longer input would be needed to see a few ms. What stays is the one-worker list. THREAD B (10-26, release build at 9030678cd0's successor): hotel_audit, 31 runs on 4 workers, 0.892x as is and 0.978x with its two small tasked loops written as non-counting whiles (revenue_report@782 `for k in 0..4`, a format and push per trip, and ledger_summary@938 `0..min2(5, ..)`), so those 8 calls of 4..5 one-iteration tasks cost about 1.5 ms of 16: a cost-gate question (kata thread). One worker: kata 28 brute_force's sequential build folds the needle (`Vec.filled(16, ..)`) through the heap, and once the needle is captured by a task it escapes, so even the loop as written in the same function loses it; 4, 8, 9, 159 and 191 pay the exact signed-sum tracking per term (an i128 total and both prefixes). Measured, not landed: a pool check that runs an auto-par loop as written on one worker (no gain on 28, 4 or 191, and kata 12 fell to 1.07x on 4 workers); i64 tracking with an i128 fallback (see B-2026-10-26-14). CORRECTED by Thread B (10-26 19:10Z): the 0.892x/0.978x pair was one noisy pass. Three more passes of 31 interleaved runs on 4 workers, same binaries: as is 0.918 / 0.927 / 0.960, without the two loops 0.950 / 1.031 / 0.974. The kata thread's few-trips gate rule also measured no gain (kata-thread/m4-item13-fewtrips-* in the shared folder), so it was not landed. Gowtham's 10-26 12:57Z call puts auto-par default-on together with threads default-on, so one worker is not what a default auto-par program gets. WASM HALF FIXED by Thread B in b657fa3413 (10-27): a wasm build always runs one worker, so `build_source` now builds in order for a wasm target. Kata 28 brute force built with `--target=wasm_wasi` took 6.9 s as tasks and 2.2 s in order (7 runs each under node WASI). Pinned by tests/mir_auto_par_wasm.rs. Native one worker (`KARAC_THREADS=1`, or a one-core host) is still open.
fix: 45524985d1 (native half; the wasm half is b657fa3413): a native build keeps both forms of what auto-par touches and picks at run time. A function that has a site, or calls one that does (the callers closure over the in-order build's calls, `AutoParHints::note_affected`), is also lowered as `<name>#seq` with no hints, which is the body KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 builds, and starts by asking `__pooled()` (runtime `karac_mir_pooled`, the existing `pooled()`: KARAC_THREADS, else the core count; the interpreter answers the same). On one worker it returns what the twin returns. A twin calls only twins (`Bx::seq_world_call`), so a one-worker run enters an in-order copy of the program at `main` (or the first such function) and stays there. A twin of the function alone was not enough: with it, kata 8 stayed at 0.69x, because `my_atoi`, now called from the twin and from the task too, stopped being inlined (callgrind: 1.744G instructions in order, 1.815G with 120M in an out-of-line `my_atoi`). Through the whole copy the instruction counts match the in-order build: kata 28 KMP 4,602,427,749 vs 4,602,440,804; kata 7 16,102,283,875 vs 16,102,294,600; 8 1,744,126,705 vs 1,744,136,642; 125 20,340,373,969 vs 20,337,384,320; 153 760,374,604 vs 760,384,571; 60 nextperm 2,210,456,228 vs 2,210,465,788; 895 298,169,006 vs 299,610,665. scripts/m4b-speedup.py over all 129 programs, 9 runs, on the tree that became 45524985d1 (review/m4b-speedup/m4b-speedup-twin-45524985d1-t1.md and -t4.md in the shared folder): one worker geomean 1.009 (0.958 at 9030678cd0), kata 28 brute force 0.264 -> 1.087, 191 0.359 -> 0.904, 4 0.560 -> 1.037; four workers geomean 1.885, 0 outputs differing. Still under 0.9 on one worker in that pass: 16 programs (7, 8, 125, 153, 895 among them) whose instruction counts equal the in-order build's, so what remains is where the code lands, not what it runs: the very same in-order kata 7 linked against the full archive (KARAC_FORCE_FULL_RUNTIME=1) ran 2.4 s against 1.6 s lean. That remainder is its own row, B-2026-10-28-1. Pinned by tests/mir_auto_par_one_worker.rs (the twin exists and the entry asks; an owned self, a borrow, an owned Vec and a destructured tuple reach it; one and four workers print the same, built and interpreted), in CI's codegen-e2e job.

title: `karac check` types a `VecDeque` with `Vec`'s whole method surface, so `d.sort()`, `d.dedup()`, `d.binary_search(x)`, `d.as_slice()` check though collections.md (857e45825) refuses them; it should refuse every method off the VecDeque table with a "no method on VecDeque" diagnostic, suggesting `Vec.from_iter(dq)` for the ones that need one contiguous slice (sort, dedup, binary_search, reverse, ranges, as_slice)
detail: Split out of B-2026-10-21-29 (its fifth part; the other four closed at 4344167c8b). The review thread decided page-vs-checker at 857e45825 (docs/library/collections.md): the VecDeque table now carries new, push_back/front, pop_back/front, front, back, get, len, is_empty, clear, contains, insert, remove (shifting from the nearer end, panicking like Vec's), swap, retain, truncate, extend; try_insert is in the fallible-twins paragraph; iteration, Clone, Display, Eq/Ord and FromIterator are elsewhere on the page. Everything else is refused. The checker today routes VecDeque through `infer_vec_method` (src/typechecker/expr_method_call.rs, the `vec_elem_for_dispatch` block), so the whole Vec surface types. Check that the MIR backends implement each table method (insert/remove/swap/retain/truncate/extend on a ring buffer) before closing. Owner: Thread A.
fix: 687ad99102. `karac check` gives a `VecDeque` collections.md's surface (857e45825). `reject_vec_method_on_deque` (src/typechecker/method_vec_mutation.rs), ahead of the aggregate and Vec-mutation surfaces in `infer_method_call`, refuses every Vec/Slice method off the deque table as "no method 'm' on type 'VecDeque'": `push`/`pop`/`first`/`last` carry a machine fix to `push_back`/`pop_back`/`front`/`back`; the methods that need one slice (sort, dedup, binary_search, reverse, as_slice, split_at, chunks, windows, ...) point at `Vec.from_iter(dq)`; max/min/sum/product/join/concat point at `dq.iter().m()`. Checked on mir-interp, mir-llvm and mir-llvm-asan with i64 and String elements; every lib:vecdeque corpus entry fails the same on the pre-change binary or passes. Measured over every corpus and kata program naming VecDeque: one newly refused, fixtures/codegen/iter_range/test_e2e_direct_vec_iterator_terminals_survive_being_chained (already refused for `xs.max()` on its Vec), flipped to an error pin. Test: tests/core_strict_check.rs a_vecdeque_has_the_page_surface_not_vecs (control 0 passed 1 failed at 2ee6abbf8e).

title: `karac check` refuses returning a `Vec[(ref Node, i64)]` whose pushed tuples hold a borrow of a parameter ("returned borrowed collection holds an element that borrows function-local storage"), because the pinning check reads the tuple literal `(c, 1)` as a local source; the same push of a bare `c` into a `Vec[ref Node]` passes, and the MIR borrow checker accepts both
detail:
MEASURED 2026-10-27 on main 0a4cfd7fc7 (release karac), Thread B, while pinning B-2026-10-14-29. Prefix `struct Node { val: i64, children: Vec[Node] }`, and `main` builds a one-child tree and prints `frames(t).len()`.

(1) `fn frames(t: Node) -> Vec[ref Node] { let mut v: Vec[ref Node] = Vec.new(); for c in t.children.iter() { v.push(c); } v }`: check passes, runs, prints 1.
(2) the same with `Vec[(ref Node, i64)]` and `v.push((c, 1))`: check refuses at the returned `v` with "returned borrowed collection holds an element that borrows function-local storage; the element's source is dropped when the function returns, leaving the collection's borrows dangling". `karac __mir-run` (which skips check) runs it and prints 1, so the MIR borrow checker accepts it.
(3) `v.push((t, 1))`, a borrow of the parameter itself: the same refusal.
(4) `let local = Node { .. }; v.push((local, 1))`: refused by check, and also by the MIR borrow checker (E0516 drop while borrowed, E0509 result borrows a local), which is right.
(5) `Vec[(i64, i64)]` with `v.push((t.val, 1))`: passes.

CAUSE (read, not bisected): src/ownership/ref_return.rs check_borrowed_collection_pinning classifies each `v.push(src)` source with classify_borrow_return, and a tuple literal is classified as DanglingSource (a literal), whatever its `ref` parts borrow. The tuple's `ref` part should be classified instead, as the bare push in (1) is. The MIR borrow checker already gives the right answer on all five, so the fix is in check only.

TOUCHES: Thread A (src/ownership/).
fix: 098fea6a67. src/ownership/ref_return.rs `check_borrowed_collection_pinning` classified each pushed element (and a returned `Some(..)` / `Ok(..)` payload) whole with `classify_borrow_return`, and a tuple literal reads as a local, so `(c, 1)` and `(t, 1)` were refused. The new `element_source_dangles` takes the element type from the return type (`first_type_arg`) and classifies only the parts at `ref` positions: a tuple literal member by member, a borrowed struct literal by its `ref` fields; a part whose type holds no `ref` is an owned value. Re-measured on the row's five cases: (1) bare `c` passes as before; (2) `(c, 1)` and (3) `(t, 1)` now check and run (`1`); (4) `(local, 1)` is still refused by check, and by the MIR borrow check; (5) `Vec[(i64, i64)]` passes. A nested `Vec[(i64, (ref Node, String))]` with `(1, (t, "a"))` checks too. Pinned by tests/core_borrowed_collection_tuples.rs.

ee104fa4a0 (with d8eb452b1e by Thread B and 95eaaa4f76). Thread B's d8eb452b1e records a function type's declared clause in `Body.fn_value_effects` for each local a call's func operand names and each annotated `let`. src/mir/effects.rs (`declared_fn_value_effects`, used by `call_effects` and `fn_value_effects`) now charges a call through such a local with exactly the declared effects, keyed as classes (`Network` / `FileSystem` as capabilities), plus the default-permitted `panics` and `allocates(Heap)`. No entry is still every effect, per core-semantics §12. The row's repro (`struct Job { run: Fn(i64) -> i64 with reads(Clock) }`, `par { (j.run)(3), (j.run)(4) }`) checks and runs (`25`); the same slot declaring `writes(Stdout)` conflicts on `writes(Stdout)`. 95eaaa4f76 makes the refusal name the unknown's reason (`unknown (a call through a value)`) instead of a bare `unknown`. Pinned by tests/mir_par_stored_callback.rs. Remainder: a call through a captured annotated `let` inside a `par` branch is still unknown, filed as B-2026-10-27-8 (Thread B).
title: A `par` over calls through a stored callback ignores the callback type's effect clause: `struct Job { run: Fn(i64) -> i64 with reads(Clock) }` and `par { (j.run)(3), (j.run)(4) }` is refused as `unknown` and `unknown`, where core-semantics §12 says a call through an escaping function value has the effects its type declares
detail: src/mir/effects.rs charges every call through a value that is not a parameter with `EffectSet::unknown("a call through a value")` (`opaque()`), and the MIR `TyKind::Fn` carries no effect clause, so the field type's `with reads(Clock)` never reaches the analysis. core-semantics.md §12 (line ~699): "A call through an escaping function value has the effects its type declares ... With no effect clause, a call through it has every effect (default 1)." So the clause-less `struct Job { run: Fn(i64) -> i64 }` refusal is right and the clause-carrying one is a false positive. Repro (release karac at 8c794cddcb): `struct Job { run: Fn(i64) -> i64 with reads(Clock) }\nfn sq(x: i64) -> i64 { x * x }\nfn main() { let j = Job { run: sq }; let (a, b) = par { (j.run)(3), (j.run)(4) }; println(f"{a + b}"); }` gives `branches 1 and 2 of the `par` conflict: `unknown` and `unknown``. The diagnostic also names nothing a reader can act on: the set's `why` ("a call through a value") is not printed, so even the correct refusal should say the callback's type declares no effects and how to declare them. Fix: carry the declared clause from the HIR field / binding type into the MIR call site's effects (channel resources as Key::Any), and print the unknown's reason in the conflict message.

fix: 0f5289b733: `strip_main` copies the source a run at a time (from the end of the last `fn main` it skipped), so characters are never split. tests/repl_v2.rs `repl_v2_items_keep_non_ascii_text` pins `héllo, wörld` through an item.
title: The v2 REPL garbles an item's non-ASCII text: `fn greet() -> Str { "héllo" }` then `println(greet());` prints `hÃ©llo`, because `strip_main` (src/repl/util.rs) copied the accumulated items a byte at a time as `char`s
detail: Found while probing B-2026-10-24-1's auto-clone columns, measured at 87001222fe. A cell `let ü = "é"; ...` was refused with the snippet `let Ã¼ = "Ã©"` and an unrelabeled `<repl>:2:5` place, while `karac check` of the same text in a file renders it correctly and a statement cell `println("é")` prints `é`. The cause is `strip_main`, which every cell's, `%show`'s and `:provide`'s program runs the items through: it pushed `bytes[i] as char`, so each byte of a multi-byte character became its own Latin-1 character. Every item holding non-ASCII text (a string literal, a comment, a char) reached the cells' programs changed, so a program's output differed from `karac run` of the same source. Pinned by tests/repl_v2.rs `repl_v2_items_keep_non_ascii_text`.

title: The v2 build refuses `--enable-hot-swap` on a default-profile project and a cross `--target` / `[build].target` by name, where legacy honoured both; 4 cli tests stay ignored
detail: The remainder of B-2026-10-23-16 (closed 392c90770a). That row asked for each flag to work or be refused by name; these two are now refused by name, so nothing is silently ignored, but neither works. (1) `--enable-hot-swap` on a project whose [package].profile is the default: `karac build` stops with `the v2 build does not honour `--enable-hot-swap` yet`. Legacy emitted PLT-style indirection for extern-public module symbols (docs/deferred.md, Continuous PGO with Shared-Object Hot-Swap, commitment 1). The wasm and embedded/kernel refusals already match legacy's wording. Ignored: tests/cli.rs test_build_project_hot_swap_accepted_with_default_profile. (2) A cross `--target=<triple>` (or `[build].target` in the manifest) naming a non-host triple: refused with `the v2 build does not honour a cross `--target` yet`. src/backend's MIR object emission uses the host target machine. Ignored: test_build_target_flag_activates_overlay_dep, test_build_target_space_separated_form_parses, plus test_build_target_from_manifest_build_section and the `--target` sibling at tests/cli.rs ~15888, each of which passes only where the target is the host. Owner for (2) is the backend (drop schedule) together with the cli driver.
fix: 6be9fd1111: both now work on v2. (1) A cross --target / [build].target triple is built for, not just used for the overlay as legacy did (legacy linked a host binary): the object is compiled for the triple (Target::initialize_all on that path only, so a host build's time is unchanged), linked with KARAC_LINKER, else the triple's GNU cross gcc on PATH (x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc for x86_64-pc-windows-gnu), else clang --target=<triple>, against the runtime archive built for the triple (KARAC_RUNTIME, else <karac>/../lib/<triple>/, else target/<triple>/release/); a missing archive fails at the link naming `rustup target add` and the cargo rustc recipe. The triple also picks the [target.<triple>.*] overlay, the walk platform, the CPU baseline arch and the .exe suffix; codegen-unit splitting is off for a cross build. Measured: hello.kara --target=x86_64-pc-windows-gnu on Linux gives a PE32+ x86-64 hello.exe (tests/build_v2_target.rs checks MZ / PE / machine 0x8664 when mingw and the archive are present). (2) --enable-hot-swap on a default profile: each non-generic module-scope pub fn (main aside) gets a slot in the external karac_hotswap_table [N x ptr]; __karac_init_hot_swap_table in llvm.global_ctors fills it; each direct call of a registered body loads its slot and calls through it, taking the callee's final param/return/function attributes (noalias is marked after lowering, so they are copied at the end) and calling convention (src/backend/mir/hot_swap.rs). Flag-off IR is byte-identical (KARAC_MIR_LL diff). Still refused on wasm (now also a wasm32-* triple) and embedded/kernel. The 4 ignored cli tests run (a cross build on a host without that triple's archive is accepted when it stops at the link with the recipe, after the overlay walk they pin) and the two cfg-gated ones run on every host; tests/project_v2_refusals.rs's cross [build].target refusal pin is flipped.

title: On the pool (threads on by default since 72ce9e026c), sleepers wake out of deadline order: the first park opens the reactor's epoll set under the executor's lock, and its F_DUPFD to descriptor 100 grows the fd table, which in a threaded process waits out an RCU grace period (48 ms under strace), stalling every worker; a 60 ms sleeper woke before 20 and 40 ms ones
detail: Found when tests/mir_reactor.rs's sleepers test went red in a gate after default-on (mir_reactor_sleepers_wake_in_deadline_order_beside_a_parked_task, 1 in 6). Built program, 100 runs on 4 cores: 76 in order, 14 with the 60 ms sleeper before the 40 ms one, one with it before the 20 ms ones. Timestamps showed the tasks spawned after the first park starting 13 to 21 ms late, all at once. strace -f -tt: fcntl(ep, F_DUPFD_CLOEXEC, 100) took 48 ms (expand_fdtable synchronizes RCU when the file table is shared by threads), inside park() -> Reactor::watch under the shared EXEC lock. A second, smaller hole: idle_wait read the timer heap and the running count under two locks, so a sleeper another worker settled in between was missed until the wait's old deadline; and a napping first worker was not roused by a new timer.
fix: 808e37ce9b. Reactor::open (runtime/src/mir_task.rs) makes the epoll set and moves it to descriptor 100. start_workers calls it before spawning any thread, so the fd table grows while the process has one thread and skips the RCU wait. watch() calls the same open() lazily, which is all the one-worker executor needs. Two smaller holes closed in the same change: idle_wait reads the timer heap and the running count under one lock (a worker settles its sleeper before it stops counting as running, so with none running every timer is already in the heap), and settling a Wait::Until / FdBy task rouses a napping first worker. Measured on 4 cores, the row's program built: 76/100 in deadline order before, 200/200 after, with task starts at 0 ms instead of 13-21 ms late. New pin tests/mir_reactor.rs mir_reactor_pool_sleepers_wake_in_deadline_order (KARAC_THREADS=4; deadlines 20/60/100/140 ms). Four tests that pinned print order across tasks now run their build on one worker (§11.1, §11.9): the same-deadline sleepers, mir_isolating_built's natives and teardown, and mir_cancel_running_and_unstarted_tasks. Task suites (34 files, 349 tests) clean 7 runs in a row.

title: A `let p: P = Json.deserialize(s).map_err(f)?` (or `.context(msg)?`) is refused with "cannot infer type parameter 'T' of `Result[T, DeserializeError]`": the annotation on the `let` does not reach the receiver of a method whose `Ok` type is the receiver's, through the `?`
detail: MEASURED 2026-10-27 on main 87001222fe plus the B-2026-10-21-22 fix (debug karac --features llvm), Thread A. Program: `import std.json.{Json};` `#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)] struct P { x: i64 }` `fn go(s: String) -> Result[i64, String] { let p: P = Json.deserialize(s).map_err(|e| e.to_string())?; Ok(p.x) }` and a `main` that calls `go(Json.serialize(P { x: 3 }))`. `karac check` says: "cannot infer type parameter 'T' of `Result[T, DeserializeError]`, this call's result: nothing in the body fixes it (design.md § Type inference); bind the result with a type annotation" at the `Json.deserialize(s)` call. The same with `.context("reading P")?` into a `Result[i64, AnyError]`. Binding the call first (`let r: Result[P, DeserializeError] = Json.deserialize(s); let p = r.map_err(...)?;`) checks and runs (prints 3). `map_err[F]` returns `Result[T, F]` and `context` returns `Result[T, AnyError]`, so the `?`'s value is the receiver's `T`, which the `let`'s `P` fixes; the checker does not carry the expected type back through the method's return type to its receiver. design.md § Type inference is bidirectional within a function body; whether a method's receiver is inferred from its result is the question (INFERRED that it should, since the `let`-then-call form needs no new information).
fix: 0ab7f4850c. The annotation reached a generic call's payload only when the call was itself the `?` or `.unwrap()` operand (`pending_expected_call_payload`, B-2026-10-21-55). src/typechecker/exprs.rs now walks a chain of methods that keep the `Option` / `Result` payload (`map_err`, `context`, `with_context`, `or_else`, `or`, `inspect`, `inspect_err`, `ok`, `ok_or`, `ok_or_else`, `filter`; `payload_preserving_root`) to the call at its root and seeds that call's payload, in three positions: a `?` operand (`let p: P = Json.deserialize(s).map_err(f)?;`, `.context("reading P")?`), an `.unwrap()` / `.expect(..)` receiver (`.map_err(f).unwrap()`), and the chain checked against its own `Option` / `Result` (`let r: Result[P, String] = Json.deserialize(s).map_err(f);`). The row's two programs check and run (`3`). Pinned by tests/core_payload_through_method_chain.rs.

802932ff9d (Thread B). The builder now also keys an annotated `let`'s declared clause by the binding's symbol (src/mir/lower.rs `Lcx::let_fn_effects`, filled in `note_declared_effects`), and `callee_effects` resolves an identifier callee through `Res::Local(sym)`, which a closure's capture of the binding resolves to as well. So the call in a `par` branch, whose func operand is the `&f` temp of an environment projection, carries the clause in `Body.fn_value_effects`. The row's program checks clean and prints 25 on the interpreter and the built binary; the same program with `writes(Stdout)` is refused as `writes(Stdout)` and `writes(Stdout)`. Found on the way: a call through a `OnceFn` field moved the field place itself, so its entry named the struct's local (a second field's call would have shared it); such a call now moves the field into a temp first, and only a projection-free func operand is recorded. Pins: the kata thread's PREDICTS fixture in tests/mir_par_stored_callback.rs, flipped to `mir_par_stored_callback_captured_from_a_let_has_its_effects`, and tests/mir_fn_value_effects.rs's capture and once-field cases (control with b09a2761b2's src/mir/lower.rs: the three fail).
title: A `par` branch that calls a captured, annotated `let` (`let f: Fn(i64) -> i64 with reads(Clock) = ..; par { f(3), f(4) }`) is still refused as `unknown (a call through a value)`: the declared clause reaches a call through a field and through a let in its own body, not through a capture
detail: Remainder of B-2026-10-27-2. d8eb452b1e records a function type's declared clause in `Body.fn_value_effects` for each local a call's func operand names and each annotated `let`, and src/mir/effects.rs (`declared_fn_value_effects`) charges a call through such a local with exactly those effects. A `par` branch is a closure body, and a `let f` it captures is reached through the closure's environment, so the call's func operand is (inferred, not dumped) a projection of the env parameter with no entry, and the call keeps every effect. `(j.run)(3)` on a captured struct works because the builder copies the field into a temp local first. Repro: `fn sq(x: i64) -> i64 { x * x }\nfn pick(n: i64) -> Fn(i64) -> i64 with reads(Clock) { sq }\nfn main() { let f: Fn(i64) -> i64 with reads(Clock) = pick(0); let (a, b) = par { f(3), f(4) }; println(f"{a + b}"); }` gives `branches 1 and 2 of the `par` conflict: `unknown (a call through a value)` and ...`, where core-semantics §12 gives the call the effects its type declares. Pinned by `mir_par_stored_callback_captured_from_a_let_is_refused_for_now` (tests/mir_par_stored_callback.rs, PREDICTS). Fix: carry the clause for a func operand that is a capture (builder), or copy the capture to a local with an entry.

fix: 75990e74c3. `karac check` reads each impl method's parameter and return types against its trait method's at the impl (src/typechecker/items.rs, check_impl_signatures_match_trait): `Self` is the impl's type, `Self.A` the impl's own binding, the trait's generics its trait arguments, and the method's generics the impl method's by position. The row's program is now refused: "the return type of impl method 'S.mk2' is `Option[i64]`, but trait 'Mk2' declares `Option[bool]` there". An impl associated type the trait does not declare is refused ("defines associated type 'B', which 'Tr' does not declare"), and a parameter-count mismatch too. Only types known on both sides are compared: a projection, an inference variable, or an `impl Trait` against a concrete type is taken to agree, and an `impl Trait` against an `impl Trait` compares the trait and its bindings. Modes stay §4.7's check, and a function type's parameter modes are compared under the mode, since D5 rewrites user `Fn(A, T)` to borrow and leaves the library's owned. Pinned by tests/core_impl_signature.rs (4 tests; on the base tree 3 fail and the accepting one passes). Corpus check sweep: 21 new refusals before two fixes (impl-side `Self`, Fn parameter modes), 0 after, apart from the twelve operator traits. DELIBERATE GAP: the operator traits (Add .. Shr, Neg, Not) are skipped, because the library declares them without the spec's `Rhs` and `Output` and every operator impl binds an `Output`; check_operator_output already holds the method's return to it, and the rest is B-2026-10-27-13.

title: Passing a function value held in a collection element to a non-escaping function-typed parameter (`apply(v[0], 4)` over `fn apply(f: Fn(i64) -> i64, x: i64)`) is refused as a move out of the element, where core-semantics §4.1 / §9.3 make a bare `Fn` parameter a borrow
detail: Measured at dcd242dbc8 plus the B-2026-10-22-43 fix: `fn doubler(n: i64) -> i64 { n * 2 }\nfn apply(f: Fn(i64) -> i64, x: i64) -> i64 { f(x) }\nfn main() { let mut v: Vec[Fn(i64) -> i64] = Vec.new(); v.push(doubler); println(f"{apply(v[0], 4)}"); }`. `karac check` gives `cannot move a non-`Copy` value out of a collection element: the collection still owns it` (src/use_classifier.rs walks the argument as Consuming: the bare `Fn` parameter's mode is owned in the front end's tables), and the MIR builder refuses the same call independently (`borrow check main: ... move of (*_17) through a shared reference [E0517]`), so the program cannot run on any path. Before the B-2026-10-22-43 fix check passed it and only the MIR refusal remained. The non-function control `fn size(s: String) -> i64 { s.len() }` with `size(w[0])` over a `Vec[String]` checks and runs. core-semantics §9.3: function-typed parameters are non-escaping by default and the callee may only call them or pass them on; §4.1: an argument to a borrowed parameter moves nothing. A local `let f: Fn(..) = doubler; apply(f, 1); apply(f, 2)` already works, because check reads a function value as `Copy`. Fix: give a bare (non-`escaping`) function-typed parameter the borrowed mode in the front end's call modes and pass it by reference in the MIR builder, together.

fix: f91c8a7d29: the twelve runtime/stdlib operator traits are declared as design.md § Operator traits writes them: `trait Add[Rhs = Self] { type Output; fn add(own self, rhs: own Rhs) -> Self.Output; }` (Sub, Mul, Div, Rem, BitAnd, BitOr, BitXor, Shl, Shr the same), `trait Neg { type Output; fn neg(own self) -> Self.Output; }` and Not. A trait's generic parameters take defaults (design.md § Default generic arguments): GenericParam.default, parsed only in a trait declaration's own list (a default elsewhere, and a defaultless parameter after a defaulted one, are parse errors), printed by the formatter. The B-2026-10-27-9 signature check fills an omitted trait argument with its default read at the impl (`impl Add for I` is `Add[I]`), reads `type Output = Self` as the impl's type, and its operator skip is gone, so the row's program is now refused: "parameter 'rhs' of impl method 'I.add' is `D`, but trait 'Add' declares `I` there: an impl method's signature is the trait's. To take a `D`, implement `Add[D]`"; with `impl Add[D] for I` it prints 3. check_operator_output is deleted (the signature check refuses the same mismatch; tests/core_strict_check.rs's pin now reads its wording) and proj_traits' OPERATORS special case goes, since the traits declare Output. An impl binding no Output is a missing associated type, now with a karac fix binding it to the operator method's written return type (missing_assoc_type_fix); it migrated corpus SRC_17, user_neg_and_not_impls_are_accepted, apps/cli/mini_bc (and kara-katas apps/cli/mini_bc), and the same test sources inline. design_md_code_blocks' `Rhs = Self` allow-list entry retired. The bounded-generic result type and type-parameter defaults are filed apart (B-2026-10-27-14, B-2026-10-27-15).

fix: 09ef1b3e15: an operator on a parameter bounded by its operator trait calls the bound's impl, so it is typed as design.md § Operator traits says. src/typechecker/expr_ops.rs `bounded_operator_types`: the right operand is checked against the bound's `Rhs` (its first type argument, `T` by default; `T: Add[D, Output = T]` now takes `a + d`), and the result is the bound's `Output`, the projection `T.Output`, which an `Output = X` in scope resolves (a `Numeric` parameter is a primitive, whose Output is itself). Unary `-` on a `T: Neg` likewise. A refused right operand types the result as an error, so nothing cascades. `unfixed_operator_output` finds a `T.Output` no `Output =` fixes and builds the machine-applicable edit `Add` -> `Add[Output = T]` (the bound for the operator when it is known; no edit when the parameter has several operator bounds and the projection does not say whose). It is refused where it is used as the `T` (check_assignable, ahead of the TypeParam wildcard of types_compatible), operated on again (`a + b + c`), compound-assigned (`x += b`), or passed to a callee whose bound requires `Output = T` (discharge_assoc_type_eq_bounds, which also normalizes a caller's parameter through its own `Output =`). The row's program is refused: "expected 'T', found 'T.Output': the result of an operator on a 'T' is its bound's `Output` ... write `Sub[Output = T]`", and `-> T.Output` runs it (prints the Du). Two fixes the migration needed: an `Output = X` discharge now reads the impl of the bound's own trait (`bound_trait_assoc`; V's `Add` binds V and its `Mul` i64, and the type-keyed lookup picked Mul's), and a trait's where-clause eqs reach its default methods (`trait Stat[T: Add[Output = T]]`). Migrated with `karac fix`: 31 corpus sources (fixtures and kata 307's two generic variants) and kara-katas 307; the inline test sources in tests/typechecker.rs, tests/core_strict_check.rs and tests/mir_build.rs (six typechecker tests now desugar first, since a bound's `Output = T` reaches the checker through the desugar pass's hoist). Pinned by tests/core_operator_traits.rs (the Instant/Duration case both ways, the chain/Neg/compound-assign refusals and their karac fix, the mixed Rhs, a generic caller, the trait selection and trait defaults). Two neighbours found on the way are their own rows: B-2026-10-27-18, `T.Output` is keyed by parameter, not by trait, so `T: Add[Output = T] + Mul` reads `a * b` as a `T`; and B-2026-10-27-19, a rigid type parameter is a wildcard in types_compatible (`fn f[T](x: own T) -> T { 5 }` passes check).
title: Arithmetic on a `T: Add` (`Sub`, `Mul`, ...) type parameter is typed `T`, not the bound's `T.Output`, so `fn g[T: Sub](a: own T, b: own T) -> T { a - b }` passes check and, at a type whose `Output` is another type, reads the result as a `T`; and a mixed-operand bound (`T: Add[D, Output = T]`, `a + d`) is refused as 'both operands must have the same type'

fix: 3bb4dac262: a struct's or enum's generic parameters take defaults, as design.md § Default generic arguments writes them. The parser accepts `= Type` on a struct's or enum's own generic list as on a trait's (`Parser::generic_defaults_ok`, set around both parse sites in src/parser/items.rs); a function's parameters still refuse it, with the message now naming trait, struct or enum, and a defaultless parameter after a defaulted one is a parse error for types too. The typechecker records each type with a default in `env.generic_defaults` (parameters in order with their defaults, in the stub pre-pass so a type is known before any field naming it is lowered), and `fill_default_generic_args` (src/typechecker/lowering.rs) appends each omitted trailing argument's default where a struct or enum path is lowered, single-segment or module-qualified, and in a struct or variant literal's `[...]` (src/typechecker/fields.rs, whose arity check now accepts the shorter write when the rest are defaulted). A default may name the parameters before it: `Pair[i64]` of `struct Pair[A, B = Vec[A]]` is `Pair[i64, Vec[i64]]`. A write with no arguments is left to inference (`P.new()`), and a write omitting an argument with no default keeps its arity, so nothing that was accepted before changes. Pinned by tests/core_generic_defaults.rs (annotation, impl target, literal and enum uses run; a mismatched field against the default refused; literal over-arity refused; parameter order). Map's and Set's hasher parameter keeps its own mechanism (take_hasher_type_arg); moving it onto this one is the drop schedule's to schedule.

detail: MEASURED at f91c8a7d29: `struct S[T = i64] { v: T }` is refused at parse: 'a default generic argument (`T = Type`) is allowed on a trait's type parameters only: a function's generic parameters take no defaults (design.md § Default generic arguments), and a type's are not supported yet'. B-2026-10-27-13 added defaults to a trait's own generic list (GenericParam.default, Parser::generic_defaults_ok) for the operator traits' `Rhs = Self`, and read them in the impl-signature check. design.md § Default generic arguments also gives a struct or enum's parameters defaults (`Map[String, i64]` uses the default hasher). Before B-2026-10-27-13 the parser stopped at the `=` with 'Expected RightBracket'. Fix: accept the default on struct/enum parameters and fill an omitted trailing argument with it wherever a type is lowered (an annotation, a constructor, an impl target); a function's parameters keep refusing it.

fix: 5fc21d28ff: per design.md § Associated types, "A projection names one trait's type" (review-thread ruling 2026-10-27, 5211fe6274): `T.Name` belongs to the one bound on `T` that declares `Name`. `Type::AssocProjection` carries `trait_name` and `WhereConstraint::AssocTypeEq` carries the trait it was hoisted from (desugar `drain_bound`; `None` for a written `where`, resolved to the one declaring bound). `enclosing_assoc_eqs` is keyed by (param, assoc, trait) and `normalize_enclosing_assoc_eqs` / `resolve_enclosing_assoc_eqs` substitute only projections of their own trait (`substitute_assoc_bindings_of`); a bound receiver's method reads only the eqs of the traits that bound declares. An operator's result `T.Output` names its operator's trait, so under `T: Add[Output = T] + Mul` the body `-> T { a * b }` is refused with the edit `Mul[Output = T]`, and `T: Add[Output = T] + Mul[Output = i64]` types `a + b` as `T` and `a * b` as `i64`. A projection that names its trait resolves through that trait's impl (`trait_impl_assoc`, matching the impl's written target to bind its parameters), so the row's program no longer reads Mul's `i64` for Add's eq; `bound_trait_assoc` is gone. MIR lowering (src/ty.rs) takes the projection's trait before the frame's `proj_traits`. A written `T.Name` (`lower_type_expr`) or `where T.Name = X` (`check_where_assoc_eqs_name_one_trait`) that two bounds declare, a supertrait's declaration counting as its subtrait's (`assoc_declaring_traits`), is `E_AMBIGUOUS_ASSOC_TYPE`, once per written span, naming the traits and the two remedies (fix each on its bound, or name it with a type parameter); no machine fix, since which bound the author meant is not in the program. The open form `fn f[T: Add[Output = A] + Mul[Output = M], A, M]` type-checks and runs, at a user type and at i64. Ten corpus sources that wrote `Add[Output = T] + Mul` (the interp_generic_impl_method_resolves_its_own_type_param__fmt family, e2e_operator_on_operator_trait_bounded_type_param) migrated with `karac fix`; a sweep of all 19,916 corpus sources found no other newly refused program. Pinned by tests/core_assoc_projection.rs.
title: An associated-type projection on a type parameter (`T.Output`) is keyed by the parameter, not by the trait that declares it, so under `T: Add[Output = T] + Mul` the `Add` eq also types `a * b` as a `T`, and an `Output = X` discharge with two bounds declaring `Output` falls back to a type-keyed impl lookup that can pick either impl

fix: d7caf55aa6: in a generic item's body, check_assignable now treats the item's own type parameter as rigid. Setting one against a concrete type at the same place is refused: `-> T { 5 }`, `let y: T = 3`, `Vec[T]` vs `Vec[i64]`, `-> i64 { x }` with `x: T`. The message is "expected 'T', found 'i64': inside this item `T` stands for whatever type the caller picks". The check is narrowed so it leaves alone parameters that belong to a callee. Inside a found type only the expected side is read, since `None` is an `Option[T]` of Option's `T`. A concrete type must be a declared one, so a trait method's unsolved `Rhs` doesn't count. Library bodies are skipped, because a program function named like a builtin replaces it there (B-2026-10-27-29). Corpus fallout over 19,926 programs was 5 ill-typed fixtures. Three copies of `wrapG[T](x: own T) -> H { H { r: x } }` now take an `H[T]`, with output unchanged. `negate[T] -> T { 0 - x }` and the Bag that pushes 99 onto a `Vec[T]` are flipped to the refusal. Pins: corpus/core/err_rigid_type_param and tests/core_rigid_type_param.rs.

title: Auto-par is not yet invisible to logging (docs/library/log.md, ruled 2026-10-27): the interim keeps every statement and loop that logs out of auto-par, so adding a log line can change what runs in parallel. Target: an auto-par task's records carry the enclosing task's `task_id` and span and reach the backend in sequential order, held per auto-par task and released in statement order at the join.
detail: Before the interim, statement auto-par (on by default) ran two `info` statements in `main` as tasks: each record carried a task id (1, 2) instead of null, and the JIT printed them in swapped order. fix: ef19081ebc: a lowercase name followed by `.` in pattern position can only be a module binding, so it now roots a pattern path (src/parser/patterns.rs), and the module-binding desugar (src/module_binding.rs `pattern`) strips the bound root from a qualified unit variant or const, which the parser stores joined (`log.Level.Debug` becomes `Level.Debug`), and from a range bound's path (`shapes.LOW..=shapes.HIGH`), as it already did for struct and tuple variant paths. This is the first of the row's two options: the pattern mirrors the expression, so `log.Level.Debug =>` names the variant `log.Level.Debug` builds. A dotted pattern whose root resolves to nothing (`zzz.Mode.Slow`, an unbound module) is `undefined name 'zzz'` in the resolver, as the struct and tuple paths already were, rather than a fresh binding that matched every value. The expression side gains the matching struct-variant literal through a binding, `shapes.Shape.Rect { w: 3, h: 4 }`, which also failed to parse. detail: src/parser/patterns.rs roots a qualified pattern path only at an uppercase identifier ("lowercase is always a plain binding"), so `log` parses as a binding and the `.` is unexpected. The spec does not say whether a module-qualified pattern path is allowed; either the parser accepts it (and the module-binding desugar strips it as it does in expressions) or it reports a diagnostic naming the fix (`import std.log.{Level};` and `Level.Debug =>`). fix:
918d380872 (its subject line reads "tests: pin column of the body Set write"; an amend kept only that line, and this note is the full description). `K: Hash + Eq` now holds wherever a `Map` / `Set` type is written, per collections.md § Map (ruling 13227bd13e, option 1).

New file src/typechecker/table_keys.rs:
- `check_declared_table_keys` is a pre-pass, run after the type environment and before bodies. It walks every struct field, enum payload, alias body, fn/method signature, impl target and trait method signature, with that item's bounds in scope. A struct's fields are lowered once, during environment building, before any bound is known, so the pre-pass is the only place they can be judged.
- `check_table_key_at` (called from lower_path_type) judges body annotations under the enclosing function's bounds.

Each write is judged once.

A key that is or contains a type parameter needs `Hash + Eq` on the declaring item, directly, through a supertrait (`Ord` gives `Eq`, `trait Key: Hash + Eq`) or through a where clause. There is one report per parameter declaration, with a fix-it adding the missing bound. param_bound_edit now also finds a struct's, enum's, alias's and trait's parameters (param_scopes_at).

A concrete key without the impls is refused where the type is written:
- a float gets a to_bits hint;
- a half-written pair is told which half is missing;
- a local non-generic struct or enum whose fields have the impls gets a `#[derive(...)]` fix-it.

title: The `K: Hash + Eq` bound on a table's key is checked only at a Map / Set method call and passes a type parameter, a type-only use and a generic ADT's arguments, where collections.md makes it a bound of every table (default hasher included); the target is a refusal naming the missing impl, with a `karac fix` that adds `#[derive(Hash)]` (owner Thread A)
detail:
Filed at the review thread's ruling on B-2026-10-25-31 stage 2 (Q2: "file a row for enforcing the bound on every table (default tables included), owner Thread A, with a corpus count"). Until then a key with no Hash impl is fed as if derived (B-2026-10-25-31's interim).
Where it is checked today: src/typechecker/stdlib_map.rs infer_map_method (and the Set arm at ~1077) call type_supports_hash on the key at each method call. src/typechecker/derives.rs type_supports_hash answers true for a TypeParam / TypeVar / AssocProjection, true for a Named type that is neither a known struct nor enum, and for a generic struct or enum reads only its own derived_traits without recursing into its arguments.
So these pass check: (a) a generic item over Map[K, _] / Set[K] with K unbounded; (b) a Map / Set type written with no method call on it (a field, a parameter, an annotated `let` of Map.new()); (c) Map[Pair[f64], _] where Pair derives Hash.
Corpus count, case (a) only (grep of generic item headers whose param keys a Map / Set with no Hash bound, a grep of corpus/ by the drop schedule, .orig copies excluded): 7 programs, 15 sites, all generic struct declarations or their impls (apps/cli/mini_difflib, mini_click and mini_intelhex share `struct Matcher[T] { b2j: Map[T, Vec[i64]], bjunk: Set[T] }`; mini_collections `struct Dict[K, V]`; mini_graphlib `TopologicalSorter[N]`; two codegen fixtures). The MIR builder lowers it once per key type as `K.eq#key(a: ref K, b: ref K)` (src/mir/lower.rs note_key_eq / lower_key_eq, recorded in Program.key_eqs). The interpreter's find_key (user_eq) and the compiled eq glue (src/backend/mir/key.rs user_eq_body) call it. title: A table key whose PART has a hand-written PartialEq is compared structurally, so `Set[(Name, i64)]` with a case-insensitive `impl PartialEq for Name` misses `(Name { text: "BO" }, 3)` after inserting `(Name { text: "Bo" }, 3)` while `==` on the same tuples says true (both backends)
detail: MEASURED at B-2026-10-25-31 stage 2 (a1e167c756): `(Name{"Bo"},3) == (Name{"BO"},3)` prints true on `karac run` and a built binary; `s.contains((Name{"BO"}, 3))` on a Set holding `(Name{"Bo"},3)` prints false on both. collections.md § Hashing: "compares keys through its PartialEq impl". Cause: src/backend/mir/key.rs consults user_eq_body only for the key's TOP-LEVEL type (a user eq makes the hash 0 and the eq glue call it); a tuple / derived struct / Vec over such a type gets KeyOp::Eq = Total cmp, structural. detail: Found while fixing B-2026-10-27-24. `karac check` passes both programs and `karac run` prints "other slow" / "other 4". fix: 192217f2f9. As the review thread ruled, when a panic is about to end the program, every record an auto-par task still holds goes to the backend before the panic is reported. They go in statement order: a hold's own records, then those of the groups its tasks made, in the order the groups were made, each group's in task order. A task still running gives what it logged so far. No statement is ordered for logging's sake. Runtime: `drain_logs` in mir_task.rs, run from `karac_mir_abort`, `karac_mir_abort_at` and `deadlock` once the panic has begun, skipped if a backend panics while records are being let go. Interpreter: `drain_logs` from `report_abort` and `deadlock`. log.md states the rule. Pinned by tests/mir_auto_par_log.rs `mir_auto_par_logs_before_a_later_panic` (run, run --interp, built x3). Control, drains disabled: no record before `runtime error: index out of bounds` on the interpreter, and none on the built binary, where the record waits behind a 30M-step loop, 3 of 3.
title: Auto-par and std.log, remainder of B-2026-10-27-22: a record an earlier auto-par statement would log can be missing when a later one panics first. Target (review-thread ruling 2026-10-27): before a panic ends the program, the runtime drains every held record in statement order to the backend, then reports the panic
detail: B-2026-10-27-22 made auto-par invisible to logging. An auto-par task logs as its spawner. Its records go on live while it is its group's first unfinished task. Otherwise they wait for the tasks before it to finish, and then go on in statement order. The gap: a panic in a later statement's task can end the program while an earlier statement's task is still running or not yet started. That task's records never reach the backend, though run sequentially they would have come before the panic report. Measured: `let a = step(1, 10); let b = boom(3000000);`, where step logs after a nested loop and boom indexes an empty Vec. Under `karac run --interp` the record is missing before `runtime error: index out of bounds`; the compiled run printed it, by timing. Not to be fixed by ordering statements: counting a record as visible to the stops rule kept the tests' statements and loops in order (most statements can panic), against design.md §12. Ruling (review thread, 2026-10-27): when a panic is about to end the program, first drain every held record, in statement order, to the backend, then report the panic. An earlier task still running contributes its records up to where it got. Needs: the drain on the fatal-panic path of the interpreter and of the runtime (runtime/src/mir_task.rs holds, mir_log.rs), on both the JIT and built binaries. The console-order rule (a statement that logs stays ordered against one that writes Stdout or Stderr or calls init) is the spec, not part of this row.

detail: MEASURED: Pipeline::ownershipcheck_phase (src/cli.rs) ran mir_borrow_errors (and with it source_effect_errors, the par check) only when `ownership.errors` was empty, and computed that before drop_library_diagnostics removed library-span errors from the report. A std.log import reaches the serde Deserialize bodies (Vec/VecDeque/Set/SortedSet/Map/SortedMap impls, json_number_text), whose `d: mut ref D` passed to `T.deserialize(d)` the front-end ownership pass reads as a move (B-2026-10-27-32): 11 hidden errors, so 'clean' was false and the MIR checks were skipped, silently. The same holds for any program whose reachable library bodies raise an ownership error. Without the import, or with std.json/std.path, the conflict was reported.

fix: 01e7e98a0c: collect_callee_param_modes (src/ownership.rs) now gives a trait's static methods mode entries ("Trait.method"; D5 adjusts a user trait's bare positions as it does other decls), and lookup_callee_param_modes falls back, on a miss for a two-segment `T.method` callee, to the modes of the traits that declare a static method of that name (collect_trait_static_methods) when they all agree. Both the ownership checker (borrow.rs callee_modes_for_call) and the use classifier use it. `T.make(s)` with `s: mut ref S` in a loop and reused after the call now passes check; an `own` parameter still moves. Pinned by tests/core_trait_static_param_modes.rs (3 tests).
title: A `mut ref S` parameter passed to a static method of a type parameter (`T.make(s)`, the serde `T.deserialize(d)`) is read as a move by `karac check`: inside a loop it is 'moved inside a loop and not assigned again', twice it is 'moved here, used again'. `karac run` accepts the program and prints the right answer.
detail: MEASURED: trait Src { fn next(mut ref self) -> i64; } trait Make { fn make[S: Src](s: mut ref S) -> Self; } fn many[T: Make, S: Src](s: mut ref S) -> Vec[T] { let mut out = Vec.new(); for _ in 0..3 { out.push(T.make(s)); } out } with a Counter source: check refuses at `T.make(s)` ("value 's' is moved inside a loop ... bound 'S' by `Clone`"); `karac __mir-run` prints 3 and 3. The callee is a method of the type parameter T, so the front-end ownership pass does not find its parameter modes and falls back to a move of the argument, though `s` is itself a `mut ref` (a reborrow). The library's serde Deserialize impls (Vec/VecDeque/Set/SortedSet/Map/SortedMap) raise 11 such errors, which check drops as library diagnostics; they hid every MIR check of a std.log program until B-2026-10-27-31. Owner: ownership errors in check (Thread A).

fix: 472e0d7dc6: an open value (`None`, `Some(x)`, `Ok(x)`, `Err(e)`) given to a table is checked against the concrete element or key slot, as `push` already checked it. src/typechecker/method_vec_mutation.rs gains is_open_value and infer_probe_arg, and infer_element_arg uses is_open_value. src/typechecker/stdlib_map.rs routes Set/SortedSet `contains | remove` and check_map_slot_arg_inner's borrowed path through infer_probe_arg. tests/mir_open_value_needle.rs checks the output on both backends and runs the program under the ASan lane, which reported the overflow before the fix.
title: `None` (or `Some(x)` / `Ok(x)` / `Err(e)`) given to a table's `insert`, `contains`, `remove`, `get` or `contains_key` is typed alone as `Option[()]`, so the compiled table reads its element out of a one-byte slot (ASan stack-buffer-overflow on `Set[Option[String]]`'s `insert(None)`)
detail: MEASURED at B-2026-10-27-26: `let mut o: Set[Option[String]] = Set.new(); o.insert(None);` under `karac __mir-llvm-asan`: READ of size 32 overflowing a 1-byte local `_3`; KARAC_MIR_DUMP=built shows `let mut _3: Option[()]; _3 = Option.None; Set[Option[String]].insert(move _4, copy _3)`. The same for `contains(None)` on a Set and SortedSet, and `get(None)` / `contains_key` on a Map keyed by an Option. `Vec.push(None)` was right: its arm checks such an open value against the slot (method_vec_mutation.rs, B-2026-10-14-19's open_value), while the table arms inferred the needle alone (infer_element_arg; the Set `contains | remove` arm; check_map_slot_arg_inner's borrowed path). The interpreter compares by value, so only compiled code misread; the wrong type was the checker's.

fix: 043ee4083f: RenameTypes (src/prelude.rs) renames a unit-variant pattern (PatternKind::Binding("Level.Debug")) as it does the other variant patterns, and privatize_unlisted_types joins the module path with `$` (`Level$std$log`) so the private name has no '.' and a dotted binding still splits at the type; display_private_names reads the new form as `std.log.Level`. Pinned by tests/gated_type_rename.rs gated_type_rename_beside_a_program_type_of_its_name (own `enum Level` with `import std.log;` prints `INFO  ready` / `WARN  careful`, run and run --interp).
title: A program with its own `enum Level` beside `import std.log;` logs every record as DEBUG: `log.init(log.text_backend(log.Stream.Stdout), level: log.Level.Info); log.info("ready")` prints `DEBUG ready`, in run and build alike, and check passes.
detail: MEASURED at B-2026-10-27-23: privatize_unlisted_types (src/prelude.rs) renames the module's Level to Level$std.log when the program declares a Level (B-2026-10-19-10), through RenameTypes. RenameTypes renamed type expressions, paths, struct literals and struct/tuple-variant patterns, but not a unit-variant pattern, which parses as PatternKind::Binding("Level.Debug"). So std_log.kara's `match level { Level.Debug => 0, ... }` (__log_rank, and the text formatter's level names) named the program's Level; the type errors that raised were library diagnostics, dropped from check's report, and the arms misbehaved at run time. A rename of the dotted binding alone is not enough: the private name Level$std.log has '.' in it, and the resolver and lowering split a dotted binding at its first '.', so `Level$std.log.Debug` read as the type `Level$std`. Any gated module type with unit variants and a program type of its name is affected (std.encoding DecodeError, std.log Stream and Level).

title: After 45524985d1 a one-worker auto-par build runs the in-order build's instructions, yet 16 of 129 M4b programs still time under 0.9x of it in one 9-run pass (kata 7 0.764, 8 0.727, 125 0.696, 153 0.798, 895 0.79, word_freq_multi 0.787): the code is the same and lands elsewhere, so the floor at one worker is at the resolution of code placement
detail: Measured on the tree that became 45524985d1 (scripts/m4b-speedup.py --threads 1 --runs 9, review/m4b-speedup/m4b-speedup-twin-45524985d1-t1.md in the shared folder; identical-binary noise band 0.970..1.045). callgrind counts, in order vs auto-par on KARAC_THREADS=1: kata 7 16,102,283,875 vs 16,102,294,600; 8 1,744,126,705 vs 1,744,136,642; 125 20,340,373,969 vs 20,337,384,320; 153 760,374,604 vs 760,384,571; 60 nextperm 2,210,456,228 vs 2,210,465,788; 895 298,169,006 vs 299,610,665 (+0.5%). Kata 7's hot loop is one function in both binaries (`karac.main` inlined whole). Placement alone moves these programs as far: the same in-order kata 7 source built with KARAC_FORCE_FULL_RUNTIME=1 ran 2.36 / 2.43 / 2.64 s against 1.72 / 1.62 / 1.62 s with the lean archive it normally gets, with identical instruction counts; and the in-order build's own kata 28 KMP ran 0.67 s where the auto-par build, executing 13,055 more instructions, ran 0.40..0.44 s. Not yet tried: aligning loop headers in the backend (an LLVM `-align-loops` setting) so both arms place hot loops alike, and timing with more runs to separate placement from noise. Whether the floor should be judged against instruction counts at one worker is the review thread's call (M4b rules). Owners: the drop schedule (src/backend/) for any placement change; the review thread for the floor rule.

fix: b9294ac5ff: a generic struct's or enum's declared parameter bounds are now judged wherever the type is written with arguments, as a type alias's are (src/typechecker/adt_bounds.rs). The model is the table-key pre-pass of B-2026-10-27-25: declarations' written types are judged under each item's own bounds in `table_keys_in`, and a body's annotations as they are lowered (`check_adt_bounds_at` in lowering.rs). A concrete argument must implement the bound ("`M` requires its parameter `T` to implement `Hash + Eq`, but `f64` does not implement `Hash + Eq`"); an enclosing type parameter must declare it, with a `karac fix` edit adding the bound where the parameter is declared. A compound argument naming a parameter (`M[Vec[T]]`) is not judged, since impls the bounds do not settle decide it. Library spans are skipped; each write is judged once. Corpus: 14 programs declare a bounded generic ADT; 2 were refused, both correctly, and were migrated with `karac fix` in the same commit (apps/cli/mini_collections: Counter, Lru, ChainMap; fixtures/codegen/map_set/test_e2e_struct_move_out_map_set_enum_field_no_crash: GMOuter); both pass on mir-interp. Pinned by tests/check_adt_bounds.rs (3 tests; control without the fix: 1 passed, 2 failed).
title: A generic struct's or enum's declared parameter bounds are not checked where the type is written with arguments: `struct M[T: Hash + Eq] { m: Map[T, i64] }` lets `fn mk() -> M[f64]` and `let x: M[f64] = mk()` pass, and the `f64` key surfaces only at a later `x.m.len()` (reported twice there); the target is a refusal at the written `M[f64]` naming the unmet bound, for every declared bound, not only `Hash + Eq`

fix: 05ba42efa8 (measured at; no code change). Wontfix: real, and measured to a standstill on this hardware. The review asked for function and loop/block alignment settings to be tried beyond the drop schedule's 10-28 set, and for one to be landed only if it removes the swing within the binary-size bars. Method: the 10-28 one (relink after a 0/16/32/48-byte .text pad, taskset -c 2, child CPU, shuffled rounds), at 05ba42efa8, on katas 125, 28 KMP, 7, 8 and 270, under six settings: base, function align 32 and 64, -align-all-nofallthru-blocks=5 and =6, and function align 64 with blocks=5. Write-up: review/m4b-speedup/placement-2026-11-02.md in the shared folder. Measured spread across the four pads (median CPU s): unaligned, kata 28 swings 21-28% (0.45-0.60 s) and kata 125 7-19%. 64-byte non-fallthrough block alignment is the only setting that removes kata 28's swing at the fast level (0.45-0.53 s, ~5%; function align 64 removes it only at the slow level, 0.56-0.60 s), and it steadies 270 (9% -> 5%, ~4% faster). But kata 125 runs ~4% slower on average under it (61 rounds: mean 1.346 -> 1.404 s), its spread stays 7-9%, and large binaries grow 5-11%: mini_lua 796344 -> 878264 bytes (+10.3%, .text +13.9%), mini_markdown +10.7%, mini_sqlite +4.7%, mini_tldextract +2.5%. 32-byte block alignment is cheaper but leaves kata 28's 20% swing. So no setting removes the swing without moving another program the wrong way or adding ~10% code, which matches the 10-28 reading. Attributing the swing needs DSB/frontend counters, and these containers have no PMU (perf_event_open: ENOENT). Reopen as a new row with a PMU host or a profile-guided block layout.
title: A compiled program's run time moves 10-20% with where its hot function lands, and the runtime archive is one of the things that moves it: kata 125 runs about 10% slower whenever karac.main sits at 16 mod 64 (the full archive's larger headers shift user code by 0x3130 bytes), kata 28 KMP 0.41 vs 0.52 s between layouts; no alignment setting tried removes the swing without slowing another program 7-20%
detail:
MEASURED 2026-10-28 at c175914b59 (drop schedule; the review thread asked for it after Gowtham's ruling on B-2026-10-28-1, where one worker is now judged by instruction count). Machine: x86-64 container, Xeon family 6 model 207, 4 cores. There is no PMU: perf_event_open returns ENOENT and perf is not installed, so there are no frontend counters. Timing is child CPU time, pinned with taskset -c 2, in shuffled rounds, at KARAC_HASH_SEED=1 and KARAC_THREADS=1. The object was kept through a `cc` wrapper and relinked by hand with a 0/16/32/48-byte .text pad object before it, against libkarac_runtime_min.a and the full archive. The unpadded link was byte-identical to karac's own. Full write-up: review/m4b-speedup/placement-2026-10-28.md in the shared folder. Experiment knobs, not committed: placement-experiment-2026-10-28.patch, which adds KARAC_MIR_FN_ALIGN and KARAC_MIR_LLVM_ARGS.

The archive is not slower code. callgrind shows lean vs full at kata 7 16,102,297,038 vs 16,102,306,810, at kata 125 20,340,386,116 vs 20,340,395,016, and at kata 8 1,744,138,428 vs 1,744,147,251. The full archive moves .text from 0x4080 to 0x7080. Kata 125 spends 83% of its instructions in karac.main, which lands at 32 mod 64 on lean and 16 on full.

Shift sweep, 25 rounds, median CPU s:
- Kata 125 lean (+0/16/32/48): 1.12, 1.14, 1.15, 1.25.
- Kata 125 full: 1.21, 1.11, 1.12, 1.12.
- The two slow arms are both karac.main at 16 mod 64.
- Kata 7 is 1.44-1.49 on all 8 arms, and kata 8 is flat. The 2.36-2.64 s vs 1.62-1.72 s that B-2026-10-28-1 recorded for kata 7 does not reproduce on this CPU.

Knobs (21 or 15 rounds):
(a) align 64 on every defined function. Kata 125 runs 1.06-1.12 on all 8 arms, and binary size grows 0-0.5%. But kata 28 KMP's seq build goes 0.41-0.43 -> 0.50-0.52, and its one-worker build 0.51 -> 0.41.
(b) -align-loops=64 or 32 on top of (a): no change from (a).
(c) -x86-align-branch-boundary=32 -x86-align-branch=fused+jcc+jmp. Kata 28 runs 0.40-0.41 on every arm. But kata 125 goes 1.09-1.10 -> 1.16-1.21, and kata 270 slows by 2-5%.

12 of the M4b one-worker under-floor programs, seq/par unaligned, 11 rounds: 7 1.03, 8 1.00, 125 1.01, 153 1.17, 60-nextperm 1.00, 270 1.08, 209 1.04, 276 0.96, 722 1.00, 13 0.99, 895 1.33 (at 10 ms resolution), 28-kmp 0.80. Only 28 is under 0.9 here.

Not yet tried: measuring on a host with a PMU (DSB and frontend stalls, to say what the 16-mod-64 layout and kata 28's loop actually hit); a profile-guided layout of hot blocks. Inferred: a fixed function alignment buys determinism, not speed, because loops still move inside the function when its code changes. BLOCKED on a host with a PMU: the cloud containers answer perf_event_open with ENOENT, so the frontend counters that would say what the swing is cannot be read here, and no further work is planned on this row without one (drop schedule, 2026-10-28).

detail: MEASURED by the kata thread's corpus sweep (review thread, 2026-10-28): mir-llvm default env vs KARAC_THREADS=1 KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, release karac c336ac98fa. The four entries refuse with that error by default and pass with KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0; KARAC_THREADS=1 alone still refuses (the twin is built either way). one_worker_twin (src/mir/lower.rs, 45524985d1) maps HK::Ref and HK::MutRef arguments to Operand::Copy. fix: a9f56911ac: crate::ast::is_mutating_collection_method (src/ast.rs) lists `extend_from_slice` and strips a `try_` prefix, so the fallible twins write what the plain forms do; MIR now borrows those receivers `&mut`, and auto-par keeps a buffer's appends in order (proto_map_field_roundtrip's encoder: 0 failures in 9,000 runs on three workers, from 56). core_ref_write and core_taskgroup's writer lists defer to the same function, so check refuses `v.extend_from_slice(w)` and `v.try_push(1)` on a `ref` parameter.
