A use of `k` as a value (push, let, own param) still retains the handle. tests/borrowed_handle_reads.rs `a_handle_bound_from_a_ref_scrutinee_is_a_ref_into_it` pins the row's program and the value uses on run and the MIR interpreter.

title: `s.substring(0, len)` with `len` a `ref i64` from `for len in lengths.iter()` is refused (E0200 "'substring' expects integer byte indices, found 'ref i64'"), with no fix-it, where a user function's `i64` parameter, `v[len]`, `v.truncate(len)` and `len.min(..)` all take the same `ref i64`; char_at, repeat, String.truncate and slice check the same way
detail: Found by a mutant of kara-katas leetcode/1001-1100/1032-stream-of-characters (sets arm: `self.stream.substring(0, len)` inside `for len in self.lengths.iter()`, `lengths: Vec[i64]`). karac 6697158faf. Reduced: `let s = "abcdef".to_string(); let lens: Vec[i64] = vec![1, 3]; for len in lens.iter() { println(take(s, len)); println(s.substring(0, len)); }` with `fn take(s: ref String, n: i64) -> String { s.substring(0, n) }`: `karac check` accepts `take(s, len)` and refuses only `s.substring(0, len)` (E0200 at the `len`, no replacement); `s.char_at(k)` is refused the same way ("'char_at' expects an integer index, found 'ref i64'"), while `v[k]`, `v.len().min(k)` and `w.truncate(k)` on a Vec check and run. With `*k` every one runs and prints the expected text under `karac run` and `__mir-run`. `s.substring(n - len)` checks, since the subtraction already yields an i64. The checks are `matches!(arg_ty, Type::Int(_) | Type::Error)` in src/typechecker/stdlib_seq.rs at the char_at (~260), substring (~515), repeat (~548), String truncate (~796) and slice (~964) arms, which do not look through a `ref` of an integer the way an ordinary `i64` parameter does. Expected: accept a `ref` to an integer there (the lowering must then load it), or at least offer `*len` as a machine-applicable fix.
fix: b740a6831e. substring, char_at, repeat, slice and String.truncate (src/typechecker/stdlib_seq.rs) now take an integer argument or a borrow of one (`is_integer_argument`), the way an `i64` parameter, `v[len]` and `Vec.truncate` already did, so `for len in lens.iter() { s.substring(0, len) }` checks. Both backends already read a borrowed integer as its value, so the change is in the checker only. Pin: tests/string_index_borrowed_int.rs runs all five methods with `ref i64` arguments and checks the output on the interpreter and compiled at -O0 and -O2. The control arm on the parent tree gave 0 passed, 1 failed. gate136 green (10064 + 10168 passed, 0 failed).

title: Kata 9's auto-par binary executes a constant +1.85G instructions (+75%) whenever it has two or more workers, flat from 2 to 18: the par lane runs 2.10x rayon's time where it ran 1.21x, the B-2026-10-28-35 signature on a loop shape its fix (5b6aab2a3c) did not cover
detail: MEASURED 2026-10-31 on the M5 Pro, karac g6697158fa, exact counts via kara scripts/pmc.c (3-run minima), bench/palindrome.kara's default (auto-par) build: KARAC_THREADS=1 2.459G instructions (= the KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 twin's 2.458G), 2 workers 4.310G, 4 4.311G, 8 4.313G, 18 4.323G; wall 0.10 s / 0.06 s / 0.02 s at 1 / 4 / 18 workers on 0.10 / 0.22 / 0.26 s of CPU. The excess does not grow with workers, so it is not idle spinning: the parallel lowering of this loop does ~1.75x the sequential work. The loop: `while k < k_iters { let idx = k % n; let x: i32 = inputs[idx]; let inc: i64 = if is_palindrome(x) { 1 } else { 0 }; sum = sum + inc; k = k + 1 }`, an i64 sum of a 0/1 if over a call whose body has its own `while` loop of i32 arithmetic. B-2026-10-28-35 (fixed) was the same signature on kata 4, caused by the task carrying its sum as i128 with prefix bounds; whether this is that shape again is not attributed. Platform-independent: the instruction counts reproduce on Linux. Seq lane separately runs 1.11x legacy dd86e3955's instructions (2.458G vs 2.214G). kara-katas re-bench 2026-10-31. SECOND INSTANCE, kata 7 (bench/reverse.kara, the same i64 sum over per-element i32 work): 14.024G instructions at 1 worker, 15.875G at 2, 15.878G at 4, 15.890G at 18, the same +1.85G excess flat in the worker count; par lane 1.15x -> 1.36x rayon. Not a fixed cost of every parallel run: the excess at 4 workers is +0.39G on kata 12, +0.38G on kata 8, +0.04G on kata 15. LINUX 2026-11-02 (drop schedule, karac at 3a1355614d, kata 9 with K cut to 5M, callgrind): 1 worker 297.7M instructions (karac.main.seq), 2 workers 352.8M (+18%), so the +75% measured at g6697158fa is mostly gone on x86. The hot loop is 59.5 instructions an iteration in order and 70.5 in the task. The difference: a bounds check on inputs[k % n] and a reload of its buffer pointer each iteration (the task no longer knows the Vec's length, and the captured reference has no dereferenceable attribute), the run's least and greatest prefix (two compare-and-cmov pairs and two moves), and the original `k < k_iters` test kept next to the chunk's bound. Candidate fixes: drop the prefix tracking for a term known non-negative (kata 9's 0/1 count), or bound-check the join against term ranges and replay on doubt; mark captured references dereferenceable.
fix: FIXED by f117a8f69f9eb1d23ba79ec433aaeded4593c983 for the prefix tracking, the parent shape. An auto-par task's wide sum skips both prefix compares when every term its statement adds is never negative: a literal that is not, an `if` of such arms, or a name an immutable `let` of the loop body binds to one (chains count operand by operand). Kata 9 then runs only rising terms, and its two-worker excess on Linux went from 55.1M to 35.1M instructions over the in-order 297.7M (K cut to 5M, callgrind). Pinned by tests/mir_auto_par_rising_sum.rs. The remainder has its own row, B-2026-11-02-17: the task's bounds check and buffer reload, and kata 7's signed term. The M5's +75% figure was measured at g6697158fa, before B-2026-10-28-35's narrow runs reached it. It needs a Mac re-bench.

title: Kata 10's regex DP runs 1.37x legacy's instructions and 1.50x its cycles on the MIR backend: the seq lane went from 1.11x to 1.60x rustc -O
detail: MEASURED 2026-10-31 on the M5 Pro by the kara-katas re-bench, karac g6697158fa vs legacy dd86e3955, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, exact counts via kara scripts/pmc.c (3-run minima): bench/regex.kara MIR 5.687G instructions / 798M cycles, legacy 4.153G / 533M. Wall: seq lane 1.11x -> 1.60x rustc -O, 1.09x -> 1.59x clang -O3; par lane 1.15x -> 1.79x rayon. Also in the legacy-vs-MIR corpus screen's tail (Kara/mir_screen/screen2.tsv, 1.37x). Cause unattributed; the instruction gap is platform-independent, so it reproduces under cachegrind on Linux.
fix: 4e55fcd778. A Slice or str parameter (or result) left a function with no by-value signature: `reg_class` (src/backend/mir/mod.rs) knew only scalars and values of 1, 2, 4 or 8 bytes, so one slice sent every parameter and the result through memory. is_match_at copied both slices into fresh 16-byte slots at each of its three recursive calls and returned its bool through a pointer, where legacy passes `{ptr, len}` and an i1. A slice, a str, and a reference to either are now the register pair `{ptr, i64}`; KARAC_MIR_SLICE_REGS=0 turns it off. Callgrind on x86, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, bench/regex.kara: 6.138G instructions before, 4.749G after, legacy dd86e3955 4.850G (1.265x to 0.979x), output unchanged. A 51-bench sample of the kata benches has geomean 0.9985 (best 0.949 on kata 395, worst 1.003), every output unchanged. Pinned by tests/mir_slice_regs.rs.

title: karac compiles a kata 1.54x slower than rustc -O at twice its peak memory on the M5 (median over 24 katas: 165 ms vs 103 ms, 59.8 MiB vs 28.3 MiB): a deliberate divergence, within ADR-2 (0.73x legacy build time over the frozen set at f1416771a4); rustc parity is not a v1 bar
detail: MEASURED 2026-10-31 on the M5 Pro by the kara-katas re-bench (karac g6697158fa, each bench.sh's cold-compile hyperfine row and /usr/bin/time -l peak), 24 katas: karac/rustc compile time median 1.54x (min 1.11x, kata 126; max 1.86x), karac median 165 ms against rustc's 103 ms; karac compile peak median 59.8 MiB (54.6-68.0) against rustc's 28.3 MiB. In July (legacy) karac compiled a kata in ~92 ms at ~24 MiB. B-2026-10-28-37 (fixed by 6bae6aa8d2) cut the library prune's share (kata 2 build 466 -> 330 ms on the cloud box); this is what remains on the M5. Not attributed further: a KARAC_MIR_TIME=1 phase breakdown of one kata build is the next measurement.
fix:
f1416771a4 (measured at; no code change). Wontfix, a deliberate divergence: the review thread's call was to fix the largest phase or close with the measured split if within the ADR-2 bars, and the bars hold with margin. The rustc ratio is not a v1 bar (the Rust/C comparison is deferred past M4, Gowtham 10-18).

ADR-2 at f1416771a4 (x86 cloud box, 4 cores) against legacy-archive 741fbf08c1 `karac build --legacy`, all 585 comparable frozen-set benches (review/adr2-dual), min of 3 interleaved runs, default auto-par: build time geomean 0.734x (max 1.318x, kata 3629 bfs_sieve; none over 1.5x), stripped size geomean 0.376x, peak RSS geomean 1.115x (median 118 vs 106 MiB). At 94c9eb83dd it was 1.155x / max 1.758x / size 1.185x.

Against rustc -O here (KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, median of 7): kata 2 iterative 0.25 vs 0.24 s (1.04x), 126 word_ladder_ii 0.42 vs 0.59 s (0.71x), 233 digit_one 0.23 vs 0.14 s (1.64x); geomean 1.07x. The M5 numbers (ld64) cannot be re-measured from here.

Split (KARAC_MIR_TIME=1, kata 233, ms): the build thread parses 13, prepares 17, resolves 2, typechecks 63 (48 when the check thread is not running beside it), ownership-checks 12, builds MIR 4, optimizes 13, emits 9 and links 99 (cc + GNU ld 70-84, strip 4-5). The check thread runs typecheck 23 and ownership+MIR 10 concurrently (B-2026-10-31-7). Kata 126: opt 180, emit 92. Link is the largest phase of a small kata, typecheck the next.

Callgrind, kata 233 build: the build thread executes 433M instructions, 323M of them in the front end. TypeChecker::check is 161M, of which check_impl_block_inner is 100M: library method bodies. The prune keeps 189 of 266 library methods for a program that names none, through ALWAYS_KEPT (src/mir/library_prune.rs). Ownership check 55M, prepare_for_resolve (desugar) 51M, compile_module 64M. The check thread executes 214M (typecheck 80M, ownership 46M, gated stdlib parse 20M).

Link: rustc 1.97 links through rust-lld (run_linker 33 ms). lld on karac's link takes 33 ms against GNU ld's 67, but the stripped kata-233 binary grows from 71,672 B to 311,376 B: lld keeps std's gimli/addr2line backtrace symbolizer, which GNU ld's --gc-sections drops. Gold gives 348,104 B. Not taken, since it breaks the size bar.

Levers for a later compile-time pass, none taken here:
- Typecheck only the library bodies the MIR builder reaches; ALWAYS_KEPT over-keeps.
- Let the build reuse the check thread's typecheck. That also removes the second AST and type environment, likely part of the peak-memory gap (inferred, not measured).
- A faster linker without lld's size cost.

title: A Rust-spelled mutable receiver or parameter type (`fn find(mut self, ..)`, `&mut self`, `ref mut self`, `self: mut ref Self`, `v: &mut Vec[i64]`) gets a bare parse error with no fix, where `mut ref self` / `mut ref T` is the one Kāra spelling; `let (mut x, ..)` already gets a named message and a machine fix
detail:
Found writing kata 1034's union-find arm (kara-katas leetcode/1001-1100/1034-coloring-a-border): the disjoint-set methods were first written `fn find(mut self, x: i64) -> i64` and `fn join(mut self, a: i64, b: i64)`. MEASURED at 6697158faf, `karac check` and `karac check --output=json` on a five-line `impl S { fn bump(<receiver>) { self.x += 1; } }`:

| receiver or parameter | code | message | fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| `mut self` | E0003 | 'mut' is a reserved keyword and cannot be used as an identifier | none |
| `&mut self` | E0002 | Expected parameter pattern, found `&` | none |
| `ref mut self` | E0003 | 'ref' is a reserved keyword and cannot be used as an identifier | none |
| `self: mut ref Self` | E0002 | Expected `)`, found `:` | none |
| `v: &mut Vec[i64]` (free fn) | E0001 | Expected type, found `&` | none |

The same slip inside a `let` pattern is already handled: `let (mut x, y, mut z) = start;` gets E0001 "`mut x` inside a pattern is Rust syntax -- in Kāra `mut` goes before the whole pattern ..." with a machine-applicable edit (src/parser/patterns.rs:218), and `karac fix` makes it `let mut (x, y, z) = start;` (kata 1033). B-2026-10-29-16 did the same for `for x in mut v`. Each spelling in the table has one Kāra meaning: a receiver that writes is `mut ref self` (corpus/katas: 60 `fn next(mut ref self`), an owned one `own self`, and a parameter that writes is `mut ref T`. For a Rust author these are the first things typed in any `impl`, so the error lands on nearly every first draft with methods; the generic message names the keyword and gives no route to `mut ref self`. Expected: a named message ("`mut self` is Rust syntax -- a receiver that writes is `mut ref self`") with a machine-applicable edit for each row, `&mut T` -> `mut ref T` and `&T` -> `ref T` in type position.
fix: 59f20988a7: the parser recognises each Rust receiver spelling (`mut self`, `&mut self`, `&self`, `ref mut self`, `self: mut ref Self` / `self: ref Self` / `self: Self`) and each Rust borrow type (`&mut T`, `&T`), and reports E0001 naming the Kāra spelling (`mut ref self`, `self`, `own self`, `mut ref T`, `ref T`) with a machine-applicable edit, so `karac fix` rewrites them and the result checks clean. A `self: <other type>` gets the message with no fix. Pinned by tests/rust_receiver_fixes.rs (both tests fail on 487927fd09). Files: src/parser/items.rs (try_parse_self_param, rust_receiver), src/parser/types.rs (the Token::Amp arm of parse_type).

title: A struct variant named like a library type (`Stmt.Match { cases: Vec[i64] }`, also `Response`, `Client`, `Regex`, `Stats`) passes `karac check` but `karac run`/`build` refuse a use of its Vec field ("a type that failed to check is not lowered yet"); check also accepts `*n` on its `i64` field
detail: MEASURED on main at cbfb4aa1ba (karac release build, no compiler change since). A program's own enum with a struct variant whose name is a scope-0 library type (`Match`, `Response`, `Client`, `Regex`, `Stats` measured; `Captures` is fine) cannot use a variant field of a generic type: `enum Stmt { Match { cases: Vec[i64] }, Other }` with `fn visit(s: ref Stmt) -> i64 { match s { Stmt.Match { cases } => cases.len(), Stmt.Other => 0 } }` passes `karac check` ("All checks passed"), and `karac run`, `karac __mir-run` and `karac build` refuse it with "error[mir]: build: 8:33 in `visit`: a type that failed to check is not lowered yet" at `cases.len()`. Renaming the variant (`Block`) makes all three print 2; a tuple variant `Match(Vec[i64])` works; scalar fields (`Match { n: i64, label: String }`) work; a bare `s: Stmt` parameter fails the same way. The checker mistypes the binding too: in `enum Stmt { Match { n: i64 }, Other { n: i64 } }`, `Stmt.Match { n } => *n` is accepted while the same arm on `Other` is refused (E0209 "a 'i64' is copied, so drop the `*`"), so the variant's field types look to be read from the library struct of that name. Found writing apps/cli/mini_symtable (a port of CPython's symtable, whose statement AST has a `Match` variant); the app names the variant `MatchStmt` with a comment naming this row. Related family: B-2026-10-25-33 (a bare use of such a variant refused by check, fixed) and B-2026-11-01-2 (check prints all-passed while MIR lowering fails).
fix: d07a6cee24: the struct-pattern arm of `check_pattern_against` (src/typechecker/patterns.rs) asked `env.structs` first, so `Stmt.Match { cases }` read its field types from the library's `Match` struct (likewise `Response`, `Client`, `Regex`, `Stats`), where `cases` does not exist: it bound at an error type, check passed, and the MIR builder refused the arm. An `i64` field bound as a borrow, so `*n` was accepted on that arm only. The scrutinee enum's struct variant now wins over a same-named struct in the field-type, generic-param, `#[non_exhaustive]` and partial-move lookups. No MIR change was needed: run, `__mir-run` and build print the right answer once the binding has its real type. Pinned by tests/struct_variant_library_name.rs (all five names with Vec fields on the interpreter and compiled at -O0/-O2, and `*n` refused on both arms); both tests fail on 63b2626725.

title: Kata 20's valid-parentheses stack scan runs 1.41x legacy's instructions on the MIR backend: the seq lane went from 0.74x to 0.90x rustc -O and the par lane from 0.68x to 1.06x rayon
detail: MEASURED 2026-10-31 on the M5 Pro by the kara-katas re-bench, karac g6697158fa vs legacy dd86e3955, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, exact counts via kara scripts/pmc.c (3-run minima): bench/valid_parentheses.kara MIR 26.257G instructions / 4471M cycles, legacy 18.591G / 3261M (1.41x / 1.37x). Also in the corpus screen's tail (Kara/mir_screen/screen2.tsv, 1.42x). The par build's instructions are flat across worker counts (26.33G at 1 worker, 26.49G at 2, 26.39G at 18), so it is not the B-2026-10-31-39 signature: the par lane's loss is this seq gap. Cause unattributed; platform-independent.
fix: 11d7eb7f01. The bracket runs are counting fills `mir::presize` now reserves: a counter reset for a second loop, and a bound the guard works out as `n - c` (`while i < depth - 1`). The reservation of an empty vector is one inline allocation of exactly the room, and the fill's pushes become `Vec.__push_within`, which skips the capacity check below the room, so a fill of one value becomes a `memset` as on legacy. Measured with callgrind on x86 against legacy dd86e3955 (the row's 1.41x is from the M5): kata 20's bench reduced to 20,000 iterations went from 1.40x to 0.99x legacy's instructions. Pinned by tests/mir_presize_fill.rs, which fills two runs this way and checks both backends print 33246.

title: Implicit auto-par no longer fires on kata 23 (merge k sorted lists), which the legacy backend parallelized: its par lane now runs the sequential program, 1.49x -> 5.15x rayon
detail: MEASURED 2026-10-31 on the M5 Pro by the kara-katas re-bench, karac g6697158fa: bench/divide_and_conquer.kara's default build has no call of karac_mir_task_spawn in its KARAC_MIR_LL IR; par lane 2579 ms against the seq twin's 2578 ms (the 2026-08-05 legacy feed ran it parallel at 1.49x rayon). KARAC_AUTO_PAR_DEBUG=1 verdicts: main@112 (the outer k-loop, `total = total + sum_list(merged)`, each iteration building its own lists) Exit and Cost("it is inside a loop"); main@116 Crossing("lists reaches the `shared` type `ListNode`"); merge_k_lists@61, merge_two_lists@31/35/40/44 and sum_list@90/95 Crossing(... the `shared` type `ListNode`); merge_k_lists@59 and merge_two_lists@23 Dependence. Whether refusing a loop whose iterations each build and consume their own `shared` values is intended (a reference count crossing threads) is for the auto-par owner to decide; if it is, this row becomes a README note and closes as wontfix. Seq lane flat (0.89x -> 0.88x rustc -O).
fix: 11d7eb7f01 (Thread B's presize change, found by bisection; the row did not name it). Reproduced on x86 by the kata thread at 6697158fa: KARAC_AUTO_PAR_DEBUG=1 gives main@112 Exit plus Cost("it is inside a loop"), the default build has no karac_mir_task_spawn symbol, and it runs 5.7 s real on 5.7 s user. A git bisect between 6697158fa and 91e1821270, with each step's release karac judged on its auto-par verdict for bench/divide_and_conquer.kara, names 11d7eb7f01 as the first commit where main@112 is a loop as tasks with its `total` reduction; its parent 55d161d5d3 still gives Exit. The cause was the reservation mir::presize puts before the inner `lists.push` fill inside the outer loop. 11d7eb7f01 joins that reserve to the region branches of the block it follows and counts its borrow with the vector's push, so the outer loop gets the verdict it had without the reserve. At head (karac 91e1821270, x86, 4 cores) the default build spawns tasks and runs 3.1-3.4 s real on 6.8 s user, against 4.5 s for its KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 twin, with byte-equal output. The inner loops' Crossing verdicts on the `shared` ListNode are unchanged and intended (deferred.md: auto-par declines a body that touches a `shared` value). The M5 par-lane ratio to rayon wants a re-bench on the Mac.

title: A call, operator or array literal reads a place operand only after the later operands have run, against core-semantics 8.1 (left to right): `pair(c.n, bump(mut c))` prints `11 11` (want `1 11`), `c.n + bump(mut c)` is 22 (want 12) and `[y, { y = 7; y }]` is `[7, 7]` on mir-interp and mir-llvm alike; when the later operand MOVES the place, `wrap(b.n, vec![b])` is refused at run and build (`use of _1.0, which may have been moved or never initialized`) though `karac check` accepts it
detail: MEASURED on main at 45e13b0a8e (karac release build; the commits since the build touch only the ledger). Wrong value, interp and build agree: `struct Counter { n: i64 }  fn bump(c: mut ref Counter) -> i64 { c.n += 10; c.n }  fn pair(a: i64, b: i64) -> String { f"{a} {b}" }` then `let mut c = Counter { n: 1 }; println(pair(c.n, bump(mut c)));` prints `11 11`; `let s = c.n + bump(mut c);` gives 22; `let mut x = 1; println(pair(x, { x += 5; x }));` prints `6 6`; `let mut y = 1; let arr = [y, { y = 7; y }];` gives `7 7`. Python, Rust and the spec (8.1: the arguments, the operands of a binary operator and the elements of an array literal are evaluated left to right) give `1 11`, 12, `1 6`, `1 7`. Refusal: `struct Node { n: i64, kids: Vec[Node] }  fn wrap(n: i64, kids: own Vec[Node]) -> Node { Node { n: n, kids: kids } }` then `let body = Node { n: 1, kids: Vec.new() }; let c = wrap(body.n, vec![body]);` passes check, and `karac run` / `karac build` both stop with `error[mir]: move check main: bb6[term]: use of _1.0, which may have been moved or never initialized`. Same with `wrap(body.n, one(body))` for a plain `fn one(k: own Node) -> Vec[Node]`, and `pair(body.n, (body, 5))`; `wrap(body.n, body)` (the move as the argument itself) works. Cause (read, not bisected): src/mir/lower.rs `expr_operand` returns `self.use_place(p, t)` for a place expression, an operand that reads the place when the Call / BinaryOp / Aggregate executes, i.e. after the statements that lowered the later operands. A later operand that writes or moves the place therefore changes what the earlier one reads. The eval_order pin (corpus/core/eval_order) uses only calls `p(x)` as operands, never a place read next to a write, so it does not see this; the interp and LLVM backends agree, so run-vs-build and the corpus A/B cannot see it either. Related, same model: `karac check` refuses `let t = (v[0], { v[0] = 9; v[0] });` with E0516 (`cannot mutably borrow v while it is still borrowed`, the borrow at the first `v[0]`), which 8.1 makes legal: the `i64` is copied out before the block runs. Remedy (a hypothesis): when lowering an operand list, copy an earlier place operand into a temp once a later operand is anything but a constant or another place read; for a Copy scalar the extra copy is free after LLVM. Found writing kara-katas apps/cli/mini_infer: its parser built `with_kids(Nk.EConstraint, body.span, vec![body])`, which `karac run` refused; the app copies the span into a local first, with a comment naming this row.
fix: d8e47c345a. src/mir/lower.rs reads a place operand into a temporary at its own position when a later operand of the same call, operator, method call, tuple / array / struct / collection literal or f-string can write or move it: one that names a local the place is rooted in (an assignment, a `mut` argument, a receiver, a move) or calls a local closure, or, for a place through a static or a shared handle, any operand that runs code (`note_eval_order`, `later_may_write`, `read_at_position`). Lists of places, constants and built-in scalar arithmetic lower as before. `pair(c.n, bump(mut c))` prints `1 11`, `c.n + bump(mut c)` is 12, `[y, { y = 7; y }]` is `[1, 7]`, `pair(x, { x += 5; x })` is `1 6`, and `wrap(body.n, vec![body])`, `wrap(body.n, one(body))` and `first(body.n, (body, 5))` are accepted, on mir-interp and mir-llvm. Pinned by corpus/core/ok_eval_order_place_then_write (14 cases incl. struct fields, f-string holes and a shared handle written through an alias; refused as a use after move on the control, spec output with the fix). Corpus: of the 328 mir-interp entries that failed a cut-off sweep, one changes verdict, test_entry_chain_places_read_and_write_the_slot, refused before only for f-string holes 8.1 makes legal; its expected refusal (line 11, 8.2) is B-2026-11-01-16. mir-llvm over core/ and apps/: 563 of 564 pass and every app, the one fail a stale legacy-run expectation. Perf: the elaborated MIR of the 1010 kata bench programs is identical for 826; in the other 184 every added local is a scalar, a reference, a str or slice view or a pair of i64, register-sized copies with no new drops. The related check refusal of `(v[0], { v[0] = 9; v[0] })` (E0516) is check's and is not changed here.

title: MIR never full-unrolls a constant-trip loop that calls or exits early, where the June legacy fix (B-2026-06-17-7) did: kata 36 went from 0.55x to 1.66x rustc -O and kata 37 from 0.97x to 1.37x
detail: MEASURED 2026-10-31 on the M5 Pro by the kara-katas re-bench, karac g6697158fa, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0. B-2026-06-17-7 (legacy, fixed 1de4eb1e) found rustc fully unrolls kata 37's candidate loop `while d <= 9 { .. if go(..) ..; d = d + 1 }` while clang's cost model declines it (recursive call + early exit), and made karac mark it `llvm.loop.unroll.full`; kata 36 led the field from it (kara-katas 5f66a192). On MIR neither kata's KARAC_MIR_LL carries an unroll hint: kata 36's is_valid nests `while r < 9 { while c < 9 { .. if .. { return false } .. rows[r] = ..; c = c + 1 } }` (a call to box_index, array stores, an early return), kata 37's loop is the one above, so mir::counters::unroll_full_latches' gate rejects both (which condition is not attributed: the call, the early exit, the stores or UNROLL_FULL_MAX_STATEMENTS = 48). Kata 36 bench/valid_sudoku.kara: 65.3 ms (June feed) -> 220.7 ms, 0.55x -> 1.66x rustc -O, with C and Rust 11-13% slower in the same sessions. Kata 37 bench/sudoku_solver.kara: 0.97x -> 1.37x rustc -O (the row's measured rolled gap was ~1.34x). The October legacy build had lost the unroll as well: MIR runs 1.02x (36) and 1.01x (37) dd86e3955's instructions, so the regression is against the June build, not the MIR switch.
fix: c26d97bd87. mir::counters::unroll_full_latches now admits a counting loop whose body calls a small leaf (no loop, no call but an element access, at most 24 scalar statements, counted into the loop's size) or the function itself, under a 128-statement limit for calling loops, and a `<=` guard counting to at most 32; src/backend/mir/mod.rs passes the program's bodies as the callee lookup. Measured with valgrind I refs (this container, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0): kata 36 bench 7.085B -> 5.748B (-18.9%), kata 37 bench 5.849B -> 4.249B (-27.4%), outputs identical. Deliberately NOT every call: an experiment admitting all calls regressed the benches' outer pass loops (187 +6.40%, 66 +3.63%, 126 +1.36%, 16 +1.14%), the shape legacy narrowed for in B-2026-08-13-10 and B-2026-08-15-31; with this gate no other of the 1016 kata benches screened gains a hint. Pinned by tests/mir_unroll_calls.rs (leaf call and self-recursive `<=` loop hinted, a pass loop calling a looping kernel not; the two positive cases fail on the base). M5 wall-time not re-measured here.

title: `unsafe { xs.get_unchecked(i) }` is bounds-checked on the MIR backend: the escape hatch design.md documents does nothing, and kata 28's unchecked KMP no longer gains on the checked one (1.14x -> 1.01x)
detail: Found 2026-10-31 by the kara-katas re-bench (karac g6697158fa). src/backend/mir/seq.rs's ("get_unchecked", [i]) arm computes the element with checked_elem, the same bounds-checked path as an ordinary index, while design.md § Bounds checks and get_unchecked (c) makes `unsafe { xs.get_unchecked(i) }` the opt-out, with Rust's contract (the caller ensures i < len). Evidence: kata 28's bench/kmp_unchecked.kara, which differs from kmp.kara by three get_unchecked calls, emits the same 11 `icmp ult` and 8 abort calls in its KARAC_MIR_LL IR. Effect: the unchecked variant ran 1.14x faster than kmp on legacy (120.1 vs 136.4 ms, 2026-07-28 feed) and 1.01x now (161.1 vs 163.3 ms); against rustc -O it went 0.87x -> 1.01x. The MIR interpreter's get_unchecked arm checks too (src/mir/interp.rs), which is fine for an interpreter but means no test can see the difference there.
fix: 62aae3a95a: the MIR backend's `get_unchecked(i)` arm (src/backend/mir/seq.rs) takes the element address with `elem_ptr` instead of `checked_elem`, so `unsafe { xs.get_unchecked(i) }` emits no bounds compare or abort, as design.md documents. tests/mir_get_unchecked.rs pins the IR (no `icmp ult` in the unchecked loop) and the printed totals on run and build.

title: `karac fix` on `println!("{}", n)` (and `print!` / `eprintln!` with format arguments) only deletes the `!`, leaving `println("{}", n)`, which fails E0202 "takes 0 or 1 argument(s)" with no fix; and on `println!("{n}")` the same edit silently changes the output from Rust's `3` to the literal `{n}`. `format!` already gets the f-string rewrite (B-2026-10-24-12)
detail:
Measured at 6697158faf (karac 0.9.0-dev.14057), each line in `fn main() { let n = 3; <line> }`, then `karac fix`, then `karac run`:

    println!("hello");                 -> println("hello");                 -> hello
    println!("{}", n);                 -> println("{}", n);                 -> E0202 println() takes 0 or 1 argument(s), found 2
    println!("{} and {}", n, n + 1);   -> println("{} and {}", n, n + 1);   -> E0202 found 3
    print!("{:03}\n", n);              -> print("{:03}\n", n);              -> E0202 found 2
    eprintln!("n={}", n);              -> eprintln("n={}", n);              -> E0202 found 2
    println!("{n}");                   -> println("{n}");                   -> prints {n}
    println!("{0}", n);                -> println("{0}", n);                -> E0202 found 2
    let s = format!("{} and {}", n, n + 1); -> let s = f"{n} and {n + 1}";    -> 3 and 4

The E0202 on the result carries no fix either, so the author hand-edits after a machine fix, which is the Mend loop's worst case: the fix made the program look done and moved the error. The `{n}` case is worse: Rust 2021 captures `n` inline, so the edit compiles and prints something else with no diagnostic.

Where: src/parser.rs report_macro_call. `println`, `print`, `eprintln` (and the other names in MACRO_FUNCTION_TWINS that take a string) fall through to the generic edit that deletes the bang. The `format` branch just above already has format_macro_rewrite (80fb30bcf3) with the safety rules a println rewrite needs.

Suggested remedy (a hypothesis): when the first argument is a string literal and more arguments follow, or the literal holds a `{ident}` hole, reuse format_macro_rewrite to emit `println(f"...")`; when it declines (positional `{0}`, `{:?}`, counts disagree), give the named message with no edit rather than the bang deletion, as `format!` does. A bare literal with no holes keeps today's edit. Seen authoring kata 1037's bench with a Rust habit (`println!("{} triples, ..", count, ..)`).
fix:
d9ce354001. In src/parser.rs report_macro_call, a println! / print! / eprintln! / panic! whose first argument is a string literal followed by more arguments, or whose literal still holds a `{` hole, now gets format_macro_rewrite's f-string edit wrapped back in the call (`println!("{} and {}", n, n + 1)` becomes `println(f"{n} and {n + 1}")`), with a message saying the call takes one string. format_macro_rewrite also carries Rust 2021 inline captures (`{n}`, `{n:02}`) as is. A call the rewrite cannot carry one-to-one (positional or named holes, mismatched counts, `{:?}`, an expression in a hole) keeps the message and gets no edit, so the `!` is no longer deleted into an arity error or a literal brace print. Pinned by tests/print_macro_fix.rs: eight sites rewritten, the result reparses and runs to "3 and 4
003
3 then 03
{3}
plain
3!
"; six no-fix shapes carry the message and no edit. Control: the row's table at 6697158faf.

title: Rust string-method carry-overs `trim_start_matches`, `trim_end_matches`, `trim_matches` and `to_owned` get a bare E0236 "no method 'X' on type 'String'" with no hint (and `trim_matches(|c| ..)` adds a cascaded E0208 on the closure), where `parse::<T>()` and `s.parse()` already get named messages that point at `i64.parse(s)`; Kāra's spellings are `strip_prefix` / `strip_suffix` and `to_string()`
detail:
Measured at 6697158faf (karac 0.9.0-dev.14057), each line in `fn main() { let s = "[12]"; <line> }`, `karac check --output=json`:

    let t = s.trim_start_matches("[");      E0236 no method 'trim_start_matches' on type 'String'
    let t = s.trim_end_matches("]");        E0236 no method 'trim_end_matches' on type 'String'
    let t = s.trim_matches(|c| c == 0);     E0236 no method 'trim_matches' .. || E0208 cannot compare '?T0' and 'i64'
    let t = s.to_owned();                   E0236 no method 'to_owned' on type 'String'
    let n = s.parse::<i64>().unwrap();      E0001 names turbofish, says `i64.parse(s)`, with a fix
    let n: i64 = s.parse().unwrap();        E0236 names the expected-type rule and `i64.parse(s)`
    let t = s.strip_prefix("[").unwrap();   clean

The typo suggester (src/typechecker/method_user_impl.rs `did you mean`) finds nothing this far from `strip_prefix` or `to_string`, so the author is left to search docs/library/strings.md. The E0208 on the closure is noise from the unknown receiver method: once the method is unknown its closure's parameter stays `?T0`, and the comparison is reported as a second error.

Suggested remedy (a hypothesis): a small table of Rust String/str method names with a Kāra twin, consulted when the lookup fails, giving a named message: `trim_start_matches(p)` -> `strip_prefix(p)` (one occurrence, returns Option) or a loop for repeated strips; `trim_end_matches` -> `strip_suffix`; `to_owned()` -> `to_string()` (machine-applicable, same meaning). Suppress the closure's follow-on error when the receiver method is unknown. Seen writing kata 1038's level-order parser with a Rust habit.
fix: da4e21d14c. In src/typechecker/expr_method_call.rs, a String or Str receiver calling trim_start_matches, trim_end_matches, trim_matches or to_owned (with no user method of that name on String / StringSlice) now gets "no method '<m>' on type '<T>': <twin> (library/strings.md)", naming strip_prefix / strip_suffix / trim / to_string, and returns Type::Error so a closure argument (`trim_matches(|c| ..)`) adds no second error. `to_owned()` with no arguments carries the edit renaming it to `to_string`. Pinned by tests/rust_string_method_hint.rs: three hints, one error each, no edit; and karac fix renames two to_owned sites, after which the program runs to "ab\n". Control: the row's table at 6697158faf, where each was a bare "no method".

title: Comparing a library lookup with an owned Option (`m.get(k) == Some(5)`, `m.get(k) == o`, `v.get(i) == o.map(..)`) fails E0208 "cannot compare 'Option[ref i64]' and 'Option[i64]'" with no fix, though the fix is the one the `.copied()` diagnostic already names: `.cloned()` on the ref side (or `?? d`), machine-applicable when the item is Copy
detail:
Measured at 6697158faf (karac 0.9.0-dev.14057), in `fn main()` with `m: Map[i64, i64]` holding 1 -> 5, `v: Vec[i64] = vec![5]`, `o: Option[i64] = Some(5)`, each printed in an f-string:

    m.get(1) == Some(5)            E0208 cannot compare 'Option[ref i64]' and 'Option[i64]', no fix
    m.get(1) == o                  E0208, no fix
    m.get(1) == o.map(|v| v + 1)   E0208, no fix
    v.get(0) == o                  E0208, no fix
    m.get(1) == m.get(2)           clean, false
    m.get(1).cloned() == o         clean, true
    m.get(1).copied() == o         E0236 names `.cloned()`, with a fix
    (m.get(1) ?? -1) == 5          clean, true

The refusal itself is the settled rule (B-2026-10-12-22: the library side is the ref; 6bbbaf1fb5 relaxed only the other direction, a constructor operand holding a ref to a Copy value). What is missing is the edit: the message names neither `.cloned()` nor `*`, so an author who meets it (here kata 1038's differential, comparing `new_shifted.get(k + c)` against `new_of.get(k).map(|v| v + c * rank)`) has to find the library page. Even `m.get(1) == Some(5)`, the most direct spelling, gets no help.

Suggested remedy (a hypothesis): in infer_binary, when the two operand types differ only by one side being `Option[ref T]` (or `Result[ref T, E]`) and the other `Option[T]` with T Copy, attach an edit inserting `.cloned()` after the ref operand, and name it in the message, as the `.copied()` branch does.
fix: f5a8142cd5. Both "cannot compare" sites in src/typechecker/expr_ops.rs (Eq/NotEq and the orderings) now go through report_compare_mismatch, which offers the `.cloned()` edit when one side is an `Option[ref T]`, the other an `Option[T]` of the same item, the item is Copy, and the viewed side ends at a known span (a method call's close paren, or a name, field, index or call). The message also names `.cloned()` and `opt ?? d`. A non-Copy item (Map[i64, String]) keeps the message with no edit, since `.cloned()` there would copy a String the author may not want. Pinned by tests/option_ref_compare_fix.rs: four edits on both sides of == / != and <, after Map.get and Vec.get, `m.get(2) == None` untouched, and the fixed program runs to "true true true true\nfalse\n"; the non-Copy case carries no edit. Control: the row's own table at 6697158faf, where every case had no fix.

title: `(x, y) = (y, x)` on two `String` bindings gets the right E0287 fix (drop the parentheses) plus four cascade E0500 move errors with `.clone()` fixes, and `karac fix` applies the clones, not the E0287 edit, leaving `(x.clone(), y.clone()) = (...)` and then `x.clone(), y.clone() = ...`, which no fix repairs; with `i64` bindings the fix works
fix: b5520ddad6 drops the cascade. The typechecker now records each assignment it refuses with E_ASSIGN_TARGET_NOT_PLACE as a span from the target's start to the value's end (`TypeCheckResult::rejected_assign_spans`, filled in `check_assignment_target_is_place`, src/typechecker/items.rs), and the check pipeline (src/cli.rs, `ownershipcheck_phase`) drops every ownership error whose use or move site lies inside one, along with its `error_fix_diffs` envelope. The ownership pass read the refused statement as plain moves of every name in it, so those errors existed only because of the refusal. Measured on the row's program: `karac check` now reports the place error alone (1 error), and one `karac fix` writes `x, y = y, x;`, which checks clean and prints `y x`. A move error elsewhere in the same function is still reported. Pinned by tests/fix_tuple_assign_cascade.rs (3 tests: check output, fix-then-check-then-run, and an unrelated `take(z); take(z);` still reported). Gate at b1379a8666 plus the fix: fmt, both clippy legs, `cargo test --all` (10068 passed, 0 failed) and `cargo test --features llvm` (10172 passed, 0 failed); after the rebase onto 0385166bd1 (no overlap with the fix's files) the cli, rust_receiver_fixes and new suites re-ran green.

title: A `mut` field of handle-aggregate type passed to a borrowed parameter (`g(h.left, h)` with `a: Option[N]`) is lent in place rather than counted (core-semantics §6.2), so a write to the field through another handle during the call changes what the parameter reads: `cut(h); match a { Some(x) => x.val, None => -1 }` prints -1, want 7
fix: bf1ae02cf1: `arg_operand_here` copies (or counts) a `mut` field of a `shared` value whose type is `Copy` or a handle aggregate into a temporary and lends that, per core semantics §6.2; `Lcx.mut_fields` records the program's `mut` struct fields, which MIR does not. Pinned by corpus/core/ok_shared_mut_field_lent_as_value (expected_from spec), which prints 7 on mir-interp and mir-llvm (the control printed -1). 0d471f66c4 removes the copy's cost where it cannot matter: rc_borrow lends the field itself when the callee is count-safe (writes no place through any `shared` handle, calls only count-safe bodies, no closures) and no `mut` borrow of anything holding a handle is passed alongside. Kata 938's differential on the interpreter: 42 s before, 62 s with the copy, 46 s with the lend. Aliases (`g(h.left, h2)` with h2 == h), a handle inside another argument, and a capturing closure argument all print 7 on both backends, since each makes the callee not count-safe and the copy stays.

title: `karac fix` gives `println!("{} {}", c.n, s.replace("a", "b"))` no edit, because format_macro_rewrite refuses any argument holding a `"`, though an f-string hole balances quotes (`f"{s.replace("a", "b")}"` parses); `println!("{} {}", c.n, s.trim())` is rewritten
detail: MEASURED in the v0.9.0 fresh-user walkthrough rehearsal: a fresh clone of main at cb012884a4, built as the README says with KARAC_RELEASE_TAG=v0.9.0 (`karac 0.9.0+gcb012884a`) and freshly built runtime archives. `println!("{} {}", c.n, s.replace("a", "b"))` gets the B-2026-11-01-8 message ("Kāra has no macros; ... write its format arguments into an f-string") and no edit, so `karac fix` leaves it and the program stays refused. With the arguments `c.n, x`, `c.n, s.len()` or `c.n, s.trim()` the same call is rewritten to `println(f"{c.n} {s.trim()}")`. The cause is the `bad` character list in `format_macro_rewrite` (src/parser.rs), which refuses an argument containing `"` along with `{`, `}`, `:`, a backslash and a newline. design.md § strings ("Full expressions") says the parser balances quotes inside a hole, and `println(f"{s.replace("a", "b")}")` parses and runs. A string argument with no brace, colon or backslash inside could be carried as is. The same list serves `format!` (B-2026-10-24-12).
fix: 51cbfabbb4: `format_macro_rewrite` (src/parser.rs) no longer refuses an argument for holding a `"`. An f-string hole balances quotes (design.md § strings, "Full expressions"), so `println!("{} {}", c.n, s.replace("a", "b"))` now gets `println(f"{c.n} {s.replace("a", "b")}")` from `karac fix`, and `format!` does the same. An argument with a brace, `:`, backslash, comment or line break still gets the message and no edit. The tests/format_macro_fix.rs pin that held `g("a")` as no-fix is flipped into the rewritten set, and `g("a:b")` takes its place as a no-fix case. Pinned by tests/rehearsal_diagnostics.rs `println_macro_argument_with_a_string_literal_gets_the_f_string_edit` (rewrites, reparses, runs to "1 xbc"), which fails on 7161c53902.

title: `karac run` with no file inside a `karac new --lib` project says "missing file argument" and suggests "`karac run` inside a project to run its src/main.kara", while the user is inside one; `karac build` there says the library has no `main`
detail: MEASURED in the v0.9.0 fresh-user walkthrough rehearsal: a fresh clone of main at cb012884a4, built as the README says with KARAC_RELEASE_TAG=v0.9.0 (`karac 0.9.0+gcb012884a`) and freshly built runtime archives. In a fresh `karac new mylib --lib`, `karac run` prints `error: missing file argument` and `help: `karac run <file.kara>`, or `karac run` inside a project to run its src/main.kara`, exit 1. The user is inside a project, so the help sends them back to the command they just ran. `karac build` in the same directory says `library package `mylib`: checked, nothing to link (a library has no `main`; the packages that depend on it build it)`. The fallback in src/cli/args.rs (B-2026-10-30-18) returns None when the project root has no src/main.kara and falls through to the generic message. It should name the library and point at `karac test`.
fix: 51cbfabbb4: in src/cli/args.rs, `karac run` with no file, inside a project whose root has src/lib.kara and no src/main.kara, now prints `error: library package `<name>` has no src/main.kara to run` with `help: a library has no `main`: `karac test` runs its tests, and the packages that depend on it run its code`, exit 1, instead of the generic "missing file argument" help. Outside a project the generic message is unchanged. Pinned by tests/rehearsal_diagnostics.rs `karac_run_in_a_library_project_names_the_library` (scaffolds `karac new mylib --lib` and runs `karac run` in it), which fails on 7161c53902.

title: `h.d ?? x` with `h` a borrowed struct whose field `d: Option[Node]` holds a `shared` handle is refused by check as a move out of a borrow; core-semantics §6.1 makes the read a count, as check already says for a bare `d: Option[Node]` parameter (B-2026-11-01-1)
fix: 8df360f9f9: `reject_nil_coalesce_out_of_borrow` (src/typechecker/expr_ops.rs) now skips any payload that copies or counts, using `index_read_part_counts_or_copies` (src/typechecker/items.rs, made pub(super)): a `shared` handle, or an Option / Result / tuple / array whose parts are such handles or Copy values (core-semantics §6.1). So `h.d ?? Node.Leaf(-1)` with `h: Holder` borrowed and `d: Option[Node]` checks clean, and run / build print 3. The source stays usable (a second `field(h)` prints 3 again), and `h.p ?? (Node.Leaf(0), -1)` over `Option[(Node, i64)]` works the same way. ASan lane clean. A payload that is neither, like `Option[String]`, is still refused with the `.clone()` fix. Pinned by tests/borrowed_field_nil_coalesce.rs; `nil_coalesce_counts_a_handle_field_through_a_borrow` fails on 2526fe4a0a, and the String guard passes on both.

title: An assignment whose place is a method-call chain evaluates the value before the place, against core-semantics 8.2 (place operands first): `m.entry(1).or_insert(Bag { n: 1 }).n = m[1].n * 2` on an empty map panics `key not found` (want: the place inserts the key, then the value reads it, which 8.2 makes a borrow error), and check accepts it
detail: MEASURED on mir-interp at 487927fd09 (before B-2026-11-01-7) and with the -7 fix alike. `struct Bag { n: i64 }  fn main() { let mut m: Map[i64, Bag] = Map.new(); m.entry(1).or_insert(Bag { n: 1 }).n = m[1].n * 2; println(f"{m[1].n}"); }` passes `karac check` and stops at run with `runtime error: key not found at 4:44`, the `m[1]` of the value: the value ran before the place's `or_insert`. Under 8.2 the place's operands run first, so `or_insert` lends `m` mutably and the value's `m[1]` reads `m` while that loan is live, the E0516 the corpus entry fixtures/interpreter/families/b_2026_10_06_114/test_entry_chain_places_read_and_write_the_slot expects (its v2_reject note cites 8.2). An index place is already place-first: `a[idx(1)] = val()` prints `place` then `value` on mir-interp and mir-llvm. core-semantics 8.2 itself says `Today = evaluates v first`; no ledger row tracked it. Found by B-2026-11-01-7's corpus comparison: that entry was refused before -7 only for its f-string holes at 15:57 and 28:25 (a `mut` loan from one hole's `or_insert` held across the next hole), which 8.1 makes legal once the first hole's `i64` is copied out; with -7 they are accepted, nothing refuses line 11, and the program runs (output `read 10 1` / `[5] 10 [x] [9]` / `ab` / `noisy` / `noisy` / `36` / `6 2 9`).
fix: edc88dd260. In the MIR builder's pre_index, a MethodCall or Call that roots an assignment place is evaluated into a pinned temporary before the value and before any index along the place (core semantics 8.2), so `m.entry(k).or_insert(d).n = v` and `at(mut b).v[p(1)] = p(9)` print place first on mir-interp and mir-llvm. A value that then reads what the place borrows is refused (E0516). Pins: corpus/core/ok_assign_place_call_first, corpus/core/err_assign_place_call_then_value_reads; the fixture test_entry_chain_places_read_and_write_the_slot notes its line 11 is refused since this fix. docs/core-semantics.md 8.2 drops its 'Today' sentence.

title: Kata 71's auto-par binary at exactly two workers runs 1.22x slower than at one on the M5 (143.1 ms against 117.6 ms at eb17818b45, from 1.6-2.6x), ATTRIBUTED to macOS's xzone allocator: free() reads mach_absolute_time on each of simplify()'s per-iteration buffer frees, not the pool; Linux scales cleanly
detail:
MEASURED 2026-11-01 on the M5 Pro (6P+12E) by the kara-katas re-bench, karac g6697158fa, bench/simplify.kara's default (auto-par) build, exact counts via kara scripts/pmc.c (whole-process): KARAC_THREADS=1 3.935G instructions / 0.643G cycles, real 0.15 s; =2 4.204G / 3.222G, real 0.24-0.39 s, user 0.47-0.77 s; =3 4.086G / 0.758G, real 0.06-0.10 s; =4 4.087G / 0.839G, real 0.04-0.05 s; =18 4.032G / 1.747G, real 0.03-0.05 s. At two workers the instruction count barely moves (+7%) while cycles go up 5x, so the two workers stall on each other (a shared cache line, a lock, or the pool's hand-off at width two); it is not extra work and not the B-2026-10-31-39 signature (that one adds instructions). Not attributed; whether it reproduces on the Linux container's homogeneous cores, or is the M5's P/E-core asymmetry at width two, is the first thing to check. The kata's published par lane (default worker count) is unaffected (0.91x rayon); a user who sets KARAC_THREADS=2 gets a program slower than its sequential build. The legacy-era KARAC_PAR_WORKERS knob is no longer read by the v2 runtime (KARAC_THREADS is). SECOND INSTANCE, kata 125 (bench/valid_palindrome.kara: `sum = sum + pass(input)` over a shared `ref String`, each pass building a fresh Vec[u8]), re-measured 2026-11-01 with the Mac awake: KARAC_THREADS=1 0.79-0.91 s, 25.19G instructions / 3.17G cycles; =2 1.29-1.51 s, 25.58G / 11.13G (3.5x the cycles for +1.6% instructions); =3 0.60-1.19 s; =4 0.29-0.32 s. NOT the P/E-core asymmetry: under `taskpolicy -b` (E-cores only, homogeneous) 1 worker 1.38-1.40 s, 2 workers 1.19-1.28 s, so two identical cores still barely beat one. Not macOS's nano allocator (MallocNanoZone=0 no better). Not every width-two reduction: synthetic reductions with the same shape scale cleanly at two workers (pure i64 arithmetic per iteration 2.59 -> 1.30 s; a 200-element Vec built and summed per iteration 0.58 -> 0.35 s), so the trigger is something these two kernels share and the probes lack (both read one shared heap object every iteration; a contended refcount or line on it is a candidate, not verified). The published par lane (default 18 workers) is unaffected: 0.62x Go-par, 1.16x rayon. LINUX 2026-11-02 (drop schedule, 4-core x86 container, karac at 3a1355614d, 3 runs each): does NOT reproduce. Kata 71 real/user: 1 worker 0.156-0.176/0.156-0.169 s, 2 workers 0.075-0.078/0.140-0.145 s, 3 0.053-0.055 s, 4 0.037-0.045 s. Kata 125: 1 worker 1.12-1.15 s, 2 0.61-0.66 s, 3 0.45-0.50 s, 4 0.37-0.40 s. Both scale cleanly at width two, so the stall is macOS-specific (os_unfair_lock PoolLock, the nap's yield_now/park_timeout, or ulock wake-ups) and needs a Mac to attribute.

M5 re-bench 2026-11-03 (scripts/bench/m5-rows.sh at kara cd7fd85dec, Darwin arm64, min of 5, outputs equal): kata 71 wall at 2 workers 165.9 ms vs 1 worker 124.4 ms, 1.334x. Still over. M5 RE-RUN 2026-11-05, Gowtham via scripts/bench/m5-pool2.sh at eb17818b45, Darwin arm64, min of 5: kata 71 base T=1 117.6 ms wall / 114.5 ms user, T=2 143.1 / 279.5, T=3 96.5 / 265.1, T=4 67.0 / 241.3; with 4096 strings of ballast T=1 121.1, T=2 157.0 (padding does not help); kata 125 scales cleanly (T=1 710.5, T=2 281.5, T=3 210.1, T=4 152.4), so its half of this row is gone. ATTRIBUTED from the saved `sample` call trees (k71_T2, k71_T4; read by the review thread): every mach_absolute_time frame, at T=2 and T=4, sits directly under `_xzm_free + 1048` in libsystem_malloc, reached from three k71 call sites (+0x1320, +0x12d4, +0x13d0; 141+92+88 samples on one worker, 125+83+103 on the other); none come from the pool (nap, fire_deadlines, worth). simplify() allocates and frees four small buffers (cs, starts, ends, out) per iteration, and compiled code calls the system malloc/free directly, so this is the OS allocator's free path at two threads. The pool needs no change. What is left: (a) whether a Rust/rayon build of the same kernel at 2 threads pays the same on the M5, which would make it a platform effect for every language on the system allocator (then wontfix with this attribution), or (b) a Kara-side cure (per-thread reuse of small Vec/String buffers, or a bundled allocator), a design decision rather than a fix.

The M5 call trees put every hot clock read under `_xzm_free` in libsystem_malloc, reached from simplify()'s per-iteration buffer frees, and Rust pays the same at two threads, worse. Gowtham's M5 run 2026-11-05, the kata's rayon comparator (bench/rayon simplify_rayon, hyperfine -N, 10 runs): RAYON_NUM_THREADS=1 155.4 +- 6.1 ms (user 152.6), 2 410.4 +- 41.0 (user 807.7), 3 191.4 +- 9.3, 4 77.6 +- 7.8; that is 2.64x slower at two threads against Kara's 1.22x (eb17818b45: T=1 117.6 ms, T=2 143.1, T=3 96.5, T=4 67.0). title: Kata 118's Pascal's-triangle build loop runs 1.72x legacy's instructions on the MIR backend (1.30x its cycles): the seq lane went from 0.56x to 0.76x rustc -O and from 1.14x to 1.48x C
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-01 on the M5 Pro by the kara-katas re-bench, karac g6697158fa, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, exact counts via kara scripts/pmc.c (3-run minima). bench/generate.kara (nested while; inner body `row.push(tri[i - 1][j - 1] + tri[i - 1][j])` or `row.push(1)` at the row edges): MIR 6.474G instructions vs legacy dd86e3955 3.760G (1.72x), 1657M vs 1277M cycles (1.30x). Unattributed: only the pre-opt IR was read (it shows the push growth path via karac_mir_vec_reserve and many 8-byte memmoves of locals, which may fold), so the hot-loop delta is not located. Platform-independent as far as known (instruction count).
fix: 11d7eb7f01. `mir::presize` now reserves a fill whose bound is an outer loop's counter (Pascal's rows, `while j <= i`), and the reservation of an empty vector is one inline allocation of exactly the room, returning the length it leaves room for. The fill's pushes become `Vec.__push_within(&mut v, x, reach)`, whose compiled form skips the capacity check below `reach`, so LLVM drops the growth path. Measured with callgrind on x86 against legacy dd86e3955 (the row's 1.72x is from the M5): kata 118's bench went from 1.48x to 0.92x legacy's instructions. title: Kata 116's populate-next-right-pointers loop runs legacy's instruction count on the MIR backend but 1.23x its cycles (M5), 1.08x wall on x86: WONTFIX, DELIBERATE: core-semantics §7 drops a struct's fields in reverse declaration order (next, right, left), legacy dropped them in declaration order, and the resulting free order is the whole gap
detail:
MEASURED 2026-11-01 on the M5 Pro by the kara-katas re-bench, karac g6697158fa, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, exact counts via kara scripts/pmc.c (3-run minima). bench/connect.kara: MIR 10.971G instructions vs legacy dd86e3955 11.025G (1.00x) but 2320M vs 1880M cycles (1.23x). Seq lane 0.90 -> 1.10x rustc -O (1.22x relative). Same instructions-flat, cycles-up signature as B-2026-10-31-37 and B-2026-10-31-38 (a store-forwarding reload in kata 64), and larger than the borderline group in B-2026-11-01-20; the mechanism is NOT verified for this kata's loop. An IPC loss, so it may be M5-specific; check x86 wall time before assuming it is shared. | 2026-11-03 (drop schedule, x86 4-vCPU, karac 4d6ced41f3 vs legacy dd86e3955, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, min of 7 wall): bench/connect 496 vs 458 ms (1.08x), outputs equal. The x86 gap is small next to the M5's 1.23x cycles; an arm64 measurement is still what attributes it.

M5 re-bench 2026-11-03 (scripts/bench/m5-rows.sh at kara cd7fd85dec, Darwin arm64, min of 5, outputs equal): kata 116 cycles MIR 2333.8M vs legacy 1906.0M, 1.224x; instructions 0.986x. Still over. | 2026-11-03 (Thread B): qemu-aarch64 counts (apple-m1, 200 reps): MIR 34.46M vs legacy 33.71M; 66% of both is malloc/free, with the same 1022 40-byte allocations per tree. The difference is the ORDER of the frees. Legacy frees the tree post-order in allocation order (8, 9, 7, 11, 12, 10, 6, ...). MIR frees along the `next` links and down the levels (256, 384, 257, 129, 448, ...), so the next tree's allocations come back from a scattered free list. That is a locality cost, which fits cycles-only. It is in drop elaboration of a `shared` node with three `Option[Node]` fields (the drop schedule's area). Not changed by 3d8ac8a2c5. Not confirmed on the M5.
fix: ac3bfa3ad1 (Thread B's attribution; no code change). WONTFIX, a deliberate trade. Mechanism: Node is `shared struct { val, left, right, next }`. Each node is held by its parent's child field and by its left neighbour's `next`. Under core-semantics §7 (struct fields drop in reverse declaration order) a node drops `next` first. The right neighbour's last reference then goes along the level, so the tree is freed along `next` links. Legacy dropped fields in declaration order, so the last reference always came from the parent's left/right and the tree was freed post-order. MEASURED x86 4-vCPU, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, at 9d4ab2635c, interleaved, outputs equal: the same bench with the fields declared `val, next, right, left`, which makes §7's order the legacy one, runs 0.534-0.558 s min against 0.578-0.585 s (about 4-9%), the whole x86 gap. So no codegen cost is left: the gap is the allocator's locality under the spec's drop order. Why not fix it: the order is normative and observable whenever any part has a Drop body. An as-if exception (declaration order when the whole type graph's drop is pure deallocation) would be a layout heuristic: it helps a type whose last field is a sibling link and hurts the mirror case, with no general locality argument either way. It would also add a second drop order for drop elaboration and the interpreter to agree on. A program that wants post-order frees can declare its link field first.

title: Kata 120's default build auto-parallelizes its one-off 200-row triangle build and then runs +2.0G instructions (+29%) whenever it has two or more workers: the default binary is 1.10x slower than its KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 twin
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-01 on the M5 Pro, karac g6697158fa, exact counts via kara scripts/pmc.c (3-run minima). bench/triangle.kara's default build emits one karac_mir_task_spawn (poll.main.ap0#task, returning TaskHandle[Vec[Vec[i64]]]): auto-par took main's triangle-build loop (`while i < nrows { let mut row = Vec.new(); while j <= i { row.push((i * 31 + j * 17) % 100) } tri.push(row) }`, N = 200 rows, ~20k pushes, run once), not the 20,000-rep min-path punch loop that dominates the run. Instructions by KARAC_THREADS: 1 6.884G (= the KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 twin's 6.883G), 2 8.892G, 4 8.906G, 8 8.932G, 18 9.001G; cycles 905M / 988M / 1015M / 1071M / 1213M. hyperfine (15 runs, same session): seq 228.2 +/- 3.2 ms [user 226.6, sys 0.9] vs default 249.9 +/- 5.8 ms [user 262.8, sys 39.2], 1.10x slower. Two defects: (1) the cost gate admits a once-run loop whose whole work is ~20k pushes, so parallelism can never pay; (2) the same flat-in-the-worker-count instruction excess as B-2026-10-31-39 (katas 9 and 7, +1.85G), here on a loop that collects a Vec[Vec[i64]], so the excess is not tied to an i64 sum reduction. Unattributed beyond that. Also: kara-katas bench.sh for this kata timed the default build as its seq lane until this re-bench (fixed to KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, as katas 81 and 90 were).
fix: FIXED by 3a1355614d98e3157c3d3187a375b4f0c4ccef97, for defect (1); defect (2) is attributed below. MEASURED on Linux, callgrind with the punch loop cut to 2,000 reps: 1 worker 530M instructions, all in karac.main.seq; 2 workers 771M (+46%), the excess in main's par twin. The extra instructions are the code AFTER the auto-par loop, not the pool. The triangle comes back through the task's join, so the punch loop no longer knows the rows' lengths, and three bounds checks per inner DP step stay where the sequential build folded them away (disassembly of both hot loops: 13 instructions against 19). So the excess is not tied to a reduction and is not B-2026-10-31-39's signature. Fix: the cost gate's loop half also weighs a top-level loop whose iterations only run inner loops of known trips, with no call that loops: constant trips times inner trips, an inner bound allowed to be the outer counter (through plain copies) at its last value. Under SMALL_WORK = 100,000 it stays in order. Kata 120's loop is 200 x 200 = 40,000. After: kata 120 at 4 workers 0.36-0.42 s against the KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 twin's 0.39-0.41 s. A screen of all 1010 kata benches changes 7 verdicts (katas 90, 120, 290, 291, 902, 914, 984), each a one-off input-building loop in main. Pinned by auto_par_top_level_loop_of_little_work_stays_in_order (kata 120's while-while shape through the real builder, a 100x100 grid refused, a 1000x1000 grid and an unknown inner bound still tasks). M5 not re-measured.

title: MIR `shared` boxes carry a 16-byte strong+weak count header where legacy carried 8, so a 24-byte node body (a tree's val + left + right) takes a 48-byte macOS malloc block instead of 32: kata 124's peak RSS went from 35.2 MB to 52.1 MB (1.48x)
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-01 on the M5 Pro, karac g6697158fa vs legacy dd86e3955, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, /usr/bin/time -l (3 runs each, stable): bench/max_path_sum.kara (2048 balanced trees x 511 `shared struct TreeNode { val: i64, mut left: Option[TreeNode], mut right: Option[TreeNode] }` = 1,046,528 nodes) peaks at 35,225,600 bytes on legacy and 52,101,120 on MIR; same sink. The MIR build calls `malloc(40)` per node and stores 1 at offset 0 and 1 at offset 8 before the body at 16, per src/mir/layout.rs `SHARED_COUNTS: u64 = 16` ("the strong and the weak count"). macOS malloc rounds 40 up to its next 16-byte quantum, 48, where legacy's 8 + 24 = 32 fit exactly: +16 bytes on each of ~1.05M nodes is +16.7 MB, the whole measured gap (+16.9 MB). Every `shared` type whose body is 17-24 bytes (or 33-40, ...) pays this on macOS; that includes the corpus's binary-tree and linked-list katas. INVISIBLE ON LINUX: glibc gives malloc(32) and malloc(40) the same 48-byte chunk, so measure on macOS. The kata's legacy-era x86 container run agrees: kāra 51.3 MiB vs C 34.3 MiB already with the 8-byte header (8 + 24 = 32 rounds to a 48-byte glibc chunk; C's 24-byte node to 32). On the M5 the MIR kāra row (49.2 MiB in results.json) now equals Rust's Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>> (49.3 MiB: strong + weak + borrow flag + body = 48), where legacy kāra matched C (33.1 MiB). A fix candidate is to drop the weak count from types no `weak` handle ever names (whole-program), restoring the 8-byte header; not attempted. Timing on this kata is not hurt measurably (seq 0.87x rustc -O); the cost is memory and cache footprint. See also the memory note that an 8-byte header was free on macOS because it filled the 32-byte slot.
fix: FIXED by 498a852019e616d880d51340d941042bb46ad0f2. Code generation takes the set of `shared` types some interned `weak` type names (TyCtxt::weak_shared_defs, once before any code). A type outside it gets an 8-byte header, the strong count alone: construction stores no weak count and the last release frees the box directly. Types a `weak` type names keep both u64 counts (16 bytes). A weak-count access on a type outside the set is a compiler error, not a write past the strong count (Cx::weak_count_ptr). Kata 124's node is now malloc(32), which fits macOS's 32-byte block, where malloc(40) took 48. Measured on x86-64 Linux, where glibc hides the RSS gap (32 and 40 both take a 48-byte chunk): across 117 shared-type kata benches vs origin/main, binary size geomean 0.999x, time geomean 0.98x, outputs identical. The macOS RSS recheck of kata 124 is still owed. Rejected alternative: strong and weak as u32 in one word. Its per-retain overflow check cost katas 865 and 99 1.4-1.65x, because it stopped retain/release pairs from cancelling. Pinned by tests/mir_shared_header.rs (32-byte box without `weak`, 40 with, built and under ASan, `shared` and `sync`).

title: Under the task pool every borrow-flag operation goes through ONE process-wide locked table, so parallel tasks that write `mut` fields of their own `shared` values serialize on it in the kernel: kata 133's par lane runs 28.8x rayon (was 1.36x) with 17 s of system time, and 45x faster with KARAC_MIR_FLAGS=0
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-01 on the M5 Pro. bench/clone_bfs_par.kara: 18 `par {}` branches each clone a 500-node `shared struct Node` graph (BFS with a visited Map, writing the clones' `mut` neighbor fields), reading one `frozen` source graph. The clones never leave their branch. karac g6697158fa (the sweep compiler): KARAC_THREADS=1 0.21 s; 4 workers 1.01-1.08 s, sys 2.5 s; 18 workers 1.11-1.18 s, user 1.0 s, SYS 16.2-17.2 s. The published par lane is 1164.9 ms vs rayon 40.4 ms (28.8x, was 1.36x on 2026-09-08) and 4.5x slower than kāra's own seq lane (258.8 ms). `sample` puts the workers in __psynch_mutexwait / __psynch_mutexdrop (pthread mutex) called from the program's own code; on that build PoolLock is std's Mutex. CURRENT MAIN (263afb2303, which has 22920fb08b's os_unfair_lock PoolLock on Apple) is barely better: 18 workers 0.89-0.90 s, user 1.3 s, sys 12.4-12.6 s, still 4.3x slower than one worker. ROOT CAUSE confirmed by switch: main with KARAC_MIR_FLAGS=0 (no borrow flags; 7 karac_mir_flag_* calls in the IR -> 0) runs 0.19 s / 0.06 s / 0.02 s at 1 / 4 / 18 workers, sys 0.01-0.02 s, same sink 500. runtime/src/mir_flags.rs keeps FLAGS and HOLDS as `program_state!`, which under the pool is a single PoolLock-guarded Vec (mir_task.rs), taken on every karac_mir_flag_acquire/_release and on every _check while any flag is held anywhere (HELD is process-wide). FIX CANDIDATES (not attempted): a per-task flag table, carried with the task across suspensions (its doc says `shared` values never cross tasks, so flags taken by one task never conflict with another's), or per-worker tables migrated at suspension; at least make the HELD fast path per-task. Platform: the global lock is platform-independent; macOS parks contended waiters in the kernel (psynch / ulock), so the cost is likely largest here; measure Linux before sizing.
fix: FIXED by 57efe5bc2fbb907120a3e7aca5bcd7dbb052c710. The flags and coroutine-frame holds were `program_state!`, one table behind the pool's lock, and the global HELD counter sent every check to it while any task held a flag. `shared` values never cross tasks, so a flag one task holds can never meet another task's access: each task now keeps its own mir_flags::Table, a thread-local while it runs, swapped in and out around each of the executor's three poll sites as its span stack is, and carried with the task when it moves between workers. No flag operation takes a lock. MEASURED on Linux (4 cores) with bench/clone_bfs_par.kara. Before: 1 worker 0.60 s, 4 workers 2.72 s real (7.7 s user, 1.7 s sys); KARAC_MIR_FLAGS=0 at 4 workers was 0.17 s. After: 1 worker 0.60 s, 2 workers 0.32 s, 4 workers 0.20 s, same sink 500. M5 not re-measured.
