title: A `shared` handle crosses a task boundary inside a function value whose type is erased by a SIGNATURE: `fn mkf(s: own S) -> Fn() -> i64 { || { s.n = s.n + 1; s.n } }` then two `TaskGroup.spawn` closures calling `f = mkf(s)` pass `karac check` and race on the non-atomic handle: 2 x 100000 increments print 166280 (run) and 150044 (ASan build) under KARAC_THREADS=4, want a check refusal (core-semantics §6.3) (WIDENED: any container of an erased function type is assumed CrossTask: a struct field `f: Fn() -> i64`, a `Vec[Fn()]` or `Map[_, Fn()]` (local or returned), `Option[Fn()]`, a returned `dyn Trait` over a shared field, a closure returning a closure, a `channel` send of the erased value, a `sync struct` field of type `Fn()`, and an erased `Fn` parameter spawned inside the callee all pass check; only a closure literal visible in the spawning body is refused)
detail: MEASURED on main at 31dae2d40 (karac release build with llvm, this container, 2026-11-01) by the core-semantics probe (cells in the probe thread's grid; the repro below is the whole program). Program: `shared struct S { mut n: i64 }  fn mkf(s: own S) -> Fn() -> i64 { || { s.n = s.n + 1; s.n } }  fn main() { let s = S { n: 0 }; let f = mkf(s); let g = TaskGroup.new(); let a = g.spawn(|| { let mut i = 0; while i < 100000 { f(); i = i + 1; } 0 }); let b = g.spawn(|| { ...same... }); a.join(); b.join(); println(f()); }`. `karac check`: All checks passed. `KARAC_THREADS=4 karac run`: 166280; `karac __mir-llvm-asan`: 150044 (want a refusal; a sequential run would print 200001). Control: the same closure bound locally (`let f: Fn() -> i64 = || { s.n = ...; s.n };` then `g.spawn(|| f())`) is refused with E_NOT_CROSS_TASK, the B-2026-10-26-13 fix. So the fix follows a function value's environment when the closure literal is visible in the same body, and loses it when the value comes back through a function's declared `Fn()` return type. §6.3: a function value is CrossTask only when everything its environment reaches is, through any depth of erased Fn / MutFn / OnceFn values. An erased `Fn` whose environment is unknown therefore cannot be assumed CrossTask: either the return type must say so (`Fn() + CrossTask`-style, the `dyn T + CrossTask` precedent) or a spawn/send of a value whose environment is unknown must be refused. Spec call for the review thread; the check gap is Thread A's. Also untested here: the same erasure through a struct field of type `Fn()`, a `Vec[Fn()]`, a `dyn Trait` returned from a function, and a `channel` send of the erased value. WIDENED by the probe's second pass (same build, cells n1/* in the shared folder's probe-core/): each of these passes `karac check` and runs (all spawn or send a function value whose environment holds `S`, a `shared struct S { mut n: i64 }`): (a) `struct W { f: Fn() -> i64 }` built locally as `W { f: || s.n }` and captured by `g.spawn(|| (w.f)())`; (b) the same built by `fn mkw(s: own S) -> W`; (c) `let mut v: Vec[Fn() -> i64] = Vec.new(); v.push(|| s.n); g.spawn(|| v[0]())` (LOCAL, no signature involved); (d) the Vec returned by a function; (e) `fn mkd(s: own S) -> dyn Get` returning `W { s: s }` and `g.spawn(|| d.get())` (B-2026-10-30-13 covered a dyn MOVED in, not one returned); (f) `tx.send(mkf(S{..}))` on a `channel(1)`; (g) `fn go(f: Fn() -> i64) -> i64 { TaskGroup.new().spawn(|| f()).join() }` called with an erased f (the closure-literal argument `go(|| s.n)` IS refused); (h) `fn mko(..) -> Option[Fn() -> i64]`; (i) `sync struct Y { f: Fn() -> i64 }` holding mkf's value (a sync field must be CrossTask, 6.3); (j) a `Map[i64, Fn() -> i64]` captured by a spawn; (k) `let mkc = || { let s = S{..}; let c: Fn() -> i64 = || s.n; c }; let f = mkc(); g.spawn(|| f())`. Refused correctly: an erased f in `par { f(), f() }` and in `par for` (the effect pass sees the captured S there), and the closure literal passed to `go`. So the gap is in the typechecker's CrossTask test on TYPES that contain an erased function type (`Fn`/`MutFn`/`OnceFn`/`dyn T`), which it answers yes; the B-2026-10-26-13 analysis of a function value's environment only reaches values whose closure literal is in the same body.
fix: 3139c3c5bf. Core semantics §6.3 as ruled at 54c572e94: an erased function type is CrossTask only when it is written `Fn(A) -> R + CrossTask with E` (also MutFn and OnceFn; the marker binds to the nearest function type). The parser reads the marker, the formatter prints it back, and the lowered type carries it outside type equality. The CrossTask walker refuses an unmarked function type at every boundary it serves: spawn and `par` captures, task results, channel sends, `sync` fields, CrossTask supertraits and auto-par legality. Its fix-it adds ` + CrossTask` where the type is declared, whether a parameter, a `let` annotation or the return type of the function a `let` is bound from. A local bound directly from a closure literal in the same body is not erased, and its environment is followed as before (B-2026-10-26-13). Each coercion into a marked type is checked to reach only CrossTask values. That covers a parameter, a `let`, a return, a field, an element, a method argument such as push or send, and a server handler. `IsolatingGroup.spawn` is a spawn too. The stdlib functions that spawn a function parameter now declare it marked: `Server.serve` and its TLS and WebSocket forms, and `std.time.timeout`. A gated module's marks are read from its own parse. Auto-par still treats a function item, a constructor and a closure literal written in the loop body as having no environment, so only a held erased value keeps a loop sequential (ruling (d)). The row's program and probe cells (a) to (d) and (f) to (k) are refused at check. The marked forms run, and their coercions are checked. Case (e), a `dyn` returned from a function and viewed by tasks, is a separate rule (the dyn view carve-out) and is filed as its own row. Pins: corpus/core ok_closure_moves_into_fn_value_call and effect_vars_par_apart take the marker, and err_fn_param_unmarked_spawned and err_effect_vars_par_unmarked are their unmarked forms. Tests: tests/fn_cross_task_marker.rs, tests/fn_cross_task_auto_par.rs and the strict-check fn-env-spawned-param case. Corpus and apps sweep under `karac check` at this build: 20,851 files, and nothing is refused beyond the err_ pins. Control on origin/main: fn_cross_task_marker failed 3 of 4. Gate on the rebase: fmt, both clippy legs, `cargo test --all` 10117 passed and `--features llvm` 10229 passed, 0 failed.

title: A task spawned into a `TaskGroup` made OUTSIDE a `with_provider` call captures the provider and outlives it: `let tg = TaskGroup.new(); let h = with_provider[Clk](F { t: vec![1] }, || tg.spawn(|| Clk.now())); h.join()` passes `karac check`, prints `dF` before the task reads, then a garbage number on run and heap-use-after-free under ASan (core-semantics §14.5 makes it a check error) (WIDENED: the group as a parameter, an isolating group, a task that reaches the provider through a named function, a nested `with_provider` with the group in the outer one, and a `Stdout` override all pass check; llvm reads freed memory or leaks, while mir-interp stops with `field access ... goes through an uninitialized value`)
detail: MEASURED on main at 31dae2d40 (karac release build with llvm, this container, 2026-11-01) by the core-semantics probe (cells in the probe thread's grid; the repro below is the whole program). Program: `effect resource Clk: ClkP;  trait ClkP { fn now(ref self) -> i64; }  struct F { t: Vec[i64] }  impl ClkP for F { fn now(ref self) -> i64 { self.t[0] } }  impl Drop for F { fn drop(mut ref self) { println("dF"); } }  fn main() { let tg = TaskGroup.new(); let h = with_provider[Clk](F { t: vec![1] }, || tg.spawn(|| Clk.now())); println("after"); println(h.join()); }`. `karac check`: All checks passed. `karac run` (KARAC_THREADS=4): `dF`, `after`, `8243122676035110500` (want a refusal; reading the live provider would give 1). `karac __mir-llvm-asan`: `ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-use-after-free ... READ of size 8 ... thread T1`, freed by the provider's drop at the end of the `with_provider` call. §14.5: a closure that uses `R` captures the hidden reference, a view of `p`, so handing it to a task that may outlive the call is the §5.7 / §9.1 error, naming `R` and the `with_provider`. §9.5: the group borrows the closure's origins until it drops, so a group declared before the `with_provider` outlives `p`. B-2026-10-30-5 (fixed) made spawns INSIDE the call work; this is the group-outside shape it did not cover. Related untested shapes: the group passed into the closure as a parameter, a task spawned on a group that is a field of a struct, and the same with a program-rooted override (`with_provider[Stdout](cap, || tg.spawn(|| println(..)))`). WIDENED by the probe's second pass (same build, cells n1/* in the shared folder's probe-core/): (a) `fn under(tg: TaskGroup) -> TaskHandle[i64] { with_provider[Clk](F { t: vec![1] }, || tg.spawn(|| Clk.now())) }`: check passes, mir-llvm prints 94126703203639, ASan aborts with an invalid access, and mir-interp stops with `in F.now at bb0[0]: field access of (*_1).0 goes through an uninitialized value` (the interpreter detects the dead provider; `karac run` prints garbage like the build); (b) `TaskGroup.isolating()` outside: same; (c) `tg.spawn(|| rd())` with `fn rd() -> i64 { Clk.now() }`: same; (d) a group made inside an outer `with_provider[Clk]` spawned into from an inner one, `h.join()` in the outer: same, the inner provider is gone; (e) `with_provider[Stdout](Cap { .. }, || tg.spawn(|| { println("x"); 0 }))` with tg outside: runs, prints 0, the text goes nowhere visible and ASan reports an 8-byte leak from the task. Control, right on every lane: the group made INSIDE the `with_provider` closure and joined there prints 1.
fix: 7bb878c704. `check_core_provider_escape` (src/provider_escape.rs) takes the type-check result and, for each `with_provider[R]` call and `providers { }` block in a user function, walks its body for `g.spawn(task)` on a `TaskGroup` or `IsolatingGroup` (by the receiver's type) whose group's root binding is not bound inside that body. Such a group was made before the call, or is a parameter, a field, or an outer `with_provider`'s group, so it outlives `p` (§9.5). The spawn is refused as the §14.5 escape ("cannot be spawned on a task group made outside the `with_provider`, which outlives it") when the task uses `R`: directly, through a named function (by the effect checker's inferred effects, as the other §14.5 candidates are), or as `Stdout` through a print. A group bound inside the body, at any depth of block, drops and joins before the provider does and stays accepted. tests/provider_escape_outer_group.rs covers all six of the probe's shapes (let, parameter, isolating, named function, nested `with_provider`, `Stdout` override) and two inside-the-call controls. Control on origin/main before it: 6 failed, 2 passed. The sweep over corpus and apps (20,851 files) refuses nothing new. Not covered: a group passed into a function that spawns on it from inside a caller's `with_provider` (the binding is out of sight there; a callee's `with_provider` is not), which would need the caller's group location.

title: A `Map` index place reads its key operand after the assigned value has run, against core-semantics 8.2 (place operands first): `let mut k = 1; m[k] = { k = 2; 5 };` inserts key 2, want key 1, on mir-interp and mir-llvm alike; a `Vec` index place (`v[i] = { i = 1; 5 }`) and a call key (`m[key()] = val()`, prints place then value) are already right (WIDENED: every plain `=` into a `Map` or `SortedMap` index place reads a place key late: a field key `m[s.k] = { s.k = 2; 5 }`, a String key, and `v[0][k] = ..` on a `Vec[Map]`; `m[k] += ..` and `m[k][0] = ..` are already right) (FIXED for Copy keys only; the moved String-key remainder is B-2026-11-01-46)
detail: MEASURED on main at 31dae2d40 (karac release build with llvm, this container, 2026-11-01) by the core-semantics probe (cells in the probe thread's grid; the repro below is the whole program). Program: `fn key() -> i64 { println("place"); 1 }  fn val() -> i64 { println("value"); 5 }  fn main() { let mut m: Map[i64, i64] = Map.new(); let mut k = 1; m[k] = { k = 2; 5 }; println(f"{m.contains_key(1)} {m.contains_key(2)}"); let mut n: Map[i64, i64] = Map.new(); n[key()] = val(); let mut v = vec![0, 0]; let mut i = 0; v[i] = { i = 1; 5 }; println(f"{v[0]} {v[1]}"); }`. `karac run` and `karac build` agree: `false true` / `place` / `value` / `5 0`. Want `true false` first: 8.2 step 1 evaluates the place's operands (the key `k`, a Copy place, read as 1) before `v`. So a call key is evaluated first, but a PLACE key is read lazily, after the value: the B-2026-11-01-7 mechanism (a place operand read only after later operands ran) at the Map-index-assignment position, which that fix did not reach. Unprobed neighbours: `m[k] += { k = 2; 1 }`, `m[s.k] = ...` with a field key, a String key moved or written by the value. WIDENED by the probe's second pass (same build, cells n1/* in the shared folder's probe-core/): wrong (insert at the late key) on mir-interp, mir-llvm and ASan alike: `m[s.k] = { s.k = 2; 5 }` with `struct K { k: i64 }`; `let mut key = "a".to_string(); m[key] = { key = "b".to_string(); 5 }` on a `Map[String, i64]` (inserts "b"); `v[0][k] = { k = 2; 5 }` on a `Vec[Map[i64, i64]]`; `SortedMap` the same as `Map`. Right: `m[k] += { k = 2; 1 }` (updates key 1), `m[k][0] = { k = 2; 5 }` on a `Map[i64, Vec[i64]]` (writes key 1's vec), and `f"{m[1]} {bumpm(mut m)}"` (8.1 operand read). So the late read is specific to the Map insert-on-assign path (`m[k] = v` lowered as an insert call whose key argument is taken after the value), not to Map index places in general.
fix: 84c96d6599. index_set (src/mir/lower.rs) now reads a Copy place key into a temporary before the value when the value may write it (the B-2026-11-01-7 later_may_write test), so `m[k] = { k = 2; 5 }` inserts key 1, as do a field key, a SortedMap and a `Vec[Map]` element (`vm[i][j] = { i = 1; j = 2; 5 }`), on mir-interp and mir-llvm. Pinned by corpus/core/ok_assign_map_key_first (fails on the base). PARTIAL by design: a moved (String) key is still read late, because reading it first refuses `m[key] = key.len()` with an internal MIR move error while the ownership check accepts it; that remainder is B-2026-11-01-46 (review thread ruled: follow 8.2, E0500 from the ownership check).

title: B-2026-11-01-16 is wider than method chains: an assignment whose place is rooted in ANY call evaluates the value first, against core-semantics 8.2: `at(mut s).n = { println("value"); 3 }` with a free `fn at(s: mut ref S) -> mut ref C` prints `value` before `place`, and so does `get(h).n = ..` with `fn get(h: H) -> H` returning a `shared` handle, on run and build
detail: MEASURED on main at 31dae2d40 (karac release build with llvm, this container, 2026-11-01) by the core-semantics probe (cells in the probe thread's grid; the repro below is the whole program). Program: `struct C { n: i64 }  struct S { c: C }  fn at(s: mut ref S) -> mut ref C { println("place"); mut ref s.c }  shared struct H { mut n: i64 }  fn get(h: H) -> H { println("place"); h }  fn main() { let mut s = S { c: C { n: 0 } }; at(mut s).n = { println("value"); 3 }; let h = H { n: 1 }; get(h).n = { println("value"); 3 }; println(f"{s.c.n} {h.n}"); }`. `karac run` and `karac build` agree: `value place value place 3 3`, want `place value place value 3 3` (8.2: the place's operands, including a call that yields it, run first). B-2026-11-01-16 (open) names the method-chain spelling `m.entry(k).or_insert(d).f = v`, and core-semantics 8.2 says 'a place rooted in a method call still evaluates v first'; these two cells show the order follows any call-rooted place, a free function returning `mut ref` and a function returning a `shared` handle alike. Filed separately rather than retitling -16 so that its owner sees the widening; the fix is probably one change for both. A field place on a local (`o.r = ..`), an index place and a tuple element place are already place-first.
fix: edc88dd260. The B-2026-11-01-16 change covers every call-rooted place, not only method chains: it pins any Call or MethodCall rooting the place. Re-measured on the fix (release with llvm), the row's own program prints `place value place value 3 3` on karac run and karac build (want met), the free `fn at(s: mut ref S) -> mut ref C` and the shared-handle `fn get(h: H) -> H` alike. Pinned: corpus/core/ok_assign_place_call_first (free fn returning mut ref) and corpus/core/ok_assign_map_key_first (shared handle, 84c96d6599).

title: A temporary created in a `match` guard drops at the end of the enclosing statement instead of the end of the guard, against core-semantics 7.4: `match 1 { x if see(mk(x)) == 1 => println("arm"), _ => {} }` prints `arm d1`, want `d1 arm`, on mir-interp, mir-llvm and the ASan build; a guard that FAILS already drops before the next arm (WIDENED: every success-path guard shape: a field read on a temporary `mk(x).id == 1`, two temporaries, a guard in a loop, a guard on a payload binding, an arm that returns)
detail: MEASURED on main at 31dae2d40 (karac release build with llvm, this container, 2026-11-01) by the core-semantics probe (cells in the probe thread's grid; the repro below is the whole program). Program: `struct R { id: i64 }  impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"d{self.id}"); } }  fn mk(i: i64) -> R { R { id: i } }  fn see(r: R) -> i64 { r.id }  fn main() { match 1 { x if see(mk(x)) == 1 => println("arm"), _ => {} } let k = match 2 { x if see(mk(x)) == 3 => 0, _ => { println("fallthrough"); 1 } }; println(k); }`. `karac run` and `karac build`: `arm d1 d2 fallthrough 1`. Want `d1 arm d2 fallthrough 1`: the table in 7.4 says a match guard's temporaries drop at the end of the guard, and the narrower-construct rule says an argument to a borrowed parameter inside a guard drops there, not at the end of the statement. The failing-guard path (second match) is right, so the success edge of the guard skips the guard-scope drop and the temp falls to the statement's. Same probe, all right on every lane: `if` condition, `while` condition, `let ... else` (both paths), `while let` scrutinee, brace-less arm, block tail, `return e`, and the guard/if-condition nested inside an f-string argument (`println(f"{if see(mk(1)) == 1 { 10 } else { 0 }}")` prints `d1 10`). ASan reports nothing (it is order, not memory). WIDENED by the probe's second pass (same build, cells n1/* in the shared folder's probe-core/): `x if mk(x).id == 1 => println("arm")` prints `arm d1` (want `d1 arm`); `x if see(mk(x)) + see(mk(2)) == 3` prints `arm d2 d1` (want `d2 d1 arm`); in `for i in 0..2 { match i { x if see(mk(x)) >= 0 => println(f"a{x}"), .. } }` prints `a0 d0 a1 d1` (want `d0 a0 d1 a1`); `Some(x) if see(mk(x)) == 7 => println(f"arm {x}")` prints `arm 7 d7`; an arm that runs `println("r"); return 1;` prints `r d1 1` (want `d1 r 1`). All lanes agree, ASan clean. So the temporaries of a guard that succeeds live until the end of the statement, and the arm body runs before they drop.
fix: FIXED by 420746ccf0f869fc37acce8d415e5ddd30ef1082. lower_match evaluated a guard in the arm's scope, so the guard's temporaries were scheduled with the arm's bindings and dropped when the arm ended; only the failing edge (exit_entries before trying the next arm) dropped them first. The guard now gets a scope of its own, popped once its value is read (owned_operand + read_before_drops, as an `if` condition is), on both edges, and the arm's scope keeps only the bindings. The row's program prints `d1 arm d2 fallthrough 1`. Pin: corpus/core/drop_temp_match_guard (success and failing edges, a payload binding, a guard in a loop, an arm that returns), matched on mir-interp, mir-llvm and __mir-llvm-asan, and read by the built_core_pins unit test.

title: `let x: i64 = None?;` passes `karac check` and stops `karac run` / `karac build` with `invalid MIR: f: bb5[0]: assigning () to _1 of type i64`; `let x: i64 = g()?;` with `g() -> Option[i64]` is fine
detail: MEASURED on main at 31dae2d40 (karac release build with llvm, this container, 2026-11-01) by the core-semantics probe (cells in the probe thread's grid; the repro below is the whole program). Program: `fn f() -> Option[i64] { let x: i64 = None?; Some(x) }  fn main() { println(f().is_none()); }`. Check passes; run prints `error[mir]: invalid MIR: f: bb5[0]: assigning () to _1 of type i64`, build fails the same way. Want `true`. Control: `let x: i64 = g()?;` with `fn g() -> Option[i64] { None }` prints `true`. So the bare `None` literal under `?` is typed by its (unconstrained) payload, and the MIR builder lowers the continue edge with a unit value. Found inside two probe cells (a `?` early exit in a `for` over a shared field, and drops on a `?` exit), where the spelling was incidental. Low: nobody writes `None?` on purpose, but `Err(e)?` in a generic position may take the same path (unprobed).
fix: 5ae1af9472: the check-mode `?` arm checks a bare `None` / `Option.None` operand against `Option[<expected>]` (src/typechecker/exprs.rs), as `let o: Option[i64] = None;` does, so `let x: i64 = None?;` no longer synthesizes as the enum's own `Option[T]` and lowers with a unit payload. `Err(e)?` under an annotation already typed its payload from the return type (probed: prints `true`). tests/none_question_payload.rs pins both spellings in functions and closures on check, interp and run.

title: A `TaskGroup` task that READS a `Copy` local does not borrow it: `let mut x = 1; let tg = TaskGroup.new(); let h = tg.spawn(|| x + 1); x = 5;` passes `karac check` and runs (prints 2, then 5), where core-semantics 9.1/9.5 make writing a place a live task captured an error; a `Vec` capture is refused correctly (WIDENED: a whole Copy tuple `t` captured by a task and reassigned is also accepted; a FIELD capture `p.a` and a task that WRITES `x` are refused correctly)
detail: MEASURED on main at 31dae2d40 (karac release build with llvm, this container, 2026-11-01) by the core-semantics probe (cells in the probe thread's grid; the repro below is the whole program). Program: `fn main() { let mut x = 1; let tg = TaskGroup.new(); let h = tg.spawn(|| x + 1); x = 5; println(h.join()); println(x); }`. `karac check`: All checks passed; `karac run` and the ASan build (KARAC_THREADS=4): `2` / `5`. Want a refusal: 9.1 says a read-only capture of a Copy place is still a `ref` capture, so writing the place while the closure is live is an error, never a silent read of a stale copy; 9.5 says while the group lives a captured place may not be written. Control: the same program over a `Vec` (`tg.spawn(|| { for x in v { .. } })` then `v.push(4)`) is refused with `v is written while a task of tg borrows it (§9.5)`, and a non-task closure (`let f = || lim + 1; lim = 4; f()`) is refused. So the task capture of a Copy place is treated as a snapshot copy, which is the stale-copy semantics 9.1 rules out (and whether the task sees 1 or 5 would depend on scheduling if it were by reference). Not a memory fault as compiled today. WIDENED by the probe's second pass (same build, cells n1/* in the shared folder's probe-core/): `let mut t = (1, 2); let h = tg.spawn(|| t.0 + 1); t = (5, 5);` is accepted and prints 2. Refused correctly: `let h = tg.spawn(|| p.a + 1); p.a = 5;` on a `struct P { a: i64, b: i64 }`, and a task that writes `x` (`tg.spawn(|| { x += 1; x })`) followed by a read of `x`. So a task's read-only capture of a whole Copy local is taken by copy.
fix: 1d70880a1f. The strict task-group pass (src/typechecker/core_taskgroup.rs) no longer skips a task's read-only capture of a Copy place: per core semantics 9.1 it is a ref capture and 9.5 keeps it borrowed while the group lives, so `let mut x = 1; let h = tg.spawn(|| x + 1); x = 5;` is refused like the Vec case, and so is the widened tuple cell (`t = (5, 5)`). A Copy place that drops before the group (a loop counter declared after it) still counts as borrowed until it dies: a later write is refused and reads are not, and `let c = k;` before the spawn compiles. Impact counted first: of the 215 task-using programs under corpus/ and kara-katas, 2 legacy codegen fixtures read the counter in the task; they moved to the 9.1 spelling (review thread approved). Pins: corpus/core/err_taskgroup_copy_read_then_written, err_taskgroup_copy_read_in_loop_then_written (both fail on the base), ok_taskgroup_copy_read_then_read. run and build still keep the task's copy (the pass is a strict-command check, as for the Vec case).

title: `with_provider[R](p, ..)` moves `p` (core-semantics 14.4), but `karac check` accepts a later use of `p`, which `karac run` and `karac build` then refuse (`move check main: bb11[0]: use of _1.0, which may have been moved`)
detail: MEASURED on main at 31dae2d40 (karac release build with llvm, this container, 2026-11-01) by the core-semantics probe (cells in the probe thread's grid; the repro below is the whole program). Program: `effect resource Clk: ClkP;  trait ClkP { fn now(ref self) -> i64; }  struct F { t: Vec[i64] }  impl ClkP for F { fn now(ref self) -> i64 { self.t[0] } }  fn main() { let p = F { t: vec![1] }; let r = with_provider[Clk](p, || Clk.now()); println(r); println(p.t[0]); }`. `karac check`: All checks passed. `karac run` and `__mir-llvm-asan`: `error[mir]: move check main: bb11[0]: use of _1.0, which may have been moved or never initialized`. Want E0500 from check (14.4: p moves into the call, which owns it; 3.2). The run refuses correctly, so nothing unsound executes; this is the check missing the move of the provider argument.
fix: 2ebd405d13. The ownership pass's intrinsic modes for `with_provider` (src/ownership.rs collect_callee_param_modes) classified the provider slot as Ref, the legacy mutation-visible-after-pop rule; core semantics 14.4 moves `p` into the call, so the slot is Own and `karac check` reports the row's program as E0500 at `println(p.t[0])`, matching run and build. Impact counted first: of 115 provider programs under corpus/, kara-katas, runtime/ and tests/, only the legacy fixture test_with_provider_e2e_mut_ref_self_mutation_visible_after_pop changes; it and tests/ownership.rs b26_with_provider_value_slot_* (which held the old borrow) are flipped to the use-after-move error. Pins: corpus/core/err_with_provider_then_provider_used, tests/with_provider_moves_check.rs (fails on the base).

title: A closure that writes one field through a `mut ref` parameter (`let mut f = || { p.a += 1; };` with `p: mut ref P2`) holds the whole `*p`, so writing a DIFFERENT field (`p.b = 5`) while it is live is refused (E0516 on check and run), against the disjoint field capture of core-semantics 9.1; the same closure over an owned local is accepted
detail: MEASURED on main at 31dae2d40 (karac release build with llvm, this container, 2026-11-01) by the core-semantics probe (cells in the probe thread's grid; the repro below is the whole program). Program: `struct P2 { a: i64, b: i64 }  fn g(p: mut ref P2) { let mut f = || { p.a += 1; }; p.b = 5; f(); f(); }  fn main() { let mut p = P2 { a: 1, b: 2 }; g(mut p); println(f"{p.a} {p.b}"); }`. Check and run: `write of (*_1).1 while it is borrowed mutably (borrow at bb1[0] at 10:23) [E0516]`. Want `3 5`. Control: the same body over an owned local (`let mut p = P2 { a: 1, b: 2 }; let mut f = || { p.a += 1; }; p.b = 5; f();`) prints 7 as expected, and writing the SAME field (`p.a = 5`) is refused correctly in both. 9.1: closures capture places, not whole bindings; a place through a `mut ref` deref is still a place (2.1). So the capture of `(*p).a` is widened to `*p`.
fix: 2bc12f367e: a closure that uses a borrowed binding (`p: mut ref P2`, `p: ref P2`, or a method's `mut ref self`) only through its fields now captures those fields through the borrow, `&mut (*p).a`, as it already did for an owned local (src/mir/lower.rs closure lowering, `disjoint_fields`, `captured_field`; core semantics §9.1, §2.1). Writing `p.b` while the closure is live checks clean, and a field the closure holds stays held (writing it is still E0516). tests/closure_field_capture_through_ref.rs pins the row's program, read-only and `ref` variants, `mut ref self`, and the two refusals on check, interp and run.

title: A generic call with a `Copy` place argument followed by an argument that writes the place (`pr(c.n, bump(mut c))` with `fn pr[T: Display](a: T, b: T)`) is refused E0516 on check and run, where the non-generic `pair(c.n, bump(mut c))` is accepted since B-2026-11-01-7 and prints `1 11`
detail: MEASURED on main at 31dae2d40 (karac release build with llvm, this container, 2026-11-01) by the core-semantics probe (cells in the probe thread's grid; the repro below is the whole program). Program: `struct C { n: i64 }  fn bump(c: mut ref C) -> i64 { c.n += 10; c.n }  fn pr[T: Display](a: T, b: T) -> String { f"{a} {b}" }  fn main() { let mut c = C { n: 1 }; println(pr(c.n, bump(mut c))); }`. Check and run: `mutable borrow of _1 while it is borrowed (borrow at bb3[0] at 8:48) [E0516]`. Want `1 11` as with the non-generic `fn pair(a: i64, b: i64)`. A bare `T` parameter borrows, so before monomorphization the first argument looks like a live `ref` to `c.n` across the `mut c` loan; 4.1 says a bare parameter of a Copy type is a copy, and 5.8 says the 5.6 checks run on the monomorphised instance, where T = i64. Low: the fix-it (bind `let a = c.n;` first) is easy, but the program is legal under the spec and the refusal depends on whether the callee is generic.
fix: 6a51dbc47e: a `Copy` place argument that a later argument may write (B-2026-11-01-7's `read_now`) is lent as a fresh temp copied at its own position, then borrowed (src/mir/lower.rs `arg_operand_here`), so a generic `pr(c.n, bump(mut c))` reads `c.n` before `bump` runs (§8.1) and the instance check (§5.8) no longer sees a live borrow of `c`. tests/copy_args_read_in_order.rs pins the generic case on check, interp and run; a non-Copy `Vec` control still reports E0516.

title: Kata 139's word-break DP inner loop ran 1.18x legacy's instructions on the MIR backend (x86 callgrind; 1.75x on M5): LLVM's O2 unroll threshold left its window loop rolled; at O3's threshold it runs 0.91x
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-01 on the M5 Pro by the kara-katas re-bench, karac g6697158fa, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, exact counts via kara scripts/pmc.c (3-run minima). bench/word_break.kara: MIR 4.494G instructions vs legacy dd86e3955 2.563G (1.75x), 835M vs 542M cycles (1.54x). Seq lane 0.99 -> 1.50x rustc -O, 1.36 -> 2.08x clang -O3, 0.76 -> 1.15x Go (1.5x relative on all three). The hot loop is pure i64 arithmetic over four Vecs with an early break: `while j >= low { let ch = s[off + j]; code = ch * pw + code; pw = pw * alpha; ln = ln + 1; if dp[j] { let key = base[ln] + code; if table[key] { dp[ii] = true; break; } } j = j - 1 }` (s: Vec[i64], dp/table: Vec[bool], base: Vec[i64]); no allocation, no maps. Unattributed; same family as the per-iteration Vec-access gaps in B-2026-10-31-40/-42 and B-2026-11-01-18/-19. Platform-independent as far as known (instruction count).
fix: 9cde7995eb closes the gap: LLVM's full-unroll threshold is now O3's 300 with the rest of the pipeline at default<O2>, so the 24-trip window loop with its inner loop unrolls. bench/word_break.kara on x86 callgrind: 4.100G to 3.164G instructions, 0.908x legacy's 3.484G, output unchanged. Cost over the 707 frozen-set programs, measured with one release binary: build time +0.7% geomean, stripped size +0.15% (28 of 707 change, at most 6%), inside ADR-2's bars. A 51-bench run sample has geomean 0.987 (worst 1.008), outputs unchanged; kata 216 is unchanged. KARAC_MIR_UNROLL_THRESHOLD=150 restores O2's value. Earlier close, kept for its measurements: Wontfix, a deliberate trade. Measured 2026-11-02 at 80a4fd013b on x86 with callgrind (KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0) on bench/word_break.kara: MIR 4.100G against legacy dd86e3955 3.484G (1.177x). The gap is LLVM's loop-unroll threshold, not the checks. The 24-trip window loop with its inner loop is fully unrolled only at the O3 threshold (300), and karac's mid-end runs default<O2> (150). With `-unroll-threshold=300`, or KARAC_MIR_OPT=3, the kernel runs 0.91x legacy (measured on a reduced input: 144M against 159M, where the default build ran 186.7M). Other forms tried: (a) the sadd.with.overflow step with a monotone fact, as legacy emits it, made no change; (b) i1 branches in place of the flag switch went from 181M to 200M, which is worse. Raising the threshold is a pipeline-wide choice that runs against the ADR-2 build-time and binary-size bars, so it is not taken for one kernel. KARAC_MIR_OPT=3 is the lever if the frozen-set geomean ever shows it pays.

title: `par { 1, 2 }` inside a `TaskGroup` task is refused as a `writes(Stdout)` conflict between its two branches when the task holds a local whose `Drop` prints and the program calls `g.cancel()`: the cancellation teardown's drop of the task's OUTER local is charged to every branch (core-semantics 11.2, 11.9)
detail: MEASURED on main at 31dae2d40 (karac release build with llvm, 2026-11-01) by the core-semantics probe; the repro below is the whole program. Program: `struct R { id: i64 }  impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"d{self.id}"); } }  fn main() { let g = TaskGroup.new(); let h = g.spawn(|| { let r = R { id: 1 }; let (a, b) = par { 1, 2 }; a + b }); g.cancel(); println(h.join()); }`. `karac check` (and run): `error[effect]: 7:22: branches 1 and 2 of the par conflict: writes(Stdout) and writes(Stdout)`. Neither branch writes anything. Delete `g.cancel();` and the program checks and prints `d1 3`; delete `let r = ...` instead and it checks too. So once a cancel exists, each `par` branch is treated as a cancellation exit that runs the teardown of every enclosing frame, and the outer frame's `Drop` effect (`writes(Stdout)` through println) lands in both branches. 11.9 tears a cancelled task down at its suspension point and runs each frame's drops once, innermost first; the outer local `r` drops once, after the `par` is torn down, not once per branch, so it cannot make two branches conflict. Found while minimising a cancellation cell (a task holding `let r = mk(1)` around a `par` with a sleeping branch). Medium: in a program that cancels anything, a `par` inside a task that owns a printing or I/O-dropping local is refused. The branches don't need to suspend (`par { 1, 2 }` here).
fix: d0ee689070. A program that cancels anything gives each TaskGroup.spawn a cancellation point whose teardown (an `__unwinding()` test, then drops of every live local of the frame, then return) sits right after the spawn; inside a par those blocks belong to each branch's block set, so the drop of the task's outer local was one of every branch's effect sites. par_conflicts (src/mir/effects.rs) now leaves out of each branch's sites a Drop on the branch's way out of the function (leaving_blocks, factored out of branch_uses, which already left those drops out of the place uses, B-2026-10-24-34) of a local the branch does not own (own_locals): the enclosing frame's teardown runs once, after the par is torn down (core 11.7, 11.9). The row's program now checks; with the cancel after the join it prints `d1` then `3` on __mir-run, __mir-llvm-run, run and build alike, where the 8f3182f638 binary refused it. A branch that prints, and a branch that drops a printing local it declares, are still refused with writes(Stdout). Pinned by tests/par_cancel_teardown_effect.rs (2 tests). Gate: fmt, both clippy legs, cargo test --all 10090 passed 0 failed; the llvm leg 10193 passed, 1 failed: mir_reactor_pool_sleepers_wake_in_deadline_order, whose interpreter run woke the 140 ms sleeper before the 100 ms one under the full leg's load; the suite passed 5 of 5 runs alone, and this change only widens what check accepts.

title: A whole `Array[i64, 2]` passed to a bare (copying) parameter is held as a borrow across the later arguments: `sh(a, set(mut a))` and `sh(a, { a[0] = 9; 9 })` are refused E0516 (the second as `write of a temporary value[a temporary value]`), where a `#[derive(Copy)]` struct or a tuple in the same position is copied and prints `1 9`
detail: MEASURED on main at 31dae2d40 (karac release build with llvm, 2026-11-01) by the core-semantics probe; the repro below is the whole program. Program: `fn sh(a: Array[i64, 2], q: i64) -> String { f"{a[0]} {q}" }  fn set(a: mut ref Array[i64, 2]) -> i64 { a[0] = 9; 9 }  fn main() { let mut a: Array[i64, 2] = [1, 2]; println(sh(a, set(mut a))); }`. Check: `cannot mutably borrow a while it is still borrowed (the borrow is taken at 5:16) [E0516]`. With the block argument `sh(a, { a[0] = 9; 9 })` the error reads `write of a temporary value[a temporary value] while it is borrowed`, and the doubled bracket text is a diagnostics bug of its own. Want `1 9`: 4.1 says a bare parameter of a Copy type is a copy, 1.1 makes `Array[T, N]` Copy when T is, and 8.1 evaluates the first argument (a copy) before the second writes `a`. Controls in the same probe, both accepted with `1 9`: `#[derive(Copy)] struct Pt { x: i64 }` passed as `sh(p, { p.x = 9; 9 })`, and a tuple `(i64, i64)` the same way. Sibling of B-2026-11-01-35 (a generic `T` instantiated with a Copy type held as a borrow); both take a Copy argument as a live `ref` across later operands. Note an unannotated `let mut a = [1, 2];` infers `Vec[i64]` here (`expected 'ref Array[i64, 2]', found 'Vec[i64]'`), so the cell needs the annotation.
fix: 6a51dbc47e: the same change as B-2026-11-01-35: a `Copy` aggregate (`Array[i64, 2]`) argument a later argument writes is copied at its position and lent from the copy (src/mir/lower.rs `arg_operand_here`), so `sh(a, set(mut a))` and `sh(a, { a[0] = 9; ... })` pass the old array and check clean (§4.1, §8.1). `karac check`'s MIR message now names an indexed temporary as one place (src/cli.rs). tests/copy_args_read_in_order.rs pins the array case on check, interp and run.

title: The drop of a `dyn` value is charged no effects, against core-semantics 12 default 3 (a drop's effects are its type's drop glue's): `par { { let d = mkr(); 0 }, { println("x"); 2 } }` with `fn mkr() -> dyn T { mk(1) }` and a printing `Drop` on the concrete type passes check, and so do two branches that each drop such a value; calls THROUGH a `dyn` are charged correctly
detail: MEASURED on main at 31dae2d40 (karac release build with llvm, 2026-11-01) by the core-semantics probe (§10, §12, §13 pass); the repro below is the whole program. Prelude `struct R { id: i64 }  impl Drop for R { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"d{self.id}"); } }  fn mk(i: i64) -> R { R { id: i } }  trait T { fn go(self) -> i64; }  impl T for R { fn go(self) -> i64 { self.id } }  fn mkr() -> dyn T { mk(1) }`. Each passes `karac check` and runs: (a) `par { { let d = mkr(); 0 }, { println("x"); 2 } }` (a returned `dyn T` with no clause, whose concrete drop prints `d1`); (b) `par { { let d: dyn T = mk(1); 0 }, { println("x"); 2 } }` (coerced locally, concrete type visible); (c) `let v: Vec[dyn T] = vec![mk(1)]` dropped in a branch beside a printing branch; (d) `par { { let d = mkr(); 0 }, { let e = mkr(); 0 } }`, two branches that both print through drops. Want a §11.2 conflict naming `writes(Stdout)` (or `unknown`): default 3 charges a drop the effects of its type's drop glue, and a `dyn T` whose type has no clause has every effect (design.md § dyn Trait, Effects: 'A type with neither a clause nor a ceiling has every effect'), so its drop glue is unknown unless the concrete type is known. Controls, refused correctly: a CALL through a returned dyn (`d.go()` beside a println: `unknown (a call through a dyn value a call hands back)`) and through a dyn field. Every non-dyn drop shape probed is charged correctly: a local, a Vec, a struct field, an Option payload, a Map value, a moved-in value, an `own` parameter's callee drop, a temporary argument, a closure capture, a generic `own T`, a `par for` body, the last `shared` handle, `defer` blocks. Two branches printing through drops interleave lines on several workers; no memory fault.
fix: 58b9c2df3e. The effect pass's parts() (src/mir/effects.rs), which drop_glue and drop_bodies walk, saw nothing inside a `dyn`, so a `dyn` drop was charged no effects. A `dyn` of trait T now owns, for the pass, every type the program coerces to a `dyn` of T (the `concrete` type of each vtable whose dyn type names T), so its drop is charged the union of their drop glue. That is a closed-world over-approximation, finer than the every-effect a call through an untraced `dyn` gets: a `dyn T` built from a silent type is still charged R's printing drop when R is coerced to `dyn T` anywhere in the program. All four row cases are now refused with `writes(Stdout) and writes(Stdout)`: a returned dyn, a locally coerced one, a Vec[dyn T], and two such drops. A `dyn T` whose only types drop silently, alone or in a Vec, still checks and runs beside a printing branch. Pinned by tests/dyn_drop_effect.rs (2 tests). Control: the row's measurement at 31dae2d40 and this thread's pre-fix binary at 7894256e59, where all four cases passed check. The four corpus programs that use both dyn and par keep their verdicts. Gate on badc77361c: fmt, both clippy legs, cargo test --all 10092 passed, the llvm leg 10196 passed, 0 failed.

title: CORRECTED 11-02 (kata thread): no index-disjointness analysis exists on v2 for `par {}` OR `par for` (`par for i in 0..2 { v[i] = i + 1 }` is refused too, and so is an Array); the analysis core-semantics 11.2 calls "existing" is deferred.md "Auto-Parallel Loops over Provably-Disjoint Indexed Writes". Was: Two `par {}` branches that write CONSTANT, different indices of one `Vec` (`{ v[0] = 1; 0 }` and `{ v[1] = 2; 0 }`) are refused as conflicting mutable borrows of `v`, where core-semantics 11.2 says disjoint index ranges proven by the disjointness analysis do not conflict
detail: MEASURED on main at 31dae2d40 (karac release build with llvm, 2026-11-01) by the core-semantics probe (§10, §12, §13 pass); the repro below is the whole program. Program: `fn main() { let mut v = vec![0, 0]; let (a, b) = par { { v[0] = 1; 0 }, { v[1] = 2; 0 } }; println(f"{v[0]} {v[1]}"); }`. Check and run: `error[effect]: branches 1 and 2 of the par conflict: mutable borrow of v and mutable borrow of v`. Want `1 2`. Writing the SAME index from both branches is refused correctly. Low: the analysis may cover only `par for` ranges, in which case the spec sentence wants narrowing instead. That is a review-thread call. ADDENDUM 11-02 (kata thread, karac release at 7894256e59): the probe guessed that only par-for ranges are analysed; refuted. `par for i in 0..2 { v[i] = i + 1; }` on a Vec is refused with "two iterations of the par for conflict: mutable borrow of v and mutable borrow of v", and `par { { a[0] = 1; 0 }, { a[1] = 2; 0 } }` on an Array[i64, 2] is refused the same way. Mechanism: each branch runs as a task closure that captures the whole binding `&mut v` (lower.rs splits captures by field only, disjoint_fields), and the element write is `Vec.index_mut(&mut (*cap).0, const 0)` inside the closure body, so the par region sees two `&mut _1` and nothing about indices. Implementing 11.2 as written needs index-disjoint captures in lowering, borrowck acceptance of two live element borrows of one Vec, and effects/place_conflict reading the constant (or range) index: a feature across three owners, not a check-side fix.
fix: 3f0754fa0. Relocated on the review thread's call: v1 ships no index-disjointness analysis. Measured on 7894256e59 (addendum): `par for i in 0..2 { v[i] = i + 1 }` on a Vec and the row's `par {}` on a Vec or an Array are all refused, because each branch captures the whole binding. 3f0754fa0 narrows core-semantics 11.2: in v1 the elements of one collection are one place, so two `par` branches or two `par for` iterations that write one Vec or Array conflict even at different indices. The way through is `split_at_mut`; the review thread checked it on the 0.8.0 binary, where `let (a, b) = v.split_at_mut(2); par { { a[0] = 1; 0 }, { b[0] = 2; 0 } }` prints `1 2`. Index-disjoint captures, borrowck acceptance of disjoint element borrows and an index-aware place_conflict belong to the deferred item.
tracker: docs/deferred.md § Auto-Parallel Loops over Provably-Disjoint Indexed Writes

title: Two later-track features named in core-semantics 13 are accepted silently and run as ordinary code: `comptime fn sq(n: i64) -> i64 { n * n }` checks and prints 9 at run time, and a `#[gpu]` function checks and runs on the CPU; `Tensor`/`Column` are refused with a clear 'not in 0.8' diagnostic

title: Kata 170's Map[i64, i64]-heavy two-sum-III runs FEWER instructions on the MIR backend than legacy (0.75x) but 1.43x its cycles: the seq lane went from 2.56x to 3.01x rustc -O ON x86 IT REPRODUCES: 1.34x legacy's wall time (3962 vs 2956 ms), all of it the Map walk's per-step work
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-01 on the M5 Pro by the kara-katas re-bench, karac g6697158fa, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, exact counts via kara scripts/pmc.c (3-run minima). bench/two_sum_iii.kara (a `counts: Map[i64, i64]` probed per query): MIR 23.461G instructions vs legacy dd86e3955 31.269G (0.75x) but 10125M vs 7059M cycles (1.43x). Seq lane 2.56 -> 3.01x rustc -O, 6.28 -> 7.60x clang -O3, 1.64 -> 1.95x Go vs the 2026-09-14 feed (that feed is in the u64 map-key miscompile window but this kata keys by i64, so it stands). Less work at a much lower IPC on a hash-map kernel: memory or branch behaviour of the MIR map path (table layout, probe order, or a call boundary that defeats prefetch), not extra instructions. Unattributed; possibly M5-specific (an IPC change); check x86 wall time. | 2026-11-03 (drop schedule, x86 4-vCPU, karac 4d6ced41f3 vs legacy dd86e3955, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, min of 7): MIR 3962 ms, legacy 2956 ms (1.34x), outputs equal. ATTRIBUTED: a variant collecting the keys into a Vec once and walking that runs 2960 ms against legacy's 2963, so the excess is the walk, not the probes. callgrind (60k queries): a Map walk step is about 29 instructions more than a Vec step (1.480G vs 1.187G over 10.1M steps): each step re-reads the table header after the hash call (handle, len, holes, buf, entry size), re-checks that the walk words are current (an acquire load of perm_len), and took `(a * i + c) mod n` by a 32-bit `div`. 591fc8693a replaced the division with the header's reciprocal: 3923 -> 3767 ms in an A/B on one karac (about 4%). LEFT: the per-step header reloads and the perm_len check, about 27% of this kata. LLVM cannot hoist them because the hash glue's cold path (seed init, karac_hash_word) may write memory and the walk words are ordered atomic loads. A fix needs both: the walk words validated once per walk (at the view's creation) and read unordered per step, and a hash call LLVM knows writes no table memory.
fix: 591fc8693a + 02b775e0e7. 591fc8693a took the walk's remainder by the header's reciprocal of n (Barrett, one correction, karac_hash::walk_index_near) instead of a 32-bit div. 02b775e0e7 reads the walk words (a, c, reciprocal) through an internal `karac.walk.words` function kept noinline/argmem-read/speculatable through O2, so LICM hoists the header reload and the perm_len check out of the walk loop even when the loop writes (a push per key), then inlines it; and the index is a `karac.walk.index` marker that mir_aot::walk_carry rewrites after the pipeline, carrying j across trips (j += (a*s) mod n, one conditional subtract) when i is an induction variable plus a constant, else expanding the Barrett remainder in place. KARAC_MIR_WALK_CARRY=0 turns the carry off, =report names carried loops. MEASURED x86 4-vCPU, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, wall-time minima of interleaved runs: kata 170 4.03 s -> 3.35 s against legacy 3.22 s (1.34x -> about 1.04x, inside this box's noise); a walk that pushes each key 146 -> 120 ms. Order: tests/mir_map_walk_reciprocal.rs builds with the carry on and off and matches __mir-run for seeds 1, 42, 31337 over sizes 0..=300 and four large tables, incl. holes, growth between walks and a writing loop. The M5 IPC measurement in detail was not re-run here (no Mac); the M5 re-bench confirms, and a remaining M5-only gap gets its own row.

title: A map index assignment still reads a moved (non-`Copy`) place key after the value, against core-semantics 8.2: `m[key] = { key = "b".to_string(); 5 }` on a `Map[String, i64]` inserts "b", want "a" (the `Copy`-key remainder of B-2026-11-01-28 is fixed)
detail: MEASURED on the B-2026-11-01-28 fix (local, karac release build with llvm, 2026-11-01), mir-interp and mir-llvm alike: `let mut key = "a".to_string(); let mut m: Map[String, i64] = Map.new(); m[key] = { key = "b".to_string(); 5 }; println(f"{m.contains_key("a")} {m.contains_key("b")}");` prints `false true`, want `true false`. The -28 fix reads a place key into a temporary before the value only when the key type is `Copy`. Doing the same for a moved key makes `let key = "abc".to_string(); m[key] = key.len() as i64;` fail with an internal `error[mir]: move check main: bbN[1]: use of _25, which may have been moved` instead of compiling, because the front-end ownership check models the value before the key's move. By §8.2 that program is an error (as `put(mut m, key, key.len())` is today, with a proper ownership diagnostic), so the fix is two-part: the ownership check moves the key at the place's position (giving the call form's diagnostic for `m[key] = key.len()`), then the MIR builder reads the key first for every key type (drop the `is_copy` test in `index_set`, src/mir/lower.rs). Needs a decision on whether `m[key] = key.len()` should stop compiling.
fix: 0e9a42f043. Core semantics 8.2 (review thread ruling: follow it): the key of `m[key] = v` is a place operand, so it is evaluated and moved before `v`. The MIR builder's index_set now reads every place key first, not only Copy ones, so `m[key] = { key = "b".to_string(); 5 }` inserts "a" on mir-interp and mir-llvm. The ownership check's CFG (src/cfg.rs) lowers an index place's index before the value, so a value that reads the moved key (`m[key] = key.len()`) is E0500 at the read, 'moved at line L:C as the key of a map assignment, which moves before the value runs', like `put(mut m, key, key.len())`. Its machine fix (src/ownership.rs map_assign_key_error, both the legacy and the core reporting paths) rewrites the statement to `let value = key.len();` then `m[key] = value;`, which `karac fix` applies. Before implementing, a sweep of all 27,250 .kara files under corpus/ and kara-katas, using an instrumented karac whose control fires on the repro, found no program this refuses. Pins: corpus/core/ok_assign_map_key_first (String-key line), corpus/core/err_assign_map_key_moved_then_value_reads, tests/map_key_move_hoist_fix.rs; both corpus pins fail on the base. docs/core-semantics.md 8.2 drops its 'Today' sentence.

title: Kata 216's combination-sum-III recursion runs 1.28x legacy's instructions on the MIR backend (x86 callgrind; was 1.41x on M5): a deliberate trade, since legacy's IPSCCP fold needs a monotone fact MIR's step shape loses and the i1-branch form that recovers 1.23x costs kata 139 10%
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-01 on the M5 Pro by the kara-katas re-bench, karac g6697158fa, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, exact counts via kara scripts/pmc.c (3-run minima). bench/combination_sum_iii.kara: MIR 4.881G instructions vs legacy dd86e3955 3.457G (1.41x), 796M vs 659M cycles (1.21x). Seq lane 1.07 -> 1.26x rustc -O, 1.11 -> 1.30x clang -O3, 0.68 -> 0.80x Go (1.18x relative on all three). The kernel is a plain recursive counter, `fn count_combos(start: i64, k: i64, remaining: i64, d_pool: i64) -> i64`, with no Vec, Map or shared values, so the extra instructions are in call/recursion lowering or per-call checks, not in container access. Unattributed; platform-independent as far as known (instruction count).
fix: Wontfix, a deliberate trade. Measured 2026-11-02 at 80a4fd013b on x86 with callgrind (exact instruction counts, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0) on bench/combination_sum_iii.kara: MIR 5.362G against legacy dd86e3955 4.175G (1.284x). The gap is legacy's monotone fact on the `d` counter, which feeds IPSCCP; legacy without its assume runs 5.19G. Two forms were tried on MIR. (a) Legacy's own shape, as the review thread asked: the counter's checked step emitted as `llvm.sadd.with.overflow` plus the `d >= start` assume. It ran 5.36G, no change, because MIR's step is still recognised as a recurrence and the assume folds before IPSCCP. (b) i1 branches in place of the switch on a zext'd flag: 5.12G (1.23x), but kata 139 went from 181M to 200M (+10%) and kata 10 rose 0.7%, so it was not kept. The monotone facts that did land (80a4fd013b, B-2026-11-01-19) recover kata 88 and leave this kernel unchanged. Nothing tried closes the 1.15x bar without a cost elsewhere.

title: Cancelling a `TaskGroup` task while it waits inside a `par {}` (or `par for`) whose other branch has already finished leaks: `par { { sleep(2 s); 1 }, 2 }` in a task cancelled after 20 ms leaks 16 bytes on four workers and 104 bytes (the `par`'s internal group from `mir_task::group_new` plus 16 from the task body's resume) on one, every run under ASan; teardown of a `par` whose branches are all still suspended does not leak
detail: MEASURED on main at bd3154b02 (karac release build with llvm, 2026-11-02) by the core-semantics probe; found because B-2026-11-01-37's fix let the cell check. Program: `import std.time.{sleep, Duration};  fn main() { let g = TaskGroup.new(); let h = g.spawn(|| { let (a, b) = par { { sleep(Duration.ms(2000)); 1 }, 2 }; a + b }); sleep(Duration.ms(20)); g.cancel(); println(h.try_join().is_err()); }`. Output `true` on mir-interp, mir-llvm and ASan (correct). `karac __mir-llvm-asan`: KARAC_THREADS=4 gives `Direct leak of 16 byte(s) ... in kara.main.c0#resume <- kara.main.c0#task#resume <- poll.main.c0#task#resume <- karac_mir_task_run`. KARAC_THREADS=1 gives 104 bytes in 2 allocations: 88 from `karac_runtime::mir_task::group_new` (the `par` block's group) and the same 16 from `main.c0#resume`. Three runs each, identical. Same with the `par` in a named function the task calls (16 bytes), and a `par for x in vec![1, 2] { sleep(2 s); x }` leaks 64 bytes. Controls, no leak: a cancelled task with no `par` (a plain sleep, a String local); a `par` whose BOTH branches are suspended when the cancel lands; the same `par` not cancelled. So the leak needs the branch that FINISHED before the teardown, which suggests the finished branch's result slot and the `par`'s group are not released on the cancellation exit (11.9: teardown runs the drops an error exit runs, so it should free what a `?` exit frees). Drops of user values are right: a task holding `let r = mk(1)` around such a `par`, with `let q = mk(2)` in the sleeping branch, prints `d2 d1 cancelled` (innermost first). ASan leak lane verified live with a planted shared-cycle canary. A server that times out requests with a `par` inside its handler leaks per cancelled request.
fix: FIXED by 59908af3782752651ec380b11bcb90bc0103f540. The par's group and its handles were unscheduled temporaries that lowering dropped by hand after the joins, so the cancel exit (§11.9: the drops an error exit runs) never saw them. A cancelled task leaving at a join leaked the group (88 bytes, at one worker) and the result a finished branch left in its handle (16). They are now scheduled from creation until the joins are done, then taken back for the existing hand-placed drops (unschedule_drops). That is par_tasks for a `par` block, and loop_tasks / par_for_join for `par for` and auto-par loops. On the exit the handles drop first (an unjoined one detaches from a running task or frees a finished one's result), then the group, whose drop waits for its torn-down tasks; a joined handle is moved and does not drop. MEASURED under ASan at 1 and 4 workers, three runs each: the row's program, its `par for` variant and a `par` in a named function are clean. The controls (both branches suspended, no cancel) stay clean, and user drops still print d2 d1. Pinned by tests/mir_cancel_par_frees.rs, which reported the block case's leak before the fix.

title: Kata 225's queue-rotation loop (Vec push + index read + field update through a `mut ref` struct) runs 1.43x legacy's instructions on the MIR backend and 1.61x its cycles: the seq lane went from 0.80x to 1.24x rustc -O
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-02 on the M5 Pro by the kara-katas re-bench, karac g6697158fa, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, exact counts via kara scripts/pmc.c (3-run minima). bench/stack_using_queues.kara: MIR 4.778G instructions vs legacy dd86e3955 3.334G (1.43x), 651M vs 405M cycles (1.61x). Seq lane 0.80 -> 1.24x rustc -O, 1.09 -> 1.70x clang -O3, 0.12 -> 0.15x Go (~1.55x relative vs Rust and C). Hot loop: `stack_push`'s rotation, each iteration `q_dequeue` (`let v = q.data[q.head]; q.head = q.head + 1`) then `q_enqueue` (`q.data.push(front)`), with `q: mut ref Queue` and `struct Queue { data: Vec[i64], mut head: i64 }` (a plain struct, not shared). Suspects, not verified: the Vec push or the field reload/store through the `mut ref` struct on each call (the helper functions may not inline the same way). Platform-independent as far as known (instruction count).
fix: 7310a8f945. A push's growth (first block, doubling, a borrowed literal's copy-out) moved out of line into one noinline cold internal function per element size, grow1.<size>, which takes and returns the header's words, so the runtime still never sees the header. In line, those three paths cost each push site about 210 of LLVM's inline budget (legacy's push: 65), and kata 225's stack_push missed inlining into main (cost 550 vs threshold 525), so its mut ref queue's head and length were loaded and stored on every rotation. x86 valgrind instruction counts (callgrind) against legacy dd86e3955, outputs equal: bench/stack_using_queues.kara 4.263G -> 3.083G vs legacy 3.107G (1.372x -> 0.992x). Marking by-value functions' mut ref params noalias, as legacy did, was tried first and changed nothing here, so it is not in the fix. Pinned by tests/mir_vec_growth.rs (every growth path's output, and the push site calling a cold noinline grow1.8 / grow1.16).
