fix: 59ca8f5a88: core_escape now walks a tuple's elements at an escaping position (the tuple's own when it is one, else "stored in a tuple"), so a closure in a tuple element escapes as in a struct field (core-semantics §9.3, 102ed9f295) and captures by move, matching what MIR lowering already did. `let t = (1, || s.len()); println(s);` is now E0500 at the reuse in check instead of passing check and failing MIR's move check. A destructured tuple literal (`let (a, f) = (1, || s.len())`) is refused the same way, as MIR already refused it. Pinned by corpus/core/err_escaping_capture_in_tuple (E0500; passes mir-interp and mir-llvm). Gate: fmt, both clippy legs, cargo test --all 10157/0 (re-run after the rebase), cargo test --features llvm 10287 passed with 5 failures (mir_panic_free_messages), which came from a lean runtime archive built before ad984ef96b; after rebuilding the archives, 5/5 pass. After the merge with Thread A's -31 change to core_escape.rs: lib + core_strict_check + mir_escaping_view + effectchecker 2990/0, and the corpus core pins pass on mir-interp and mir-llvm.

title: The empty effect clause `with ()` on a function type (design.md § How a call through a function value gets its effects, Gowtham 2026-11-03) was a parse error ("Expected effect verb"), so a stored callback could not be declared pure and two `par` branches calling stored callbacks always conflicted
detail: Decided 2026-11-03 (design.md 8fbfc5ea2e, 280c279049): `Fn(A) -> R with ()` in a field, a collection element, a parameter or a return type declares the empty set. A stored value may have only default-permitted effects (allocates(Heap), panics), and a call through it has none. On a `fn` declaration `with ()` is a parse error with a fix-it that removes it. The probe saw `Expected effect verb` for every position. Found alongside: storing into a field of an UNANNOTATED struct local (`let mut bus = Bus { handlers: Vec.new() }; bus.handlers.push(printer)`) was not checked against the field's clause for any clause, named or empty, while the same push through a `mut ref Bus` parameter or an annotated local was.
fix: 1446dde436: the parser takes `with ()` after a function type in every type position (src/parser/types.rs), including a return tail, where it can only be the type's; on a `fn` declaration it is a parse error whose fix-it deletes it (src/parser/items_effects.rs). The formatter prints the empty list as `()`. MIR reads a collection element's declared clause through an index and a `for` binding over a local or a struct field (src/mir/lower.rs `declared_elem_effects`), so a call through a `with ()` element has no effects and two `par` branches calling stored pure callbacks run apart. The effect checker's slot walk now records an unannotated `let` bound to a plain struct literal, so `bus.handlers.push(printer)` is checked against the field's clause (src/effectchecker/subtyping.rs `literal_struct_type`). Pins: corpus/core/effect_empty_clause_par_apart, err_effect_empty_clause_exceeded, tests/empty_effect_clause.rs.

title: Kata 302's default build no longer auto-parallelizes on the MIR backend: the item 13 cost gate declines min_area's group as reached from a loop, a 1.9x loss on x86 at 4 workers that no static rule can take without flipping kata 165's 318x pin; relocated to a runtime work estimate
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-02 on the M5 Pro, karac 0.8.0-dev.14217+g7310a8f94, bench/blackpixels.kara: no call of karac_mir_task_spawn in the default build's IR, and the par and seq binaries are both 68,552 B. The 2026-08-28 feed (karac dev.7481) fired: par 146.5 ms at 332% CPU, seq 151.0 ms. So the par lane's move against rayon (0.74 -> 0.95x), pthreads C (1.29 -> 1.69x) and Go-par (1.44 -> 1.91x) is the lane going sequential; seq is flat (1.02 -> 0.98x rustc -O). Little wall time is lost, and declining may be the cost gate doing the right thing, but rayon and Go do gain here, so the parallelism is available in principle. ATTRIBUTED to the auto-par gate, not a recognizer miss: `karac query concurrency bench/blackpixels.kara` still reports parallel_groups [0,1,2,3] on min_area ("no data or effect dependencies"), and its auto_par entry for min_area is tasks:false, "min_area is recursive or reached from a loop" (main calls it from the 1200-query loop). Whether that rule should decline this shape is not judged here. Compare B-2026-10-31-43 (kata 23). | 2026-11-03 (kata thread, x86 4 cores, origin/main 4d6ced41f3 + a local probe that skips hot_reason's hot-body check, uncommitted): outputs md5-equal for seq / default / probe. seq (KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0) 0.690 / 0.646 s; default build at 4 workers 0.655 / 0.631 s (declined, binary identical in size to seq); probe at 1 / 2 / 4 workers 0.671 / 0.365 / 0.341 s (second round 0.639 / 0.357 / 0.340 s; user 0.70 s at 2, 0.90 s at 4). So declining costs about 1.8x on x86: each of min_area's four statements is a bisection loop over a 4096-element scan loop (weight 2, about 50k reads per task), so the per-task work pays, though main calls min_area from a 1200-trip loop. The hot rule ("recursive or reached from a loop") refuses regardless of the group's own weight. A narrower rule is the drop schedule's call (owner of the cost gate); the candidate sent to it is to keep the hot refusal unless every task of the group has weight 2.
fix: c0bc5a3e9b relocates this to docs/deferred.md § Runtime Work Estimate for Auto-Par Groups in Hot Bodies; the review thread kept the item 13 ruling (2026-11-03). The candidate carve-out (allow a group in a body hot only through a loop when every statement weighs 2) flips the ruling's own pin, kata 165. compare_version's `revisions(v1)` and `revisions(v2)` are each a nested loop (weight 2), and main reaches the body from a 10M-trip loop, where legacy lost 318x. It also flips `compare` in auto_par_statements_in_hot_code_stay_in_order. No static signal separates 302 from 165. Both have weight-2 statements over dynamic sizes (the image's width, a string's length), called from a literal-trip loop in a body that is not hot (1200 trips against 10M), so a trip cap would be tuned to benchmarks. The gain is real (1.9x on x86 at 4 workers), so the decision moves to run time: the builder keeps the group as tasks and spawns or runs them inline from a cheap work estimate. Running inline is a scheduling choice, so the parallelization graph stays deterministic. src/mir/effects/auto_par.rs is unchanged.
tracker: docs/deferred.md § Runtime Work Estimate for Auto-Par Groups in Hot Bodies

title: `[|x: i64| x + 1].to_vec()` into a `Vec[Fn(i64) -> i64]`, and `.clone()` of a `Vec[Fn(i64) -> i64]`, pass `karac check` and fail at run ('clone of Fn(i64) -> i64 needs its Clone body'): a value of function type is move-only (design.md § Escaping function values), but require_elements_clone reported nothing for an element that does not clone unless it was a derivable type or a `dyn`
detail: Found by Thread B, routed by the review thread 2026-11-03. `let fs: Vec[Fn(i64) -> i64] = [|x: i64| x + 1].to_vec();` checks clean; `karac __mir-run` stops with `run: in main at bb13[term]: clone of Fn(i64) -> i64 needs its Clone body`. Same for `fs.clone()` on a `Vec[Fn(i64) -> i64]`. type_supports_clone answers false for Type::Function, but require_elements_clone (src/typechecker/dyn_trait.rs) only reported when a `#[derive(Clone)]` fix or an uncloneable `dyn` was inside the type, so the false fell through silently. Which side is wrong: design.md § Escaping function values says a value of function type is move-only and only a closure literal that core-semantics §1.1 makes Copy is copied; the element of a `Vec[Fn(..)]` is an erased function value, not a literal, so check is the side to fix. The typechecker types an unannotated `[|x: i64| x + 3].to_vec()`'s element as the same `Fn(i64) -> i64` (its Copy rule has no closure-literal case either), and that also fails at run today, so it is refused the same way.
fix: f907cfec34. `require_elements_clone` (src/typechecker/dyn_trait.rs) refuses `.to_vec()` / `.clone()` on a collection whose element type holds a function value (`fn_within`), naming design.md § Escaping function values: a value of function type is move-only. The hint says to build the Vec with `vec![..]` or `push`, or wrap the function in a `shared struct`. The check side was the one fixed: core-semantics §1.1 makes only a closure literal Copy, and as a collection element it is an erased Fn (review thread, 11-03). The unannotated `[|x| x + 3].to_vec()` is refused too; it failed at run the same way. Pinned by tests/fn_value_clone_and_move_prefix.rs.

title: `move |..|` is refused with 'use `own |...|` for closure capture-by-value', naming a capture prefix core semantics §9.6 removed (and refuses as E0519)
detail: Found by Thread B, routed by the review thread 2026-11-03. src/parser/exprs.rs (the Token::Move closure arm) reported `the move keyword is not used in Kāra; use own |...| for closure capture-by-value` and parsed the rest as an `own` closure. §9.6 removed every capture prefix: captures are inferred from the body, and a copy is a `.clone()` taken before the closure. Following the advice gets E0519. Expected: say to delete `move`, with the edit, and recover as a bare closure.
fix: f907cfec34. The parser's `move |..|` error (src/parser/exprs.rs) now says to delete `move`, because captures are inferred (core-semantics §9.6), and to clone a value before the closure for a copy. It carries a machine-applicable deletion of `move`, so `karac fix` produces a bare closure that checks and runs, and the parser recovers as a bare closure. Pinned by tests/fn_value_clone_and_move_prefix.rs.

title: A method call on a function value (`f.clone()`, `f.foo()`) checks to an error with no diagnostic; MIR then reports "a type that failed to check is not lowered yet"
detail: `let f: Fn(i64) -> i64 = |x: i64| x + 1; let g = f.clone();` fails `karac check` with only `3:9: a type that failed to check is not lowered yet` (from src/mir/lower.rs, HK::Error), at the `let`, not the call. Any method name does the same (`f.foo()`). The receiver falls through every arm of `infer_method_call` to `Type::Error` without a type error. design.md § Escaping function values: a value of function type is move-only; only a closure literal core-semantics §1.1 makes Copy is copied. Wanted (review thread, 11-03): the move-only message family for `clone`, with the `shared struct` hint, and a named no-method error otherwise.
fix: ea349dd9ce. `infer_method_call` (src/typechecker/expr_method_call.rs) now stops a method call whose receiver, after peeling a ref, is a function value. `clone` gets "a value of function type '..' is move-only; it cannot be cloned" (design.md § Escaping function values), with hints for copying a Copy closure literal by assignment (`let g = f;`) and for a `shared struct` to give one function many holders. Any other method gets "no method '..' on function type '..': a function value has no methods". Both are reported at the call. Pinned by tests/fn_value_clone_and_move_prefix.rs (a_method_on_a_function_value_is_named).

title: Moving a place a live closure captures by `ref` (`let f = || s.len(); let t = s; f()`) is refused with the §3.3 LOOP message ('value s is moved inside a loop and not assigned again before the next iteration') in straight-line code with no loop
detail: §9 round-3 probe at head. `fn main() { let s = "abc".to_string(); let f = || s.len(); let t = s; println(f()); }` is correctly refused, but by error[ownership] at the closure's capture span (1:51) saying 's is moved inside a loop and not assigned again before the next iteration (moved at 1:68; core-semantics.md §3.3)', with a help about `own` callee parameters. There is no loop. Expected: the §5.6 / §9.1 conflict, as the explicit form gives: `let r = ref s; let t = s; println(r);` reports E0516 'cannot move s while r still holds a borrow of it'. When the closure is not used after the move (`println(t)` instead of `f()`) the program is accepted, as it should be. Cell k10 in probe-core/gen59c.py.
fix: faa987cba1. When the RC witness's earlier use is the body of a `let`-bound closure that is used again after the move (rc_predicate::live_closure_over_consume: a use of the closure binding that the consume precedes), core_move_errors now reports "cannot move 's' (moved at line L:C) while the closure `f` still borrows it: the closure reads it here and is used after the move (core-semantics.md §5.6, §9.1)", with help to clone at the move or finish using `f` first. A closure that is not used after the move, or a move carried around a real loop, keeps the §3.3 message. Pin: corpus/core/err_move_while_closure_borrows. The sweep for -03-8 also looked for this message: no other file gets it.

title: `Err(1)?;` as a statement (nothing fixes the Ok type) is refused by `karac check` with the MIR builder's internal message `an expression whose type does not lower (Type(UnknownParam("T"))) is not lowered yet` (E0516, class TYPE_MISMATCH) instead of design.md § Type inference's `cannot infer type ...; annotation needed`, which `let x = None;` already gets
detail: Repro (fcd788977, check, run, __mir-run all the same): `fn f() -> Result[i64, i64] { if true { Err(1)?; } Ok(0) }  fn main() { println(f().is_err()); }`. Same inside `for` and `par for` (found by the round-3 §11.7 cell b32: `par for i in 0..2 { if i == 1 { Err(1)?; } }`). Refusing is right (Rust refuses it too: the Ok parameter of `Err(1)` is unsolved at the end of the body), so this is only the wording: the message leaks a Debug value, says 'not lowered yet' (reads as a missing feature, inviting a workaround hunt), and names no fix. Control: `let x = None;` gets `cannot infer type parameter 'T'; add a type annotation to this binding`; `let e: Result[i64, i64] = Err(1); e?;` runs (prints true). design.md:2881 says an unsolved variable is an error at the end of the body, naming the unsolved parameters. Suggested wording points at `Err(1)` and offers `return Err(1)` (the usual intent) or an annotation; B-2026-10-29-36 (9d8dfb194d, check_unsolved_call_results) is the sibling for comparison operands, and a `?` operand is one more position that check misses.
fix: d168fd2a53. `check_unsolved_call_results` (src/typechecker/items.rs) now also walks the statements whose expression is a `?`: the statement discards the value, so nothing after it can fix the operand's `Ok` type, and an unbound parameter there is final. It reports design.md § Type inference's "cannot infer type parameter 'T' of `Result[T, i64]`, this `?` operand's type" at the operand. The hint is `return Err(..)` for an `Err` literal and a type annotation otherwise. Covers `Err(1)?;`, a generic `g()?;` and the `par for` shape. Not covered: `Ok(1)?;` with an unsolved error type, which already gets its own (different) check error. Pinned by tests/question_operand_unsolved.rs.

title: A `shared` handle enters a `par` branch or `par for` body through a local closure's environment: `let a = n(1); let f = || a.id; let (x, y) = par { f(), 2 };` and `par for i in 0..4 { f() + i }` pass `karac check` and run, while the direct capture (`par { a.id, 2 }`), a closure defined inside the branch, and the TaskGroup.spawn form (`g.spawn(|| f())`) all get E_NOT_CROSS_TASK
detail: Spec: §6.3 (a function value is CrossTask only when everything its environment reaches is; a local bound from a closure literal in the same body is checked as the literal's) and §11.3 (shared handles may not enter a task; par branches are tasks under the same rule, 'one worker as on many'). At 9e8c6100f: (1) `shared struct N { id: i64, mut items: Vec[i64] } ... fn main() { let a = n(1); let f = || a.id; let (x, y) = par { f(), 2 }; println(x + y); }` prints 3 on check/run. (2) The same with `let f = || get(a)` (fn get(h: N) -> i64). (3) `let r = par for i in 0..4 { f() + i };` prints 4. (4) `let f = || { let h = a; h.id }; par for i in 0..20000 { f() + i }` under KARAC_THREADS=4 runs on __mir-run and __mir-llvm-run (sum 200010000; no race observed in one run, but every iteration copies a non-atomic count from up to four workers, the B-2026-10-26-13 race). Controls, all refused correctly with E_NOT_CROSS_TASK: `par { a.id, 2 }`; `par { { let f = || a.id; f() }, 2 }` (closure literal inside the branch); `let f = || a.id; g.spawn(|| f())` (the fn_env_cross_task pass names `a` via the function value's environment). So the environment walk that B-2026-10-26-13 added for spawn closures is not applied to par-branch captures: a par branch that captures a function-valued local is not looked through. Expected: E_NOT_CROSS_TASK at the branch, naming `a` through `f`'s environment, as the spawn form says. A closure that mutates through the handle (`|| { a.items.push(1); 0 }`) is refused, but by E0517 (mutable borrow through a shared reference), not by the cross-task rule, so read-only and count-copying closures are the gap.
fix: 21c89bae17. The function-environment walk (typechecker/fn_env_cross_task.rs, the pass B-2026-10-26-13 added for TaskGroup.spawn) now treats a `par` block and a `par for` body as task boundaries: it collects what the function values a branch uses reach, as it does for a closure literal, and refuses a reached capture that cannot cross with E_NOT_CROSS_TASK ("a `par` branch / a `par for` body uses a function value whose environment captures `a` (type `N`), which cannot enter a task (core semantics §6.3, §11.3)"). This covers the row's four shapes, a closure calling another closure, and a function value through a helper call. A capture the branch names itself stays cross_task_check.rs's. A `frozen` handle (parameter or `let x = freeze y`) is exempt, as §11.3 allows; closures capturing one are refused separately by the ownership pass anyway. Outside the core rules a `shared` leaf keeps its sole-ownership carve-out. Pins: corpus/core/err_par_branch_uses_closure_over_shared, err_par_for_uses_closure_over_shared, and the control ok_par_branch_uses_closure_over_owned (interp, llvm and ASan). A check-only sweep of 27,386 corpus, example, test and kata files found no other program this refuses; the instrument was confirmed on the pins.

title: `karac __mir-run` runs an iterator adaptor chain with a closure (`v.iter().filter(|x| ..).count()`, `.map(|x| *x).max()`) about 11x slower than the same hand loop, about 2.9 us an element; kata 1040's iterator arm times out at 102 s against the corpus's 60 s cap
detail: Kata 1040 (kara-katas leetcode/1001-1100/1040-moving-stones-until-consecutive-ii, corpus/katas/.../moving_stones_iter) writes each window of n slots as `s.iter().filter(|x| *x >= start and *x <= start + n - 1).count()` and its last stone as `.filter(..).map(|x| *x).max().unwrap()`, O(n^2) over two 2000-stone sets. `karac __mir-run` takes 102 s on it (classify.py bucket timeout); the other four arms take 0.56 to 13.6 s and the compiled iter arm 50 ms (against 10 ms for the sliding window). Reduced, on a release build of kara 8876b6f720 (built before a rebase that slid parser and typechecker changes in beneath it; src/mir unchanged): 1000 passes of `s.iter().filter(|x| *x >= start and *x <= start + 999).count()` over a 2000-element `Vec[i64]` take 5.70 s, against 0.51 s for the same count as `for x in s.iter() { if .. { c += 1; } }` (2M elements each, one run each), and 1000 passes of `s.iter().map(|x| *x).max().unwrap()` take 6.83 s. Callgrind on 40 filter passes (80000 elements): 2.29 G instructions, about 28 k an element. The hot list is the general interpreter path, not the decoded fast path of src/mir/interp_fast.rs: run_body 12.2%, operand_slow 7.3%, statement 6.5%, local_fields_mut 5.1%, call_body 4.8%, resolve 4.6%, malloc/free about 10%, TyInterner::kind 2.2%, memcmp 2.1%, plus split_method, native, collection_method and a SipHash write. call_erased (the closure calls) is 24% inclusive, so most of the cost is the adaptor machinery around them (inferred from the profile; not traced to a line). Wanted: the adaptor chain near the hand loop's cost, at least enough to bring the kata arm under the 60 s cap without changing the kata.
fix: dff4157d25 (with the fixture in 27e2fffd45). The interpreter's decoded form (src/mir/interp_fast.rs) now covers the steps an iterator adaptor's bodies are made of, which all ran on the general path before. Decoded now: a scalar field read or stored through a reference (`(*l).f`, a closure's `*(*l).f`); `&(*l).f` and `&(*(*l).f)`; `discriminant`; an enum variant's field; an enum or struct built from scalars and references; a copy or move of a no-drop enum local; `StorageDead` of a no-drop local; reference arguments to a decoded call; a call through a reference to an erased closure (Term::CallErased, its body found through a cache keyed by the name's address); and `Vec[T].get` returning `Option[ref T]` (Term::VecGet). Each falls back to the general step off its happy path. Measured (callgrind, 40 passes over 2000 elements): `filter(..).count()` 22k -> 8.2k instructions an element (the hand loop is 2.2k); `map(..).max()` 2.57 G -> 1.22 G instructions. Kata 1040's iterator arm on __mir-run: 94.3 s -> 30.8 s on this machine, same output, under the 60 s cap. Full interp corpus: no new failure against a baseline build of e87b92a440 (10 entries that timed out under load pass on a re-run, at the baseline's time). Not closed: the chain is still about 4x the hand loop, mostly call and frame overhead per adaptor body.

title: `karac fix` left two edits its diagnostics name unapplied: `==` / `!=` on a type without `PartialEq` says "add #[derive(PartialEq)]" with no fix-it (the `Clone`, `Copy` and table-key derives carry one), and `lossless_cast` offered no fix on a dereference (`*v as i64`)
detail: Found porting the mini_roaring app through the Mend loop. After `karac fix` reached a fixed point, `karac check --output=json` still held E0208 "type 'Op' does not implement PartialEq; add #[derive(PartialEq)] to use == or !=" twice (an `op == Op.And` match guard on a unit enum) with no `fixes`, and three W0291 "unnecessary cast: 'u16' widens to 'i64' implicitly here" on `*v as i64` / `*x as i64` (a `Vec[u16]` iterated by reference, its element passed where an `i64` is wanted), also with no `fixes`. The derive is the edit the message prescribes, and the same derive fix already exists for `.clone()` / `.eq()` without the derive (B-2026-10-18-32, `missing_derive_fix_it`) and for a table key (`table_key_derive_fix`). `lint_unneeded_cast` offered its deletion only on an identifier, field, tuple index, call, method call or index operand; a dereference's span also ends where the `as` starts, so deleting from there to the end of the type keeps `*v`. Both are fix-rate gaps, not wrong answers: the hand edit compiles and the app's output matched its oracle on every backend.
fix: 67f5b2209d: `==` / `!=` on a struct or enum of the program that neither derives nor implements PartialEq now carries the `#[derive(PartialEq)]` edit its message names (`partial_eq_derive_fix` in src/typechecker/table_keys.rs, sharing the declaration lookup `derivable_decl` and the `derive_line` edit with `table_key_derive_fix`), when the type is not generic and every field or payload compares, so the derive compiles as written; a type with a field that does not compare keeps the message without an edit, and a type with a hand-written PartialEq keeps the "add impl Eq" message. `lint_unneeded_cast` now offers its deletion on a dereference operand (`*v as i64` -> `*v`). tests/fix_derive_partial_eq.rs pins all three (the derive on a unit enum and on a struct that already derives Clone, then the program runs; no edit when a field lacks PartialEq; the deref cast deleted and the program prints the same). Re-checking mini_roaring's pre-fix source, `karac fix` reaches a clean check with no hand edit for these two.

title: `s + t` with a `Str` on the left said only "type 'Str' does not implement trait Add", with no hint and no `karac fix` edit, where `String + Str` already names the `.to_string()` and fixes it
detail: Found porting the mini_lsm app through the Mend loop. `let k = prefix + fname(i).substring(1, 6);` with `prefix: Str` was refused with E0208 "type 'Str' does not implement trait Add" and no `fixes`, so `karac fix` stopped short of a clean check; the same program's `"data/" + name` (a `String` on the left, a `Str` on the right) got "'+' on 'String' requires a 'String' right operand, found 'Str' ... Take an owned copy with `.to_string()`" and an edit (B-2026-10-24-24). Minimal: `fn f(p: Str) -> String { p + "x" }` and `let t = s + "b";` with `s: Str` both get the bare message. `arithmetic_rejection_message` names the view only when it is the right operand; a `Str` on the left fell through to the missing-impl wording, which is true of `Str` but says nothing about what to write.
fix: 592000a587: `s + t` with `s` a `Str` (or a borrow of one) and `t` a `Str` or a `String` now says "'+' on 'Str' needs an owned 'String' on its left: a `Str` is a view and `+` appends to an owned `String` (design.md § Operator traits). Take an owned copy with `.to_string()`" and carries the edit that appends `.to_string()` to the left operand where its end is known (`str_concat_left_fix` in src/typechecker/expr_ops.rs; the end-of-operand logic is now `to_string_fix`, shared with the right-hand `str_concat_operand_fix`). With a `Str` on both sides, the next `karac fix` run owns the right one through the existing fix. tests/fix_str_concat_left.rs pins `prefix + f"{n}"` (one run) and `a + b` (two runs), then checks and runs both. mini_lsm's pre-fix source now reaches a clean check through `karac fix` alone, apart from two edits no fix could make (a typo and a const name).

title: Mixed-width arithmetic is refused where design.md § Mixed-width operands widens the narrower operand within its kind: `u + w` (u: u8, w: i64), `s * i` (s: i16, i: i64) and `f + d` (f: f32, d: f64) each get `cannot mix integer/float types ... cast the 'u8' operand up to 'i64' with as`, and the cast the message asks for is the one the spec says is implicit there
detail: design.md § Numeric semantics > Mixed-width operands: 'In a binary operator, the narrower operand widens within its kind. When the two operands have different numeric types of the same kind, and one converts losslessly to the other, that operand widens and the result has the other operand's type' (integer rows of the widening table; f32 to f64), covering + - * / %, & | ^ and the comparisons; and 'Each operation runs in its own operands' type', so `a_i32 * b_i32 + c_i64` computes the product in i32 (traps there) then widens. Repro at head: `fn main() { let u: u8 = 200; let w: i64 = 1000; println(u + w); let s: i16 = -5; let i: i64 = 3; println(s * i); let f: f32 = 1.5; let d: f64 = 2.25; println(f + d); }` expected 1200 / -15 / 3.75; check refuses all three (E: cannot mix integer types 'u8' and 'i64' in arithmetic ...; cannot mix float types 'f32' and 'f64'). `let a: i32 = 2147483647; let b: i32 = 2; let c: i64 = 0; println(a * b + c);` should panic with integer overflow (the product traps in i32) and is refused instead. Bindings and arguments do widen (`let b: i64 = u;` passes), and `u as i64 + w` passes with no `lossless_cast` warning, though design.md § as casts says that lint flags an `as` whose widening is implicit where it stands; so the spec, the lint and the operator check disagree three ways. Either the operator check implements the rule, or the spec section is rewritten to require `as` (and the lint's 'implicit where it stands' reads accordingly). Spec call for the review thread before code.
fix: 6f7041393d: the typechecker widens the narrower operand of a binary arithmetic or bitwise operator within its kind (an integer to a wider integer that holds every value it can take, f32 to f64); the result is the wider operand's type and the operation runs there, so an overflow in it still traps (pin panic_mixed_width_narrow_product_traps). Integer with float stays an error, and so does a pair where neither type holds the other (`i32 + u32`, pin err_mixed_signedness_operand), with a message that says so; explain.rs's rejection text follows. `lossless_cast` now fires on an operand cast the widening makes redundant and `karac fix` deletes it (tests/cast_lints_operands.rs); it skips a cast whose sibling is an unsuffixed literal or takes its type from context, since `old as i64 - 97` is not `old - 97`. Check-only sweep over 27,386 corpus and kata programs: only the two legacy fixtures that expected the refusal change verdict (flipped to the spec's output); 1,680 programs gain 3,566 lossless_cast warnings, none an error. Pin ok_mixed_width_operands_widen passes on interp, mir-llvm and ASan.

title: `String.from_utf8(v)` moves its argument, though strings.md declares `from_utf8(bytes: Slice[u8])`, a borrowed parameter: calling it twice on one local `Vec[u8]` or byte array is refused with `value 'v' moved here, used again here`
detail: strings.md § Building: `from_utf8 | fn from_utf8(bytes: Slice[u8]) -> Result[String, Utf8Error]`. Parameters borrow by default (core-semantics §4), so the argument should stay usable. Repro: `fn main() { let v: Vec[u8] = [1u8, 2u8].to_vec(); println(String.from_utf8(v).is_ok()); println(String.from_utf8(v).is_ok()); }` -> E (ownership) value 'v' moved. Same with `let a = [104u8, 195u8, 169u8];`. Control: a user `fn f(b: Slice[u8]) -> i64 { b.len() }` called twice on the same array passes. If the intent is Rust's `from_utf8(Vec<u8>)` (reuse the buffer, no copy), the doc signature should say `own Vec[u8]`; otherwise the native's parameter mode is wrong.
fix: d41d935108. String.from_utf8 lends its bytes, as strings.md's Slice[u8] parameter says: the builtin's signature lives only in the typechecker (env_build.rs), so the ownership pass had no modes for it and took the consume default; it is now Ref among the intrinsic modes (src/ownership.rs collect_callee_param_modes), and the MIR builder lends a non-Copy argument as a shared reference, as print does (src/mir/lower.rs builtin_call), so the Vec stays its holder's to use and drop. Pinned on check, interp, a built binary and ASan in tests/mir_from_utf8_lends.rs (a Vec twice, an invalid Vec, an array, a struct field, a temporary).

title: A generic parameter fixed only by an integer literal is reported unsolved instead of taking the literal's default: `c.or_else(|e| Err(0))` (c: Result[i64, i64]) and `g.or_else(|e| if e > 3 { Ok(e) } else { Err(0) })` get `cannot infer type parameter 'F'`, though design.md § Type inference says literals default last (`let x = identity(3.14)` is f64)
detail: design.md § Type inference: 'Literals default last. A numeric type variable takes its default (i64, f64) only at the end of the body, after every use has had its chance to fix it ... `let x = identity(3.14);` is f64.' So the error type F of `or_else`'s closure result `Err(0)` should be i64. Repro: `fn main() { let c: Result[i64, i64] = Err(4); let r = c.or_else(|e| Err(0)); println(r.is_err()); }` -> 'cannot infer type parameter F; add a type annotation to this binding'. Inside an expression (`po(c.or_else(...).ok())`) it reads 'nothing in the body fixes it'. Control: `d.or_else(|e| if e > 3 { Ok(e) } else { Err(e) })` passes (F fixed by e). The unsolved check appears to run before literal defaulting for a type parameter that only an integer literal reaches.
fix: 8e206842a3: the closure body is checked against `or_else`'s signature before the call's parameters are instantiated, and the Ok/Err/Some arm that lets an unsuffixed integer payload adopt its slot returned the expectation unchanged when the slot was the callee's `F`, so nothing solved it (a float or string payload went through synthesis and worked). When the slot is an unsolved metavar or the callee's own parameter the payload is now synthesised and unification solves the slot; a parameter of the enclosing item stays rigid. Both forms in the title are accepted; `Ok(0)` into `or_else` still leaves `F` unconstrained and is still refused. Pin core/ok_closure_literal_solves_callee_param (also a generic free function over `Some(5)`) passes on interp, mir-llvm and ASan.

title: A negative capacity: `String.with_capacity(-3)` gives an empty string on the interpreter and panics with a bare `explicit panic` on the compiled backend (and ASan lane); `Vec.with_capacity(-3)` panics `explicit panic` on both, while `Vec.filled(-3, v)` is empty and `reserve(n <= 0)` does nothing
detail: Repro: `fn main() { let s = String.with_capacity(-3); println(s.len()); }`: __mir-run prints 0; __mir-llvm-run and __mir-llvm-asan: 'runtime error: explicit panic at 1:31', exit 101. `let v: Vec[i64] = Vec.with_capacity(-3);` panics 'explicit panic' on both lanes. Docs: strings.md/collections.md give with_capacity no negative rule; `String.reserve` says 'additional <= 0 does nothing', and B-2026-10-22-38 made `Vec.filled(n < 0)` empty 'as from_fn and resize treat it'. Whichever rule is chosen (empty like filled/reserve, or a panic), the two backends must agree and a panic should name the method and the value, not 'explicit panic'. A one-line doc rule for negative capacities would settle it.
fix: 3331af4516 (with 3dda4504bc). A negative capacity counts as 0, as in Vec.filled (B-2026-10-22-38): String/Vec.with_capacity and try_with_capacity in the compiled backend (src/backend/mir/call.rs, a select via the new clamp_non_negative helper, also used by filled) and Vec's with_capacity on the interpreter (the over-max-allocation panic stays); try_with_capacity(n < 0) is Ok(empty). One-line rule in collections.md and strings.md. The corpus fixture interpreter/vecs/test_vec_with_capacity_negative_runtime_error flips from panic to stdout 0 (decision); the lib unit test display_keys_stderr_and_narrow_floats flips to exit 0 (3dda4504bc). Pinned on interp, a built binary and ASan in tests/mir_saturating_bounds.rs.

title: `substring` with a negative start gives "" instead of clamping the start to 0 as strings.md says ("Out-of-range, negative or inverted bounds saturate"): `"hello".substring(-5, 2)` is "" (want "he"), `"hello".substring(-1)` is "" (want "hello"), `"日本語".substring(-2, 3)` is "" (want "日"); several pins hold the "" and flip with the fix
detail: Review-thread ruling 2026-11-03: the doc stands; saturate means each bound clamps to [0, len]. B-2026-10-22-38 pinned only the end-inside-a-code-point panic. Repro at 1265979dc on __mir-run and __mir-llvm-run alike: `fn main() { let s = "hello"; println(s.substring(-5, 2)); println(s.substring(-1)); println(s.substring(-1, 100)); println(s.substring(0, 2)); }` prints '', '', '', 'he' (want he / hello / hello / he). Pins that hold the empty answer and must flip: tests/mir_library.rs:1223 (`[{s.substring(-2, 3)}]` expected `[]`, want `[日]`); corpus/fixtures/mir_library/substring_panics_on_an_end_inside_a_code_point (same line); corpus/fixtures/codegen/strings/e2e_string_substring_two_arg_codegen and corpus/fixtures/interpreter/strings/test_string_substring_two_arg_interpreter (`substring(-2, 4)` on "hello world", expected '' want 'hell'); corpus/fixtures/codegen/strings/test_e2e_string_substring_basic and corpus/fixtures/interpreter/strings/test_string_substring_interpreter (`substring(-1)`); re-read each expected.out before flipping.
fix: 3331af4516 (with 3dda4504bc). `substring` clamps each bound to [0, len] (strings.md: "Out-of-range, negative or inverted bounds saturate"; review-thread ruling 2026-11-03) on the interpreter (src/mir/interp.rs) and in the runtime's str_range / str_range_panic mode 0 (runtime/src/mir.rs); 3dda4504bc uses max/min rather than i64::clamp, whose assert linked std's panic hook (tests/mir_panic_free_messages.rs). An end inside a code point still panics, an empty range there included. "hello".substring(-5, 2) is he, substring(-1) is hello, "日本語".substring(-2, 3) is 日. Pins flipped: tests/mir_library.rs substring_panics_on_an_end_inside_a_code_point and its corpus fixture ([日]), the two substring_two_arg fixtures (hell), the two substring_basic fixtures (/todos/42). Pinned on interp, a built binary and ASan in tests/mir_saturating_bounds.rs.

title: A binding destructured from a `Map` / `SortedMap` `iter_mut()` item is typed `V`, not `mut ref V`, when `V` is Copy: `for (k, v) in m.iter_mut() { *v = 9; }` (m: SortedMap[i64, i64]) is refused ("unary '*' requires 'ref T' ... found 'i64'; a 'i64' is copied, so drop the `*`"), though collections.md gives the item as `(ref K, mut ref V)` and design.md says assigning through a `mut ref` needs an explicit `*`
detail: collections.md § Iteration: Map and SortedMap iter_mut() item `(ref K, mut ref V)`. design.md (§ assignment, line ~2034): 'Assigning through a mut ref needs an explicit *: *counter = 0;'. Repro: `fn main() { let mut m: SortedMap[i64, i64] = SortedMap.new(); m.insert(1, 1); for (k, v) in m.iter_mut() { *v = 9; } println(m[1]); }` -> refused at check; `*k` likewise ('found i64'). The fix-it offered (drop the `*`) gives `v = 9` / `v += k * 10`, which check accepts and which does write through on both backends (`for (k, v) in m.iter_mut() { v += k * 10; }` makes {1:11, 2:22}), so the program works but only in the spelling the doc says is wrong. Controls: `for x in w.iter_mut() { *x += 1; }` on a Vec passes; with V = String, `*v = "z".to_string()` in the same pattern passes. So the tuple pattern over a Copy V drops the reference from the binding's type. __mir-run/__mir-llvm-run run the `*v` form correctly (they skip this check), so only check is wrong.
fix: 597c6ce7e2: `iter_mut()` over a `Map` or `SortedMap` now yields `(K, mut ref V)` in the checker, the key part read as a `for` over the map reads it, so a `Copy` V binds as `mut ref V`: `*v = 9` is accepted and writes the entry, and `v = 9` gets the "write `*v`" diagnostic instead of writing through. The MIR builder already bound both parts in place, so no backend change. The writable key this exposed is its own soundness row, B-2026-11-03-26, fixed by the same commit. Pins core/ok_map_iter_mut_lends_values and err_map_iter_mut_value_plain_assign pass on interp, mir-llvm and ASan; the 112 corpus and kata programs that call iter_mut check the same before and after.

title: `Client.get` / `Client.post` under a `Network` fake crash on every lane: the interpreter stops with `in Fh.__get at bb13[term]: a String place holds no box`, the compiled build segfaults (`karac run` exit 139) or fails `memory allocation of 94402663242032 bytes`, and ASan reports a stack-buffer-overflow in `kara.Fh.__get`; `c.request(..).send()` under the same fake works
fix: 17c180c647 (CI list in f0d327e1d6). src/mir/providers.rs `owned_texts` formatted only a literal url or body into the owned `String` that the library's `__get(.., url: own String)` / `__post` take. A `String` argument went through as the `&url` the native `str` parameter takes, so `__get` read a reference as the `String` it owns. It now formats any borrowed text (a `ref String` or a view) into an owned temporary; the caller's `String` stays borrowed and is dropped as before. Pinned by tests/mir_network_owned_text.rs on the interpreter, a built binary and the ASan lane: get and post with a `String`, an f-string and a literal, under a fake that counts its calls.

title: `Some(ref place)`, the spec's own way to build an `Option[ref T]` (design.md § `ref place` borrows a place: `let first = Some(ref self.items[0]);`), is refused as "`ref` is not written at call sites", and `karac fix` deletes the `ref`, turning the borrow into a move that a later fix then clones
detail: mini_raft passes `Some(ref g)` to `fn leader_node(self, among: Option[ref Vec[i64]]) -> i64` so a group of node ids is viewed, not moved. The parser's argument list (src/parser/exprs.rs parse_arg_list_inner) rejects any `ref` or `mut ref` before an argument as the call-site mode marker of design.md Rule 4, whatever the callee is, and attaches a machine-applicable deletion. Reduced: the spec's line `let first = Some(ref self.items[0]);` in a method gives the same error, as do `longest(Some(ref g))` and `Pick.One(ref g[1])`. After `karac fix`, `Some(g)` moves `g`; the next check reports a use after move and the fix inserts `g.clone()`, so the program copies the vector on every call it meant to borrow. A constructor has no parameter modes, so the marker rule has nothing to say there; `ref place` in it is the borrow expression.
fix: 53e7f5f11a: src/parser/exprs.rs parses a call whose callee is named in Type case (an enum variant or tuple-struct constructor: `Some`, `Ok`, `Pick.One`) with parse_ctor_arg_list, which leaves `ref place` and `mut ref place` to parse_expression as the borrow expression instead of rejecting them as call-site mode markers; `MAX`-style constant names do not count. The spec's `let first = Some(ref self.items[0]);`, `longest(Some(ref g))` and `Pick.One(ref g[1])` now check and run; `show(ref s)` and `grow(mut ref s)` are still refused. Pinned by tests/parse_ctor_ref_arg.rs (check and MIR output).

title: `karac check` refuses moving a binding after an adaptor chain rooted at a range reads it (`let rest: Vec[i64] = (1..n + 1).filter(|i| not side.contains(i)).collect(); self.groups = Some((side, rest));`) as "moved inside a loop" with no loop in the program; B-2026-10-29-43's fix covers only a chain rooted at a collection
detail: mini_raft's partition action collects the nodes outside one side with a range filter and then stores both sides. check: "value 'side' is moved inside a loop and not assigned again before the next iteration (moved at line 616:37; core-semantics.md §3.3)" on the closure's read, and `karac fix` clones `side`. Reduced to `let side: Vec[i64] = [1].to_vec(); let k = (0..n).filter(|i| side.len() > i).count(); Some(side)`: refused; the same chain over `all.iter()` is accepted. src/use_classifier.rs record_statement_closures counts a chain's closures as statement-local only when the chain's root receiver's type holds no closure, and holds_no_closure did not list the range types, so a `(a..b)` root fell to `false`.
fix: 53e7f5f11a: src/use_classifier.rs holds_no_closure lists Range, RangeInclusive, RangeFrom, RangeTo, RangeToInclusive and RangeFull, so record_statement_closures (B-2026-10-29-43) treats a chain rooted at a range like one rooted at `v.iter()`: its closures run within the statement, and a later move of a binding they read is an ordinary move. The row's collect, a count over `0..n` and a sum over `1..=n` are accepted with the right MIR output; the chain and the move inside one loop are still refused. Pinned by tests/core_range_closure_read_before_move.rs.

title: A type mismatch whose found type is an `Option`/`Result` wrapping the expected one (`s.push(t.char_at(i))`, `let c: char = t.char_at(0)`, `take(t.char_at(1))`, an if/else or match with a `char` branch and an `Option[char]` one) gets no hint to unwrap; only the arithmetic mismatch carried it (B-2026-07-30-13)
detail: Kata 1041 (Robot Bounded In Circle), written through the Mend loop: `out.push(letters.char_at(c % 3))` drew `'push' expects a Char argument, found 'Option[char]'` and `if k % 2 == 0 { "GLR".char_at(r % 3) } else if .. { 'G' }` drew `if/else branches have incompatible types: 'Option[char]' and 'char'`, each with no hint and no fix, and `karac fix` reported nothing fixable. The canonical assignment / argument mismatch (`expected 'char', found 'Option[char]'`) and the match-arm join said the same bare thing. `arith_wrapper_unwrap_hint` (src/typechecker/expr_ops.rs) already gave the hint for `s = s + q.pop_front()`. `v.first()` into `let x: i64` (an `Option[ref i64]`) got none either, though `.unwrap()` of it checks there.
fix: 1a547cb615. The canonical assignment / argument mismatch (src/typechecker.rs), `String.push`'s argument (src/typechecker/stdlib_seq.rs), the if/else join (src/typechecker/exprs.rs) and the match-arm join (src/typechecker/patterns.rs) now append the hint the arithmetic mismatch carried, renamed `wrapper_unwrap_hint` (src/typechecker/expr_ops.rs), with `branch_unwrap_hint` trying either branch as the wrapped one: `expected 'char', found 'Option[char]' — `Option` wraps the 'char'; unwrap it first (`.unwrap()`, `.unwrap_or(<default>)`, or a `match`)`. An `Option[ref T]` counts as wrapping `T` (`let x: i64 = v.first()`), since `.unwrap()` of it checks there. The hint is text, not a machine-applicable fix: which unwrap is right is the author's call. Fixture: tests/option_unwrap_hint.rs (8 tests: let, argument, push, if/else, match, Result, Option of a ref, and two mismatches that wrap nothing and get no hint). Control: a release build from before the change (8876b6f720) printed the bare messages for the let, argument and push programs.

title: `karac fix` on `'L' => (dx, dy) = (-dy, dx),` (a braceless match arm) writes `'L' => dx, dy = -dy, dx,`, which does not parse, so it refuses to write the file; a Mend-loop dead end
detail: Kata 1041's rotate arm: `match c { 'G' => { .. } 'L' => (dx, dy) = (-dy, dx), _ => (dx, dy) = (dy, -dx), }`. `karac check` gives E_ASSIGN_TARGET_NOT_PLACE (a parenthesized tuple is a value; drop the parentheses, `a, b = b, a`) with a machine-applicable fix from `unparenthesized_multi_assign_fix` (src/typechecker/items.rs). In statement position the fix is right. As a braceless arm body the multi-assign does not parse, since the arm ends at the first `,` (`Expected =>, found =`), so `karac fix` prints `applying 2 fix(es) would leave robot_bounded_rotate.kara with MORE parse errors than it started with -- refusing to write`. `{ a, b = b, a }` without the `;` does not parse either (`Expected ;, found }`); `{ a, b = b, a; }` does and runs.
fix: 1a547cb615. The typechecker marks the block the parser builds for a braceless arm body (`recover_assignment_arm_body`, src/parser/exprs.rs): one `Assign` statement whose span is the block's own, where a written block's span takes in its braces (`braceless_arm_block`, src/typechecker/items.rs). `infer_block` and `check_block_against` set `braceless_arm_assign` to that statement's offset while they check it, saving and restoring the outer value. When the refused tuple target starts there, `unparenthesized_multi_assign_fix` writes `{ dx, dy = -dy, dx; }` instead of the bare multi-assign, and the message says to brace it as an arm's body. Fixture: tests/multi_assign_arm_fix.rs: the braceless arms fix to `'L' => { dx, dy = -dy, dx; },` and run (`-1 0`); a statement and a braced arm still drop only the parentheses; a braceless single assignment still checks. Control: a release build from before the change (8876b6f720) refused to write the first program (more parse errors after the fix).

title: `let undo = vec!["LR", "RL"][k];` (an element of a TEMPORARY, binding only read) gets E_INDEX_MOVE_NON_COPY's borrow fix `ref vec![..][k]`, and `karac fix` then leaves an E0516 (the temporary drops while `undo` borrows it) with no fix
detail: Kata 1041's differential: `let undo = vec!["LR", "RL", "LLLL", "RRRR"][next_random(mut seed) % 4];`. B-2026-10-24-18 replaced the `.clone()` fix with `ref` when the binding is only read (`core_read_only_index_lets`, src/ownership/index_let.rs), and the rule did not ask whether the indexed object is a place. For a temporary (`vec![..]`, a call result) the borrow outlives it: the second `karac check` gives `cannot drop the temporary value of the expression at 274:20 while undo still borrows it [E0516]`, and `karac fix` finds nothing fixable. `.clone()` checks and runs.
fix: 1a547cb615. `read_only_index_lets` (src/ownership/index_let.rs) now skips a `let` whose indexed object has no place root (`place_root` is None: a `vec![..]` literal, a call result, any temporary), so the typechecker's `.clone()` fix stands there and the `ref` borrow is offered only for an element of a binding, a field or `self`. Fixture: tests/index_let_temporary_fix.rs: `let undo = vec!["LR", "RL", "LLLL"][k];` and `let w = words()[1];` fix to `.clone()`, then check clean and run; `let undo = names[k];` still fixes to `ref names[k]`. Control: a release build from before the change (8876b6f720) wrote `ref vec![..][k]` and then reported the E0516.

title: `karac fix` appends `.to_string()` / `.clone()` after an expression that binds looser than a postfix `.`, so `names.contains(*r)` (r: ref Str, names: Vec[String]) becomes `names.contains(*r.to_string())`, which binds the call to `r` and no longer checks
detail: mini_crdt's loader checks each word of a line against the replica names with `self.names.contains(*r)` in a `for r in w[1..w.len()].iter()` over a `Vec[Str]`. check: "expected 'ref String', found 'Str': `.to_string()` copies the text into a `String`", with a machine fix inserting `.to_string()` at the end of the span. `karac fix` writes `*r.to_string()`, which parses as `*(r.to_string())`; the next check says "unary '*' requires 'ref T' ... found 'String'" with no fix, a Mend-loop dead end. The mismatch fixes in check_assignable (`.clone()`, `.to_string()`, `.to_vec()`, `.ok()`) all insert a suffix at the span's end without looking at the expression there, so a prefix unary, a binary or a cast operand gets the call on its last operand.
fix: c42cbe441c: src/typechecker.rs `parenthesize_suffix_fixes` rewrites a TypeMismatch whose machine fix is a zero-length insert at the span's end beginning with `.`, when the span is an expression that binds looser than a postfix `.` (a Unary, Binary, Cast, Range or Closure, recorded by `note_loose_expr` in src/typechecker/exprs.rs at the top of check_expr/infer_expr): the fix becomes two edits, `(` before and `)` plus the suffix after, so `names.contains(*r)` is fixed to `names.contains((*r).to_string())`. Pinned by tests/fix_suffix_on_loose_expr.rs (the fixed source is re-checked and run); mini_crdt's Mend loop now reaches a clean check on `karac fix` alone.

title: `*a` on a non-reference, non-`Copy` value compared with `==` (`seqs.iter().position(|el| el.id == *a)` with `a: (i64, String)` bound by value) gets "unary '*' requires 'ref T' ..." and no fix, though a comparison borrows both operands, so dropping the `*` is always right there
detail: mini_crdt matches `Edit.Insert { after, text }` on an owned op, so `Some(a)` binds an `Id` (a `(i64, String)`) by value, and the RGA anchor search writes `el.id == *a`. The deref check (src/typechecker/expr_ops.rs, UnaryOp::Deref) offers to drop the `*` only for a `Copy` value; for anything else it reports with no edit. design.md § References: operators that borrow their operands, such as `==` and `<`, borrow `*r` and need no copy, so in a comparison `a` reads the same value and moves nothing.
fix: c42cbe441c: src/typechecker/expr_ops.rs, UnaryOp::Deref error arm: the drop-the-`*` fix now applies when the operand is a comparison operand (`borrowed_deref_operands`) as well as when the value is Copy, with the message naming the reason ("a comparison borrows its operands, so drop the `*`"). Pinned by tests/fix_suffix_on_loose_expr.rs (`*id == a` with an `own Option` parameter, fixed and run).

title: A `Map` / `SortedMap` key is writable through `iter_mut()`: `for (k, v) in m.iter_mut() { k.push_str("x"); }` (m: Map[String, i64]) is accepted and changes the key in place on every backend, which breaks the map's hash or order; collections.md gives the item as `(ref K, mut ref V)`
detail: Found while fixing B-2026-11-03-17. The checker typed the item `mut ref (K, V)`, so a non-Copy key destructured as a writable view; `core_ref_write` treats a `for` over `.iter_mut()` as writable and did not tell the key from the value. Measured: the program above printed `ax` under `karac run` after a later `for (k, v) in m.iter()`. A lookup of the old key after such a write misses.
fix: 597c6ce7e2: `core_ref_write` binds the key part of `for (k, v) in m.iter_mut()` over a `Map` / `SortedMap` read-only (Origin::MapKey), with an error that says `iter_mut()` lends only the values and points at `remove` + `insert`; the checker types the key as a `for` over the map does. Pin core/err_map_iter_mut_key_write. CHANGELOG 0.8.1 lists it under "Programs 0.8.0 accepted that are now refused".

title: Rust's `&` sigil gets no fix in a pattern (`for &(x, y) in v.iter()`, `|&x| ..`, `&3 =>`, `&mut z`), on an argument (`f(&x)`, `f(&mut x)`) or as a borrow (`let r = &v;`, `match &v[0]`): only `Expected pattern / parameter pattern / expression, found `&``, and in a `for` the failure cascades into a top-level-statements error
detail: Kata 1042 (Flower Planting With No Adjacent), probing the Rust-shaped phrasings through the Mend loop: `for &(x, y) in paths.iter()` drew `Expected pattern, found `&`` with no fix, followed by `Expected expression, found `}`` and `file contains both top-level statements and an explicit `fn main()``, both cascades; `.filter(|&x| x > 1)` drew `Expected parameter pattern, found `&``; `total(&v)` and `let r = &v;` drew `Expected expression, found `&``. `karac fix` applied nothing. The type position already had a fix (`&T` -> `ref T`, B-2026-11-01-5) and so did `&self` receivers; the pattern, argument and expression positions did not, though `&` is the most common Rust borrow spelling.
fix: 25a40f3d26. A pattern (src/parser/patterns.rs, `skip_rust_amp_pattern`, called from `parse_single_pattern` and from `parse_param_pattern` in src/parser/items.rs for closure parameters) now says "`&` before a pattern is Rust syntax -- a Kāra pattern already matches through a reference, so drop the `&`" (and the same for `&mut` and `&&`), with an edit deleting the sigil, and parses on, so the `for` no longer cascades. An argument (src/parser/exprs.rs, the call-argument loop) drops the `&`: `f(&x)` becomes `f(x)` and `f(&mut x)` becomes `f(mut x)`, the call-site marker. A borrow in any other expression (`parse_prefix`) becomes `ref x` or `mut ref x` and parses as that borrow. Fixture: tests/rust_amp_sigil_fix.rs (4 tests: a `for` pattern is one diagnostic with an empty replacement; closure, `&(a, _)` closure, `&mut` loop patterns; `&` and `&mut` arguments; `&` and `&mut` borrows and `match &v[0]`; each fixed file checks clean and runs). Control: the release build at 27f59a0e9c printed the bare `Expected pattern, found `&`` with no replacement, then the two cascades, for kata 1042's probe.

title: `x.as_str()` passed where a `ref String` is wanted (`["rc", "si", "ser"].contains(w[2].as_str())`, `w: Vec[String]`) gets the fix that appends `.to_string()`, so `karac fix` writes `w[2].as_str().to_string()`, a copy of text the place already holds, where dropping the `.as_str()` borrows the `String` itself
detail: mini_mvcc's loader checks a transaction's level with `["rc", "si", "ser"].contains(w[2].as_str())`. The array's elements are `String` (a string literal is `String` by default), so `contains` wants a `ref String` and the `Str` from `.as_str()` mismatches. check: "expected 'ref String', found 'Str': `.to_string()` copies the text into a `String`", whose machine fix appends `.to_string()` at the end of the span; `karac fix` writes `contains(w[2].as_str().to_string())`, which checks and runs but allocates a copy to compare against, and reads as a round trip. The same happens for a user function whose bare `String` parameter is borrowed (`named(names, name.as_str())`). The `.to_string()` arm in check_assignable (src/typechecker.rs) does not look at the expression it fixes; for a `.as_str()` call on a `String` receiver where a reference is wanted, deleting the call is the whole fix. Where an owned `String` is wanted (`s: own String`, `let x: String = ..`), dropping it would move the receiver, so `.to_string()` is right there.
fix: 3bd1b54849: src/typechecker.rs `drop_as_str_fix`, called from the `.to_string()` arm of check_assignable: when the mismatched value is an `x.as_str()` call with no arguments (recorded by `note_loose_expr` in src/typechecker/exprs.rs as `as_str_calls`, call span to receiver span), a reference is wanted, and the receiver's recorded type is `String` (or a reference to one), the fix deletes `.as_str()` instead of appending `.to_string()`, with the message "drop the `.as_str()`, and the `String` itself is borrowed". An owned `String` wanted keeps the `.to_string()` fix. Pinned by tests/fix_as_str_borrow.rs (both shapes fixed, re-checked and run); mini_mvcc's loader now reads `["rc", "si", "ser"].contains(w[2])`.

title: `mir_serve_ws_upgrades_while_serving` is schedule-sensitive: under the full `cargo test --features llvm` load the built server's output lacks `closed 1001`, because the session that says `bye` calls `exit(0)` while the other session's handler has not yet printed the close it received
detail:
Seen once in a full `cargo test --features llvm` gate at 3bd1b54849's parent (the apps thread's typechecker change, which touches no runtime or net code): 'serve-ws: the build and the interpreter differ', the build's stdout missing the line `closed 1001` (`request /chat
request /chat
request /health
text two
text one
request /chat
request /elsewhere
text bye
close true`), while the client transcript matched, so the close frame was echoed. Run alone it passed 6 of 6. SERVE_WS_SRC's `chat` handler prints `closed {n}` after `ws.recv()` returns the client's Close, and the other session's handler calls `exit(0)` on `bye`. The client in `upgrades` sends Close on session two, reads the echo, then makes two plain requests and sends `bye` on session one without waiting for anything the server prints, so when session two's task is descheduled between the echo and its `println`, the process exits first. Whether the remedy is in the test (wait for the server to report before `bye`, or exit only after every session ended) or in the runtime (a pending task's output before `exit`) is for the owner; the measurement is the one failure under load and the six clean solo runs.
fix: 8c67849f18. A test race, not a runtime one: SERVE_WS_SRC's chat handler printed `closed 1001` after recv returned the client's Close, and the client went on to session one's `bye` (whose handler calls exit(0)) without waiting for that line, so a session-two task descheduled between the Close echo and its println lost the line. The handler now writes SESSION_CLOSED on stderr after the line and the client waits for it (Ports::wait_for in tests/mir_tls_ws.rs) before its next request; exit(0) ending other tasks mid-handler is the specified behaviour, so the runtime is unchanged. Measured: unfixed, 60 of 60 under 4-way load (window narrow); with a 400 ms sleep before the println the old client failed 2 of 2 with the row's exact output (missing `closed 1001`) and the fixed client passed 120 of 120 (plain + TLS, 60 rounds under load), and 120 of 120 without the sleep; full gate green.

title: `let s = mut place;` (a call argument's marker where a borrow for writing is wanted) is refused as "'mut' is a reserved keyword and cannot be used as an identifier" with no fix; `karac fix` should write `mut ref place` (core-semantics §5.1)
detail: Found porting mini_tsdb (kara-katas apps/cli/mini_tsdb): `let samples = mut self.series[key].samples;` written the way a `mut` call argument is. The parser's prefix-expression path had no arm for a bare `mut` followed by a place, so it fell to the identifier path and reported the reserved-keyword error, with no fix-it. Repro: `fn main() { let mut v = [1, 2].to_vec(); let first = mut v[0]; first += 10; println(f"{v[0]}"); }` under `karac check`.
fix: 4230ad12ec. The parser's prefix-expression path has an arm for a bare `mut` before anything other than `ref` or a closure's `|`: it reports "`mut place` is the marker a call argument takes; a borrow for writing is `mut ref place` (core-semantics §5.1)", attaches a fix-it that inserts ` ref` after the `mut`, and parses the operand as `mut ref`, so the rest of the file still checks. Pinned by `a_let_of_mut_place_gets_mut_ref` (tests/fix_mut_place_and_borrowed_moves.rs), which also asserts the reserved-keyword text is gone and that the fixed program prints `11 2` on the MIR interpreter. mini_tsdb Mends with it.

title: `items.into_iter()` on a bare `Vec[Item]` parameter whose `Item` is not clonable gets the fix `items.clone().into_iter()`, which does not check either and then asks for `#[derive(Clone)]` on `Item`; the fix should take the parameter `own`
detail: Found porting mini_tsdb: `fn ingest(parsed: Vec[Scrape])` with `for s in parsed.into_iter()`. The clonable-receiver sweep in the typechecker treated any type with a `.clone()` method as clonable, and `Vec[T]` has one whatever `T` is, so the fix offered `.clone()` rather than `own`, which it already offers for a type with no `.clone()`. A `Vec` clones only when its elements do.
fix: 4230ad12ec. The end-of-check sweep that builds `clonable_expr_spans` (src/typechecker.rs) now requires `type_supports_clone` as well as `clone_receiver_self_type`, so a span is clonable only when its `.clone()` both resolves and checks; for `Vec[Q]` with `Q` not clonable the typechecker refuses the call ("clones each element, and 'Q' has no `.clone()`"), and the fix now takes the parameter `own` as it does for a type with no clone. The ownership hint's no-clone sentence now reads "exists only on `String`, RC types and the built-in heap collections whose elements have one". B-2026-09-03-26's fixture `uam_hint_offers_clone_for_vec_of_non_clone_element` pinned that `Vec[Q].clone()` resolved, which the typechecker has since refused; it is flipped and renamed `uam_hint_withholds_clone_for_vec_of_non_clone_element` (tests/ownership.rs). New pin `into_iter_on_a_bare_vec_of_unclonable_items_takes_it_own` (tests/fix_mut_place_and_borrowed_moves.rs).

title: `let s = v[i].field;` with `s` only read gets the fix that clones the field, where `let s = v[i];` already gets `ref`; under `self`, a write to any other field of `self` also ruled the borrow out
detail: Found porting mini_tsdb: `let samples = self.series[key].samples;` then only reads of `samples`, while the method pushes to `self.out`. The read-only-binding borrow fix in `src/ownership/index_let.rs` recognised only a bare `Index` initializer, not a field or tuple-index chain over one, and its place root for `self.x[...]` was `self`, so a write to `self.out` counted as a write to the indexed place. The MoveOutOfPlace error on the field kept its `.clone()` suggestion.
fix: 4230ad12ec. `src/ownership/index_let.rs` recognises a field or tuple-index chain over an `Index` as an indexed place, and its place root for `self.f[...]` is `self.f`, matched against writes at a `.` boundary, so a write to `self.out` no longer rules out borrowing from `self.series`, while a write to `self.series` still does. `src/cli.rs` turns the MoveOutOfPlace error on such a read-only binding into the `ref` borrow ("the binding is only read, so the fix borrows the field"). Pinned by `a_read_only_field_of_an_element_is_borrowed` and `a_field_of_self_s_element_is_borrowed_unless_that_field_is_written` (tests/fix_mut_place_and_borrowed_moves.rs). `derive_clone_reaches_through_option_and_payloads` (tests/core_strict_check.rs) only read its field, so it now borrows; its program moves the field on into a `Vec` to keep testing the derive.

title: `for f in rx.into_iter()` over a `Receiver[Fn(i64) -> i64 + CrossTask]` passes `karac check` and fails the MIR borrow check inside the library: `borrow check ReceiverIter[Fn(i64) -> i64].next: ... the result borrows (*_1).0, which the receiver owns [E0509]`, on __mir-run, __mir-llvm-run and `karac run`; `while let Some(f) = rx.recv()` on the same channel works
detail: concurrency.md § Channels: `Receiver[T]` implements IntoIterator with item T, so `for msg in rx.into_iter()` receives until closed and drained; T may be any CrossTask type, and a marked function type is CrossTask (core semantics §6.3). Repro at head: `fn main() { let (tx, rx): (Sender[Fn(i64) -> i64 + CrossTask], Receiver[Fn(i64) -> i64 + CrossTask]) = channel(4); tx.send(|x| x * 3).unwrap(); { let d = tx; } let mut t = 0; for f in rx.into_iter() { t += f(10); } println(t); }` -> check 'All checks passed.', then 'error[mir]: borrow check ReceiverIter[Fn(i64) -> i64].next: 3838:9: bb1[term]: the result borrows (*_1).0, which the receiver owns; an item may borrow only what its `ref` fields borrow (borrow at bb0[0] at 3838:9) [E0509]'. Controls: the same with `while let Some(f) = rx.recv()` prints 30; `Receiver[String]` with `for s in rx.into_iter()` works. So the library's ReceiverIter.next, specialised at an erased function item type, is judged as returning a borrow of the receiver (the instance name also drops the `+ CrossTask` marker). App shape: a worker task draining a channel of jobs/handlers (probe cell s04 in probe-core/gen_app.py).
fix: 555b8efd68: the result of a channel's recv / try_recv was taken to carry a borrow of the receiver, so the library's ReceiverIter.next, which returns it from a mut ref self method, moved out of a borrow (E0509) once the item type was one whose moves the checker tracks (a CrossTask Fn value); a program's own Iterator.next returning try_recv failed the same way. A received value is moved out of the channel, so recv and try_recv join the moves_out natives in src/mir/lower.rs result_borrows, whose result holds no receiver borrow. tests/mir_channel_fn_values.rs pins the for-loop over rx.into_iter() (41) and an Iterator whose next is try_recv (10) on __mir-run; both fail with E0509 on the parent tree. Gate green (test0 10210 passed, test1 10371 passed).

title: Remainder after c2a612b69c (which names and fixes a Rust `::` path in an expression or a pattern: `Vec::new()`, `String::from("ab")`, `i64::MAX`, `HashMap::new()`, `std::cmp::max`, `Dir::Up =>`): an import path `import std::collections::HashMap;` (what `karac fix` makes of Rust's `use`) still gets only `Expected ';', found '::'` with no fix, and once `HashMap::new()` is fixed to `HashMap.new()` the resolver says only "undefined name 'HashMap'" with no hint toward Kāra's `Map`; likewise `HashSet` ("did you mean 'Hasher'?"), `BTreeMap`, `BTreeSet` and `BinaryHeap`, where the rename must also flip the direction (`BinaryHeap::from(v)` is `PriorityQueue.max_first_from(v)`: Kāra's queue pops the smallest first)
detail: Mend loop (CLAUDE.md § Writing Kāra): blind-authored Kāra goes through check --output=json and karac fix. Repros at head, each a one-liner `fn main() { ... }`: `let v: Vec[i64] = Vec::new();` -> 1:34 Expected `;`, found `::`; `let s = String::from("ab");` -> Expected `;`, found `::`; `println(i64::MAX);` -> Expected `)`, found `::`; after `karac fix` turns `use std::collections::HashMap;` into `import std::collections::HashMap;`, the `::` in the import and in `HashMap::new()` stay, with the same bare error. Kāra spells these `Vec.new()`, `"ab".to_string()` (or `String.from`), `i64.MAX`, `import std.collections...` (design.md § paths), so the fix is the same `::` -> `.` edit in every position (and `HashMap` -> `Map` as a did-you-mean). src/parser/exprs.rs `reject_method_turbofish` already names `::` after a METHOD; a path `Ident :: Ident` after a type or module name is the uncovered case. This is the commonest single Rust-ism in blind LLM output, so it costs the Mend fix rate most. | 2026-11-04 (kata thread): c2a612b69c adds Parser::rewrite_rust_path, called at an identifier expression and a pattern: the whole path is one diagnostic naming the Rust-ism, its fix writes the Kāra spelling (`.` for `::`, a std/core module prefix dropped), and the tokens are rewritten so the parse continues (no cascade; the `;` after a tail expression that the old recovery offered is gone). Pinned by tests/rust_path_fix.rs. Not covered: the import path (src/parser/items.rs parse_import_subtree expects `.`), and the HashMap->Map did-you-mean in the resolver. | 2026-11-04 (kata thread, kata 1046): a Rust-shaped ★ arm (`use std::collections::BinaryHeap;`, `BinaryHeap::from(stones)`) reaches `undefined name 'BinaryHeap'` with no hint after the `::` fix; `HashSet.new()` draws "did you mean 'Hasher'?", and `BTreeMap`/`BTreeSet` nothing, while `TreeMap`/`TreeSet` already rename to `SortedMap`/`SortedSet` (src/resolver.rs renamed_stdlib_type). A plain rename of `BinaryHeap` would turn Rust's largest-first heap into Kāra's smallest-first one and change the program's answer, so its constructor needs `max_first` / `max_first_from`.
fix: 75832f76f1 closes the remainder. The import: src/parser.rs reject_rust_prelude_import (called at `use` and at `import` in src/parser/items.rs) takes `use std::collections::HashMap;`, a `{..}` group of them, `std::cmp`/`std::mem` names and the module imports `use std::mem;` as one diagnostic naming Kāra's prelude names (`Map`, `Set`, `SortedMap`, `PriorityQueue`, `max`), whose fix deletes the line with its newline, in place of the `use` -> `import` diagnostic so the edits never overlap; a renaming import (`as`) is left to the next rule. rewrite_rust_import_path gives any other `::` import path one diagnostic whose fix writes `.` for each `::` (`import std.process.exit;`) and rewrites the tokens so the parse continues. The names: resolver renamed_stdlib_type adds crate::parser::rust_collection_rename (HashMap -> Map, HashSet -> Set, BTreeMap -> SortedMap, BTreeSet -> SortedSet, BinaryHeap -> PriorityQueue for a type). In a name position report_rust_binary_heap says Rust's heap is largest-first and attaches the edit the parser recorded at `BinaryHeap.new()` / `BinaryHeap.from(v)` (Program::rust_heap_ctor, beside rust_box_new): `PriorityQueue.max_first()` / `PriorityQueue.max_first_from(v)`. Pinned by tests/rust_std_import_fix.rs: seven cells (HashMap, a HashSet/BTreeMap group, BinaryHeap.from -> pops 8, BinaryHeap.new with a typed binding -> pops 9, std::cmp::max, `use std::mem;` + `mem::swap`, std::process::exit) each carried by `karac fix` to a clean check and the expected output under __mir-run. Not covered: a dotted `import std.collections.HashMap;` (written by hand, not by fix) still gets "unknown module `std.collections`".

title: Rust angle-bracket generics on a DECLARATION (`struct Bx<T> { v: T }`, `impl<T> Bx<T> { .. }`) get `Expected '{' or ';' after struct name` with no fix, though the same brackets in a type position (`Vec<i64>`, `Result<i64, String>`, `Box<..>`) are named and machine-fixed to `[..]`
detail: Repro: `struct Bx<T> { v: T }\nimpl<T> Bx<T> { fn get(self) -> T { self.v } }\nfn main() { let b = Bx { v: 4 }; println(b.get()); }` -> error[parse] 1:10 Expected `{` or `;` after struct name; `karac fix` changes nothing. Kāra writes `struct Bx[T]` and `impl[T] Bx[T]` (design.md § Generics). Expected: the `Vec<..>`-style diagnostic ('`<..>` is Rust's spelling: Kāra writes generic parameters in brackets') with the bracket edit, for struct, enum, trait, fn and impl headers.
fix: 6932c9f1e9: a `<` straight after the name in a struct, enum, trait, fn or impl header (`struct Bx<T>`, `impl<T: Copy> Bx<T>`) gets the same diagnostic as `Vec<..>` in a type position, "`Bx<..>` is Rust's spelling: Kāra writes generic parameters in brackets, `Bx[..]`", with the bracket edit, and the header parses on as if bracketed (`parse_optional_generic_params` -> `angle_generic_list`). tests/rust_spelling_decl_fix.rs rust_angle_generic_params_on_declarations_are_bracketed: the row's struct + impl plus enum, trait and fn, `karac fix` in one pass, then run.

title: Two Rust-isms are fixed into a program that is still refused: `fn first(s: &[i64])` is fixed to `ref [i64]`, whose `[T]` diagnostic then offers no machine edit to `Slice[i64]`; `-> Box<dyn Fn(i64) -> i64>` is fixed to `Box[dyn Fn(i64) -> i64]`, which then fails to parse (`Expected ']', found '('`)
detail: Repros: (1) `fn first(s: &[i64]) -> i64 { s[0] }\nfn main() { let v = [9, 8].to_vec(); println(first(&v[..])); }`: karac fix (repeated to a fixpoint) gives `fn first(s: ref [i64])` and `first(v[..])`; check then says '`[T]` is Rust's slice type -- in Kāra a view of a run of elements is `Slice[T]`' with no edit, so the loop stalls one step short. Wanted: `&[T]` -> `Slice[T]` in one edit (a bare parameter already borrows), or the `[T]` diagnostic carrying the `Slice[T]` edit. (2) `fn mk(k: i64) -> Box<dyn Fn(i64) -> i64> { Box::new(move |x| x + k) }`: the `Box<..>` edit produces `Box[dyn Fn(i64) -> i64]`, a new parse error; Kāra's answer is `-> Fn(i64) -> i64` returning the closure (an escaping function value), with no Box. Either a dedicated `Box<dyn Fn..>` diagnostic, or no edit that cannot parse.
fix: 6932c9f1e9: (1) `&[T]` is now named as Rust's slice and fixed to `Slice[T]` in one edit (`&mut [T]` to `mut Slice[T]`), replacing the `ref [T]` step whose `[T]` diagnostic had no edit. (2) `Box<dyn Fn(A) -> R>` (and MutFn/OnceFn/FnMut/FnOnce) gets its own diagnostic, "`Box<dyn Fn(..)>` is Rust's boxed closure: in Kāra a function value has its own type, `Fn(A) -> R`", whose edit deletes `Box<dyn ` and `>`; the generic `Box<..>` -> `Box[..]` edit that produced the unparsable `Box[dyn Fn(..)]` no longer fires there. tests/rust_spelling_decl_fix.rs rust_borrowed_slice_types_are_slice_in_one_edit and rust_boxed_closure_type_is_the_function_type fix the row's programs and run them. The body of repro (2), `Box::new(move |x| x + k)`, is B-2026-11-04-43 (fixed in the same push), so the whole program now mends (tests/mend_rustisms.rs r20_box_dyn_fn).

title: UFCS on a program trait (`A.m(s)`, design.md §9 Method resolution) is refused by `karac check`, `karac run` and `karac build` with "a call that leaves out default arguments is not lowered yet"; this is the fix the ambiguity diagnostic points at, so two traits sharing a method name have no way out, and inside a generic body under `T: A + B` the UFCS call `A.m(x)` is itself reported as ambiguous
fix: 5bb971cb18: three parts. (1) `karac check` and `run` lowered the MIR check's copy of the program before the UFCS rewrite the build frontend does, so `A.m(s)` reached `def_call` as a path call without its receiver; the copy now takes `lowering::rewrite_ufcs` (src/cli.rs). (2) Two traits' methods of one name for one type got one MIR name (`S.m`), so `A.m(s)` and `B.m(s)` both ran the first impl's body; each is now named apart with its trait (`S.m#A`, `S.m#B`), as a trait method beside an inherent one already was (src/mir/lower.rs). (3) In a generic body under `T: A + B`, `A.m(x)` keeps only the named trait's bound (src/typechecker/expr_method_call.rs `dispatch_bounded_receiver_method`), and lowering takes that trait's impl. Pinned by corpus/core/method_ufcs_names_the_trait (default method, two traits, generic) and tests/trait_bound_dispatch.rs, on check, interp and run. A default body's own `self.m()` on such a type is still refused as ambiguous: B-2026-11-04-40.

title: In a generic body under `T: Named`, `T.label()` calls the concrete type's INHERENT associated function of the same name instead of the trait's (prints "inherent", expected "trait") on every lane; the method form `x.m()` under the same shape correctly calls the trait's
fix: 5bb971cb18: the checker records, for `T.f()` dispatched through one bound, the bound's trait under the call's span (`method_typeparam_trait_key`, src/typechecker/expr_method_call.rs `try_dispatch_typeparam_assoc_fn`), and MIR lowering's `type_param_call` takes that trait's impl function for the instance's type (`bound_impl_fn`, src/mir/lower.rs) before the inherent lookup. `via[T: Named]` prints trait; `P.label()` stays inherent. Pinned by corpus/core/method_generic_assoc_fn_through_bound and tests/trait_bound_dispatch.rs, on check, interp and run.

title: A program associated function named like a comptime reflection method (`fn name() -> String` in a trait or inherent impl) passes `karac check` but `P.name()` / `T.name()` lowers to the native `Type.name`: `karac run`/interp stops with "`Type.name` runs only at compile time, inside a `comptime` evaluation" and the LLVM lane with "native `Type.name` is not lowered yet"
fix: 5bb971cb18: MIR lowering's comptime-native arm took `P.name()` (any reflection method name on a struct, enum or union) as the reflection native `Type.name`; it now does so only when the checker did not resolve the call to a program function (src/mir/lower.rs `comptime_native`). `T.name()` under `T: Named` goes through the bound (B-2026-11-04-9). Pinned by corpus/core/method_user_fn_named_like_reflection (trait impl, inherent, generic) and tests/trait_bound_dispatch.rs.

title: A generic body under one bound `[T: B]` calling `x.m()` is refused ("the method call `.m` with no resolved callee is not lowered yet") when the concrete type also implements ANOTHER trait with a method `m`; design.md §9 says lookup uses the bound and gives one candidate
fix: 5bb971cb18: when the receiver's type has several traits' `m`, method-call lowering in a generic instance now takes the impl of the trait the bound names (`bound_impl_fn` from `method_typeparam_trait_key`, src/mir/lower.rs) instead of giving up; with two traits' `m` named apart (B-2026-11-04-8) the existing bound path finds it too. `g[T: B]` prints 2, `h[T: A]` prints 1. Pinned by corpus/core/method_bound_picks_one_of_two_traits and tests/trait_bound_dispatch.rs.

title: The ownership check charges `s.m()` with the TRAIT method's `own self` when an inherent `m(self)` is the method chosen: `let s = S {}; println(s.m()); println(s.m());` is refused "value 's' moved here, used again" though inherent methods win (design.md §9 Method resolution) and interp runs it (inh, inh)
fix: ee3803b7f8. The ownership check's receiver-mode table (collect_method_self_modes in src/ownership.rs, and its copy collect_method_self_modes_in_items in src/ownership/concurrent_shared.rs) keyed `S.m` by source order, so a trait impl written after the inherent impl overwrote the inherent `m(self)` with the trait's `m(own self)`, and `s.m()` moved `s`. Both now go through insert_self_mode: an inherent entry always wins and a trait impl never overwrites it (design.md §9 Method resolution). The probe's q.kara and t14 (`s.m()` then `T.m(s)`) check and print inh/inh and inh/tr; a type with only the trait method still refuses the second `s.m()`. Pinned by corpus/design/ok_inherent_method_receiver_mode_wins (inherent impl first, as in the probe); the pre-fix binary refused it with "value 's' moved here".

title: An impl method with a STRONGER mode than its trait (`fn look(mut ref self)` for the trait's `fn look(self)`) is not refused at the impl (design.md §9 Conformance: the impl's modes may be the trait's or weaker); the method silently gets the trait's `self`, so with no write it is accepted, and a write in its body reports "the receiver is `ref self` ... Declare the method `mut ref self`", which it already is
fix: d9cf47b567. The cause was D5's rewrite, not the §4.7 check: `d5_params::borrow_bare_params` gave every method of an impl of a user trait the trait's borrowed receiver, overwriting a written `mut ref self` with `ref self`, so `check_impl_modes_not_stronger` saw the trait's mode on both sides. Only a bare `self` takes the trait's borrow now (src/d5_params.rs), and the check reports "impl method 'S.look' takes its receiver as `mut ref self`, but 'T.look' declares `self` ... Declare `self`" at the receiver, with a fix (its label for the rewritten borrow is now `self`, D5's spelling). Weaker receivers (`self` for `own self` or `mut ref self`) still pass. Pinned by tests/coherence_impls.rs (both directions) and corpus/fixtures/coherence/impl_receiver_stronger. A corpus-wide check scan found no program refused by it.

title: Coherence is not checked where impls are declared for three overlap shapes: a duplicate `impl T for S` twice, `impl[X: Eq] T for B[X]` beside `impl[X: Ord] T for B[X]`, and a second `impl Iterator for Up` with another `Item`; each is accepted and the first call says "ambiguous ... Use UFCS" listing two identical candidates (`T.f(S)` twice) that UFCS cannot separate
