detail: Repros (probe d1/t09, t11, t28; d1x/g, n, o): `impl T for S { fn f(self) -> i64 { 1 } }\nimpl T for S { fn f(self) -> i64 { 2 } }` -> check passes with no call; with `S {}.f()` -> "ambiguous method 'f' on receiver of type 'S': multiple candidates apply. Use UFCS to disambiguate: `T.f(S)` -> i64 / `T.f(S)` -> i64". Same for the Eq/Ord pair on B[X] (`T.f(B)` twice) and for two Iterator impls (`Iterator.next(Up)` -> Option[i64] / -> Option[String]). Spec: §9 Coherence "Overlap is an error. Two impls of one trait overlap when their headers unify, ignoring their bounds ... The error is reported at the second impl"; "A type implements a trait once"; Associated types "ERROR: CountUp already implements Iterator, with Item = i64". The concrete-vs-generic shape (`impl T for B[i64]` + `impl[X] T for B[X]`, t10) IS refused at the second impl ("conflicting impl"), so the check exists and misses exact duplicates and bound-differing headers.
fix: d9cf47b567. A second trait impl whose header unifies with an existing one's (same trait arguments, same target arguments or both generic on the name), bounds ignored, is refused at the second impl (src/typechecker/env_build.rs `ImplOverlap::Duplicate` in `impl_overlap_conflict`), naming the first impl's associated types ("`Up` already implements `Iterator`, with Item = i64"). A library source re-stating a baked impl still replaces it; `From`/`TryFrom` with no trait argument are told apart by the method's source parameter (tests/typechecker.rs `test_try_into_multi_impl_disambiguates_by_source`). MEASURED: the row's three repros (t09, t11, t28) each refused at the second impl; t10 (concrete vs generic) refused as before. Pinned by tests/coherence_impls.rs and corpus/fixtures/coherence/{duplicate_trait_impl,overlap_bounds_ignored,second_iterator_impl} (expected_from = spec). A corpus-wide check scan found no program refused by it.

title: An inherent impl on a standard type, `impl Vec[i64] { fn total(self) -> i64 { .. } }`, is accepted and runs (prints 3), though design.md §9 Coherence says a package may write `impl Type { .. }` only for a type it declares, the application exemption not changing this
detail: Repro (probe d1x/l.kara): `impl Vec[i64] { fn total(self) -> i64 { let mut t = 0; for x in self { t += x; } t } }\nfn main() { let v: Vec[i64] = [1, 2].to_vec(); println(v.total()); }` -> check passes, run prints 3. Spec: §9 Coherence "Inherent impls only on your own types. A package may write `impl Type { ... }` only for a type it declares; the application exemption does not change this. Outside the standard library, `impl Vec[i64] { ... }` is an error. Write a trait, or wrap the type in a `distinct type`." Expected: refused at the impl with that advice. (Program-trait impls on Vec, `impl Local for Vec[i64]`, are allowed and work, t13.)
fix: d9cf47b567. An inherent impl whose target is not a type the program declares (a struct, enum, union, distinct type, opaque extern type, or an alias of one) is refused at the impl with the spec's advice (src/typechecker/items.rs `check_inherent_impl_locality`): "inherent impl on `Vec[i64]`, a type this program does not declare ... Write a trait and implement it for `Vec[i64]`, or wrap the type in a `distinct type`". The appended library sources, spliced gated modules and a baked module compiled as its own program are exempt. FLIPPED pins: seven legacy-derived corpus fixtures that ran a program's `impl i64 { .. }` / `impl Column[i64] { .. }` now carry `v2_reject`; tests/typechecker.rs (Column/Tensor admission, `impl i64 { fn lt }`) assert the refusal; tests that used an inherent primitive impl to test something else (cast/cmp/shout dispatch, mir_build assoc fns and comparison methods, mir_library and a lower.rs unit test on Option) now use a trait impl, and their corpus fixtures with them. Pinned by tests/coherence_impls.rs and corpus/fixtures/coherence/inherent_impl_on_std_type. An impl through an alias of the program's own struct is admitted but fails in MIR: B-2026-11-04-50.

title: A blanket impl of the program's own trait, `impl[T: Display] Twice for T { .. }` (design.md §9 Coherence: allowed when the package defines the trait), is accepted but never found: `5.twice()` is "no method 'twice' on type 'i64'", `"ab".twice()` "no method on 'String'", and UFCS `Twice.twice(5)` the same
detail: Repro (probe d1/t61, d1x/f.kara): `trait Twice { fn twice(self) -> String; }\nimpl[T: Display] Twice for T { fn twice(self) -> String { f"{self}{self}" } }\nfn main() { println(5.twice()); println("ab".twice()); }` -> error[typecheck] 7:21 "no method 'twice' on type 'i64'", 7:41 "no method 'twice' on type 'String', did you mean 'slice'?". Expected 55, abab. Spec: §9 Coherence "Blanket impls. `impl[T: B1 + B2] Trait for T` is allowed only if the package defines `Trait` (or is the application)", with the example `impl[T: SomeForeignTrait] MyTrait for T { ... }   // OK`. Conditional impls on a named type (`impl[T: Display] Sh for W[T]`, t21) work, so it is the bare-`T` Self that lookup does not match.
fix: d9cf47b567. A method call on a concrete receiver that no impl answers tries the program's own blanket impls over a bare parameter (src/typechecker/method_user_impl.rs `blanket_impl_candidates` / `blanket_impl_method`, hooked where the primitive, String and named-type lookups would report no method): one whose bounds the receiver meets is dispatched as the trait's method and recorded in `method_typeparam_trait_key` with no `Type.method` callee (`blanket_method_spans`), so the MIR builder's `blanket_method` instances the impl at the receiver, as under a bound. UFCS `Trait.m(x)` on a type with no impl of the trait takes the blanket impl's `m` past an inherent `m` (checker and MIR). The library's own blanket impls are left to their surfaces (core_strict_check pins `(1..).into_iter()` refused with a fix). MEASURED: `5.twice()`, `"ab".twice()`, `P { n: 1 }.twice()`, `Twice.twice(7)` print 55 / abab / P1P1 / 77 on run and --interp; pinned by tests/coherence_impls.rs and corpus/fixtures/coherence/blanket_impl_bare_param (passes mir-interp, mir-llvm, mir-llvm-asan). A default method calling another trait method through a blanket impl is B-2026-11-04-49.

title: `for x in it` with `it: I` or `it: mut ref I` (I: Iterator[Item = i64], a borrowed iterator) reports "expected 'i64', found 'ref I'" at the first use of `x`, typing the loop variable as the iterator; design.md §9 says a `for` over a type that is neither Iterator nor Iterable is an error naming the missing impl
detail: Repro (probe d1x/e.kara, r.kara): `fn total[I: Iterator[Item = i64]](it: I) -> i64 { let mut t = 0; for x in it { t += x; } t }` -> error[typecheck] 1:85 (`t += x`) "expected 'i64', found 'ref I'"; with `it: mut ref I` -> "expected 'i64', found 'mut ref I'". Same with `it: impl Iterator[Item = i64]` ("found 'ref T_impl_arg_0'"). `it: own I` works (t27). Spec: §9 Iterator and Iterable "An `Iterator` is consumed. `for x in it` moves `it`"; "A `for` over a type that is neither an `Iterator` nor `Iterable` is an error naming the missing impl"; "To loop over an iterator without consuming it, write `for x in it.by_ref()`". Expected: an error at `it` saying a borrowed iterator cannot be consumed, suggesting `own I` or `.by_ref()` (whether `mut ref I` should iterate is the spec's call). Blind authors write `fn f(it: impl Iterator[..])` first, so this is the first thing they hit.
fix: ee3803b7f8. The `for` arm (src/typechecker/exprs.rs) now asks borrowed_iterator_for (src/typechecker/bounds.rs): a `ref` or `mut ref` of a type parameter bounded by `Iterator` and not `Iterable` (including the synthetic parameter of `impl Iterator[..]`) is refused at the iterable, since the loop consumes an Iterator (design.md § `Iterator` and `Iterable`). For `ref I` the message names `it: own I` and the fix-it inserts `own` at the parameter; for `mut ref I` it names `it.by_ref()` and the fix-it appends `.by_ref()`. The loop's item type is also normalized against the enclosing `Item = T` bounds, so `for x in it.by_ref()` binds `i64`, not `I.Item` (it did not check before). All three probe shapes go through `karac fix` to a program that checks and prints 6 (tests/borrowed_iterator_for.rs); corpus/design/err_for_over_a_borrowed_iterator pins the refusal. Whether `mut ref I` should iterate directly was left to the spec: as written, `for` consumes, so the by_ref form is the fix. A borrowed CONCRETE iterator type (e.g. a `ref` of a library iterator struct) is not covered by this check. A check sweep of 3371 corpus and kata programs changed no verdict besides the new pins.

title: The effects of the `From` impl that a `?` inserts are not charged to the enclosing function (design.md §10: "The conversion is a real call for effects"): a `pub fn` whose `?` converts through `impl From[E1] for E2 { fn from(..) -> E2 with writes(Log) }` passes `karac check` with no effect clause and reports no effects, while the same conversion written as `E2.from(e)` is refused for the undeclared `writes(Log)`
fix: 7c0ff1e85c. The typechecker's `?` From success (src/typechecker/expr_ops.rs) now also records `{target}.from` in user_operator_calls at the `?` span. The AST effect checker's Question arm (src/effectchecker/inference.rs) charges that key as it does an operator's program impl. The repro's `pub fn f` is now refused with "performs effects [writes(Log)] but has no effect declaration", the private `h` shows writes(Log) in program_effects, and declaring the clause is accepted and runs. On the MIR side the `?`'s From is already a real Call to the impl body, and its user-resource clause is charged by the B-2026-11-04-25 fix in the same commit. Pins: corpus/core/err_question_from_effects, ok_question_from_effects_declared.

title: Script mode's implicit `main` returns `()`, so a top-level `?` is refused with "'?' requires the enclosing function to return `Result` or `Option`, found '()'"; design.md §10 Script mode gives it `fn main() -> Result[(), AnyError]` so that `?` works and an `Err` exits 1 with `Error: ..`
detail: Repro (probe d1x/sm2.kara): `fn h() -> Result[i64, AnyError] { Ok(2) }\nlet x = h()?;\nprintln(x);` -> error[typecheck] 2:9 "'?' requires the enclosing function to return `Result` or `Option`, found '()'". Also d2/e27 (top-level `let v = chk(2)?;` with a program `Error` type; expected stdout a, 4 then exit 1 with stderr `Error: bad:neg-1`). Spec: §10 Script mode "A file with top-level statements, not just items, gets an implicit `fn main() -> Result[(), AnyError]`" and "`?` works, because the implicit main returns a Result", "it ends with `Ok(())`". The parser's synthesis (src/parser.rs ~788) says the Result upgrade "is deferred until a catch-all `Error` type exists in v1"; `AnyError` exists since B-2026-10-21-22, so the deferral's premise is gone. Script mode itself works (`let x = 1; println(x);` runs), and the both-main-and-statements error matches the spec (d2/e28). Side note for the doc: the §10 script example uses `File.read("input.csv")?`, while library/io.md has `fs.read_to_string`.
fix: ab80e422aa (pin a480a6b665). Script mode's implicit main is `fn main() -> Result[(), AnyError]` ending with `Ok(())` (design.md § Script mode); the deferral's premise (no catch-all error type) ended with AnyError. src/parser.rs script_main_signature parses the signature and tail from their own text with offsets past the file's end, so no synthesized node shares a written node's span. The probe's sm2 repro prints 2; d2/e27's shape prints a, 4 and exits 1 with `Error: bad:neg-1`, on interp, the JIT and a built binary. The parser pin script_mode_synthesizes_main_from_top_level_statements flips (Result return, Ok(()) tail). Pinned in tests/script_and_package_shapes.rs and corpus fixtures/script_mode/question_in_implicit_main (spec, every lane). Side effect noted as its own row: `karac fmt` already rewrote a script into an explicit main, and now writes the Result signature and Ok(()) too. The doc's File.read example is left for the doc owner.

title: `#[track_caller]` on a program function is accepted but does nothing: a wrapper `#[track_caller] fn must(o: Option[i64]) -> i64 { o.unwrap() }` called at line 10 panics with `at <file>:6:5`, the `unwrap()` inside the wrapper; design.md §10 says user code may use it on its own panicking wrappers and that it is transitive
fix: aed0200c63 (Thread B). Lowering records each `#[track_caller]` function's instances in `Program.tracked` (a provider specialisation of one is tracked too). The interpreter places a panic in a tracked body as it places one in a library body (`Program::defers_location`, used by `report_abort` and the isolating-group unwinding), so the report lands on the first untracked frame's call. The LLVM backend makes a tracked body that can abort a located one (src/backend/mir/debug.rs `located`, `own_body`): it takes its caller's place as two trailing parameters and forwards it to the library bodies and tracked functions it calls. The repro now reports the call `must(None)`, on run, --interp and build; through two tracked functions the report is the outer call, and an untracked wrapper reports its own call into the tracked one. Pinned by corpus/core/panic_track_caller_reports_the_call (design.md §10, via TaskFailed.Panicked's location; interp, mir-llvm, mir-llvm-asan) and tests/track_caller_location.rs (three cases on stderr; all three fail with the tracking disabled).

title: In a package, importing a NESTED module itself (`import db.connection;`, then `connection.open(7)`) is refused with "error[E0112]: unknown module `db`" by `karac check`, `run` and `build`; design.md §4 Imports binds the module as `connection`, and a top-level module import (`import util;`) works
detail: Repro (probe mp/m04_module_import, mp/u): kara.toml `[package] name = "app"`; src/db/connection.kara `pub struct Connection { pub port: i64 }\npub fn open(p: i64) -> Connection { Connection { port: p } }`; src/main.kara `import db.connection;\nfn main() { let c: connection.Connection = connection.open(7); println(c.port); }` -> error[E0112] src/main.kara:1:1 "unknown module `db`". Same with `import db.c;` + `c.f()`. Control: src/util.kara + `import util;` + `util.f()` prints 1. Item imports from the same nested module work (`import db.connection.{Connection, open};`, m01; wildcard `import db.connection.*;`, m05). Spec: §4 Imports `import db.connection;  // the module itself, as connection` and Binding rule "`import db.connection;` binds the module `connection`, so its items are `connection.Connection`". B-2026-10-23-14 fixed the whole-module import for a single segment.
fix: ab80e422aa (pin a480a6b665). src/resolver/collect.rs collect_import: a dotted prefix that names no module (db/ with no db.kara) passes when every name imported is a module under it, so `import db.connection;` binds the module `connection` (design.md § Imports) and `import db.connection as c;` binds `c`; `import db.nothere;` is still unknown. The probe's m04 shape prints 7 under check, run and build. Pinned in tests/script_and_package_shapes.rs and corpus fixtures/packages/nested_module_import_whole (spec, mir-build: the corpus runs a package only through `karac build`).

title: Struct field visibility does not follow design.md §5's three levels: a field with no keyword is refused from another module of the SAME package ("private field 'inner' of struct 'S' is not visible outside its defining module", coded E0221 PrivateTypeInPublicSignature), though the default is package-visible, and `private inner: i64` (directory-only) is a parse error "'private' is a reserved keyword"
detail: Repro (probe mp/m25_default_field_cross_dir_ok): src/db/c.kara `pub struct S { pub a: i64, inner: i64 }\npub fn mk() -> S { S { a: 1, inner: 2 } }`; src/main.kara `import db.c.{mk};\nfn main() { let s = mk(); println(s.inner); }` -> error[E0221] src/main.kara:2:35 "private field 'inner' of struct 'S' is not visible outside its defining module"; expected 2. And mp/m24: `pub struct S { pub a: i64, private secret: i64 }` -> error[parse] 1:28 "'private' is a reserved keyword and cannot be used as an identifier". Spec: §5 "Field visibility takes the three levels of §4 Visibility: a field is visible in its package by default, to users of the package with `pub`, and in its directory only with `private`"; shared struct fields list `private mut field: T`, `private field: T`. The rule in src/typechecker/fields.rs check_cross_module_field_access refuses any non-`pub` field outside its defining MODULE, which is the module-private default §4 "Why the default is package-internal" rejects. Item visibility already follows the three levels (default fn across directories works, m15; `private fn` same-directory works and other-directory is E0111, m12..m14). A field access the rule should refuse would be E0111 PrivateItemAccess, not E0221.
fix: c32f787973: struct fields follow design.md §5's three levels. A field with no keyword is visible in the whole package; `private` (now parsed on a field, `StructField.is_private`) limits it to files in the module's directory; `pub` exports it. `check_cross_module_field_access` and `infer_imported_field_access` share `field_visibility_refusal`, whose messages name the level crossed ("is `private`: visible only to files in the same directory as module `db.c`" / "is not `pub`: only `pub` fields are visible outside package `..`"). The error keeps its code E0221 rather than a new one. tests/field_visibility_levels.rs pins the row's repro (default field read from another directory: accepted) and a `private` field read from another directory (refused); core_strict_check a_private_field_is_refused_through_an_imported_call is flipped to the `private` spelling. CHANGELOG 0.8.1 lists it under "Wrong behaviour fixed".

title: `karac run` in a package whose src/ has both main.kara and lib.kara runs main.kara and exits 0, while `karac check` and `karac build` refuse it ("a Kāra package cannot contain both ... a package is either an executable or a library, never both", design.md §4 Entry points)
detail: Repro (probe mp/m28_main_and_lib_refused): src/main.kara `fn main() { }`, src/lib.kara `pub fn f() -> i64 { 1 }`; `karac check` -> error (walker) "a Kāra package cannot contain both `.../src/main.kara` and `.../src/lib.kara`"; `karac build` -> the same error[walker]; `karac run` -> rc 0 with no diagnostic. Spec: §4 Modules "Entry points. `main.kara` for an executable, `lib.kara` for a library. A package cannot have both." Expected: `run` refuses with the walker's error, as build does.
fix: ab80e422aa (pin a480a6b665). `karac run` (and `karac build <file>`, through the same run_v2 package_source) now asks the walker first (src/cli/project_v2.rs package_walk_refusal) when the file is under a package's src/, and refuses what the walker refuses (both main.kara and lib.kara, a mod.kara, a module written twice) with the walker's error and exit 1; package_tree read a refused walk as 'no package' and ran the file alone. A missing src/ is not a refusal there. Pinned on both run lanes in tests/script_and_package_shapes.rs and corpus fixtures/packages/run_refuses_main_and_lib (spec, mir-build).

title: A type mismatch between two same-named types from different modules prints the compiler's internal mangled names: `expected 'ref P__a', found 'P__b'` for `a.P` and `b.P` imported as `AP` and `BP`
fix: 3942d674ca. The project amalgam renames a same-named item from another module (`P` in a.kara becomes `P__a`) and now records each rename's shown name, its module path (`a.P`). src/cli/project_v2.rs demangles every remapped message and the JSON "expected"/"got" fields by whole-word replacement, quotes the file's own line in the snippet where the combined source's line differs, and moves the caret by a word-aligned column map between the two lines; the header and JSON column are remapped the same way. title: Two `par` branches that write the same USER-DECLARED resource are never refused: with `effect resource Db;` and `fn put() with writes(Db)`, `par { put(), put() }`, `par { { put(); }, { put(); } }` and `par { put(), rd() }` (rd: reads(Db)) all pass `karac check` and run, though `karac query effects` lists writes(Db) on both; design.md §12's own AuditLog example is refused only through its `writes(Stderr)`
fix: 7c0ff1e85c. A declared user resource has no operation a body performs, so the MIR effect pass, which sums what bodies do, never charged it. Lowering now keeps each function's clause effects on the resources the program declares (`effect resource`) in Program.clause_effects (src/mir/lower.rs, src/mir/interp.rs), and src/mir/effects.rs Analysis::user_clause adds them to that body's summary with Key::Any. Value-rooted clauses (`sends(self)`, which tests/effect_value_roots.rs keeps unrefused across two receivers) and built-in resources are left to the body's own sites. Every repro shape is now refused: `par { put(1), put(2) }`, the block form, a private wrapper, writes against reads, and design.md's AuditLog example without its eprintln. Auto-par measured too: before the fix, a reduction loop `for i in 0..64 { t += put(i); }` with put writes(Db) ran its iterations as tasks (KARAC_AUTO_PAR_DEBUG "loops as tasks: main@19"). Now it reports Conflict writes(Db)/writes(Db) and stays in order. Pins: corpus/core/err_par_user_resource and ok_par_user_resource_disjoint (reads/reads of one resource and writes of two different ones still run together). Five legacy IR fixtures in corpus/fixtures/par_codegen whose branches each write one `Log` are now refused (check-refuses:E0418), per §12. A declared but unused BUILT-IN effect is not charged; that is B-2026-11-04-26 (apps thread).

title: Call sites are charged the callee's BODY effects, not the declared contract: a `pub fn g() -> i64 with writes(Stdout) { 1 }` called in two `par` branches is not a conflict, and a call through `[T: Storage]` whose trait method has the ceiling `with writes(Stdout)` is charged the instance impl's (empty) effects, so `par { via(a), via(b) }` passes
fix: 9ae967f6a6. A caller is now charged a function's declared clause, not only its body (design.md §12: "a call to a public function contributes its declared set"; "a call through a type-parameter bound has the clause's effects, whatever the instance's impl does"). Lowering records a clause's plain effects on the host's named resources as well as the program's own (Channel and value-rooted resources stay with the body's own keyed sites), and a trait impl's method with no clause of its own carries its trait method's clause, so `via[T: Storage]` over a no-op `Ro.save` is charged writes(Stdout). user_clause keys Network and FileSystem as Fresh (capabilities, core §12 item 5), as clause_set does. Both probe repros are refused with "branches 1 and 2 of the `par` conflict: `writes(Stdout)` and `writes(Stdout)`". A whole-corpus interpreter run showed no new failures. Pins: corpus/core/err_par_pub_clause_contract, err_par_bound_clause_ceiling, par_clause_capabilities_apart (reads/reads, Network and FileSystem stay apart).

title: A declared effect clause is not verified on a PRIVATE function or on a trait's DEFAULT method body: `fn f() with reads(Clock) { println("x"); }` and `trait T { fn m(self) -> i64 with reads(Clock) { println("x"); 1 } }` pass `karac check`, though design.md §12 says a private function's declared set "is checked like a public one" and default bodies "are checked against their method's clause"
fix: 98ef92e24b (with a5c8c061f2, ad1725a4ec, 511d4becec). verify_written_declarations (src/effectchecker/verify.rs) checks every written `with` clause the public pass did not: private free functions, inherent-impl methods public or private, and a private trait's default bodies (apply_unimpled_private_trait_rule no longer makes a trait method with a written clause Polymorphic). An undeclared effect is E0400 "function 'f' performs writes(Stdout) ... but its `with` clause does not declare it". title: `#[no_effect(allocates(Heap))]` (design.md §12's real-time guarantee) misses most allocations: `[1, 2].to_vec()`, `"a".to_string()`, an f-string, a `Vec` literal `let v: Vec[i64] = [1, 2]`, `Vec.filled(3, 0)`, `String + Str` and `(0..3).collect()` all pass under it; only `push` is caught
detail: Repro (probe d1x/na.kara, one body per line): `#[no_effect(allocates(Heap))]\nfn f() -> i64 { <body> }\nfn main() { println(f()); }` with body `let v = [1, 2].to_vec(); v.len()` -> All checks passed; likewise `let s = "a".to_string(); s.len()`, `let s = f"{1}"; s.len()`, `let v: Vec[i64] = [1, 2]; v.len()`, `let v = Vec.filled(3, 0); v.len()`, `let s = "ab".to_string() + "c"; s.len()`, `let v: Vec[i64] = (0..3).collect(); v.len()`. Control: `let mut v: Vec[i64] = Vec.new(); v.push(1); v.len()` -> error[E_NO_EFFECT_VIOLATED]; a helper that pushes is caught transitively (d4/f15), and the bare `#[no_effect(allocates)]` form catches push too. Spec: §12 Default-permitted effects "A function under `#[no_effect(allocates(Heap))]` is proven allocation-free for the whole call: the checker follows the full transitive call graph and rejects any callee that allocates" (game loops, audio callbacks). The library functions that allocate do not carry allocates(Heap) in their effect sets (`to_vec`, `to_string`, `filled`, collect, string concat, f-string formatting, Vec literals).
fix: 98ef92e24b. The effect checker charges `allocates(Heap)` at `collect`, `to_vec` and `to_string` calls, interpolated strings with holes, map literals, `Vec[..]`/`Set[..]` prefix literals, `Vec.filled`, String `+` (String.add), and a list or repeat literal the typechecker typed as a heap collection (NodeTypeFacts.heap from lib.rs::node_type_facts). A fixed `[0; 4]`, a hole-free f-string and a literal stay free. Pins: corpus/core/err_no_effect_heap_allocations, no_effect_heap_free_loop; tests/effects_spec_atoms_and_clauses.rs.

title: Integer `/` and `%` and checked-mode overflow arithmetic are not `panics` atoms: `#[no_effect(panics)] fn f(a: i64, b: i64) -> i64 { a % b }` (and `a / b`, `a + b`) passes `karac check`, and `f(1, 0)` then panics at run time with "division by zero"
fix: 98ef92e24b. Integer `/`, `%` and the checked operators `+ - * << >>`, unary `-`, and their compound assignments are `panics` atoms (design.md §12). The lowered operator call (`call_path([i64, div], ..)`) and the typed Binary/Unary/CompoundAssign forms on integer operands (NodeTypeFacts.ints) push __builtin_div_rem or __builtin_int_overflow. wrapping_*/saturating_*, bitwise ops, comparisons and float arithmetic stay pure. Fixtures that asserted an arithmetic function is pure now use wrapping_* (lsp hover, book appendix D kernel example) or expect `panics` (tests/cli.rs test_query_effects_of_an_arithmetic_function). Pins: corpus/core/err_no_effect_panics_arithmetic, no_effect_panics_wrapping_arithmetic.

fix: 76e7c027a5 (the corpus copy of kara-katas d6d1a5e8; the fix is in the kata, not the compiler). The Kara arm's deserialize now keeps its tokens as views (`Vec[Str]`), as the Rust mirror borrows `&str`, instead of copying 400k heap Strings a round. Re-run on the M5 by Gowtham with scripts/bench/m5-rows.sh at kara a3df76e55c, kara-katas ee3012e4, Darwin arm64, 5 runs, against the kata's Rust mirror built with rustc -O: peak RSS 172.7 vs 172.8 MiB = 0.999x, wall 502.9 vs 500.3 ms = 1.005x, both within; the sink is the same.
title: Kata 297's peak RSS is 1.35x Rust's (233-235 MiB vs 173 MiB) on the MIR backend, where the 2026-08-28 feed read 179.9 vs 174.3 MiB
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-04 on the M5 Pro with /usr/bin/time -l on bench/target binaries: kara 233.1-233.5 MiB on gd33cb285d and 233.5-235.0 MiB on g7310a8f94 (so no change between those), rust 173.0 MiB, C 14-20 MiB. The harness's own sampler read kara 215.5 and rust 174.3 MiB on 2026-11-02 and 179.9 MiB for kara on 2026-08-28, so the comparison with the older feed is across builds, not one tool. Legacy dd86e3955 cannot compile this kata, so there is no legacy A/B. The program allocates one String per token from String.split in a loop, so macOS retention on large frees (see the 2026-11-02 kata 280/283 finding) has not been ruled out; Rust's mirror also allocates per token and stays at 173 MiB. 2026-11-06 drop schedule, x86 cloud box at fdc7656606 (peak RSS from wait4, 3 runs each, same checksum 397546302): kara 45.8 MiB 1.31-1.41 s, rustc -O mirror 25.7 MiB 0.88-0.90 s (results.container-x86.json had 48.3 vs 27.0 MB, 1571 vs 892 ms). The arms are not the same algorithm: the Kara arm's deserialize copies every token into its own heap String (`s.split(",").map(|p| p.to_string()).collect()` into `Vec[String]`, 400k Strings a round), where the Rust mirror borrows (`Vec<&str>`). With `let tokens: Vec[Str] = s.split(",").collect();` and `de_at(tokens: ref Vec[Str], ..)`, the Kara arm runs 0.88-0.93 s (Rust's time) at 31.7 MiB, 1.23x Rust; what is left is the `shared struct` node's count against Rust's `Box`. So the fix is in the kata (kara-katas leetcode/201-300/297-*/bench/treecodec.kara, routed to the kata thread), not the compiler; the row closes on an M5 re-run of the fixed arm.

title: Kata 1665 (a gated `sort_by` partition) still executes 1.17x legacy's instructions on the M5 at 3dc7786b7f; 314 and 318 are within the 1.15x bar, and 214, 247, 288 and 895's par lane wait on their first M5 figures since filing
detail: MEASURED on the M5 Pro by the kara-katas re-bench, vs legacy dd86e3955, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, exact counts via scripts/pmc.c (3-run minima). On karac 0.8.0-dev.14370+gd33cb285d (2026-11-04): 314 vertical: instr 1.08x, cycles 1.13x (1.950G vs 1.808G); seq 1.16 -> 1.31x rustc -O, the largest move here. 318 max_product: instr 1.09x, cycles 1.12x (3.998G vs 3.682G); seq 1.26 -> 1.33x. 1665 greedy: instr 1.20x, cycles 1.16x (0.066G vs 0.055G), a 3 ms kernel; seq improved against the 2026-06-16 feed (2.83 -> 1.28x). Carried from earlier runs on g6697158fa: 214 shortest_palindrome: instr 1.08x, cycles 1.05x (4.360G vs 4.022G); seq 0.98 -> 1.10x. 247 strobogrammatic_ii: instr 1.07x, cycles 1.03x (8.076G vs 7.533G); seq 1.09 -> 1.23x, mostly comparator drift. 288 uniqueabbr: instr 1.08x, cycles 1.08x (2.108G vs 1.960G); seq 1.60 -> 1.81x. 895 freq_stack: seq is better than legacy (instr 0.84x, cycles 0.92x) but par went 6.85 -> 7.72 ms on a 7 ms lane, 1.90 -> 2.31x rayon and 1.52 -> 1.77x Go-par; seq-to-par gain is 3.5x against rayon's 4.6x. X86 2026-11-05 (callgrind, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, main 0901a9fe6c vs legacy dd86e3955, outputs equal): 314 vertical 1.071x instructions, 318 max_product 1.192x, 214 shortest_palindrome 1.007x, 247 strobogrammatic_ii 1.015x, 288 uniqueabbr 0.926x, 1665 greedy 1.288x (78.3M vs 60.8M, a sort_by comparator kernel, not attributed). 318 IS ATTRIBUTED: `write_word(mut letters, mut lens, ...)` is called from two sites and stays a call on MIR (its body is over the inlinehint bounds in src/backend/mir/mod.rs, 32 blocks / 32 statements), so `lens` lives in memory across it, LLVM cannot know its length is still 6000, and the hot `j` loop keeps `lens[j]`'s bounds check and reloads its data pointer on every match (14 instructions a match against legacy's 10). With write_word's body pasted into both call sites the MIR build runs 2.458G instructions, legacy's 2.458G exactly. A fix is an inlining decision (a larger hint bound, or hinting a body whose callers pass a local Vec by `mut ref`), which needs a frozen-set run for code size and build time. 1665 ATTRIBUTED AND PARTLY FIXED 2026-11-06 (drop schedule, callgrind on x86): the comparator key (b.1 - b.0) has 50 distinct values, so sort_by takes the gated partition, whose counting pass tagged each element `1 + gt - lt` from the adapter's order; LLVM cannot see through the inlined comparator that the order is -1, 0 or 1, and spent 25 instructions an element where legacy's count pass spends 13 (legacy calls the comparator again in its scatter pass instead of keeping tags). baceefb375 tags `trunc(order) + 1`: 21 an element, 78.3M -> 71.6M instructions (legacy 60.8M), 1.29x -> 1.18x. The rest is the tag store and a loop-invariant overflow check of the pivot's key that stays in the loop (`test cl; jne` per element); calling the comparator twice, as legacy does, would change the call schedule the interpreter pins. 318 MEASURED 2026-11-06 (drop schedule): `opt -passes=default<O2> -pass-remarks-missed=inline` on the -O0 IR says write_word is 'too costly to inline (cost=370, threshold=225)' at both call sites, after its three `next` calls are inlined into it (cost 60 each). It is 22 blocks and 41 statements, so the inlinehint bound (32/32) leaves it unhinted; hinting it changes nothing (bounds 32/48 and 48/64 gave the same binary, 2.930G instructions), as the hint's threshold is 325. Inlining it needs a threshold over 370, a global change for code size and build time; not landed. M5 RE-RUN 2026-11-07, Gowtham's Mac via scripts/bench/m5-rows.sh at kara 3dc7786b7f, kara-katas 3fc59b3f, LLVM 22.1.8, 5 runs, sinks equal: 314 1.107x cycles (1.084x instructions) and 318 1.086x instructions within; 1665 1.167x instructions over (x86 1.18x after baceefb375). The script carried only those three; 214, 247, 288 (pair, instructions) and 895 (par, wall) are in it from 2026-11-07. X86 RE-MEASURED 2026-11-09 (Thread C, callgrind, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, the bench's greedy.kara, outputs equal): main c1a8b938ff 68.2M instructions against legacy dd86e3955 (built against LLVM 18, as the M5 script builds it) 60.8M, 1.12x, inside the 1.15x bar; it was 71.6M (1.18x) after baceefb375. a806504986 (the own-order sort_by path) does not apply: the comparator is a key difference, not `a.cmp(b)`. The legacy-archive head 741fbf08c1 built against LLVM 22 runs it in 78.5M, so the reference is dd86 on LLVM 18. Closing needs the M5 figure (1.167x at 3dc7786b7f, when x86 read 1.18x).

title: A closure or task made in each arm of an `if`, each moving the same value in, is refused as "moved into a closure, used again here" (or "moved into a task of `group`"), though no run makes both; inside a loop it fires even when the value is declared in the loop body
detail: Found porting mini_ledger (kara-katas apps/cli/mini_ledger): `if name.ends_with(".journal") { handles.push(group.spawn(|| Loaded.Journal(parse_journal(path, fidx, text)))) } else { handles.push(group.spawn(|| Loaded.Csv(import_csv(path, fidx, text, rules)))) }` inside `for (fidx, name) in names.iter().enumerate()`, with `path` and `text` declared in the loop body. The same shape with a direct call `work(text, i)` in each arm checks; with a closure `let c = || work(text, i); c()` (taking `own String`) or a task it was refused. The RC predicate's mutual-exclusion rule (B-2026-07-31-28) is gated to `Direct` consumes, since a closure body's blocks are not on the CFG's paths; a capture consume was left with dominance incomparability alone, which two `if` arms satisfy.
fix: f575bce6f0. The RC predicate (src/rc_predicate.rs, `first_witness`) now gives a capture consume the mutual-exclusion test that B-2026-07-31-28 gave a direct one, asked where the closures are made rather than where their bodies' blocks sit: a closure moves its captures in when it is made (core semantics §9.3, §9.6), and a use in another closure's body runs no earlier than that one is made. When the two creation blocks (or the creation block and a plain use's block) reach neither each other, along paths that do not pass a fresh `let` or assignment of the binding, the pair is dropped. The second clause is what clears the loop case: a value declared in the loop body is a new value on each turn, so the back edge does not join the two arms. A closure made inside another closure's body is left alone, since when it is made is not on the edges (that kept `a_closure_returning_a_capturing_closure_is_once` refusing). Pinned in tests/closure_moves_on_exclusive_paths.rs: tasks in each arm of an `if`, with and without a loop, and plain closures in each arm, all check and run on the MIR interpreter; the value declared outside the loop, a use after the `if`, two tasks in a row, and tasks in each arm inside a loop over an outer value still refuse. mini_ledger spawns its two kinds of parse tasks this way again.

title: `match p.c { C.At(s) => .. }` with `p` from `.iter()` is taken as consuming `p.c`, so it is refused as "cannot consume `p.c` while closure at line N captures `p.c` by `ref`" when a live closure reads `p.c`
detail: Found porting mini_ledger: in `Ledger.book`, `let fits = |l: Lot| match p.cost { Cost.At(ca) => .., _ => true };` and later `let what = match p.cost { Cost.At(ca) => f"..", _ => c.clone() };`, with `p` from `t.postings.iter()`. The same match with no closure checks, since `p` is a borrow and its field cannot be moved out; but the per-arm consume of a place scrutinee ran the closure-capture conflict check first. Repro: `for p in ps.iter() { let fits = |x: i64| match p.c { C.At(s) => s.len() == x, _ => true }; let w = match p.c { C.At(s) => s.clone(), _ => "".to_string() }; println(f"{fits(1)} {w}"); }`.
fix: f575bce6f0. `is_borrow_typed_scrutinee` (src/ownership/expr_check.rs) also answers true for a field or tuple-index chain whose root is typed `ref T` or `mut ref T` (a binding from `.iter()`, a `ref` parameter): such a place is matched in place and its bindings borrow (core semantics §4.6), so the match reads the scrutinee and the closure-capture conflict check no longer runs on it. Pinned by `a_match_on_a_field_a_closure_reads_through_a_borrow` (tests/closure_moves_on_exclusive_paths.rs), which checks and prints `true x` / `true ` on the MIR interpreter. mini_ledger's `Ledger.book` matches `p.cost` after its `fits` closure again.

title: `karac fmt` rewrites a script-mode file into an explicit `fn main()`, its top-level statements moved after every item; since B-2026-11-04-19 it also writes the implicit main's `-> Result[(), AnyError]` and `Ok(())`, so formatting a script changes its shape (design.md § Script mode)
fix: e5ccf4fc0c. The parser marks the main it synthesizes around a script's top-level statements (Program::script_main, src/parser.rs), and the formatter (src/formatter.rs format_program, format_top_level_stmt in src/formatter/stmts.rs) writes those statements back at the top level in file order among the items, consecutive statements in one paragraph, and never writes the implicit main, its `-> Result[(), AnyError]` or its `Ok(())` (review-thread ruling 2026-11-04: fmt preserves a script's form). The row's repro `let x = 1;\nprintln(x);\n` formats to itself. Pinned in tests/fmt_script_mode.rs: a script using `?` with an item between its statements formats to an exact text, is a fixed point, contains no `fn main` or `Ok(())`, and runs the same (2, big, 4) before and after; tests/fmt_round_trip.rs over the corpus stays green.

title: A trait's default method body calling `self.m()` is refused as ambiguous ("ambiguous method 'm' on receiver of type 'S'") in the copy for a type that also implements another trait with a method `m`; inside trait `A`'s default, `self.m()` is `A.m`
fix: d78c610976. The typechecker marks a trait impl's method whose span lies outside the impl block (a default body copied in by desugar keeps the trait's spans) with its trait (current_default_trait), and dispatch_user_impl_method narrows a `self.m()` lookup with several candidates to that trait's impl when exactly one matches, as `self: Self: A` has in the trait. A call on the concrete type (`s.m()`) stays ambiguous. MIR lowering needed nothing further: the repro with both traits defaulting over two types prints 11/102/15/110 on interp, `karac run`, `karac build`, mir-llvm and ASan (pin corpus/design/ok_trait_default_self_call_names_its_trait; tests/mutfn_owned_arg_and_trait_default_check.rs).

6dcdc1a604 (karac on LLVM 22, inkwell llvm22-1 / llvm-sys 221): as attributed, the cause was the LLVM version, not Kara's IR. LLVM 22 counts the two-pointer loop and vectorizes the reversed swap, with no change to what karac emits for it. x86 (drop schedule, callgrind, bench/reverse_string.kara): 0.254G instructions against 3.604G on the LLVM 18 build, same sink, wall 0.073 s against 0.295 s. M5 CONFIRMATION, Gowtham via scripts/bench/m5-rows.sh (row added 386feaf5f9) at eb17818b45, Darwin arm64, 5 runs: 816.0M instructions against legacy's 4015.1M (0.203x), at the row's bar of rustc -O's 0.819G.
title: Kata 344's two-pointer reverse stays scalar: LLVM 18's SCEV cannot count a loop whose bound moves (`while i < j { ...; i += 1; j -= 1 }`) and its dependence analysis rejects the reversed swap, where LLVM 22 (rustc 1.98) and Apple clang vectorize it; 4.5x instructions on x86, 4.9x on the M5
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-04 on the M5 Pro, karac 0.8.0-dev.14374+gf0017054a, bench/reverse_string.kara, exact counts via scripts/pmc.c: kara 4.017G instructions, 471M cycles; rustc -O 0.819G, 196M; rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on 0.818G, 194M; clang -O3 0.814G, 194M. Legacy dd86e3955 is 4.015G, 470M (1.00x, 1.00x). Wall: 2.47x Rust at either safety, 2.48x C. The kernel is a two-pointer swap, `while i < j { let t = s[i]; s[i] = s[j]; s[j] = t; i += 1; j -= 1; }`, and the checked Rust build shows overflow checks cost nothing here, so the gap is not the overflow-check cost. #345 (reverse-vowels, which branches on each byte) is 0.88x Rust. Not attributed: whether the comparators vectorize this loop and Kara's bounds checks prevent it has not been confirmed. ATTRIBUTED 2026-11-04 (drop-schedule thread, Linux x86, callgrind): rustc 1.98 -O on the comparator source runs 0.804G instructions against Kara's 3.604G (same sink 258295624; a counter confirms Rust does all 400M swaps). rustc's binary vectorizes the inlined loop (movdqu, pshufd $0x1b, movdqu: 8 swaps an iteration); Kara's is the scalar two-load/two-store loop with its bounds checks already gone. The cause is the LLVM version, not Kara's IR: clang-18 -O3 on the C comparator with rev inlined and the length known stays scalar ("could not determine number of loop iterations"), while rustc 1.98 bundles LLVM 22.1. A counted form (trip count d/2 + (d&1) precomputed, `for k < cnt`) gets LLVM 18 to 2.403G and 211 ms against 4.003G and 259 ms for the C loop, but still not vectorized ("unsafe dependent memory operations in loop"), so a two-pointer rewrite in the backend would buy about 1.67x instructions and 1.2x wall, not the gap; it was not done (review thread, 2026-11-04). Left open against the LLVM upgrade question.

fix: a723c25762. SimplifyCFG's two-entry phi-node folding threshold is 6 rather than LLVM's 4 in the AOT pipeline (mir_aot.rs, KARAC_MIR_PHI_FOLD_THRESHOLD), so kata 342's `n > 0` is folded beside the ctpop and the arm64 loop branches once per element. M5 pass (review thread's m5-rows, kara 6e709e5fdd, Darwin arm64, 5 runs each): 342 vs legacy 521.6M vs 521.4M cycles, 1.000x (instructions 1.049x); 342 at 6 vs 4 517.2M vs 682.5M, 0.758x; 229 0.992x; 391 0.996x; 467 0.983x; kata 7 1.111x, the one regression (x86 1.05x). Kata 7's cause is attributed and filed as B-2026-11-07-1 (low): its rare `result == min_div and digit < -8` overflow guard is folded into a select computed every digit. All within the 1.15x bar.
title: Kata 342 ran 1.20x legacy's instructions and 1.39x its cycles on the MIR backend; arm64 loop branched twice (ctpop over SimplifyCFG's phi-fold threshold); FIXED a723c25762 (threshold 4 -> 6), M5 1.000x legacy, kata 7 +11% filed as B-2026-11-07-1
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-04 on the M5 Pro, karac 0.8.0-dev.14374+gf0017054a vs legacy dd86e3955, bench/power_of_four.kara, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, exact counts via scripts/pmc.c (3-run minima): 0.819G vs 0.683G instructions, 723M vs 522M cycles. First M5 run, so no earlier ratio. Wall 2.45x rustc -O, but 1.02x rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on, so most of the gap to Rust is overflow checks. Read from rustc's assembly, not measured: `-O` makes the 50M-iteration classification loop branchless (csel/cinc), while the checked build branches on each acceptance and carries adds/b.vs for `count += 1` and `sum += x`. The 1.39x is what MIR adds on top of legacy, and is not attributed. ATTRIBUTED 2026-11-04 on x86 (callgrind, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0): 1.111x legacy's instructions (587.1M against 528.3M), unchanged by the -39 call-convention fixes. The hot loop over `a` is the same shape in both builds, unrolled by two. Per element MIR spends `xor; popcnt; cmp; jae` where legacy spends `lea; and; jne` (LLVM's InstCombine turned the i32 `n & (n - 1) == 0` into `ctpop(n) < 2`; legacy's IR sign-extends first and keeps the and), and MIR carries a second per-element induction variable that the hit count's overflow check compares against a limit (`cmp %r15,%rax; je`) where legacy uses `inc; jo`. Both are LLVM's choices from equivalent IR; nothing backend-specific found. The 1.39x cycle ratio on the M5 is not explained by two instructions an element and needs the Mac's counters. ATTRIBUTED 2026-11-06 on arm64 (Thread B, karac's real pipeline cross-built for aarch64-apple-darwin with the object kept): the hot loop branched twice per element on data, `cmp w11,#1; b.lt` for `n > 0` and then a ccmp chain's `b.ne`, where legacy's loop (LLVM 18, apple-m1) branches once on a three-way ccmp chain. After the early sroa/instcombine prefix, InstCombine turns `(n & (n - 1)) == 0` into `ctpop(n) < 2` before SimplifyCFG folds the short-circuit; a ctpop costs more than LLVM's two-entry phi folding threshold of 4 on aarch64, so `n > 0` stays a branch. On random data both branches mispredict, which fits cycles rising at the same instruction count; x86 shows nothing because both compilers branch three times there and run level (0.356 s vs 0.354 s). a723c25762 sets the threshold to 6 (KARAC_MIR_PHI_FOLD_THRESHOLD): the arm64 loop then has one branch. x86 frozen set: 29 of 707 change, 0.969x geomean, 229 0.68x best, 7/391/467 1.03-1.05x worst. The close waits on m5-rows: the env:KARAC_MIR_PHI_FOLD_THRESHOLD=4 rows for 342, 229, 7, 391 and 467, and the pair row against legacy.

title: Kata 333 executes 1.28x legacy's instructions on the M5 at 3dc7786b7f (1.19x at eb17818b45): ce0cf3209b's `dereferenceable` on its `mut ref` parameter added 6.0% (x86 too); 321, 337, 338, 339 and 343 are within
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-04 on the M5 Pro, karac 0.8.0-dev.14374+gf0017054a vs legacy dd86e3955, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, exact counts via scripts/pmc.c (3-run minima). First M5 runs, so no earlier wall ratio. 321 create_max_number instr 1.14x, cycles 1.04x (15.180G vs 13.284G). 333 largest_bst 1.21x, 1.01x (1.155G vs 0.952G). 337 house_robber_iii 1.21x, 0.88x (3.774G vs 3.123G). 338 counting_bits 1.26x, 1.06x (4.367G vs 3.465G). 339 nested_weight_sum 1.17x, 1.06x (3.134G vs 2.668G). 343 integer_break 1.24x, 1.08x (6.122G vs 4.946G). And the reverse shape: 326 power_of_three instr 0.99x, cycles 1.13x (0.394G vs 0.400G; 460M vs 408M). Same set's clear wins, sinks agreeing across languages: 331 verify_preorder instr 0.16x, 341 flatten_iterator 0.37x, 325 max_sub_len 0.51x. ATTRIBUTED AND PARTLY FIXED 2026-11-04 on x86 (callgrind instruction counts, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, MIR against legacy dd86e3955). Before: 337 1.323x, 343 1.141x, 338 1.151x, 333 1.123x, 321 1.124x, 339 1.093x. Three backend causes, fixed in 4286297660: (1) a 16-byte result (337's `(i64, i64)`) had no register class, so the whole call went through memory and each `ref Vec` parameter arrived as a pointer to a slot holding the reference; a tuple or plain struct of two scalars now returns in a register pair (KARAC_MIR_PAIR_REGS=0 reverts). (2) A larger result (333's four-field `Info`) did the same; it is now written through a pointer the function takes first, the parameters staying in registers (KARAC_MIR_SRET_REGS=0 reverts). (3) The runtime's vector and string growth entry points were declared without `nocapture`, so a local vector's slot escaped and every store through its buffer reloaded its length and data pointer (343's `best[i] = whole`). After: 337 1.035x, 333 1.050x, 343 1.084x, 338 1.101x. Pinned by tests/mir_pair_and_sret_calls.rs. LEFT: 338's `for i in 1..=n` lowers to a header Le test plus a latch Eq exit, which keeps `ans[i]`'s bounds check in the loop (13 against 11 instructions an iteration); MIR-builder shaped, sent to Thread B. 321 (1.124x, unchanged): legacy inlines `shrink` into `main`, where `nums` and `out` are distinct locals; the MIR build calls it, and with no `noalias` on its `ref`/`mut ref` parameters the loop reloads `nums.len()` after each `out[top]` store and keeps `nums[i]`'s bounds check. The fix would be `noalias` on reference parameters whose referent holds no inline interior mutability (`Atomic`, `Mutex`), as Rust marks `&T` and `&mut T`; not done here, as it needs a soundness review against core-semantics 5.9 and 6.2. 339 (1.093x, unchanged): `text.chars().collect()` runs 17 instructions a char against 10: the source String's header is reloaded after each store into the new buffer (the collect's outlined grow returns `{ptr, cap}`, so LLVM cannot see the buffer is fresh), plus a bounds check and a width test the legacy loop folds. Close on the M5 re-run: scripts/bench/m5-rows.sh carries the six katas. M5 RE-RUN, Gowtham via scripts/bench/m5-rows.sh, 2026-11-04 at 4286297660: 337, 343 and 321 within the bar; 333 1.192x, 338 1.173x, 339 1.154x still over. 338's `..=` loop shape is the MIR builder's (Thread B took it). Kept open for the three. M5 RE-RUN 2026-11-05, Gowtham via scripts/bench/m5-rows.sh at eb17818b45 (LLVM 22), kara-katas cac611dc, 5 runs: 337 1.026x, 343 1.098x, 321 1.084x, 339 1.137x within; 333 1132.7M vs 952.4M instructions 1.189x and 338 4066.8M vs 3465.3M 1.174x still over, against x86's 1.05x and 1.10x. Kept open for those two; the arm64-only part of their gap is unattributed. 338's `..=` LATCH FIXED 2026-11-05 at 9b61847653 (Thread B): the latch tests `i == MAX` of the counter's type instead of `i == n`, so LLVM keeps `i <= n` and drops `ans[i]`'s bounds check. Callgrind x86 against legacy dd86e3955: 338 6.599G -> 6.300G (1.101x -> 1.051x of 5.992G); 529 10.19G -> 8.66G (legacy cannot build it); 526 5.134G -> 5.923G (0.866x -> 0.999x of 5.930G, LLVM's loop strength reduction picks a worse counter); the 13 other corpus benches with a `..=` loop within 0.1%. Still open for 333 and the M5 re-run of 338. M5 RE-RUN 2026-11-07, Gowtham's Mac via scripts/bench/m5-rows.sh at 3dc7786b7f, kara-katas 3fc59b3f, LLVM 22.1.8, 5 runs, sinks equal: 337 1.027x, 343 1.097x, 338 0.914x (the `..=` latch fix), 321 1.090x, 339 1.137x within; 333 1.284x over, up from 1.189x. ATTRIBUTED 2026-11-07 on x86 (callgrind, drop schedule): 333 ran 1.160G instructions at eb17818b45 and 1.230G at 3dc7786b7f; KARAC_MIR_DEREF_PARAM=0 gives 1.160G back, and so does leaving the attribute off `mut ref` parameters alone (a scratch switch), with teemo's `ref` win kept (1.530G either way; without `ref` 1.705G). `visit(..., best: mut ref i64)` may now load `*best` speculatively, so `bst and size > *best` folds to a flag `or`, and the flags live across the recursive call in a stack slot. x86 wall time does not show it (5 interleaved runs each). Dropping the attribute on every `mut ref` was swept over the 719 kata benches with a `mut ref`: 697 identical binaries, 22 changed, instruction geomean 1.000 (529 0.787x and 17% faster wall, 333 0.943x, 980 0.962x; 157 1.089x and 6% slower wall, 158 1.066x, 348 1.053x, 702 1.048x), so it was not landed. A fix is a per-site decision (the speculated load folding a short-circuit `and`, as B-2026-11-07-1's phi fold does), not the attribute. RE-MEASURED 2026-11-09 at 5cfb46bd3d (Thread B, x86 callgrind, bench/largest_bst.kara, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, sinks equal): 1.219G, KARAC_MIR_DEREF_PARAM=0 1.159G, legacy dd86e3955 1.104G, so 1.104x of legacy on x86; d308599fbb did not move it. Optimized IR: with the attribute, SimplifyCFG turns `bst and size > *best` into `select bst_false, true, size <= *best` with the load speculated, so `bst` is no longer a constant per edge and its phi lives across the second recursive call. That is the extra callee-saved value. Still open for the M5's 1.28x.

title: The MIR effect pass gives every call of an `extern` function every effect, ignoring its declaration: two `par` branches that each call a `pure fn` from an `unsafe extern "C"` block are refused with `unknown (native labs)` and `unknown (native labs)`, though design.md § Effects ("an `extern` function ... has the effects it declares, none if it is declared `pure`") and core-semantics §12 item 2 give it none
fix: b8f73d1a3f. The MIR effect pass now charges an `extern` call the clause its declaration carries. `ExternSig` gained `effects: Option<Vec<DeclaredEffect>>`, filled in `lower.rs` from the extern declaration: `pure` is the empty list, a declared clause is its list, and no clause stays `None`. In `effects.rs` the native-call arm looks the extern up and charges `clause_set(declared)`, the same mapping `declared_fn_value_effects` uses for fn values (network and file-system resources keyed fresh, others Any); `None` stays `EffectSet::unknown()`, so an extern with no clause is still treated as doing anything. Pin: corpus/core/ok_par_pure_extern, two `par` branches each calling a helper that calls `pure fn labs` from an `unsafe extern "C"` block; it prints "3 4", and a release build from before the fix refuses it with the row's `unknown (native labs)` conflict. A first draft of the pin with both `unsafe` blocks inside the `par` was refused by tests/fmt_round_trip.rs after formatting, filed as B-2026-11-04-53. Gate: fmt, both clippy legs, `cargo test --all` (10249 passed) and `cargo test --features llvm` (10411 passed), 0 failed.

title: Rust's `Box.new(e)` (what `Box::new(e)` becomes) gets `undefined name 'Box', did you mean 'Hex'?` with no fix, though Kāra has no `Box` (design.md § dyn Trait: "There is no `Box`: the owned form is the handle") and the answer is `e` itself
detail: Found closing B-2026-11-04-7, whose repro (2) is `fn mk(k: i64) -> Box<dyn Fn(i64) -> i64> { Box::new(move |x| x + k) }\nfn main() { let f = mk(2); println(f(3)); }`. The return type now gets its own diagnostic and edit (`-> Fn(i64) -> i64`); the body does not. `fn mk(k: i64) -> Fn(i64) -> i64 { Box.new(|x| x + k) }` and `let b = Box.new(5);` -> error[resolve] "undefined name 'Box', did you mean 'Hex'?" (the suggested edit renames it to `Hex`). Since c2a612b69c reads `Box::new` as `Box.new`, `karac fix` applies the suggestion and writes `Hex.new(|x| x + k)`, a new error ("`Hex.new` is removed"); before it, the parser's recovery inserted `;` after `Box` (`Box;::new(..)`). Expected: a Rust-ism diagnostic naming the heap box, with the edit `Box.new(e)` -> `e`, when no `Box` is declared.
fix: a3e6d2fd30: the resolver names Rust's heap box for an undeclared `Box` ("`Box` is Rust's heap box: Kāra has none (design.md § dyn Trait) ... so `Box.new(e)` is `e`") and offers no near-name rename, so `karac fix` no longer writes `Hex.new(e)`. For `Box.new(e)` / `Box::new(e)` with one unlabeled argument the parser records the edit that writes `e` in the call's place (`Program::rust_box_new`, keyed by the offset of `Box`), and the resolver attaches it. tests/rust_spelling_decl_fix.rs karac_fix_writes_the_value_for_rusts_box_new (a returned closure and a `Box.new(5)` value, fixed and run); tests/mend_rustisms.rs r20_box_dyn_fn (the B-2026-11-04-7 repro) now mends end to end.

title: An empty list literal with no expected type (`let mut w = [];`) is refused by `karac check` with MIR's internal "a type that failed to check is not lowered yet", not a diagnostic saying the element type is needed
fix: aa857c6355. An unannotated `let` (and `let ... else`) whose value is the empty list literal reports E_EMPTY_PREFIX_LITERAL_NEEDS_ANNOTATION, "cannot infer the element type of the empty list literal `[]`: this `let` does not say what it holds", with a `Vec.new()` fix-it (src/typechecker/items.rs, report_empty_list_literal in src/typechecker.rs); `let mut w = []; w.push(1)` fixes to `Vec.new()` and prints [1]. The row's caution held: reporting EVERY synthesized `[]` refused `report([])` in 31 corpus katas, because call arguments are synthesized and then unified, so the report is limited to the `let`, where the literal can get no expected type. Remaining internal-message case, not in this row's repro: `v == []` still reaches MIR's "not lowered yet". A full check sweep (27,484 programs) against the previous binary changed no verdict. Pinned by tests/literal_temporaries_and_empty_let.rs.

title: A `let` keeping a borrow of a prefix `Vec` literal's temporary (`let g = Vec["a"].last();`, and `vec!["a"].last()`, the same node) is refused late, as E0516 "cannot drop the temporary value ... while `g` still borrows it", where the list literal `["a"].last()` gets the §5.5 rule "a reference to a temporary outlives its statement"; next to another refusal the late E0516 never shows
fix: aa857c6355. core_expr_is_temp (src/typechecker/items.rs) counts a prefix literal (`Vec[..]`, and `vec![..]`, the same node), a repeat literal and a map literal as temporaries, as the list literal already was; the ref-returning tail's `fresh` list the same. `let g = Vec["a", "b"].last();` is now refused at 2:13 with "a reference to a temporary outlives its statement (core-semantics.md §5.5)", not later by MIR's E0516, and so is `[["a"]; 2].last()` and `["a": 1].get("a")`. The full check sweep changed exactly one diagnostic list, the b_2026_09_30_80 fixture the row came from, which now shows the §5.5 refusal. The interim formatter note is gone: since the review thread's ask the formatter prints a literal as written (`(Vec[..]).m()`), so it no longer needs this fix to write `[..]`. Pinned by tests/literal_temporaries_and_empty_let.rs.

title: Reading a `private` field from another directory is refused with code E0221 (PrivateTypeInPublicSignature) instead of E0111 PrivateItemAccess, which design.md §4 names for direct access to an invisible item (leftover of B-2026-11-04-22)
detail: Repro (probe mp/m24_private_field_other_dir): src/db/c.kara `pub struct S { pub a: i64, private secret: i64 }\npub fn mk() -> S { S { a: 1, secret: 2 } }`; src/main.kara `import db.c.{mk};\nfn main() { let s = mk(); println(s.secret); }` -> error[E0221] src/main.kara:2:35 "field 'secret' of struct 'S' is `private`: visible only to files in the same directory as module `db.c`". The refusal and message are right (B-2026-11-04-22 fixed, a3e6d2fd30 era); the code is not. Spec: §4 Visibility "A non-`pub` type in a `pub` signature is `E0221 PrivateTypeInPublicSignature`. Direct access to an invisible item is `E0111 PrivateItemAccess`"; §5 field visibility takes the three levels of §4. Item-level E0111 is already used for a `private fn` imported from another directory (m12). Expected: E0111 on the field access (and on a struct literal naming the field).
fix: 3942d674ca. A new TypeErrorKind::PrivateFieldAccess carries the field refusal (src/typechecker/fields.rs, both sites) and maps to E0111 in src/cli/diag_json.rs and build_cmds.rs type_error_code; it counts as a module-boundary rule like E0221 did. E0111 is now minted by the resolver (an item) and the typechecker (a field), both for design.md §4's "direct access to an invisible item", so src/cli/explain.rs names it in SPEC_SHARED_CODES, which the two-phase guard skips and checks for staleness; `karac explain E0111` keeps its one row. The row's second expectation found a missing refusal: a struct literal naming a `private` field from another directory was ACCEPTED. infer_struct_literal_expected now runs the same visibility check on each named field, so the literal is refused with E0111 too. Pinned by tests/private_field_code.rs (read and literal); tests/module_graph.rs field cases assert the new kind.

title: With two `From` impls on one type, `Out.from(c)` calls the FIRST impl's `from` whatever the argument (prints 6 for `Out.from(C { n: 6 })` whose impl multiplies by 10), on run and --interp; with argument-less headers (`impl From for Out` twice, told apart by the parameter) `.into()` picks the first impl too
fix: c922a27b91 (Thread B), with 4159d2c978. A path call `Out.from(x)` resolved to one `from` by name and took the first impl. `trait_sibling_by_args` in src/mir/lower.rs now looks at the sibling functions of the same trait on the same target (same name, arity, no `self`, no own generics) and picks the unique one whose parameter types equal the argument types; it runs just before the call is built, so a single impl is untouched. 4159d2c978 covers the argument-less headers: two `impl From for Out` used to share one MIR instance name, so the second body was never emitted and `.into()` and `Out.from(..)` both reached the first; `impl_suffix` now numbers impls with no trait arguments too. The repro prints 50 / 60 under `karac run` and `run --interp`, and the argument-less form prints 50 / 60 / 7. Pinned by corpus/core/conversion_from_picks_impl_by_argument (design.md § Conversion traits, 2000/610/7/4/305/1000) and tests/trait_bound_dispatch.rs `from_impls_without_trait_arguments`. The checker half for a user generic trait (`impl Make[i64]` + `impl Make[String]`, `Out.make(s)` refused at check) is its own row, B-2026-11-04-54.

title: `self.raw()` in a method of a `distinct type` whose receiver is a bare (borrowed, D5) `self` is refused after check: "`raw` of a borrowed distinct value is not lowered yet"
detail: Repro: `distinct type Ids = Vec[i64];\nimpl Ids { fn first(self) -> i64 { self.raw()[0] } }\nfn main() { let ids = Ids([7, 8].to_vec()); println(ids.first()); }` -> `karac check` passes; `karac run --interp` -> error[typecheck] 2:36 "`raw` of a borrowed distinct value is not lowered yet" (the MIR builder's `unsupported`, src/mir/lower.rs `method == "raw"` arm); same at the control binary e87b92a440. design.md § Coherence now points authors who want methods on a library type at a `distinct type` (B-2026-11-04-15), and a bare receiver borrows under D5, so this is the natural shape. Expected 7.
fix: 36c03e2120. `.raw()` of a borrowed distinct value whose base is not Copy (a bare `self` under D5, `ref self`, a borrowed parameter) is now a borrow of the base, `ref Base`: the checker knows when `self` is a borrow (current_self_borrowed) and types it so, and the MIR builder borrows field 0. A Copy base is still copied and an owned receiver still gives up its base. Deliberate reading of design.md's 'returns the base type' for a borrowed receiver, so `fn f(self) -> Vec[i64] { self.raw() }` is now a type error rather than a MIR refusal. Pinned by corpus/fixtures/distinct_types/raw_of_borrowed_receiver (interp, llvm, asan).

title: A trait default method that calls another of the trait's methods (`fn shout(self, n: i64) -> String { let s = self.tag(); .. }`), reached through a blanket impl over a bare parameter (`impl[T: Display] Shout for T`), is refused after check: "the method call `.tag` with no resolved callee is not lowered yet", by a bound (`fn go[U: Shout](u: U) { u.shout(3) }`) and on a concrete receiver alike
fix: 36c03e2120. In a blanket impl's body, a method of the impl called on the impl's own parameter (`self.tag()` in `impl[T: Display] Shout for T`, written there or in a trait default copied into it) now calls that impl's method at the instance, ahead of an inherent method of the receiver's type: the MIR builder's no-callee fallback looks up the blanket fn's sibling (blanket_sibling). Not specific to default bodies: the same call written in the impl failed too. Pinned by corpus/fixtures/coherence/blanket_impl_sibling_call (interp, llvm, asan) and tests/coherence_impls.rs a_blanket_default_body_calls_the_impls_own_method.

title: An inherent impl on a type alias of the program's own struct (`type Wrap = W; impl Wrap { fn get(self) -> i64 { .. } }`) passes check, then `W { n: 4 }.get()` fails in MIR: "call of unknown function W.get" (--interp), "native `W.get` is not lowered yet" (run)
fix: fbe0caf3bc. An impl through a non-generic alias of the program's own struct is that struct's: the def table interns the impl target through the alias (aliases are added before impls), the checker types the impl's self as the aliased struct, and UFCS through either name (Wrap.get(w), W.get(w)) is the receiver call, recorded under the name as written so lowering rewrites it. Pinned by corpus/fixtures/coherence/inherent_impl_through_alias (interp, llvm, asan) and tests/coherence_impls.rs an_inherent_impl_through_an_alias_of_an_own_struct_is_the_structs.

title: An iterator method called straight on a sequence draws an edit-distance guess with no fix for `find`, `position`, `nth`, `rev` and `flatten`: `windows.windows(2).find(|p| p[0] == p[1])` (kata 1044's Rust-shaped iterator arm) gets "no method 'find' on type 'Vec', did you mean 'fill'?", where `map`, `filter` or `any` get the `.iter()` hint and a fix
detail: Found writing kata 1044's iterator arm the way Rust does (`.windows(2).find(..)`, no `.iter()`). The typechecker's list of iterator-surface names (`is_iterator_surface_method`, src/typechecker/expr_method_call.rs), which says to keep in sync with `infer_iterator_method`'s own list (src/typechecker/stdlib_iter.rs), had drifted: it lacked find, flatten, nth, position and rev (and last and peek, which a sequence owns or which only Peekable has). Measured at b8f73d1a3f (the fix's parent) on Vec, Slice, Array and VecDeque receivers: `v.find(|x| x > 1)` -> "no method 'find' on type 'Vec', did you mean 'fill'?" plus a cascade "cannot compare '?T0' and 'i64'"; `v.position(..)`, `v.nth(1)`, `v.flatten()` -> "no method '<m>' on type 'Vec'" with no help; `v.rev()` -> "did you mean 'get'?". None carries a fix, so `karac fix` leaves the program refused. The cascade on the closure body is common to every name on the list (`v.filter(|x| x > 1)` has it too) and does not block the fix.
fix: 6ef646c141. `is_iterator_surface_method` (src/typechecker/expr_method_call.rs) gains `find`, `flatten`, `nth`, `position` and `rev`, the names of `infer_iterator_method`'s list it had drifted from; `last` (owned by Vec, Array and Slice, with its own VecDeque hint) and `peek` (Peekable only) stay off, and the doc comment says why. A direct call of any of the five on a Vec, VecDeque, Slice or Array now gets "iterator adaptors/terminals require an explicit `.iter()`" with the fix that inserts it. tests/mend_iter_surface.rs runs eight cells through check, fix to a fixpoint and `__mir-run`: find, position, nth and rev on a Vec, position on a Slice, find on an Array, and kata 1044's `w.windows(2).find(|p| p[0] == p[1])`, each printing the task's answer; `g.flatten()` over a `Vec[Vec[i64]]` gets the hop and then the open B-2026-11-04-52. Before the fix, each of the five drew a guess or nothing (measured at b8f73d1a3f). Kata 1044's Rust-shaped iterator arm now mends with `karac fix` and matches the mirror. The cascade "cannot compare '?T0' and 'i64'" on the closure body remains for every name on the list; it does not block the fix.

title: `.iter().flatten()` over collection items names the exact rewrite ("write `.flat_map(|v| v.iter())` in place of `.flatten()`") but carries no fix, so `karac fix` leaves `g.iter().flatten().collect()` on a `Vec[Vec[i64]]` refused
detail: Found with B-2026-11-04-51: once `g.flatten()` on `g = [[1, 2], [3]]` gets the `.iter()` hop, the next check refuses `g.iter().flatten()` with "`flatten` needs items that are themselves iterators (docs/library/iterators.md: `where Self.Item: Iterator`), and `ref Vec[i64]` is not one: write `.flat_map(|v| v.iter())` in place of `.flatten()`", and no fix. The message is emitted from two places (src/typechecker/exprs.rs, the projection-bound discharge, which already picks `iter` or `into_iter` by the item's mode; and src/typechecker/method_user_impl.rs, the IterFlatten bound), both with the whole call's span, so the edit needs the span of `.flatten()` alone. A Rust author writes `.flatten()` over `Vec[Vec[T]]` as a matter of course (Rust's `&Vec` is IntoIterator), so this is the common shape. Pinned as the first-step-only cell `vec_flatten` in tests/mend_iter_surface.rs.
fix: e9fa6bddd1. Each `.flatten()` call with no arguments records, by its span, the source span from the end of its receiver to its `)` (`flatten_calls`, filled in `infer_method_call`; the receiver's end comes from the new `receiver_end`, which `iter_hint_fix` now shares). Both places that refuse a `flatten` over collection items, the projection-bound discharge in src/typechecker/exprs.rs and the IterFlatten bound in src/typechecker/method_user_impl.rs, attach a fix rewriting that span to `.flat_map(|v| v.iter())`, or `v.into_iter()` where the items are owned. Measured on five shapes with check, fix to a fixpoint and `__mir-run`: `g.flatten()` on a `Vec[Vec[i64]]` (the `.iter()` hop, then this fix), `g.iter().flatten().collect()`, `g.into_iter().flatten().collect()`, `g.iter().flatten().map(..).count()` and `for x in g.iter().flatten()`, each now mending to a program that prints the right answer; before, each stopped at the refusal. tests/mend_iter_surface.rs: the `vec_flatten` cell now runs to "3", and a new `into_iter_flatten` cell prints "123". Gate: fmt, both clippy legs, `cargo test --all` (10254 passed) and `cargo test --features llvm` (10416 passed), 0 failed; after a rebase onto 14 commits, fmt, both clippy legs, the lib tests and the typechecker, mend and core_strict_check suites again.

title: `karac fmt` breaks an expression holding two `unsafe { .. }` blocks over lines, and the `undocumented_unsafe` lint then fires on the second though the statement carries a `// Safety:` comment: `// Safety: ..` above `let (a, b) = par { unsafe { labs(-3) }, unsafe { labs(-4) } };` is clean, and its formatted form is not, with no place a comment could go

With two impls of a user generic trait on one type (`impl Make[i64] for Out` + `impl Make[String] for Out`, `fn make(x: T) -> Self`), `Out.make("abcd".to_string())` is refused at check ("expected 'i64', found 'String'"): the checker picks among `From` impls by the argument's type but takes the first impl of any other trait
fix: 2b657fbeba. The checker picks among two or more impls of one trait on a type by the argument types of the associated function `T.f(args)` they declare (`impl Make[i64] for Out` + `impl Make[String] for Out`), as it already did for From/TryFrom, with an error naming each impl's parameters when none or several fit. `T.make(5)` under `T: Make[i64]` also binds the trait's parameter now ("expected 'T', found 'i64'" before, at the control too). MIR's own pick is B's c922a27b91. Pinned by corpus/fixtures/coherence/assoc_fn_impl_by_argument (interp, llvm, asan) and tests/coherence_impls.rs an_assoc_fn_of_two_impls_of_one_trait_is_picked_by_argument.

title: `PriorityQueue.pop` sifts down by swapping, two comparisons a level, where Rust's `BinaryHeap::pop` sifts a hole to the bottom with one: kata 1046's bench (1000 piles of 3000 stones, 3 rounds of the heap game) runs 2.66x Rust's time under overflow checks, of which the compiler is about 1.15x and the heap algorithm the rest
detail: Measured 2026-11-04 on a 4-core Linux container, kara f55808f63d release, eight interleaved runs: kata 1046's bench/last_stone.kara (KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0) median 1.618 s; rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on with std BinaryHeap 0.608 s; rustc -O 0.624 s; clang -O3 with a swap-sifting array heap like Kāra's 1.131 s; Go container/heap 2.896 s. Same sink everywhere (total 1563, checksum 142150343). Attribution: the same swap-sifting heap written by hand in Kāra runs 1.53-1.64 s and in Rust with overflow checks 1.32-1.39 s (C 1.12-1.15 s), so Kāra's codegen on that loop is about 1.15x checked Rust and the library's per-compare `if self.max` branch adds little (hand heap 1.53 s vs PriorityQueue 1.62 s); the remaining ~2.2x is the algorithm. runtime/stdlib/source/priority_queue.kara `pop` swaps the last element to the root and `sift_down` compares both children and the parent at each level, swapping; Rust's `pop` (`sift_down_to_bottom`) moves the root's hole to a leaf with one child comparison a level, moving rather than swapping, then sifts the last element up from there, which is fewer comparisons on random keys because the element usually belongs near the bottom. Remedy (a hypothesis): the same hole-based pop and sift_up (move, don't swap) in priority_queue.kara, and in its baked twin if that is still compiled.
fix: 5bd3da78cc. runtime/stdlib/source/priority_queue.kara and the baked runtime/stdlib/priority_queue.kara: `pop` calls a new `sift_down_to_bottom`, Floyd's pop as Rust's BinaryHeap::pop and Python's heapq do it (walk the root's slot to a leaf along the better child, one comparison a level, then sift the carried element back up; ties take the right child, as heapq). Moving rather than swapping, the row's other half, is not expressible for a generic T in Kāra (no hole), so it still swaps. MEASURED x86, best of 3-5, outputs equal: last_stone 1.96 s -> 0.91 s against Rust's 0.61 s (the row's 1.618 s / 0.608 s were another container). The row's hypothesis was half the story: the Floyd walk alone cut instructions 10.64G -> 7.34G (31%) and changed no wall time, because each level still branched on `self.max` (outranks) and on the random child pick. One loop per direction removed the first (1.68 s); picking the child as `c + (xs[c] <= xs[c + 1]) as i64`, which LLVM lowers to setcc/add instead of a branch, removed the second (0.91 s). The remaining 1.5x to Rust is the per-level bounds checks (the Vec's length reloads after each swap's stores) and the `2 * i + 1` overflow check. All 17 PriorityQueue benches: same output, 0.48x-1.03x the time. The other 186 PriorityQueue corpus programs pass on mir-interp and mir-llvm (COLLECTIONS_PAGE and kata 778's differential interp timeout were red before). Gate: fmt, both clippy legs, cargo test --all 10345/0, cargo test --features llvm 10513/0. Kata thread refreshes the 1046 README timings.

title: `karac check` does not run the MIR borrow check on a function that `main` never reaches, so a library package's `pub fn bad() -> Str { let s = "abc".to_string(); s.as_str() }` (a view of its own local escaping, E0516/E0509) is reported clean; the same function called from `main` is refused by check
detail: Repros (probe d1x/sv.kara, sv2.kara, mp/lb): `pub fn bad() -> Str { let s = "abc".to_string(); s.as_str() }\nfn main() { }` -> All checks passed; a package with only src/lib.kara holding that fn -> `karac check` All checks passed. Control: with `fn main() { let v = bad(); println(v); }` -> error[typecheck] 1:46 "cannot drop `s` while it is still borrowed ... [E0516]" (the MIR borrow check: `__mir-run` names E0516 and "the result borrows _1, which this function owns [E0509]"). Typecheck and the ownership pass DO run on unreached functions (`fn bad() -> i64 { let x: i64 = "a"; x }` and a use-after-move in an uncalled fn are refused, sv3/sv4), so it is the MIR-based checks that only see reachable functions. Spec: design.md §5 Strings "Returning a view of a `String` the function owns is an error"; core-semantics §5. A library is exactly where nothing is reachable from a `main`: its author gets a clean check and the error lands on the first dependent that calls the function. The same gap presumably covers every MIR-only check (par conflicts, effects inferred on MIR) in unreached code; worth confirming when fixing.
fix: 8c480bd9df (Thread B). A check (`lower_program_inner` with `signatures_only_from`) now also roots every function of the program's own that has no type parameters of its own or of its impl (not comptime, not a trait's default body), and needs no `main`. Those roots are built after everything `main` reaches, and the lowering errors they alone add are dropped: what the builder does not lower yet in a function nothing reaches is a build's to report, not check's. Over 3635 corpus programs (corpus/core, corpus/apps and 3000 sampled), the check verdict is unchanged with and without the change. A first cut without the error split refused 3 of them on builder gaps in unreached functions (a user Hasher's `write_u8`, a `T` that does not lower). Both repros are now refused at 3:5 with E0516: the uncalled `pub fn bad()` beside an empty `main`, and the lib-only package. Pinned by tests/check_unreached_fns.rs: an uncalled fn, an uncalled method, a library package, and sound uncalled and generic functions that still pass.

title: Three pattern shapes design.md §5 specifies pass the front end but are refused with "this pattern is not lowered yet": an or-pattern whose alternatives bind under a guard (`E.A(x) | E.B(x) if g(x) =>`), an or-pattern nested inside a variant (`Out.Foo(In.A | In.B) =>`), and an or-pattern in `if let` (`if let Lr.Left(x) | Lr.Right(x) = v`); a distinct type's literal pattern (`Uid(0) =>`) is refused the same way ("this variant is not lowered yet")
fix: 6ad941be02. All four shapes lower. A binding or-pattern under a guard binds through the first alternative that matches, runs the guard once against those bindings (design.md § Or-patterns and guards), goes on to the next arm when it is false, and moves a payload the arm takes only once the guard holds, from the alternative that matched. A binding or-pattern where the pattern is known to match (if let, while let, a nested alternative) binds through the first alternative that matches. A name resolving to a unit variant is not a binding, so `Out.Foo(In.A | In.B)` and `if let K.A | K.B = k` are tested rather than refused. `Uid(0)` / `Uid(n)` test and bind a distinct type's base, and exhaustiveness reads `Uid(n)` as covering every value (it was reported non-exhaustive at check too). Pinned by corpus/fixtures/or_patterns/{guard_after_binding_alternative,nested_in_variant,if_let_and_while_let} and corpus/fixtures/distinct_types/literal_pattern (interp, llvm, asan).

title: A list literal with a `Set[T]` expected type is refused: `let s: Set[i64] = [1, 2, 2, 3];` -> "expected 'Set[i64]', found 'Vec[i64]'", though design.md §5 Collection literals says the literal follows the expected type and builds a `Set` there
detail: Repro (probe d5/l02): `fn main() { let a: Array[i64, 3] = [1, 2, 3]; let z = [0u8; 4]; println(a[2]); println(z.len()); let s: Set[i64] = [1, 2, 2, 3]; println(s.len()); }` -> error[typecheck] 6:116 "expected 'Set[i64]', found 'Vec[i64]'" (expected 3, 4, 3). The Array and SortedMap/Map forms of the same rule work (l02 without the Set, l05). Spec: §5 Collection literals "`[a, b, c]` is a `Vec` by default and follows the expected type: with an `Array[T, N]` or `Set[T]` annotation it builds that type", example `let s: Set[i64] = [1, 2, 3];  // Set[i64]`; and "There is one way to write each collection" lists `Set.from([..])` only "where no expected type is available".
fix: 167711e424. A list literal checked against an expected `Set[T]` (an annotation or a parameter) checks each item against `T` and is recorded as the `Set`, which MIR builds as the prefix literal does (design.md § Collection literals). `let s: Set[i64] = [1, 2, 2, 3]` checks, and run and build print the set's size 3. Pinned by corpus/design/ok_list_literal_builds_a_set (interp and llvm) and tests/spec_section5_checks.rs. A check sweep of 27,484 corpus and kata programs against the previous binary changed no diagnostic list.

title: Mixed-width compound assignment passes `karac check` and then fails in MIR: `total_i64 += n_i32` (legal per design.md §5) stops `run`/`build` with "invalid MIR: binary operands of different types i64 and i32", and the illegal narrowing `n_i32 += total_i64` is accepted by check and fails the same way; `let w: Slice[i64] = v;` (a let does not coerce, §5 Slices) is likewise accepted by check and fails in MIR
