detail: Repros (probe d5/n18, n19, c08): `let mut total: i64 = 5; let n: i32 = 3; total += n; println(total);` -> check: All checks passed; `__mir-run` and `run`: "error[mir] run: invalid MIR: main: bb5[0]: binary operands of different types i64 and i32" (expected 8). `let total: i64 = 5; let mut n: i32 = 3; n += total;` -> check passes; MIR "binary operands of different types i32 and i64"; expected a refusal at check. `let v = [1, 2, 3]; let w: Slice[i64] = v;` -> check passes; MIR "assigning Vec[i64] to _3 of type Slice[i64]"; expected a refusal pointing at `.as_slice()`. Spec: §5 Mixed-width operands, Compound assignment "`p op= e` computes `p op e` by the same rule, and the result must then convert implicitly to the type of `p`. So `total_i64 += n_i32` is legal, and `n_i32 += total_i64` is an error"; Slices "`let` and assignment do not convert". The plain binary form `let s = a + c` (i32 + i64) works (n14), so the widening coercion is missing only on the compound-assignment path.
fix: c25557486e. design.md §5, Compound assignment: `p op= e` computes `p op e` by the mixed-width rule and the result must convert implicitly to `p`'s type. MIR's `compound_assign` (src/mir/lower.rs) now widens the right operand losslessly into the place's type, as the plain binary form does, so `total_i64 += n_i32` runs (8 on interp, JIT and build alike). The checker's CompoundAssign arm (src/typechecker/items.rs) now checks a numeric result against the place: `n_i32 += total_i64` gets the narrowing diagnostic a `let` gives, and so does the float case `f_f32 += d_f64`, which also used to stop in MIR. design.md § Slices: `let w: Slice[i64] = v;` and an assignment of a `Vec` or `Array` to a `Slice` binding are refused at check (`reject_slice_conversion`) with a machine-applicable `.as_slice()` (`.as_slice_mut()` for a `mut Slice`) fix; a range write `v[1..] = [5, 6]` is not a conversion and stays accepted. Pinned by corpus/core/ok_compound_assign_widens (spec; interp, llvm, ASan) and err_compound_assign_narrows, err_compound_assign_float_narrows, err_let_does_not_convert_to_slice. An interpreter sweep of corpus katas, fixtures/core_strict_check and apps found no new failure against the pre-change binary.

title: Small §5 divergences in refusals and lints: an or-pattern whose alternatives bind different names (`E.A(x) | E.B(y)`) is accepted; `mut port: i64` on a plain struct field and `struct Marker;` are accepted; the `redundant_alias_bound` warning never fires; a shift amount out of range reports "integer overflow" instead of "shift amount out of range"; and the alias-bound and range-bound errors carry E0262/E0263 where §5 names E_TYPE_ALIAS_BOUND_NOT_SATISFIED / E_RANGE_PATTERN_BOUND_NOT_CONST
detail: Repros (probe d5): p02 `enum E { A(i64), B(i64) }\nfn main() { let e = E.A(1); match e { E.A(x) | E.B(y) => println(1) } }` -> check passes, runs (spec §5 Or-patterns: "`A(x) | B(y)` is an error"). s03 `struct P { mut port: i64 }` -> accepted (spec §5 Structs: "`mut port: i64` on a plain struct field is a compile error"). s04 `struct Marker;` -> accepted ("The form `struct Marker;` is not valid"). a03 `type Sk[T: Ord] = SortedMap[T, i32];` -> no warning (spec Type aliases: `warning[redundant_alias_bound]`). n10 / d1x/sh.kara `let x: i32 = 1; let n = 32; x << n` and `x << -1` -> runtime "integer overflow" (spec §5 Division, remainder and shifts: panic with "shift amount out of range"). a01 `type Counts[T: Eq + Hash] = Map[T, i64];` with `Counts[f64]` -> code E0262 (twice, once per bound); p06 range bound `FOO` -> E0263; the messages match the spec's text, only the codes differ. Each is one small check or string; filed together because each alone is cosmetic.
fix: 167711e424, all but two pieces, which have their own rows: the shift message (B-2026-11-04-74, drop schedule) and `mut` on a plain struct field (B-2026-11-04-79; 305 corpus programs write it, so it needs a migration decision). Fixed: an or-pattern whose alternatives bind different names is refused, naming the names (unit variants, bare or qualified, bind nothing); `struct Marker;` is a parse error with a ` {}` fix-it and recovers as the braced form; an unmet alias bound is one E0262 naming the whole bound in the spec's words; `redundant_alias_bound` (W0293, E0293 under deny) fires for an ordered collection's key `Ord` or a user type's declared parameter bound. `Map`/`Set` keys are deliberately left out of the lint, because design.md's own example of an enforced bound is `type Counts[T: Eq + Hash] = Map[T, i64]`. On the codes, the review thread decided to keep the numeric catalogue codes, so design.md §5 now names E0262 TypeAliasBoundNotSatisfied and E0263 RangePatternBoundNotConst. The new or-pattern check also exposed a formatter bug, fixed in the same commit: `karac fmt` wrote `x @ (1 | 2)` as `x @ 1 | 2`, a different pattern. Pins: tests/spec_section5_checks.rs, the respelled unit-struct tests in tests/parser.rs. A check sweep of 27,484 corpus and kata programs changed no diagnostic list.

title: `m.get(k) == Some(v)` with a non-Copy value (Map[String, String]) refuses E0208 "cannot compare 'Option[ref String]' and 'Option[String]'" with no edit, and `karac fix` instead applies E0200's `.clone()` inside the `Some`, leaving the E0208 standing; the no-copy edit `Some(ref v)` (design.md § Views) is never offered
fix: be4628d4bc. `report_compare_mismatch` (src/typechecker/expr_ops.rs) now offers, when the Copy-only `.cloned()` edit does not apply, `option_some_view_fix`: the edit writing `ref ` before a place argument (identifier, field, index, tuple index) of a `Some(e)` literal compared with an `Option[ref T]`, for any T, so `m.get(l.key) == Some(l.value)` becomes `Some(ref l.value)` (design.md § Views). The same call drops the `borrow_projection_copy` `.clone()` lint on that argument and records the argument in `core_ref_copy_spans`, so the ownership pass's use-after-move of the same place (with its `.clone()` replacement) is dropped too; viewed in place nothing moves, and `karac fix` no longer writes `Some(ref s.clone())`. A temporary argument (`Some("x".to_string())`) keeps the message with no edit. Pins: tests/option_ref_compare_fix.rs `karac_fix_views_a_some_place_compared_with_a_non_copy_lookup` (field, local on both sides, fix then __mir-run prints `true true true`) and `a_non_copy_item_compare_with_a_temporary_keeps_the_message_without_an_edit`, which replaces the old no-edit pin for a local.

title: Rebinding an `own MutFn` / `own Fn` parameter with `let mut f = f;`, the spelling design.md §7 Function types and kinds prescribes for calling an owned MutFn, is refused by karac check as binding a non-escaping function value; the backends run it
detail: design.md §7 Function types and kinds: "Calling a local MutFn needs let mut. An own parameter is rebound first: let mut f = f;", and the spec's own example is `fn repeat(n: i64, f: own MutFn()) { let mut f = f; ... }` called as `repeat(3, || { count += 1; })` printing 3. karac check (and so karac run / build) refuses: "parameter `f` is a non-escaping function value and cannot be bound to a variable ... Declare it `f: escaping Fn(...)`" (core-semantics §9.3). `karac __mir-run`, `__mir-llvm-run` and ASan print 3. Same refusal for an Fn passed where MutFn is expected (`repeat(2, || println(k))`, spec Subsumption) and for `let mut g = f; g();`. With no way to rebind, an `own MutFn` parameter cannot be called at all: calling `f()` directly needs `let mut`. A local rebind of a non-escaping parameter does not escape it; the §9.3 rule is about storing or returning. Cells: probe-core d7 c06_repeat_mutfn, c13_fn_subsumes_mutfn, c27_own_mutfn_rebind (also blocks c20).
fix:
e06766fe96. src/core_escape.rs: `let mut g = f;` where `f` is a non-escaping parameter now keeps the binding classified as that parameter (Bound::NonEscParam) instead of refusing it, so the §7 spelling for calling an owned MutFn checks and runs ("3
7
7
" on interp and llvm, pin corpus/design/ok_own_mutfn_parameter_rebound). A genuine escape of the rebinding is still refused, and the message now reads "`g` holds parameter `f`, which ...".

title: A struct pattern with a `..` rest in parameter position is a parse error ("Expected identifier, found `..`"), though design.md §7 Destructuring parameters shows `fn inspect(Request { headers, .. }: Request)`
detail: design.md §7 Destructuring parameters: `fn handle(Request { headers, body }: own Request)` and `fn inspect(Request { headers, .. }: Request) { log(headers); }`; an own parameter drops its unbound parts at the end of the function. Any parameter pattern containing `..` fails: `fn inspect(Req { headers, .. }: Req)` gives error[parse] "Expected identifier, found `..`" on all four lanes. Without `..` (all fields named) the parameter destructures and runs fine (cell d04). So the drop-of-unbound-parts rule (spec cell d07: `fn h(W { a, .. }: own W)` should print a, body, drop a, drop b) cannot be exercised. `..` works in let and match patterns. Cells: d7 d05_bare_destructure_borrows, d06_bare_destructure_move_refused (refused, but by this parse error), d07_own_destructure_drops_unbound.
fix: 1776ad9f5e. The parameter pattern parser accepts a trailing `..` in a struct pattern (`fn inspect(Request { headers, .. }: Request)`), with E_REST_PATTERN_NOT_LAST for one before a field, as in any struct pattern. A bare parameter borrows its fields (moving one out is refused: "expected 'D', found 'ref D'"), and an `own` one drops its unbound parts at the end of the function (cell d07: a, body, drop a, drop b). Pinned by corpus/fixtures/params/destructure_with_rest (interp, llvm, asan) and tests/param_rest_pattern.rs.

title: An unbound method value `User.adult` gets the type `Fn() -> bool` with the receiver dropped, so `let check = User.adult; check(u)` is refused ("expected 0 argument(s), found 1") and `.map(User.adult)` fails to infer
detail: design.md §7 Function values: "Unbound methods are function values. User.validate is a function whose first parameter is the receiver ... let check = User.validate; has type Fn(User) -> Result[...]". With `impl User { fn adult(self) -> bool { self.age >= 18 } }`: `let check = User.adult; println(check(u));` -> error[typecheck] expected 0 argument(s), found 1. `let r: Vec[bool] = us.iter().map(User.adult).collect();` -> expected 0 arguments / cannot infer OutV. Expected `true` and `[true, false]`. Cells: d7 v02_unbound_method_value, v10_unbound_method_in_map.
fix: 8b04a3215e. design.md §7 Function values: an unbound method is a function whose first parameter is the receiver. The checker's path type for an inherent `Type.method` (`resolve_path_type` in src/typechecker/expr_ops.rs) left `self` out because `FunctionSig.params` excludes it; it now prepends the receiver in the mode the method declares (`self` -> `User`, `ref self` -> `ref User`, `mut ref self` -> `mut ref User`; `inherent_self_param` in method_ufcs.rs), and opens a generic impl's parameters as fresh type variables so a use (`let get: Fn(Wrap[String]) -> String = Wrap.get;`) solves them. In MIR (src/mir/lower.rs) a call through such a value passes the receiver first as a direct call does (`call_value`), and `fn_item_value` instances a generic impl's method from the receiver type its value is given. `let check = User.adult; check(u)`, `.map(User.adult)`, a `Fn(User) -> bool` parameter, `ref self` / `mut ref self` methods and `Wrap.get` agree on interp, JIT and build, ASan clean. As with a generic free function, an unannotated `let wg = Wrap.get;` still asks for an annotation. Pinned by corpus/design/ok_unbound_method_is_a_function_value (spec; interp, llvm, ASan).

title: An escaping closure that captures a String and calls `println(s)` is classified OnceFn ("consumes captured binding `s`") and refused for an Fn slot; `println(f"{s}")`, `show(s)` and `s.len()` in the same closure are Fn
detail: Escaping closures capture by move (design.md §7 Escaping function values) but a body that only reads the capture is still an Fn (Function types and kinds: most permissive kind the body allows). `fn mk() -> (Fn() with writes(Stdout)) { let s: String = "abc"; || println(s) }` called twice should print abc twice. karac check: "cannot pass once-callable closure where 'Fn()' is expected ... it consumes captured binding 's'". Replacing the body with `println(f"{s}")` or `show(s)` (fn show(s: String)) runs and prints abc abc; `|| s.len()` also works. The same `println(s)` in a NON-escaping closure called twice is fine. Also hits an escaping parameter: `subscribe(mut b, || println(s))` with `h: escaping Fn()`. println borrows its argument, so the kind inference treats println's argument slot as a move only in the by-move capture case. Cells: d7 e16_escaping_closure_println_capture, e05 (refused for this reason rather than the intended use-after-move).
fix: e06766fe96. src/typechecker/items.rs callee_borrow_positions: print, println, eprint, eprintln and dbg borrow their argument when no user function of that name exists, so `println(s)` in a closure no longer counts as consuming the captured `s` and the closure is an Fn. Pin corpus/design/ok_escaping_closure_prints_its_capture ("abc\nabc\n").

title: A function type with no effect clause in a struct field or a return type is treated as pure ("has effect writes(Stdout) not declared in slot [pure]"); design.md §12 says a call through it has every effect, and the same unannotated type on an escaping parameter does accept it
detail: design.md §12 (effects of function values, line ~5581, Gowtham 2026-11-03): "An escaping value (an escaping parameter, a struct field, a collection element) has the effects its type declares ... With no clause, a call through it has every effect. To declare one with no effects, write the empty clause with ()"; §7 Escaping: "or every effect if its type declares none"; return_clause_on_fn warning text itself says a returned function value with no clause "keeps every effect". Repro: `struct R { h: Fn(i64) }  fn mk() -> Fn(i64) { |x| println(x) }  fn main() { let r = R { h: |x| println(x) }; (r.h)(1); let g = mk(); g(2); }` -> error[effect] field `h` ... slot [pure]; returned value ... slot [pure]. Expected 1, 2. Contrast: `fn subscribe(bus: mut ref Bus, h: escaping Fn(i64)) { bus.hs.push(h); }` with `hs: Vec[Fn(i64)]` and a println closure runs (d7 e02). After B-2026-11-03-1 (with ()) the no-clause and with () cases look merged for literal fields and returns. Also `let f: Fn(i64) = |x| println(x);` is refused with slot [pure]; the spec does not list a local annotation among escaping slots, so the right reading there is for the owner (probably the inferred effects of a non-escaping local). Cells: d7 c25 (original form), d7t repro in probe-core.
fix: d50ea9e470: src/effectchecker/subtyping.rs fn_annotation_slot_effects returns None (no check) for a function type with no clause, where it returned the empty set; `with ()` (EffectSpec::Specific with no items) is still the empty set, admitting only default-permitted effects. That one function serves every declared-slot position (a `let` annotation, an assignment, a return type, a struct-literal field, and a container element reached by a literal or a receiver store), so all of them now read a missing clause as design.md § How a call through a function value gets its effects says: every effect. MIR's effect pass already charged a call through such a value every effect (src/mir/effects.rs), so `par` safety is unchanged. The cause was the 08-24 slot rule (4f67f9d135, 536c495113), written when a bare slot meant pure, not B-2026-11-03-1: that commit added `with ()` but left the bare reading in place. The `let f: Fn(i64) = |x| println(x);` case the row left to the owner is accepted too: a local is no escaping slot. tests/effectchecker.rs: the twenty tests that pinned the old reading spell their pure slots `with ()` (SLOT_PRELUDE's `struct H` included), test_other_verbs_still_constrain_a_bare_fn_slot is renamed ..._an_empty_clause_slot, and a_function_type_with_no_clause_admits_every_effect pins field, return, let, element and `blocks`-through-a-return as accepted. corpus/core/ok_effect_no_clause_fn_slot runs the row's program (1, 2) on mir-interp, mir-llvm and mir-llvm-asan.

title: A use after move of a function value (a OnceFn closure called twice, or an Fn value called after `let h2 = h`) passes karac check and is refused only by the MIR move check with an internal message ("move check main: bb10[term]: use of _3")
detail: design.md §7 Diagnostics for a kind mismatch: calling a OnceFn twice is an error, and the diagnostic must point at the capture that makes the closure OnceFn and at the use that moves it. Repro: `let s: String = "a"; let f = || s; let a = f(); let b = f();` -> karac check: All checks passed; karac run and karac build: error[mir]: move check main: bb10[term]: use of _3, which may have been moved or never initialized (no span, no names). Same for `let h = mk(); let h2 = h; println(h());` with mk returning an Fn (design.md: a value of a function type is move-only). Passing the closure twice to an argument (`call(g); call(g);`) IS caught by check with a good message, so only a direct call of a moved closure binding is missed. Cells: d7 c08_oncefn_called_twice_refused, e12_stored_fn_move_only.
fix: e06766fe96. karac check now runs the use-after-move rule on function values: a closure body is walked as consuming under the core rules, so a closure that moves a capture out is an OnceFn and a second call is refused at check with "it is an OnceFn because its body moves captured `s` out at line L:C" and a help to call it once or clone; an erased `Fn` local (a `let` bound to anything but a closure or function path, or a parameter that is `own`/escaping) is move-only, so `let h2 = h; h(1)` is refused with "a function value is move-only (design.md § Escaping function values): borrow it (`ref h`) ... or wrap it in a `shared` type". Pins corpus/design/err_once_closure_called_twice_names_its_capture and err_function_value_used_after_move; tests/closure_kinds_check.rs. A 27,484-program sweep found 12 codegen heap_env and 7 asan legacy fixtures newly refused at check; MIR's move check already refused every one.

title: A named-parameter default that names a function (`g: Fn(i64) -> i64 = id`) is refused ("'id' is not a known const"); design.md §7 says a function name is a constant expression for defaults
detail: design.md §7 Named and default parameters: "Defaults are constant expressions: whatever a const initializer allows. A function name is one; a closure literal is not." `fn id(x: i64) -> i64 { x }  fn f(a: i64; g: Fn(i64) -> i64 = id) -> i64 { g(a) }` with `f(4)` and `f(4, g: dbl)` should print 4 and 8; check: error[typecheck] const expression: 'id' is not a known const. The closure-literal default is correctly refused (n12). Cell: d7 n13_default_fn_name.
fix: e06766fe96. src/typechecker/bounds.rs: a named-parameter default may name a top-level function item (design.md §7, a function name is a constant expression), so `g: Fn(i64) -> i64 = id` checks and runs. Pin corpus/design/ok_default_parameter_names_a_function ("4\n8\n").

title: §7 functions/closures: five spec errors accepted (MutFn called from a plain `let`; OnceFn bare parameter; UFCS receiver without `mut`; `a == r` with non-Copy `r: ref T`; `own escaping`) and two misleading diagnostics (refutable parameter pattern; `f[i64]` value)
detail: All from design.md §7. (1) Calling a local MutFn needs let mut: `let mut n = 0; let f = || { n += 1; }; f();` accepted, prints 1 (c09). (2) A MutFn or OnceFn parameter is declared own: `fn call(f: OnceFn() -> String)` accepted and runs; MutFn bare is correctly refused (c10 vs c11). (3) A UFCS call marks its receiver: `Counter.bump(c)` for `fn bump(mut ref self)` accepted, prints 1 (k10; `Counter.bump(mut c)` works). (4) For non-Copy T, `a == b` with b: ref T is a type error with fix-it `*b`: `let r = ref b; println(a == r);` on Strings accepted, prints true (s04). (5) own is not written beside escaping: `h: own escaping Fn(i64)` accepted (e04). Diagnostics: (6) `fn f(Some(x): Option[i64])` says "`Some` is Type-class but parameter names must be Value-class" instead of refutable pattern in a parameter (d03). (7) `let f = srt[i64];` says "'i64' is a type, not a function: a numeric conversion is the cast" instead of no call-site type arguments (§8) (v09).
fix: e06766fe96 lands six of the seven items. (1) A plain `let` bound to a capture-writing closure and then called is refused: "`f` is a `MutFn` (it writes captured `n`), so calling it needs `let mut f`", with a machine-applicable "mut " fix (8 corpus closure fixtures migrated by karac fix). (2) A bare OnceFn parameter that is called is refused: "`f` is a borrowed `OnceFn`, so it cannot be called ... Declare the parameter `f: own OnceFn(...)`", with an "own " fix (3 corpus programs and 2 test fixtures migrated). (3) A UFCS receiver of a `mut ref self` method without `mut` is refused (MissingMutMarker, "mut " fix). (5) `own escaping` is a parse error with a fix deleting `own`. (6) A refutable parameter pattern says "a parameter's pattern must be irrefutable, and `Some(..)` matches only some values (design.md § Destructuring parameters)". (7) `srt[i64]` as a value says a function takes no type arguments where it is used (design.md §8). Item (4), `a == r` with a non-literal operand beside `r: ref T`, is split to B-2026-11-05-1 under the review thread's 5966d6bd81 ruling (a literal beside a `ref T` is a `ref T`). Tests in tests/closure_kinds_check.rs.

title: A closure cannot capture a `frozen` binding at all ("`frozen` alias `g` is captured by a closure"), and a TaskGroup.spawn closure over one is also E_NOT_CROSS_TASK; design.md §11 Handles in closures says such a closure is a view that may be called, passed down and enter par branches and TaskGroup tasks
detail: design.md §11 Handles in closures: "A frozen handle is never counted, so a closure that captures one is a view. It may be called, passed down, and enter par branches and TaskGroup tasks, but it may not escape." The frozen table row says capturing n in a closure: yes. Repros (shared struct Node { val: i64 }; let g = freeze r;): (1) `let f = || g.val; println(f());` -> error[ownership] `frozen` alias `g` is captured by a closure; the backends (__mir-run, llvm, ASan) print 2. (2) `let f = || g.val + g.neighbors.len(); let (a, b) = par { f(), f() };` same refusal; backends print 6. (3) `tg.spawn(|| { c.fetch_add(g.val); })` -> E_NOT_CROSS_TASK capture of `g` (type `Node`) cannot cross a TaskGroup.spawn task boundary, plus the closure-capture error; the same program with literals in place of g runs. Direct use of g in a par branch (`par { g.val, g.val + 1 }`) and in a par for body works, so only the closure path is missing. The escape case (`fn mk(n: frozen Node) -> Fn() -> i64 { || n.val }`) is correctly refused, but by the same blanket rule. Cells: probe-core d11 f14_frozen_closure_par, f21_frozen_taskgroup, d11e.
fix: bf270628d9. The frozen escape pass (src/ownership/frozen_escape.rs, `ExprKind::Closure`) now reads the typechecker's v2 core §9.3 escape set (`core_escaping_closures`): a frozen place inside a NON-escaping closure is judged by the same place rules as a direct use (scalar reads, `len`, frozen-slot pass-through), and only a closure that escapes (returned, also through a local; stored in a field or collection; passed to an `escaping` parameter), or any closure when the core rules are off, reports, now as "`frozen` ... is captured by a closure that escapes" with help naming what may capture it. `check_cross_task_safe_captures` (src/typechecker/cross_task_check.rs) lets a `frozen` parameter or `freeze` binding cross `TaskGroup.spawn`/`IsolatingGroup.spawn` when its only unsafe leaf is the shared-ness, as a `par` branch already did. The row's three repros check and run (2; 6; the TaskGroup sum). Pins: corpus/core ok_frozen_closure_view (called, passed to a non-escaping `Fn` param, two par branches, two TaskGroup tasks; prints 4/60/10/14 on interp, llvm and ASan) and err_frozen_closure_escapes (a closure bound to a local and returned; in borrowck.rs not_mir).

title: design.md §11 #[must_use] mandate unmet: a discarded `m.lock()` guard, iterator adapter (`v.iter().map(..);`) and `s.trim()` give no warning, so a lock released at the wrong point is silent; also no `.unwrap()` -> `.expect` suggestion and no warning on a deprecated enum variant
detail: design.md §11 #[must_use] Standard library mandate: category 2 every iterator adapter, category 3 every guard type such as MutexGuard[T] (message names the resource: "the mutex is released when this guard drops; bind it to a name to keep the lock"), category 5 pure transformations such as String.trim(). karac check on `let m = Mutex.new(1); m.lock();`, `let v = [1, 2]; v.iter().map(|x| x + 1);` and `let s: String = " a "; s.trim();` reports All checks passed. runtime/stdlib/source/sync.kara Mutex.lock, iter.kara map, collections.kara trim carry no #[must_use], and the `missing_must_use` stdlib lint (karac lint --list) does not flag them. Categories 1 (Result/Option, user code) and user #[must_use] on types and fns do warn (cells u01..u05, u08, u11). Also from §11: (a) Ergonomics: `.unwrap()` on any Option gets a suggestion to use .expect("...") with a machine-applicable fix; `let o: Option[i64] = Some(1); println(o.unwrap());` gives no diagnostic (w11). (b) #[deprecated]: every use of the item, including a variant constructor or a pattern, emits the deprecated lint; `enum E { #[deprecated(note: "gone soon")] A, B }` with `E.A` and a match on it: no warning (x07); deprecated fn and struct uses do warn (x01, x06). Cells: d11 u06, u09, u10, w11, x07.
fix: 75fe0ae07f. design.md § #[must_use] mandate, categories 2, 3 and 5. `MutexGuard` (runtime/stdlib/source/sync.kara) carries #[must_use("the mutex is released when this guard drops; bind it to a name to keep the lock")], so `m.lock();` warns; String/Str `trim`, `trim_start`, `trim_end` (collections.kara) carry a function-level #[must_use]. With the library compiled from source each adapter is its own struct (IterMap, VecIter, IterFilter, ...), not the `Iterator` pseudo-struct the iterator message lived on, so src/must_use_lint.rs now treats every library-defined struct (span past `library_start`, or stdlib_origin) with an `Iterator` impl as must_use with that message; a user iterator stays silent. The note spells #[must_use("...")], not Rust's `= "..."` (B-2026-11-04-72 item 8). No corpus app or core pin gains a warning. Pin: tests/must_use_library_mandate.rs. The missing_must_use hygiene lint is unchanged (the discard warnings are the mandate's effect). Remainder, its own row B-2026-11-04-80: the `.unwrap()` -> `.expect` suggestion and the deprecated enum variant warning.

title: §11 sharing roll-up: `own self` on a sync type and `weak` on a non-shared type accepted; borrow-flag panic does not name the field or both spans; several sharing diagnostics give stale or wrong wording
detail: From design.md §11. Accepted though the spec says error: (1) sync methods take a borrowed self only; `impl C { fn done(own self) }` on a sync struct is accepted and runs (the shared-type twin h18 is refused) (y06). (2) `weak` is for back-edges between shared/sync handles; `shared struct H { mut w: weak Pl }` with a plain struct Pl, and even a plain `struct H { w: weak Pl }`, are accepted; using it fails with unrelated borrow errors (E0516/E0509 on a temporary) (w10, d11g/d11h). Diagnostics: (3) a conflicting access through another handle panics with "already borrowed: this `shared` field is borrowed through another handle" and one span; the spec says the message names the field and the source spans of both accesses (h15). (4) writing a plain field of a sync struct says "shared struct field 'Sx.x' is not declared mut", which points at a fix (`mut`) that is illegal on sync (y14). (5) `mut ref self` on a sync method says "method `clear` on `par Counter` ... a `par` value is always Arc-allocated", stale naming (y05). (6) `shared struct Nd { mut next: Nd }` is reported as a cycle that will leak rather than as a type no value can inhabit (w05; the tuple form w06 is worded right). (7) writing through a frozen parameter, and writing the source after freeze, say "cannot be projected through `.neighbors` yet" rather than that frozen is deeply immutable (f03, f04, f17). (8) the must_use note prints the Rust spelling `#[must_use = "..."]`; Kāra writes `#[must_use("...")]` (u01).
fix: b378b20b59. (1) `own self` on a sync type is refused by check_core_shared_receivers (src/typechecker/items.rs), extended from shared types with its `self` fix; (2) a `weak` field (struct or enum struct variant) pointing at a plain type is refused at the declaration (check_weak_field_targets), a type parameter left to its instantiation; (4) writing a plain sync field says the field is fixed at construction and state lives in Atomic/Mutex fields (src/typechecker/fields.rs), not "is not declared mut"; (5) the sync `mut ref self` error names the sync type, not "par Counter ... Arc-allocated"; (6) an all-shared cycle (`shared struct Nd { mut next: Nd }`) says no value can be constructed and advises Option/Vec, as the tuple form did, not "will leak, add weak" (src/ownership.rs); (7) a mutating method through a frozen place, on the parameter or on the source after a freeze, reports "cannot be written through" (src/ownership/frozen_escape.rs) instead of "cannot be projected ... yet"; (8) fixed with B-2026-11-04-71 at 75fe0ae07f. Pins flipped in tests/ownership.rs (two cycle rows, three frozen-method rows, test_weak_breaks_cycle now on shared types). New: tests/sharing_diagnostics_roll_up.rs, corpus/core err_sync_own_self, err_weak_plain_target. Remainder, its own row B-2026-11-04-81: item (3), the borrow-flag panic text.

title: A `for` over a borrow of a concrete non-`Copy` iterator (`it: VecIntoIter[i64]`, a user `impl Iterator for Up`) is refused with MIR's internal "a `for` loop over a collection is not lowered yet" instead of the borrowed-iterator diagnostic B-2026-11-04-17 gives a bounded type parameter
fix: aa857c6355. borrowed_iterator_for (src/typechecker/bounds.rs) now also takes a `ref` / `mut ref` of a concrete named type that implements `Iterator`, not `Iterable`, is not a core collection and is not `Copy` (a `Copy` iterator such as `Range` is consumed by copying it and still iterates). The repro is refused at `it` with "`it` is 'ref VecIntoIter[i64]', a borrowed iterator, ... take the parameter by value, `it: own VecIntoIter[i64]`", and `karac fix` writes `own` and the program prints 3. Pinned by the VecIntoIter case in tests/borrowed_iterator_for.rs. Filed and closed together: found and fixed in the same slice as -44/-45.

title: A shift by an out-of-range amount (`x << 32` on an i32, `x << -1`) panics with "integer overflow" on run and build; design.md §5 says it panics with "shift amount out of range" (split from B-2026-11-04-60)
fix: 6f9132f62b: the checked binop lowering (src/mir/lower.rs) gives a Shl/Shr range check its own abort reason, `AbortReason::ShiftOutOfRange` (code 5, src/mir/syntax.rs), whose text in the MIR interpreter and the compiled backend is "shift amount out of range". A negative amount or one at least the operand's width now panics with that message on `__mir-run` and on a built binary; a shift by width-1 stays legal (`1i32 << 31` prints -2147483648, `-8i32 >> 31` prints -1). Pinned by tests/mir_shift_out_of_range.rs (shl at width, negative shl, u8 shr at width, `<<=` at width; interp unconditional, build under llvm). Control: the pre-fix karac printed "runtime error: integer overflow" on all four.

title: An empty list literal compared with a typed `Vec` (`v == []`) is refused with MIR's internal "a type that failed to check is not lowered yet"; the other operand gives `[]` its element type, so it should check
fix:
e06766fe96. src/typechecker/expr_ops.rs infer_binary: when a comparison has an empty list literal on one side, the other side is inferred first and the empty literal is checked against its type, so `v == []` and `[] == v` check and run. Pin corpus/design/ok_empty_literal_compared_with_a_vec ("false
true
true
").

title: A closure parameter written `mut acc` (Rust's `fold(init, |mut acc, x| ..)`) is refused with "'mut' is a reserved keyword and cannot be used as an identifier" and a cascade error at the closing `)`, with no fix; a `fn` parameter written `mut x` gets a diagnostic naming the Kāra spelling (`let mut x = x;` in the body)
detail: Mend loop (CLAUDE.md § Writing Kāra), kata 1047's fold arm. Repro at 75832f76f1: `fn main() { let v = [1, 2, 3]; let s: i64 = v.iter().fold(0, |mut acc, x| { acc += x; acc }); println(s); }` -> d1 parse E0003 "'mut' is a reserved keyword and cannot be used as an identifier" at the `mut`, d2 E0002 "Expected expression, found `)`", neither with a fix. The `fn f(mut x: i64)` case gets src/parser/items.rs's "a parameter's mode is written in its type, not before its name ... or `x: own T` and `let mut x = x;` to change your own copy" (also with no fix). A closure parameter's mode comes from the slot (`fold` passes `own A`), so the Kāra spelling is the bare name plus `let mut acc = acc;` as the body's first statement, which kata 1047's remove_dups_fold.kara uses; that is a machine-applicable edit when the body is a block (insert after `{`) and a wrap (`{ let mut acc = acc; <expr> }`) when it is an expression. `|mut acc, x|` is the commonest spelling of a fold over an owned accumulator in Rust, so blind LLM output hits it.
fix: dd0d3d3fa3. design.md § Patterns has no `mut name` pattern, so the spec answer is a refusal with a fix, not a parse. `|mut acc, x|` is now one error naming the Kāra spelling, and its machine-applicable fix drops the `mut` and opens the body with `let mut acc = acc;`, wrapping an expression body in a block (`|mut n, x| n + x` becomes `|n, x| { let mut n = n; n + x }`). The same fix now covers a `mut` nested in a parameter's tuple pattern (`|acc, (mut a, b)|`, and `(mut a, b): (i64, i64)` on a `fn`, impl method or trait default method), which also used to fail as "'mut' is a reserved keyword" (src/parser/items.rs `report_param_pattern_mut`, fixed through the existing `pattern_muts` / `fix_pattern_muts`). A `-> T` on the same closure keeps its own deletion fix, and the two compose. Pinned by tests/closure_mut_param.rs (block body, expression body, nested in a closure and a `fn`: check, fix, run).

title: `Vec` has no `drain(range)`: Rust's `v.drain(i..i + 2);` gets only "no method 'drain' on type 'Vec'" with no hint, though `remove`, `truncate` and `split_off`-style edits exist
detail: Kata 1047's scan arm, which takes an adjacent pair out of a `Vec[char]`. Repro at 75832f76f1: `fn main() { let mut v = [1, 2, 3, 4]; v.drain(1..3); println(v.len()); }` -> typecheck "no method 'drain' on type 'Vec'", no suggestion. docs/library/collections.md's Vec table has `remove` (one index, shifting) and `truncate`, nothing that takes a range out, and deferred.md does not list `drain`. The kata writes `v.remove(i + 1); v.remove(i);`, which is O(n) per call as `drain` is. Either `drain(r: Range[i64]) -> VecIntoIter[T]` in runtime/stdlib/source/collections.kara (removes eagerly, so a dropped iterator still removes, as Rust's does; documented in the Vec table), or a diagnostic naming `remove` / `truncate` for the common statement form. A library addition, so routed to the stdlib owner.
fix: 4e87c65465. `Vec.drain(r: Range[i64]) -> VecIntoIter[T]` is library source (runtime/stdlib/source/collections.kara, per docs/library/collections.md): it removes the range at the call, shifts the tail down, and yields the taken elements front to back, so an iterator dropped unread still removed them; an out-of-bounds or reversed range aborts. A checker arm (src/typechecker/method_vec_mutation.rs) types it where the library source is not loaded, and 'drain' is in the did-you-mean list. Rust's spellings `a..`, `..b`, `..` and `a..=b` are refused with a machine-applicable rewrite to `start..end` (`drain_range_spelling` in src/typechecker/expr_method_call.rs; `i..=i + 1` becomes `i..i + 2`, `..` becomes `0..v.len()`). Pinned by corpus/fixtures/mir_collections/vec_drain_range (spec; green on mir-interp, mir-llvm and mir-llvm-asan, including the drop of read and unread elements) and tests/vec_drain_range.rs (each spelling's fix, then a run). Kata 1047's scan arm on `v.drain(i..i + 2);` gives the same output as its two `remove` calls under run and build.

title: A borrowed parameter passed where a library constructor takes `own Vec[T]` (`PriorityQueue.from(v)`, `max_first_from(v)` with `v: Vec[i64]`) draws "expected 'Vec[T]', found 'ref Vec[i64]'" and a cascade "cannot infer type parameter 'T'", with no fix; the same parameter given away by `let`/return gets "cannot give away parameter `v`" with its `own` / `.clone()` fix
detail: Mend loop, kata 1046's Rust-shaped ★ arm re-run after 75832f76f1 (B-2026-11-04-5) fixed its `use std::collections::BinaryHeap;` and `BinaryHeap::from(stones)`: the next stop is `fn last_stone_weight(stones: Vec[i32]) -> i32 { let mut heap = PriorityQueue.max_first_from(stones); ..`. Repro at 4bfe8f296b: `fn f(v: Vec[i64]) -> i64 { let q = PriorityQueue.from(v); q.len() }  fn g(v: Vec[i64]) -> Vec[i64] { let w: Vec[i64] = v; w }  fn main() { println(f([1, 2])); println(g([3]).len()); }` -> 1:55 "expected 'Vec[T]', found 'ref Vec[i64]'" (no fix), 1:36 "cannot infer type parameter 'T'; add a type annotation to this binding" (no fix, a cascade of the first), and for `g` the good one: "cannot give away parameter `v`: a bare parameter borrows (core-semantics §4.1), and an owned 'Vec[i64]' is wanted here. Take it by value with `v: own Vec[i64]`, or hand on a copy with `.clone()`" with a fix. The argument to a generic `own` parameter of a library method is the uncovered case: the unifier reports the `ref` mismatch before the give-away check sees it. Rust code passes its owned `Vec<i32>` parameter this way constantly (`BinaryHeap::from(v)`, `HashSet::from_iter(v)`, `v.into_iter()`), so D5 borrow-by-default makes it common in blind output.
fix: 5190a456b6: pass 1 of a generic call's argument check solves an owned slot (not `ref`, `Slice` or a bare `T`) from what a bare parameter borrows, and pass 2 reports the parameter given away through d5_give_away, with the `own` fix, in place of the `ref` mismatch and the unsolved `T`. `PriorityQueue.from(v)`, `max_first_from(v)`, `Set.from(v)` and a user `take[T](v: own Vec[T])` now get "cannot give away parameter `v`" and `karac fix` writes `v: own Vec[i64]`; `id[T](x: T)`, `ref Vec[T]` and `Slice[T]` slots still take the borrow. Pinned by tests/generic_own_slot_give_away_fix.rs.

title: Tracker for the next minor release: `mut` on a field of a plain (non-`shared`) struct or enum becomes a compile error; in 0.8.x it is a `deprecated` warning with a `karac fix` that deletes it (ad5c10d728, design.md §5 Structs 25d27bd53a)

Remainder of B-2026-11-04-71: `.unwrap()` on an Option gets no `.expect("...")` suggestion with a fix (design.md §11 Ergonomics), and a use of a `#[deprecated]` enum variant (constructor `E.A` or pattern) gives no deprecated warning
detail: Split from B-2026-11-04-71, whose must_use part (guard, library iterators, trim) is fixed at 75fe0ae07f. (a) design.md § weak Ergonomics: ".unwrap() on any Option gets a suggestion to use .expect("…") with a machine-applicable fix". `let o: Option[i64] = Some(1); println(o.unwrap());` checks clean (probe cell w11). Open question before a fix: the corpus and katas call `.unwrap()` on Options thousands of times, so a warning-level suggestion would be loud; the spec says "suggestion", which may mean a note-level hint or an LSP code action rather than a `karac check` warning. (b) `enum E { #[deprecated(note: "gone soon")] A, B }` then `let e = E.A; match e { E.A => .., E.B => .. }` checks clean (cell x07), while a deprecated fn or struct use warns (x01, x06). The resolver records the variant's Deprecation against its SymbolId (src/resolver/collect.rs collect_enum), but no typechecker site calls `check_deprecated_use_at` for a variant path or a variant pattern, and the by-name fallback (global scope, bare variant name) would pick the wrong enum's variant when two enums share a name, so the lookup needs the enum.
fix: 7d007768dd. (b) A #[deprecated] enum variant now warns at every use: unit, tuple and struct constructors (Enum.Variant, Enum.Variant(..), Enum.Variant { .. }) and the matching patterns, qualified or bare. The table (src/typechecker/deprecated_variant.rs) is keyed by (enum, variant), so a same-named variant of another enum stays silent. (a) Per design.md §11 weak Ergonomics (8c5e67ab81): .unwrap() directly on a weak read (k.parent.unwrap(), k.parent.upgrade().unwrap()) is the weak_read_unwrap lint (W0294), with a machine-applicable fix to .expect("the referent is alive"); karac fix rewrites it and the program runs unchanged. Any other Option's unwrap is not a check warning; the LSP code action for that case is not part of this commit. Pinned by tests/deprecated_variant_and_weak_unwrap.rs (4 tests); corpus files with weak fields or #[deprecated] gain no new warnings.

title: Remainder of B-2026-11-04-72: the shared-field borrow-flag panic says "already borrowed: this `shared` field is borrowed through another handle" with one span; design.md §11 says it names the field and the source spans of both accesses
detail: Split from B-2026-11-04-72 (item 3; the other items are fixed at b378b20b59). A conflicting access to a `shared` field through a second handle while the first borrow is live panics at run time with "already borrowed: this `shared` field is borrowed through another handle" and the span of the second access only (probe cell h15). design.md §11 says the message names the field and the source spans of both accesses. The borrow flag records no field name or first-access span today, so the fix needs the flag to carry (or the panic site to be handed) the field and the span of the access that set it, on both the MIR interpreter and the LLVM runtime.
fix: 872c092c69. A §6.2 borrow flag now records where the borrow that took it was made: the MIR interpreter's Flag keeps the acquiring statement's place, and the runtime's (runtime/src/mir_flags.rs) keeps a file:line:col constant the compiled acquire passes (two constant arguments, stored only when the flag is first taken). On a conflict the message names the field and that place, and the abort's own place is the conflicting access, on the interpreter, `karac run` and a built binary alike, across a suspension too: `runtime error: already borrowed: `Bag.items` is borrowed through another handle at m.kara:3:5 (core semantics §6.2)` then `  at m.kara:4:9`. The compiled message is built only on a conflict (karac_mir_flag_conflict sets the panic message before the abort). Readers that join a held flag keep the first reader's place. Pinned by tests/borrow_flag_conflict_names_both.rs (2 interpreter + 2 compiled tests, the latter added to CI's codegen-e2e job). The TSan archive was not rebuilt in this container (it has none).

title: An integer tuple literal passed as a collection key or compared with `==`/`<` keeps the default (i64, i64) layout instead of the declared narrow tuple type: `s.contains((1, 2))` on a `SortedSet`/`Set`/`Vec[(i32, i32)]` and `m.contains_key((1, 2))`/`m.get((1, 2))` on a `Map[(i32, i32), _]` answer false/None on compiled code, and `a == (1, 2)` with `a: (i32, i32)` is invalid MIR on run and build
detail: Found by the LLVM 22 mir-llvm lane: fixtures/codegen/families/b_2026_10_03_23/e2e_narrow_tuple_literal_into_container_keeps_declared_layout prints `set 2 false false` against `set 2 true true`. It fails the same on the LLVM 18 build at c420c96612, so the upgrade did not cause it. MEASURED 2026-11-04 on main 80e7fba5c8, x86 Linux: with `let mut s: SortedSet[(i32, i32)]` holding (1, 2), `s.contains(k)` for a bound `let k: (i32, i32) = (1, 2)` is true on every backend, but `s.contains((1, 2))` is false on `__mir-llvm-run` and `karac run` and true on `__mir-run`. The same literal key answers false (or None) for `Set[(i32, i32)].contains`, `Map[(i32, i32), i64].contains_key` and `.get`, `SortedSet[(u8, u8)].contains`, `SortedSet[(i16, i16, i32)].contains` and `Vec[(i32, i32)].contains`. `SortedSet[(i64, i64)]` and `SortedSet[(i32, i64)]` work, which fits the literal being laid out as all-i64. The IR (KARAC_MIR_LL) builds the argument in a 16-byte slot with `store i64 1` / `store i64 2` and hands it to `karac_mir_map_lookup` with `cmp.(i32, i32)`, which reads two i32s at offsets 0 and 4. So the literal argument's type is not taken from the parameter's element type. The interpreter compares by value and hides it. In an operator, the same literal is refused by the MIR verifier: `let a: (i32, i32) = (1, 2); println(f"{a < (3, 4)} {a == (1, 2)}")` passes `karac check` and then fails with `invalid MIR: field 0 of (i64, i64) has type i64, but the projection says i32` on `__mir-run` and `__mir-llvm-run`. Insert and push take the literal at the right type, since `s.insert((1, 2))` followed by a bound-key lookup finds it. The fix belongs in the typed HIR's expected-type propagation into a library method's key argument and into a comparison's right operand (Thread B's area).
fix: 89324c3d8f. The typechecker retypes a tuple literal of integer literals to the tuple type its slot expects, element by element, wherever it already retyped a tuple of string literals (check_assignable's retype_literal): each unsuffixed integer literal (and `-n`) is recorded with its node ids when synthesised, and an `(Int|UInt)` element whose slot wants another integer type is range-checked (check_int_literal_fits, so `(300, 1)` into `(u8, u8)` is refused) and re-recorded at the slot's type. check_expr no longer overwrites the retyped tuple node with its synthesised `(i64, i64)`, which was why `Vec.contains` still built an i64 pair. A comparison retypes a tuple-literal operand to the other side's tuple type (infer_binary's compare block), so `a == (1, 2)` with `a: (i32, i32)` builds an `(i32, i32)` and no longer emits invalid MIR. Pinned by corpus/core/literal_tuple_takes_the_slot_int_types (spec: design.md § Numeric literals; `SortedSet`, `Set`, `Vec.contains`, `Map.contains_key`/`get`, `==`/`<` on i32, u8 and i16 tuples; interp, mir-llvm and ASan agree) and e2e_narrow_tuple_literal_into_container_keeps_declared_layout.

title: The backend does not emit the facts LLVM 19-22 added: `range` attributes on parameters and returns, `nuw`/`nusw`/`inbounds` flags on GEPs beyond inbounds, `nuw`/`nsw` on `trunc`, `samesign` on `icmp`, and `captures(address/read_provenance)` beyond `captures(none)`
detail: Gowtham's LLVM 22 decision asked for a follow-up row naming the new facts LLVM accepts, kept out of the upgrade slice (6dcdc1a604), which changed only what LLVM 22 required. The upgrade replaced `nocapture` with `captures(none)` and kept range metadata on loads (src/backend/mir/drop.rs), and emits none of the following. (1) `range(i64 lo, hi)` on parameters and return values (LLVM 19): integer-typed indices, lengths and enum tags whose bounds the MIR knows (`len >= 0`, a discriminant in 0..n) could carry it through calls that are not inlined. (2) GEP `nusw`/`nuw` (LLVM 19): element addressing from a bounds-checked index is non-negative and in-bounds, and `nuw` lets SCEV prove more loops countable. (3) `trunc nuw`/`nsw` (LLVM 19): narrowing casts after a range check. (4) `icmp samesign` (LLVM 20): comparisons of two values both known non-negative, such as indices against lengths. (5) the finer `captures(...)` (LLVM 21): `captures(address)` for pointers that are only compared. Each one is an opportunity, not a bug. It should be measured on the frozen bench set (ADR-2) before it lands, because a wrong fact is UB. No program is known to be slower for lack of them.
fix: e75d97a500 (part 1), 18fba62c62 (part 2). Two of the five facts land; the other three are B-2026-11-05-25. (2) An element address from a bounds-checked index (Vec/Array checked_elem and some_elem in seq.rs, and body.rs index()) is now `mul nuw nsw` then `getelementptr inbounds nuw`, through clone.rs elem_ptr_nuw and mark_index_nuw. This is provable: the index is in [0, len) and the offset is less than the allocation's size. elem_ptr itself is unchanged, since some of its 75 callers step backward. (3) `T.try_from(n)` truncates under `fits`, so the trunc is `nsw` for a signed target and `nuw` for an unsigned one, or for a signed one from an unsigned source (num.rs int_try_from). A boundary probe (i8/u8 from i64 and u64, i16/u16 from i32) prints the same under run and build. KARAC_MIR_INDEX_NUW=0 turns the index facts off for A/B. Measured on the frozen set (502 programs), one pass each: geomean on/off 1.013. All 39 movers re-timed interleaved, best of 3: geomean 1.016 and none over 1.25x. The four worst, re-timed best of 7, were byte-identical binaries (ratio 0.87 to 1.03). Only 5 of 502 binaries change at all, so LLVM 22 was already deriving most of this. ASan lane on the 5 changed programs, 7 index-heavy movers and corpus/core: 242 of 244 pass. The 2 failures are timeouts that also occur with the facts off (28 brute_force, 798 best_rotation). Data: c-notes/b83/ in the shared folder.

title: `a == r` with a non-Copy `T` beside a non-literal `ref T`: Gowtham decided 2026-11-05 that comparisons see through `ref` on either side for any T (design.md e6d39e4575), so the accepted behaviour is the spec; pinned (was: the spec wanted a type error with fix-it `*r`, and refusing it turned 573 swept programs red)
detail: Split from B-2026-11-04-69 item (4). Ruling 5966d6bd81: a literal beside a `ref T` is itself a `ref T`, so `s == "("` stays accepted; the T-vs-ref-T refusal stands for every non-literal operand. Repro: `fn main() { let a = "x".to_string(); let b = "x".to_string(); let r = ref b; println(a == r); }` -> check passes, prints true. Measured at e06766fe96 + an env-gated check (KARAC_EXP_REFCMP, both `==`/`!=` and `<`/`>` arms, string/byte/c-string literal operands exempt, Copy inner types exempt): a 27,484-program check sweep (kara corpus + kara-katas) flags 1,106 sites in 573 programs, 334 distinct (operand, line) pairs once corpus copies of katas are folded. By origin: 106 kara-katas katas, 170 kara-katas apps sources, 278 corpus/katas + corpus/apps copies, 19 corpus fixtures (18 memory_sanitizer). By type: 994 String vs ref String, 112 other (Vec[..], user enums/structs, generic T/V). Shape: the `ref` operand is a bare identifier in all 334 distinct sites, overwhelmingly a parameter that borrows by default under D5 (`fn f(name: String)` is `ref String`), a closure parameter or a `for` element; the other operand is a local (114), an index (63, `lines[0] != header`), a call (17), a field (12, `c.name == name`), other (37) or unparsed (90). So the rule as written asks for `c.name == *name` wherever a borrowed parameter meets an owned value. Patch and per-site list: shared folder threadA-patches/B-2026-11-05-1-refcmp_patch.py and -sites.tsv (report_value_compared_with_ref in src/typechecker/expr_ops.rs).
fix: 2a3202d89d. Settled by Gowtham's 2026-11-05 decision, option (c) of the review thread's card: design.md § No automatic dereference in operators now says (e6d39e4575, with syntax.md) that `==`, `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=` compare the values whether either operand is `T`, `ref T` or `mut ref T`, for any T, and move neither; arithmetic keeps the Copy-only rule. So the accepted behaviour this row reported is now the spec, and the refusal patch measured here (573 programs) is discarded. Pin corpus/design/ok_comparison_sees_through_ref: String vs ref String on all six arms, a D5-borrowed parameter against an owned value, a `mut ref String`, a derived struct, generic `T: PartialEq` / `T: PartialOrd`, and `*pa == *pb` (checks with no borrow_projection_copy lint); passes on mir-interp, mir-llvm and mir-llvm-asan, and in tests/design_pins.rs.

title: A MutFn closure passed to an `own MutFn()` parameter twice (`take(f); take(f);`) is accepted on every lane and runs as if copied; design.md §7 says a MutFn is never Copy, so the second call is a use after move
detail: Exposed by the -62 fix (e06766fe96), which made the spec cell reachable: before it, `let mut f = f;` in the callee refused the program for another reason. design.md §7 Function types and kinds: "A MutFn or OnceFn closure never is [Copy]"; core-semantics §1.1. Repro (probe d7 c20_mutfn_not_copy): `fn take(f: own MutFn()) { let mut f = f; f(); }  fn main() { let mut n = 0; let f = || { n += 1; }; take(f); take(f); }` -> karac check: All checks passed; __mir-run, llvm and ASan run it, and with `println(n)` after it prints 2. Same with a Drop-carrying capture written through (`d.t.push_str("!")`): prints a!! then drop a!! once, ASan clean, so no memory error was observed: both calls see one set of captures, sequentially. Contrast, both correctly refused: `let g = f; let mut a = f;` (typecheck: "use of moved value `f` ... a MutFn is never Copy"), and `both(f, f)` with two own MutFn parameters (MIR E0516: two live mutable borrows). So only the move of a MutFn binding into an own argument, in two separate calls, is not recorded as a move. A OnceFn passed twice the same way IS refused ("value 'g' moved here, used again here").
fix: d78c610976. src/typechecker/core_ref_write.rs note_mut_fn_moved_into_param: a MutFn local passed to an owned parameter (`own MutFn()`, or `escaping`, which is owned) is recorded as moved, beside the `let g = f` move the walker already tracked, under the same rule (a call in the local's own scope, outside any closure, so one move per branch is not a use on another). A later use is refused: "use of moved value `f`: it writes a captured binding, so it is a MutFn, and a MutFn is never Copy (core-semantics §1.1), so passing it to `take`'s owned parameter `f` moved it". Lending first (`twice(mut f); take(f);`) and one move on each `if` branch stay accepted. Pins corpus/design/err_mutfn_moved_into_own_parameter_twice and ok_mutfn_moved_into_own_parameter_on_each_branch; tests/mutfn_owned_arg_and_trait_default_check.rs. A 27,484-program check sweep at d78c610976 found no program newly refused by it.

title: Remainder of B-2026-11-04-80: the editor code action that rewrites `.unwrap()` on an ordinary (non-`weak`) Option to `.expect("…")` does not exist; design.md §11 weak Ergonomics (8c5e67ab81) offers it as an LSP code action, never a check warning
detail: Split from B-2026-11-04-80, whose check-warning half landed at 7d007768dd (weak_read_unwrap, W0294, only on a direct weak read). design.md §11: "On any other `Option`, the same rewrite is offered as an editor code action, never as a check warning". kara-lsp's code actions (lsp/src/analysis.rs `code_actions`) come only from diagnostics with machine-applicable fixes, so there is no way to offer an edit at an Option `.unwrap()` that carries no diagnostic. Needs the typechecker to record the user-source `unwrap()` sites whose receiver is an `Option` (and not a weak read), a lib API that returns them, and a non-diagnostic code action (kind refactor.rewrite) in the LSP over them.
fix: 5fd8c20172. The typechecker records the `unwrap()` text of each builtin `Option.unwrap` in the program's source, recorded before the library-from-source dispatch and excluding library spans and `weak` reads (TypeCheckResult::option_unwrap_sites). `karac::option_unwrap_sites(source)` returns them for an editor buffer through the same pipeline `karac check` runs. kara-lsp offers a non-preferred `refactor.rewrite` code action "Replace `unwrap()` with `expect("…")`" at each one overlapping the request, with no diagnostic, and advertises `refactor.rewrite` beside `quickfix`. A `weak` read's `.unwrap()` keeps its weak_read_unwrap warning and quick fix and gets no rewrite. `karac check` output is unchanged. Pinned by lsp/src/analysis.rs tests `unwrap_on_an_option_offers_the_expect_rewrite` and `a_weak_read_unwrap_keeps_its_quick_fix_without_the_rewrite`, plus the capability assertion in lsp/tests/server.rs.

title: Teemo_attacking ran 2.8x slower on LLVM 22 than on LLVM 18 (x86, 357 ms vs 126): LLVM 22's LICM stopped hoisting the Vec's data-pointer load on karac's dereferenceable assume, and the deeper load chain made the cmov converter branch the loop's `min` (min_stack and hsearch, filed here too, have other causes: B-2026-11-05-27)
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-05 on the 4-core x86 cloud container. Builds: main bd14c35815 (LLVM 22.1.8) against c420c96612 (the last LLVM 18 commit, worktree build). The pre-optimization IR karac emits is the same on both, apart from file paths in panic strings (teemo, KARAC_MIR_LL diff), so the difference is LLVM's. Over the 502 frozen-set programs both built: run-time geomean LLVM 22/18 0.995, 29 programs over 1.25x slower, 47 under 0.8x; two LLVM 22 runs of one binary differ by geomean 0.983 with 8 over 1.25x, so most single movers are noise. Re-timed best of 3: teemo_attacking (495) 357 ms vs 126, callgrind 1.705G vs 1.530G instructions; min_stack (155) 900 vs 423 at 2.206G vs 2.407G; hsearch (275) 925 vs 471 at 1.800G vs 1.625G. TEEMO is attributed: LLVM 18 emits `cmp; cmovge` for `(t[i+1] - t[i]).min(duration)`, LLVM 22 a `cmp; jl` branch on random gaps (0-99 against durations 0-49, about half mispredicted). On karac's post-pass IR (KARAC_MIR_CARRY_STORE=report KARAC_MIR_OPT_LL), llc-22 keeps the cmov only with `-x86-cmov-converter=false`, so X86CmovConversion makes it. With that option set for every build (an experimental KARAC_MIR_CMOV_CONVERT=0, not landed), teemo is 130 ms, but find_peak (162) runs 2.23x slower and find_k_closest (658) 1.79x, and the frozen-set geomean moves 0.978, inside the noise. So a global switch is wrong; a cure would keep the converter and mark the select (unpredictable metadata on a `min`/`max` of loaded data, which the converter honours), and that needs its own measurement. MIN_STACK and HSEARCH are not the cmov converter (the option changes neither: 923 vs 933 ms, 877 vs 922). Their cause is not found, with fewer or about the same instructions; the next step is perf counters (branch misses, store-forwarding stalls), which this container lacks, or a diff of their hot loops. Summary and raw files: shared folder m2-bench/summary-2026-11-05-adr2-llvm22.md. The ADR-2 build and size bars are met on LLVM 22 (build 0.829x, size 0.328x of legacy).
fix: ce0cf3209b (with 0901a9fe6c putting its test in CI). src/backend/mir/mod.rs mark_deref_params: a by-value function's `ref T` / `mut ref T` parameter carries `dereferenceable(size of T) align(align of T)`, what a borrow guarantees for the whole call. CAUSE, found by running each LLVM's opt and llc on the other's IR: llc-18 and llc-22 both keep teemo's cmov on LLVM 18's post-pass IR and both branch on LLVM 22's, so the codegen was not the change. LLVM 18's LICM hoisted the Vec's data-pointer load (`load ptr, ptr %0`) out of find_poisoned_duration's loop on karac's `dereferenceable` llvm.assume; LLVM 22's LICM no longer speculates on that assume (between the assume and the hoist point it must prove nothing frees the memory, and the abort on the bounds-check path defeats it), so the pointer reloaded every trip and the deeper load chain made X86CmovConversion branch the `min`. On the parameter attribute the fact holds for the whole function and the hoist comes back. `!unpredictable` on the min's select was tried first and cannot work: instcombine folds the select into llvm.smin and drops the metadata. MEASURED x86, best of 5, outputs equal: teemo_attacking 379 ms -> 133 ms (LLVM 18 124 ms); a full frozen-set pass with the attribute on and off, movers re-timed head to head: heaters 0.62x, trapping_rain_water 0.75x, partition_max 0.80x, find_peak and find_k_closest unchanged (the rejected global KARAC_MIR_CMOV_CONVERT=0 cost them 2.23x and 1.79x); the programs that read slower in the single pass compile to identical code. Gate: fmt, both clippy legs, cargo test --all 10337/0, cargo test --features llvm 10503 passed plus the one signature pin (mir_pair_results_and_sret_results_keep_parameters_in_registers) updated for the new attributes; corpus mir-llvm lane no new failures. New test tests/mir_deref_params.rs. KARAC_MIR_DEREF_PARAM=0 leaves the attribute out. min_stack and hsearch are NOT this cause (the attribute changes neither) and moved to B-2026-11-05-27.

title: Two `par` branches that each apply `?` to a `Result[D, E]` whose `D` has a printing Drop body conflict on writes(Stdout), though nothing drops inside the branches; the same branches without `?` are accepted
detail: design.md §13 par blocks: a conflict is a write/move/mutable borrow/drop of a place or resource that another branch uses; Failure: on an error exit the block's other values drop after every branch is done, in reverse source order, i.e. outside the branches. Repro: `struct D { t: String }  impl Drop for D { fn drop(mut ref self) { println(f"drop {self.t}"); } }  fn mk(t: own String) -> Result[D, String] { Ok(D { t: t }) }  fn p() -> Result[i64, String] { let (a, b) = par { mk("a")?, mk("b")? }; Ok(1) }  fn main() { println(p().is_ok()); }` -> karac check: error[effect] branches 1 and 2 of the `par` conflict: `writes(Stdout)` and `writes(Stdout)`; MIR effects says the same. Expected: drop b, drop a, true. Control: `let (a, b) = par { mk2("a"), mk2("b") };` with `mk2 -> D` passes and prints joined, drop b, drop a. So the `?` expansion's drop of the Result temporary (whose Err path holds no D) charges D's Drop effect to each branch. Any par over fallible constructors of a type with an effectful Drop (a connection, a file, a guard-like type that logs) hits this. Cells: probe-core d13 p22_par_drops_on_err_reverse, pd2.kara.
fix: 8982776215: the effects pass skips blocks no run reaches (src/mir/effects/feasible.rs). A forward dataflow over the facts a switch on `discriminant(l)` establishes ("is v", "is none of vs"), killed by any write to l, a SetDiscriminant, FreeBox, StorageDead or Drop of it, or a call into it, with locals ever borrowed untracked, prunes the switch edges an earlier switch on the same unchanged enum already decided. The residual drop of the `?` temporary's Ok arm, after the Err arm took the payload, is such a block, so it no longer charges D's writes(Stdout) to each `par` branch. The repro checks clean and prints drop b, drop a, true on mir-run, mir-llvm-run and ASan; branches that really drop a D (`{ let d = mk2("a"); 1 }`) still conflict. Test: tests/par_try_effectful_drop.rs.

title: §13 concurrency roll-up: `return` out of a `par for` body accepted; par conflicts never carry E0408; E_NOT_CROSS_TASK calls a type that contains a shared handle "a shared handle" and gives no field path; freeze refused after pushing a temporary into a mut field; design.md and core-semantics disagree on disjoint element writes in `par for`
detail: From design.md §13. (1) `par for`: "break, continue and return may not cross out of the body"; `fn f() -> i64 { par for i in 0..3 { if i == 1 { return 5; } i }; 0 }` is accepted on every lane and returns 5 (with 16 iterations returning i it returns the earliest, 0, deterministically) (q09). break is correctly refused (q08); `return` in a `par {}` branch is allowed by the spec and works (p31). (2) "The error, E0408, names both accesses": every par/par for conflict diagnostic (p05, p06, p07, p27, q03...) is `error[effect]: branches 1 and 2 of the par conflict: ...` with no E0408 code. (3) Diagnostic shape (What may cross a task boundary): for a type that contains a shared handle the diagnostic names the path (`note: Server contains the shared type Entries at field path inner.cache.entries`). `struct Srv { inner: In }`, `struct In { cache: Ct }`, shared Ct, used in a par branch says "`s` (a `shared` handle of type `Srv`) cannot enter a `par` branch" with no path note; the help does name Ct (p25). `Vec[Ct]` is likewise called "a shared handle of type Vec[Ct]" (p24). (4) design.md §11 freeze site refuses a non-unique source; `let r = Nd { val: 2, kids: [] }; r.kids.push(Nd { val: 3, kids: [] }); let g = freeze r;` is refused "`Nd` has mutable state, so it cannot be frozen yet", though r is the only handle (the pushed node is a temporary). Building the same tree in a helper and freezing its result, or writing the child in the literal, is accepted (fz.kara). (5) Doc contradiction: design.md §13 par for says "Iterations that write disjoint elements of one collection, as the compiler's disjointness analysis proves, do not conflict", while core-semantics §11.2 (ruling 2026-11-02, B-2026-11-01-40) says elements of one collection are one place in v1. The compiler follows core-semantics (`par for i in 0..4 { v[i] = i * 3; }` is refused, q12); design.md needs the v1 caveat.
fix: c519e4b881 for items (3) and (4); (1), (2) and (5) were doc-only. (1) `return` in a `par for` body is core-semantics §11.7's early exit (the earliest iteration's value wins), so the compiler was right and design.md:5809 was wrong; the review thread corrected it in 38455d5c77 ("`return` and `?` end the iteration as an early exit, as they end a `par` branch"). (2) The par conflict does carry a code, E0418 (ParBranchConflict, src/cli/diag_json.rs), visible in `--output=json`; E0408 is ModuleBindingWriteInPar, and the four doc mentions now say E0418 (47adf8ce34). (5) design.md now carries the v1 caveat (ea5cf4556e). (3) src/typechecker/cross_task_check.rs: a value that contains a shared handle is described "`s` (of type `Srv`, which contains the `shared` type `Ct`)" with "note: `Srv` contains the shared type `Ct` at field path inner.cache" (a non-field step, such as a `Vec` argument, is named as it is); a shared handle itself keeps the old wording. (4) src/ownership/frozen_escape.rs walk_fresh_insert_into_field: a statement `r.f.push(..)` / `push_back` / `push_front` / `insert` on a field path of a plain local, whose arguments hold no handle (literals, composite literals of them, Copy locals), does not count as a use of `r` for the freeze-site uniqueness check, so `freeze r` after it is accepted; pushing an existing handle (`r.kids.push(c)`) is still refused. Pin corpus/design/ok_freeze_after_pushing_a_fresh_child; tests/par_cross_task_and_freeze_check.rs.

title: In a package (kara.toml + src/), `import std.sync.{..}`, `import std.net.{..}` and `import std.json.{..}` are refused "unknown module `std.sync`" by check, run, build and test; the same import in a single file works, and `std.time`, `std.log`, `std.process` work in a package
detail: Found probing design.md §14 (a `_test.kara` importing Atomic), then reduced to plain packages. Repro: `kara.toml` = `[package]\nname = "app"` (also with version/edition), `src/main.kara` = `import std.sync.{Atomic};\nfn main() { let a = Atomic.new(1); println(a.load()); }` -> `karac run`: error[E0112] src/main.kara:1:1: unknown module `std.sync`; karac check and karac test (resolve_error event) the same. The same file run alone (`karac run main.kara`) prints 1. Table, package vs single file: std.sync {Atomic}, {channel}, {TaskGroup}: refused vs ok; std.net {TcpListener}: refused vs ok; std.json {Json}: refused vs ok; std.time {Instant}, std.log, std.process: ok in both. So no multi-file program can use Mutex/Atomic/channels/TaskGroup/net/json, i.e. any service-shaped app in package form. Pointer, not a diagnosis: src/resolver/collect.rs collect_import's tree branch validates `imp.path` against `tree.graph.by_path` (the package's own modules), and its comment says valid gated std imports are spliced and removed by prelude::expand_gated_stdlib_imports before resolution; the modules that fail look like the ones that splice path does not cover in tree mode. No existing corpus/example package imports std.sync/net/json (grep examples/*/src), which is why nothing caught it. Cells: probe-core t14/imp.
fix: 8b95f3e4b1. A library module whose items are globals (std.sync, std.net, std.json, std.io, std.hash, std.iter, std.regex) has no node in a package's module graph, so collect_import's tree branch refused it as an unknown module. It now resolves it, or refuses it item by item, through the same check a lone file uses (report_library_global_items in src/resolver/collect.rs). The bare-import message is shared too. A gated module's globals (std.time.{Clock}) bind nothing in a package either, since a lone file's pipeline drops them; that case was found by the new fixture. tests/package_std_imports.rs checks one item of every importable std module (27) in a package against a lone file, diagnostics included, plus bad imports and a two-module run with Atomic, Mutex and Json.

title: `assert_eq(v, e)` and `assert_ne(s, "b")` move a non-Copy operand, so using it afterwards is E0500; design.md §14 says both operands are borrowed and stay usable
detail: design.md §14 Assertions: "They borrow both operands, so neither moves: after assert_eq(v, expected), v is still usable." Repro (plain file, no test needed): `fn main() { let v: Vec[i64] = [1, 2]; let e: Vec[i64] = [1, 2]; assert_eq(v, e); println(v.len()); println(e.len()); let s: String = "a"; assert_ne(s, "b"); println(s); }` -> karac check: error[ownership] value 'v' moved here, used again here; same for e and s. In a test block `karac test` reports the same E0500 with a `.clone()` fix. Expected 2, 2, a. Every test that asserts on a collection or String and then keeps using it hits this, and the suggested fix (clone) is the opposite of the spec's promise. Cell: probe-core t14 t15_assert_eq_borrows, ae.kara.
fix: c519e4b881. src/ownership.rs collect_callee_param_modes: `assert`, `assert_eq` and `assert_ne` take every argument as Ref, beside the print family, so neither operand nor the message moves (design.md §14). `assert_eq(v, e); println(v.len()); println(e.len()); assert_ne(s, "b"); println(s)` prints 2, 2, a on interp, llvm and ASan (pin corpus/design/ok_assertions_borrow_their_operands). The 27,484-program sweep found one program newly accepted, corpus/fixtures/codegen/enums/test_e2e_assert_eq_compares_an_enum_by_content's .orig source, and none newly refused.

title: §14 testing roll-up: assert_eq/assert_ne failure messages omit the `left:`/`right:`/`value:` lines; assert_eq accepts a type with no Debug; `karac test` panics in Rust on a closed stdout
detail:
design.md §14 Assertions table. (1) assert_eq failure message is "assertion failed: a == b
  left:  <a>
  right: <b>"; karac test gives message "assertion failed: add(1, 2) == 4" with no left/right lines (the separate `left`/`right` JSON fields are present, "3"/"4"); assert_ne should end "
  value: <a>" and gives "assertion failed: add(1, 2) != 3" only. Same on JIT and --interp (t03, t04). (2) assert_eq[T: PartialEq + Debug]: `struct P { x: i64 }` with a hand impl of PartialEq and no Debug, `assert_eq(P { x: 1 }, P { x: 1 })` in a test passes check and the test passes (t18). (3) `karac test | head -1` makes karac panic: "thread '<unnamed>' panicked at library/std/src/io/stdio.rs ... failed printing to stdout: Broken pipe" with a Rust backtrace from karac::cli::test_cmd::emit_test_event; a JSONL producer should stop quietly on EPIPE (CLAUDE.md: never panic on user input). Everything else in §14 held on both lanes: discovery by block only (test_ helpers not run), E_TEST_BLOCK_NOT_TOP_LEVEL, tset/pub/private parse errors, duplicate names, private access from the same module and a submodule, filter semantics and total_tests, a panicking test failing alone, test_fail fields, exit codes, karac build ignoring a broken _test file.
fix:
984142c99a. (1) The test_fail message keeps the `
  left:  <a>
  right: <b>` lines (and assert_ne's `
  value: <a>`); src/cli/test_v2.rs no longer cut the message back to its head. Verified on JIT and --interp: `assert_eq(add(1, 2), 4)` reports "assertion failed: add(1, 2) == 4
  left:  3
  right: 4", `assert_ne(add(1, 2), 3)` "... != 3
  value: 3". (2) assert_eq / assert_ne check their operands' type against Debug (src/typechecker/expr_call.rs, through type_supports_debug): a type with no Debug, derived or written, is refused with TraitBoundNotSatisfied naming the type and the §14 signature, and suggests `#[derive(Debug)]` or `assert(a == b)`. Pin corpus/design/err_assert_eq_operand_without_debug; two corpus fixtures that compared non-Debug types gained the derive (f3e512ae99). (3) Every stdout line on the test and JSON/JSONL paths goes through `print_stdout_line` (src/cli/diag_json.rs), which exits 141, the status a SIGPIPE'd process reports, on BrokenPipe instead of panicking; SIGPIPE's disposition is left alone. Tests: tests/jsonl_stream_and_closed_stdout_check.rs (karac_test_into_a_closed_pipe_ends_quietly, assert_eq_refuses_operands_that_cannot_print), tests/test_v2.rs's message pin. A 27,484-program check sweep changed nothing else.

title: Kata 73's bench runs 21x slower on the default pool than on one worker (10.1 s against 0.48 s, 4 workers, x86): auto-par runs its 20-row matrix build (400 pushes) as tasks on every one of 100,000 outer trips, since a loop inside a loop was refused only at 16 trips or fewer
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-05 on the 4-core x86 container, main bd14c35815: corpus/katas/1-100/73-set-matrix-zeroes/bench/set_matrix_zeroes 10.086 s default (4 workers), 5.29 s at KARAC_THREADS=2, 8.65 s at 3, 0.478 s at KARAC_THREADS=1, 0.507 s built with KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0; the 10-29 baseline had it at 0.395 s, and the LLVM 18 build at c420c96612 is as slow (8-10 s), so it is not the LLVM upgrade. KARAC_AUTO_PAR_DEBUG: `loops as tasks: main@89` with `reductions: main@89 (m at 96)`, the `while i < rows` loop that builds a fresh 20x20 Vec[Vec[i64]] inside `while k < total` (100,000 trips). The cost gate (src/mir/effects/auto_par.rs) refuses a nested loop only when it makes at most FEW_TRIPS (16) trips, and applies the SMALL_WORK test (all trips times inner trips under 100,000) to top-level loops only; and its counter `i` is reset with `i = 0` for the fold loop that follows, so `constant_trips` saw two literal writes and gave up, which also lets a loop of unknown trips through. Found while re-measuring ADR-2 after the LLVM 22 upgrade: it is the frozen set's worst run-time ratio (24.7x the 10-29 legacy figure).
fix: ebd092c397. src/mir/effects/auto_par.rs: a loop inside another loop whose iterations only run inner loops of known trips is sized by all of that work (trips x inner trips) and stays in order under SMALL_WORK, with the refusal "its N trips run about W inner trips each time, inside a loop, too few to pay"; before, a nested loop was refused only at FEW_TRIPS or fewer trips. loop_trips also takes a counter reset to the same literal before a second loop (kata 73's `i = 0;`) as its start, since this only sizes a loop for the cost gate. MEASURED x86, 4 workers, best of 5, outputs equal: kata 73's set_matrix_zeroes 8.70 s -> 0.44 s (legacy-level 0.48 s); over the frozen set exactly three verdicts change, all to this refusal: 73, 130 surrounded_regions 0.41 -> 0.34 s, and 631 excel 0.66 -> 0.77 s wall, which a control build of the parent (8ad41b4a1a) shows is layout: 6.324G instructions both ways under callgrind, and the control's own in-order twin (KARAC_THREADS=1) runs 0.66 s, so the par loop itself never paid (676 cheap gets per round). Unit test auto_par_nested_loop_of_little_work_stays_in_order (a 20x20 build inside a loop stays in order; a 1000x1000 one still goes). Gate on the rebased tree: fmt, both clippy legs, wasm clippy, cargo test --all 10318/0, cargo test --features llvm 10484/0. m5-rows.sh carries a par-lane row for the M5.

title: The target gate never refuses ProcessTable on wasm_wasi: a program that spawns a process passes `karac check --targets=all` and a `[build] targets = ["native", "wasm_wasi"]` matrix, and `karac build --target=wasm_wasi` emits a module that runs; design.md §16 makes it error E0411 with the call chain
fix: 8982776215: the gate did find ProcessTable, at Command.status's own node, but at a span in the library's text, and check drops every diagnostic there (drop_library_diagnostics), so nothing reached the user. The gate now reports a use inside library text at the program's last call on the chain, once per call and resource (src/effectchecker/target_gate.rs). The repro now fails `karac check --target=wasm_wasi` with one error at 2:30, "target `wasm_wasi` does not provide resource 'ProcessTable' — required on the call chain main → helper → spawn_it → Command.status", and passes on native. Test: tests/target_gate_library_process.rs.

title: §16 targets roll-up: artifact paths differ from the spec; the multi-target check JSON is neither tagged nor deduplicated; `--targets=all` also runs wasm_browser and gpu, so every printing program fails it; `[profile.release]` is ignored; `--target-cpu=help` prints to stderr; wasm builds need the host's rustc with the wasm32-wasip1 target
detail: From design.md §16. (1) Build artifacts: native at `dist/native/<pkg>`, wasm_wasi at `dist/wasm/<pkg>.wasm`. A package `karac build` writes `dist/app`, and `--target=wasm_wasi` writes `dist/app.wasm`; `karac build --help` itself says `dist/wasm/<pkg>.{wasm,js,d.ts}` for wasm (k01, k02). (2) Checking several targets: a finding identical on every target is reported once in a `shared_diagnostics` array (JSON). With targets [native, wasm_wasi] and one type error, `karac check --output=json` prints two separate top-level `{"diagnostics": [...]}` objects with no target field and no shared_diagnostics (k09). (3) The v1 target set is closed at native and wasm_wasi; `--targets=all` checks native, wasm_browser, wasm_wasi and gpu, and gpu refuses any program that prints ("target `gpu` does not provide resource 'Stdout'"), so `--targets=all` fails on hello world; that gpu diagnostic also suggests `#[target(...)]`, an attribute the spec does not have (#[cfg(target: ..)]) (k08). (4) Build profiles / CPU override: `[profile.release] target-cpu = "bogus9"` builds with "warning[manifest]: unknown key `[profile].release` ignored in 0.8 (reserved)", so the third rung of the CPU and feature precedence is not there (c05); flag and env rungs work and refuse unknown names (c01, c04, c06-c09). (5) `--target-cpu=help` / `--target-features=help` print the list on stderr with empty stdout (c02, c10). (6) Runtime: "The compiler distribution contains bin/karac and the runtime archive ... no runtime to install"; `karac build --target=wasm_wasi` resolves wasi-libc through `rustc --print target-libdir --target wasm32-wasip1` (src/backend/driver.rs resolve_wasi_self_contained_dir), so outside a directory pinned to a toolchain with that target installed it fails "wasm32-wasip1 self-contained sysroot not found ... rustup target add"; with RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN=1.98.0 every wasm cell passed. Held: wasi hello/par/par for/TaskGroup/channels/fs/panic 101, recv deadlock panic, _start export, -simd128, panic handler on native, interp and wasm, one-handler rule, handler panics once, no drops, run/build exit 1, -O0/-O3 same output, panic file:line, --platform refused by build/run, platform file suffix.
fix: c48ad61f26 (items 1 to 5) and 7c8f15e8fd (item 6). (1) USER-VISIBLE PATH CHANGE: a package build now writes dist/native/<pkg>, and --target=wasm_wasi dist/wasm/<pkg>.wasm, as §16 says; they were dist/<pkg> and dist/<pkg>.wasm, so a script running the built binary needs the new path. karac install takes the binary from dist/native; examples/slipstream updated; CHANGELOG 0.8.1 "Changed" says so.
