fix: 34cb06e29c: a plain binding of a non-`Copy` part of a `shared` value is typed `ref T` (src/typechecker/patterns.rs, core_shared_part_depth), as the same binding over a `ref` scrutinee already was, in both the strict check and the build's check. So a tuple of such bindings holds references and `match e { E.R { xs, ms } => (xs, ms) }` checks the same under `e: E` as under `e: ref E`. The nested case is covered: a part that is itself a handle copies the handle, and a pattern over it binds `ref`s again. The MIR already bound these by reference. Moving one out (an `own` parameter, a returned tuple, `push`) is still refused. Pins: corpus/core ok_shared_part_bindings_are_refs, err_shared_part_ref_moved_out. Full interp corpus: no new failures. A broader first draft also typed borrowed-place and explicit `ref name` bindings as `ref T`. It refused writes through `mut ref` places (14 corpus programs) and changed the `Drop`/clone diagnostics two strict-check tests pin, so it was narrowed. The explicit `ref name` half is filed separately as B-2026-11-06-4. Not changed: style_lints.rs `redundant_ref_param` still exempts destructured parameters citing this row.

title: Rust's map methods `values_mut`, `retain`, `into_values`/`into_keys`, and on `SortedMap` `first_key_value`/`last_key_value`/`pop_first`/`pop_last`, are a bare `no method 'X' on type 'SortedMap'` that names no Kāra twin; whether `SortedMap` (which has `floor`/`ceiling` but, unlike `SortedSet`, no `min`/`max`) and `Map` should gain some of them is a library-spec question
detail: Found writing apps/cli/mini_jobqueue (kara-katas d04a3f89). A job queue keeps jobs in a `SortedMap[i64, Job]` and promotes due jobs in place; the natural first draft is `for j in m.values_mut() { if j.due <= now { j.state = State.Available; } }`, which karac refuses with `error[typecheck]: no method 'values_mut' on type 'SortedMap'` and nothing else. docs/library/collections.md specs `iter_mut()` with item `(ref K, mut ref V)` for `Map` and `SortedMap` (Iteration table), so `for (_, j) in m.iter_mut()` is the spelling, and it runs on interp, mir-llvm and build. The same bare error, at 5:13 on `let x = m.<call>;` over a `SortedMap[i64, i64]`, for: `values_mut()`, `retain(|k, v| true)`, `first_key_value()`, `last_key_value()`, `pop_first()`, `pop_last()`, `into_values()`, `into_keys()`, `get_or_insert_with(1, || 2)`, `remove_entry(1)`, `get_key_value(1)`, `range_mut(1..3)`, `append(o)`. The twins that work today (checked on interp and `karac run`): `m.keys().next().cloned()` and `m.keys().last().cloned()` / `m.iter().rev().next()` for the first and last key, then `m.remove(k)` to pop; `h.into_iter().filter(|(_, v)| v > 2).collect()` for a retain. Precedent: B-2026-11-01-9 names the Kāra twin of Rust `str` methods (`rust_string_method_twin` in src/typechecker/expr_method_call.rs), and `matches!` already gets a twin in the parser. Two parts: (1) diagnostics, owned here: name the twin for each Rust map method that stays absent, as B-2026-11-01-9 does; (2) design, for the library spec owner: `SortedMap` is the ordered map an event queue, timer list or scheduler reaches for, and it has no first/last/pop at all while `SortedSet` has `min`/`max`; `Map`/`SortedMap` have no `retain` while `Vec` and `VecDeque` do. If the spec adds any of these, part (1) drops them.
fix: 2a3f845fd5. Per the library spec ruling (docs/library/collections.md, 5033cb49da): Map and SortedMap have `values_mut`, `into_keys`, `into_values` and `retain(pred: own MutFn(K, mut ref V) -> bool)` (SortedMap's in key order); SortedMap has `first`/`last` (borrowed pair) and `pop_first`/`pop_last` (owned pair); SortedSet has `pop_first`/`pop_last` and `retain`. They are library methods in runtime/stdlib/source/collections.kara over two new cursor natives, `take_entry_at(i)` and `value_at_mut(i)`, on the interpreter (src/mir/interp.rs) and the LLVM backend (src/backend/mir/table.rs). Rust names Kara spells otherwise (`first_key_value`, `last_key_value`, a sorted set's `first`/`last`) now say which method Kara has. Pinned by corpus/design/ok_map_retain_values_mut_and_pops (interp, llvm, asan and build at KARAC_THREADS 1 and 4) and tests/sorted_collection_rust_names.rs; corpus/apps/cli/mini_jobqueue promotes with the natural values_mut loop again.

title: In a package, `import utils;` naming no module is reported as E0223 `circular module dependency: <crate root> → <crate root>` instead of an unknown module: the module graph's longest-prefix fallback turns a bare import that names nothing into an edge to the crate root, so main.kara imports itself
detail: Found while pinning B-2026-11-05-15. Repro: pkg/kara.toml `[package]\nname = "app"`, pkg/src/util.kara `pub fn f() -> i64 { 1 }`, pkg/src/main.kara `import utils;\nfn main() { println(utils.f()); }`. `karac check src/main.kara` (and `karac check` in pkg): `error[E0223]: src/main.kara:1:1: circular module dependency` with `cycle: <crate root> → <crate root>` and a suggestion to extract shared items into a lower layer. Cause: `collect_import_edges` in src/module.rs tries the whole path (`["utils"]`), then the path with the tail stripped, which for a bare import is `[]`, the crate root; from main.kara that is a self-edge, and Tarjan reports it as a one-node cycle. The cycle check runs before resolve, so the resolver's unknown-name error never appears.
fix: 8dff1b2177. In collect_import_edges (src/module.rs) a module importing from itself adds no graph edge, so `import utils;` in the crate root naming no module is no longer a self-cycle E0223; the resolver reports the unknown module with its did-you-mean (`util`). An `import z;` of a crate-root item from another module still adds its edge, so real cycles through the root are still E0223 (tests/cli.rs module-cycle tests). Pinned by tests/import_unknown_module_in_package.rs, for `karac check <file>` and the package check.

title: An explicit `ref name` pattern binding over an owned scrutinee cannot go into a tuple: `match p { P.R { ref xs, ms } => (xs, ms) }` (and `let H { ref xs } = h; (xs, 1)`) is refused as `cannot move 'xs': it borrows its value`, while the same tuple of a binding over a `ref` scrutinee holds the reference (core semantics §4.6)
detail: The remainder of B-2026-11-05-40 (fixed for parts of `shared` values in 34cb06e29c). Minimal: `enum P { R { xs: Vec[i64], ms: i64 }, N } fn f(p: own P) -> i64 { let (xs, ms) = match p { P.R { ref xs, ms } => (xs, ms), _ => return 0 }; xs.len() + ms }` -> `error[borrow_projection_copy]: cannot move 'xs': it borrows its value` at the tuple; under `p: ref P` with a plain `xs` it checks and runs. The `ref name` binding is typed as the plain part (T) and marked a view, so a tuple of it reads as a move. Typing it `ref T` (tried in the -40 draft) accepts the tuple on interp, but changes two pinned diagnostics: tests/core_strict_check.rs `a_drop_value_behind_a_ref_binding_derives_clone` (`h.f = r` loses its `Drop` message and derive-Clone fix to a bare `expected 'R', found 'ref R'`) and tests/core_match_result_is_a_ref.rs `the_ref_a_match_binds_cannot_be_moved_out_or_written_through` (`v.push(r)`). A fix needs those messages kept, either by teaching the mismatch path the move-out-of-a-ref wording and fix, or by exempting a view identifier in a tuple element and typing the slot `ref T`. The let-destructure spelling goes through a different binding site.
fix: 5f60e598f2: an inferred tuple literal types an element that names an explicit `ref name` binding (not `mut ref`, of a non-`Copy` type) as `ref T`, and the tuple's element move check skips it (src/typechecker/items.rs tuple_slot_holds_ref_pattern / is_ref_pattern_ident, called from exprs.rs; the binding is marked in LocalTypeScope.ref_patterns at both binding sites in patterns.rs). So `match p { P.R { ref xs, ms } => (xs, ms) }` and `let H { ref xs } = h; (xs, 1)` hold the reference, as a tuple of a binding over a `ref` scrutinee does (core semantics §4.6), on interp and llvm. The binding keeps its type `T`, so the two pinned diagnostics the -40 draft broke (core_strict_check `a_drop_value_behind_a_ref_binding_derives_clone`, core_match_result_is_a_ref `push`) are unchanged. Taking the part back out of the tuple as an owned value is still refused. Pins: corpus/core ok_ref_pattern_binding_into_tuple, err_ref_pattern_tuple_part_moved_out. The 1432 corpus entries that use a ref pattern: no new interp failures.

title: `karac query` refuses a program that uses a library type `karac check` resolves (`undefined type 'WsMessage'`), so every query kind fails on the `karac new` backend scaffold: the query pipeline is built without `.with_library()`
detail: Found while fixing B-2026-11-05-29. `fn f(m: WsMessage) -> i64 { match m { WsMessage.Close(_) => 1, _ => 0 } } fn main() { println(2); }` passes `karac check` ('All checks passed.'), but `karac query effects ws.kara` stops with `error[resolve]: ws.kara:1:9: undefined type 'WsMessage'`. The same happens to `karac query queries` (and every other kind) in a fresh `karac new hello` package, whose src/main.kara names `WsMessage.Text` / `.Binary` / `.Close`. The cause is in src/cli/query_cmd.rs `cmd_query`: it builds `Pipeline::new(filename, &source)` and resolves it, where `karac check` (src/cli/run_check_cmds.rs) builds `Pipeline::new(..).with_lint_overrides(..).strict_core().with_library()`. src/cli/explain_item.rs (`karac explain <file>.<item>`) builds its pipeline the same way, so it presumably has the same gap; that was not measured. A fix probably adds `.strict_core().with_library()` to the query pipeline. The whole-program answers (query effects / ownership / concurrency on a bare file) would then need to leave out the library's own functions, as check's reports do through `library_len`. design.md § Compiler query API: the query runs 'enough of the pipeline to answer', which has to be the same program check sees.
fix: 02a406c30c: `karac query` (src/cli/query_cmd.rs) and `karac explain <file>.<item>` (src/cli/explain_item.rs) build `Pipeline::new(..).strict_core().with_library()`, as `karac check` does. Every answer is about the program's own items: `own_program` clones the program truncated at `library_start` (a byte offset, so `partition_point` on item offsets), and whole-program ownership answers are filtered to `own_function_names`. src/style_lints.rs had read `library_start` as an item index; it now partitions the same way. src/layout_queries.rs peels `ref` / `mut ref` off the iterated collection, so a loop over a bare (borrowed) `Vec[S]` parameter still gets its layout query. Four cli pins that held pre-core answers are flipped: a bare closure parameter borrows (tests/snapshots/closure_query.kara now writes `own` for its consume case), and the RC-fallback query and cost-summary entries do not arise (core §6.4); the remaining RC-fallback reporting on programs check refuses is B-2026-11-06-9. Pinned by tests/derivation_and_fixes.rs `query_and_explain_see_the_library_check_sees` (query effects lists exactly f and main, ownership two functions, explain succeeds on a WsMessage program). Gate green on this change before its final rebase (10457 + 10627 passed).

title: two impls of one trait whose headers do not unify, `impl[T] Name for W[A[T]]` and `impl[T] Name for W[B[T]]`, are refused as a conflicting impl ("`W` already implements `Name`"), and in the standard library the second is dropped silently
fix: 30f3ec3af7. The overlap check (src/typechecker/env_build.rs impl_overlap_conflict) keyed a generic impl on its target's name, so impl[T] Name for W[A[T]] and W[B[T]] (or W[B[i64]]) were refused as 'already implements'. Two trait impls now overlap only when their written targets unify (headers_unify, each impl's params standing for any type, conservative where it cannot compare); inherent impls keep the name rule, since disjoint inherent impls would be dispatched by Type.method to the first. So each call reaches its own impl: impl_shape_fits (src/typechecker/env.rs) no longer lets two different type constructors fit, and MIR's user_impl_method (src/mir/lower.rs), used by calls through a bound, picks the impl whose written target the receiver is, binding its params with written_fits. In the standard library the refusal had been dropped with the library's other type errors, the second impl skipped silently; src/cli.rs drop_library_diagnostics now keeps a library ConflictingImpl, prefixed 'in the standard library:' (shown with a planted duplicate), except a package member's restatement of a baked impl, which leaves the baked one standing as before. tests/library_coherence.rs checks the whole unpruned library. B-2026-11-05-35's private StepBack is replaced by DoubleEndedIterator for IterStepBy[Range[T]] and [RangeInclusive[T]]. Pinned by corpus/design/ok_impls_whose_headers_do_not_unify (direct, via a bound, a default method) on mir-interp, mir-llvm and mir-llvm-asan.

title: A type parameter that only a call's return type names is refused at the `let` (`let mut heap = PriorityQueue.new()`, a user `Bag.new()`, `fn empty[T]() -> Vec[T]`) with 'cannot infer type parameter T', though a later use in the body (`heap.push(x)`) fixes it; design.md §8 solves type variables by unification within the body
detail: Found by kata 1057's heap arm, written the way Rust writes it: `let mut heap = BinaryHeap::new(); for i in 0..n { heap.push(Reverse((d, i, j))); }`. `karac fix` carries it to `let mut heap = PriorityQueue.new(); heap.push((d, i, j))`, and `karac check` then refuses the binding: 'cannot infer type parameter 'T'; add a type annotation to this binding'. The same holds for `PriorityQueue.max_first()`, for a user `impl[T] Bag[T] { fn new() -> Bag[T] }` used as `let mut b = Bag.new(); b.push((3, 4));`, and for a free `fn empty[T]() -> Vec[T]` used as `let mut v = empty(); v.push(3);` (all three probed on the release build of 52c81c1375). `Vec.new()`, `VecDeque.new()`, `Set.new()`, `SortedSet.new()`, `Map.new()` and `SortedMap.new()` work because src/typechecker/expr_call.rs special-cases them ('Built-in collection constructors with no syntactic stdlib declaration') with fresh type variables that a later `push` solves; a declared generic function or constructor instead leaves the return-only parameter a `TypeParam`, and `check_unsolved_type_param` (src/typechecker/items.rs) reports it at the binding. design.md §8 says type variables are solved by unification within one function body, which a later `push` is. Remedy hypothesis, unverified: instantiate a return-only parameter as a fresh type variable at the call and report it only if the body leaves it unsolved, as `check_unsolved_call_results` already does for a call result used as a receiver; MIR lowering would need the solved type. The kata's heap arm writes `let mut heap: PriorityQueue[(i64, i64, i64)] = PriorityQueue.new();` by hand and its README cites this row.
fix: 2783b8c546. A generic call's type parameter that nothing at the call fixes stays a type variable inside the call's type (src/typechecker/exprs.rs, `late_var_ids`), so a later use in the body solves it: `PriorityQueue.new()` / `max_first()`, a user `Bag.new()` and `fn empty[T]() -> Vec[T]` followed by a push now check and run. One still unsolved when the program has been checked is refused at the call (`report_unsolved_call_vars`), and the impl bounds of a method call made while the receiver's argument was a variable (`T: Ord` on `push`) are checked against the type the use fixed (`report_deferred_receiver_bounds`; env.rs treats a variable argument as undecidable, as it does a parameter). Pinned by corpus/design/ok_a_later_use_fixes_a_call_s_type_parameter (interp, llvm, asan) and tests/later_use_fixes_call_type.rs. Option/Result results, a bare-parameter result and a parameter named like the caller's own keep the old path: B-2026-11-06-11.

Relocated to B-2026-11-06-34 (drop schedule's sort work), by agreement with the drop schedule, 2026-11-07. 5e869cb573 took the LIS phase: src/mir/halving.rs turns a signed `x / 2^k` of a provably non-negative `x` into `x >> k`, which removes the arm64 sign fixup and lets the midpoint facts apply. scripts/bench/probes/354 splits the kata by phase for m5-rows.sh. M5 at 7708b0aae5 (5 runs, cycles vs rustc -O): whole kata 1.237x (was 1.304x); gen 1.018x; LIS 1.088x (halving on vs off 0.886x); sort 1.316x. The remaining gap is the sort phase, the large-n merge path that -06-34 describes.
title: Kata 354 on arm64 ran 1.36x rustc -O's cycles after d70e6d474a and 1.237x after 5e869cb573 (LIS phase 1.088x); what remains is the sort phase (1.316x), relocated to B-2026-11-06-34
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-06 on the M5 Pro (review thread's m5-rows run at kara 4471044a8a, 5 runs, bench/russian_doll.kara, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0): 757.1M cycles against rustc -O's 556.6M, 1.360x; against legacy dd86e3955 0.954x cycles at 0.824x instructions, so B-2026-11-06-1's legacy half is closed. On x86 the same commit runs 0.53 s against rustc -O's 0.52 s, so the remaining gap is arm64's. Not attributed. Candidates from the x86 work, unmeasured on arm64: the fused partition loop still branches on the comparator's own `a.0 != b.0` (apple-m4 llc output: `cmp; b.ne` per element, the less test is a csel since d70e6d474a), and the patience LIS binary search, whose select x86's cmov converter turned back into a branch (that half was left alone; on arm64 there is no cmov converter, so check what llc emits there). Rust's std sort is a different algorithm (ipnsort), so compare the two loops' branch counts before blaming the sort.

fix: f053625e94: the strict pipeline (src/cli.rs `ownershipcheck_phase`, the `strict_core` block that turns each RC-fallback site into its E0500 and drops the RC note) now also clears the ownership result's `rc_values`, `arc_values` and `suppressed_rc_fn_keys`, because under core semantics §6.4 no value is shared to make a program legal and each of those sites is already an error. `karac query queries` no longer answers an `rc_fallback_decision` with keep_rc / prefer_rc, `query cost-summary` counts no `rc_ops` (suppressed or not), and `query ownership` lists no `rc_values`, for a program check refuses with the move. Pinned by tests/query_core_no_rc.rs (the closure-capture and maybe-moved shapes from this row). The `#[prefer_rc]` / `#[no_rc]` / `#[allow(rc_fallback)]` attribute surface is unchanged: under the core rules those attributes no longer have anything to act on. Gate green on this change before its final rebase (10463 + 10635 passed).
title: `karac query queries` and `query cost-summary` still report RC fallbacks (`rc_fallback_decision` with keep_rc / prefer_rc, `rc_ops`), which core semantics §6.4 removed: they now appear only on programs `karac check` refuses with E0500
detail: Found while fixing B-2026-11-06-5, which made `karac query` run the core rules as check does (02a406c30c). Core semantics §6.4: 'The compiler never turns an owned value into a shared or atomically counted one. design.md Part 4 (RC fallback) ... removed. Where the fallback would have fired, the program has an E0500 (§3.2) or an escaping capture (§9.3).' Under the core rules the four cli pins that held RC fallbacks no longer produce one, because their bare parameters borrow (§4.1); they were flipped in 02a406c30c. Writing the move explicitly still produces one. `struct Owned { x: i64 } fn take(o: own Owned) { } fn main() { let o = Owned { x: 1 }; let _f = || take(o); let _u = o; }`: `karac check` says `error[ownership]: value 'o' was moved into a closure ... used again here`, while `karac query queries` answers an `rc_fallback_decision` whose options are keep_rc ('accept the reference-counting overhead'), prefer_rc ('confirm the RC fallback is intended with `#[prefer_rc]`') and no_rc. Adding `#[prefer_rc]` does not make check accept it. Likewise `fn consume(d: own Data) {} fn use_d(d: own Data) {} #[allow(rc_fallback)] fn process(d: own Data) { match d.value { 0 => consume(d), _ => {} } use_d(d); }`: check gives E0500-style 'may have been moved', while `query cost-summary` reports `rc_ops: {count: 1, rc: 1, suppressed: 1}` with derivation 'Rc fallback for `d` — direct re-use after consume'. So the query offers resolutions that do not exist and counts RC operations no build will emit. The likely remedy (a hypothesis): drop `crate::rc_fallback_queries::analyze` from `karac query queries` (src/cli/query_cmd.rs) and the RC-fallback entries from src/cost_summary.rs, and decide whether the `#[prefer_rc]` / `#[no_rc]` / `rc_fallback` lint surface goes with them or is refused with a diagnostic pointing at §6.4. Shared-handle counting (`shared struct`) is a different category and is unaffected.

fix: bd1c1521a1: core semantics §4.6 now holds for `let` destructuring as it does for `match` (B-2026-11-05-40). Typecheck: the let-route struct arm in src/typechecker/patterns.rs (`bind_pattern_types`) accepts a `Type::Shared` scrutinee of the pattern's struct, and types a non-`Copy`, non-handle part as `ref T` (a handle part still copies the handle, §6.1). MIR: src/mir/lower.rs destructures a `shared` value in a place where it is, rather than copying the handle into a statement temporary and moving the parts out of it, and `bind_irrefutable` binds a shared value's parts through `bind_pattern`, the match lowering's path. A temporary scrutinee (`let H { xs, .. } = make();`) is E0516, because the temporary ends at the `;` (§4.6, §7.4). Pins: corpus/core ok_shared_let_destructure_binds_refs (nested shared parts, a bare shared parameter, the handle still usable after) and err_shared_let_part_moved_out (moving a bound part into `own` is refused, §3.7). Gate green on this change before its final rebase (10458 + 10629 passed); the core-pin unit tests were re-run after it.
title: `let H { xs, n } = h` on a `shared struct H` is refused with `struct pattern `H` used but type is `H``, though core semantics §4.6 lets a shared scrutinee bind its parts as `ref`s and the same pattern in `match` / `if let` checks clean
detail: Found while narrowing redundant_ref_param for B-2026-11-06-5. `shared struct H { xs: Vec[i64], n: i64 } fn main() { let h = H { xs: [1, 2], n: 3 }; let H { xs, n } = h; println(xs.len() + n); }`: `karac check` says `error[typecheck]: 4:9: struct pattern `H` used but type is `H``. The same program with `match h { H { xs, n } => xs.len() + n }` or `if let H { xs, .. } = h { .. }` passes check. Spec: core semantics §4.6 'A shared scrutinee ... counts as a ref scrutinee ... A plain binding of a part is therefore a ref automatically, and moving it is an error whose fix is .clone()', and §4.6 covers `let` destructuring. Two layers, measured at 5aa778b57e. (1) Typecheck: src/typechecker/patterns.rs, the `let`-route `PatternKind::Struct` arm (`field_source_ty`), accepts only `Type::Named { name == struct_name }`; a shared struct's value is `Type::Shared(name)`, which falls to the mismatch error (type_display renders both as `H`, hence the message). The `match` route (`check_pattern_against`) peels refs and does not refuse it. (2) MIR: with (1) patched locally to accept `Type::Shared(name)` when name == struct_name (not landed), check then fails at the `let` with `error[mir]: build: 4:5: cannot move a non-`Copy` value out of a `shared` value ... (core semantics §3.7)`, though nothing is moved (only `xs.len()` reads it). So the MIR lowering of a `let` struct pattern moves parts out of a shared scrutinee where §4.6 binds them as `ref`; the `match` lowering does not. With the patch, a program that does move the part (`keep(xs)` with `fn keep(v: own Vec[i64])`) gets the right error at the move site (`borrow_projection_copy: cannot move 'xs': it borrows its value`), so only the read-only case is wrong. The fix probably needs both layers; the typecheck half is the 15-line arm above.

title: Remainder of B-2026-11-06-7: a later use still does not fix a call's return-only type parameter when the result is an `Option`/`Result` (`let mut best = none_of(); best = Some(3)`), is the bare parameter (`let x = make(); let y: i64 = x`), or the parameter shares a name with the caller's own (`fn g[T]` calling `Bag.new()` then `b.push(1)`: "expected 'T', found 'i64'")
detail: 2783b8c546 (B-2026-11-06-7) keeps a call's unfixed type parameter a type variable, so a later use in the body solves it, when the variable sits inside a struct, a collection, a tuple or a reference in the result (`PriorityQueue.new()`, `Bag.new()`, `fn empty[T]() -> Vec[T]`). Three shapes keep the old path, where an unsolved parameter comes back as `TypeParam(name)`: (1) `Option`/`Result` results, because the unbound `E` of `Ok(5)` is read off the call's type by `resolved_node_tables` and the `?`-operand diagnostics (tests/question_operand_unsolved.rs, tests/core_closure_question_err.rs) name `TypeParam`; `fn none_of[T]() -> Option[T] { None }` then `let mut best = none_of(); best = Some(3);` is refused at the `let` with 'cannot infer type parameter 'T''. (2) A bare parameter result, because `collect`'s `C` is fixed from the binding's annotation through `record_declared_type_for_polymorphic_rhs` and node call subs (tests/mir_iterators.rs went to 'the method call `.collect` with no resolved callee' when it was a variable); `fn make[T: Default]() -> T` then `let x = make(); let y: i64 = x;` is refused at the `let`. (3) A parameter whose name is in scope at the caller: a library default body copied into `impl[K, V] Iterator for MapValues[K, V]` reads `self.next()`'s unsolved `V` as the impl's own `V` (the receiver is the bare target type), so names in `enclosing_bounds` stay `TypeParam`; a user `fn g[T](x: T) -> i64 { let mut b = Bag.new(); b.push(1); b.len() }` is refused with "expected 'T', found 'i64'" because the call's `T` aliases the caller's; renaming the caller's parameter to `U` makes it pass and print 1. All probed on the release build of 2783b8c546. design.md § Type inference solves all three by a later use in the body.
fix: 5f1222f497. A `let` whose initializer leaves a type parameter unbound (`let mut best = None;`, `let mut r = Ok(1);`, `let mut lo = none_of();`, `let x = make();`) now opens it as a fresh variable in the binding's type (src/typechecker/items.rs, `open_unsolved_let_params`), judged once the program has been checked; an assignment to such a binding (`best = Some(x)`, `r = Err("bad")`) unifies the slot with the value before checking it (`solve_open_slot_from`). A callee parameter spelled like the caller's own (`Bag.new()` inside `fn g[T]` or `impl[T] Holder[T]`) is the callee's (exprs.rs); only a method call on a receiver inside an impl, whose bare `self` leaves the impl's own parameters unsolved (`self.drain_entries()` in `impl[K, V] Map`), keeps naming them, and an unsolved variable spelled like a parameter in scope still names it at the end. Pinned by corpus/design/ok_a_later_use_fixes_an_option_or_bare_result (interp, llvm, asan) and two tests in tests/later_use_fixes_call_type.rs.

title: Polymorphic recursion hangs the compiler: `fn deep[T: Display](x: own T, n: i64) -> i64 { .. deep([x], n - 1) + 1 }` makes `karac check` (and the interpreter lane) run forever instead of refusing the program
detail: Repro: `fn deep[T: Display](x: own T, n: i64) -> i64 { if n == 0 { 0 } else { deep([x], n - 1) + 1 } }\nfn main() { println(deep(1, 3)); }`. `timeout 100 karac check` exits 124 with no output; `__mir-run` also times out. RSS was about 58 MB at 22 s. The same with `deep(Some(x), n - 1)` and no bound: no output after 60 s. Each call instantiates `deep` at a strictly larger type (Vec[i64], Vec[Vec[i64]], ...), so design.md §8 Monomorphization (one instance per argument tuple) needs unboundedly many instances; expected since 1326cb22a7 (design.md §8 Monomorphization, `Polymorphic recursion is an error`): karac check refuses the program with a diagnostic at the recursive call, instead of looping. Ordinary generic recursion at the same instance (`fn cnt[T](v: Vec[T], i: i64) -> i64 { .. cnt(v, i + 1) }`) works on all four lanes. At 760d8f9ec.
fix: d4c94d8b4b. `karac check` (and every build) now refuses polymorphic recursion at the recursive call, before any instance is made (design.md §8). src/mir/poly_recursion.rs builds a graph over generic parameters: a call in `f` to a generic `g` whose j-th type argument holds f's i-th parameter d levels down is an edge (f,i)->(g,j) of weight d (`T` 0, `Vec[T]`/`Option[T]`/`(T, i64)` 1); a method call that dispatches on a receiver of a parameter's type reaches each impl of that method that could take it, weighing d minus the depth of the impl's parameter in its target. Instances are finite exactly when no cycle weighs more than 0, so each positive call that closes such a cycle (Bellman-Ford within its strongly connected component) is refused with the cycle and the growing argument: "polymorphic recursion: `deep` calls itself with `Vec[T]` in place of `T`, so the argument grows on every round ...". lower_program_inner runs it first and seeds no instance when it refuses, so check ends in about 0.1 s where it ran forever. Pins: corpus/core err_poly_recursion_{vec_grows,some_grows,mutual_grows,through_dispatch} (the row's two repros, a two-function cycle, and a cycle through trait dispatch that the first, unweighted version missed and still hung on) and ok_recursion_{same_or_other_type,through_dispatch_peels} (same, swapped, unrelated and outside-a-cycle growth; a `Tree[T]` method passing its children to a `show_all[U]` that dispatches back at the same `T`), pass on mir-interp and mir-llvm; tests/mir_poly_recursion.rs runs check on each under a one-minute watchdog. A `karac check` sweep over every corpus entry and kara-katas program refused nothing else and timed out on nothing. Not covered: a cycle through a function value (`Callee::Value`) or through a method's own (non-impl) generic parameters under dispatch.

title: [Literal half split to B-2026-11-07-3; this row closed on shapes 5-6] Numeric literals do not default last: a literal bound by `let` (directly or pushed into `Vec.new()`) is fixed at i64 before a later use can fix it, so design.md §8's own example (`let x = 5; take_i32(x); let mut v = Vec.new(); v.push(7); sum(v)`) is refused; `.collect()` passed straight to a generic `Vec[T]` parameter leaks `UnknownParam("T")`
detail: design.md §8 Type inference: a numeric literal starts as a type variable that later uses may fix, and takes its default only at the end of the body. Refused at 760d8f9ec on every lane: (1) the spec demo `fn sum(xs: Vec[i32]) -> i32 {..} fn take_i32(n: i32) {..} fn demo() -> i32 { let x = 5; take_i32(x); let mut v = Vec.new(); v.push(7); sum(v) }`: `implicit coercion from 'i64' to 'i32' would narrow` at `take_i32(x)` and `expected 'ref Vec[i32]', found 'Vec[i64]'` at `sum(v)`; (2) `let a = 255; let b: u8 = a;`: same narrowing error; (3) `let mut v = Vec.new(); v.push(7); v.push(250); tot(v)` with `tot(xs: Vec[u8])`: Vec[i64] found; (4) `let x = 2000000000; let y = x + x; take_i32(y);` is refused instead of typing x as i32 and panicking with overflow. (5) `let mut best = None; for x in [3, 9, 4] { if best.is_none() or x > best.unwrap() { best = Some(*x); } }` is refused `cannot infer type parameter 'T'` at the `let` (plus a cascade `may have been moved`); this is the `None` literal, not a call, so it is not B-2026-11-06-11's `none_of()` shape, though it may share its Option path. (6) `fn largest[T: Ord + Copy](v: Vec[T]) -> T` called as `largest(w.iter().map(|s| s * 2).collect())` (single file and package) is refused with the internal `an expression whose type does not lower (Type(UnknownParam("T"))) is not lowered yet`; the argument's expected type `Vec[?T]` should fix collect's target and the item type should solve ?T. Not refiled: B-2026-11-06-11's three return-only-parameter shapes. Working correctly: a literal checked directly against an annotation or parameter, `Vec.filled(2, 0)` defaulting to Vec[i64], `id(3.5)` as f64, closures typed by a later call, `Map.new()` fixed by insert, `util.empty()` fixed by push across modules.
fix: 9bee6df335. The two non-literal shapes are fixed: (5) a comparison or arithmetic operand still a type variable (`x > best.unwrap()` after `let mut best = None;`) is fixed by the other operand (src/typechecker/expr_ops.rs infer_binary), and (6) a bare `collect()` handed to a generic collection parameter solves the slot from the iterator's item before the argument is checked, peeling a borrowed slot (src/typechecker/exprs.rs solve_collect_slot_from_items), so `largest(w.iter().map(|s| s * 2).collect())` prints the largest on every lane. Pinned by corpus/design/ok_a_later_use_fixes_a_compare_and_a_collect_slot (interp, llvm, asan). Shapes 1-4, literals defaulting last, moved to their own row B-2026-11-07-3 with the work plan (review thread, 11-07). The same commit refuses a let whose initializer leaves its own variable open at the end of the body (B-2026-11-06-15 items 3 and 4); two legacy-sourced fixtures flipped.

title: Const generic parameters cannot be used as values or solved from the expected type: `N` in a body is `a type that failed to check is not lowered yet`, `[0; N]` is refused as a non-literal count, and `fn zeros[const N: i64]() -> Array[i64, N]` with `let a: Array[i64, 8] = zeros();` finds `Array[i64, N]`
detail: design.md §8 Const generic parameters (and its note that Array[T, N] is the implemented case): a const parameter is a value fixed per instance; one that appears only in the return type is solved from the expected type (the spec's own `zeros` example); `[v; n]` takes a constant n. At 760d8f9ec, single file and package alike: (1) `fn cap[const N: i64](arr: Array[i64, N]) -> i64 { N }` -> error[typecheck] at `N`: `a type that failed to check is not lowered yet` (no underlying error is printed, so the message is also a diagnostics gap); `while i < N - 1` in a rotate body fails the same way. (2) `fn zeros[const N: i64]() -> Array[i64, N] { [0; N] }` -> `Array[T, N] repeat-literal requires a non-negative integer literal count`, and `let a: Array[i64, 8] = zeros();` -> `expected 'Array[i64, 8]', found 'Array[i64, N]'`. Working: N solved from an argument's Array type (`first(a)` on Array[i64, 3] and Array[String, 2] when the body does not name N), `let b = zeros();` refused, the same N at two sizes refused, String/f64/usize const parameters refused, a runtime value as a const argument refused.
fix: c79be19373. The typechecker keeps the enclosing function's `const` parameters with their declared types (`current_fn_const_params`), so `N` in a body types as `i64` (resolve_identifier_type) and `[v; N]` is an `Array[T, N]` in check and synthesis alike. The expected-return seeding at a generic call now also fires when the instantiated return holds a const variable, so `let z: Array[i64, 4] = zeros()` solves `N`. In MIR, `N` lowers to a constant read from the instance's arguments (see B-2026-11-06-17 for how the value is carried). The `cannot infer const parameter` diagnostic no longer suggests call-site generic arguments, which design.md §8 rules out. Pinned on interp, mir-llvm and mir-llvm-asan by corpus/core/ok_const_param_is_a_value (`N`, `N - 1` in a while, `[0; N]`, `[v; N]`, return-only N from an annotation) and err_const_param_unsolved. A later use fixing N (`let b = zeros(); let c: Array[i64, 4] = b;`, design.md § Const generic parameters, Inference) is still refused at the `let`, now B-2026-11-07-9.

title: §8 roll-up: a `where` bound on a struct is never checked and an inline struct bound is not checked on an unannotated literal; `if c { 1i32 } else { 2i64 }` joins to i64 though §8's LUB has no rule for it; an unsolved `Vec.new()` used only for `.len()` and a never-called `|x| x` are accepted
detail: At 760d8f9ec against design.md §8. (1) `struct Q {}\nstruct Pair[T] where T: Ord { a: T, b: T }` then `let p = Pair { a: Q {}, b: Q {} };` passes check and runs; with an inline bound `struct Pair[T: Ord]` the annotation `Pair[Q]` and a return type `-> Pair[Q]` are refused correctly, but the unannotated `let p = Pair { a: Q {}, b: Q {} };` is still accepted. (2) `let v = if c { 1i32 } else { 2i64 };` passes and prints 2: LUB rule 4 says two different types have no LUB (widening is defined for operator operands only); either refuse or record the widening in §8. (3) `let v = Vec.new(); println(v.len());` passes; §8: an unsolved variable is `cannot infer type ...; annotation needed` at the end of the body. (4) `let f = |x| x; println(1);` passes; §8: a closure parameter still unknown at the end of the body is `cannot infer closure parameter type`. Everything else of §8 (87 single-file cells x 4 lanes, 10 package cases) matched: qualified receivers, call-site type arguments refused, Vec of Fn indexed and called, function values at a chosen type, closures from expected types, no let-generalization, Never from generics/closures/Some(todo()), LUB with unknown Result/Option/Vec arguments, known-argument conflicts refused, Never arms, bounds (method/operator outside a bound refused, missing impl named at the call, where on fn/impl/after effects, T.Output with default Rhs, Map/Set key bounds, default generic args, fn defaults refused, defaults ordering, CrossTask by hand refused), Fn as MutFn, Vec invariance, monomorphized identity/structs/trait calls/nested generics, and generics across package modules.
fix: bd8e607903 fixes items (1), (2) and the range-bound width laxity folded into this row; items (3) and (4) landed in Thread C's 9bee6df335. (1) An unannotated struct literal now judges the struct's bounds (inline and `where`) against the arguments its fields fixed (src/typechecker/fields.rs, infer_struct_literal_expected via judge_adt_bounds), so `Pair { a: Q {}, b: Q {} }` is refused like the annotation. (2) join_branch_types returns no LUB for two different numeric types (LUB rule 4), so `if c { 1i32 } else { 2i64 }` is refused; an unsuffixed literal tree in one branch (a literal, or a block/if/match whose tails are literal trees) takes the sibling's type, so `if c { x } else { 0 }` still works. (3, folded) A literal integer range-pattern bound is range-checked against an Int/UInt scrutinee (patterns.rs check_range_pattern_bounds), so `0i8..=300` is refused; an in-range bound of another width is accepted per design decision (B). Pins: corpus/core/ok_branch_join_by_annotation, ok_branch_literal_tree_takes_sibling_type, err_struct_literal_bound_unmet, err_branch_join_mixed_width, err_range_bound_out_of_range. mini_pymodbus had a genuine mixed-width join (kara-katas 75ede910 annotates it).

title: A `const` in a pattern binds a fresh name instead of comparing against the constant: with `const LIMIT: i64 = 3`, `match x { LIMIT => .., _ => .. }` takes the LIMIT arm for every x (`if let LIMIT = 5` and `Some(LIMIT)` against Some(5) match too); path constants such as `i64.MAX` in a pattern are refused as enum-variant patterns
detail: design.md §5 pattern table: a `const` name in a pattern matches that value (and §3's naming rule makes a SCREAMING_CASE name a constant, never a binding). At 760d8f9ec: `const LIMIT: i64 = 3;\nfn cls(x: i64) -> String { match x { LIMIT => "limit", _ => "other" } }\nfn main() { println(cls(3)); println(cls(5)); match Some(5) { Some(LIMIT) => println("some-limit"), _ => println("no") } if let LIMIT = 5 { println("iflet-wrong") } else { println("iflet-ok") } }` prints `limit limit some-limit iflet-wrong` on `karac run`, `__mir-run`, `__mir-llvm-asan` and the built binary (expected `limit other no iflet-ok`). `karac check` passes with only `warning[unreachable_arm]` on the `_` arm, which shows the pattern is typed as an irrefutable binding. The same for a `String` const (`const NAME: String = "bo"` matched "al"). Path constants: `match x { i64.MAX => .., _ => .. }` is refused `pattern i64.MAX is an enum-variant pattern, but the scrutinee has type i64`; a path to an associated or module constant must match its value as well. Silent wrong values on every lane, so high. Route: Thread A (after its B-2026-11-06-10), per the review thread.
fix: 473651262e. A new desugar pass (src/const_patterns.rs) runs after desugar_selects and rewrites every binding pattern that names a module `const` into a comparison: an integer or `char` constant becomes a one-value range pattern on the constant's path (so exhaustiveness and the range checks see its value), and a `Str`, `bool` or float constant with a literal value becomes that literal. A dotted integer limit (`i64.MAX`, `u8.MIN`) in a pattern becomes the same one-value range, resolved by the new `int_type_limit` in src/exhaustive.rs and by resolve_range_bound_value in the typechecker. The rewrite covers match arms, `if let`, `while let` and let-else, and recurses through at-bindings, struct, tuple-variant, tuple, or and slice patterns. A constant with neither an ordinal type nor a literal value is refused with "constant 'X' in a pattern must be of an integer or `char` type, or have a literal value". Pinned on interp, mir-llvm and mir-llvm-asan by corpus/core/ok_const_in_pattern_compares (16 shapes, including Some(LIMIT), an at-binding, or-patterns, struct fields and let-else), err_const_pattern_not_exhaustive and err_const_pattern_without_value.

title: Const-generic functions pass `karac check` but do not compile: the instance is named `first[i64, ()]` (N instantiated as `()`), so `a.len()` / `a[0]` on `Array[T, N]` fail with `Array[i64, N] has no layout` (llvm) or `index into non-array Array[i64, N]` (MIR), and `for x in a` is `a for loop over a collection is not lowered yet`
detail: design.md §3/§8 const generic parameters (`Array[T, N]` is the implemented case). At 760d8f9ec, all pass `karac check`: (1) `fn f[const N: i64](a: Array[i64, N]) -> i64 { a.len() }` called on `[1, 2, 3]` -> `karac run` and `karac build`: `Array[i64, N]` has no layout (the interpreter lane printed 3). (2) `fn first[T: Copy, const N: i64](a: Array[T, N]) -> T { a[0] }` -> `first[i64, ()]: bb1[0]: index into non-array Array[i64, N]` on run and `__mir-run`. (3) `for x in a { .. }` over `a: Array[i64, N]` -> typecheck-time `a for loop over a collection is not lowered yet`. The instance name shows the const argument is dropped at monomorphization, so the parameter's type is never substituted. Related but separate: B-2026-11-06-14 (N unusable as a value).
fix: c79be19373. A generic call records each solved `const` parameter with its type arguments, carried as the length of a `()` array (`N` -> `Array[(), 3]`, or the caller's `Array[(), M]` when it passes its own parameter through). The instance is therefore keyed by the length, and `TyCtxt::subst` (new `subst_len`) reads a const parameter's length from the type argument in its position, so `Array[T, N]` in the body is `Array[T, 3]`: `a.len()`, `a[0]` and `for x in a` lower and have a layout on every backend. typed_hir's return-type binding (`bind_params`) binds a const parameter the same way. A `D: Dim` shape parameter is left out of the record. Pinned on interp, mir-llvm and mir-llvm-asan by corpus/core/ok_const_param_instances (two lengths per function, a `char` and a `String` element, a body passing its `N` through).

title: §3 roll-up: the value-class naming rule is enforced only on parameters, `struct _Hidden` / `const _MAX` are accepted, `requires`/`ensures`/`invariant` are reserved, a nested f-string is accepted, and doc-comment misuse is a parse error or silent (fixed; the nested f-string is deliberately a 0.8.x deprecation warning, the error comes at the next minor release)
detail: At 760d8f9ec against design.md §3. (1) CN-2 value class (snake_case): `let Count = 1`, `let COUNT = 1`, `let X = 1`, `let (Ab, b) = (1, 2)`, `for Ix in 0..3`, `match o { Some(Val) => .. }` all pass check and run; the same names as fn parameters are refused correctly. (2) CN-5: a leading underscore marks only an unused binding; `struct _Hidden {}` and `const _MAX: i64 = 1` are accepted. (3) `requires`, `ensures`, `invariant` as identifiers are refused as reserved words; §3 lists them as deferred, not keywords in v1 (`lock`, `suspends`, `providers` behave as specified). (4) `f"a {f"{x}"} b"` is accepted and prints the inner value; §3 says a nested f-string is an error. (5) `///` before a statement in a function body is `Expected expression, found a doc comment` (parse error); §3: a doc comment that documents nothing is discarded with a warning. A detached `///` at top level and `///` on an `impl` block produce no warning at all. Everything else in §3 (136 cells x 4 lanes) matched: E0003, E0004, non-ASCII byte literal, E_INTERIOR_NUL_IN_C_STRING, E_MOVE_NOT_USED, raw/triple-quoted strings, escapes, numeric literal forms and suffixes, format specs, keyword list, prefix-must-touch rules.
fix: d978271697 + dfc1f834c3. (1) CN-2: let, for, closure and pattern bindings are refused unless Value-class (resolver E0127, with a rename suggestion and a guard hint when the name is a constant). A Type-class name in a refutable pattern may be the scrutinee enum's bare variant (a library enum's `NotFound`, or `Fn`), which only the type checker knows, so the type checker reports it there (E0128) once it is not a variant: `Some(Val)` over i64. Reserved names (`let Fn`) keep their single ReservedIdentifier report. (2) CN-5: a leading `_` on a type or const name is a parse error with the trimmed rename. (3) requires / ensures / invariant are contextual words, not keywords (lexer and selfhost lexer); contracts still parse, and an effect clause stops before `requires`/`ensures` (examples/weave's `with panics ensures(result) ..`). (4) DELIBERATE DIVERGENCE: a nested f-string is a `deprecated` warning in 0.8.x, not the error design.md §3 states, because 162 programs in the corpus and katas nest them; when the hole is the inner f-string alone, `karac fix` writes its text in the hole. design.md §3 now says so, as for implied derives and field `mut`; it becomes the error at the next minor release. (5) A `///` that documents nothing is discarded with an `unused_doc_comment` warning (W0296, new lint): before a statement (was a parse error), before an `impl` (was silent and leaked onto the impl's first undocumented method), before a blank line, comment, `}` or end of file, or before a declaration that takes none. Three stdlib impl docs moved onto their methods. Collateral fixed: uppercase locals renamed in 8 corpus fixtures, corpus/core/ok_const_field_paths, two kata benches and mini_readelf (kara-katas copies prepared as a patch for the apps thread, since this session cannot push kara-katas); the typechecker and mir_build fixtures that pinned uppercase locals as valid now pin the refusal; the book's module-level lets are consts. tests/core_naming_lexical.rs (5 tests). Sweep: 0 unexpected new refusals over 27,970 programs.

title: A cycle between constants crashes the compiler: `const AA: i64 = BB; const BB: i64 = AA;` (or `const AA: i64 = AA + 1;`) aborts `karac check` and `karac run` with `thread has overflowed its stack` (exit 134) instead of a diagnostic
detail: design.md §4 Constants: an initializer may name other constants; a cycle has no value and must be refused with a diagnostic naming the cycle (CLAUDE.md: never panic on user input). At 760d8f9ec, single file: `const AA: i64 = BB;\nconst BB: i64 = AA;\nfn main() { println(AA); }` -> `karac check` prints `thread '<unknown>' has overflowed its stack / fatal runtime error: stack overflow, aborting`, exit 134; `karac run` the same. The self-reference `const AA: i64 = AA + 1;` crashes the same way. Across package modules the same cycle is refused, but only as E0223 circular module dependency, because the two imports form a module cycle. Forward references without a cycle (`const AA: i64 = BB + 1; const BB: i64 = 2;`) work.
fix: 609dbaa6da. check_const_decl walks the constants each initializer names (TypeChecker::const_cycle) and refuses a cycle once, at its first-declared constant, before MIR lowering inlines anything: `constant `AA` is defined through itself (`AA` -> `BB` -> `AA`), so it has no value; give one of them a value that does not name the others`, at the name that starts the cycle. Covers self-reference, longer cycles and constants of any type (a `Point` cycle). Pins: corpus/core err_const_cycle_{mutual,self,struct}. A check sweep over the 483 corpus programs with constants and every kara-katas program refused nothing else. Gate: default 10503 passed, llvm 10674 passed.

title: Constant initializers are not evaluated at compile time: `const SH: i32 = 1 << 40` silently reads as 0 (the same shift in a function panics `shift amount out of range`), and `const XX: i64 = 9223372036854775807 + 1` / `1 / 0` pass check and panic at run time at each use
detail: design.md §4 Constants: the initializer is a compile-time constant and the constant exists in the binary as data; no code runs before main. So an initializer that overflows, divides by zero or shifts out of range has no value and must be a compile-time error. At 760d8f9ec on run, __mir-run and __mir-llvm-run: (1) `const SH: i32 = 1 << 40; fn main() { let n: i32 = 1; let s = 40; println(SH); println(n << s); }` prints `0`, then panics `shift amount out of range` at the second line: the constant evaluator and the run-time rule disagree, and the constant gives a silent wrong value. (2) `const XX: i64 = 9223372036854775807 + 1;` -> check passes; run panics `integer overflow at :2:17` (the initializer's span) at the use. (3) `const XX: i64 = 1 / 0;` -> check passes; run panics `division by zero`. Correct today: an out-of-range literal (`const XX: i8 = 200`), a type mismatch, calls, closures, method calls, String/Vec types and `"a" + "b"` are refused.
fix: 609dbaa6da. An integer, bool or char constant's initializer is evaluated at check with the const evaluator at its declared type (design.md § Constants), and an overflow, division by zero, out-of-range literal or out-of-width shift is refused: `const SH: i32 = 1 << 40` -> `const expression overflow: 1i32 << 40i32 overflows i32`; `9223372036854775807 + 1` and `1 / 0` likewise, where they read 0 or panicked at each use. A negated literal evaluates as one literal, so `const NN: i8 = -128` and `const ZZ: i64 = -9223372036854775808` stay legal. Float, aggregate and cast initializers are left to the existing constness checks (the evaluator does not fold them). Pins: corpus/core err_const_init_{shift_out_of_range,overflow,div_by_zero} and ok_const_init_evaluated (in-range forms incl. a forward reference, mir-interp and mir-llvm). Check sweep over corpus constants and katas: no other refusals.

title: A constant is treated as a place, not a fresh value: a second use of a non-Copy constant is `value 'ORIGIN' moved`, `ORIGIN.x` on a struct constant is `this name is not lowered yet`, `T_THREE.1` is a parse error, while `XX = 5;` and `TABLE[0] = 3;` on constants are accepted and do nothing
detail: design.md §4 Constants, "Each use is a fresh value": every use of a constant builds its own value, which the user owns and may move; constants are not variables (no module-level let mut, no mutable globals). At 760d8f9ec, single file (package the same): (1) `struct Point { x: i64, y: i64 }\nconst ORIGIN: Point = Point { x: 0, y: 0 };\nfn eat(p: own Point) {..}` then `let a = ORIGIN; let b = ORIGIN; eat(a); eat(b);` -> error[ownership] `value 'ORIGIN' moved here, used again here`; `for i in 0..3 { let mut p = ORIGIN; .. }` -> `value 'ORIGIN' is moved inside a loop`. (2) `println(ORIGIN.x)` -> error[typecheck] `this name is not lowered yet` (check and run); `let o = ORIGIN; println(o.x)` works; across modules `import cfg; cfg.ORIGIN.x` and `import cfg.ORIGIN; ORIGIN.x` fail the same way. (3) `const T_THREE: (i64, i64, i64) = (1, 2, 3); println(T_THREE.1)` -> error[parse] `Expected ), found 1` (a lower-case tuple binding `t.1` parses). (4) `const XX: i64 = 1; fn main() { XX = 5; println(XX); }` passes check and prints 1; `const TABLE: Array[i64, 2] = [1, 2]; TABLE[0] = 3; println(TABLE[0]);` passes and prints 1: assigning to a constant must be refused, not silently dropped. Copy constants, Array constants (`let mut t = TABLE; t[0] = 99` leaves TABLE[0] = 1), indexing and iterating a const Array, Str constants, enum and Option constants, and constants imported, re-exported and qualified through a module work.
fix: 8f0eb3eae2. Every shape in the row, plus the two the probe found beside it. (1) The use classifier reads a constant's name (one no local or parameter shadows) as a read, so `let a = ORIGIN; let b = ORIGIN; eat(a); eat(b)` and `let mut p = ORIGIN` in a loop check and print 0 0 0 1 2 (src/use_classifier.rs). (2) MIR lowering builds a path rooted at a constant (`ORIGIN.x`, `NESTED.i.n`) as the constant's value in a temporary, then each field (`const_path_place`, src/mir/lower.rs); a library method of such a field (`ORIGIN.n.abs()`, `NESTED.i.s.len()`) takes it as the receiver, and so does a field of an uppercase local (`Wv.i.s.len()`, which was `the builtin StringSlice.len is not lowered yet`). Imported forms (`cfg.ORIGIN.x`, `import cfg.ORIGIN; ORIGIN.y`, `BX.p.x.abs()`, `cfg.TRIPLE.1`) print the same on run and build. (3) The parser leaves a dot before anything but a name to the postfix loop, so `T_THREE.1` and `T_THREE.1.1` index the tuple (src/parser/exprs.rs). (4) Writes are refused at check: `XX = 5`, `TABLE[0] = 3`, `ORIGIN.x += 1` (typecheck, `check_const_assignment`), and a `mut ref self` method on a constant, `TABLE.sort()` / `CC.bump()`, which the row did not name and which also wrote a copy no one reads (ownership, `report_write_to_constant`). A local of the same name shadows the constant in each. Pins: corpus/core ok_const_each_use_fresh, ok_const_field_paths, err_const_assign, err_const_assign_part, err_const_mut_method; every corpus/core pin passes on mir-interp and mir-llvm-asan.

title: `#[target]` is not honoured on impl members, struct fields or enum variants: with `#[target(native)] fn f(self) -> i64 { 1 }` and `#[target(wasm_wasi)] fn f(self) -> i64 { 2 }` in one impl, a native run prints 2; a wasm-gated field is still required in a native struct literal and a wasm-gated variant is still required in a native match
fix: e963bf0239. `target::filter_inactive_items_in` now also drops, from each item it keeps, the impl methods, struct fields and enum variants whose own `#[target(..)]` does not admit the target, and `extra_check_targets_for` counts member gates, so `karac check` still reads a member gated to another target. The row's three shapes: twin `#[target(native)] fn f` / `#[target(wasm_wasi)] fn f` prints 1 natively (was 2, the wasm member's value); `S { a: 1 }` with a wasm-only field `b` and a `match` without a wasm-only variant `B` both run. Pinned by tests/design_section4_gates.rs (twin methods, field and variant, a type error in a wasm-gated member body still reported by check).

title: §4 roll-up: the spec's own `[build].target = "x86_64-linux"` makes `karac build` demand a runtime archive for that triple, `main_linux.kara` is ignored beside `main.kara`, the unknown-edition message differs from §4's text, `karac init --backend` is accepted, and a constant of a struct with a String field is accepted
detail: At 760d8f9ec against design.md §4. (1) Manifest with `[build]\ntarget = "x86_64-linux"` (§4's example): check and run pass, `karac build` fails `a build for x86_64-linux needs the runtime archive built for it`. §4 says [build].target selects the manifest-overlay triple and code generation targets the host; the overlay triple must not change the codegen triple (or §4/§16 should say it does and use a real triple in the example). (2) `src/main.kara` plus `src/main_linux.kara`: on Linux, run and build execute main.kara's `main`; by the platform-file rule the Linux file replaces the shared one (or the spec should exclude the entry file). (3) `edition = "2027"` -> `unknown [package].edition = "2027". Supported editions: 2026.`; §4 gives `unknown edition "2027"; this compiler supports editions up to "2026"`. title: A generic function returning `impl Iterator[Item = T]` cannot be consumed: `fn evs[T](xs: own Vec[T]) -> impl Iterator[Item = T] { xs.into_iter() }` then `evs(["a"]).collect()` is `the method call .collect with no resolved callee is not lowered yet`

title: CString lacks the CStr reading surface (to_str, to_string) and has no constructor from Slice[u8], which strings.md says exists
detail: strings.md C strings: `CString` owns and `ref CStr` borrows, as `String` owns and `Str` borrows, and the CStr table lists as_ptr, len, is_empty, bytes, to_str, to_string. `A CString can also be built from a Slice[u8]`. Release karac at 2fc16b773: `let cs = s.to_cstring().unwrap(); cs.to_string()` -> `no method 'to_string' on type 'CString'` (typechecker/stdlib_seq.rs infer_cstring_method knows only as_ptr, bytes, is_empty, len). For the Slice constructor, `CString.from(..)`, `CString.new(..)`, `CString.from_bytes(..)`, `CString.from_slice(..)` and `slice.to_cstring()` are all refused, and the doc names no API, so either the doc needs the name or the constructor is missing. The rest of the C-string surface (c".." len/is_empty/bytes/to_str/to_string, String.to_cstring NUL error, no implicit CStr->Str) is correct on all four lanes.
fix: 69889deae9. A `CString` has `ref CStr`'s reading surface: `to_str` and `to_string` type as `CStr`'s do (src/typechecker/stdlib_seq.rs) and run on the interpreter and LLVM, where the CStr-only guard on that arm is gone (src/mir/interp.rs, src/backend/mir/cells.rs). The constructor is `CString.from_bytes(bytes: Slice[u8]) -> Result[CString, NulError]`, now named in strings.md: it borrows the bytes (ownership mode `Ref`, lent at lowering like `String.from_utf8`), copies them and refuses an interior NUL like `to_cstring`, and the bytes need not be UTF-8 (`to_string` on them is then `Err`). A `Vec[u8]`, `.as_slice()` and `s.bytes()` all pass. Pin: corpus/design/ok_cstring_reading_surface on mir-interp, mir-llvm, mir-llvm-asan and mir-build. Gate as B-2026-11-06-30.

title: `c.to_digit(10)` on a char compiles to a `karac_mir_char` call that matches the method's name among twenty strings: half of kata 1058's benchmark
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-06 on the 4-core cloud container, kara 4975afc0a9, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build of kata 1058's bench/rounding.kara (40 lists of 500 prices, every target, 8 rounds; each price read digit by digit with `c.to_digit(10).unwrap()`): 3.0-3.2 s against rustc -O's 0.67-0.88 s and rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on's 0.75-0.88 s. Callgrind on a 10-list, 1-round cut: 1.725G instructions, 865.5M (50.2%) in `karac_mir_char`. The runtime function (runtime/src/mir.rs) looks the op's index up in `CHAR_OPS` and then matches the name against each string in turn, for every char; codegen (src/backend/mir/num.rs `char_op`) computes the ASCII classes and case maps in line (B-2026-10-13-31) but sends `to_digit` and `is_digit` to the runtime for every char. A radix outside 2..=36 still goes to `karac_mir_char`, which words the panic. An integer receiver (a byte) keeps the runtime path. title: `Vec.sort_by(|a, b| b.cmp(a))` on 500 `i64`s takes about 1.9x Rust's `sort_by` in kata 1058's benchmark (2.5x before a53992a785), where a plain `sort()` keeps pace
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-06 on the 4-core cloud container, kara with kata 1058's to_digit fix, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build of kata 1058's bench/rounding.kara against rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on (two runs each): as written 1.45-1.53 s against 0.82-0.83 s; with the sort line deleted 0.73-0.84 s against 0.54-0.56 s; with `fractions.sort()` in place of `fractions.sort_by(|a, b| b.cmp(a))` 1.03-1.11 s. So the descending `sort_by` costs Kāra about 0.7 s where Rust's costs about 0.28 s, and the ascending `sort()` about 0.3 s. The IR (KARAC_MIR_LL) sorts through `merge_sort.by.closure`, `merge_widths.by.closure` and `partition.by.closure`, which call the comparator `sort_by.closure` and branch on the `Ordering` it returns; callgrind put 195M instructions (35.7%) in one unnamed sort function of a 10-list, 1-round cut, against 140M in Rust's quicksort and smallsort for the same calls. What remains with the sort gone, about 1.4x, is the per-call price reading and the answer's f-string. PARTLY FIXED a53992a785 (2026-11-07): callgrind on the full bench put 6.35G of 22.0G instructions in `merge_widths.by.closure`, the comparator inlined; a Rust copy of the schedule showed the 16-element insertion runs alone (a mispredicted branch per element moved) costing as much as Rust's whole sort_by, and the one-ended merge waiting on each comparison. Every backend now sorts runs of four with core's sort4_stable network and merges from both ends at once (interp.rs `merge_order`, runtime `merge_widths`, callable.rs `build_merge_widths`, same calls in the same order). Six interleaved runs, medians: as written 1.65 s -> 1.49 s, sort line deleted 0.84 s, rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on 0.94 s and 0.59 s without the sort: the sort costs Kara about 0.65 s (was 0.81 s) against Rust's 0.35 s. What is left is instruction count: seven merge passes from width 4 at about 17 instructions per element; Rust's driftsort quicksorts input with no runs (a branch-free stable partition) down to small-sorted runs. A partition here must keep the interpreter's calls (src/mir/interp.rs `sort_order`, PART_MIN 4096). TRIED 2026-11-07 (drop schedule, x86, a 375-element descending sort_by 120000 times: Kara 7.69G instructions and 0.51-0.62 s against rustc -O 4.89G and 0.29-0.43 s; valgrind's branch model puts Kara's mispredicts at 2.2% against Rust's 13.6%, so the gap is instruction count). The bidirectional merge loop is 64% of instructions at 35 an iteration (two elements). PART_MIN 256 (partitioning input with no runs from 256 elements, both backends) changed nothing measurable (7.39G, same wall). A Rust model of the same merge with pointer cursors ran 7% more instructions; with pointer cursors chosen by a select, 10% fewer in the merge, with no wall difference above noise. Not landed: what is left is the algorithm (driftsort's partition), which would change the comparator call schedule every backend pins.
fix: a806504986. A sort_by / sort_unstable_by whose comparator is exactly the element type's own order or its reverse (|a, b| a.cmp(b), |a, b| b.cmp(a)) over integers, char or bool is recognised from its MIR shape (src/backend/mir/sort_order.rs): it reads only its two elements and calls nothing, so its call order is unobservable, and equal elements are identical bits, so stable and unstable agree. The vector is then sorted by the runtime integer sort (karac_mir_sort_int) and reversed for the descending order, instead of the merge sort's comparator call per pair. Any other comparator keeps the merge sort; KARAC_MIR_SORT_BY_OWN=0 turns the path off. tests/mir_sort_by_own_order.rs pins run == build and that the integer sort is called. Kata 1058's bench (KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, hyperfine, 7 runs): 1.219 s before, 0.917 s after, rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on 0.845 s (1.44x to 1.08x); outputs identical.

title: `Vec` has no `rotate_left` or `rotate_right`: `v.rotate_left(1)` is refused with "no method 'rotate_left' on type 'Vec'"
detail: Kata 1058's differential turned a list of prices round by one, the Rust way, with `turned.rotate_left(1)`, and `karac check` refused it: no method 'rotate_left' on type 'Vec', with no suggestion. docs/library/collections.md lists no rotation on `Vec` or `Slice`. The differential built the turned list by hand (`prices[1..]` collected, then `prices[0]` pushed).
fix: 2fee84b590 adds `Vec.rotate_left(mid)` and `Vec.rotate_right(k)` to runtime/stdlib/source/collections.kara, by three reversals in place, panicking when the count is outside 0..=len, and lists both in docs/library/collections.md; 1502aac7f4 keeps both names in library_prune's ALWAYS_KEPT, since the integer rotates share them. tests/kata_1058_digits_and_rotate.rs runs both on `Vec[i64]`, `Vec[String]` and an empty `Vec` on `__mir-run` and `__mir-llvm-run`; kata 1058's differential now turns its prices with `rotate_left(1)`.

title: A closure in a method chain that ends in `?` (`let h = half(n).map_err(|_| bad.clone())?;`) is paired with a later move of what it reads (`return Err(bad)`) as "moved inside a loop and not assigned again before the next iteration", with no loop in the program
detail: Found writing apps/cli/mini_logbroker: a record parser keeps one error string and hands a clone to each `map_err`, then returns the string itself on a later check. `fn parse(n: i64) -> Result[i64, String] { let bad = "bad".to_string(); let h = half(n).map_err(|_| bad.clone())?; if h > 10 { return Err(bad); } Ok(h) }` is refused at the closure's read of `bad` (karac check, 4975afc0a9). The same chain without the `?` (`let r = half(n).map_err(|_| bad.clone()); let h = r?;`) passes, as do a `let`-bound closure and `unwrap_or_else`. Cause: B-2026-10-29-43's statement-closure rule (`record_statement_closures` in src/use_classifier.rs) walks a statement's receiver chain only through `MethodCall`s, so a `Question` at the top (or mid-chain) hides the closure, and `first_witness` pairs the closure-body read with the later consume. `karac fix` then offers `return Err(bad.clone())`, which the app had taken; the closure's read was further rewritten to a fresh literal.
fix: aeb2ac0023. `record_statement_closures` (src/use_classifier.rs) walks a statement's receiver chain through `?` as well as method calls, so a closure handed to a method before a `?` (at the top or mid-chain) counts as run by the statement's end, as B-2026-10-29-43 already did without the `?`. `let h = half(n).map_err(|_| bad.clone())?; if h > 10 { return Err(bad); }` now checks and prints `Ok(2) Err(bad) Err(bad)` for 4, 3, 40; the same pair inside a loop is still "moved inside a loop". Pinned by tests/core_question_closure_read_before_move.rs (return, tail and mid-chain shapes accepted with their MIR-interpreter output; the loop shape refused). mini_logbroker's record parser is back to `map_err(|_| bad.clone())?` and a plain `return Err(bad)`.

title: `Slice[T]` has no `iter_mut`, though docs/library/collections.md lists it (`mut ref T` items): `fn bump(xs: mut Slice[i64]) { for x in xs.iter_mut() { .. } }` and `v[0..n - 1].iter_mut()` are "no method 'iter_mut' on type 'Slice'"
detail: Found writing apps/cli/mini_logbroker: compaction rewrites every segment but the active one in place, naturally `for seg in part.segs[0..n - 1].iter_mut() { seg.recs.retain(..) }`. collections.md's iteration table gives `Vec[T]`, `Array[T, N]` and `Slice[T]` an `iter_mut()` of `mut ref T` items in index order; Vec and Array have it, a `mut Slice[T]` parameter and a range view receiver do not (karac check, 4975afc0a9). The library source (runtime/stdlib/source/collections.kara) has `SliceIter` but no mutable twin. Once the method exists, a range view receiver is also refused by the ownership pass ("`v` cannot be borrowed as `mut ref T` because it is also borrowed as `Slice[T]`") because `iter_mut` is not in `SLICE_MUTATING_METHODS`, the list that makes `v[a..b].sort()` take a `mut Slice[T]` view (B-2026-10-12-24). The app used `part.segs.iter_mut().take(n - 1)` meanwhile. Not covered: `let s = mut ref v[1..3];` is "this unary operator is not lowered yet".
fix: aeb2ac0023. runtime/stdlib/source/collections.kara gains `SliceIterMut[T]` (`mut ref T` items, double-ended, as `VecIterMut`) and `impl[T] Slice[T] { fn iter_mut(mut ref self) }`, and `iter_mut` joins `SLICE_MUTATING_METHODS`, so a range view receiver (`v[a..b].iter_mut()`) takes a `mut Slice[T]` view as `v[a..b].sort()` does: it needs `let mut v`, and writing `v` in the loop body is refused (core-semantics §5.6). Pinned by corpus/design/ok_slice_iter_mut (a `mut Slice` parameter, `v[2..]`, `segs[0..k - 1]` with a struct element, `.rev()`; passes mir-interp, mir-llvm, mir-llvm-asan and mir-build at KARAC_THREADS=1 and 4). mini_logbroker's compaction is back to `part.segs[0..n - 1].iter_mut()`. Not covered, as noted: `let s = mut ref v[1..3];` is still "this unary operator is not lowered yet".

title: A `TaskGroup.spawn` closure whose `Result` error type only a later annotation fixes is refused at lowering when its handles are kept in a `Vec`: `let r: Result[i64, String] = h.join();`, the annotation `?`'s own diagnostic asks for, leaves `let mut hs = Vec.new()` as "an expression whose type does not lower (Type(UnknownParam(\"E\"))) is not lowered yet"
detail: Found writing apps/cli/mini_logbroker: recovery reads each topic's partitions in a task, `handles.push(group.spawn(|| { let mut got = Vec.new(); for p in 0..t.partitions { got.push(load_part(t.clone(), p)?); } Ok(got) }))`, then `let got = h.join()?;` per handle. karac check (4975afc0a9) says "cannot infer type parameter 'E' of `Result[..., E]`, this `?` operand's type: nothing in the body fixes it; annotate the operand (`let r: Result[..., String] = ..; r?`)". Doing exactly that passes `karac check` when the function is unreachable and fails `karac run` once it is called. Minimal: `fn main() { let group = TaskGroup.new(); let mut hs = Vec.new(); hs.push(group.spawn(|| { let h = half(4)?; Ok(h + 1) })); for h in hs.into_iter() { let r: Result[i64, String] = h.join(); .. } }` with `half: fn(i64) -> Result[i64, String]`. Without the Vec (`let h = group.spawn(..)`) the refusal is "cannot infer type parameter 'E'; add a type annotation to this binding" at the `let`, though the later annotation fixes it; a plain closure in a Vec (`fs.push(f); let r: Result[i64, String] = g();`) works. Related to B-2026-11-06-11 (1): an unsolved `E` of an `Option`/`Result` result stays `TypeParam` rather than a type variable a later use solves. The app annotates the closure's tail meanwhile (`let done: Result[Vec[(Part, Option[String])], String] = Ok(got); done`). Re-probed at 9cb9fc2928 (after 5f1222f497, B-2026-11-06-11): the bare `let h = group.spawn(..)` shape now checks; the handles-in-a-`Vec` shape is still refused at lowering as above.
fix: b07a360a6d. A closure tail whose `Result` error type nothing in the body fixes now leaves that parameter open as a type variable instead of a `TypeParam`: `open_unsolved_closure_tail` (src/typechecker/items.rs, called from the checked closure arm in src/typechecker/exprs.rs) opens it when the closure's expected return is itself unsolved, `open_unsolved_let_params` also rewrites the call's recorded substitution (`node_call_subs`) with the opened variables, and `Vec.push`'s element inference opens its argument the same way (src/typechecker/method_vec_mutation.rs). So `hs.push(group.spawn(|| { let h = half(4)?; Ok(h + 1) }))` followed by `let r: Result[i64, String] = h.join(); r?`, the form `?`'s diagnostic asks for, solves `E` at the join and runs; the bare-handle form (`let h = group.spawn(..)`) too. A closure whose `E` nothing ever fixes is still refused with "cannot infer type parameter 'E'". Test: tests/core_spawn_result_error_later_use.rs (2). apps/cli/mini_logbroker's load task now ends in plain `Ok(got)` (kara-katas f19a85ee) and passes mir-interp, mir-llvm, mir-llvm-asan and mir-build at KARAC_THREADS=1 and 4. Gate: fmt, both clippy legs, test --all, test --features llvm (10670 passed, 0 failed).

title: A let-chain (`if let Some(s) = v and kind == "group" { .. }`, Rust's `if let .. && ..`) gets two unrelated errors ("logical operator requires 'bool', found 'Option[String]'" and a pattern-against-`bool` mismatch) and no word that Kāra has no let-chains or how to nest the `if`
detail: Found writing apps/cli/mini_logbroker, rebuilding consumer groups from the offsets topic: `if let Some(v) = v and f[0] == "group" { .. }`. The parser reads the scrutinee as `v and kind == "group"`, so check (4975afc0a9) reports a `bool` operand error at `v` and "pattern `Some(..)` is an enum-variant pattern, but the scrutinee has type `bool`". design.md has no let-chain form, so the program is wrong, but the diagnostic should name the shape (a refutable `let` joined with `and`) and offer the nested `if let .. { if .. { .. } }`, machine-applicable where the chain is two operands. Same family, also met here: a type alias named `TP` gets "consider renaming to `Tp`" with no machine-applicable edit (parser.rs `check_ident_class` says this site carries none), and Rust's `Vec.last_mut` (not in the spec) is a bare "no method 'last_mut'" with no pointer to indexing at `len() - 1`. The app uses nested `if`s, which is natural Kāra.
fix: b07a360a6d. `if let P = v and c { .. }` is now one parse error naming the shape ("`if let` cannot be joined with `and`: Kāra has no let-chains"), from `refuse_let_chain` in src/parser/exprs.rs, in place of the `bool` operand error and the pattern-against-`bool` mismatch. With no `else` it carries a machine-applicable fix that nests the test (`if let P = v { if c { .. } }`), which `karac fix` applies and the program then runs; with an `else` the error is reported without a rewrite, since the `else` would need duplicating. A `let true = a and b`-style literal, binding or wildcard pattern is not refused. The side items: Vec's `last_mut`/`first_mut` now say to write through an index (`v[v.len() - 1] = ..`), in src/typechecker/method_user_impl.rs; the `TP` alias's "consider renaming to `Tp`" stays without a machine fix by design, because a rename must reach every use of the name and the parser sees only the declaration. Tests: tests/let_chain_refused_with_nesting_fix.rs (4). Gate as B-2026-11-06-38.

5e869cb573: src/mir/rare_exits.rs finds the arm of a short-circuit inside a loop's early-return guard that can reach the return. The arm must test two computed integers of 32 bits or more for equality, like kata 7's `result == min_div`. Codegen weighs that arm 1:2000 through the existing `rare_edge`, so SimplifyCFG keeps it as a branch at the phi-fold threshold of 6. `KARAC_MIR_RARE_EXITS=0` turns it off. Kata 7's arm64 object is byte-identical to the threshold-4 one, and x86 runs it in 763 ms against 1113. Of 1035 kata benches only kata 7's code changes; weighing ordering and byte-literal tests slowed 729, 731 and 777, so those are not weighed. M5 at 7708b0aae5 (review thread's m5-rows run, 5 runs): threshold 6 vs 4 is 1.009x and 1.006x (was 1.111x), rare exits on vs off is 0.812x, and B-2026-11-04-37's phi-fold row is 0.997x.
title: Kata 7 runs 1.11x the cycles on arm64 at SimplifyCFG's phi-fold threshold 6 (a723c25762) than at 4: the rare `result == min_div and digit < -8` guard is now computed every digit
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-07 on the M5 (review thread's m5-rows env rows for B-2026-11-04-37, kara 6e709e5fdd, 5 runs): kata 7 (bench/reverse.kara) 1.111x cycles at the default threshold 6 against KARAC_MIR_PHI_FOLD_THRESHOLD=4; x86's frozen set showed 1.05x. ATTRIBUTED (Thread B, karac's real pipeline cross-built for aarch64-apple-darwin, object kept): the digit loop of `reverse` checks two overflow guards, `result > max_div or (result == max_div and digit > 7)` and `result < min_div or (result == min_div and digit < -8)`. At 4 the second guard's `and` arm is a branch (`cmp w15,w16; b.ne` skips `cmn w0,#8; b.lt`), taken almost never and well predicted. At 6 SimplifyCFG folds it into a select: every digit computes `add; cmp; ccmn; cset` and then branches on the materialized bool (`cbz w1`), four more ALU ops on the loop's critical path for the same six branches. The first guard was already folded at 4. Nothing else in the object differs. Possible remedies: keep a short-circuit `and` whose arms compare against a loop-invariant boundary as a branch (an `llvm.expect` or branch weights on overflow guards that end in `return`), or a per-loop cost check; the global threshold stays at 6, which is worth 0.758x on kata 342 and 0.68x on x86's 229.

fix: 957a835c43. The checker's identifier arm gives a generic function item named as a value (not as a call's callee, whose call instantiates it) fresh type variables at each use, and check_expr solves them from an expected `Fn` slot (`let f: Fn(own Vec[T], i64) -> i64 = shout`). `apply(shout, [7], 1)` now builds `apply[Vec[i64]]` and `shout[Vec[i64]]` and prints `[7]` on mir-interp, mir-llvm and the ASan lane (no leak); inside a generic body the item's `T` is its own (`apply(shout, v.len(), 2)` in `count[T]` checks and prints 1). src/mir/poly_recursion.rs reads a function value's instance off its `Fn` type, so `apply(deep, [x], n - 1)` inside `deep[T]` is refused as polymorphic recursion at the use (design.md §8) where it ran `deep[i64]` on a `Vec`. Pins: corpus/core ok_generic_fn_value_own_instance (direct, generic body, annotated let, unannotated let) and err_poly_recursion_through_fn_value; tests/mir_poly_recursion.rs covers both. Whole corpus on mir-interp: no new failures against a control with the freshening switched off (the two 60 s timeouts in the full run pass alone). Gate: default 10491 passed, llvm 10657 passed.
title: A generic function passed as an `Fn` value is instanced with its type arguments unsolved: `apply(shout, [7], 1)` with `fn apply[U](g: Fn(own U, i64) -> i64, u: own U, n: i64)` builds `apply[()]` and `shout[()]`, which print a `Vec` as garbage under llvm; inside a generic body the item's `T` is taken for the caller's
detail: Found while checking the function-value gap of B-2026-11-06-12 (Thread B, karac 30ae813fb6). Repro: `fn apply[U](g: Fn(own U, i64) -> i64, u: own U, n: i64) -> i64 { g(u, n) }\nfn shout[T: Display](x: own T, n: i64) -> i64 { println(x); n }\nfn main() { println(apply(shout, [7], 1)); }`. `karac check` passes. `__mir-run`: `in apply[()]{fn#963} ... in shout[()] at bb0[term]: print cannot show Agg([Int(7)])`; `__mir-llvm-run` of the same shape inside a generic (`fn wrap[T: Display](x: own T) -> i64 { apply(shout, [x], 1) }`) prints heap addresses (94054773382704) where it should print `[7]`: the value is instanced at the wrong type, so the callee reads a `Vec` as something else (memory-unsafe), and the `Vec` passed in is never dropped (`leaked at exit: a0 (count 1)` in the interpreter). Second shape: in a generic `fn wrap2[T: Display](x: own T) -> i64 { ...; apply(shout, v.len(), 1) }` the checker refuses `expected 'T', found 'i64': inside this item `T` stands for whatever type the caller picks` at the argument, so `shout`'s own `T` is unified with `wrap2`'s `T` of the same name. In a recursive generic (`fn deep[T](x: own T, n: i64) -> i64 { .. apply(deep, [x], n - 1) .. }`) the self reference is instanced at the enclosing `T`, so the polymorphic recursion check of B-2026-11-06-12 has no edge to see and the program runs `deep[i64]` on a `Vec[i64]` instead of being refused (design.md §8). Expected: the item's own parameters are fresh at each use as a value and solved from the expected `Fn` type, the instance is `shout[Vec[i64]]` (and `apply[Vec[i64]]`), and a growing self reference is a polymorphic recursion error.

title: Numeric literals do not default last (split from B-2026-11-06-13): an unsuffixed literal is typed i64/f64 when inferred, so a later use cannot fix it; design.md §8's own demo (`let x = 5; take_i32(x); let mut v = Vec.new(); v.push(7); sum(v)`) is refused
detail: design.md § Type inference: 'An integer or float literal starts as a type variable that later uses may fix. If nothing fixes it by the end of the function body, it defaults to i64 or f64', and 'Literals default last'. The checker has no literal type variables: `infer_expr` types an unsuffixed literal i64 (f64) on the spot, and only a literal CHECKED against a known type takes that type.
