Refused at 760d8f9ec on every lane (B-2026-11-06-13's shapes 1-4): (1) the spec demo `fn sum(xs: Vec[i32]) -> i32 {..} fn take_i32(n: i32) {..} fn demo() -> i32 { let x = 5; take_i32(x); let mut v = Vec.new(); v.push(7); sum(v) }`: 'implicit coercion from i64 to i32 would narrow' at `take_i32(x)` and 'expected ref Vec[i32], found Vec[i64]' at `sum(v)`; (2) `let a = 255; let b: u8 = a;`; (3) `let mut v = Vec.new(); v.push(7); v.push(250); tot(v)` with `tot(xs: Vec[u8])`; (4) `let x = 2000000000; let y = x + x; take_i32(y);` refused instead of typing x as i32 and panicking with overflow. Work plan (review thread, 11-07: do the full literal type variables, not a let-retype partial): an unsuffixed integer or float literal synthesizes a fresh literal variable (integer or float kind) recording its span and value; unification binds it to an integer (float) type and refuses any other; every site that needs a concrete number settles an unbound literal variable to its default before use: binary operators and comparisons (both operands, the result of arithmetic on two literal variables is that variable), unary minus, method receivers (`x.abs()`), indexing and the index operand, `for` items and ranges, f-string and `println` arguments, casts, match patterns against literals; at the end of the body the remaining literal variables take i64 / f64 (before `report_unsolved_call_vars` and `resolved_node_tables`), and each literal's range check (`check_int_literal_fits`, `wide_int_literals`) runs then against the type it ended with. MIR reads literal types from the resolved node tables, so no MIR change is expected; pin with §8's demo and shapes 1-4 on interp, llvm and asan.
fix: 87e598fee9. design.md § Type inference: an integer or float literal is a type variable a later use may fix (a let's value, an operator's operand, a slot whose type is itself a variable, a Vec push, a generic struct's method argument), defaulting to i64 / f64 at the end of its body; anywhere else it takes its type where it is written, as before. Each literal is range-checked against its final type, so let a = 300; let b: u8 = a; is refused at the literal and x = 2000000000 fixed to i32 by a call traps in i32. A literal beside a narrower binding keeps its default and the binding widens (h ^ b over u8), a compare with a literal the peer cannot hold widens (c < 300), a receiver whose method only an impl for one instantiation has takes its defaults first (impl Total for Vec[i64]). Pins: corpus/design/ok_a_literal_takes_the_type_a_later_use_gives_it, err_a_literal_a_later_use_narrows_must_fit, panic_a_literal_a_later_use_narrows_overflows_there (interp, llvm, asan). Full interp corpus: 0 new failures; gate green.

f50642eaba. src/use_classifier.rs: the statement-closure rule of B-2026-10-29-43 asks the typechecker's struct and enum tables, so a chain rooted at user records whose fields hold no closure counts as closure-free (holds_no_closure_in, the standard types asked first), and an `if`'s condition, as a statement or a block tail, is recorded with the condition as its extent (record_chain_closures). src/rc_predicate.rs: B-2026-11-04-34's mutual-exclusion test also covers a plain move on one path and a read in a closure made on another, since a closure that borrows its capture dies with the frame. The row's `if ps.iter().any(..) { return .. } Ok(P { name })`, the tail `if` with a move in either branch, and a `find` in one `match` arm with the move in another are accepted with the right MIR output; the same pairs inside a loop are still refused. Pinned by tests/core_record_closure_read_before_move.rs; mini_blinker's natural shapes check.
title: `karac check` refuses moving a binding after an iterator chain's closure that reads it when the chain's root holds user records (`if ps.iter().any(|p| p.name == name) { .. } Ok(P { name })` over a `Vec[P]`), when the chain is an `if` condition, or when the move is in another `match` arm ("moved inside a loop", no loop in the program)
detail: Found writing mini_blinker (karac c8ca0ca768). `fn add(ps: Slice[P], name: own String) -> Result[P, String] { if ps.iter().any(|p| p.name == name) { return Err(..); } Ok(P { name }) }` with `struct P { name: String }` is refused as "value 'name' is moved inside a loop". Three gaps in B-2026-10-29-43's statement-closure rule: its root-type test `holds_no_closure` admits only standard types, so a `Vec[P]` of plain records is refused; it looks only at `let` and expression statements, so a chain in an `if` condition (statement or block tail) is never recorded; and a chain over records that do hold a closure (`signals.iter().find(|s| s.name == opt)` where a Signal holds `Fn` values) in one `match` arm is paired with a move of `opt` in another arm, which no run reaches together. The same pair inside a loop is a real error and must stay refused.

fix: f50642eaba. A variant constructor's payload is a positional field, so a closure in it escapes even in a local value (core semantics §9.3): src/core_escape.rs gives an `E.V(..)` payload "stored in an enum payload" when the enclosing position is not already an escape, and src/mir/lower.rs let_closure_escapes counts a `let`-bound closure passed to a variant constructor. The closure now captures `seen` by move (a counted handle), the reads-and-writes and re-wrapped shapes run, and a non-Copy capture used after the store is E0500 as for a struct field. Pinned by tests/core_enum_payload_closure_escapes.rs.
title: A `let`-bound closure stored in an enum payload (`let c = |d| seen.n + d; let l = L.F(c);`) captures by `ref` and is refused with E0509 "a view of a temporary value is stored in an escaping closure"; inline in the constructor, or stored in a struct field, it is accepted
detail: Found writing mini_blinker (karac c8ca0ca768): `let trace = |d: Delivery| { seen.n += 1; Ok(Some(..)) }; self.connect(sig, "trace", None, Link.Func(trace))` with `seen` a `shared` handle. core semantics §9.3: a field of function type is escaping by nature, so the closure escapes and captures by move. The MIR builder's `let_closure_escapes` counted struct literals, tuples, arrays, `return` and storing methods but not a variant constructor, and `core_escape` passed a variant payload the enclosing value's position (a `let` binding is not an escape), so check's ownership pass and MIR disagreed with the spec in different ways. The borrow checker's wording ("a view of a temporary value") names no temporary the program has.

fix: f50642eaba. src/typechecker/items.rs check_signature_visibility skips the library's own items (offset at or past library_start), so the name-keyed visibility map no longer applies a program's private `Receiver` or `Sender` to the library's `channel`. The row's program prints 8 on run; a program's own `pub fn make() -> Receiver` over a private struct is still refused. Pinned by tests/library_type_name_reused_by_program.rs.
title: A program whose private type reuses a library type's name (`trait Receiver`, `struct Sender`) passes `karac check` but every `karac run` and `karac build` stops at "private type 'Receiver' leaks through return type of 'channel'", a line of library source
detail: Found writing mini_blinker (karac c8ca0ca768), whose plugins implement `trait Receiver`. Repro: `trait Receiver { fn receive(self, n: i64) -> i64; } struct Dbl {} impl Receiver for Dbl { .. } fn main() { println(f"{Dbl {}.receive(4)}") }` prints `error[mir]: typecheck: 4548:44: private type 'Receiver' leaks through return type of 'channel'`; `pub trait Receiver` runs. `check_signature_visibility` keys types by name and walks the library's items too, so the library's `pub fn channel` read the program's private `Receiver`. The program's own `pub` signatures must still be held to its own types.

fix: f50642eaba. src/typechecker/exprs.rs: an identifier read of a `ref weak T` binding upgrades to `Option[T]` as a `weak T` one does (B-2026-10-25-45), recorded as a weak slot read so `.upgrade()` on it is the same read; the MIR builder already upgraded through a reference. A `Vec[weak T]` walked by `for w in v.iter()` (live and dead elements) and a `weak` payload bound by `match` print the right answers on the MIR interpreter and ASan. Pinned by tests/weak_read_through_ref_binding.rs.
title: A `weak T` reached through a `ref weak T` binding (a loop over a `Vec[weak T]`'s `iter()`, a `weak` payload bound by a `match`) cannot be read or upgraded: the binding types as an error with no message and run/build stop at "a type that failed to check is not lowered yet"
detail: Found writing mini_blinker (karac c8ca0ca768): `enum Link { Strong(Sub), Weak(weak Sub) }` matched as `Link.Weak(w) => match w.upgrade() { .. }`. design.md § Cycles and `weak`: reading a `weak` slot yields `Option[T]` and `.upgrade()` does the same. design.md's own `Vec[weak GraphNode]` example cannot be walked: `for w in a.neighbors.iter() { match w.upgrade() { .. } }` fails the same way, as does `match w { Some(n) => .. }`. `v[0]` (an indexed read) and a `weak` local or parameter already upgrade (B-2026-10-25-45); the identifier read did not cover `ref weak T`.

title: Since 5f1222f497 (B-2026-11-06-11) a method call on a part of a tuple element of a generic `Vec[(K, K)]` walked by `for` is left unsolved: `for (k, v) in d.iter() { s = s + k.show(); }` under `K: Show` is refused by `karac check` with `a type that failed to check is not lowered yet`; corpus apps/cli/mini_collections (e-spec) regressed with it
fix: fbf880fff9. A method call's rigid parameters (the caller's own that the receiver's type names, which stay themselves rather than becoming the call's variables) were collected from named types' arguments only, so the K of a Vec[(K, K)] receiver was opened as d.iter()'s variable. Before 5f1222f497 an unsolved variable read back as its name at once; since B-2026-11-06-11 it stays open for a later use and is bound to K only at the end, so the walked tuple part had no type while k.show() was checked. collect_type_param_names (src/typechecker/expr_method_call.rs) now walks tuples, references, arrays, slices, function and dyn types. The row's program prints its oracle; pinned by corpus/design/ok_a_tuple_part_of_a_generic_vec_calls_its_bound (both destructured parts and p.0), and corpus apps/cli/mini_collections checks clean again.

title: A const parameter only the return type names is not solved by a later use: `let b = zeros(); let c: Array[i64, 4] = b;` is refused at the `let` with `cannot infer const parameter 'N'`
detail: design.md § Const generic parameters, Inference: `let b = zeros();  // error unless a later use fixes N`. At c79be19373, with `fn zeros[const N: i64]() -> Array[i64, N] { [0; N] }`, `let z: Array[i64, 4] = zeros();` works (the annotation solves N, B-2026-11-06-14), but `let b = zeros(); let c: Array[i64, 4] = b;` is refused at the first `let` with `cannot infer const parameter 'N'`. Type variables get this through the late-variable path (B-2026-11-06-7 / -11: `unsolved_call_vars`, `report_unsolved_call_vars`); the call's return resolves an unsolved const variable to the callee's `ConstParam(N)` instead, and `find_unbound_const_param` refuses it at the binding. The remainder of B-2026-11-06-14; the late-variable machinery is Thread C's.
fix: 8a446aedae. A call's const parameter that only its result names now stays a const variable in the call's type (check_call_args_with_substitution_full, late_const_var_ids), as a type parameter does since B-2026-11-06-7. check_assignable takes the array length from the slot a value flows into: an annotated binding, a call argument (through a borrowed parameter's ref), a struct field, or the caller's own Array[i64, M]. One nothing fixes is reported at the call by report_unsolved_call_vars once the program is checked ("nothing in the body fixes it"). A second use that disagrees is a mismatch. A D: Dim shape parameter, a rigid one and one spelled like a parameter in scope keep their old paths. Pins: corpus/core/ok_const_param_later_use (interp, llvm and ASan), err_const_param_later_use_clash; err_const_param_unsolved's wording is updated. Gate green: 10604 + 10777 passed, 0 failed, then 10605 passed on the default leg after the rebase.

title: Tracker for the next minor release: an implied derive (`Copy` without `Clone`, `Eq` or `PartialOrd` without `PartialEq`, `Ord` without `PartialOrd`/`Eq`, `Hash` relying on the filled-in `Eq`) becomes a compile error; in 0.8.x it is a `deprecated` warning with a `karac fix` that adds the derive (bb8531c2c4, design.md §9 37d71cee7f)
detail: Split from B-2026-11-06-27 items 1, 2 and 7 under the review thread's ruling (37d71cee7f): design.md §9 says a derive never adds another, and `derive(Hash)` does not add `Eq`. `add_implied_derives` (src/typechecker.rs) still fills Copy->Clone, Hash->Eq, Eq->PartialEq for 0.8.x, and `warn_implied_derives` (src/typechecker/derives.rs) reports each fill-in, Ord's chain included, as W0245 `deprecated` with a machine-applicable fix that appends the missing names to the `#[derive(..)]` list. kara's corpus, examples and runtime/stdlib were migrated in bb8531c2c4 (126 files, 151 fixes). Remaining before the error: kara-katas (apps thread migrates with `karac fix`), then at the next minor delete `add_implied_derives`, turn the warning into an error, and flip tests/core_derive_lists.rs `implied_derive_is_a_deprecation_warning_with_a_fix`. Repro: `#[derive(Copy)] struct B { x: i64 }` warns `Copy` needs `Clone`.

title: §9 remainder of B-2026-11-06-27: `dbg` on a Display-only type and derived `Debug`/`Clone` on a generic type ignore the bound (items 8, 9); `Option.from`, `Result.from` and `i64.try_into` are missing, and an ambiguous `into()` reports `no method 'into'` instead of asking for an annotation (items 12, 13)
detail: Re-probed at bb8531c2c4 (all four lanes agree): (8) `#[derive(Display)] struct Pt { x: i64 }` then `dbg(Pt { x: 1 })` prints `Pt { x: 1 }`; §9 says there is no fallback and the error names Debug. `struct Nd {}` plus `#[derive(Debug)] struct W[T] { v: T }`, `W { v: Nd {} }.fmt_debug()` prints `W { v: Nd }`; the derived impl is `impl[T: Debug]`. (9) `struct NoC { v: Vec[i64] }` plus `#[derive(Clone)] struct Pair[T] { a: T }`: `p.clone()` deep-copies NoC (pushing to the copy leaves p unchanged), though `impl[T: Clone]` should refuse the call. (12) `Option.from(3)` is `no associated function 'from' on type 'Option'`, `(7i64).try_into()` is `no method 'try_into' on type 'i64'` (i32.try_from works); §9's std conversion table lists both. (13) with `impl From[i64] for A` and `impl From[i64] for B`, `let x = 3.into();` reports `no method 'into' on type 'i64'` rather than asking for a type annotation.
fix: 4fdb64b0c6 closes all four items. (8) dbg of a named type without Debug is refused with no Display fallback; a derived Debug on a generic type holds only where the type arguments are Debug, so `W { v: Nd {} }.fmt_debug()` is `no method 'fmt_debug' on type 'W'` and `dbg(W { v: Nd {} })` names 'W[Nd]'. (9) A derived Clone holds only where the arguments clone, so `Pair[NoC].clone()` is refused ("clones each element, and 'NoC' has no `.clone()`"). (12) `Option.from(x)` and `Result.from(x)` desugar to `Some(x)` / `Ok(x)`. An annotated `try_into` (`let r: Result[i32, String] = 9.try_into()`) already worked. An untargeted one, including `7.try_into().unwrap()` with only the outer annotation, now gets the annotation-asking error, which matches §9's "picks it by the expected type". (13) An untargeted `x.into()` / `x.try_into()` asks for an annotation and lists the targets the source converts into (`i64` converts into `A`, `B`). Eleven corpus dbg fixtures and their tests/cli.rs sources relied on "every type has Debug" and gained `#[derive(Debug)]`. A differential sweep of 27,970 programs found no other newly refused program. Pinned by tests/core_debug_clone_bounds_conversions.rs. Gate 69: test --all 10536, --features llvm 10707. The two clippy nits it found were fixed before the push, and both clippy legs were re-run clean.

9d3631f381. src/mir/lower.rs: the builder's `scrutinee()` treats a place whose path passes through a `shared` handle (`m.a` with `m` a local handle) as a `ref` scrutinee, as core semantics §4.6 says, unless it is a `mut` field read as a value (§6.2); `let` destructuring of such a place takes the same path. A plain binding of a non-`Copy` part is then a `ref` into the handle, and moving it stays the §3.7 error. match, guarded match, if let, while let, let-else, `mut ref` bindings and tuple `let` all check and print the right answers on mir-interp, mir-llvm and ASan. Pinned by tests/shared_local_field_scrutinee_binds_refs.rs (fails on origin/main 01b60e526c) and by corpus/apps/cli/mini_transitions.
title: A plain binding of a non-`Copy` part of a `shared` value held in a local (`match m.a { Some(i) => .. }`, `if let`, `while let`, `let`-`else`, `let (s, k) = m.pair`) is refused as "cannot move a non-`Copy` value out of a `shared` value" by `karac check` and every backend, though core semantics §4.6 makes it a `ref`
detail: Found writing mini_transitions (karac f88c012a03): `let Some(m) = cur else { return; }; match m.initial { Some(i) => { m.state = i.clone(); machines.push(m); } None => .. }` with `m` a `shared struct` handle. Core semantics §4.6: a `shared` scrutinee, or any place reached through one, counts as a `ref` scrutinee, so a plain binding of a part is a `ref` and only moving it is the §3.7 error. The smallest refusal is `shared struct S { a: Option[String] }` with `let m = S { .. }; match m.a { Some(i) => println(i), None => .. }`: every form (match, if let, while let, let-else, tuple `let` destructuring) is refused at the scrutinee by check, mir-interp, mir-llvm and ASan. The same match over a borrowed parameter's field (`fn show(m: S)`) passes, because that place goes through a `Deref`. Cause: the MIR builder's `scrutinee()` returned a by-value scrutinee for a field place with no `Deref` or index in its projection, so each binding moved its part out of the handle and `forbidden_moves` reported it; `let` destructuring took the same path only for `Deref` places. `Some(ref i)` was the only spelling that checked.

fix: 9d3631f381. src/typechecker/patterns.rs: a dotted unit-variant pattern no longer sets `pattern_may_move` on the MIR pipeline, so its scrutinee is not recorded as moving and the closure-kind walker reads it; a closure matching a captured enum against unit variants stays `Fn` on run and build, as `karac check` already had it. Pinned by tests/unit_variant_match_in_stored_closure.rs (fails on origin/main 01b60e526c) and by corpus/apps/cli/mini_transitions.
title: A closure that matches a captured enum against dotted unit variants only (`match cmp { Cmp.Lt => x < v, Cmp.Ge => x >= v }`) types as `OnceFn` on the MIR pipeline, so storing it in a `Fn` slot fails every run and build while `karac check` passes
detail: Found writing mini_transitions (karac f88c012a03): conditions are kept as `type Test = Fn(Slice[Var]) -> bool` closures built from a parsed `enum Cmp { Eq, Ne, Lt, Le, Gt, Ge }`; `self.conds.insert(name, test)` failed `karac run` and every corpus backend with "cannot pass once-callable closure where 'Fn(..)' is expected ... (closure becomes once-callable because it consumes captured binding 'cmp')", while `karac check` printed "All checks passed." A unit-variant pattern binds nothing, so it moves nothing (core semantics §4.6), and the closure is `Fn`. Cause: the closure-kind walker reads a `match` scrutinee as consumed when the checker recorded it in `moving_scrutinees`; the binding arm of `check_pattern_against` stops at a dotted unit variant only under `strict_core` (`karac check`), so on the MIR pipeline (`library_methods_from_source`) `Cmp.Lt` fell through to the binding path and set `pattern_may_move`. `match cmp { _ => .. }` was accepted on both.

fix: 78f0e2b7e5. src/cfg.rs: the `LetElse` arm records a `Define` marker for each binding after the RHS, as the `Let` arm does, so `loop_of_consume_candidates` sees a binding a `let .. else` makes inside a loop as fresh each iteration. Moving it, or a field of it, inside the loop now checks; a `let .. else` binding made outside the loop and moved inside it is still refused. Pinned by tests/let_else_in_loop_binds_afresh.rs (2 of 3 fail on origin/main cf70e4747f) and corpus/apps/cli/mini_rq (8/8 on mir-interp, mir-llvm, ASan and mir-build at KARAC_THREADS=1 and 4).
title: `karac check` refuses moving a binding made by a `let .. else` inside a loop (`let Some(done) = rx.recv() else { .. }; out[done.slot] = Some(done.outcome);`) as "moved inside a loop and not assigned again before the next iteration", though it binds afresh each iteration and every backend runs it
detail: Found writing mini_rq (karac 9d3631f381): the main task collects a round's outcomes with `for _ in 0..n { let Some(done) = self.from_workers.recv() else { return Err(..); }; outcomes[done.slot] = Some(done.outcome); }`. `karac check` reported E0500 at `done.outcome`, and the same for moving the whole binding (`kept.push(done)`) or with `continue` in the else block; `karac fix` offered `done.outcome.clone()`. mir-interp ran the program and printed the right answer. The same loop with `let done = next(k).unwrap();` or `if let Some(done) = .. { .. }` checked. Cause: the use classifier's CFG (src/cfg.rs) records a `Define` marker for each name a plain `let` introduces, which `loop_of_consume_candidates` uses to tell a loop-local binding from one made outside the loop; the `LetElse` arm recorded none, so the move paired with the next iteration's use of the same name.

fix: 849eb1f1b9. src/ownership/index_let.rs finds, beside the read-only index lets, each `let t = v[i];` (or `v[i].f`) on a collection the function may write (a `mut ref` parameter, `mut ref self`, a `let mut`) whose binding's fields are written afterwards: a field or compound store through `t`, a `mut` argument or `mut ref` operand rooted at it, or (in src/cli.rs) a use the ownership pass refuses as a write to a binding without `mut`, such as `t.items.push(x)`, which used to get the `ref` fix. src/cli.rs rewrites the E_INDEX_MOVE_NON_COPY / E0515 repair for those to `mut ref ` and drops the `let mut` refusals of the writes, since the borrow allows them. The borrow is exclusive, so when the collection is used where a later use of `t` can follow (not in another branch of the same if/match; anywhere in a loop that holds both), no fix is offered and the message says to borrow with `mut ref`; a collection the function may not write keeps the copy. On mini_rq with both sites written plainly, `karac fix` restores `let job = mut ref self.jobs[j];` at both, byte for byte. Fixture tests/index_let_written_fields_fix.rs (8 tests); control arm on origin/main 7ce41fe933: 1 passed; 6 failed (the one passing there pins the unchanged copy for a read-only collection; the eighth test, the kept `let mut` refusal on a Copy element, was added after the control arm ran). Gate on the tree before its final rebase (main moved in typechecker and docs only; the four fix suites re-ran green after it): test --all 10552 passed, --features llvm 10723 passed, 0 failed.
title: For `let job = jobs[j];` whose fields are then written (`job.status = 2`), `karac fix` derives `Clone` on the element type and adds `mut`, steering toward a copy that would drop the writes; the repair that keeps them is `let job = mut ref jobs[j];`
detail: Found writing mini_rq (karac 9d3631f381): `fn bump(jobs: mut ref Vec[Job], j: i64) { let job = jobs[j]; job.status = 2; }`. `karac check` reports E_INDEX_MOVE_NON_COPY at `jobs[j]` ("`Job` has no `.clone()` yet: the fix derives one, so that a copy can be taken") and E0384-style "cannot assign through `job` -- declared without `mut`" with help `let mut job`. `karac fix` applies both: `#[derive(Clone)]` on `Job` and `let mut job = jobs[j];`. The next check offers `ref jobs[j]`, `jobs[j].clone()` or `swap`, with no machine fix; `.clone()` would compile and silently lose `job.status = 2`, and `ref` is refused for the write. A binding only read already gets the `ref ` fix (B-2026-10-24-18, `core_read_only_index_lets`). For a binding whose only uses are reads and field writes, over a place reached through a `mut ref` or a `mut` local, the fix should be `mut ref ` (core semantics §5.1), with no `let mut` fix and no derive. Repro: /mnt/attach/project-files/apps-thread/repro-B-2026-11-07-15.kara.

title: Option.take / replace / get_or_insert / get_or_insert_with (all `mut ref self`) are accepted through a bare borrowed parameter, a field of one, an index of an immutable Vec, and (take, replace) on a non-mut local; every backend then mutates the caller's value
fix: 44258c543c. take and replace are builtins with no Kāra body, so neither the ownership pass's stdlib receiver table nor the core ref-write walk knew they take `mut ref self` (get_or_insert / get_or_insert_with had their mode from option.kara's body, which covered the bare-parameter case but not every path). Added the four Option methods to `stdlib_method_self_borrow_kind` (src/ownership.rs) and to `method_writes_receiver`'s by-type fallback (src/typechecker/core_ref_write.rs); Option.replace joins the effect seeds beside take/get_or_insert. Now refused: a bare parameter's o.take() / o.get_or_insert(..) / o.get_or_insert_with(..), a field of one (s.o.replace(..)), and take/replace on a non-mut local or an immutable Vec's element (v[0].take()), with the same messages as Vec.push. Correct shapes (mut ref parameter, mut local, mut Vec element, owned parameter, Iterator.take(n)) check clean and print the same on interp and LLVM: tests/core_option_mut_ref_self.rs (3 tests). Not changed: a Copy-typed bare parameter (Option[i64]) is a copy, as for any Copy struct with a mut ref self method, so writing it changes only the callee's copy; that matches the existing Copy-parameter rule and the caller is not modified. Sweep of 27,970 programs: no new refusals.

title: i128.MIN, i128.MAX and u128.MAX are refused with the internal `a type that failed to check is not lowered yet`; the other widths' MIN/MAX work
detail: Release karac at f02e013e5 (probe of docs/library/core-types.md). design.md §3 and §5 name `i64.MAX` as a type path and every integer type has MIN/MAX. `fn main() { let x = i128.MAX; println(x); }` -> check: `error[typecheck]: 1:17: a type that failed to check is not lowered yet` (the same text from __mir-run / __mir-llvm-run / __mir-llvm-asan as `error[mir]: build:`). Same for `i128.MIN` and `u128.MAX`. `i64.MAX`, `u64.MAX`, `i32.MAX`, `u8.MAX`, `f64.MAX` print correctly. i128/u128 arithmetic methods (checked_neg, saturating_neg, overflowing_shl(128), checked_shl(127)) work on all four lanes, so only the constants fail. The message is internal and gives no hint; a user cannot write `x == i128.MAX`.
fix: a44db5f5ac. The type checker reads a primitive type's constants from `PRIMITIVE_CONSTS` (src/prelude.rs), which had rows for every integer width but the 128-bit ones, so `i128.MAX`, `i128.MIN` and `u128.MAX` failed to check and reached lowering as `a type that failed to check is not lowered yet`; lowering already computed their values (`int_limit`). Added i128 MIN/MAX and u128 MIN/MAX. They print 170141183460469231731687303715884105727, -170141183460469231731687303715884105728, 340282366920938463463374607431768211455 and 0 (checked against Python's 2**127-1, -2**127, 2**128-1) on run, build and mir-llvm-asan, and serve as a const initializer (`const HALF: u128 = u128.MAX / 2`), in a comparison and as a pattern. Pin: corpus/core/ok_int128_limits.

title: f32 copysign / pow / hypot / atan2 refuse a negative float literal argument (`h.copysign(-1.0)`: expects f32, got f64); a positive literal, and min / max / clamp / total_cmp with a negative one, are accepted
detail: Release karac at f02e013e5 (probe of docs/library/core-types.md). core-types.md float methods take `y: Self`. `fn main() { let h: f32 = 2.0; let r = h.copysign(-1.0); println(r == r); }` -> `copysign expects an argument of type f32, got f64`. Same for `pow(-1.0)`, `hypot(-1.0)`, `atan2(-1.0)`. Accepted: `h.copysign(1.0)`, `h.min(-1.0)`, `h.max(-(1.0))`, `h.clamp(-1.0, 1.0)`, `h.total_cmp(-1.0)`, `take32(-1.0)` for `fn take32(x: f32)`, `h + -1.0`. So the arm in typechecker/method_numeric.rs that checks these four arguments takes a literal's expected type only when it is a bare literal, not a unary minus applied to one. Workaround `-1.0f32`. Neighbour of B-2026-11-07-3 (literals default last) but narrower: here the expected type is known at the call.
fix: d411135900. typechecker/method_numeric.rs: the float binary methods (copysign, pow, hypot, atan2) promote a suffix-free float literal argument through unsuffixed_num_literal / record_promoted_literal, as wrapping_* and min / max do, so a negated one is the receiver's type. Not covered by B-2026-11-07-3: a literal there was already written into a known slot. Pin: corpus/design/ok_a_negative_float_literal_is_an_f32_method_s_argument (f32 and f64; checked against numpy float32), interp, llvm and asan.

title: BufReader.read_line / read_to_string and ChildStdout.read_to_string append into a `mut ref String` whose buffer is still a string literal's static data: segfault on build and run, ASan global-buffer-overflow WRITE in karac_mir_buf
fix: a17505d129. runtime/src/mir_io.rs `push_bytes` (shared by BufReader read_line / read_to_string and ChildStdout.read_to_string via runtime/src/mir_process.rs) tested its free room as `s.cap - s.len < b.len()`. A literal's String has cap 0 and len > 0, so the subtraction wrapped to a huge value, read as room to spare, and the bytes were copied into the literal's static data. It now compares `s.cap < s.len + b.len()`, which takes the existing fresh-allocation path (it already skipped freeing a cap-0 buffer). No compiler change: src/backend/mir/io.rs is untouched. Verified: the row's program prints 4 / >abc on __mir-run, __mir-llvm-run and __mir-llvm-asan (ASan clean). tests/io_append_into_literal_string.rs pins read_line and read_to_string into literal-initialised Strings on both backends. Runtime archives rebuilt (all, including TSan).

title: par branches writing two different Files conflict when both pass the same read-only buffer (`par { f.write(b.as_slice()), g.write(b.as_slice()) }`), and the error blames `writes(File @ l1)` vs `writes(File @ l4)`
detail: Release karac at f02e013e5, runtime archives rebuilt there (probe of docs/library/io.md). io.md Effects: an open file is keyed by its value, and operations on two different files do not conflict (core-semantics §12 item 5). With f and g two File.create results and `b: Vec[u8] = [1]`: `par { f.write(b.as_slice()), g.write(b.as_slice()) }` -> `branches 1 and 2 of the par conflict: writes(File @ l1) and writes(File @ l4)`. Same with `b[..]` and with `.is_ok()` on both. Accepted: two different buffers (`g.write(c.as_slice())`), `par { f.write(b.as_slice()), b.len() }`, `par { f.write(b.as_slice()), g.flush() }`, and moving each write into a helper `fn wa(f: File)`. Same-file pairs (write/write, flush/flush, write/flush, seek/write) are refused correctly. So two shared reads of one buffer make the two distinct file keys collide, and the message names the files, which points the user at the wrong cause.
fix: 39dbc078da: a collection, tuple, array or slice of scalars and strings holds no resource, so it carries no origin in the effects pass (`carries_at` in src/mir/effects.rs). The shared read-only buffer passed to both writes had joined the two files through the store-through-a-writable-argument edge (the buffer into `mut ref f`, which runs back to `f`), so `f` and `g` shared an origin. Verified on the row's program with release karac: `par { f.write(b.as_slice()), g.write(b.as_slice()) }` checks clean, and the same on two channels; one channel twice is still refused. Pinned by `effects_par_shared_scalar_buffer_keeps_two_channels_apart`; `effects_par_capabilities_do_not_conflict_but_parameters_may_alias` now gives its two aliasing handles a struct type (85169d33d5), as a `Vec[i64]` no longer aliases.

title: check accepts Atomic[T] for T outside the documented set (i8, u8, i16, u16, i128, usize all pass); Atomic[i128] then fails to link under ASan (undefined __atomic_load_16)
detail: Release karac at f02e013e5 (probe of docs/library/concurrency.md). concurrency.md: `Atomic[T]` exists for T = bool, i32, i64, u32 and u64. The checker already refuses f64, char and String with `Atomic[X] is not a valid atomic type: ...`. But `import std.sync.{Atomic}; fn main() { let a: Atomic[i8] = Atomic.new(127); println(a.fetch_add(1)); println(a.load()); }` passes check and prints 127 / -128 on __mir-run and __mir-llvm-run; the same for u8, i16, u16 (u16 fetch_sub(1) from 0 gives 65535) and usize. `Atomic[i128]`: check passes, `karac build` and __mir-run give the right values, and `__mir-llvm-asan` fails at link: `undefined reference to __atomic_load_16` / `__atomic_fetch_add_16`. Either the checker refuses every T outside the five (the existing message), or the doc widens the set and the 16-byte case links (libatomic or a lock).
fix: 3f39b2aafd (tests in 407b63262b): library/concurrency.md § Atomics. atomic_ineligible_inner_kind (src/typechecker/expr_call.rs) accepts exactly bool, i32, i64, u32 and u64 and refuses every other integer width (i8, u8, i16, u16, usize, isize), a 128-bit integer (the ASan link failure on __atomic_load_16 can no longer be reached) and a raw pointer (design.md §11 makes no thread-safety claim about one; the E_NOT_CROSS_TASK help no longer suggests Atomic[*mut T]). An argument the call leaves open (a literal under `let a: Atomic[i8] = Atomic.new(127)`) is judged at the end of the program, and the checked path reports E0272 on the annotated type. Folded in: `import std.sync.{RecvTimeoutError, SendTimeoutError}` now binds the two timeout errors (src/prelude.rs LIBRARY_GLOBAL_MODULES). Pins: corpus/design/err_atomic_outside_the_five, corpus/design/ok_std_sync_names_the_timeout_errors. Remainder: a generic `Atomic.new(x)` over `x: own T` is not judged at the instance, filed as B-2026-11-07-35.

title: A struct literal of another package's struct is refused even when every field is `pub` (`Opts { port: 1 }` -> E0111 field 'port' is not `pub`); the literal path calls the cross-module check without the is_pub test the field-access path makes
detail: Release karac at f02e013e5. Two path packages: lib (kara.toml name lib) and app with `[dependencies] lib = { path = "../lib" }`; lib/src/lib.kara = `#[non_exhaustive] pub enum Kind { A, B }  pub fn get() -> Kind { Kind.A }  pub struct Opts { pub port: i64 }  pub fn mk() -> Opts { Opts { port: 3 } }`. app/src/main.kara `import lib.{Opts}; fn main() { let o = Opts { port: 1 }; println(o.port); }` -> `error[E0111]: field 'port' of struct 'Opts' is not pub: only pub fields are visible outside package lib`. Accepted: `lib.mk().port` and `let Opts { port } = lib.mk();`. design.md §5 Field visibility: a field is visible to users of the package with `pub`; code that cannot see a field cannot name it in a field access or a struct literal, so a `pub` field may be named in a literal. Cause read at src/typechecker/fields.rs: the struct-literal loop (about line 1266, added by 3942d674ca for B-2026-11-04-46) calls `check_cross_module_field_access` for every named field, and that function refuses any non-private field from another package; the field-access sites (lines 336 and 360) call it only when `!is_pub`. So every cross-package struct literal is refused, and the message is false. Found while checking std.encoding's #[non_exhaustive] (next row).
fix: b92f71fe7d: the struct-literal loop in src/typechecker/fields.rs calls check_cross_module_field_access only for a field that is not `pub`, the same test the field-access sites make, so `Opts { port: 1 }` of another package's struct with a `pub` field checks, and a literal naming a non-pub field is still E0111. Pinned by tests/cross_package_struct_literal.rs (both directions).

title: #[non_exhaustive] is not enforced outside the defining package: a match naming every variant with no wildcard is accepted, for a user package's enum and for std's DecodeError
detail: Release karac at f02e013e5. Two path packages: lib (kara.toml name lib) and app with `[dependencies] lib = { path = "../lib" }`; lib/src/lib.kara = `#[non_exhaustive] pub enum Kind { A, B }  pub fn get() -> Kind { Kind.A }  pub struct Opts { pub port: i64 }  pub fn mk() -> Opts { Opts { port: 3 } }`. design.md §11 #[non_exhaustive]: on an enum, a match outside the defining package needs a wildcard arm, even when it names every current variant, with a machine-applicable fix adding `_ => todo()`. app: `import lib.{Kind, get}; fn main() { match get() { Kind.A => println("a"), Kind.B => println("b") } }` passes check and runs. Same for encoding.md's `#[non_exhaustive]` DecodeError (runtime/stdlib/std_encoding.kara marks it): `match base64_decode("x") { Ok(_) => .., Err(DecodeError.InvalidByte(_)) => .., Err(DecodeError.InvalidLength) => .. }` is accepted. src/prelude.rs builds library stubs with `is_non_exhaustive: false`. The struct half (a literal outside the package must be refused naming the constructor; a pattern must end with `..`) could not be checked because of B-2026-11-07-22, which refuses every cross-package literal.
fix: 03ecef223d: design.md § #[non_exhaustive]. (1) The cross-package rule fired only for library types; `sees_from_outside` (src/typechecker/fields.rs) also asks whether the type's package is the current module's, so a user package's enum, struct literal and struct pattern without `..` are covered. (2) A qualified unit variant (`Kind.A`) parses as a dotted Binding and pattern_is_catchall read it as a catch-all, so the top-level wildcard check never fired on the usual spelling; that is why std's DecodeError matched at the top passed too. (3) Exhaustiveness treats such an enum as open (TypeEnv.open_enums, set per function), so it needs a wildcard wherever it sits (`Err(DecodeError.InvalidLength)`), reported as E_NON_EXHAUSTIVE_CROSS_PACKAGE_MATCH so a package check keeps it. (4) A package-mode `karac fix` applies these module-boundary fix-its (wildcard arm, `..`). Two legacy pool fixtures and two backend tests that matched PoolError exhaustively gained `Err(_)` arms. Pins: corpus/design/err_non_exhaustive_std_enum_needs_a_wildcard, tests/cross_package_non_exhaustive.rs.

title: std.secret exports only Secret: Zeroize and ConstantTimeEq cannot be imported or named (so the documented user `impl Zeroize` cannot be written), and `impl Debug for Secret[i64]` is accepted though secret.md makes it a compile error
detail: Release karac at f02e013e5 (probe of docs/library/secret.md; regex.md, crypto.md, pool.md and log.md clean). secret.md (post-v1 library): `Secret`, `ConstantTimeEq` and `Zeroize` live in std.secret; `Drop (where T: Zeroize)` zeroizes; under Not yet implemented it says the library's own Zeroize impls are missing but `A user impl Zeroize works`; and `Writing impl Debug for Secret[T] ... is a compile error whose diagnostic points to this section`. Measured: (1) `import std.secret.{Secret, ConstantTimeEq, Zeroize};` -> `unknown item ConstantTimeEq in module std.secret; available: Secret` (same for Zeroize). (2) Without the import, `struct Key { b: i64 } impl Zeroize for Key { fn zeroize(mut ref self) { self.b = 0; } }` -> `undefined type 'Zeroize'`, so no user type can opt in and `Secret[Key]` never zeroizes. (3) `impl Debug for Secret[i64] { fn fmt(self, f: mut ref Formatter) -> Result[(), FmtError] { Ok(()) } }` passes check and runs. Correct: `expose` / `expose_mut`, `ct_eq` (method works without importing the trait), refusals of Display, ==, Copy and use as a Map key, and `#[derive(Debug)]` on a struct holding a Secret printing `token: <redacted>` through dbg. Either secret.md's Not yet implemented list gains these three items, or the trait names are exported and the impl refused.
fix: RELOCATED: std.secret is post-v1. 07d1b1f0c4 lists the missing Zeroize/ConstantTimeEq exports and the unenforced impl Debug refusal under secret.md's Not yet implemented, tracked with the other std.secret items in docs/implementation_checklist/phase-11-stdlib-longtail.md (review-thread ruling 2026-11-07).

title: A compiled TLS server (Server.serve_tls, TlsListener) is killed by SIGPIPE (exit -13) when a client disconnects without close_notify: one client that sends a request and drops the TCP connection takes the whole HTTPS server down
detail: Release karac at f02e013e5 with archives rebuilt there (probe of the io.md network half; driver scripts in the shared folder probe-core/srvp/). Program: `fn handle(req: Request) -> Response { Response { status: 200, body: f"tls {req.path()}" } } fn main() { let c = fs.read_to_string(chain).unwrap(); let k = fs.read_to_string(key).unwrap(); match Server.serve_tls("127.0.0.1:0", c, k, handle) { .. } }` with a CA-signed leaf for 127.0.0.1. A Python ssl client sends `GET /a` with Connection: close and gets `200 tls /a`; a second client sends `GET /b` and closes the TCP socket without close_notify and without reading. The `karac build` binary then exits with signal 13 (SIGPIPE) and the next client gets ECONNREFUSED. `__mir-run` survives and answers the third request. Same with a hand-written TlsListener loop (accept, read until error, return): after a client's unclean close the server logs `Tls(UnexpectedClose)` correctly and then dies of SIGPIPE when the TlsStream drops (io.md: dropping a stream sends close_notify, as far as the socket takes it). Plain TCP is fine: `TcpStream.write` to a peer that closed returns Err and the process lives, and the plain HTTP server survives clients that reset mid-request. So the TLS write path (runtime tls_conn / rustls over the socket) writes without MSG_NOSIGNAL, and only mir_process.rs ignores SIGPIPE (and only before spawning a piped child). The interpreter never sees it because Rust's own runtime ignores SIGPIPE. Any internet-facing HTTPS service built with karac can be killed by one client. Expected: Err(Tls(..)) or a dropped connection, the process keeps serving.
fix: 81bda056fb. A compiled program ignores SIGPIPE from the start of main (runtime/src/fatal.rs ignore_sigpipe, called by karac_mir_run_main), as the interpreter's Rust start up does, so a TLS or TCP peer that drops its connection fails only that connection's write. The console keeps the quiet ending (io.md 32a347fd0a): a stdout or stderr write that fails with EPIPE restores the default disposition and raises SIGPIPE, so prog | head still ends with status 141. Test: tests/mir_server_disconnect.rs mir_tls_server_outlives_a_client_that_drops_mid_response, two clients drop a serve_tls connection mid-response and the server answers the next on both backends; against the old archive the compiled server died and the next connect was refused.

title: For an absolute-form request target (`GET http://example.com/z?k=v HTTP/1.1`) the server's Request.path() returns `http://example.com/z` and for `GET http://example.com` returns `http://example.com`, not `/z` and `/`
detail: Release karac at f02e013e5 with archives rebuilt there (probe of the io.md network half; driver scripts in the shared folder probe-core/srvp/). io.md HTTP server: `path` and `query` read the target, which for an absolute URL (`http://host/items?id=3`) is its path and query, `/` when it has neither. A handler printing `req.path()` behind Server.serve, sent `GET http://example.com/z?k=v HTTP/1.1` (Host: example.com), sees path `http://example.com/z` (query() is right: k=v); `GET http://example.com HTTP/1.1` gives path `http://example.com`. Identical on __mir-run, __mir-llvm-run and __mir-llvm-asan. A Request built in the program does it right: `Request.new("GET", "http://host/items?id=3").path()` is `/items`, `Request.new("GET", "http://host").path()` is `/`, `https://h:8443/p/q?z` gives `/p/q`. So the server's parsed request skips the absolute-URL split that Request.new does. Absolute form is what a client sends through a forward proxy, so routing on path() breaks there.
fix: 81bda056fb. src/http1.rs reads an absolute-form request target as its origin form (origin_target, shared with Request.new): GET http://example.com/z?k=v gives path() /z and query k=v, and GET http://example.com gives /. Also per io.md: a request line that is not method, target and HTTP/x, or a header without a colon, makes Server.__install return -2, and http_server.kara answers 400 Bad Request without calling the handler and closes the connection (it reached the handler with path HTTP, or closed unanswered). Test: tests/mir_server_disconnect.rs mir_server_reads_absolute_targets_refuses_garbage_and_outlives_a_dropped_client, on both backends.

title: Socket methods with no declared effects (local_addr, set_read_timeout, try_clone on TcpListener/TcpStream/UdpSocket) carry an `unknown (native ..)` effect, so a par branch calling one conflicts with any branch that prints, reads the clock or uses another socket
detail: Release karac at f02e013e5 with archives rebuilt there (probe of the io.md network half; driver scripts in the shared folder probe-core/srvp/). io.md declares `fn local_addr(self) -> Result[String, NetError]`, `fn set_read_timeout(self, ms: Option[i64]) -> Result[(), NetError]` and `fn try_clone(self) -> Result[TcpStream, NetError]` with no effects. `let (a, b) = par { l.local_addr().is_ok(), println("x") };` -> `branches 1 and 2 of the par conflict: unknown (native TcpListener.local_addr) and writes(Stdout)`. Same against `Clock.now()` / `sleep(..)` (reads(Clock)) and against `cl.write(..)` on another stream (sends(Network @ l4)); not against a pure expression or `fs.exists`. Reproduced for TcpStream.set_read_timeout, TcpListener.local_addr, TcpStream.try_clone, UdpSocket.set_read_timeout, UdpSocket.local_addr, UdpSocket.try_clone. The natural shape `par { { sv.set_read_timeout(Some(40)).unwrap(); sv.read(mut buf) }, { sleep(..); .. } }` is refused for it. These natives need an effect entry (none, or keyed by the socket value).
fix: 39dbc078da: `local_addr` on TcpListener, UdpSocket and TlsListener, `try_clone` on TcpStream and UdpSocket, and `set_read_timeout` on TcpStream, UdpSocket, TlsStream and WebSocket now have known effects in `native_effects` (src/mir/effects.rs): allocates(Heap) for the address and the handle, nothing for the timeout, as docs/library/io.md gives them no effect clause. Verified with release karac: `par { println(l.local_addr().unwrap()), u.set_read_timeout(Some(5)).unwrap() }` checks clean and runs, where 6e709e5fdd refused it as `unknown (native TcpListener.local_addr)` vs `unknown (native UdpSocket.set_read_timeout)`. Pinned by `effects_socket_address_clone_and_timeout_are_known`.

title: A compiled HTTP client sends a plain HTTP request for any URL scheme (`ftp://127.0.0.1:P/x` and `gopher://..` get `OK 200` from an HTTP server), while the interpreter refuses them with `Unknown Scheme`; io.md allows only http:// and https://
detail: Release karac at f02e013e5 with archives rebuilt there (io.md network-half probe; scripts in the shared folder probe-core/srvp/cli/, program ftp.kara). io.md HTTP client: `A URL is http:// or https://`. Program: `Client.new().get("ftp://127.0.0.1:<port of a plain HTTP server>/ftpprobe")`, the same with `gopher://`, and `127.0.0.1:<port>/noscheme`. __mir-run prints `ERR ftp://...: Unknown Scheme: unknown scheme 'ftp'` and the same for gopher. __mir-llvm-run and __mir-llvm-asan print `OK 200 plain GET /ftpprobe` and `OK 200 plain GET /gprobe`, and the server's log shows both GETs arrived, so the compiled client spoke HTTP to a URL that names another protocol. With no explicit port it connects to port 80 (`ftp://127.0.0.1/x` gives `connect failed: Connection refused`, where the interpreter says Unknown Scheme). The scheme-less URL is refused the same way on both lanes (`bad url: invalid format`). Likely site: runtime/src/lib.rs around line 7192, where `scheme_str().unwrap_or("http")` is compared only with "https", so every other scheme takes the http path (and the proxy lookup is keyed on it). ASan clean. The spec does not say how a refused scheme reads, so any Err naming the scheme satisfies it; the divergence is that compiled code sends the request at all.
fix: a3e88251f4. The compiled client (runtime/src/lib.rs `http_fetch_once`) now refuses any scheme other than http and https before it resolves or connects, in the interpreter's words: `ftp://127.0.0.1:P/ftpprobe: Unknown Scheme: unknown scheme 'ftp'`, the same for gopher. tests/mir_http_client_wire.rs `http_client_refuses_a_scheme_other_than_http_or_https` runs ftp://, gopher:// and http:// against one loopback server on the interpreter and built: both print the two refusals and `200 ok`, and the server takes exactly one connection per run. Control at the parent tree: the built lane printed `200 ok` three times (0 passed; 2 failed with the -29 test), fix: 2 passed. A redirect to another scheme goes back through `http_fetch_once`, so it is refused the same way.

title: Through a CONNECT tunnel (`https_proxy` set, https:// URL) the interpreter's client sends the request in absolute form (`GET https://proxied.invalid:P/tunnel`), where compiled code sends origin form (`GET /tunnel`); a Kara server then reads the wrong path (B-2026-11-07-26)
detail: Release karac at f02e013e5 (io.md network-half probe; scripts in probe-core/srvp/cli/: servers.py runs an HTTP proxy that maps *.invalid to 127.0.0.1 and a TLS echo server; program c2.kara). io.md Proxies: an http:// URL goes to the proxy in absolute form; an https:// URL goes through a CONNECT tunnel, with the certificate checked as without a proxy, i.e. the tunnelled request is the one sent to the origin directly, which is origin form (RFC 9112 3.2.1: absolute form is for a request to a proxy other than CONNECT). Run with `https_proxy=http://127.0.0.1:<proxy>` and KARAC_HTTP_EXTRA_CA set, request `https://proxied.invalid:<tls>/tunnel`. The proxy logs `CONNECT proxied.invalid:<tls>` on all lanes; the TLS server echoes the request target: __mir-run `OK 200 tls GET https://proxied.invalid:43789/tunnel`, __mir-llvm-run and __mir-llvm-asan `OK 200 tls GET /tunnel`. RFC servers must accept absolute form, so this is low on its own, but a Kara server reached this way reports path() as the whole URL, per B-2026-11-07-26. Interpreter's client is ureq (src/mir/interp.rs); compiled is runtime/src/lib.rs. Direct https (no proxy) sends origin form on both lanes.
fix: a3e88251f4. `ureq` 2.12 writes the absolute form whenever an HTTP proxy is configured, for a tunnelled https request too (unit.rs `send_prelude`). The interpreter (src/mir/interp.rs `http_exchange`) no longer gives ureq the proxy for an https URL: `http_agent_tunnelled` builds an agent whose resolver maps every name to the proxy, and whose TLS step (`TunnelTls`) sends `http_proxy::connect_request`, checks `connect_refusal`, then does the rustls handshake with the origin, so ureq sends origin form as the compiled client does. A refused tunnel or an unreachable proxy reads in the compiled client's words, as before (`http_client_goes_through_the_environment_proxy_on_both_backends` still passes). Plain-http requests through a proxy keep absolute form. tests/mir_http_client_wire.rs `http_client_sends_origin_form_inside_a_proxy_tunnel`: an echoing TLS origin behind a loopback CONNECT proxy prints `200 GET /tunnel?q=1` on both lanes; at the parent tree the interpreter printed `200 GET https://example.invalid/tunnel?q=1`.

title: A bare `for a in args` over an owned `Vec` (an `own` parameter not used after the loop) whose element's payload is moved out (`Value.List(items) => ls.push(items)`) gets the fix `items.clone()`, though the message itself names the repair that takes no copy, `for a in args.into_iter()`
detail: Found writing mini_dask (kara-katas apps/cli/mini_dask, `apply`). Repro /mnt/attach/project-files/apps-thread/repro-dask-for-own-vec-clone.kara: `fn lists(args: own Vec[Value]) -> Vec[Vec[i64]] { let mut ls = Vec.new(); for a in args { match a { Value.List(items) => ls.push(items), Value.Int(_) => {} } } ls }`. `karac check` (849eb1f1b9): error[borrow_projection_copy] "cannot move 'items': it borrows its value (a bare `for` element, ...). For a `for` element, iterate with `.into_iter()` to move the elements out of the collection. Write `.clone()` to take a copy, or keep using it in place", and the machine-applicable edit is `.clone()` after `items`; `karac fix` applies it, so every list is copied out of a vector the function owns and drops right after. Writing `for a in args.into_iter()` checks clean and prints 1 under `__mir-run`. Where the iterated place is an owned local or `own` parameter with no use after the loop, the fix should be `.into_iter()` on the iterable; the copy fits only where the collection is used again or is borrowed.
fix: ec6e5415ba. A move out of a bare `for` element whose type has `.clone()` records its site when the loop iterates an owned collection (src/typechecker/exprs.rs keeps, per `.into_iter()` site, the variable and first field the iterable hangs off, and the loop's span); at the end of the function src/typechecker/items.rs (`offer_for_into_iter_fixes`, `consumable_after`) replaces the `.clone()` fix with `.into_iter()` on the loop's iterable when nothing the loop can reach afterwards uses the collection (a use of another field of the root, or one past a block that holds the loop and ends in `return`, does not count) and no loop around it began before the collection was declared (a `for`/`while let`/`match` pattern binding it counts as declared inside). A collection used after the loop, or iterated inside an outer loop that does not redeclare it, keeps the copy. On mini_dask's first draft, `karac fix` now writes `args.into_iter()` and `step.inputs.into_iter()`. Fixtures tests/for_into_iter_and_ref_list_fixes.rs (six of its eight tests); tests/core_strict_check.rs a_for_over_a_temporary_collection_binds_refs flipped from `.clone()` to `mk().into_iter()` and `m.into_iter()`, the repairs it already accepted. Control arm on origin/main 7a8be14476: 2 passed; 6 failed for the file (the two passing pin the kept copy). Full gate on the tree before rebases: one failure, that pin, flipped; after the rebases --lib, core_strict_check, typechecker and the fix suites re-ran green.

title: An unannotated list literal of a `ref` to a `Copy` value (`let chain = [k];` with `k` from `order.iter()`) is typed `Vec[ref i64]`, and its later use where a `Vec[i64]` is wanted is refused "expected 'Vec[i64]', found 'Vec[ref i64]'" with no fix, though annotating the `let` (`let chain: Vec[i64] = [k];`) checks and runs
detail: Found writing mini_dask (kara-katas apps/cli/mini_dask, the fuse step: `let mut chain = [k];` then `units.push(Unit { chain: chain, .. })`). Repro /mnt/attach/project-files/apps-thread/repro-dask-list-literal-ref-copy.kara: `fn chains(order: Vec[i64]) -> Vec[Vec[i64]] { let mut out: Vec[Vec[i64]] = Vec.new(); for k in order.iter() { let chain = [k]; out.push(chain); } out }`. `karac check` (849eb1f1b9): error[typecheck] at `out.push(chain)`: expected 'Vec[i64]', found 'Vec[ref i64]', no hint and no edit; `karac fix` reports no fixable diagnostics. With `let chain: Vec[i64] = [k];` it checks and prints 2 under `__mir-run` (B-2026-10-22-6 made the annotated literal read the `ref` as the value). Either the literal's element type should be taken from the later use, as §5.10 reads a `ref` to a `Copy` value where the slot is that value, or the refusal should carry the annotation as its fix.
fix: ec6e5415ba. src/typechecker/items.rs `offer_ref_list_annotations` runs at the end of each function under the strict commands: a TypeMismatch with no fix whose expected type is `Vec[T]` and found `Vec[ref T]`, at an identifier bound by the nearest earlier un-annotated `let name = [..];`, gets the fix `: Vec[T]` after the name and a sentence saying the list holds borrows; the annotation reads each `ref` as its value (B-2026-10-22-6). On mini_dask's first draft `karac fix` writes `let mut chain: Vec[i64] = [k];`. Fixtures tests/for_into_iter_and_ref_list_fixes.rs an_unannotated_list_of_copy_refs_is_annotated and an_unannotated_mut_list_of_copy_refs_is_annotated; both fail on the control arm (origin/main 7a8be14476) and pass with the fix.

title: Tracker for the next minor release: an f-string inside an f-string's `{..}` becomes a compile error; in 0.8.x it is a `deprecated` warning with a `karac fix` that writes the inner f-string's text in the hole when the hole is that f-string alone (d978271697, design.md §3 Interpolated strings)
detail: Split from B-2026-11-06-18 item 4 under the review thread's ruling (accepted with the -79 and -07-10 precedent): design.md §3 says a nested f-string is an error, but 162 programs in kara's corpus and kara-katas nest them, so 0.8.x warns. The parser records each inner f-string literal in `Program::nested_fstrings` (`record_nested_fstrings`, src/parser/exprs.rs) with the flattening edit when the hole is the inner literal alone and has no format spec (`{f"<{x}>"}` becomes `<{x}>`); `warn_nested_fstring` (src/typechecker/exprs.rs) reports W0245 `deprecated`. A hole that uses the inner f-string inside a larger expression (`{g(f"{a}{b}")}`) gets no fix, since binding it first needs a name. Remaining before the error: migrate kara's corpus and kara-katas (`karac fix` for the flattenable ones, a hand-written `let` for the rest), then at the next minor turn the warning into a parse error and flip tests/core_naming_lexical.rs `a_nested_f_string_is_deprecated`. Repro: `fn main() { let x = 4; println(f"a {f"<{x}>"} b"); }` warns at 1:37.

fix: d308599fbb (B-2026-11-09-8, `noalias` on a frozen `ref` parameter) fixed the appends: x86 callgrind, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, karac 2f76d840df, outputs identical: 473 7.30G against checked Rust's 7.66G (8.69G with both noalias flags off), 498 4.40G against 6.26G. 404 stays 2.607G against 2.113G and every remedy is slower. (1) LLVM infers no `readonly` for visit's header pointer (minimal .ll: a self-recursive fn that reads through a pointer loaded from %p gets nothing on %p), hence the reload; emitting `readonly` for a frozen `ref` in mark_deref_params drops the reload and second check, but the data pointer and offset then take a fourth saved register plus an alignment push: 2.680G. (2) The drop schedule's header by value: one struct 2.782G (473 7.82G); three words 2.684G (473 7.67G, 498 4.61G). Rust keeps one element pointer, three saved registers; no IR form tried reaches it, so the x86 remainder is measured to a standstill. The arm64 share (M5 1.73x) is B-2026-11-09-22.
title: Kata 404's recursive `visit(nodes: Vec[Node], ...)` reloads its Vec header after the first recursive call: 1.23x checked Rust's instructions on x86, where every remedy tried (readonly, header by value) is slower; 473 and 498 were fixed by `ref` noalias (d308599fbb)
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-07. M5 (review thread's 400-426 batch, kara-katas 3d7ad5f1 on the Mac): kata 404 (bench/sum_of_left_leaves.kara, 50 random trees of 30000 nodes, 50 rounds) 1.73x rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on. x86 container (drop schedule, kara b3904f35ce, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, sinks equal): wall 1.04-1.16 s against Rust's 0.79-0.88 s and clang -O2's 0.85-0.95 s; callgrind 2.607G instructions against Rust's 2.113G and C's 1.707G, of which `visit` is 2.486G against Rust's 2.015G (about 150M calls, 16.6 against 13.4 instructions a call). The bare parameter borrows, so `visit` receives a pointer to the caller's Vec header (`ptr align 8 dereferenceable(24)`), where Rust's `&[Node]` arrives as a data pointer and length in two registers. Kara's machine code loads the length for the bound check and the data pointer on entry, and after the first recursive call loads both again and repeats the bound check, as LLVM cannot tell the call left the header alone. Marking the parameter `noalias readonly` by hand in the IR (opt -O3, llc) drops the reload and the second check but costs a fourth callee-saved register, and ran 2.665G against 2.580G for the same pipeline without it. What would match Rust is passing a read-only borrowed Vec of a by-value function as its data pointer and length (LLVM's ArgumentPromotion does not fire on this recursive function), or `noalias` on `ref` parameters once their soundness against core-semantics 5.9 and 6.2 is settled (B-2026-11-04-39's 321 needs the same). The arm64 part of the gap (1.73x against x86's 1.3x) is unattributed. Kata 401 from the same batch (M5 1.25x legacy's instructions, 1.42x cycles) is at parity with Rust on x86 (6.04G against 6.09G instructions, the same wall), about a quarter of it in malloc and free, so it was not filed. APPENDED 2026-11-08 (kata thread's parity pass, x86, release karac 0.8.1-dev.14849+g8cdef3b93): (a) kata 473 (matchsticks-to-square, after its bench moved `sides` to Array[i64, 4], kara-katas 8ccfc5705): 8.69G against checked Rust's 7.66G (1.135x). In the recursive `place(sticks: Vec[i64], i, sides: mut ref Array[i64, 4], side)` the `sticks` data pointer, length and sticks[i] are reloaded and bounds-checked in each of the 4 unrolled side iterations and after every recursive call; in the IR %0 (sticks) is readonly but %2 (sides) is not noalias and the function has only nounwind, no memory(argmem..), so a store to sides or the recursive call may clobber sticks. Also every call stores three panic-location values to the stack in the prologue (`lea r8,[rip+..]; mov [rsp],r8; mov edi,0x11; ..`), the phi feeding karac_mir_abort_at in the merged abort1/abort2 blocks, about 6 instructions x 98M calls. KARAC_MIR_OPT=3 changes nothing. (b) UNVERIFIED on arm64: kata 498 (diagonal-traverse, M5 1.27x; x86 shows no gap, 4.505G against checked Rust's 6.264G) reloads and bounds-checks the outer matrix header per element in its 100M-iteration traversal (`cmp r12,[r9+r10+0x8]; jae`; `mov rax,[r9+r10]`). In the IR the loads through the inlined find_diagonal_order argument carry `!noalias !4` where `!alias.scope !4` belongs, so the scope cannot prove the push store and the grow call leave all[k] alone; karac_realloc_or_panic is declared with no allocator attributes. Needs an M5 profile. TRIED 2026-11-08 (drop schedule), NOT LANDED: a `ref Vec`/`ref String` parameter passed as three words {ptr, len, cap} (len and cap with range(i64 0, i64::MAX); caller loads through load_len; off when a call would need more than six register words). Sweep of all 1036 kara-katas benches, x86 callgrind, header words on vs KARAC_MIR_HEADER_REGS=0 on one binary: 389 differ, geomean 0.9795 over them, 44 better than 0.95, no output differs, but 5 worse than 1.05: 330 1.180, 581 1.145, 236 1.131, 871 1.107, 592 1.057, against the bar (none worse than about 1.05). 330's cause, read from opt -O2 -print-after-all on kara.min_patches: with the length a load carrying !range, JumpThreading (through LVI) drops the index's `i >= 0` check and the loop test and bounds check fuse into one `samesign ult`; with the length an argument carrying the same range attribute, an assume, or both, LVI does not use it, and the separate sign check stays (`cmp; jg; test; js` per element). Patch and sweep in the shared folder, drop-schedule/header-abi-B-2026-11-07-33.patch and header-abi-sweep-2026-11-08.txt. Next for this row: give LVI the length's range at the callee another way, or pass header words only where the callee never indexes. APPENDED 2026-11-08 (Mac bench thread's 498 profile, routed by the review thread): kata 498 (diagonal-traverse) reloads the outer `mat` header (len and data pointer) on every element of its zigzag loop because the `out.push` store may alias `mat`, which arrives by pointer: the same shape. Its larger arm64 cost, if-converted selects, is B-2026-11-08-73.

title: A `collect` into a written collection whose items hold a call's unsolved parameter (`let mut cells: Vec[Vec[String]] = tops.iter().map(|_| Vec.new()).collect();`) is refused with "cannot infer type parameter 'T' of `Vec[T]`": the end-of-check unsolved-variable report runs before the deferred `FromIterator` bound that would solve it
detail: Found re-checking kara-katas apps after 0.8.x: apps/.../mini_pandas_display.kara:1791-1792 (`let mut cells: Vec[Vec[Val]] = tops.iter().map(|_| Vec.new()).collect();`) no longer checks. Repro: `fn main() { let tops: Vec[i64] = [1, 2, 3]; let mut cells: Vec[Vec[String]] = tops.iter().map(|_| Vec.new()).collect(); cells[0].push("x".to_string()); println(cells.len()); }`. `karac check` on main at 9b29e7486e: error[typecheck] 3:59 "cannot infer type parameter 'T' of `Vec[T]`: nothing in the body fixes it". The Nov 4 release build (karac 0.8.0-dev.14446) accepts it. In `check` (src/typechecker.rs), `report_unsolved_call_vars()` (added by 2783b8c546, B-2026-11-06-7) ran before `discharge_deferred_call_bounds()`, whose `solve_collected_item_vars` unifies the items `Vec[?T]` with the written element `Vec[String]` (instrumented: concrete `Vec[Vec[Str]]`, want `[Vec[?T]]`, one offer `[Vec[Str]]`). So the variable is solved, just after it has been reported. design.md § Type inference reports a variable only if no later use solves it, and the written collect is such a use.
fix: bf2c7db3d5: `check` now settles the deferred receiver bounds and aliased variables, discharges the deferred call bounds (whose written-collect pass solves the items' variables), and only then reports a variable still unsolved (src/typechecker.rs; `settle_deferred_call_vars` split out of `report_unsolved_call_vars` in src/typechecker/exprs.rs). tests/collect_solves_item_call_vars.rs: the repro checks clean and prints [[x], [], [y, z]] under __mir-run, and an unwritten collect of the same items is still refused at the inner `Vec.new()`; the control on origin/main 9b29e7486e fails the two positive tests and passes the negative. Full gate green on the tree before its final rebase (test --all 10577 passed, --features llvm 10750 passed); after the rebase, lib, typechecker, core_strict_check, example_corpus and the unsolved-variable suites re-ran green.

title: A generic function's `Atomic.new(x)` over `x: own T` is not judged at the instance: `wrap(1i8)` with `fn wrap[T](x: own T) -> Atomic[T]` passes check and runs, though Atomic[i8] is outside concurrency.md's five
detail: Release karac at 407b63262b (after B-2026-11-07-21 restricted Atomic[T] to bool, i32, i64, u32, u64). `fn wrap[T](x: own T) -> Atomic[T] { Atomic.new(x) }  fn main() { let a = wrap(1i8); println(a.load()); }` passes `karac check` and prints 1 on __mir-run. The eligibility check (src/typechecker/expr_call.rs atomic_ineligible_inner_kind) defers a TypeParam inner so a generic body is not refused, and nothing judges the instance: the call site's type arguments are never checked against the five. Either a `where`-style implicit requirement on T judged at each instantiation (like the deferred call bounds), or a check at monomorphization in MIR. A concrete annotation, a concrete argument and a literal fixed later are all refused since 3f39b2aafd.
fix: efeab13898: an `Atomic.new(x)` whose element is a bare type parameter (at the call, or once the body settles a variable to one) is recorded under its body's callee key (`f` or `Type.method`), and each strict-mode call that instantiates the body is judged against library/concurrency.md's five with E0272 at the call, naming the parameter, the type argument and the line where the body puts it in an Atomic (src/typechecker/items.rs emit_atomic_instance_errors). A generic caller that passes its own parameter on (`twice[U]` calling `wrap(x)`) carries the requirement up, to a fixed point, so the call that names a type is refused; a generic impl's method is covered through node_method_callees. Instances at i32/i64/u32/u64/bool stay accepted. Pin: corpus/design/err_atomic_generic_instance.

title: Number parsing in two `par` branches or a `par for` is refused as a conflict: `par { i64.parse(a), i64.parse(b) }` reports `unknown (native str.char_at_byte)` vs `unknown (native str.char_at_byte)`; `f64.parse` adds `unknown (native str.is_empty)`
detail: Release karac at 20203bbb6 (second core-semantics pass, launch-audience shapes; gen_c2.py in the shared folder probe-core/). core-semantics §11.2: branches conflict only when one writes, moves, mutably borrows or drops what another uses, or writes a resource another uses; parsing a borrowed string does neither. Repros, each refused by `karac check` (so on every lane): (1) `fn main() { let a = "1"; let b = "2"; let (x, y) = par { i64.parse(a), i64.parse(b) }; println(x.unwrap() + y.unwrap()); }` -> `branches 1 and 2 of the par conflict: unknown (native str.char_at_byte) and unknown (native str.char_at_byte)`; the same with String locals. (2) `par for s in v.iter() { i64.parse(s).unwrap_or(0) }` -> `two iterations of the par for conflict` with the same pair. (3) `par { f64.parse("1.5"), "a,b".split(",").count() }` -> `unknown (native str.is_empty)` vs `unknown (native str.char_at_byte)`. (4) The launch shape `fn both(a: Str, b: Str) -> Result[i64, ParseError] { let (x, y) = par { p(a)?, p(b)? }; Ok(x + y) }` with `fn p(s: Str) -> Result[i64, ParseError] { i64.parse(s) }` is refused the same way. `par { a.to_uppercase(), b.trim().len() }` checks clean, so the gap is the natives the Kara-source `parse` reaches. B-2026-11-07-27 (fixed 39dbc078da) added the socket natives to `native_effects` (src/mir/effects.rs) one by one; this is the same family for str natives. A sweep of every native the stdlib's Kara sources call, giving each its known effect, would close the family rather than this pair.
fix: 670fbcb5ec: `native_effects` (src/mir/effects.rs) had no entry for base `str`, the borrowed-string natives (`str.char_at_byte`, `str.char_before_byte`, `str.find_at_byte`, `str.len`, `str.is_empty`, `str.contains`, `str.replace`, ...) that the library's Kāra `parse`, `split`, `lines`, `split_whitespace`, `chars` and `trim_*` call. Each was `unknown`, so two branches conflicted. `str` now sits with `String` and the other natively implemented collections: allocates, may panic. A sweep over a program using every integer and float `parse` and the split, trim, search and replace methods found no other unknown native. The unit test `effects_every_str_native_the_text_library_reaches_is_known` walks every `str` native such a program reaches; it fails without the fix (`str.len in StrLines.next`). The row's four repros check clean and run on __mir-run, __mir-llvm-run and __mir-llvm-asan. Pin: corpus/core/ok_par_parse_branches.

title: `karac check` accepts calling an `OnceFn` struct field twice (`(job.run)(); (job.run)();`); every run lane then stops with the internal `move check main: bb10[term]: use of _2.0, which may have been moved or never initialized` instead of E0500 at the second call
detail: Release karac at 20203bbb6 (second core-semantics pass; gen_c2.py cell f16). core-semantics §9.6: an `OnceFn` may be called once; the call moves the value (§3), so a second call is E0500. Program: `struct T { n: i64 }` with a printing Drop, `fn consume(t: own T) { }`, `struct Job { run: OnceFn() }`, `fn main() { let t = T { n: 9 }; let job = Job { run: || consume(t) }; (job.run)(); (job.run)(); }`. `karac check`: All checks passed. `__mir-run`, `__mir-llvm-run` and `__mir-llvm-asan`: `error[mir]: move check main: bb10[term]: use of _2.0, which may have been moved or never initialized`, with no source span and MIR names, so nothing runs (not unsound), but check is wrong and the diagnostic does not say what to change. The same through a parameter (`fn call_twice(f: own OnceFn()) { f(); f(); }`, corpus/core/err_once_called_twice) is refused by check correctly, and a single `(job.run)()` runs and drops as specified (cell f15), so the gap is the move of a field-place callee in the check-side move analysis. Expected: E0500 at the second `(job.run)()`, naming the first call as the move, as the parameter form reports.
fix: 3dacb8cfc5 (check: an OnceFn field call moves the field). The use classifier walks a field or tuple-index callee whose type is OnceFn as a consuming use (src/use_classifier.rs, Call arm), and check_fn_kinds records the once-call for any callee whose node type is OnceFunction, not only an identifier (src/typechecker/core_ref_write.rs). The ownership pass's projection rewrite then names the rule: `(job.run)(); (job.run)();` is refused at check time with E0500 "job.run moved by the first call at line L:C (an OnceFn is called once, §9.6)" and a fix-it to call it once or make it an Fn, so no run lane reaches the MIR move check. Through a shared ref, the field call is "cannot move `job.run`: it is reached through a shared `ref`". Fn field calls stay accepted. Pinned by tests/core_strict_check.rs once_fn_field_called_twice_is_refused and corpus/core/err_once_field_called_twice.

title: An early exit in a `par {}` branch does not cancel the branches after it: with `par { quick()?, slow()? }` where `slow` sleeps 2 s, the function returns its Err only after `slow` wakes and runs to its end (prints, 2000 ms), though §11.7 cancels later branches at their next suspension point; `par for` cancels correctly
detail: Release karac at 20203bbb6 with archives rebuilt there (second core-semantics pass, cancellation batch; gen_c3.py cell x10 in the shared folder probe-core/). core-semantics §11.7 (from M4 item 5, landed 10-25 for TaskGroup.cancel / with_deadline / timeout): when a branch exits early, every branch after it in source order is cancelled; it stops at its next suspension point; §11.9: a task suspended at a wait is torn down there. Program: `fn quick() -> Result[i64, String] { Err("x".to_string()) }`, `fn slow() -> Result[i64, String] { defer { println("slow defer"); } sleep(Duration.ms(2000)); println("slow woke"); Ok(1) }`, `fn f() -> Result[i64, String] { let (a, b) = par { quick()?, slow()? }; Ok(a + b) }`, main prints `f().is_err()` and the elapsed ms. __mir-run, __mir-llvm-run and __mir-llvm-asan, with KARAC_THREADS=1 and the default pool: `slow woke`, `slow defer`, `true`, `2000` (2006 on llvm). Expected: `slow defer`, `true`, and well under 2000 ms, with no `slow woke`. The same with block branches and `return`: `par { { return Err(..); 0 }, { sleep(1500 ms); println("b woke"); 1 }, { sleep(1500 ms); 2 } }` prints `b woke` and takes 1500 ms. The result is right (the earliest Err), so the gap is the cancellation: the later branches' effects after their wait still happen, and a request handler that fans out with `par` waits for its slowest call after one has already failed. `par for i in 0..3 { h(i)? }` where iteration 0 errs and the others sleep 1500 ms returns in under 1000 ms on all three lanes, so the `par for` lowering cancels and `par {}` does not. ASan clean.
fix: e0b7c1b723: `par_tasks` (src/mir/lower.rs) joined every branch before reading any result, so a later branch ran to its end. The joins now check each result as it arrives, in source order. The first early exit joined (`?` or `return`) is therefore the source-earliest one. It calls `TaskGroup.cancel` on the block's group, so the later tasks are torn down at their next wait and run their defers (§11.7, §11.9). It returns once the group is done. The branches before it have already finished; a later branch with no wait left completes, so `par_error_runs_siblings` is unchanged. The probe's program now prints `slow defer` and `true` and takes 108-456 ms on __mir-run, __mir-llvm-run and __mir-llvm-asan, with KARAC_THREADS=1 and 4, and prints no `slow woke`. The `return` block form prints `b torn down`. In `par { first()?, bad()?, late()? }` (first sleeps 300 ms), `late` is torn down after `first` finishes. Pin: corpus/core/par_early_exit_cancels_later, passing on all three lanes and failing on the build before. Deliberate limit, within §11.9's timing freedom: a later branch is cancelled once the branches before the failing one have finished, not the moment it fails.

title: The item of a bare `for x in xs` over a borrowed parameter cannot be returned: `fn last(xs: Slice[String]) -> ref String { let mut best = ref xs[0]; for x in xs { best = x; } best }` is `returned borrow does not originate from a ref parameter` and `for x in xs { if .. { return Some(x); } }` into `Option[ref String]` is `cannot move 'x'`; the same bodies over `xs.iter()` check clean
detail: Release karac at 20203bbb6 (second core-semantics pass, views batch; gen_c5.py cell v09 in the shared folder probe-core/). core-semantics §4.6: `for x in e` on a non-Iterator borrows `e` through Iterable and `x` is the iterator's item, `ref T` for the standard collections; §5.4: a function's result borrows its borrowed non-Copy and view parameters, and items borrow what the receiver borrows, so an item of a borrowed parameter may be returned. Refused by `karac check`: (1) `fn pick(xs: Slice[String]) -> ref String { let mut best = ref xs[0]; for x in xs { if x.len() > best.len() { best = x; } } best }` -> `error[ownership]: returned borrow does not originate from a ref parameter; its source is dropped when the function returns, leaving a dangling reference` at `best`; (2) the same with `xs: Vec[String]`; (3) `for x in xs { best = x; } best`; (4) `fn find(xs: Slice[String]) -> ref String { for x in xs { return x; } ref xs[0] }`; (5) `fn find(xs: Slice[String], n: i64) -> Option[ref String] { for x in xs { if x.len() as i64 == n { return Some(x); } } None }` -> `error[borrow_projection_copy]: cannot move 'x': it borrows its value (a bare for element ...)`, though `Some(x)` here builds an `Option[ref String]` and moves no String. Accepted: the same bodies with `for x in xs.iter()` (Slice or Vec parameter), `ref xs[0]` returned directly, and `let best = ref xs[0]; best`. The corpus backends, which skip the check refusal, run (1) and print `ccc` on __mir-run, __mir-llvm-run and __mir-llvm-asan, ASan clean, so the analysis, not the lowering, is what is wrong. This is the find/longest/first-match shape a service writes over a request's headers or a config list.
fix: 3dacb8cfc5 (check: ... a bare for item of a borrowed param may be returned). ref_return.rs core_defs_in_expr's For arm now treats the iterable itself as the borrowed place when it is a plain path (identifier, self, field, tuple index) and no borrowed_walk_place applies, so a bare `for x in xs` item over a borrowed parameter derives from that parameter (§4.6 bare for borrows; §5.4 result borrows) and may be returned, stored in a `ref` local that is returned, or wrapped as `Some(x)` into `Option[ref T]`. The `Some(x)` case also needed the element-drop lint deferred in the infer pass (no expected type yet) and judged at the expected `Option`/`Result` slot (src/typechecker/exprs.rs, items.rs). Pinned by tests/core_strict_check.rs for_item_of_borrowed_param_may_be_returned and corpus/core/ok_for_item_of_borrowed_param_returned (ccc / bb / none / a / 3).

title: `karac fix` applies did-you-mean edits to foreign keywords and builtins that produce nonsense: `null` -> `Mul`, `nil` -> `n` (or `Div`), `range(3)` -> `Range(3)`, `fmt` -> `Not`, `func` -> `fence`; `func main() {` and `def main():` get `expected ;` with a fix inserting `;` (`func; main(); {`)
detail: Release karac at 20203bbb6 (first-hour newcomer pass, review thread 11-07 19:39Z; programs in the shared folder probe-core/nb/). design.md §17: `karac fix` applies the machine-applicable fixes, the primary fix path for an AI author, so a fix that rewrites a program into a different wrong program is worse than none. Each line is the program, the message as printed, and the message expected.
