(1) `fn find(v: Vec[i64]) -> Option[i64] { if v.len() > 0 { Some(v[0]) } else { null } }` -> `undefined name 'null', did you mean 'Mul'?` with a machine fix; after `karac fix` the program reads `else { Mul }` and fails with `a type that failed to check is not lowered yet`. Expected: `Kāra has no null: an absent value is None (Option[T])`, fix `null` -> `None`. (2) `let (n, err) = i64.parse("12"); if err != nil { return; }` -> `undefined name 'nil', did you mean 'n'?`; the fix makes `err != n`. In `fn main() { let x = None; if x == nil {..} }` the suggestion is `Div`. Expected: `Kāra has no nil: compare with None, or match on Ok/Err`; Go's `(v, err)` tuple from a Result deserves `i64.parse returns a Result: use match, ? or let ... else`. (3) `for i in range(3)` -> `undefined name 'range', did you mean 'Range'?`; the fix gives `Range(3)`, then `'Range' is a type, not a function`. Expected: `range(n) is Python: write 0..n`, fix to `0..3`. (4) `func main() { fmt.Println("hi") }` -> `expected ; after this expression statement` at `func` and at `main`, fixes inserting `;`, giving `func; main(); { .. }` then `undefined name 'func', did you mean 'fence'?` and `'fmt', did you mean 'Not'?`. Expected: `func is Go: Kāra declares a function with fn`, fix `func` -> `fn`; `fmt.Println(x)` -> `println(x)`. (5) `def main():` gives the same `;` insertions. Expected: `def is Python: Kāra declares a function with fn name() { .. }`. The edit-distance suggester runs over type and variant names (`Mul`, `Div`, `Not`) for a lowercase value name and marks the suggestion machine-applicable; a suggestion with a different name class, or of distance at most 2 against a 3-4 letter word, is a guess, not a fix. Mend-style rustism tables already cover Rust (`::`, `&`, `impl Fn`, `vec!`, `println!`, `HashMap`, all well handled in this pass); Go and Python day-one words have no entries.
fix: c15666711c. The resolver names a newcomer's foreign words instead of an edit-distance guess: null/NULL/nullptr/undefined (fix: None), nil (message only: Kāra has no nil, use Option), True/False (fix: true/false), Python's range(n)/range(a, b) (fix: 0..n / a..b) and Go's fmt.Println(x)/fmt.Print(x) (fix: println(x)/print(x)); the parser records the call rewrites in Program::foreign_calls, as it does for Rust's Box.new. At an item head, Go's func and JavaScript's function/fun are one diagnostic fixed to fn and parsed as a function; Python's def is one diagnostic naming fn and braces, and its indented body is skipped. A two-element tuple pattern over a Result names Go's (v, err) and the match / ? / let-else remedies and is not also called refutable. suggest_similar offers a name of five letters or fewer only a one-edit neighbour (an adjacent swap counts as one), and an undefined value name is offered only names of its own case class, so null -> Mul, nil -> n, fmt -> Not and range -> Range are gone. Pinned by tests/newcomer_foreign_words.rs (4 tests, each fixed program checks); tests/cli.rs test_json_suggestion_in_hints now uses a real one-edit typo. Gate195 on the rebase: leg1 10616/0, LLVM leg 10789/0.

title: `std::thread::spawn(|| ..)` is told `Kāra's spawn needs no module path: write spawn`, and that fix is then refused as `free spawn is removed (§11.1)`; the first message should point at `TaskGroup.spawn` / `par`
detail: Release karac at 20203bbb6 (first-hour newcomer pass, review thread 11-07 19:39Z; programs in the shared folder probe-core/nb/). design.md §17: `karac fix` applies the machine-applicable fixes, the primary fix path for an AI author, so a fix that rewrites a program into a different wrong program is worse than none. Program: `fn main() { let h = std::thread::spawn(|| 1); println(h.join().unwrap()); }`. Printed: `error[parse]: 1:21: std::thread::spawn is a Rust path -- Kāra's spawn needs no module path, and a path is written with .: write spawn`, machine-applicable. After `karac fix`: `let h = spawn(|| 1);` and check reports `free spawn is removed (§11.1); a task starts only in par { … }, par for or TaskGroup.spawn, so it cannot outlive its scope` (plus `no method unwrap on i64`). core-semantics §9.3 and §11.1: there is no free spawn. So the parse-stage message asserts something the spec denies and its fix leads straight into the second error. Expected at the first diagnostic: `std::thread::spawn is Rust: Kāra has no free spawn; start tasks with let g = TaskGroup.new(); g.spawn(|| ..) (joined when g drops) or par { .. }`, with no machine fix (the rewrite needs a group), or a fix to the TaskGroup form.
fix: 71eb8d8b97. rewrite_rust_path (src/parser.rs) recognizes a path ending in thread/task/tokio then spawn (std::thread::spawn, thread::spawn, tokio::spawn) and reports "`std::thread::spawn` is Rust: Kāra has no free `spawn` (core-semantics §11.1); start a task in a group, `let g = TaskGroup.new(); let h = g.spawn(|| ..);` (joined when `g` drops, its value read with `h.join()`), or run branches with `par { .. }`", with NO machine fix, as the row allows (the rewrite needs a group the program does not have). Other std:: paths keep their fix (std::cmp::max -> max, pinned). Pinned by tests/newcomer_rust_shapes.rs rust_thread_spawn_names_task_group_and_par_without_a_fix (karac fix leaves the file unchanged). Gate195 green.

title: A `Self { x: x }` struct literal in a method body is `expected ; after this expression statement` at `Self`, and `karac fix` inserts the `;` (`Self; { x }`), which then fails as `expected P, found i64`; it should say to write the type's name (`P { x }`)
detail: Release karac at 20203bbb6 (first-hour newcomer pass, review thread 11-07 19:39Z; programs in the shared folder probe-core/nb/). design.md §17: `karac fix` applies the machine-applicable fixes, the primary fix path for an AI author, so a fix that rewrites a program into a different wrong program is worse than none. Program: `struct P { x: i64 }\nimpl P { fn new(x: i64) -> Self { Self { x } } }\nfn main() { let p = P.new(1); println(p.x); }`, the constructor every Rust user writes. Printed: `error[parse]: 2:35: expected ; after this expression statement` with the caret on `Self`, and a machine fix inserting `;`; after `karac fix` the body is `Self; { x }`, refused as `expected 'P', found 'i64'`. design.md uses `Self` as a type (`-> Self`, `own Self`) and never as a struct-literal head; no corpus or stdlib program writes `Self { .. }`. Expected: either accept `Self { .. }` as the impl's type (a design call), or `Self { .. } is Rust's struct literal: write the type's name, P { x }`, with that machine fix. The same program with `-> P { Self { x: x } }` gives the same message.
fix: 71eb8d8b97. Took the message-plus-fix branch, not acceptance. The parser tracks the impl block's target type name (Parser::impl_self_name, set in parse_impl_block_scoped from the target path's last segment, saved and restored around each impl), and at `Self` followed by a struct-literal body reports "`Self { .. }` is Rust's struct literal: Kāra writes the type's name, `P { .. }`" with a machine fix replacing `Self` by the name, then parses the literal as the fixed text would, so there is no `;` cascade. Generic impls take the bare name (`impl[T] Pair[T]` -> `Pair { a: a, b }`, inferred); trait impls work (`impl Mk for P`). `Self` elsewhere (-> Self, Self.new()) is unchanged. Pinned by tests/newcomer_rust_shapes.rs self_struct_literal_is_written_with_the_impl_type_name (fixed programs check and run). Gate195 green.

title: Two obvious repairs have no machine fix: a function whose last statement is `a + b;` under `-> i64` (fix: drop the `;`), and `?` in a `fn main()` returning `()` (fix: `fn main() -> Result[(), AnyError]` with `Ok(())`); the second's message also names no remedy
detail: Release karac at 20203bbb6 (first-hour newcomer pass, review thread 11-07 19:39Z; programs in the shared folder probe-core/nb/). design.md §17: `karac fix` applies the machine-applicable fixes, the primary fix path for an AI author, so a fix that rewrites a program into a different wrong program is worse than none. (1) `fn add(a: i64, b: i64) -> i64 { a + b; }`: printed `function 'add' declares return type 'i64' but its body can complete without producing a value — end it with a tail expression, return on every path, or declare no return type`, caret on the return type, no fix. The last statement is an expression statement of exactly the return type, so the repair is unambiguous: remove its `;` (the caret should be on that `;`). Expected: the same text plus `the last statement a + b; has type i64: remove the ; to return it`, machine-applicable. (2) `fn main() { let n = i64.parse("12")?; println(n); }`: printed `'?' requires the enclosing function to return Result or Option, found '()'`, no fix and no remedy. design.md §10 allows `fn main() -> Result[(), E]` with `E: Display` (exit 1 with `Error: e`), and script mode's implicit main is `Result[(), AnyError]`. Expected: `main returns (): to use ? here, declare fn main() -> Result[(), AnyError] and end it with Ok(())`, machine-applicable for `main` (one signature edit and one tail insertion); for another function, the same advice without the fix. Both are day-one shapes for a Rust or Go developer.
fix: 71eb8d8b97. (1) The parser records each expression statement's `;` (Program::expr_stmt_semis, keyed by the expression's span). A tail-less body under a non-unit return whose last statement is an expression of exactly the return type keeps the old text and adds "Here the last statement `a + b;` has type 'i64': remove the `;` to return it", caret on the `;`, with a machine fix deleting it (works for String and a generic T too). A last statement of another type keeps the old message, no fix. (2) `?` in a function returning `()` now names a remedy. In a top-level `fn main()`: "`main` returns `()`; to use `?` here, declare `fn main() -> Result[(), AnyError]` and end it with `Ok(())`", with a two-edit fix (signature before the body's `{`; `Ok(())` before the closing `}` for a one-line body, on its own line otherwise, or `; Ok(())` after a unit tail expression), attached to the first `?`. Any other function gets the advice without a fix. Pinned by tests/newcomer_rust_shapes.rs (a_trailing_semicolon_on_the_return_value_is_removed, question_mark_in_unit_main_declares_a_result_main: one-line, multi-line and tail-expression mains; each fixed program checks, and `i64.parse("x")?` exits 1 with `Error:`). Gate195 green.

title: `karac fmt` moves comments off the item they annotate: a `// first` after a parameter lands after the fn's `{` (where it reads as a comment on the body), a `/* second */` after a parameter moves into the body, and a `// one` after a call argument goes to the end of the statement; design.md § Canonical formatting says comments travel with their item
fix: 8b1e2b6970. A parameter list or call argument list (function call and method call; trait method signatures keep one line) with a comment between two elements, or after the last one before the `)`, is laid out one element per line with a trailing comma, and each comment is flushed right after the element it follows, so `// first` stays after `a: i64,`, `/* second */` after `b: i64,` and `// one` after `1,`. Lists without such a comment are unchanged, and a comment inside an element does not trigger the layout (only the gaps between elements are read, Formatter::comment_between). Output is idempotent. The struct-literal layout note in the row is not a bug and is unchanged. Pinned by tests/fmt_comment_lists.rs (3 tests: free fn and call, method with receiver and method-call args, a flat list stays flat); fmt_round_trip over the corpus green. Gate195 green.

title: kara-lsp go-to-definition returns null on a method call (`u.greet()`), a field access (`u.age`, `self.name`) and a library call (`xs.iter()`), and hover returns null on a `let` binding's own name; definition works only for names the resolver binds (locals, params, free functions, types)
detail: Program: struct User { name: String, age: i64 } with impl User { fn greet(self) -> String }, and main doing `let u = User {..}; let t = total(v); println(u.greet()); println(u.age + t);`. textDocument/definition at `greet` in `u.greet()`, at `age` in `u.age`, at `name` in `self.name`: all result null. Definition at `total`, `u`, `t`, `xs`, `User`: correct. Hover at `t` in `let t = total(v);`: null; at a later use of `t`: `i64`. Hover at `greet` shows `String` (the call's type) where hover at `total` shows `Fn(ref Vec[i64]) -> i64` with effects. Cause: karac::goto_definition (src/lib.rs) searches only resolved.resolutions, and a method or field is resolved by the typechecker. deferred.md's LSP floor lists go-to-definition and hover (type + effect signature); a newcomer's first click is on a method. kara-lsp rebuilt at 7708b0aae.
fix: 981a577ebb (lsp: go-to-definition on methods, fields and library calls; hover on a binding's name). New `src/cli/editor_nav.rs` reads the tables `karac check` builds for the buffer: a method call's name resolves through `node_method_callees` (and `node_method_impls` between two impls) to the impl method's name; a field's through the receiver's recorded type to the struct field's `name_span`; a binding pattern's hover through `node_types`. A method in the Kāra library is located in its `LIBRARY_SOURCES` file; `karac::goto_definition_site` returns `DefSite::Library`, and kara-lsp answers with a read-only copy of that file under the temp directory (`kara-library-<version>/source/...`). `karac::goto_definition` keeps its buffer-only contract. Hover on a method's name now shows its declaration header and effects (`fn greet(self) -> String`) instead of the call's result type. Measured with the probe's d5.py driver against the rebuilt kara-lsp on probe-core/tool/prog.kara: definition at `greet` -> L3:8, at `u.age` -> the field on L1, at `self.name` -> the field on L1, at `xs.iter` -> collections.kara L245; hover at `let t` -> i64, at `let u` -> User. Pinned by lsp analysis test `definition_and_hover_reach_members_and_bindings`.

title: kara-lsp diagnostics carry the phase (`ownership`, `typecheck`) as the LSP `code` instead of the diagnostic code (`E0500`), and drop the help line, so an editor user sees `value 'u' moved here, used again here` with no remedy and no code to `karac explain`
detail: `let w = u; println(u.name);` in main: publishDiagnostics gives {severity 1, code "ownership", source "kara", message "value 'u' moved here, used again here (moved at line 16:13)"}. `karac check` prints the same message plus `help: add #[derive(Clone)] to 'User' and clone 'u' at the move site ...`, and --output=json has code E0500 with that hint. The LSP's code action does offer the derive edit, but the diagnostic itself has no code and no hint text. lsp/src/analysis.rs:361 sets `code: d.phase`. Expected: code = the JSON `code` (E0500), the help text in the message or relatedInformation, and ideally codeDescription pointing at the explain entry. deferred.md's floor says diagnostics stream over the structured JSON.
fix: a9fd3117a5 (lsp: diagnostics carry the catalogue code and the help lines). `PlaygroundDiagnostic` gains `code` and `help`, read from `karac check --output=json`'s `code` and `hints[].description` (src/cli/editor.rs); the package path codes type errors through `type_error_code`. kara-lsp uses the code (the phase only where a path has none) and appends each hint as a `help:` line under the message. Probe driver: the ownership diagnostic now arrives with code E0500 and its `help: add #[derive(Clone)] ...` line, the type error with E0200. The pins that held phase names (`resolve`, `parse`, `typecheck`) are flipped to E0100, E0002, E0200; new test `diagnostics_carry_the_catalogue_code_and_help_line`. The wasm playground path still carries no code (it never builds the JSON); `check_source_matches_run_playground_static_prefix` compares the rest.

title: `karac explain E0517` prints the TYPE_MISMATCH class text ("Operand, argument, or return-value type doesn't match ...") for the write-through-a-borrowed-parameter error, because E0517 is classed TYPE_MISMATCH in JSON too; and 8 codes a newcomer hits print no explanation at all (E0001, E0002, E0205, E0254, E0506, E0509, E0510, E_NOT_CROSS_TASK)
detail: E0517 is `u` is a bare parameter, which borrows ... so an assignment through `u` cannot modify it` (fn bump(u: U) { u.age += 1; }). --output=json gives class TYPE_MISMATCH, concept ownership/borrowing; `karac explain E0517` then explains a type mismatch. Expected: an ownership/borrow class and prose about parameter modes. The 8 stub codes print phase, kind, concept and `class: OTHER — this diagnostic has no class page yet ... the message text is the authoritative description`, so `karac explain E0506` (let without mut, reassigned) says nothing a newcomer can use; `karac explain <concept>` does list the spec sections. design.md §17: karac explain explains a diagnostic code from the code catalogue. Codes taken from the newcomer pass (B-2026-11-07-40..43). Also: `karac explain e0500` (lowercase) answers `unknown concept`.
fix: e2e61a6643 (explain: E0516/E0517 are borrow conflicts; prose for the codes a newcomer meets). `class_for_type_error_kind` classes BorrowConflict and WriteThroughSharedRef as OWNERSHIP_BORROW_CONFLICT (JSON and `karac explain` alike), and that class's page names the write-through-`ref` case. A per-code prose table in src/cli/explain.rs explains E0001, E0002, E0205, E0254 and E_NOT_CROSS_TASK (one rule, two names), E0506, E0509, E0510, E0516 and E0517, each restating its rule from design.md / core-semantics and naming the section (§5.4, §5.6, §5.7, §5.9, §6.3, § Pattern exhaustiveness, § Variable binding rules, § CrossTask); none prints the "no class page yet" stub in text or JSON. `karac explain e0500` reads a catalogued code in lower case as the code. Tests `newcomer_codes_have_prose`, `lowercase_explain_code_is_the_code`; the pin `near_code_shapes_do_not_masquerade_as_codes` that held `e0200` as a concept is flipped.

title: The v0.8.0 Linux release binaries need glibc 2.39 (karac, karac_jit_runner and kara-lsp import pidfd_spawnp/pidfd_getpid@GLIBC_2.39 and __isoc23_strtol@GLIBC_2.38), so they cannot start on Ubuntu 22.04, Debian 12, RHEL 9 or Amazon Linux 2023; the release is built on ubuntu-24.04 and neither the README nor the tarball's README states the floor
detail: Downloaded karac-0.8.0-x86_64-linux.tar.gz from the v0.8.0 release, sha256 OK. `objdump -T bin/karac | grep -o 'GLIBC_[0-9.]*' | sort -V | tail -1` = GLIBC_2.39 (also GLIBCXX_3.4.30 in karac_jit_runner). The symbols: pidfd_getpid, pidfd_spawnp (2.39, from Rust std's process spawn on a new glibc), __isoc23_strtol/strtoll/strtoul/strtoull (2.38, C23 headers in the LLVM build), arc4random (2.36), hypot (2.35). The release jobs in .github/workflows/release.yml run on ubuntu-24.04 / ubuntu-24.04-arm. Common servers and CI images (ubuntu-22.04 = glibc 2.35, Debian 12 = 2.36, RHEL 9 = 2.34, AL2023 = 2.34) fail with `version GLIBC_2.39 not found`. Binaries karac builds need only GLIBC_2.34. On this Ubuntu 24.04 container every step works: install, --version, run, build, new --cli/--backend/--lib, test. Remedy options: build the release in an older container (e.g. manylinux-style or ubuntu-20.04/22.04 image with LLVM 22 from source), or state the floor in both READMEs. aarch64 not measured (same runner family).
fix: 533b9ea5e9 + 5a09777302 + a18c57396a. .github/workflows/release.yml builds and smoke-tests the Linux bundles on ubuntu-22.04 / ubuntu-22.04-arm (was 24.04, glibc 2.39), keys the build cache by runner image (a 24.04 cache's llvm-sys build script could not start on 22.04), and a new "Check glibc floor" step fails the build when any bundled executable references a glibc symbol version above 2.35 (objdump -T). The first 22.04 dry run reported GLIBC_2.35 as the highest, so the floor is 2.35: Ubuntu 22.04 and Debian 12 run the tarballs; RHEL 9 and Amazon Linux 2023 (2.34) build from source, as README and CHANGELOG say. Verified by release dry run 42414585261 at a18c57396a: all three builds and all three clean-runner smokes green (hello via JIT, AOT, wasm, par), highest glibc symbol GLIBC_2.35 on x86_64 and aarch64. 0.8.0's own tarballs are unchanged; 0.8.1 is the first release with the floor.

255b769106: an inferred tuple's `self` element in a `ref self` (`mut ref self`) method takes a `ref` (`mut ref`) slot when its type is not `Copy`, as a `ref` pattern binding's does (`tuple_slot_holds_ref_pattern`, src/typechecker/items.rs), so MIR copies the reference instead of moving the value. tests/mrjob_check_gaps.rs: the repro over `ref self` and over `mut ref self` checks and prints true twice under __mir-run; mini_mrjob's `impl Ord for Value` matches on `(self, other)` and passes all four backends at KARAC_THREADS=1 and 4. Full gate green on the tree before its final rebase (test --all 10586 passed, --features llvm 10759 passed, both clippy legs, fmt); after the rebase lib, typechecker, core_strict_check, resolver and mrjob_check_gaps re-ran green, as did clippy --features llvm. Control on origin/main 6f95a14ab8: tests/mrjob_check_gaps.rs 0 passed, 4 failed.
title: `match (self, other)` in a `ref self` (or `mut ref self`) method is refused as "cannot move a non-`Copy` value out of a borrowed place", though the same match over two borrowed parameters (`fn f(a: ref V, b: ref V) { match (a, b) { .. } }`) is accepted
detail: Found writing mini_mrjob (kara-katas apps/cli/mini_mrjob, `impl Ord for Value`'s `cmp`). Repro: `enum V { I(i64), T(String) }` with `impl V { fn same(ref self, other: ref V) -> bool { match (self, other) { (V.I(_), V.I(_)) => true, (V.T(x), V.T(y)) => x.len() == y.len(), _ => false } } }`. `karac check` on main 6f95a14ab8 (before this fix): error 17:15 "cannot move a non-`Copy` value out of a borrowed place: take a copy with `.clone()`, use it in place, or take it with `mem.replace` / `mem.swap` / `Option.take()` (core semantics §3.7)", reported from MIR (`forbidden_moves`). `(other, self)`, `(self, self)` and `let p = (self, other)` fail alike, and so does a `mut ref self` method; the free function with `a: ref V, b: ref V` (and `a: mut ref V`) checks and prints true. Cause: the checker types the expression `self` as `current_self_type`, the value, while a `ref` parameter's name is typed `ref V`; an inferred tuple takes its elements' types, so the tuple was `(V, ref V)` and MIR lowered the `self` slot as a read of the value, a move out of the borrow.

fix: 255b769106: the refusal now says `partial_cmp` returns `Some(self.cmp(other))` and carries the `impl PartialOrd for T { fn partial_cmp(ref self, other: ref T) -> Option[Ordering] { Some(self.cmp(other)) } }` edit, inserted before the `impl Ord` at its indentation (`partial_ord_from_ord_fix`, src/typechecker/items.rs), for a non-generic type and an impl without attributes, where that text compiles as written. tests/mrjob_check_gaps.rs: `karac fix` writes it, the program then checks clean and sorts mixed values (1, 3, a, b). Full gate green on the tree before its final rebase (test --all 10586 passed, --features llvm 10759 passed, both clippy legs, fmt); after the rebase lib, typechecker, core_strict_check, resolver and mrjob_check_gaps re-ran green, as did clippy --features llvm. Control on origin/main 6f95a14ab8: tests/mrjob_check_gaps.rs 0 passed, 4 failed.
title: `impl Ord for T` with no `impl PartialOrd for T` is refused ("impl Ord for Value requires impl PartialOrd for Value") with no `karac fix` edit, though the missing impl is mechanical: `partial_cmp` returns `Some(self.cmp(other))`
detail: Found writing mini_mrjob (`impl Ord for Value` for its value order). The refusal is right (Ord's supertrait is PartialOrd, as in Rust), but the message names no repair and offers no edit, so the Mend loop stops on it; the author has to know Kāra's `partial_cmp` signature (`fn partial_cmp(ref self, other: ref Value) -> Option[Ordering]`). Rust's own documentation prescribes `Some(self.cmp(other))` for a type with a total order, which is exactly what an `impl Ord` declares. Emission: src/typechecker/items.rs, the supertrait check in the impl pass ("impl {} for {} requires impl {} for {}").

title: `Dict[String, i64]` / `Dict.new()` (Python's `typing.Dict`) is "undefined type 'Dict', did you mean 'Div'?"; `HashMap`, `BTreeMap` and `HashSet` already name their Kāra collections
detail: Found writing mini_mrjob from a Python mirror. `let mut b: Dict[String, i64] = Dict.new();` gives two errors, each suggesting `Div` (the operator trait) by edit distance, and `karac fix` would rename it to `Div`. B-2026-11-04-5 routed Rust's collection names through `renamed_stdlib_type` in src/resolver.rs (`HashMap` -> `Map`, `BTreeMap` -> `SortedMap`, `HashSet` -> `Set`), and `TreeMap`/`TreeSet` were there before; `Dict` was not, so the typo matcher picked `Div`.

fix: 670fbcb5ec, per design.md d9a74163ea: `infer_binary` (src/typechecker/expr_ops.rs) now checks a comparison operand against the other operand's type when the operand is a string literal, or a `Some` / `Ok` / `Err` / tuple built of string literals (`text_literal_takes`), and the other side has a `Str`, `ref Str` or `ref String` where the literal sits. So `first(v) == Some("")` with `Option[Str]`, `lines.last() == Some("")` over `Vec[Str]`, `w.last() == Some("x")` over `Vec[String]` and `r == Err("bad")` with `Result[Str, Str]` are accepted and run on every lane. A non-literal `Option[ref T] == Option[T]` stays refused. For a non-`Copy` `T` that no `Some(ref e)` view reaches, the error now carries the `.cloned()` edit, which `karac fix` applies. Before, it had none: the `a_non_copy_item_compare_with_a_temporary_*` fixture is flipped. Note: the ruling also names `.copied()`, but `Option` has no `.copied()` method; `.cloned()` is the edit. Pin: corpus/core/ok_compare_literal_in_some.
title: `opt == Some("")` with `opt: Option[Str]` is refused ("cannot compare 'Option[Str]' and 'Option[String]'") though `let a: Option[Str] = Some("")` is accepted; `lines.last() == Some("")` over a `Vec[Str]` (and `v.last() == Some("x")` over a `Vec[String]`) is refused with no hint, and the forms the i64 hint names do not compile for a literal
detail: Found writing mini_mrjob (`input`: drop the empty piece after a final newline). Repros on main 6f95a14ab8 (before this fix): (1) `fn first(v: ref Vec[String]) -> Option[Str] { v.first().map(|s| s.as_str()) }` then `if first(v) == Some("")`: "cannot compare 'Option[Str]' and 'Option[String]'", while `let a: Option[Str] = Some(""); if first(v) == a` checks: a string literal inside `Some` takes `Str` from an expected type but not from the other side of `==`, though design.md § `*` and `ref` in expressions says comparisons read both operands and `s == "("` with `s: Str` is accepted. (2) `let mut lines: Vec[Str] = text.split("\n").collect(); if lines.last() == Some("")`: "cannot compare 'Option[ref Str]' and 'Option[String]'" with no hint; `v.last() == Some("x")` over `Vec[String]` likewise. For `Option[ref i64]` vs `Some(2)` the message names `.cloned()` (B-2026-11-01-10) and `option_some_view_fix` offers `Some(ref e)` for a place (B-2026-11-04-61), but for a literal `Some(ref "")` is E_REF_OPERAND_UNSUPPORTED and `lines.last().cloned() == Some("")` is refused as (1). So none of the named repairs reaches a literal. Whether `Option[ref T] == Option[T]` should itself look through (as top-level comparisons do since 2026-11-05) is a spec question for the review thread; (1) is a plain false positive either way. mini_mrjob writes `lines.last().is_some_and(|l| l.is_empty())` meanwhile.

title: Katas 100 and 101 (recursive `shared` tree code) ran about 1.5x slower on the M5 at karac 97681763d than at 6697158fa while checked Rust held steady (100 98.0 -> 153.5 ms, 101 131.3 -> 205.3); the Mac bisect put it at bf1ae02cf1, where one of two field arguments to a reading call stopped being lent and paid a clone; kata 113's slowdown in the same window is a separate cause (B-2026-11-08-2)
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-07 on the M5 (M5 bench thread, filed at Gowtham's request before the bisect). Kata 100 same_tree, 101 symmetric_tree, 113 path_sum_ii benches against rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on: at karac 6697158fa (2026-11-01) 98.0 / 131.3 / 200.3 ms, at 97681763d (2026-11-07) 153.5 / 205.3 / 300.0 ms; Rust 88.9 -> 82.8, 117.6 -> 112.3, 232.2 -> 205.7 ms over the same two sessions, so the ratio moved 1.10x -> 1.85x (100), 1.12x -> 1.83x (101), 0.86x -> 1.46x (113). Next: kata 100's instruction count on x86 at both ends; if x86 shows the jump, bisect in the container, else the Mac bisects. 6dcdc1a604 (LLVM 22) is in the window.

The pass now repeats until nothing more is lent. x86 callgrind at 97681763d2: kata 100 3.118G -> 2.057G, 101 3.583G -> 2.297G, same output. Kata 113 was split out: the Mac bisect put it at d273d89f37, and it was the bench's push-loop copy against its Rust mirror's clone (B-2026-11-08-2, invalid). Not yet re-measured on the M5.

title: A method called straight on a constant whose value is a bare literal reads it at i64, not its declared type (corrected: not only wide ones; `CC.leading_zeros()` with `const CC: u8 = 200` gives 56): `BIG.to_string()` with `const BIG: i128 = 10**38` prints 687399551400673280, and `DEC_SIGN.to_string()` with `const DEC_SIGN: u64 = 0x8000000000000000` prints -9223372036854775808
detail: Found while testing B-2026-11-07-3, at 87e598fee9 and on the control karac built at 3cfa1f8a15 (pre-existing). `const AA: i128 = 100000000000000000000000000000000000000; const BB: u64 = 0x8000000000000000; fn main() { println(AA); println(BB); println(AA.to_string()); println(BB.to_string()); let y = AA; println(y.to_string()); println(f"{BB}"); println((BB + 0).to_string()) }` prints 1e38, 9223372036854775808, then 687399551400673280 and -9223372036854775808 for the two direct `.to_string()` calls, then the right values for `y.to_string()`, the f-string and `(BB + 0).to_string()`. Same under `karac run` and `karac build`. Any constant past i64 does it (`const CC: u64 = 9223372036854775808` gives -9223372036854775808, `const DD: i128 = 10**20` gives 7766279631452241920), so it is the receiver path of a method call on a constant whose literal is past i64: the receiver is typed or lowered as the literal's i64 rather than the constant's declared type. corpus/apps/cli/mini_bson declares `const BIG_INT: i128` of this size.
fix: a3a7d1eeb0. `literal_value_at_declared_type` (src/typechecker/items.rs), called from `check_const_decl` and the annotated arm of `check_module_binding_decl`, records a constant's bare literal value (an unsuffixed integer or float, or its negation) at the declared type in typed HIR, where it kept the literal's `i64` / `f64`. `CC.method()` parses as a path call and the MIR builder makes its receiver from the constant's value at that value's own type (`const_segments_place`), so `CC.leading_zeros()` on `const CC: u8 = 200` called `i64.leading_zeros` (56), and a `u64` / `i128` past `i64` printed negative or truncated through `to_string()`; `println(CC)` and `let v = CC` were already right because they retype the value at the use. Pinned by corpus/design/ok_a_constant_s_methods_read_it_at_its_declared_type (u8, i8, u64, i128, f32, f64, a tuple field), identical on mir-interp and mir-llvm; the row's own program prints 10**38 in full or 9223372036854775808 on each of its seven lines, on both.

title: A literal's type variable is not fixed by an assignment or a generic call (follow-up of B-2026-11-07-3; corrected: the `b += y` shape is a deliberate divergence, design.md §8 Literals at 8686d0ee18, an operator operand does not fix a literal): `let mut b = 0; b = y; b` with `y: i32` in a fn returning `i32`, and `let b = 0; max(b, y)`, are refused 'implicit coercion from i64 to i32 would narrow'
detail: design.md § Type inference: 'An integer or float literal starts as a type variable that later uses may fix', 'Literals default last'. B-2026-11-07-3's fix (87e598fee9) covers a let's value, an operator's operand, a Vec push and the rest its close lists; at 8cdef3b93a (release, interp check) these are still refused, each at the line that returns the binding: (1) `fn g(y: i32) -> i32 { let mut b = 0; b = y; b }`; (2) `fn plus(y: i32) -> i32 { let mut b = 0; b += y; b }`; (3) `fn h(y: i32) -> i32 { let mut b = 0; b = max(b, y); b }`; (4) `fn arg(y: i32) -> i32 { let b = 0; max(b, y) }`. `fn f() -> i32 { let mut b = 0; b }` is accepted, so the return fixes the variable when nothing else touched it; an assignment of an i32 (or `+=`) widens the i32 into the i64 the literal defaulted to instead of fixing it, and `max(b, y)` takes T = i64. Met by kata 1062's Rust template arm (`let mut best = 0; ... best = std::cmp::max(best, dp[i][j]); best` in a `-> i32`), which Rust infers as i32; the arm writes `let mut best: i32 = 0` until this lands (kara-katas leetcode/1001-1100/1062-longest-repeating-substring/lrs_solution.kara). No machine fix is offered.
fix: b85cf41506. An assignment's target binding is inferred open (`fix_literal_from_assigned`, src/typechecker/items.rs): a literal no use has fixed takes the assigned value's number type, read through a borrow, or settles to its default for anything else; `solve_open_slot_from` leaves such a slot open so the value's own literal (`b = 5`) is not settled first. A generic call's argument that is a binding, for a by-value `T` parameter, is inferred open in the pass that solves the call's variables (`check_call_args_with_substitution_full`, src/typechecker/exprs.rs), so `max(b, y)` fixes `b` to `y`'s type; a borrowed `T` is left alone (`take(mut x)` would otherwise bind the variable to the reference). A later literal that does not fit is refused there (`b = y_u8; b = 300`). Shapes (1), (3) and (4) of the row are accepted; (2) `b += y` stays refused by the review's ruling (design.md §8 Literals, 8686d0ee18: an operator operand does not fix a literal), and the refusal's missing annotation fix is B-2026-11-08-20. Pinned by corpus/design/ok_an_assignment_or_a_generic_call_fixes_a_literal (mir-interp and mir-llvm).

title: The overflow-safe midpoint `lo + (hi - lo) / 2` keeps its signed division: halving (B-2026-11-06-8) does not see `hi - lo` as non-negative under the loop's `lo < hi`, so kata 1064's binary search runs 1.6x rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-08 on x86 (4-core container, kara 3565136cc1, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build, 10 interleaved runs, medians): kara-katas leetcode/1001-1100/1064-fixed-point/bench/fixed.kara, 8 sorted arrays of 1000000 numbers each searched on 500000 suffixes, `while lo < hi { let mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2; if arr[mid] < mid { lo = mid + 1 } else { hi = mid } }`. As written 0.297 s; with `(lo + hi) / 2` 0.189 s; with `lo + ((hi - lo) >> 1)` 0.197 s; rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on (usize indices) 0.184 s; clang -O3 (int64_t) 0.217 s; building the arrays alone 0.044 s. So the search phase is about 0.253 s against 0.145 s, 1.7x, and all of it is the midpoint. The as-written binary's search loop (objdump, in karac.main after inlining) is `mov; sub; mov; shr $63; add; sar $1; add; jo; cmp; jae` before the load: the sign fixup sits on the critical path, the checked `lo + half` keeps its overflow branch, and the index check against the length stays, so the midpoint's range facts (B-2026-10-28-41) do not fold it. src/mir/halving.rs's fixpoint counts sums, products, quotients and remainders of non-negative values but not a difference, and `hi - lo` is non-negative only on the path the loop guard `lo < hi` dominates. `(lo + hi) / 2` is halved today, which is why the sum form matches Rust. `lo + (hi - lo) / 2` is the form written to avoid overflow and the one LeetCode's templates and most references use (kata 1064's ★ arm, bench and Rust-template arm all write it), so every such search pays this. A fix would treat `b - a` as non-negative in a block dominated by a branch on `a < b` (or `a <= b`) with neither written in between, which the midpoint recognizer's own `lo < hi` header already establishes.
fix: a8696f186e. midpoint.rs's guarded walk from a `lo < hi` switch already knew `hi - lo` as Diff. It now also records each `Div(Diff, 2)` it passes (guarded_diff_halvings). halving.rs rewrites those to `Shr 1` alongside its fixpoint's rewrites, since past the guard the dividend is at least 1. A difference outside a guard keeps its division (unit test a_difference_under_its_guard_halves_with_a_shift, with lo starting at 0 and at a parameter, plus a bare `lo + (hi - lo) / 2` control). Kata 1064's bench on x86, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, 5 runs: as written 166-185 ms, against 255-287 ms with KARAC_MIR_HALVING=0 (the pre-fix code) and 164-189 ms for a hand-written `>> 1`. Output is unchanged. Gate green: 10607 + 10782 passed, 0 failed.

title: Kata 113's bench copies each hit path with a Vec.new() + push loop where its Rust mirror calls path.clone(), so since d273d89f37 (first block of 4 elements, as Rust's Vec) each 5-element copy grows once and the bench reads 1.46x Rust on the M5; like-for-like, Kāra is faster than Rust in both shapes
detail: Split from B-2026-11-07-55 (whose 100/101 half was bf1ae02cf1). The M5 bisect (AUTO_PAR=0, best of 5) put kata 113 path_sum_ii's jump at d273d89f37 (B-2026-11-04-38: min_first_cap 8 -> 4 for elements of 2..=256 bytes, matching Rust's RawVec): 782-798M before, 1313M at it. x86 callgrind at 97681763d2 (rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on for Rust): Kāra bench as written (copy = Vec.new(); 5 x copy.push(path[i])) 3.622G; the same Kāra with out.push(path.clone()) 2.272G; Rust mirror as written (out.push(path.clone())) 2.469G; Rust with Kāra's push loop 4.699G. So the two benches differ in shape, not the compilers: the push loop now grows 4 -> 8 per copy (5.7M grows over 300000 reps, about 175 instructions each through malloc + memcpy + free), exactly as Rust's Vec does for the same loop, and Kāra stays ahead of Rust in each matched pair (0.77x push loop, 0.92x clone). Reverting d273d89f37 would bring back kata 3629's 89 MiB RSS (Rust 60).
fix: 29e0d50c90 (corpus: refresh ... kata 113's bench; kara-katas ece173b8f). Not a compiler regression: the bench's Kāra arm now copies with path.clone(), as its Rust, C and Go mirrors do, and is judged against the mirror. With matched shapes Kāra was already ahead of Rust on x86 (clone 2.272G vs 2.469G; push loop 3.622G vs 4.699G), and d273d89f37's first block of 4 (B-2026-11-04-38) stays, since reverting it brings back kata 3629's RSS.

title: Kata 277's bench runs 1.83x Rust's instructions at karac's default O2 (3.19G vs 1.74G, x86 callgrind) and 0.62x at O3 (1.08G): O2 misses the verify loop's simplification once the candidate is the planted celebrity
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-07 at 97681763d2, x86 callgrind, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 against rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on (kara-katas leetcode/201-300/277-find-the-celebrity/bench). Everything inlines into main in both. knows(a, b) returns early for b == star and a == star, so in find_celebrity's verification loop, once cand == star, knows(cand, j) is false and knows(j, cand) true for every j; Rust's O2 pipeline exploits that and Kāra's O2 does not, while Kāra's IR through O3 does (1.08G, ahead of Rust). Next: diff the O2 pass pipeline on the loop (loop unswitching / jump threading on the cand == star condition) and see which IR shape of the kara.find_celebrity loop blocks it at O2. APPENDED 2026-11-08 (kata thread's parity pass, x86, release karac 0.8.1-dev.14849+g8cdef3b93): kata 492 (construct-the-rectangle, M5: 1.33x the legacy instructions) is the same shape. Its divisor walk `while area % width != 0 { width -= 1 }` (286M iterations) keeps the `area == i64.MIN` half of the `MIN % -1` check in the loop (`cmp rsi,rdi; jne`, 2 instructions an iteration, 0.57G, the whole gap: 4.024G against checked Rust's 3.455G). Rust unswitches it (`neg rax; jno` before the loop selects a check-free copy). With KARAC_MIR_OPT=3 Kāra runs 3.453G and the compare is gone, so O2's loop unswitching is the missing piece here too.
fix: 03e9186ea3. Non-trivial loop unswitching runs at O2: src/backend/mir_aot.rs passes `-enable-nontrivial-unswitch` to LLVM (it is on only at O3 in LLVM's pipeline, while rustc's O2 build unswitched 492's loop on `area == i64.MIN`); KARAC_MIR_UNSWITCH=0 turns it off and KARAC_MIR_UNSWITCH_THRESHOLD sets LLVM's cost bound (default 50). Pinned by tests/mir_unswitch.rs (492's loop, aarch64 object: the default build carries the extra loop copy). MEASURED x86 callgrind, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0: 277 3.19G -> 1.08G (Rust 1.74G), 492 4.02G -> 3.45G (checked Rust 3.455G). All 1036 kata benches against 2b8a45f360 (with b8e953e4f9's count change): 319 change, geomean about 0.98, outputs identical, 16 slower than 2%, worst 229 at 1.17x; of the four worst, 59, 229 and 255 stay at or under checked Rust's instructions (0.88x, 1.01x, 0.83x) and 97 goes from 1.02x to 1.13x Rust's. Smaller thresholds (25, 10, 5) kept fewer of the wins without clearing those losers.

title: `karac fix` rewrites Rust's `BinaryHeap<Reverse<i32>>` in a type (a struct field) to `PriorityQueue[Release[i32]]`: the Reverse-around-heap-items fix covers `push(Reverse(x))` and `Some(Reverse(p))` but not the type argument, which takes the resolver's did-you-mean `Release`; it should be `PriorityQueue[i32]`
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-08 (kara 92cb060c1): kara-katas leetcode/1401-1500/1500-design-a-file-sharing-system/files_solution.kara, LeetCode's Rust template with a field `free: BinaryHeap<Reverse<i32>>`, `self.free.pop()` matched as `Some(Reverse(id))`, and `self.free.push(Reverse(user_id))`. `karac fix` in three rounds (39, 11, 1 edits) turns the heap into `PriorityQueue.new()` and drops `Reverse` at the push and the pattern (src/resolver.rs report_rust_reverse, rust_reverse_wraps), but the field's type becomes `PriorityQueue[Release[i32]]`: the undefined-type path offers the did-you-mean `Release` (an atomic ordering), which report_rust_reverse's doc says must never happen for the name (kata 1057). Six errors follow (match arms `Release[i32]` vs `i32`, `push(user_id)` expected `Release[i32]`, two moves of `id`) with no fix. With the type written `PriorityQueue[i32]` by hand, check passes and __mir-run prints the kata's expected output. Expected: in a program whose Rust heaps pop smallest first, `Reverse[T]` as a heap's item type is fixed to `T`; elsewhere no did-you-mean `Release` for `Reverse` in a type either. The kata's Rust arm stays blocked on this row. The 2001+ kata thread is fixing it (Parser::rust_reverse_wraps plus error_undefined_type), per the 1001+ kata thread 11-08.
fix: cdb6382000. The Reverse-around-heap-items fix (kata 2008) now reaches the heap type argument too: `BinaryHeap<Reverse<i32>>` in a type, a struct field included, is written `PriorityQueue[i32]` rather than taking the resolver's did-you-mean `Release`. Measured with a struct field `free: BinaryHeap<Reverse<i32>>`, `push(Reverse(3))` and `if let Some(Reverse(x)) = p.free.pop()`: three `karac fix` rounds give `free: PriorityQueue[i32]`, `push(3)`, `Some(x)`, which checks and prints `1`. Pinned for a `let` annotation by tests/kata_2008_check_gaps.rs; the struct-field shape was measured by hand.

title: Kata 481's bench calls karac_mir_vec_reserve on every entry to its inner push loop (66.3M calls): the presize lowering of a counting loop that refills an existing Vec reserves through the runtime with no inline len + n <= cap check, 2.47x checked Rust's instructions
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-08 on x86 (4-core container, release karac 0.8.1-dev.14849+g8cdef3b93, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build, against rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on; callgrind instruction counts, sinks equal) by the kata thread's parity pass over the M5 batches 452-510 (review thread, 11-08): the bench does the same work as its Rust mirror. kara-katas leetcode/401-500/481-magical-string/bench: 5.24G instructions against 2.13G, wall 0.41 s against 0.245 s (M5: 1.35x). Hot spot: `for _ in 0..s[read] { s.push(next) }`. The presize MIR pass (src/mir/presize.rs) reserves room at the entry of the counting loop; its backend lowering, the ("Vec" | "String", "presize") case in src/backend/mir/call.rs, calls reserve_via_copy whenever n > 0 and the Vec is not empty, so each of the 66.3M runs calls karac_mir_vec_reserve (about 20 instructions in the runtime plus about 12 in karac.main to spill and reload the Vec header around the call) even when the capacity is already there. Rust inlines the push and calls grow_one 16K times. Expected: compare len + n with the capacity inline and call the runtime only to grow. Secondary, same bench: `for i in 0..n { if s[i] == 1 .. }` keeps a bounds check per element (10 instructions an element against Rust's 6-7). Routed to the drop schedule.
fix: bfa904694f: the presize lowering (src/backend/mir/call.rs, the ("Vec"|"String", "presize") case) now compares the wanted room with cap - len inline and calls karac_mir_vec_reserve only when the room is short, so a counting loop that refills a vector already holding elements no longer calls the runtime on every entry. Kata 481: 5.24G -> 3.65G instructions (x86 callgrind; Rust 2.13G); the reserve calls are gone, and the remaining gap is in the loop body, not this row's call. Pinned by tests/mir_presize_refill.rs (LeetCode 481's counts on both backends; the fill function's IR tests %presize.short).

title: Iterating a String's chars costs 17 instructions a char against Rust's 11 when collected, 35 against 27 in a for loop: the inlined decode reloads the String's pointer and length each char, tests ASCII twice and checks the byte cursor for overflow (katas 459, 467, 484); 459's `cs[i] != cs[i - d]` loop also keeps two bounds checks and the `i - d` overflow check
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-08 on x86 (4-core container, release karac 0.8.1-dev.14849+g8cdef3b93, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build, against rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on; callgrind instruction counts, sinks equal) by the kata thread's parity pass over the M5 batches 452-510 (review thread, 11-08): the bench does the same work as its Rust mirror. Decode: `s.chars().collect()` (459, 484) inlines from karac_mir_char_at_byte, and per char reloads the String's ptr and len from memory and bounds-checks them (`mov (%r12),%rdi; mov 0x8(%r12),%rsi; cmp %rsi,%rbx; jae`), tests ASCII twice (`test; jns`, then `cmp $0x80,%eax; jae`) and compares the capacity with a stack slot: 17 instructions a char against Rust's 11 (59.6M chars in 459, about 360M instructions). `for c in s.chars()` (467, 100M chars): 35 against 27, with a duplicate end test and bounds test on the same index (`cmp %r15,%rbx; jge` then `cmp %r15,%rbx; jae`), the data pointer reloaded from the stack, the redundant `mov $1,%ecx; cmp $0x80,%eax; jae` after the ASCII path, and `add %rcx,%rbx; jo` on the cursor; Rust walks a pointer with one end compare. 467: 3.54G against 2.73G (1.29x; M5 2.05x). Indexed loop, 459 (kara-katas leetcode/401-500/459-repeated-substring-pattern/bench): 3.77G against 2.43G (1.55x; M5 2.52x); `for i in d..n { if cs[i] != cs[i - d] ..` runs 170.7M times at 12 instructions against Rust's 7: a bounds check on cs[i] (`cmp %rcx,%rdx; jae`), the `i - d` overflow check (`sub %r9,%rdx; jo`) and a bounds check on cs[i - d], where Rust folds all three into the loop bound (`lea (%r9,%rax),%rdx; cmp %rcx,%rdx; jae` once). That loop is about 853M of 459's 1.34G gap. 484 (after its bench fix, 1.46x) also keeps an unhoisted bounds check in both D-scan loops (about 53M instructions) and fills `(1..=n).collect()` scalar with a capacity check (6 instructions an element against Rust's vectorized 2). Routed to the drop schedule.
fix: d026b1bc15 + f9b9e70667. Decode (d026b1bc15): `char_at_byte` (src/backend/mir/seq.rs) returns the char as an i32 phi, with the ASCII fast path a bare `zext` and only the slow path calling the runtime, so the ASCII test runs once a char; `StrChars.next` / `StrViewChars.next` (collections.kara) compare the cursor with the end as u64 and step it with `wrapping_add(c.len_utf8())`, so the cursor's overflow test is gone. Overflow tests (f9b9e70667): `range_bounds::elide_proven_overflow` (src/mir/range_bounds.rs, run last in finish_build) turns a CheckedBinaryOp's `switchInt(flag)` into a Goto when the operands' intervals prove the result in range (not for Add/Sub with a constant operand, which the loop-shape passes match on), and `untested_checks` lets the backend emit such an op as a plain nsw/nuw op (src/backend/mir/body.rs). Pinned by tests/mir_chars_step.rs (`%ch = phi i32`, no `with.overflow` in StrChars.next) and range_bounds unit tests `mir_range_overflow_drops_a_test_the_loops_disprove` / `..._keeps_a_test_a_negative_start_needs`. MEASURED (x86 callgrind, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, against rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on): 467 3.54G -> 3.04G (Rust 2.73G); 459 3.77G -> 2.97G (Rust 2.43G): `cs[i - d]`'s bounds check and the `i - d` overflow test are gone; 741 2.39G -> 2.22G; 484 848M -> 788M (Rust 550M). Sweep of all 1036 kata benches against e9e2b015ca: 152 changed, geomean 0.972, none slower than 2%, outputs identical. What is left (459's `cs[i]` check, 484's D-scan checks and its scalar `(1..=n).collect()` fill) is B-2026-11-08-61.

title: A Map or Set allocates five buffers for its first entry and frees five (the MirMap header, buf, hashes, index, dead): kata 491's bench makes 13.0M mallocs against Rust's 5.6M for the same 3.53M clones, and insert plus free are 47% of its instructions
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-08 on x86 (4-core container, release karac 0.8.1-dev.14849+g8cdef3b93, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build, against rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on; callgrind instruction counts, sinks equal) by the kata thread's parity pass over the M5 batches 452-510 (review thread, 11-08): the bench does the same work as its Rust mirror. kara-katas leetcode/401-500/491-non-decreasing-subsequences/bench: 5.38G instructions against 3.80G (1.42x; M5 1.57x), wall 0.52-0.64 s against 0.41-0.49 s. Both sides use SipHash-1-3, create the set lazily and clone `current` the same 3.53M times. Kāra: 13.04M mallocs and 13.04M frees; Rust 5.60M each. Each Set that receives a value costs five allocations: `empty()` in runtime/src/mir_map.rs allocates the MirMap header, then buf, hashes, index and dead are each a buffer of their own; karac_mir_map_free is called 1.86M times and frees 9.33M blocks. hashbrown allocates one block per table (2.06M reserve_rehash calls). karac_mir_map_insert_hv (1.61G inclusive) and karac_mir_map_free (0.89G) are 47% of Kāra's instructions. Expected: one allocation per table (header inline in the handle, or the arrays in one block). Routed to the drop schedule.
fix: 267075716b. runtime/src/mir_map.rs: the header's own allocation now also holds room for a table's first four entries (when they fit 256 bytes) with their hashes, and eight index cells, so a table of up to four entries is one malloc. A hashed table keeps each slot's hash after the entries in the same block as `buf`; the index is the `cells`/`ncells` words compiled code already reads, inline or one block; `dead` is allocated only once a slot becomes a hole. The first ten header words keep their offsets, so compiled code is unchanged. Measured on x86 against a control archive built at f071e8e56e (KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, identical output): kata 491's bench 13,059,058 allocations to 5,594,664 (Rust mirror 5.60M), 5.38G instructions to 4.07G (Rust 3.80G per the row), wall 0.45 s to 0.35 s; 454 and 347 1-2% fewer instructions. Runtime unit tests cover growth out of the header room, removal, clear and refill for hashed and sorted tables with 8- to 200-byte entries, and are clean under AddressSanitizer. Full gate green (10649 + 10826 passed, 0 failed).

title: A Map lookup calls SipHash out of line, reloading the hash state from a global and checking the seed on every call, and probes its index one 8-byte cell at a time: kata 454 runs 1.03x Rust's instructions but 2.9x its branch mispredicts and 2.5x its data reads
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-08 on x86 (4-core container, release karac 0.8.1-dev.14849+g8cdef3b93, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build, against rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on; callgrind instruction counts, sinks equal) by the kata thread's parity pass over the M5 batches 452-510 (review thread, 11-08): the bench does the same work as its Rust mirror. kara-katas leetcode/401-500/454-4sum-ii/bench (M5 1.42x): Rust HashMap against Kāra Map, both SipHash-1-3, the same entry().or_insert and get structure. cachegrind: instructions 2.81G against 2.73G, data reads 454M against 183M, branch mispredicts 8.2M against 2.8M, L1d misses 44.7M against 42.4M; wall 0.95-1.12 s against 0.65-0.74 s. SipHash is an out-of-line call (20M calls, about 78 instructions each) that reloads its state from the global karac_hash_word_state and tests karac_hash_seed_ready each time; after the hash Kāra probes a table of 8-byte index cells one cell at a time and then reads the entry from the separate buf array (22.7M probe iterations; 7.2M of the mispredicts are in those loops in karac.main). Rust inlines the hash and probes 16 control bytes at a time with SSE2. So the time goes to mispredicts and memory traffic, not instruction count. Routed to the drop schedule.
fix: 42bfb964f0. The Map index is now a grouped control-byte table (runtime/src/mir_map.rs, src/backend/mir/table.rs): one byte per cell (empty 0xFF, deleted 0x80, else the top seven hash bits), the first group of eight mirrored past the end, then the u32 slot array. A lookup loads eight control bytes as one unaligned word, matches the tag with SWAR arithmetic, compares keys only where the tag matches, and stops at the first group holding an empty byte; probing steps by groups, triangularly, at load at most 7/8 counting deleted cells. Measured on release builds: kata 454 ~620 -> ~520 ms (Rust 411), branch misses 8.2M -> 4.06M; kata 219 ~760 -> ~690 ms (Rust 599); katas 1, 128, 347 flat; 491 ~2% slower. Deliberately NOT changed: the hash stays out of line. Inlining karac.hash.word measured slower on 219 (660 -> 696-736 ms) under both the old and the grouped index, so the SipHash half of the title is measured and left as is. Pinned by the runtime test the_grouped_index_matches_a_model (60K steps against a BTreeSet) and the Map corpus on mir-llvm and mir-llvm-asan, identical to a main control.

title: Dropping a shared-struct handle calls an out-of-line, self-recursive drop function even when the count does not reach zero (154M calls, 21% of kata 510's instructions), and each weak upgrade adds 2 to the count and then calls that drop to take 1 back
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-08 on x86 (4-core container, release karac 0.8.1-dev.14849+g8cdef3b93, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build, against rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on; callgrind instruction counts, sinks equal) by the kata thread's parity pass over the M5 batches 452-510 (review thread, 11-08): the bench does the same work as its Rust mirror. kara-katas leetcode/501-600/510-inorder-successor-in-bst-ii/bench (M5: 1.43x the retired legacy compiler's instructions): a `shared struct` Node with a `weak` parent against Rc<RefCell<..>> with Weak, which does slightly more (RefCell borrow flags). 5.79G instructions against 5.01G (1.16x), wall 3.4-3.7 s against 2.5-2.8 s. Each Node handle is released through an out-of-line function (main+0x10, at 0x3740 in the binary): `push %rbx; mov (%rdi),%rbx; test; je; decq (%rbx); jne -> pop; ret`, called 154M times for 1.226G instructions; Rust inlines the decrement and branch and calls only drop_slow (28M instructions). Each weak upgrade does `add $0x2,%rax; mov %rax,(%r14)` and then calls that drop function to take one back (at 0x34a8, 0x352b, 0x353a, 0x3578, about 25M times each). Expected: the decrement and zero test inline at the drop site with only the free out of line, and an upgrade that adds 1. Routed to the drop schedule.
fix: ca44c9a984: call_glue (src/backend/mir/drop.rs) now drops a shared handle, or an Option of one held as a bare pointer, in line: the decrement and zero test sit at the drop site and only last.shared T is called out of line. And a weak slot read as a value is lowered (src/mir/lower.rs, the Upgrade temp in expr_place_here) as a move of the fresh upgrade rather than a clone of it, so one count is taken, not two then one given back. Kata 510: 5.79G -> 4.53G instructions (x86 callgrind; Rust 5.01G). Pinned by tests/mir_shared_release_inline.rs (values and drop order on both backends and the build; climb's IR calls no clone and no drop glue).

title: PriorityQueue's sift loops (runtime/stdlib/priority_queue.kara) take 24-27 instructions a level against Rust BinaryHeap's 9-12: bounds checks on every access, the Vec header reloaded from self each level, `self.max` tested inside the loop, and a swap where Rust moves a hole (kata 480)
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-08 on x86 (4-core container, release karac 0.8.1-dev.14849+g8cdef3b93, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build, against rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on; callgrind instruction counts, sinks equal) by the kata thread's parity pass over the M5 batches 452-510 (review thread, 11-08): the bench does the same work as its Rust mirror. kara-katas leetcode/401-500/480-sliding-window-median/bench: 4.52G instructions against 3.63G (1.24x; M5 1.38x), wall 0.96-1.10 s against 0.68-0.86 s. The same pop algorithm as Rust's BinaryHeap; the hashing of the lazy-deletion Map is the same count (14.2M) on both sides. sift_down_to_bottom: about 27 instructions a level against 12, with 4-5 bounds checks a level (`cmp %r15,..; jae`), the Vec's pointer and length reloaded from self every level, and a swap (2 loads, 2 stores) where Rust moves a hole (1 load, 1 store). sift_up: about 24 against 9, with `self.max` tested in the loop (`cmpb $0x0,0x18(%rbx)`) rather than hoisted, and 2 bounds checks a level. About 70M levels, roughly 1.1G extra instructions. Owner: Thread A (runtime/stdlib .kara), per the review thread.
fix:
833870bb07. The sift-up and Floyd sift-to-bottom loops (runtime/stdlib/source/priority_queue.kara) moved into free functions, `pq_sift_up` and `pq_sift_to_bottom`, that take the backing vector as a `mut Slice[T]`. A slice's pointer and length are values, so they stay in registers across element stores. Through `self.xs` they were reloaded every level, because a store into the buffer may alias the Vec header, and each index was checked against the reloaded length. Each direction keeps its own loop, so `max` is tested once rather than once a level. The down loop goes from 22 to 18 instructions a level, with no header reloads and only the swap's two bounds checks left.
Measured on x86 with callgrind, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0:
- push/pop microbench (400,000 i64, both directions): 268.5M -> 213.5M instructions.
- kata 480 bench: 4.92G -> 4.36G instructions, output byte-identical to the Rust mirror. Wall time is within noise, about 0.62 s for old, new and Rust alike on this container.
Not done:
- Rust's hole technique (one load and one store a level instead of a swap), which needs moving a value out of a slot.
- Dropping the overflow check on 2*i+1.
Both are what is left of the 18 against Rust's 9-12.
The 312 corpus programs that use PriorityQueue, skip or nth fail exactly the same set as a main control on mir-interp, mir-llvm and mir-llvm-asan. Pinned by corpus/design/ok_priority_queue_sifts_through_a_slice_view.

title: Rust's `mut arr: Vec<i32>` parameter has no `karac fix` edit even in a program written as Rust, where it always means an owned copy (`arr: own Vec[i32]` + `let mut arr = arr;`), and the one error is reported four times
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-08 (kara 83c2a5580): kara-katas leetcode/1501-1600/1502-can-make-arithmetic-progression-from-sequence/progression_solution.kara, LeetCode's Rust template `pub fn can_make_arithmetic_progression(mut arr: Vec<i32>) -> bool { arr.sort(); let d = arr[1] - arr[0]; arr.windows(2).all(|w| w[1] - w[0] == d) }`. `karac fix` makes five edits and then has nothing: `karac check` prints `error[parse]: ...:8:44: a parameter's mode is written in its type, not before its name ...: write `arr: mut ref T` to change the caller's value, or `arr: own T` and `let mut arr = arr;` to change your own copy` FOUR times for the one parameter. src/parser/items.rs gives the `mut` mode no edit by design ("which one was meant is not written down"). In Rust, though, `mut name: T` is unambiguous: the function owns `name` and may change it, never the caller's value; that is Kāra's `own T` plus `let mut name = name;`. So when the program is Rust-shaped (the same signals the other Rust-template fixes use: `Vec<..>`, `Solution::`, `&self`), the edit is safe. With that edit by hand, one more `karac fix` round and the arm checks and prints the ★ arm's output. Expected: (a) the edit in Rust-shaped programs, (b) the error reported once. The kata's Rust arm stays blocked on this row.
fix: 0919199c6f (test pin). The edit itself landed in cdb6382000 (katas 2007, 2008, 2001+ kata thread): Rust's `mut v: T` parameter is written `v: own T` with `let mut v = v;` opening the body, in every program. A Rust-shaped-only version of the same edit was in flight here and was dropped at the rebase in favour of cdb6382000. tests/fix_rust_mut_param.rs pins the row's own shape (an `impl Solution` template with `Vec<i32>` and a `::` call) through every `karac fix` round to a program that checks, and that the error is reported once (the row's "reported four times" did not reproduce: once at 2c6f3d5ad0 and after).

title: `karac check` refuses `let (at, _) = v[i..j].iter().enumerate().min_by_key(..).unwrap(); v.remove(at);`: it keeps the range slice `v[i..j]` borrowed through the tuple pattern's `_`, so a later `mut ref` use of `v` is E-conflict; `.unwrap().0`, or `v.iter()` without the range, checks, and __mir-run accepts the program
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-08 (kara 83c2a5580): kara-katas leetcode/1501-1600/1505-minimum-possible-integer-after-at-most-k-adjacent-swaps-on-digits/swaps_iter.kara, `let (offset, _) = digits[i..end].iter().enumerate().min_by_key(|(_, d)| *d).unwrap(); let d = digits.remove(i + offset); digits.insert(i, d);` -> `error[ownership]: `digits` cannot be borrowed as `mut ref T` because it is also borrowed as `Slice[T]` at line 12:27` at both the remove and the insert. Five-line repro: `let mut v: Vec[i64] = [3, 1, 2]; let (at, _) = v[0..3].iter().enumerate().min_by_key(|(_, x)| *x).unwrap(); v.remove(at); println(f"{v.len()}");` -> 1 error. Same with `let at = ....unwrap().0;` -> 0 errors; with `v.iter()` for `v[0..3].iter()` -> 0; `let (at, _) = v.iter().enumerate().next().unwrap();` -> 0; `let (at, x) = ...next().unwrap(); let y = *x;` then `v.remove(at)` -> 0. So the front-end ownership pass ties the `_` component of the destructured tuple to the range slice's borrow and keeps it live; `_` binds nothing, `at` is an i64. `karac __mir-run` runs every variant and prints the expected output (MIR borrowck accepts). The kata's iterator arm stays blocked on this row.
fix: edc6b01e22: a `let` that destructures a slice read keeps the slice borrowed only through the parts that still borrow it. src/ownership.rs adds deeply_owned_pattern_names (a binding of a deeply owned type, through tuple patterns), and src/ownership/block_stmt.rs ends the slice borrow when every bound part is owned, or holds it through the remaining parts otherwise. `let (at, _) = v[i..j].iter().enumerate().min_by_key(..).unwrap(); v.remove(at);` checks and runs; a part that is still a `ref` keeps the slice borrowed. Tests: tests/ownership_slice_destructure.rs (2). Kata 1505's swaps_iter.kara checks and runs.

title: `karac fix` rewrites Rust's `if let Some(&i) = pos[d].last()` to `if let Some(i) = ...`, which changes `i` from a copied usize into a borrow of `pos[d]`, so the later `pos[d].pop()` is refused (E0516) with no fix; the meaning-keeping edit is `pos[d].last().cloned()`
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-08 (kara 83c2a5580): kara-katas leetcode/1501-1600/1505-minimum-possible-integer-after-at-most-k-adjacent-swaps-on-digits/swaps_solution.kara, LeetCode's Rust template with `if let Some(&i) = pos[d].last() { ...; pos[d].pop(); ... }` (pos: Vec<Vec<usize>>). `karac fix` (7 edits, then 4) drops the `&` in the pattern, as it does for `for &c in &v` (which it turns into `for c in ref v`, fine for a loop that only reads). Here the binding outlives a mutation: `error[typecheck]: cannot mutably borrow `pos` while `i` still holds a borrow of it, taken at 21:34 (core-semantics.md §5.6) [E0516]` at `pos[d].pop()`, no fix offered. In Rust `&i` copies the Copy value out of the `Option<&usize>`, so the edit that keeps the program's meaning is `if let Some(i) = pos[d].last().cloned()` (karac fix already maps `copied()` to `cloned()`). With that written by hand (plus `before: i32` for B-2026-11-07-57), `karac fix` makes 8 more edits and the arm checks and prints the ★ arm's output. Expected: a `&x` pattern on an `Option<&T>` of a Copy T becomes `.cloned()` on the scrutinee (or `Some(i)` plus `*i` uses), never a bare `Some(i)` that keeps the borrow. The kata's Rust arm stays blocked on this row.
fix: f4b3b2a3b7: the Rust `&` pattern sigil's fix no longer drops the copy. When `Some(&i)` is the pattern of an `if let` / `while let`, the sigil's deletion becomes `.cloned()` appended to the scrutinee (src/parser.rs amp_sigils, src/parser/patterns.rs clone_through_some_amp, src/parser/exprs.rs at the if-let and while-let sites), so `if let Some(&i) = pos[d].last()` is fixed to `if let Some(i) = pos[d].last().cloned()` and `i` stays a copied value. Tests: tests/fix_some_amp_pattern.rs. Kata 1505 written with `Some(&i)` fixes to a program that runs.

title: Read-only iteration of a field of a `shared` struct that is not declared `mut` pays a run-time borrow flag (acquire + release through the thread-local list) per loan: the flag pass flags every non-Copy field because MIR does not record which fields are `mut`
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-08 (kara acb9d4c5b, release karac, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0). kara-katas leetcode/1501-1600/1506-find-root-of-n-ary-tree, `shared struct Node { val: i64, children: Vec[Node] }` (no `mut` field). The bench (200 root finds over 20 trees of up to 50000 nodes, `for node in nodes.iter() { total += node.val; for child in node.children.iter() { total -= child.val; } }`) runs in 0.277 s against rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on 0.189 s (1.47x), C 0.100 s. callgrind on the Kara binary: karac_mir_flag_acquire 23% inclusive, karac_mir_flag_release 15.6% of instructions. Micro repro (the same struct, a root with two leaves, the double loop 100000 times): acquire 46.08% and release 30.72% of 16,276,599 Ir; the emitted IR (KARAC_MIR_LL) has 2 calls to karac_mir_flag_acquire. Cause, from src/mir/flags.rs's own header: 'MIR does not record which fields are `mut`; the type checker rejects a write or `mut` borrow of any other field, so flagging every field of the right type changes nothing for those.' It changes nothing for the answer, but every shared loan of `children` takes and gives back a flag through runtime/src/mir_flags.rs's per-task list. A field that is not `mut` can never be written through any handle, so no conflict is possible and no flag is needed (core semantics 6.2 flags `mut` fields only). Suggested: Carry the field's `mut`-ness into MIR (the struct's layout, or a per-field bit the type checker already has) and have flagged_prefixes skip non-`mut` fields; pin with an IR fixture that a read-only loop over a non-`mut` field of a shared struct emits no karac_mir_flag_acquire.
fix: 4fdf0cf1e3. The lowering's struct fields a handle may write (declared `mut`, or an `Atomic` or `Mutex`, as the type checker's shared_struct_mut_field_names has them) reach insert_borrow_flags as Lowered.writable_fields. flagged_prefixes skips a struct field outside that set (may_be_written), and a variant's field is flagged as before. KARAC_MIR_FLAG_ALL_FIELDS=1 restores the old behaviour. Unit test mir_flags_skip_a_field_that_is_not_mut: 0 acquires for a non-mut field, 1 for a mut one. Kata 1506's bench on x86, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, 6 runs: 139-243 ms with one outlier of 372, against 268-403 ms with KARAC_MIR_FLAG_ALL_FIELDS=1. The emitted IR has 0 karac_mir_flag_acquire calls, against 1. Output is identical. Gate green: 10622 + 10797 passed, 0 failed.

title: `s.split_whitespace().rev()` (and `s.split(" ").rev()`) is refused with a bare "no method 'rev' on type 'StrWords'": the string-splitting iterators are not double-ended, though Rust's `split_whitespace` is, and the diagnostic gives no hint or fix
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-08 (kara acb9d4c5b). kara-katas leetcode/1501-1600/1507-reformat-date/reformat_iter.kara: `let words: Vec[String] = date.split_whitespace().rev().map(|w| w.to_string()).collect();` gives `error[typecheck]: 18:30: no method 'rev' on type 'StrWords'`, and `karac __mir-run` stops at the same error. The five-line probe `s.split(" ").rev()` gives the same for 'StrSplit'. docs/library/iterators.md lists the double-ended iterators (Vec, Array, Slice, VecDeque, ranges, step_by over a range, a String's chars()) and the splitting iterators are not among them, so this matches the library as written; in Rust `SplitWhitespace` is DoubleEndedIterator, and `str::split` is too for a char pattern, so Rust-shaped code that reverses words (a common LeetCode idiom: reverse words, reformat a date) is refused. With `let mut words: Vec[String] = date.split_whitespace().map(..).collect(); words.reverse();` the arm checks and prints the expected output on every lane, so only `rev` is missing. Either: make StrWords and StrSplit double-ended (splitting at whitespace or a fixed separator walks backward as easily as forward, like chars()), or at least have the 'no method rev' diagnostic say the iterator is not double-ended and suggest collecting first.
fix: fd8d318ca2: `StrSplit` and `StrWords` (runtime/stdlib/source/collections.kara) keep a back cursor and implement DoubleEndedIterator, so `s.split_whitespace().rev()` and `s.split(sep).rev()` work. `split(sep).rev()` yields exactly the forward pieces reversed: a separator that cannot overlap itself is found from the back with rfind; one that can (`aa`) is matched forward. The empty separator's lead/char/trail pieces mirror too; `splitn` keeps its rest-of-text piece; mixed next/next_back meet in the middle. docs/library/iterators.md lists both and notes the difference from Rust's rsplit. Pin: corpus/design/ok_string_splits_walk_from_both_ends (Python mirror), passing on mir-interp, mir-llvm and mir-llvm-asan; the 536 corpus programs that split strings were re-run on interp and native with no new failure. Kata 1507's reformat_iter.kara (`split_whitespace().rev()`) runs and matches its Python mirror.

title: A `usize` length from a Rust template (`let n = n as usize; Vec::with_capacity(n * (n + 1) / 2)`) is refused as an implicit `usize` to `i64` coercion whose message says to write `as i64`, but `karac fix` has no edit for it
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-08 (kara acb9d4c5b). kara-katas leetcode/1501-1600/1508-range-sum-of-sorted-subarray-sums/sums_solution.kara, LeetCode's Rust template `pub fn range_sum(nums: Vec<i32>, n: i32, left: i32, right: i32) -> i32 { let n = n as usize; let mut sums: Vec<i64> = Vec::with_capacity(n * (n + 1) / 2); ... }`. `karac fix` makes 9 edits and then 2, and leaves one error: `error[typecheck]: 10:52: implicit coercion from 'usize' to 'i64' would narrow or change sign; an out-of-range value is not caught at compile time. Write an explicit 'as i64' to acknowledge the truncation`, with no fix. B-2026-10-25-11 routed library length arguments through check_i64_arg, and B-2026-10-25-10 gives a drop-the-cast fix when the argument is itself `x as usize` over an i64; an expression over a `usize` binding (`n * (n + 1) / 2` after `let n = n as usize;`, the usual first line of a Rust template) gets neither. The message names the edit (`as i64`), which keeps the meaning for any length a Vec can hold, so it could carry it as a machine-applicable fix, at least for library length and capacity arguments. With `Vec.with_capacity((n * (n + 1) / 2) as i64)` written by hand, the arm checks and prints the expected output on every lane (indexing `nums[j]` and slicing `sums[(left - 1) as usize..right as usize]` with `usize` are accepted).
fix: 20031ded3d, d9ec6ec5fd, c6def19faf: a `usize` / `isize` size expression where an `i64` is wanted carries `as i64` as a machine fix (operand parenthesized unless postfix), in src/typechecker/exprs.rs. Since c2c1c98fa5 and 0600aebf3b (B-2026-11-08-49) fix the `usize` root itself (every `as usize` cast, `usize` type and suffix in a program with no FFI items), the use-site edit is dropped whenever the same check fixes a root (src/typechecker/pointer_ints.rs, usize_use_site_fixes), so the row's template `let n = n as usize; Vec.with_capacity(n * (n + 1) / 2)` is fixed at the cast alone with no redundant casts left. A use whose root is kept (a program with an `unsafe extern` block) gets the `as i64`. Tests: tests/fix_usize_size_args.rs (the template, a `usize` parameter, a float cast, and the FFI program).

title: A known unit variant (`None`) in a `match` arm over a scrutinee that already failed to type is also reported as `` `None` is Type-class but binding names must be Value-class ``, a second diagnostic on top of the real one
detail: Found by Thread A's corpus check sweep (11-07, release-equivalent debug karac at 08e2acd80b + -40..-43): 68 corpus fixtures whose scrutinee has its own error, e.g. corpus/fixtures/codegen/numerics/test_e2e_soa_pop_front_shifts_each_group (`match entities.pop_front() { .. None => println(-1) }` on a `Vec`: `no method pop_front on type Vec`, then at the `None` arm `` `None` is Type-class but binding names must be Value-class (snake_case) (design.md §3 CN-2); consider renaming to `none` ``). Introduced with the CN-2 binding check of B-2026-11-06-18 (d978271697, in 0.8.1): the check runs when the pattern was not recorded as a variant, which happens when the scrutinee type is already an error. Noise only: the scrutinee's own error is always reported first, so no valid program is affected. Valid shapes checked clean before and after: `None` over `Option[ref T]`, `ref Option[i64]`, `it.next()`, `r.ok()`, `m.get(..)`, a `for o in Vec[Option]` match, user-enum unit variants over `id(Dir.Up)` and an inferred `Vec.new()` element.
fix: 8b1e2b6970. The CN-2 binding-class check in src/typechecker/patterns.rs is skipped when the name is a known unit variant (`is_variant_pattern`) and the peeled scrutinee type is already `Type::Error`, so only the scrutinee's own error is reported. A known variant over a real non-enum scrutinee still gets the scrutinee-mismatch error (`match x_i64 { None => .. }`). The 68 corpus fixtures that showed it now report only their real error. Gate195 green.

title: A binding whose literal keeps `i64` because only an operator or a method receiver used it is refused far from the binding, with an `as` cast as the only advice: `let mut b = 0; b += y; b` in `-> i32` says 'implicit coercion from i64 to i32 would narrow ... write an explicit as i32' at the return, with no machine fix; the fix is the binding's annotation (`let mut b: i32 = 0`)
detail: design.md §8 Literals (8686d0ee18): an assignment, an argument, a return and an annotation fix a literal's type; an operator operand and a method receiver do not, and beside a narrower operand the literal keeps its default. The review asked (B-2026-11-07-57 ruling) that the refusal this leaves point at the binding with a machine-applicable annotation. At b85cf41506 `fn g(y: i32) -> i32 { let mut b = 0; b += y; b }` is refused at line of the return `b` with the narrowing message and `karac check --output=json` carries no fix. Met by kata 1062 (`+=` arm), kata 1067 (`let mut res = 0; let mut p = 1; while p <= n { .. res += ..; p *= 10; } res` in `-> i32`), katas 2013 and 2006 (`ans += a * b * c` returned as i32) and kata 2012 (`Vec.filled(n, 0)` whose element is a method receiver `pre[i - 1].max(nums[i])`); each writes the annotation by hand. Wanted: when the narrowing's source is a binding whose type came from a defaulted literal, a fix that annotates the binding (or suffixes the literal) at the declared type the refusing use wants.
fix: 7ae9bc82c0. An unannotated `let` whose value is an integer literal tree is noted by name with its literal's type variable and value (`literal_lets`, `note_literal_let`); `check_int_widening_coercion` (src/typechecker/exprs.rs), refusing an i64 that reaches a narrower integer, looks for such a binding in the refused expression (the expression itself or an operand of its operator tree) whose variable kept the default, and names it with a machine fix that inserts `: <type>` after the binding (`literal_let_annotation`), when the literal fits that type. `let mut b = 0; b += y; b` in `-> i32` gets 'b is an i64 because its literal kept the default ... declare it b: i32' and `karac fix` writes `let mut b: i32 = 0`; kata 1067's `res`/`p` takes two fix rounds (`res` at the return, then `p` inside the `+=` operand). tests/fix_literal_binding_annotation.rs. Not reached: an element whose literal is no binding's (kata 2012's `Vec.filled(n, 0)` read through a method receiver), which the 2001+ kata thread may add on top.

title: A binding's literal is not fixed by a collection literal it is an element of: `let p = 0; let v: Vec[i32] = [p, 1];` and `a.push([p, 1])` on a `Vec[Vec[i32]]` are refused 'implicit coercion from i64 to i32 would narrow', though `a.push(p)` on a `Vec[i32]` fixes `p`
detail: design.md §8 Literals (8686d0ee18): an annotation and an argument fix a literal's type. At b85cf41506 (after B-2026-11-07-57) an element of an array literal checked against `Vec[i32]` settles the binding's literal to i64 first: `fn main() { let p = 0; let v: Vec[i32] = [p, 1]; println(v.len()) }` and the same with `[p]` are refused at the literal; `let mut a: Vec[Vec[i32]] = Vec.new(); a.push([p, 1]);` likewise; `let mut a: Vec[i32] = Vec.new(); a.push(p);` is accepted. Met by kata 2015's Rust arm (`let mut prev = 0; .. ans.push([prev, pos, avg]); prev = pos;` into a `Vec[Vec[i32]]`), which writes `prev: i32` by hand. Likely the array literal's elements are inferred bare (settling) before they are checked against the element type.
fix: b07678a0f8. `fix_element_literals` (src/typechecker/exprs.rs), run in `check_expr_inner` before the numeric-collection adoption path: a sequence literal (`[..]` or `Vec[..]`) checked against a `Vec`, `VecDeque` or slice of a number type first fixes each element that is a binding whose literal no use has fixed to the element type, where the adoption path inferred the elements bare and so settled the binding to i64. `let p = 0; let v: Vec[i32] = [p, 1];`, `t([p, 1])` into a `Vec[i32]` parameter, and kata 2015's `ans.push([prev, pos, avg])` into a `Vec[Vec[i32]]` are accepted; `let p = 300; let v: Vec[u8] = [p];` is refused at the literal. Pinned by corpus/design/ok_a_collection_literal_s_element_fixes_a_literal (mir-interp and mir-llvm). A map's inserted literals not fixed by the parameter the map is handed to is B-2026-11-08-42.

title: `m.get(k) == Some(3)` (Map[String, i64]) is refused with "cannot compare 'Option[ref i64]' and 'Option[i64]'", as are `it.peek() == Some('a')`, `fl.first() == Some(1.5)` and `bs.first() == Some(true)`; design.md §5 says a literal inside the constructor takes the element type the other side fixes, but the B-2026-11-07-54 fix promotes only string literals
detail: At 4b2971e1a, on check and every run lane: `let mut m: Map[String, i64] = Map.new(); m["k"] = 3; println(m.get("k") == Some(3));` gives error[typecheck] cannot compare 'Option[ref i64]' and 'Option[i64]' (with the `.cloned()` hint, and `karac fix` applies it).
