The same happens with the operands swapped, with `!=`, and for Some(1.5) over Vec[f64], Some(true) over Vec[bool], and Some('a') against `s.chars().peekable().peek()`. `v.first() == Some("a")` over Vec[String] is accepted. design.md (Auto-deref at `.`, the B-2026-11-07-54 paragraph) says: "except that a literal inside the constructor takes the element type the other side fixes, so xs.last() == Some("") over a Vec[Str] is accepted". The wording covers any literal; the implementation (`text_literal_takes` in src/typechecker/expr_ops.rs) covers string literals only. `counts.get(word) == Some(1)` and `it.peek() == Some(':')` are everyday service and parser lines. Either extend the promotion to numeric, bool and char literals (a Copy item, so reading through the ref is free), or narrow the design.md sentence to string literals. The fix is machine-applied either way, so this is low severity.
fix: 36f65c6291. `text_literal_takes` (src/typechecker/expr_ops.rs) promoted only string literals inside a constructor or tuple. An unsuffixed number literal (or its negation into a signed or float type), a char or a bool now fits a matching element too, viewed (`Option[ref i64]`) or narrower (`Option[i32]`, `Option[ref f32]`), and is checked against it, so a literal out of the element's range is still refused at the literal. A bare literal operand keeps its own rule (`c < 300` over a u8). Measured on the row's shapes, swapped operands, `!=`, Ok(..) and tuples: correct true/false on __mir-run and __mir-llvm-run. Pin corpus/core/ok_number_literal_in_some_compares_with_view. tests/option_ref_compare_fix.rs pinned the literal refusal; it now compares places, which still get the `.cloned()` fix.

title: `collect()` into an annotated `Result[Vec[i64], String]` does not fix the error type of the mapping closure's `Ok(..)`: `let m: Result[Vec[i64], String] = xs.iter().map(|p| Ok(p.len())).collect();` is refused "cannot infer type parameter 'E' of `Result[i64, E]` ... add a type annotation to the binding", though iterators.md gives `Result[C, E]: FromIterator[Result[T, E]]` with the same E, and the closure has no binding to annotate
fix: cb995527b5. The solver that lets a collect's target fix what its items left open (solve_collected_item_vars) required the target's one FromIterator impl to be fully concrete; the library's `impl[T, E, C: FromIterator[T]] FromIterator[Result[T, E]] for Result[C, E]` leaves T to the items, so it was skipped and a closure's `Ok(p.len())` kept an unsolved E. The impl's unfixed parameters are now fresh variables, so `let m: Result[Vec[i64], String] = xs.iter().map(|p| Ok(p.len())).collect();`, the Map form and the `?`-then-Ok(n) validation shape all check. Found on the way: items whose error type is a different concrete type (`Err(5)` into Result[Vec[i64], String]) were accepted; they are now refused (wrapped_collect_mismatch compares E). And `Ok[i64, String](3)` is refused by check with the qualified form `Result[i64, String].Ok(..)` (design.md §8: no call-site type arguments). Pins corpus/design/ok_collect_into_a_result_types_the_closure_s_ok, err_collect_into_a_result_needs_the_same_error; test tests/variant_call_site_type_args.rs.

title: `Option`'s derived order puts `None` after every `Some(x)` (it is declared `Some(T), None`), so `sort()` on a `Vec[Option[T]]` puts `None` last; the review-thread ruling (core-types.md 0ec0d51d29) is `None` < `Some(x)` and `Ok(x)` < `Err(e)`, as Rust, Haskell and OCaml order them
detail: Found by the core-semantics probe's newest-features pass at 4b2971e1a. Option is declared `enum Option[+T] { Some(T), None }` in runtime/stdlib/option.kara, so the derived Ord ranks variants by declaration order and None compares greater than any Some. The docs did not state an order; the review thread ruled 2026-11-08 that None is least (core-types.md, Option § Ordering). Result is declared Ok, Err, which already gives Ok < Err. Fix by reordering the declaration or an explicit Ord/PartialOrd impl, whichever keeps layout and codegen assumptions about the variant tags intact; pin `[Some(2), None, Some(1)].sort()` -> `[None, Some(1), Some(2)]` and `None < Some(0)` on interp, llvm and ASan. A behaviour change in 0.8.2: CHANGELOG under Changed.
fix: 9972d813a None now orders before every Some(x). Option keeps its declaration (Some(T), None) and its tags; the three places that order variants by index swap Option's two: the MIR builder's derived cmp (enum_cmp in src/mir/lower.rs: <, cmp, min/max), the interpreter's order form (src/mir/interp.rs unsigned_order: sort, SortedSet/SortedMap keys, PriorityQueue), and the LLVM backend's key compare (src/backend/mir/key.rs). Result was already Ok < Err; checked on both backends. Pin corpus/core/ok_option_none_orders_first (sort, comparisons, min/max, SortedSet, PriorityQueue, a tuple key, Option[Option], Result) passes on mir-interp, mir-llvm and mir-llvm-asan; the pre-fix binary fails it. A sweep of the 445 corpus programs that both hold an Option in a collection and sort or compare found no expectation that relied on None last (the 11 differences were interpreter timeouts on benches and two dataframe fixtures that do not lower). CHANGELOG 0.8.2 Changed.

title: A program that `karac check` passes fails on every run lane with the internal `error[mir]: borrow check patch: ... drop of _24 while it is borrowed [E0516]` when a function reached from a `Server.serve` handler matches `(k.as_str(), val)` with `val` an enum carrying a String payload and another arm returns early; the same function called from `main` or a TaskGroup task runs
fix: 2eed872610: in a program that cancels tasks (Server.serve's per-connection isolating group does), every call that may suspend or panic has a cancel exit (core-semantics §11.9) that runs every scope's exit sequence. A call made while an early return was itself running those sequences (here the `for` loop's reverse of its vector) took a cancel exit that ran again the scopes the return had already left, so borrow checking saw a second drop of the `(k.as_str(), val)` tuple after `k`'s drop and reported E0516; and it skipped the entries of the scope being left, which leaked them (a `defer` that panics on the way out of an isolating task never dropped the outer scope's values). exit_to (src/mir/lower.rs) now pops each scope before running its sequence and restores them after, and exit_entries, where a cancel exit is possible, runs each entry with the entries still to run as the innermost scope. The probe's program builds and serves (`true` over HTTP from __mir-run and from `karac build`). Pinned by tests/mir_exit_cancel_scopes.rs: the probe's program lowers and passes compiled_check, and a panic in an early exit's defer prints "drop inner / drop outer / panicked" on the interpreter and compiled (the control fails all 3: E0516, and "a drop is missing").

title: Declaring `struct Response { status: i64, body: String, headers: Vec[(String, String)] }`, the form io.md § HTTP server documents for sending headers, draws `warning[prelude_shadow]: declaration of 'Response' shadows the prelude type ...; built-in paths keyed on 'Response' no longer apply to this type`, which reads as if the server will stop using it, but the server sends its headers correctly
detail: io.md: "A program may declare its own Response as struct Response { status: i64, body: String, headers: Vec[(String, String)] } to send headers." Doing exactly that in a Server.serve program prints the warning on every check, run, build and test (at 4b2971e1a). The server then sends the Location header from it on all three lanes, so the warning's "built-in paths ... no longer apply" is wrong for this type. Expected: no warning for the documented shape (or the documented shape gets a non-shadowing name, e.g. the library's Response gains an optional headers field).
fix: a8cbf37e72: the documented `struct Response { status: i64, body: String, headers: Vec[(String, String)] }` (io.md § HTTP server, the form a handler declares to send headers) draws no prelude_shadow warning: src/typechecker/items.rs is_documented_response accepts a non-generic `Response` with `status` and `body` whose every field is one of the three io.md names with its documented type, and warn_prelude_shadow skips it. A `Response` of any other shape still draws the warning. Tests: tests/response_shape_no_shadow_warning.rs (the documented shape, with and without headers and in any field order, is quiet; another shape still warns).

title: `Json.deserialize` errors give a byte offset and no field (`expected '"' at character 13`) where `Json.parse` on the same text gives `expected value at line 2 column 12`; a wrong-typed field (`{"title": 3}` into `title: String`) also reads `expected '"' at character 10`, naming neither the field nor the type
detail: At 4b2971e1a, all lanes. Program: #[derive(Deserialize)] struct N { title: String }; text "{\n  \"title\": }". Json.parse(t) -> JsonError 2:12 "expected value at line 2 column 12" (json.md: the serde_json form, 1-based line and byte column). Json.deserialize(t) -> "expected '\"' at character 13". Json.deserialize("{\"title\": 3}") -> "expected '\"' at character 10". A service returns this text to its client (400 bad json), so a client author sees a byte offset and a quote character. Expected: the same line/column form as parse, and for a type mismatch the field path and the expected type (`title: expected a string, found 3 at line 1 column 11`). Found in the HTTP JSON service probe (probe-core/svc/). Owner: B (Json).
fix: bdf7c200c3. runtime/stdlib/source/serde.kara, JsonDeserializer: an error now gives the 1-based line and byte column, as JsonError does; prefixes the path of the struct fields being read (`inner.n: ...`, kept through deserialize_mark/reset); and says what the slot wanted and what the text holds (`expected a string, found 3`, `expected an array, found an object`), or `expected value` where no value starts. Measured on both lanes: the row's `{\n  "title": }` gives `title: expected value at line 2 column 12` (Json.parse: `expected value at line 2 column 12`), `{"title": 3}` gives `title: expected a string, found 3 at line 1 column 11`; a column after a two-byte character counts bytes. The two serde fixtures that pinned `at character N` are updated (tests/mir_serde.rs and their corpus copies). Full gate green (10665 + 10842 passed, 0 failed).

title: `karac run --interp prog | head -1` keeps running after the pipe closes and exits 0, printing nothing more but running every remaining iteration (a 2,000,000-line loop: 2.1 s, then its trailing eprintln runs); the JIT and a built binary stop at once with status 141 as io.md specifies
detail: pipe.kara: fn main() { let mut i = 0; while i < 2000000 { println(f"line {i}"); i += 1; } eprintln("finished loop"); }. `karac run --interp pipe.kara | head -1`: rc 0, 2.09 s, stderr "finished loop". `karac run pipe.kara | head -1`: rc 141 in 0.16 s, nothing on stderr; a built binary the same (lgrep CLI: `lgrep error r | head -2` rc 141 built and JIT, 0 under --interp). io.md § HTTP server: "Standard output and standard error are the exception: a write to a closed pipe there ends the program as SIGPIPE would, so prog | head stops quietly with status 141." B-2026-11-07-25's fix (81bda056fb) restored this for compiled code (EPIPE on stdout/stderr re-raises SIGPIPE); the interpreter ignores SIGPIPE at startup and swallows EPIPE on the console, so a script run with --interp that filters a large input keeps reading and computing after its consumer is gone. Owner: C (interpreter natives / I/O). At 4b2971e1a.
fix: 456b9c6e58. The interpreter's console writes and flushes go through console_written (src/mir/interp.rs): a BrokenPipe restores SIGPIPE's default action and raises it (exit 141 as a fallback), so `karac run --interp prog | head -1` stops when head does, as the JIT and a built binary do. Before: the 2,000,000-line loop ran to the end, printed 'finished loop' to stderr and exited 0; after: status 141 in about 0.2 s. Pinned by tests/interp_closed_stdout.rs.

title: The unimported, deferred `std.cli` parser's types sit in the prelude, so a program declaring its own `Parser`, `Arg`, `Args`, `CliError` or `SubcommandResult` gets `warning[prelude_shadow] ... built-in paths keyed on 'Parser' no longer apply to this type` on every check, run, build and test; deferred.md § std.cli says the module is imported (`import std.cli`, `cli.Parser`) and no library doc lists these names
detail: At 4b2971e1a: `struct Parser { x: i64 }` (or Arg, Args, CliError, SubcommandResult) in an otherwise empty program draws the warning; Config, Error, Token, Lexer, Node, Store, Item do not. `fn main() { let p = Parser.new("t"); }` checks with no import. The names come from runtime/stdlib/cli.kara ("std.cli — argument parser ... Spec: deferred.md § std.cli"), whose items are evidently injected into the prelude. A CLI written the obvious way (`enum CliError { Usage(String), Io(String, IoError) }`) repeats the 4-line warning before every run (the lgrep probe printed it 9 times in one session), and a parser written for a kata or a config format (`struct Parser`) does the same. docs/library/README.md's prelude list does not mention them, and deferred.md shows them reached as `cli.Parser` after `import std.cli`. Expected: std.cli's items only under `import std.cli` (or not shipped until it is undeferred), so the natural names are free. Related: B-2026-11-08-26 (the documented user `Response` also warns).
fix: b130382d0c: std.cli's `Parser`, `Arg`, `Args`, `CliError`, `Subcommand`, `SubcommandResult`, `ArgEntry`, `FlagEntry` and `ParsedValue` are reached through `import std.cli` (deferred.md § std.cli), as `std.regex` and `std.json` are: src/library_imports.rs lists them in IMPORT_REQUIRED_MODULES (the refusal cites deferred.md § std.cli, with the import as its machine fix), and src/prelude.rs puts them under LIBRARY_GLOBAL_MODULES `std.cli`. A program's own `enum CliError` or `struct Parser` no longer draws a prelude_shadow warning, and `karac build` / `run` are unchanged. The 21 corpus fixtures that use the parser now import it. Tests: tests/std_cli_import.rs (a bare use is refused with the import as its fix; a program's own `Parser` and `CliError` draw no warning).

title: `IoError` and `VarError` display as their variant names (`PermissionDenied`, `NotPresent`, `Other(disk full)`), and `IoError` has no `Debug` (`dbg(IoError.NotFound)` is refused); io.md (8b7176574f) rules Display as readable phrases (`not found`, `permission denied`, ..., `Other`'s message as it is; VarError `environment variable not found`) and Debug as the variant
detail: At 4b2971e1a, interp and JIT alike: println(f"{IoError.PermissionDenied}") -> PermissionDenied; VarError.NotPresent -> NotPresent; IoError.Other("disk full") -> Other(disk full). dbg(IoError.NotFound): error[typecheck] dbg() argument must implement `Debug`, and 'IoError' does not. Ruling: io.md § Errors, 8b7176574f (review thread 2026-11-08): Display is `not found`, `permission denied`, `already exists`, `invalid input`, `unexpected end of file`, `invalid UTF-8`, `interrupted`, `unsupported`, `provider unavailable`, and Other's message alone; VarError is `environment variable not found` / `environment variable is not valid unicode`; Debug shows the variant. Seen in the lgrep CLI probe, which prints `lgrep: nope: NotFound` to its user. Owner: C (I/O).
fix: adf37211ee. IoError and VarError write Display out with the io.md § Errors phrases (not found, permission denied, ..., Other's message as is; environment variable not found / is not valid unicode) and derive Debug, so dbg shows the variant. The MIR pipeline runs IoError's impl from runtime/stdlib/source/io_error.kara. main's Err exit still printed the variant: a library source's re-statement of a baked impl was lowered as T.to_string#1 (after the baked #0), and the backends look up T.to_string. The impl-name suffix now counts the impls lowered (src/mir/lower.rs), which also fixes AllocError's exit line (Error: CapacityOverflow -> capacity overflow). Pinned by corpus/design/ok_io_and_var_errors_display_as_phrases and tests/io_error_display.rs; six fixtures holding the variant names were flipped.

title: (corrected: the `a += n` shape is a deliberate divergence, design.md §8 Literals at 7a4e06ce1c, beside an i32 the literal keeps i64; its refusal now offers the annotation, B-2026-11-08-20) A literal bound by `let` is fixed to `i32` or `u32` by a later use but never to `u64` or `usize`: `fn f(i: u64) -> u64 { let k = 2; i - k }` is refused 'cannot mix integer types u64 and i64', so Rust's `let mut k = 1; while k * k <= i` over a `usize` fails; and a compound assignment fixes nothing: `fn f(n: i32) -> i32 { let mut a = 0; a += n; a }` is refused 'implicit coercion from i64 to i32' (kata 1518)
detail:
MEASURED 2026-11-08 (kara 1dce193ad, release karac). Five-line probe `fn f(i: T) -> bool { let k = 2; i - k * k > 0 }`: T = i32 and T = u32 check; T = u64 and T = usize are refused at `i - k * k` with `cannot mix integer types 'u64' and 'i64' in arithmetic` (and `'usize' and 'i64'`). `i - 2 * 2 > 0` with the literal written in place checks for u64 too, so only a literal held in a `let` binding stays at its i64 default; `fn f(i: u64) -> u64 { let k = 2; i - k }` is refused the same way and `karac __mir-run` stops at it. With usize the comparison form `let mut k = 1; while k <= i` is refused 'cannot compare i64 and usize' and then 'this type mixes with i64, and usize and isize are for FFI signatures'. design.md (Type inference: 'An integer or float literal starts as a type variable that later uses may fix'; 'Literals default last') has no exception for 64-bit unsigned types, and the i32/u32 cases show the mechanism exists. Met by kata 1510's Rust template (kara-katas leetcode/1501-1600/1510-stone-game-iv/stones_solution.kara): `let n = n as usize; ... for i in 1..=n { let mut k = 1; while k * k <= i { if !dp[i - k * k] { ... } k += 1; } }`, which Rust infers as usize; after `karac fix` it is left with these two errors (and B-2026-11-08-16's `Vec.filled(n + 1, false)` with a usize length). Related to B-2026-11-07-57 (an assignment or generic call does not fix the variable), which is about i32 and the return; this one is the operand case that works for i32 and not for u64/usize. No machine fix is offered.

EXTENDED 2026-11-08 (kata 1518): `+=` does not fix a literal's type either, for i32 too. `fn f(n: i32) -> i32 { let mut a = 0; a += n; a }` is refused at `a` with 'implicit coercion from i64 to i32 would narrow'; the same through a tuple, `let mut (a, b) = (0, n); a += b; a`. `a` stays i64 and `a += n` widens n. LeetCode's Rust template for 1518, `let (mut drunk, mut full, mut empty) = (0, num_bottles, 0); while full > 0 { drunk += full; ... } drunk`, is refused this way after `karac fix`; typing the tuple `(i32, i32, i32)` makes it check. Re-measured on main at fd68cca28 (after b85cf41506, 'an assignment or a generic call's argument fixes a literal'): the u64 probe, the `+=` probe and the 1518 template are all still refused the same way.
fix: 7ae9bc82c0. `literal_binary` (src/typechecker/expr_ops.rs): a binding's literal beside an integer operand whose type does not widen into i64 (u64, usize, i128, u128) is unified with that type instead of settled to its default, per design.md §8 Literals (7a4e06ce1c). `fn f(i: u64) -> u64 { let k = 2; i - k }`, Rust's `let mut k = 1; while k * k <= n` over a usize, `k * i` over an i128 and `s = s + x` over u128 elements are accepted; beside a type that widens (u8..i32) the literal keeps i64, so the -07-3 FNV pin is unchanged. The row's `a += n` with `n: i32` returned as i32 stays refused by the ruling and now offers `let mut a: i32 = 0` (B-2026-11-08-20). Pinned by corpus/design/ok_an_operator_beside_a_wide_integer_fixes_a_literal, values from Python, mir-interp and mir-llvm. An isize beside an i64, which check accepts and the MIR builder refuses, is B-2026-11-08-48.

title: An untyped `Map.new()` whose key type comes from a `for x in v.iter()` element is inferred `Map[ref i64, _]`; `*m.entry(x).or_insert(0) += 1` then checks and runs under the interpreter, but the compiled program passes the key by value to `hash.ref i64` and segfaults (exit 101 with no message, 139 under karac run/build)
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-08 (kara 1dce193ad, release karac with LLVM 22). Seven lines: `fn main() { let nums: Vec[i64] = [1]; let mut count = Map.new(); for x in nums.iter() { *count.entry(x).or_insert(0) += 1; } println(f"{count.len()}"); }`. `karac check`: All checks passed. `karac __mir-run` prints 1. `karac __mir-llvm-run` exits 101 with empty stdout and stderr; `karac run` and a `karac build` binary die with SIGSEGV (139). `karac __mir-llvm-asan`: 'SEGV on unknown address 0x000000000001 ... #0 in hash.ref i64, #1 in kara.main': the key's value 1 is read as a pointer. So the map's key type is `ref i64` (the element binding of `nums.iter()`), but the key that reaches the hash is the copied i64. Variants that work on every lane: `let mut count: Map[i64, i64] = Map.new()` (the type written), keys from `nums[i]` or from a range, `count.insert(..)` with no loop, `let c = count.entry(1).or_insert(0)` with a literal key. The same inference shows in check with insert: `for x in nums.iter() { count.insert(x, 1); }` on an untyped map is refused 'cannot write to `x` while `count` still holds a borrow of it' (E0516), so the checker does see a `ref` key there, but `entry(x)` takes it with no borrow error. A `Copy` element yielded by `iter()` should not make a map's key a reference (Rust infers HashMap<i32, i32> from `for &x in nums.iter()` and `HashMap<&i32, _>` only without the `&`; LeetCode's template `for &x in nums.iter() { let c = count.entry(x).or_insert(0); ... }` reaches this shape after `karac fix` drops the `&` pattern). In the kata's own arm (keys from a `Vec[i32]`) `__mir-llvm-asan` reports instead 'stack-buffer-overflow ... READ of size 8 ... #0 in hash.ref i32, #1 in kara.Solution.num_identical_pairs'. Met by kara-katas leetcode/1501-1600/1512-number-of-good-pairs/pairs_solution.kara: the arm checks and prints the expected output under `karac __mir-run`, and exits 101 silently under `__mir-llvm-run`. Either the inference should fix K to the copied element type, or the compiled path must pass what the type says; a silent crash with no message is the worst of the outcomes.
fix: df02f42eac. Both halves of the review-thread ruling. (a) Lowering: `entry`'s key goes through `arg_operand` against the map's key type, as `insert`'s does, so a value is never passed where the type says a reference. (b) design.md §8 (2870295951): an unannotated Vec, VecDeque, Set or Map whose element or key variable is first solved from a `ref T` with `T: Copy` at a by-value slot is solved to `T`. The typechecker records a late-solved constructor's element variables (`collection_vars`) and solves them from a Copy reference's referent in `infer_element_arg` (push, push_back, Vec.insert, entry), the map slot check (Map/Set insert), call pass 1 and `check_assignable`; an unannotated `[x, x]` / `Vec[..]` / `Set[..]` literal of such references holds the values. Measured: the row's program prints 1 on every lane; kata 1512's pairs_solution prints the Python mirror's three checksums on __mir-run, __mir-llvm-run and __mir-llvm-asan; push and insert from `nums.iter()` into untyped collections now run (they were E0516). A written `Map[ref i64, i64]` still refuses the loop's per-item lend. Pins: corpus/core/ok_untyped_collection_takes_copy_ref_value, corpus/core/err_written_ref_map_key_lends_loop_item. tests/for_into_iter_and_ref_list_fixes.rs pinned the old refusal of `let chain = [k]` (its fix annotated it); those two cases now check as written.

title: A `ref u8` from a `Slice`'s `iter()` passed where an `i64` parameter is expected is accepted as an implicit widening, but the compiled program passes the reference's address (195 prints as 279565490929665) and the interpreter stops on `Add on Int and Ref`; `karac fix`'s lossless_cast removal of `b as i64` produces exactly this
fix: b4a08a05b1. `owned_operand` (src/mir/lower.rs) read a `ref` argument through only when its referent was exactly the slot's type; a `ref u8` for an `i64` slot fell through to the widening of the reference itself, so the compiled program passed the address and the interpreter added Int to Ref. It now reads the referent and widens it when the widening is lossless, and leaves any other mismatch to the ordinary operand path. Measured on the row's program: 195 on __mir-run, __mir-llvm-run and __mir-llvm-asan. Pin corpus/core/ok_ref_element_widens_into_param (u8 into i64, i32 into f64, a method argument).

title: A blanket impl whose method calls its bound's method (`impl[S: Store] Counter for S { fn peek(self) -> i64 { self.get() + 1 } }`) is refused at check once a concrete type uses it: "a type that failed to check is not lowered yet" at `self.get()` (design.md §9 Coherence allows the impl; B-2026-11-04-16/-49 fixed the lookup and sibling calls, not a call into the bound)
fix: 2731d331f0. The impl's self type (src/typechecker/items.rs) kept the blanket target as `Named { name: "S" }`, a type no lookup knows, so `self.get()` inside the impl failed to check and MIR refused it. A target that is one of the impl's own type parameters now stays `Type::TypeParam`, and the impl's trait is recorded as that parameter's blanket bound (a separate `blanket_impl_bound`, consulted only by `dispatch_typeparam_receiver_method`, so `impl[I: Iterator] IntoIterator for I` sees no extra bound on `I.Item`). The body therefore calls the bound's methods and its own trait's siblings. Pinned by corpus/design/ok_a_blanket_impl_calls_its_bound_s_methods (the row's program and the generic-trait form with `?? 0`, `match`, `unwrap_or`), which prints `4 4 8 1 2 0` on every lane.

title: `assert_eq(s, "x")` with `s: Str` is refused: "`assert_eq` of two types is not lowered yet"; the literal should take `Str` from the other operand (strings.md: a literal is `Str` where a `Str` is expected), while `version() == "0.1.0"` on a `Str` already works
detail: let s: Str = "x"; assert_eq(s, "x");  -> error[typecheck] "`assert_eq` of two types is not lowered yet" on check and every lane (karac 0.8.1-dev+g4b2971e1a). `s == "x"` and `assert(s == "x")` are accepted. Hit in a library's test of `pub fn version() -> Str`. If Str/String mixing is meant to be refused, the message should say which two types and suggest `.to_string()` / `as_str()`. Repro probe-core/libp/m/a3.kara.
fix: 2660652075. MIR's `assert_eq` lowering (src/mir/lower.rs) refused any operand pair whose types differ unless both were integers. A pair of text types (`Str` and a literal's static string) now goes the same way `==` does, through the binary Eq path, so `assert_eq(s, "x")` with `s: Str` compares the text. Pinned by corpus/design/ok_assert_eq_of_a_str_and_a_literal, which prints `ok`. Str against String is left as it was: design.md's `assert_eq[T](a: T, b: T)` does not say they mix.

title: `karac doc` renders wrong signatures and drops members: generic arguments vanish (`-> Result`, field `Vec`, `SortedMap`, `fn add_to(s: mut ref S, ..)` with no `[S: Store[String, i64]]`), a struct page lists no methods from its `impl`, a trait page lists no trait methods, and `builtins/` documents `collect_all`, which core-semantics §11.7 removed (check refuses it)
detail: Library package textkit (3 modules, doc comments on every pub item and member). design.md §3 Doc comments: "Each documented item gets a page with its signature"; "An impl block takes no doc comment; its methods document themselves"; members include trait methods. Observed in dist/doc: load_lines.html `fn load_lines(path: Str) -> Result with blocks + reads(FileSystem)` (source `Result[Vec[String], IoError]`); Table.html fields `headers Vec`, `rows Vec`, and none of Table's four documented pub methods (new, len, push, render); MemStore.html `items SortedMap`, no methods; Counter.html / Store.html show the trait doc but not `add`, `bump`, `get`, `put` or their docs; add_to.html loses its type parameter list. builtins/collect_all.html still describes collect_all while `karac check` says "`collect_all` is removed (§11.7)"; the builtins index also omits `panic`. Also observed, not claimed as a bug since the spec is silent: non-pub items (package-internal `fn widths`, non-pub field `rows`) get pages. `karac doc --help` prints the general help. Cross-references ([Table], [MemStore]) and effects on pub signatures work. Package in probe-core/libp/textkit.
fix: a165a62532. `karac doc` (src/doc.rs) now renders signatures with the formatter (new `render_fn_head`, `render_trait_method_head`, `render_impl_head`, `render_generic_params`, `render_where_clause` in src/formatter.rs), so type parameters, receivers, generic arguments (`Result[Vec[String], IoError]`, `Vec[String]`, `SortedMap[String, V]`) and declared effects appear as written. A struct or enum page lists the public methods of the impl blocks in its module, with their docs, and the traits it implements there. A trait page lists its associated types and its required and provided methods with their docs. The builtins registry drops `collect_all`, adds `panic`, and gives `assert_eq`/`assert_ne` design.md § Assertions' signature `[T: PartialEq + Debug](a: T, b: T)`. Pinned by tests/doc_signatures.rs (three tests) and the updated doc_surfaces_compiler_builtins_under_builtins_module. The row's unclaimed notes (non-pub items get pages; `karac doc --help`) are not changed.

title: E0113 for an unknown item in a dependency lists non-importable names as available: `import textkit.nope` says "available: Table, Store, Counter, MemStore, add_to, version, load_lines, clean, log_line", where `clean` is package-internal and importing it is E0111
detail: Dependent package with `textkit = { path = "../textkit" }`. The suggestion list should hold only `pub` items when the importer is another package. Otherwise cross-package visibility is right: package-internal fn, `private` fn, non-pub field (read and struct literal) all refused with E0111 and a help line.
fix: 380985f138. The resolver's E0113 path (src/resolver/collect.rs) built its "available:" list and its did-you-mean candidate from every top-level name of the target module. Both now keep only names the importer could import, using the same visibility test as E0111 (module item visibility at the item's canonical origin, and `pub` when the importer is another package). Pinned by tests/xpkg_unknown_item_list.rs: `import textkit.nope` lists `version, shout` and not the package-internal `clean`, and `import textkit.clea` does not suggest `clean`.

title: A `fold` closure whose parameters are annotated bare (`|acc: Vec[i64], row: Vec[i64]|`) checks, but the program fails on both backends: the interpreter stops on `deref of non-reference Box` in the closure and the compiled program exits 101 with no message; unannotated or `own` parameters run
fix: 1740abdd1 typecheck: when a closure's synthesized type still names a generic parameter (a collect() tail), the checker recorded the slot's whole function type for the closure node (src/typechecker/exprs.rs, the mentions_foreign_param record after a check-position expression), replacing the closure's own `ref Vec[i64]` parameters (an annotated bare parameter borrows) with the slot's owned ones while MIR built the body borrowed. A closure now keeps its own parameter types and takes from the slot only the parts that still name a parameter (merge_closure_foreign_params). The check side was the wrong one: the closure is legal as written. Pin: corpus/core/ok_annotated_closure_param_borrows_from_owned_slot (fold, a Fn(own Vec) slot, and a let-annotated Fn), which fails without the fix on every backend and passes on interp, llvm and ASan. Kata 1519's labels_iter.kara (kept as karac fix left it) now prints the expected output on both backends. Gate: fmt, both clippy legs, cargo test --all 10621 passed, cargo test --features llvm 10798 passed.

title: Networking on `wasm_wasi` passes `karac check --targets=wasm_wasi`, then `karac build --target=wasm_wasi` dies in wasm-ld with raw runtime symbols (`undefined symbol: karac_mir_tcp`, `karac_mir_sock_close`; `karac_mir_ready_http`, `karac_runtime_http_client_mir_send` for `Client.get`); design.md §16 lists `Network` as provided on wasm_wasi, so the program should build, or the gate should refuse it with E0411 and the table should change
detail: karac 0.8.1-dev+g52dadc1b9 with the wasm runtime archive rebuilt at that commit; modules run under node 22 WASI and wasmtime (Python bindings). Repro tcp.kara: `import std.net.{TcpStream}; fn main() { match TcpStream.connect("127.0.0.1:1") { Ok(_) => println("connected"), Err(e) => println("connect failed") } }` -> check (both targets) All checks passed; build --target=wasm_wasi: `error[link]: wasm-ld failed: rust-lld: error: /tmp/karac_mir_..._tcp.wasm.o: undefined symbol: karac_mir_tcp` and `karac_mir_sock_close`. http.kara (`Client.new().get(url)`) the same with karac_mir_ready_http and karac_runtime_http_client_mir_send. A launch reader sees an internal symbol, not a reason. WASI preview 1 has no socket connect or bind, so the likely outcome is a spec ruling (drop Network from the wasm_wasi column, letting E0411 refuse it with the chain) rather than an implementation; until then the build should refuse before linking. Files in probe-core/wasi/.
fix: c33623ba28. Network is no longer in wasm_wasi's resource set (src/target.rs target_provides), per design.md § Resources each target provides (1a4b304562): WASI preview 1 has no socket connect or bind. A TcpStream, the HTTP client or a server reached from main is refused by `karac check --target=wasm_wasi` and `karac build --target=wasm_wasi` with E0411's call chain (main → dial → TcpStream.connect), before any link; native still accepts it. Test tests/target_gate_wasi_network.rs.

title: In a package whose kara.toml declares two or more `[build] targets`, `karac check` runs a different checker: `s.split(" ").count()` and `s.split_whitespace().count()` are refused with E0200 "no method 'count' on type 'Vec' ... write `s.split(" ").iter().count(...)`", every error is coded E0200 (a type mismatch too), the text has no source snippet, and identical findings are repeated per target instead of the "all targets" group; the same file with `--targets=native,wasm_wasi`, or with one declared target, checks clean and `karac build` builds and runs it
detail: karac 0.8.1-dev+g52dadc1b9 with the wasm runtime archive rebuilt at that commit; modules run under node 22 WASI and wasmtime (Python bindings). kara.toml: `[package] name="p" version="0.1.0"` + `[build] targets = ["native", "wasm_wasi"]`; src/main.kara: `fn main() { let s = "a b".to_string(); println(s.split(" ").count()); let x: i64 = "no"; }`. `karac check` in the package prints under each of `── target: native ──` and `── target: wasm_wasi ──`: `error[E0200]: src/main.kara:1:48: no method 'count' on type 'Vec'` and `error[E0200]: src/main.kara:1:84: expected 'i64', found 'String'`, no snippet, then "2 of 2 target(s) failed". `--output=json` does put both in shared_diagnostics, but keeps the false count error. The same file outside the package with `karac check m3.kara --targets=native,wasm_wasi` reports only the mismatch, as error[typecheck] with a snippet, once under "── all targets ──" (design.md §16 Checking several targets: Deduplication). `targets = ["native"]` alone checks clean. strings.md: split/split_whitespace return lazy iterators. `v.iter().count()` and `for w in s.split_whitespace()` pass in the matrix; only an iterator method on split's result fails, which looks like an older string-method table on this path. Found on a wcount package (stdin word count with `#[target]`-gated fns): build and run were right on native, node and wasmtime while check refused it.
fix: bfe76c98a7: a multi-target sweep (`[build] targets` with two or more) checks each target the way a one-target `karac check` does: src/cli/run_check_cmds.rs check_package_for_target runs the v2 check of the package's combined source when the package check refuses only by type, and reports its errors (remapped to the package files) in place of the per-module typecheck's, so `s.split(" ").count()` and `s.split_whitespace().count()` pass under every target. A diagnostic every target reports is printed once under "── all targets ──", and each target ends "N error(s) under target 'T'.", as a file sweep does. Tests: tests/check_package_targets.rs (a two-target package passes the row's program; a real type error is reported once, under all targets).

title: The E0411 target-gate message cites a section that does not exist ("design.md § Cross-target Compilation"; the rule is §16 "Effect-driven target gating") and offers "bind a provider for 'ProcessTable'", which has no provider trait to bind (io.md has none, and no fake is planned)
detail: karac 0.8.1-dev+g52dadc1b9 with the wasm runtime archive rebuilt at that commit; modules run under node 22 WASI and wasmtime (Python bindings). `import std.process.{Command}; fn run_it() -> i64 { match Command.new("echo").arg("x").output() { Ok(o) => o.stdout.len(), Err(_) => -1 } } fn main() { println(run_it()); }` with `--targets=wasm_wasi`: error E0411 "target `wasm_wasi` does not provide resource 'ProcessTable' — required on the call chain main → run_it → Command.output; gate it with `#[target(...)]`, bind a provider for 'ProcessTable', or keep it off this target's entry path (design.md § Cross-target Compilation)". The chain and span are right. The text header says error[effect] while JSON says E0411. `karac explain E0411` describes the family generically and gives no example of the target gate.
fix: 42045bc039: the E0411 target-gate message (src/effectchecker/target_gate.rs) cites "design.md § Effect-driven target gating", the section that states the rule, and offers "or provide a '<R>' provider" only for a resource a provider can bind: NO_PROVIDER_RESOURCES (`ProcessTable`, `Heap`, `Hardware`, `GpuBuffer`) get "gate it with `#[target(...)]`, or keep it off this target's entry path". Tests: tests/target_gate_message.rs (the citation; `FileSystem` on wasm_browser offers a provider, `ProcessTable` on wasm_wasi does not); tests/target_gate_library_process.rs now counts 'ProcessTable' once.

title: `karac::run_playground` (the playground, and the book test's only gate for `kara,run` blocks) runs a program that `karac check` and kara-lsp refuse: the book's ch14 TaskGroup example (`for handle in handles { total = total + handle.join(); }`) is E0515 on the CLI and in the editor, yet tests/book_snippets.rs passes it because a Run block never goes through `check_source`
detail: karac 0.8.1-dev+g1a4b30456. docs/book/src/ch14-concurrency.md line 54, fence `kara,run`. `karac check` and kara-lsp (didOpen): error E0515 at 15:25 "cannot move a `for` element out of the collection: a bare `for` borrows it, and this method takes `self` by value; help: iterate with `.into_iter()`" (core-semantics: a bare `for` borrows). `cargo test --release --test book_snippets` at the same tree: 1 passed. In tests/book_snippets.rs, Class::Run calls only `run_playground(&src)` and accepts `r.ok`; `run_playground` runs `run_static_checks`, not the editor pipeline that B-2026-10-31-19 (afe068e2fe) gave `check_source` (strict_core + library), so the move error never fires and the program runs and prints 30. Two consequences: the book shows a newcomer code that does not compile, and the playground accepts programs the compiler rejects. Fix both: make `run_playground` run the same checks as `check_source` before executing, or have the harness run `static_check` on Run blocks too. The book block itself needs `.into_iter()` (sent to the review thread with the prose list).
fix: 91d981fdda: `karac::run_playground` (src/lib.rs) refuses exactly what `karac check` refuses: it takes the error diagnostics of check_source, the path kara-lsp and the editor use, instead of the older run_static_checks, so a program `karac check` refuses never reaches the playground's interpreter and one it accepts is not refused. The ch14 atomics example drops its MemoryOrdering arguments (`fetch_add(1)`, `load()`), which the older checks demanded and `karac check` does not. Tests: tests/playground_matches_check.rs (a bare `for` moving its elements out, which check refuses, does not run; an atomic without an ordering, which check accepts, runs); src/lib.rs playground_tests::check_source_matches_run_playground_static_prefix compares the two whole, codes and help included; tests/book_snippets.rs passes.

title: Some diagnostics print two headers on one line: `error[typecheck]: f.kara:2:1: error[E_SECRET_TRAIT_FORBIDDEN]: cannot implement ...` and `error[resolve]: f.kara:2:1: error[E_MODULE_BINDING_NAMING]: module-level binding name ...`, where every other error has one `error[CODE]:` prefix
detail: karac 0.8.1-dev+g1a4b30456. `import std.secret.{Secret}; impl Display for Secret[String] { fn fmt(ref self) -> String { "leak" } } fn main() {}` and `#[thread_local] let mut request_count: i64 = 0;` (both from the book: ch19-secrets L58, appendix-d L125). The inner code is part of the message text, so the JSON `code` field and the text header disagree about which code the error has. The book quotes the E_SECRET_TRAIT_FORBIDDEN text with one header.
fix: 89825abf23: a diagnostic whose message carries its own catalogue code prints it as its one header: src/cli.rs render_text_diagnostics turns `error[typecheck]: f.kara:2:1: error[E_X]: msg` into `error[E_X]: f.kara:2:1: msg` (hoist_embedded_code, strip_embedded_code), and the JSON entry (src/cli/diag_json.rs) carries the message without the code and the name as a `"symbol"` field beside `"code"`. Tests flipped to the one header: comptime_mir, core_assoc_projection, core_cross_task_bound, core_cross_task_generic, core_default_copy_dedup, core_strict_check, literal_temporaries_and_empty_let, core_derive_lists, cli run_value_corrupting_cast_aborts, and the design pin err_non_exhaustive_std_enum_needs_a_wildcard's expected.out.

title: A literal inserted into a `Map` or `SortedMap` is not fixed by the parameter the map is handed to: `let mut d = SortedMap.new(); d.insert(1, 2); m(d);` with `fn m(d: SortedMap[i32, i64])` is refused 'expected SortedMap[i32, i64], found SortedMap[i64, i64]', though the same with `Vec.new()`, `push` and a `Vec[i32]` parameter is accepted
detail: design.md §8 Literals / § Type inference: a later use fixes a literal, and the -07-3 pin (corpus/design/ok_a_literal_takes_the_type_a_later_use_gives_it) has a Vec's pushes fixed by the parameter the Vec is handed to. At b85cf41506: `fn m(d: SortedMap[i32, i64]) { println(d.len()) } fn main() { let mut d = SortedMap.new(); d.insert(1, 2); m(d); }` is refused at the call with 'a number held inside a collection ... keeps its type'; `Map` likewise ('expected Map[i32, i64], found Map[i64, i64]'); `let mut v = Vec.new(); v.push(1); vv(v);` into `Vec[i32]` prints 1. `push` keeps its argument's literal open (`method_vec_mutation.rs`, infer_expr_open); the map's `insert` settles its key and value at i64 first. Found while pinning B-2026-11-08-21 (a SortedMap[i32, ..] built from literals in a test program).
fix: 695f9ff6f4, with ee2d9fee79. An insert into an unannotated Map/SortedMap takes its key and value literals open (check_map_slot_arg_inner, typechecker/stdlib_map.rs), as Vec.push does, so the map handed to a SortedMap[i32, i64] or Map[i32, i8] parameter fixes them; a literal lookup key (contains_key(1)) stays open too, and a pushed or inserted tuple literal's numbers are open. Closing the hole the gate found (B-2026-11-08-89) was part of this: an open key had let Map[?, i64] pass for Map[i64, u64]. Printing a value read out of the map still settles it at i64, as it does for a Vec. Pinned by corpus/design/ok_a_map_s_inserted_literals_take_the_type_a_later_use_gives_them; the strict-check fixture defaulted-map-into-a-u64-field now refuses only a typed i64 value and map-literal-into-a-u64-field accepts the literal.

title: A temporary passed to a `mut ref` parameter (`total(mut v.iter().map(..).collect())`) checks clean and is then handed over as if it were a reference: the interpreter stops with `deref of non-reference Box`, and a `karac build` binary segfaults
detail: Found writing kata 2007's differential, where an arm took `mut ref Vec[i64]` and a mutation passed it `mut xs.iter().map(..).collect()`. Minimal: `fn total(xs: mut ref Vec[i64]) -> i64 { xs.push(1); xs.len() }` and `println(total(mut v.iter().map(|x| x * 2).collect()));` with `v = [1, 2, 3]`. `karac check` passes. `__mir-run`: `error[mir]: run: in main at bb7[term]: in total at bb0[0]: deref of non-reference Box(AllocId(2))`. `__mir-llvm-run`: exit 101 with no output; a `karac build` binary: segfault (139). Measured with a release karac on 2026-11-08 (origin/main c2c1c98fa5 plus the kata 2007 and 2008 fix commits). Either the checker refuses `mut <temporary>` (Rust's `&mut vec![..]` is accepted, so the natural reading is a borrow of a temporary that lives to the end of the statement) or MIR lowering spills the temporary to a local and passes its address; today it passes the value.
fix: 4f7a9a30a8. The checker typed a bare `collect()` at a `mut ref Vec[i64]` parameter as the slot itself: check_expr bound `collect`'s `C` (and recorded the node's type) from the expectation as it stood, so typed HIR said the argument was already a `mut ref`. Lowering then passed the Vec value where the callee expected an address, which gave `deref of non-reference Box` in the interpreter and a segfault in the binary. Fix (src/typechecker/exprs.rs, check_expr): lent to a borrowed slot, a bare `collect()` builds the value the borrow is of (core-semantics §4.1, §5.5). The expectation is peeled before `C` is bound and the node type recorded. Lowering already spills a value argument at a `mut ref` parameter into a statement-long temporary and drops it at the `;`, as `total(mut make())` always did, so no lowering change was needed. A second shape fixed with it: `let q: ref Vec[i64] = it.collect();` used to check clean and then stop the interpreter. It is now refused by the §5.5 temporary rule, as `let q: ref Vec[i64] = make();` already was (CHANGELOG, refusals). Pins: corpus/core/ok_collect_temporary_lent_to_mut_ref (a Vec[i64] and a Vec[String] temporary; passes on mir-interp, mir-llvm and mir-llvm-asan, so LeakSanitizer sees the String temporary dropped) and corpus/core/err_collect_temporary_kept_by_ref_let.

title: `v.iter().skip(1).fold(0, |x, a| x + 1)` returned as `i32` is refused (`implicit coercion from 'i64' to 'i32'`), though `v.iter().fold(0, ..)` and `(0..3).fold(0, ..)` take `i32` from the return; a follow-up of B-2026-11-07-57
detail: Found writing a mutation of kata 2011's Rust-template arm (`operations.iter().skip(1).fold(0, ..)` in a method returning `i32`). Minimal: `fn steps(v: Vec[i64]) -> i32 { v.iter().skip(1).fold(0, |x, a| x + 1) }`: `error[typecheck]: implicit coercion from 'i64' to 'i32' would narrow or change sign` on the whole call. Without `.skip(1)`, and over a range, the same fold checks clean and the `0` takes `i32`. The adapter's fold is the library's generic `fold[AccV]` (runtime/stdlib/source/iter.kara), checked through `check_call_args_with_substitution_full`, where the literal is fixed to `i64` when it is checked rather than unified with the expected return; the direct `Vec.iter().fold` goes through the built-in path in stdlib_iter.rs that defers it. Same family as B-2026-11-07-57 (a literal not fixed by a generic call), filed apart because the shape and the code path differ. Measured with a release karac on 2026-11-08 (origin/main c2c1c98fa5 plus the kata 2007 and 2008 fix commits).
fix: af14c52dbd (with acff3747c3, 5f6bdc9460). A literal written as the argument of a generic call that returns that parameter (fold, id, max) stays open, so the call's result fixes it: `v.iter().skip(1).fold(0, ..)` returned as i32 counts in i32. The literal stays typed at the call where only a bound reads the parameter (`open(2, 3)` returning T's Add output) or a constructor wraps it (`Some(5)`), or where the slot cannot be a number. A literal variable now meets an empty sibling's slot at an if/match join (`if c { Some(x) } else { None }`), takes the function's error type at `Err(1)?`, settles inside a constructor before a comparison reads item types, and its call frame is recorded once it settles (the monomorphization budget counts it). Pin corpus/design/ok_a_generic_call_s_literal_argument_takes_the_type_of_its_result.

title: Rust's `scan` closure over a `&mut` state (`|m, x| { *m = (*m).max(x); Some(*m) }`) draws six `drop the *` fixes that leave `Some(m)` and a type error `expected 'Option[(i64, OutV)]', found 'Option[i64]'`, with no fix and no word that Kāra's `scan` closure returns `Some((next_state, item))`
detail: Found writing kata 2012's scan arm in Rust's shape first. Minimal: `let m: Vec[i64] = v.iter().scan(0, |m, x| { *m = (*m).max(x); Some(*m) }).collect();`. `karac check`: three `unary '*' requires 'ref T' ... a 'i64' is copied, so drop the `*`` errors; `karac fix` drops them, leaving `m = (m).max(x); Some(m)`, which reports `expected 'Option[(i64, OutV)]', found 'Option[i64]'` at `Some(m)` and `expected 'Fn(i64, ref i64) -> Option[(i64, OutV)]'` at the closure. The program a Rust author meant is `let m = m.max(x); Some((m, m))`. Wanted: when a `scan` closure's body returns `Option[T]` rather than `Option[(S, T)]`, say that Kāra's `scan` closure takes the state by value and returns `Some((next_state, item))`, and ideally offer that rewrite when the state was assigned in the body. Measured with a release karac on 2026-11-08 (origin/main c2c1c98fa5 plus the kata 2007 and 2008 fix commits).
fix: 3af0db7bb7. src/typechecker/rust_scan.rs: after a `scan` call whose check failed inside its closure, `explain_rust_scan` (hooked in `infer_method_call`) looks for Rust's shape. The shape is a closure whose first parameter is a plain name that the body only ever dereferences, with a tail `Some(item)` where `item` is not a pair. When it finds that shape, the call's errors inside the closure are replaced by one: "this closure writes the state `m` through `*m`, as Rust's `scan` does; Kāra's `scan` closure takes the state by value and returns `Some((next_state, item))`, where Rust's lends it to be written in place". When every write of the state is a top-level statement of the body and there is no `return`, the diagnostic also carries a whole-closure fix: `*m = e` becomes `let m = e`, `*m op= e` becomes `let m = m op e`, every other `*m` becomes `m`, and the tail becomes `Some((m, item))`. The fix is rendered on one line when the closure is short; for the row's cell `karac fix` writes `|m, x| { let m = m.max(x); Some((m, m)) }`. A state written under a branch gets the message with "bind each new state with `let m = ..` and return `Some((m, item))`" and no fix. A `scan` written Kāra's way is untouched, since the rewrite only runs on a failed check. Pins: tests/rust_scan_and_last_mut_fixes.rs (one error instead of the six `drop the *` fixes, the rewrite and its output on the row's cell and on `*acc += x`, the branch case, and a Kāra-shaped scan left alone).

title: Rust's `match ans.last_mut() { Some(last) if last[1] == prev && last[2] == avg => last[1] = pos, _ => ans.push(..) }` gets `no method 'last_mut' on type 'Vec': write through an index instead` with no machine fix, though the index form it describes is mechanical for this shape
detail: Found carrying kata 2015's Rust template (kara-katas leetcode/2001-2100/2015-average-height-of-buildings-in-each-segment/average_solution.kara) through `karac fix`: three rounds (32, 2, 6 edits) leave `match ans.last_mut() { Some(last) if last[1] == prev and last[2] == avg => last[1] = pos, _ => ans.push([prev, pos, avg]), }`, refused with `no method 'last_mut' on type 'Vec': write through an index instead (`v[v.len() - 1] = ..`, or `v[v.len() - 1].field = ..`), after checking the vector is not empty` and no fix. Written by hand as `let n = ans.len(); if n > 0 and ans[n - 1][1] == prev and ans[n - 1][2] == avg { ans[n - 1][1] = pos; } else { ans.push([prev, pos, avg]); }` the arm checks and prints the mirror's output (with `prev: i32`, B-2026-11-08-21). The `match v.last_mut() { Some(x) if g => body, _ => other }` and `if let Some(x) = v.last_mut() { body }` shapes are the common Rust idioms for growing-or-extending a run (LeetCode merge-intervals, run-length and segment problems), and both rewrite mechanically: bind `n = v.len()`, guard `n > 0 and g[x := v[n - 1]]`, substitute `v[n - 1]` for `x` in the body. Wanted: that rewrite as a machine fix where the body only reads and writes through `x`; the message as it is where it does more. Measured with a release karac on 2026-11-08.
fix: 3af0db7bb7. src/typechecker/rust_last_mut.rs notes a rewrite when a `match`/`if let` is inferred, keyed by the receiver span (`end_mut_rewrites`). The shapes are `match v.last_mut() { Some(x) if g => body, _ => other }` and `if let Some(x) = v.last_mut() { body } [else ..]`, and `first_mut` too. The receiver must be a plain place (`v`, `self.runs`), and neither the guard nor the body may name the receiver's root or rebind `x`. The refusal of `last_mut`/`first_mut` (method_user_impl.rs, B-2026-11-06-39) then carries a whole-expression fix: `if v.len() > 0 and g' { body' } else { other }`, where `x` and `*x` read `v[v.len() - 1]` (or `v[0]`). The fix is indented to the expression's column; when it is longer than one line, the message says it "rewrites mechanically, as `karac fix` writes it". When the shape doesn't hold, the message is unchanged and there is no fix. Kata 2015's average_solution.kara now carries through `karac fix` to a clean check (its other blocker, B-2026-11-08-21, was already fixed), and its output matches average.py byte for byte. Pins: tests/rust_scan_and_last_mut_fixes.rs (the kata's guarded `match` and an `if let` with `*r += 4`, rewritten text and output; an arm naming the vector keeps the plain message).

title: A sequence has no `split` by a predicate: Rust's `line.split(|&ch| ch == '#')` over a `&Vec<char>` is refused "no method 'split' on type 'Vec'" with no fix and no other spelling named, and draws two cascade errors on the closures that read the pieces
detail: Kata 2018's Rust-template arm (LeetCode's natural Rust for Check if Word Can Be Placed In Crossword) cuts each line at its walls with `for seg in line.split(|&ch| ch == '#')`. After `karac fix` drops the `&`, `line.split(|ch| ch == '#')` on a `Vec[char]` is E0236 "no method 'split' on type 'Vec'", with no fix and nothing in the message pointing at a spelling. docs/library/collections.md has `windows`, `chunks` and `split_at` on sequences and `Str.split(sep)` on text, but nothing splits a `Vec` or `Slice` at the elements a predicate picks. The same check also reports two cascade errors, "tuple pattern used but type is `?T5`" and `?T6`, on `seg.iter().zip(w.iter()).all(|(a, b)| ..)`, which only read the unknown pieces. With the split written by hand as a loop that starts a new piece at each wall, the arm checks clean and prints the mirror's output. Shape: kara-katas leetcode/2001-2100/2018-check-if-word-can-be-placed-in-crossword/crossword_solution.kara.
fix: 3af0db7bb7, per the review thread's ruling at e4dc0fb948 (docs/library/collections.md § Slice). `fn split(self, pred: own MutFn(T) -> bool) -> Vec[Slice[T]]` is written in the library (runtime/stdlib/source/collections.kara, beside `partition_point`): the runs between the elements `pred` accepts, which are dropped, empty runs kept at either end and between adjacent separators, so the result has one more run than there are separators, as Rust's `slice::split`. `Vec` and arrays reach it as every `Slice` method, and a `Slice[T]` parameter or range view too. With the method there, the kata 2018 shape `for seg in line.split(|&ch| ch == '#')` checks after `karac fix` drops the `&`, and the two cascade errors on `seg.iter().zip(..)` are gone because the pieces are typed. Pins: tests/slice_split_by_predicate.rs (Vec, `Vec[String]`, an array, a `Slice` view, a stateful predicate, an empty vector; byte-identical on __mir-run, __mir-llvm-run, run and the built binary; and kata 2018's Rust arm carried by `karac fix` to a clean check that prints `true`), in CI's codegen-e2e line.

title: An `isize` operand beside an `i64` passes `karac check` and the MIR builder then refuses the program: `fn f(i: isize, k: i64) -> i64 { i - k }` is 'invalid MIR: binary operands of different types isize and i64'
detail: Found while fixing B-2026-11-08-18, at b07678a0f8 and on the binary before it. `fn f(i: isize, k: i64) -> i64 { i - k } fn main() { println(f(10, 2)) }`: `karac check` says 'All checks passed.' and `karac __mir-run` stops with 'error[mir]: run: invalid MIR: f: bb0[0]: binary operands of different types isize and i64'. The same with `let k = 2; i - k` over `i: isize` (the literal keeps i64 because the checker treats isize as widening into i64). design.md § Mixed-width operands lists no isize row; either the checker refuses the mix (as `i32 + u32` is) or the builder widens the isize operand, per a spec call.
fix: af14c52dbd. isize and usize widen as 32-or-64-bit types (design.md § Mixed-width operands, 91324ad352): the MIR builder widens an isize beside an i64 (and a usize beside a u64) instead of emitting mismatched operands, so `fn f(i: isize, k: i64) -> i64 { i - k }` builds and runs; and the checker's widening rule counts them as 64 bits as a source and 32 as a destination, so i64 or u32 into isize and u64 into usize now need `as` at a binding, argument or return (they were accepted). Pins corpus/design/ok_isize_and_usize_widen_as_32_or_64_bits and err_an_i64_into_isize_needs_as.

title: `karac fix` half-rewrites `usize` to `i64`: the 'usize mixes with i64' fix retypes a nested `fn dfs(u: usize, p: usize, adj: ref Vec[Vec[usize]])`'s parameters and one `let n = n as usize`, but leaves the callers' `e[1] as usize` pushes and `usize.MAX`, so a Rust template that checked up to that round ends with mismatches the fix created
detail: Repro (LeetCode's Rust template shape, kata 1519): a method with a nested `fn dfs(u: usize, p: usize, adj: &Vec<Vec<usize>>, ans: &mut Vec<i32>) -> i32`, adjacency built by `adj[e[0] as usize].push(e[1] as usize)`, started by `dfs(0, usize::MAX, &adj, &mut ans)`. `karac fix` makes 20, 2, 7, 5 edits over four rounds and then has nothing to apply. Round 4's diagnostics are 'this type mixes with i64 ... write i64 here' on the three parameter types and 'this `as usize` makes a usize that mixes with i64 ... cast to i64' on `let n = n as usize` only; the fix applies those four (plus `vec![..; n]` to `Vec.filled`). Left behind: `adj` is now `Vec[Vec[i64]]` by the parameter but filled with `e[1] as usize` (error: expected `ref Vec[Vec[i64]]`, found `Vec[Vec[usize]]` at the call), and `usize.MAX` passed to `p: i64` (implicit coercion from usize to i64 would narrow). Before round 4 neither error existed: the half-applied rewrite created them. Expected: either retype every `as usize` / `usize.MAX` that flows into the retyped parameters (`usize.MAX` has no i64 equivalent a fix can pick blindly; `-1` is the template's intent) or not offer the parameter rewrite as machine-applicable when its arguments stay usize. The other errors left (`[0; 26]`, `Vec.filled(n, 0)` staying i64 where i32 is wanted) are B-2026-11-08-18.
fix: 0600aebf3 karac fix: every user-written `as usize` now gets the cast fix whenever the program mixes usize with i64 (drop it over an i64, else cast to i64), not only the initializer of an unannotated let, and `usize.MAX` / `isize.MAX` become `i64.MAX` with the written types (src/typechecker/pointer_ints.rs, exprs.rs Cast arm, fields.rs). The row's repro (kata 1519's template shape) now goes through karac fix to a program that checks and prints the subtree sizes on both backends. Pinned by tests/fix_usize_every_use.rs, which fails without the fix. In a program that declares FFI items the casts are still left alone, as the let-initializer fix already did. What remains of that template (`Vec.filled(n, 0)` handed to a `Vec[i32]` parameter) is collection literal typing, not this row.

title: A `ref` number passed to a library native reaches it as its address: `"A".repeat(n)` with `n` a `ref i64` from `.iter().map(|n| ..)` stops the interpreter with "expected a library value, found Int(999)" and panics the LLVM backend at compile time; `substring` and `rotate_left` fail the same way
detail: FOUND 2026-11-08 writing kara-katas leetcode/1001-1100/1071-greatest-common-divisor-of-strings, whose ★ arm prints `[999, 600, 250, 1].iter().map(|n| gcd_of_strings(a1000, "A".repeat(n)).len())`. `karac check` accepts it: core semantics §5.10 reads a `ref` to a `Copy` value as the value wherever the value is expected, an argument included. MIR lowering's library-method argument loop passed the `ref i64` operand through unchanged, so `karac __mir-run` stopped with `expected a library value, found Int(999)` and `karac __mir-llvm-run` panicked in int_arg (src/backend/mir/call.rs) compiling the call. The same holds for `s.substring(n)`, `s.substring(0, n)` and `w.rotate_left(n)` with `n` a `ref i64`, and for `(i, j)` bound over `pairs.iter()` passed to `w.swap(i, j)`. A user function taking `i64` already read the value; only library natives took the reference.
fix: 9671efaf31. MIR lowering's library-method argument loop (src/mir/lower.rs) now reads a scalar referent (integer, float, bool, char) as its value when the native's parameter slot is not itself a reference and the receiver's element types hold no references, so repeat, substring, rotate_left, swap and Map.get take the number. Pinned by corpus/core/ok_ref_number_as_native_argument (spec, §5.10) and tests/kata_1071_native_ref_arg.rs (interp and compiled; control 0/2, fix 2/2). Kata 1071's ★ arm prints the same 14 lines on every lane.

title: Two `format!` calls in one condition (`if format!(..) != format!(..) {`) end the condition at the first call's name: only that call is reported, the `!=` throws the rest of the function out of step ("expected `;`", "Expected expression, found `}`", top-level statements), and karac fix puts a `;` after the function's tail expression
detail: FOUND 2026-11-08 carrying LeetCode 1071's Rust template (`if format!("{}{}", str1, str2) != format!("{}{}", str2, str1) { return String::new(); }`) to Kāra with karac fix. The Rust-macro recovery reported `format!` where a statement or the condition began, but the condition's expression parser stopped at the identifier `format` and handed `!` back as a prefix operator, so the second call was never seen as a macro call. The cascade produced half a dozen diagnostics far from the cause, and karac fix's machine-applicable `;` after the function's tail expression turned the function's result into unit, so a second round failed differently. With one `format!` per condition the fix converted it in one round.
fix: 9671efaf31. The parser's identifier primary (src/parser/exprs.rs) now recognises a Rust macro call (`name!(..)`, `name![..]`, `name!{..}`) where an operand's name is parsed: it reports the macro, skips the bracketed group and yields an error operand, so the rest of the condition and the function parse in step. Both `format!` calls are reported and karac fix converts them to f-strings in one round, with no `;` after the tail. tests/kata_1071_check_gaps.rs (control 0/2, fix 2/2); tests/parser.rs 922 passed.

title: `v.iter().skip(k)` walks the k skipped items one at a time, so a `skip(i * n).take(n)` row walk over a Vec is quadratic where Rust's slice iterator jumps
detail: Found writing kata 2022's iterator arm (kara-katas leetcode/2001-2100/2022-convert-1d-array-into-2d-array): each row was first `original.iter().skip(i * n).take(n).collect()`, which ran over 120 s under `karac __mir-run` with m = 50000 rows of 1. Measured alone: 50000 calls of `v.iter().skip(i).take(1).sum()` over a 50000-element Vec take 0.91 s under `__mir-llvm-run` against 0.23 s with `skip(0)`; rustc -O runs the same loop in 0.002 s, since `Skip` over a slice `Iter` calls `nth`, which moves the pointer. The interpreter shows the same walk. The kata's iter arm now shares one iterator across the rows through `by_ref().take(n)`, which is linear; the `skip` spelling is kept in the row's shapes. Shape: `fn main() { let v: Vec[i64] = (0..50000).collect(); let mut total = 0; for i in 0..50000 { total += v.iter().skip(i).take(1).sum(); } println(total); }`.
fix:
871134eeb3. `IterSkip.next` and the provided `nth` (runtime/stdlib/source/iter.kara) now step past their items with one `advance_by`. VecIter, VecIterMut, SliceIter and SliceIterMut (collections.kara) override `advance_by` to move their index; a range already did. Iterators without an override keep the walking default, so an adaptor's closure still runs on each skipped item. `nth(-1)` stays None. The row's shape, 50,000 `v.iter().skip(i).take(1).sum()` over a 50,000-element Vec, runs in 0.30 s under `__mir-run` and 0.24 s under `__mir-llvm-run`, compile time included; it was over 120 s under the interpreter. The 312 corpus programs that use skip, nth or PriorityQueue fail exactly the same set as a main control on all three lanes. Pinned by corpus/design/ok_skip_and_nth_jump_on_index_iterators, which covers:
- skip past the end
- nth past the end, and a negative nth
- iter_mut().skip
- a mapped iterator
- a range's skip then nth

title: `karac fix` drops a closure's `-> i32` and with it the type of the literal-typed tuple binding it returns, leaving `res.max(x as i32)` ("`max` expects an argument of type `i64`, got `i32`") and a narrowing at the caller with no fix and no binding named
detail: Kata 2024's Rust-template arm (LeetCode's natural Rust for Maximize the Confusion of an Exam, kara-katas leetcode/2001-2100/2024-maximize-the-confusion-of-an-exam/confuse_solution.kara) is `let longest = |c: u8| -> i32 { let (mut l, mut cnt, mut res) = (0usize, 0, 0); for r in 0..s.len() { if s[r] != c { cnt += 1; } while cnt > k { if s[l] != c { cnt -= 1; } l += 1; } res = res.max((r - l + 1) as i32); } res }; longest(b'T').max(longest(b'F'))` in an `i32` function. `karac fix` makes ten edits in two rounds (8, 2), among them dropping the closure's `-> i32` (a Kāra closure declares no return type) and 8bee9acf06's usize-suffix edit, and ends with two refusals and no fix: "`max` expects an argument of type `i64`, got `i32`" at `res.max(..)`, and the implicit narrowing `i64` to `i32` at `longest(b'T').max(longest(b'F'))`. In Rust the `-> i32` typed `res`; once it is dropped the literal `0` keeps its default (design.md § Type inference), and neither refusal names `res` or the tuple. 7ae9bc82c0's literal-annotation fix covers `let name = <literal>` at a narrowing site, but not a tuple-pattern element and not a method-argument refusal. Written by hand as `let mut (l, cnt, res): (i64, i32, i32) = (0, 0, 0);` the arm checks clean and prints the mirror's output.
fix: bfd2f7b286: the checker records a literal-typed tuple or fill binding with the binding it should fix (its own, or the one a `let y = x` copies), so the suffix fix lands on the declaration, also when the literal reaches the tuple through `min`/`max`. Pinned by tests/kata_2024_check_gaps.rs; kata 2024's Rust arm reaches a clean check through karac fix alone.

title: Rust's array type inside a generic argument (`Vec[[i64; 2]]`) is taken for a shape literal: check reports "Expected `]`, found `;`" instead of the `[T; N]` diagnostic, and karac fix inserts a second `;` (`Vec[[i64; 2;]]`)
detail: FOUND 2026-11-08 writing kara-katas leetcode/1001-1100/1072-flip-columns-for-maximum-number-of-equal-rows, whose trie arm was first written `let mut next: Vec[[i64; 2]] = [[-1, -1]];`. On its own `[T; N]` is reported as Rust's array type with a machine fix to `Array[T, N]` (B-2026-10-20-27, src/parser/types.rs), but in a generic argument list (src/parser/generics.rs) a `[` always started a shape literal (`Tensor[f64, [3, 4]]`). The shape parser read `i64` as a dimension and stopped at the `;`: "Expected `]`, found `;`", then "expected `;` after this expression statement" and "Expected expression, found `]`" for `Map[String, [i64; 3]]` in a let. karac fix applied the `;` fix, giving `Vec[[i64; 2;]]`, which still fails. The same holds for a parameter type `rows: Vec[[i64; 2]]`.
fix: 274ec2990d. In a generic argument list (src/parser/generics.rs) a `[` whose bracket holds a `;` at its own depth (Parser::bracket_holds_semicolon, src/parser.rs) is no shape literal, so it is parsed as a type, and the type parser's recovery reports Rust's array type with the machine fix to `Array[T, N]`. `Vec[[i64; 2]]`, `Map[String, [i64; 3]]` and a parameter `Vec[[i64; 2]]` fix in one round and run (tests/kata_1072_check_gaps.rs; control on the pre-fix binary: three parse errors and `Vec[[i64; 2;]]` after fix). Shape literals keep parsing (tests/parser.rs 922 passed).

title: A call to a closure puts its arguments' borrows in the closure itself, not in what the closure's `mut ref` captures reach: `|extra: Vec[i64]| total += extra.len()` called twice with temporaries is a false E0516, and `|s: Str| keep.push(s)` with `keep: Vec[Str]` lets a view of a freed String through
fix: b4d55d0ffb: transfer_call stores a `mut ref` argument's loans through store_through_call. For a closure-typed target it forwards them to what the closure's `mut ref` captures borrow (and into an owned capture only when its type holds borrows), instead of keeping them in the closure. So a closure whose captures hold no borrow is called twice without a false E0516, and a closure that pushes a borrowed String into a `mut ref` capture is refused (E0516) rather than printing freed memory. Pinned by corpus/core/ok_a_mutating_closure_keeps_no_argument_borrow and err_a_closure_stores_its_argument_in_a_capture; mini_prometheus_client's parallel workers now check and match on all 8 lanes.

title: RULING WANTED (Str vs String): `["inc", "dec"].contains(cmd)` with `cmd: Str`, and `names.contains(s)` on a `Vec[String]`, are refused "expected 'ref String', found 'Str'" with a `.to_string()` fix, while `Map[String, _].contains_key(s)` takes the view and `let cmds: Vec[Str] = [..]; cmds.contains(cmd)` works
detail: Found writing apps/cli/mini_prometheus_client: `fn is_update(cmd: Str) -> bool { ["inc", "dec", "set", "observe", "state", "reset"].contains(cmd) }`. The literals default to `String`, so the list is a `Vec[String]` and `contains(val: T)` wants a `String`; `karac fix` applies `cmd.to_string()`, which allocates per call. Measured at karac 0.8.1-dev+g17e2a7ea2: the same with a `ref Vec[String]` parameter is refused the same way; `Map[String, i64].contains_key(s)` with `s: Str` checks and runs (collections.md: a view and its owner compare identically as keys); an annotated `Vec[Str]` list works. The spec does not say whether a list of literals checked against a `Str` argument takes `Str` (strings.md: a literal is `Str` where a `Str` is expected), or whether `Vec[String].contains` accepts a view the way map lookups do. The review thread asked for a row rather than a choice in code (after B-2026-11-08-33). The app uses the fix's `.to_string()` meanwhile.
fix: e59006b616: per the review thread's ruling (652da777a5, docs/library/collections.md "Lookup by view"), `contains` on a Vec, Slice or VecDeque of String or Vec[T] elements and `binary_search` on a Vec or Slice take the element's view. The typechecker's Slice/Vec probe arms and the library-method view hook accept a Str / Slice[T] needle once the element type is solved (is_elem_view); a Vec or VecDeque `contains` with a view lowers to the library's new vec_contains_str/_slice and deque_contains_str/_slice, whose needle is the view; a Slice's contains and binary_search keep their natives, which already read either form. The list's literals stay Strings. Pinned by corpus/design/ok_a_sequence_search_takes_the_element_view (interp, llvm, ASan, build). 62e20a9d06 flips the two karac fix pins that relied on the refusal (tests/fix_as_str_borrow.rs, tests/fix_suffix_on_loose_expr.rs). mini_prometheus_client drops its .to_string() (kara-katas 82853165).

title: An unannotated array or `Vec` literal's element type is not fixed by where the binding goes: `let mut cnt = [0; 26]; ..; cnt` returned as `Array[i32, 26]`, and `let mut ans = Vec.filled(n, 0); dfs(.., mut ans)` into `ans: mut ref Vec[i32]`, are refused, and the binding annotation the message itself names gets no machine fix
detail: Found re-carrying kata 1519's Rust template (labels_solution.kara) after B-2026-11-08-49: the usize half is now carried, and four errors are left. (1) `fn dfs(..) -> Array[i32, 26] { let mut cnt = [0; 26]; for v in ref adj[u] { .. let sub = dfs(..); for c in 0..26 { cnt[c] += sub[c]; } } .. cnt[c] += 1; ans[u] = cnt[c]; cnt }`: `ans[u] = cnt[c]` is refused 'implicit coercion from i64 to i32' and the tail `cnt` 'expected Array[i32, 26], found Array[i64, 26]'. Rust fixes the literal's type from the return type (and from `cnt[c] += sub[c]` with `sub: [i32; 26]`). (2) `let mut ans = Vec.filled(n, 0); dfs(0, i64.MAX, adj, labels, mut ans); ans` in a function returning `Vec[i32]`, with dfs's `ans: mut ref Vec[i32]`: 'expected mut ref Vec[i32], found Vec[i64]: a number held inside a collection .. keeps its type .. annotate the binding (`let x: Vec[i32] = ...`)', and the same at the tail. The message names the edit but carries no fix. B-2026-11-08-18's fix (7ae9bc82c0) covers a scalar binding's literal (`: i32` on its `let` as a machine fix); this is the collection half. Sibling of B-2026-11-08-42 (a literal inserted into a Map not fixed by the parameter the map is handed to). Wanted: either the literal's element type fixed by the return / the `mut ref` parameter it is handed to (design.md §8 Literals decides), or the `let cnt: Array[i32, 26]` / `let ans: Vec[i32]` annotation as a machine fix where one use fixes it. Hand-edited with those two annotations, the arm checks and prints the other arms' output on every lane. Measured with release karac at 218952d3b.
fix: 8da3c36f75: an unannotated `let` whose value is `[v; n]` or `Vec.filled(n, v)` leaves v's number literal open (src/typechecker open_collection_let, set at the let in items.rs and read by the RepeatLiteral arm in exprs.rs and Vec.filled in expr_call.rs), so a return, an argument or an assignment fixes it, as design.md §8 Literals says: `let mut cnt = [0; 26]; .. cnt` returned as `Array[i32, 26]` and `let mut ans = Vec.filled(n, 0); dfs(.., mut ans)` into a `mut ref Vec[i32]` now check and run. Where an operator settles the element at i64 first (kata 1519's `cnt[c] += sub[c]` with `sub: [i32; 26]`, which widens), the refusal of the whole collection (returned, or handed to a parameter) names the binding and carries the literal's suffix (`0i32`) as its machine fix (literal_collection_annotation, reading the fill's LiteralLet entry B-2026-11-08-53 records), the same edit as the element-read refusal, so kata 1519's labels_solution.kara checks after one `karac fix` and matches the Python mirror. Not covered: a plain list literal (`let v = [0, 0]`), whose elements stay closed (opening them regressed two design pins), filed as its own row. Tests: corpus/design/ok_a_repeat_literal_s_element_is_fixed_by_its_use (spec); tests/repeat_literal_annotation_fix.rs (the 1519 template).

title: A closure returning `Some((Vec.new(), x))` to a generic `Fn(S) -> Option[(S, O)]` leaves `O` uninferred, and with the state unannotated reports two unifiable function types as a mismatch: `.scan(Vec.new(), |seen, x| Some((Vec.new(), seen.len())))` is refused 'expected Fn(Vec[?T3], ref i64) -> Option[(Vec[?T3], OutV)], found Fn(Vec[i64], ref i64) -> Option[(Vec[i64], OutV)]' and 'cannot infer type parameter OutV'
fix: fbc3d33e01. check_expr's Some/Ok/Err pushdown checked a payload holding Vec.new() against the slot and returned the expected type, which still named the callee's O for a closure checked against Fn(S) -> Option[(S, O)]; the call's unification never saw the payload's type. When the slot is not concrete the constructor's type is now built from the payload's (typechecker/exprs.rs). step(v, |seen| Some((Vec.new(), seen.len()))) and the scan state reset check and run on interp and llvm. Pinned by corpus/design/ok_a_closure_s_some_of_a_tuple_solves_the_callee_s_parameter.

title: An undefined `Deque`, `ArrayDeque`, `deque` or `Queue` gets no suggestion, though `HashMap`, `HashSet`, `BTreeMap` and `BinaryHeap` are each pointed at Kāra's name and a typo like `VecDequ` gets 'did you mean VecDeque': `let mut q: Deque[i64] = Deque.new();` says only 'undefined name Deque' / 'undefined type Deque'
detail: Found writing kata 1522's breadth-first arm, whose first draft spelled the queue `Deque` (Java's and Kotlin's interface name; Python's is `collections.deque`). Measured at 218952d3b with `fn main() { let q: T[i64] = T.new(); }`: HashMap -> 'did you mean Map?', HashSet -> 'Set', BTreeMap -> 'SortedMap', BinaryHeap -> the PriorityQueue explanation, VecDequ -> 'VecDeque'; Deque, ArrayDeque, deque, Queue and LinkedList -> no suggestion. The renames come from `rust_collection_rename` (src/parser.rs), which holds Rust's names only, and the edit-distance suggestion does not reach `Deque` (distance 3 from `VecDeque`). A name that is a suffix of a library type's name, or a short table of other languages' queue names, would cover it; `karac fix` could then rewrite it as it does `HashMap`.
fix: e99826bcc0: an undefined `Deque`, `ArrayDeque`, `deque`, `Queue` or `LinkedList` is renamed to `VecDeque` through the resolver's renamed_stdlib_type (src/resolver.rs), the path `HashMap`, `TreeMap` and `Dict` take, so `karac check` says "did you mean 'VecDeque'?" for the type and the name and `karac fix` rewrites both. A program's own `Queue` is not renamed. Tests: tests/queue_names_suggest_vecdeque.rs (each name is refused, fixed and runs; an own `struct Queue` runs untouched).

title: A `const` declared inside a function body (`const MOD: i64 = 1_000_000_007;`, the usual first line of a LeetCode Rust solution) is a parse error that says 'const is a reserved keyword and cannot be used as an identifier; write `r#const`', advice that does not apply, with no fix; design.md § Constants does not say whether a block may declare one
fix: a90821c8d. Ruled (a) by the review thread (design.md § Constants, 335cdef9b): a block may declare a constant. The parser reads `const NAME: T = e;` in a block as the `let` it is written like and marks it by its name's span in Program::block_const_spans (the freeze_spans channel, so no walk meets a new statement kind), and refuses a value-class name in the initializer: 'the constant `LIMIT` cannot use `x`: a constant is computed at compile time, so its initializer may name other constants but no local binding, parameter or function'. The new first desugar pass, src/block_consts.rs, hoists each to module scope as `NAME__BLOCKn` just before its item and renames the uses its scope reaches (rest of the block, nested blocks and closures, constant patterns and range bounds), up to a later declaration of the same name, which shadows it as a let would; a use before the declaration or outside the block keeps the source name. From there the type and initializer get the module-scope checks and each use is a fresh value. The formatter writes `const` back, and constant diagnostics (heap type, write through a constant, pattern constant) show the source name.
