Tests: tests/block_const.rs (scoping and shadowing, the LeetCode method shape, a local in the initializer, the source name in a diagnostic, use outside the block); pin corpus/core/ok_block_const_first_line (interp, llvm, asan). Kata 1524's Rust template now checks after karac fix and joins its differential.

title: An index into a local Vec, inside a loop bounded by that Vec's length, keeps its bounds check: 459's `for i in d..n { cs[i] .. }` (n = cs.len()) and 484's `while i < letters.len() and letters[i] == 'D'`; 484's `for i in 0..n { perm.push(i + 1) }` fill also stays scalar with a capacity test (remainder of B-2026-11-08-6)
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-08 on x86 at f9b9e70667 (release karac, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build, callgrind against rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on), after B-2026-11-08-6's decode and overflow-test fixes: 459 (kara-katas leetcode/401-500/459-repeated-substring-pattern/bench) 2.97G against Rust's 2.43G; 484 (leetcode/401-500/484-find-permutation/bench) 788M against 550M. 459, optimised IR of the inlined repeated_substring_pattern: the inner loop's latch tests `icmp slt i64 %i1, %len` and the header tests `icmp ult i64 %i, %len` before `cs[i]` (abort at repeated_substring.kara:16:16, `index out of bounds`), so one bounds check runs each of the 170.7M iterations; the loop starts at d >= 1 (phi of 1 and d + 1) and steps `add nuw nsw`, but LLVM does not carry the signed latch test to the unsigned check. `cs[i - d]`'s check and the `i - d` overflow test are gone since f9b9e70667. The facts that would drop it at MIR level: n is `cs.len()` read once into a local, cs is a local Vec not written in the loop, and i < n from the range; range_bounds / guard_bounds take a slice's length from a ref parameter, not from a local Vec's saved length. 484: the same shape in `while i < letters.len() and letters[i] == 'D'` (both D-scan loops, about 53M instructions) where the length is re-read each test, and the fill `for i in 0..n { perm.push(i + 1) }` runs 6 instructions an element with a capacity test where Rust's `(1..=n).collect()` is vectorized at about 2 (presize_fill does not match a push of `i + 1` from a range).
fix: 774d3877a5: src/mir/guard_bounds.rs proves `h <s len` for an index into a local vector written once, whole, and never borrowed mutably (`let cs: Vec[char] = s.chars().collect()`), through the copies a `for` loop makes of its counter (`i = copy counter`) and of its end (`end = copy n`), and against any once-assigned `len` read of the vector rather than one saved local, so 484's `while i < letters.len() and letters[i] == 'D'` counts too; codegen then checks only `i >= 0`. Kata 459 on x86 (callgrind, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0): 2.93G -> 2.76G against Rust's 2.43G (KARAC_MIR_GUARD_BOUNDS=0 gives back the old count). 484's `(1..=n).collect()` (the kata no longer pushes from a `for`) now lowers in src/mir/lower.rs `collect_range` to `Vec.new()` and a counting push loop, `a..=b` run as `a..b + 1` below the type's largest value, which presize reserves for: 843M -> 742M against Rust's 551M. The rest, the presized fill's second exit (7 instructions an element, not vectorized) and the chars decode (14 a char against Rust's 11), is B-2026-11-09-26. Pinned by tests/mir_guard_bounds_local.rs (459's and 484's shapes check only their sign and answer as before, the full checks are back under the flag, and a vector reassigned or popped in the loop keeps its check and still panics) and tests/mir_range_collect.rs (edge ranges on the interpreter and the built binary, the fill reserved for, no library collect called). Of the 197 corpus entries that collect a range, mir-interp failed only 2003 (no expected.out) and mir-llvm that and ten bench entries whose expectation is a legacy-build timeout (502's meta: expect error:codegen, bucket timeout), which now print their answer.

title: A copy of a defaulted literal binding gets no annotation fix: `let mut carry = 0; let mut x = carry; x += d; out.push(x & 1)` with `out: Vec[i32]` is refused with only 'write an explicit as i32', so karac fix has nothing to apply (remainder of B-2026-11-08-20)
detail: FOUND 2026-11-08 carrying LeetCode 1073's Rust template (kara-katas leetcode/1001-1100/1073-adding-two-negabinary-numbers/negabinary_solution.kara) through karac fix. After the syntax round, check refused `ans.push(x & 1)` (`ans: Vec[i32]`) with E0200 'implicit coercion from i64 to i32 would narrow or change sign ... Write an explicit as i32'. `carry`'s literal kept its default `i64` because only operators use it (design.md §8 Literals: an operator operand does not fix a literal), and `x` is `let mut x = carry;`, sharing that variable. B-2026-11-08-20's annotation fix (`literal_let_annotation`, src/typechecker/exprs.rs) looks only for a literal `let` named in the refused expression, and `x` is not one, so the refusal named no binding and offered no fix. Rust infers `carry: i32` here, so the template carries no annotation.
fix: a0bb430292. `note_literal_let` (src/typechecker/exprs.rs) also notes a `let` whose value is a binding already noted as a defaulted literal and that shares its literal's variable, with that root binding's entry (span, variable, value and name; `literal_lets` carries the root name, src/typechecker.rs). A narrowing refused at the copy then names the root and `karac fix` writes its annotation: the 1073 template's `let mut carry = 0;` becomes `let mut carry: i32 = 0;` and the arm checks clean in a second fix round. tests/kata_1073_check_gaps.rs (the copied carry; a copy of a fixed binding left alone); tests/fix_literal_binding_annotation.rs unchanged and passing.

title: A constant whose value is computed from another constant is refused as a pattern: `const AA: i64 = 5; const BB: i64 = AA + 1;` then `match 6 { BB => .. }` says 'this range pattern bound is not lowered yet', though a constant in a pattern is its value (design.md § Pattern matching) and `BB` checks and prints 6 anywhere else
fix: 429cb5a08c: a constant whose initializer is built from integer literals, other constants, negation and arithmetic is its value as a pattern: src/mir/lower.rs range_bound folds it (fold_const_int) before asking for the constant's operand, so `const BB: i64 = AA + 1;` matches 6 rather than being refused as "this range pattern bound is not lowered yet". A block constant computed from another (`const MOD_UP: i64 = MOD + 1;`) matches too. Pin: corpus/design/ok_a_constant_computed_from_constants_is_a_pattern (spec, design.md § Pattern matching).

title: A mutating method on a read-only Slice binding (`let mut b = s.bytes(); b.swap(i, j)`, also sort, reverse, fill, sort_by, sort_by_key, split_at_mut) says only 'Slice.swap() requires a mutable slice (`mut Slice[T]`)', with no hint or fix; an index assignment through the same binding names `.to_vec()` but is reported twice
fix: 34d42091dd: a method that changes a slice in place (sort, reverse, swap, fill, sort_by, sort_by_key, split_at_mut) on a read-only view bound to a local names the binding and says `let mut` does not make a view writable (src/typechecker/stdlib_seq.rs read_only_slice_method_error), and when the binding's unannotated initializer is a postfix expression other than a range subscript (`s.bytes()`) it carries `.to_vec()` on that initializer as its machine fix (read_only_slice_lets). An assignment through such a binding carries the same fix from the core check (src/typechecker/core_ref_write.rs to_vec_fix), and the older typecheck report of it (items.rs check_read_only_slice_write) is skipped under the core check, so `b[0] = 120` is reported once. A range view (`let mut w = v[0..2]`) is named but gets no fix, since `mut v[a..b]` may be what was meant. Tests: tests/read_only_slice_to_vec_fix.rs (the row's program is fixed by `karac fix` and runs; the range view gets no fix); tests/core_strict_check.rs check_write_through_a_read_only_slice now expects the core check's wording.

title: `karac fix` carries LeetCode's binary-tree template (`use std::rc::Rc; use std::cell::RefCell;`, `Option<Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>>`, `n.borrow()`) to `import std.rc.Rc` and `Option[Rc[RefCell[TreeNode]]]`, then stops at 'unknown module `std.rc`, did you mean `std.io`?' with no word of `shared struct`, Kāra's spelling of a reference-counted mutable node
detail: Found starting kata 1530, whose Rust template is LeetCode's standard binary-tree signature; every LeetCode tree problem's Rust template has the same shape. At 899b8af74, a 52-line program (the TreeNode definition LeetCode prints in its comment, `count_pairs(root: Option<Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>>, distance: i32)`, a helper taking `&Option<Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>>`, `Rc::new(RefCell::new(TreeNode { .. }))` and `n.borrow()`): `karac check` reports 25 errors; one `karac fix` round applies 48 edits (the generics to `[..]`, `::` to `.`, `&`/`&mut` to `ref`/`mut ref`, `Self::` to `Solution.`, `&&` to `and`, and the two `use` lines to `import std.rc.Rc;` / `import std.cell.RefCell;`); the next rounds stop at two errors, 'error[resolve]: unknown module `std.rc`, did you mean `std.io`?' and 'unknown module `std.cell`', with nothing fixable. The `did you mean std.io` suggestion is wrong-headed, and nothing names the idiom: design.md's `shared struct` is reference counted with mutable fields (katas 226, 919, 938, 979, 993 and 998 write `shared struct TreeNode { mut val, mut left: Option[TreeNode], mut right: Option[TreeNode] }`), so `Option<Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>>` is `Option[TreeNode]` on a `shared struct TreeNode`, `Rc::new(RefCell::new(x))` is `x`, `.borrow()` / `.borrow_mut()` are the handle itself, and `Rc::clone(&x)` is `x`. At the least the resolver could say so for `std::rc` / `std::cell` (and `Rc` / `RefCell` used as types); a machine-applicable rewrite for the template's fixed shape would carry every LeetCode tree template.
fix: a4aa93dce. src/parser/rust_rc.rs: at a `use std::rc::Rc;` / `use std::cell::RefCell;` line (also the `import std.rc.Rc;` an earlier round made) the parser reports one diagnostic naming `shared struct`, whose fix deletes the line and, for the first such line, rewrites the file in one envelope: each struct T held in an `Rc<RefCell<T>>` (or `Rc[RefCell[T]]`) becomes `shared struct` with `mut` fields, the type becomes T, `Rc::new(RefCell::new(x))` / `RefCell::new(x)` / `Rc::clone(&x)` become x, and `.borrow()` / `.borrow_mut()` go. When another fix overlaps it the envelope waits a round. The resolver names `shared struct` for `Rc` / `RefCell` as a name or type and for an unknown `std.rc` / `std.cell` module (no more 'did you mean std.io'). Pinned by tests/fix_rust_rc_refcell.rs: LeetCode's TreeNode template with a count_pairs solution converges in six fix rounds, checks clean and prints the right answer, with a write through a second handle seen by the first. Shapes the envelope does not know (`Rc<Vec<T>>`, `Weak`) keep only the pointer to `shared struct`.

title: `rest = rest[1..]` on a `Slice[T]` local is refused E0516 ("cannot assign to `rest` while ... borrow") while the `Str` twin `t = t[1..]` is accepted
detail: Found writing apps/cli/mini_graphviz: the `attr` command takes an optional first keyword off its words with `let mut rest = words[1..]; if not rest.is_empty() and not rest[0].contains("=") { kw = Some(rest[0].clone()); rest = rest[1..]; }`. Measured at karac 0.8.1-dev on 8f588ae843: `fn f(xs: Slice[i64]) -> i64 { let mut rest = xs; rest = rest[1..]; rest.len() }` is refused E0516 at the assignment, the same with `Slice[String]` and with a local `v.as_slice()`; `fn g(s: Str) -> i64 { let mut t = s; t = t[1..]; t.len() }` checks and runs. Core semantics §5.2 lists `Slice[T]` with `Str` as views. In src/mir/borrowck.rs `transfer_call`, a `ResultBorrows::Receiver` native's result takes the pointee's origins for a `ref str` receiver (`refers_to_str`) but the receiver place's for a `ref Slice`, so the sub-slice borrowed `rest` itself and the assignment overwrote a borrowed local. MIR's `TyKind::Slice` does not record whether the slice is `mut`, and for a `mut Slice` the stricter reading is what keeps `let a = xs[0..1]; xs[0] = 5; a[0]` refused.
fix: 76bc1b9842: in src/mir/borrowck.rs `transfer_call`, a `ResultBorrows::Receiver` native whose receiver is a shared reference to a `Slice` now takes the pointee's origins, as a `ref str` receiver already did (`refers_to_read_only_slice` beside `refers_to_str`), so `rest[1..]` borrows what `rest` borrows and `rest = rest[1..]` is accepted (core semantics §5.2 lists `Slice[T]` with `Str` as views). MIR's `Slice` type does not say whether it is `mut`, so a body with any `mut` loan of a `Slice` place keeps the old reading (`Cx::writes_slices`). Pins: corpus/core/ok_a_slice_rebinds_to_its_own_reslice (a `Slice[i64]` and a `Slice[String]` parameter, a local `as_slice()`, the `Str` twin; interp, llvm, ASan and build) and err_mut_slice_written_while_its_sub_slice_is_live (a sub-slice of a `mut Slice`, then a write, stays E0516). apps/cli/mini_graphviz keeps the natural `rest = rest[1..]`.

title: A number literal checked against a closure's return type or a map entry's value keeps its default `i64`: `let g: Fn() -> i32 = || 5` returns an `i64` (a build reads garbage, the interpreter prints `5` for an `f32`), and `*m.entry(k).or_insert(0) += 1` on a `Map[i32, i32]` stores 8 bytes into a 4-byte value (ASan stack-buffer-overflow, wrong counts in a build)
detail: FOUND 2026-11-08 by kata 1074's lanes (kara-katas leetcode/1001-1100/1074-number-of-submatrices-that-sum-to-target): the Rust-template arm carried by `karac fix` keeps LeetCode's `let mut count: Map[i32, i32]` and `*count.entry(sum).or_insert(0) += 1`. `__mir-run`, `__mir-llvm-run` and `run` printed the mirror's output; `__mir-llvm-asan` aborted with a stack-buffer-overflow WRITE of size 8 on the `entry` temporary in `Solution.num_submatrix_sum_target`, and a `karac build` binary counted 2 for LeetCode's first example (want 4). MIR showed `Map[i32, i32].entry_or_insert(move _3, const 1_i32, const 5_i64)`: the key went through `arg_operand` at the key type (B-2026-11-08-19), the value through `expr_operand` at the literal's recorded type, which the checker leaves at the default `i64` (a fn's tail literal is recorded `i64` too; MIR fits that constant to the return place). A `Map[i64, i32]` hid it in the entry's padding. Probing found the same root in closures: the closure check arm took the body's type as the closure's return type, so `|| 5` for `Fn() -> i32`, `|| 6` for `Fn() -> f64`, `|| { return 12; }` for `Fn() -> f32`, `or_insert_with(|| 6)` on a `Map[i64, f32]`, `x.unwrap_or_else(|| 8)` on an `Option[f32]` and `call(|| 7)` for an `Fn() -> f32` parameter were closures returning `i64`: a build printed `2 3e-323 3.5e-323 2 0` for `5 6.0 7.0 2 200`, the interpreter `5` for `5.0`. `karac check` passed all of them.
fix: 1de47226fa. The closure check arm (src/typechecker/exprs.rs) gives a closure whose body, or a `return` in it, is a number of another type than the expected `Fn`'s return type that return type, as a fn's tail and its `return`s already are: a literal kept at its default `i64` for `Fn() -> i32`/`f32`, an `i32` widened for `Fn() -> i64`. MIR lowering (src/mir/lower.rs) stores the value of the fused `m.entry(k).or_insert(v)` at the map's value type (`widen` fits a constant, widens a narrower number), as `insert` does, and `lib_param_tys` gives `Entry[K, V].or_insert` its `V` for the chained form. Pinned by corpus/core/ok_literal_takes_closure_and_entry_slots (closures for `i32`, `f64`, `u8`, `f32`, a `return`, widening, `or_insert_with`, `unwrap_or_else`, an `Fn() -> f32` parameter; `entry().or_insert(0)` on `Map[i32, i32]` and `SortedMap[i32, i32]`, `Map[i64, f32]` fused, `or_insert_with` and held), run on the interpreter and compiled by tests/kata_1074_literal_slots.rs (in ci.yml's codegen-e2e line). Control: the pre-fix karac at d95eccd728 printed `2 3e-323 3.5e-323 2 0` from a build for the closure probe (want `5 6.0 7.0 2 200`) and the interpreter `5` for `5.0`; ASan reported the stack-buffer-overflow on `Map[i32, i32]`. Kata 1074's six arms and differential agree on all five lanes after it.

title: A call to a method returning `Self` in an impl of a `shared struct` is refused against any annotation: `let y: Node = Node.new(2);` and `Some(Node.new(1))` as an `Option[Node]` say "expected 'Node', found 'Node'", and the cascade reports later uses of the binding as moves
detail: Found fixing B-2026-11-08-65: LeetCode's TreeNode template has `impl TreeNode { pub fn new(val: i32) -> Self { .. } }`, and once `karac fix` makes TreeNode a `shared struct`, `Some(TreeNode.new(v))` is refused. Repro: `shared struct Node { val: i64 }`, `impl Node { fn new(val: i64) -> Self { Node { val } } }`, then `let y: Node = Node.new(2);` -> 'expected 'Node', found 'Node''. A plain struct checks. The bare name `Node` lowers to `Type::Shared(Node)` (typechecker/lowering.rs), but the impl method's registered signature kept `Self` (env_build.rs), which the associated-call path resolved to the plain `Named` type, so the two never unify; both display as 'Node'. `-> Node` written out checks.
fix: a4aa93dce. src/typechecker/env_build.rs: an impl method's registered signature resolves `Self` to `Type::Shared(T)` when the impl's target is a non-generic shared or sync struct, the type the bare name lowers to, so an associated call's result unifies with an annotation. Pinned by self_return_of_a_shared_struct_is_the_handle_type in tests/fix_rust_rc_refcell.rs.

title: Assigning the `ref i32` a `SortedMap` walk yields to an `i64` local, `cur = d`, is refused E0509 "a view ... is stored in an escaping closure, a `shared` value or a channel", though `cur` is a plain local
detail: Found mutating kata 2021's Rust arm (kara-katas leetcode/2001-2100/2021-brightest-position-on-street; the mutation `cur += d` -> `cur = d`). Shape: `let mut m: SortedMap[i64, i32] = SortedMap.new(); m.insert(1, 5); let mut cur: i64 = 0; let mut best = 0; for (x, d) in m.iter() { cur = d; best = best + cur; } println(best);`. `karac check` reports E0509 at `cur = d` ("a view of a temporary value is stored in an escaping closure, a `shared` value or a channel, where its borrow is not kept ... store an owned copy instead"), and `__mir-run` reports the same from the MIR borrow checker ("a view of _1 ..."). `cur` is neither a closure nor `shared` nor a channel. The same program with `let mut cur: i32 = 0` checks and prints 12; with `let mut cur = 0` (the literal then takes `i32` from the assignment) it checks too; `let mut (cur, z) = (0, 0)` (the tuple's literal settled to `i64`) is refused like the `i64` annotation. `cur += d` with `cur: i64` checks. So a copy-typed view assigned with a widening (`ref i32` into `i64`) seems to be lowered as storing the reference rather than reading and widening the value, which `unkept_loans` in src/mir/borrowck.rs then reports with E0509's text. Design §5.10: a `Copy` value read through a view is its value.
fix: bb6dcf8503. `assign_stmt` (src/mir/lower.rs) reads a view of a number assigned to a wider number slot and widens it when the widening is lossless, so `cur = d` with `d: ref i32` into an `i64` local is accepted and runs. Pin: corpus/core/ok_view_of_number_widens_on_assignment (interp and mir-llvm agree).

title: Kata 520's `word.chars().filter(|c| c.is_ascii_uppercase()).count()` branches on each char's answer and overflow-tests the count, where Rust's `Filter::count` adds `pred(x) as usize`: the same instructions run 1.85x Rust's time on x86 (4.93x, then 1.84x on the M5)
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-08 on x86 (release karac at 2b8a45f360 plus 03e9186ea3's unswitching, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build, against rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on; kara-katas leetcode/501-600/520-detect-capital/bench, 20,000 words of 1 to 100 letters checked 200 times; outputs equal). Callgrind: Kara 2.548G instructions against Rust's 2.436G, cachegrind's branch model 7.58M mispredicts against 7.95M and D1 misses 7.07M against 5.93M, but wall 415-570 ms against 221-257 ms (five runs each). The hot loop, per char: Kara `add $0xffffffa5,%eax; cmp $0xffffffe6,%eax; jae` (a branch on is_ascii_uppercase) then `inc %r12; jno` on the count; Rust `add $0xffffffbf,%r14d; cmp $0x1a,%r14d; adc $0x0,%rbx`, no branch on the answer. A fifth of the words mix cases at random, so the branch mispredicts on real hardware where valgrind's model does not show it. Reported by the M5 bench thread at 4.93x checked Rust (gd96014a9d), 1.84x after -08-6's decode fixes (g2b8a45f36).
fix: b8e953e4f9. `IterFilter.count` (runtime/stdlib/source/iter.kara) adds `(it.pred)(x) as i64` for each item rather than branching on it, as Rust's `Filter::count` does, and `Iterator.count` steps with `wrapping_add` (a walk of 2^63 items would take centuries, and the test kept a filtered count from being a branch-free add). Pinned by tests/mir_filter_count.rs (counts on empty, all-kept, none-kept and mixed input, and a predicate with side effects still runs once an item in order; interp and llvm). MEASURED x86: 520 wall 214-246 ms against Rust's 214-266 (was 415-570 against 221-257), instructions 2.605G against 2.433G. The three kata benches that call count(): 520 1.02x instructions, 794 1.04x, 975 0.99x.

title: Kata 540's binary search divides `(low + high) / 2` and tests `mid % 2 == 1` as signed `i64`s, 3 instructions a step more than Rust's `usize` (8.08G against 6.21G on x86, 1.53x on the M5), though the loop keeps both indices non-negative
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-08 on x86 (release karac at 2b8a45f360 plus 03e9186ea3, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build, against rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on; kara-katas leetcode/501-600/540-single-element-in-a-sorted-array/bench; outputs equal): callgrind 8.078G against 6.208G, wall 790-887 ms against 653-693 ms. The search loop runs 281.6M steps at 18 instructions against Rust's 15: the signed `/ 2` is `mov; shr $0x3f; add; sar $1` where Rust's unsigned one is `shr $1`, and the signed `% 2 == 1` is `and; xor; cmp $1; sete; sub` (the `mid -= 1` folded in) where Rust has `shl $0x3e; sar $0x3f; add`. low starts at 0 and only becomes mid + 2, high starts at len - 1 and only becomes mid, and the loop runs while low < high, so low + high >= 1 and mid >= 0 on every step: unsigned division gives the same values. LLVM does not prove it (the facts are loop-carried); MIR's range analysis (src/mir/range_bounds.rs) can, from `low < high` and low >= 0. Routed from the M5 bench thread's 529-555 batch (kara-katas 4d21830b, 1.53x checked Rust).
fix: 871ac6133e: src/mir/range_bounds.rs `unsigned_divisions` runs the value-range analysis over the body and marks each local every Div or Rem into which has a dividend whose interval starts at 0 or above and a divisor whose interval starts at 1 or above; codegen (src/backend/mir/body.rs) emits those as `udiv` / `urem` (no overflow test, which cannot fire), so `(low + high) / 2` becomes a shift and `mid % 2` an and. `KARAC_MIR_UNSIGNED_DIV=0` divides as the types say. Kata 540 on x86 (callgrind, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0): 8.08G -> 6.67G against Rust's 6.21G. Pinned by tests/mir_unsigned_div.rs (answers for negative, mixed and non-negative operands; IR division counts with the proof and without).

title: arm64: kata 498's zigzag loop in find_diagonal_order is if-converted into about 20 selects on its loop-carried path where Rust keeps a `tbz` branch on the direction, 1.27x checked Rust on the M5; x86 is not affected (0.72x Rust's instructions, 0.8x its time)
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-08. M5 (Mac bench thread, karac gd96014a9d and again g2b8a45f36, kara-katas leetcode/401-500/498-diagonal-traverse/bench): 1.27x checked Rust at both, about 95% of samples in the zigzag loop of find_diagonal_order. Its profile shows two costs: LLVM if-converts the up and down arms into about 20 selects on the loop-carried path where Rust's arm64 code keeps a `tbz` branch on the direction, and the outer `mat` header (len and data pointer) is reloaded on every element because the `out.push` store may alias `mat`, which arrives by pointer (that half is B-2026-11-07-33's shape and is appended there). x86 (drop schedule, release karac at 2b8a45f360 plus 03e9186ea3, against rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on): callgrind 4.505G against Rust's 6.264G, wall 311-375 ms against 372-484 ms, so the select conversion is an arm64 cost that x86 does not show and it can only be measured on the Mac. A lead to try there: whether `-two-entry-phi-node-folding-threshold=6` (src/backend/mir_aot.rs, B-2026-11-04-37, which raised it from LLVM's 4 for kata 342 on arm64) is what lets SimplifyCFG fold the arms; KARAC_MIR_PHI_FOLD_THRESHOLD=4 builds with LLVM's own. RE-CHECKED 2026-11-10 at 5a072c1314 on x86, cross-building the bench for aarch64-apple-darwin (the object only; KARAC_LINKER keeps it). The lead is refuted: KARAC_MIR_PHI_FOLD_THRESHOLD=4 and the default 6 build byte-identical objects. At karac's darwin default CPU (apple-m1) and at apple-m4, the optimized IR has no `select` and the zigzag loop branches on the direction with tbz/tbnz, as Rust's does: 3 csel/cset in the whole object, with or without auto-par, KARAC_MIR_UNSWITCH=0 or the 4-entry jump-table floor. At --target-cpu=apple-m5 the object has 7. The ~20 selects were profiled at 2b8a45f36 on the M5 itself, whose CPU and build flags this container cannot reproduce. NEXT: an M5 re-run of 498 at HEAD, and the CPU the bench build targets there.

title: A closure whose whole body is an assignment (Rust's `m.entry(k).and_modify(|v| *v += 1)`, `.for_each(|x| last = *x)`) stops the parser at the operator with "Expected `)`, found `+=`", and `karac fix` has nothing to apply
detail: FOUND 2026-11-08 probing `Entry` chains for kata 1074's Rust-template arm (kara-katas leetcode/1001-1100/1074-number-of-submatrices-that-sum-to-target): `m.entry(1).and_modify(|v| *v += 1).or_insert(5);` was refused with `error[parse]: Expected `)`, found `+=``. Assignment is a statement (design.md § Assignment: "It may also be the body of a `match` arm"), a closure's body an expression, so the closure takes a block, `|v| { *v += 1; }`, which the corpus already writes (corpus/fixtures/codegen/map_set/e2e_entry_chain_on_a_map_field). The parse error named neither the assignment nor the block, and offered no fix, so a Rust author carrying `and_modify(|v| *v += 1)`, a common idiom, got a dead end. Whether a closure body should accept a bare assignment as a `match` arm's does is a language question; this row only makes the refusal name it and fix it.
fix: 5fe8006173. `parse_closure` (src/parser/exprs.rs) hands a non-block body to the new `closure_assignment_body`: when the next token is `=` or a compound assignment operator, it reports "a closure's body is an expression, and `+=` is an assignment, a statement (design.md § Assignment) ... write the body as a block", reads the assignment as the one statement of a block body so the rest of the file still parses, and registers a two-edit fix in `fix_diffs` that inserts `{ ` before the body and `; }` after the value. Pinned by tests/kata_1074_check_gaps.rs: `m.entry(k).and_modify(|v| *v += 1).or_insert(1)` and `.for_each(|x| last = *x)` each get the error, one `karac fix` writes `|v| { *v += 1; }` and `|x| { last = *x; }`, leaves `.for_each(|x| seen.push(*x))` alone, and the result checks clean and prints `2 1 [4, 5] 8` on the interpreter. Control: the pre-fix karac at 1de47226fa reported only "Expected `)`, found `+=`" and fix applied nothing. A bare assignment as a closure body stays refused (design.md § Assignment allows it only as a `match` arm's body).

title: A float format spec without a precision is refused (`{x:>8}`, `{x:+}`, `{x:<5}` on an f64: "a float format spec needs a precision"), and any spec on a `bool` or `char` is refused ("format specifiers apply to int, float, and string values only"); design.md §3's grammar makes precision optional and puts no type limit on fill, align and width
detail: karac 0.8.1-dev+g27fedd3da, every lane (refused at check). design.md §3 Format specifiers: `spec := [[fill] align] ['+'] ['0'] [width] ['.' precision] [type]`; "`align` places the value left, right or centered within `width`"; "`+` prints a sign on non-negative numbers too"; only "an unrecognized specifier" is a compile error. Cells: `let z = 0.0; let n = z / z; let i = 1.0 / z; println(f"[{n:>5}][{i:<5}][{-i:^6}]")` owes `[  NaN][inf  ][ -inf ]`; `let b = -0.0; println(f"{b:+}")`; `let b = true; let ch = 'x'; println(f"[{b:>6}][{ch:^3}]")` owes `[  true][ x ]`. A width-only float should pad the shortest round-trip Display form (`{0.1:>6}` -> `   0.1`), which is what a report aligning a float column without fixing its digits wants; Python and Rust both accept all four. The checks are deliberate in src/typechecker/exprs.rs (format-spec validation: `fs.precision.is_none()` on a float, and the int/float/string fallthrough), so either the spec gains these limits or the checks go. Found writing a CSV report (probe-core/dp/); everything else in it (fill/align/zero-pad/`+`/precision/radix, the CSV, Map/SortedMap grouping, regex captures, total_cmp sort) matched a Python oracle on interp, JIT, the built binary and ASan.
fix: 4be4cb4b9c, per the review thread's ruling at c6016977c7 (design.md §3 Format specifiers, "Which parts apply to which values"): fill, align and width apply to every value; `+` and `0` to numbers; `type` to integers; `.precision` to floats. `check_format_spec_for_type` (src/typechecker/exprs.rs) is narrowed, not removed: a float spec without a precision is accepted, and a bool, char, user `Display` type or generic `T: Display` takes fill/align/width; `+`, `0`, a radix or a precision on one of those is an error at the hole naming the part and what it is for; a string precision stays refused ("not in v1"). Runtime: a float without a precision padded Rust's `{v}` digits (`1e16` as `10000000000000000`); `FormatSpec::float_digits` now writes the magnitude's `Display` text (`write_display_f64`), and an `f32` its own shortest digits (`write_float32`; the interpreter's F32 arm; kind 6 through `karac_mir_fmt_spec` on the compiled path), so `{x:>8}` pads exactly what `{x}` prints; the core-formatting oracle's no-precision arm moved to `display_f64` with it. Pins: tests/format_spec_parts_by_type.rs, the row's cells plus `{x:>8}`, `{x:+}`, `{nan:>5}`, `{flag:>6}`, `{c:^3}`, -0.0, 1e16, f32 and a user Display type, byte-identical on __mir-run, __mir-llvm-run, run and the built binary; and each refused part's message at its line. Added to CI's codegen-e2e line.

title: A `select` whose value is the function's result (its tail expression) gets false W0278 "discarded `Result` value" warnings (five for a two-arm select); and because the library's own `recv_timeout` is such a select, every program that calls `rx.recv_timeout(d)` prints 3 of these warnings at a line past its end (`svc.kara:5439:9`, `rt.kara:5022:9`) on check and on every `karac run`
detail: karac 0.8.1-dev+g27fedd3da. (1) `fn get(rx: Receiver[i64]) -> Result[i64, String] { select { v = rx.recv() => match v { Some(v) => Ok(v), None => Err("closed".to_string()) }, _ = after(Duration.ms(5)) => Err("timeout".to_string()), } }` -> 5x `warning[must_use]: sel.kara:4:5: discarded `Result` value`; the program prints 3 (correct). The select's value is returned, so nothing is discarded (concurrency.md: "The block's value is the chosen arm's value"). (2) `let (tx, rx): (Sender[i64], Receiver[i64]) = channel(1); let _ = tx.send(3); match rx.recv_timeout(Duration.ms(10)) { Ok(v) => println(v), Err(_) => println("timeout") }` -> 3x W0278 with file `rt.kara` and line 5022, a line of runtime/stdlib/source/channel_timeout.kara's `select` as baked into the program (BAKED_SOURCES, src/mir/lower.rs); `--output=json` gives file rt.kara line 5022. So a user sees warnings they cannot act on, at a line their file does not have, every build. Library text's diagnostics are dropped elsewhere (drop_library_diagnostics), not for baked sources. Found writing a job service with graceful shutdown (probe-core/gs/), which otherwise works on every lane.
fix: 2233d104ea. Both halves. (1) `select_desugar` gives every node of its template the select's span, so the must_use walker looked up the probe statements (`if r.is_some() { break k; }`, `__select_park(e, until);`) at the select's own recorded type and read a Result-valued select tail as one discarded Result per probe. `Walker::walk_block` (src/must_use_lint.rs) now walks, but does not check as a discard, a statement whose span is its block's span: a desugar made it, since a statement the program wrote is always narrower than its braces. A `select { .. };` written as a statement is still checked at its own site and warns once (pinned). (2) The lint walked the library's bodies too, so `recv_timeout`'s probes were printed against the user's file at line 5009. `check_implicit_must_use` now drops any finding at or past `user_text_end(program)` (`library_start`, else the gated span base), and `diag_json::lint_entries_for_compile_path` applies the same cut to undocumented_unsafe, unsafe_op_in_unsafe_fn, ffi_float_eq and ambiguous_not_comparison, so neither the text nor the JSON renderer can print a library lint. Pins: tests/select_tail_must_use.rs (select tail silent on check and run, recv_timeout silent, a discarded select warns exactly once at 5:5).

title: A user type that implements both `Iterable` and `IntoIterator` cannot be the subject of a bare `for`: "type 'Bag' cannot be iterated by a `for` loop: it implements `IntoIterator` but not `Iterator`, and `for` never calls `into_iter`"; design.md §9 says `for x in c` over a non-Iterator borrows through `Iterable`, which `Vec` (implementing both) already does, and the same type with only `Iterable` loops fine
fix: c8a1782220. lowering.rs only_into_iterator: a type that also implements Iterable is not IntoIterator-only, so a bare for borrows it through iter() as design.md § Iterator and Iterable says. Pin corpus/design/ok_a_type_that_is_iterable_and_into_iterator_is_borrowed_by_for (a Ring[T] with both impls, two bare loops and one into_iter).

title: Two impls of one generic trait on a type (`impl Conv[String] for N`, `impl Conv[f64] for N`) leave the method uncallable: `n.conv()` is ambiguous (right, §9 step 2), but the diagnostic's fix `Conv.conv(N)` is listed for both candidates and is itself refused as ambiguous, and the qualified form `Conv[String].conv(n)` is refused with "no method 'conv' on `Conv[…]`" (plus a cascading "value 'n' moved" error)
fix: 3d45c76221. Per design.md §9 UFCS (ruling 4c798a759c), `Conv[String].conv(n)` names the instance. It parses as a method call on a one-segment `Path` with generic arguments. That used to reach the concrete-type UFCS path, which looked for a type named `Conv`, reported "no method 'conv' on `Conv[…]`", and then inferred the arguments as moved, which produced the spurious move error. A trait head with arguments now goes through the trait UFCS path (`try_ufcs_trait_instance`, src/typechecker/method_ufcs.rs). That path limits method lookup to impls of the trait whose `trait_args` equal the written ones (`env.ufcs_trait_args`, checked in `ufcs_admits`). `rewrite_ufcs_call` (src/lowering.rs) also accepts the `Path` receiver, so MIR sees `n.conv()` with the impl the checker resolved. Bare `Conv.conv(n)` and `n.conv()` stay ambiguous whatever the expected type. The receiver-form diagnostic now names each candidate with its trait arguments: `Conv[String].conv(N) -> String` and `Conv[f64].conv(N) -> f64`, where it used to show `Conv.conv(N)` twice. The row's three repros give `n3 1.5` (a09b) or the new diagnostic (a09, a09c). A wrong instance, `Conv[bool].conv(n)`, reports "no method 'conv' on type 'N'" alone. Pins: corpus/design/ok_a_generic_trait_named_with_its_arguments_picks_its_impl covers two generic traits, `mut ref self` with a `mut` receiver marker, and a type with one instance; it passes on mir-interp, mir-llvm and mir-llvm-asan. Also corpus/design/err_bare_trait_ufcs_over_two_instances_is_ambiguous.

title: `#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]` on a struct with a tuple field (`pair: (i64, bool)`) fails: alone it is refused at check with an internal message (E_COMPTIME_PANIC "derive `derive_serialize` could not be compiled: 6399:13 in `derive_serialize`: the method call `.name` with no resolved callee is not lowered yet"), and inside a larger program check passes and every run lane fails with "error[mir]: typecheck: 18:1: no method 'serialize' on type '(i64, bool)'"
fix: ef6cd921e9. Two causes. (a) The derives' own `comptime fn derive_serialize(comptime T: own Type)` reflects with `T.name()`, and try_identifier_receiver_method (src/typechecker/method_identifier_receiver.rs) took any identifier naming a program type as a type receiver before looking at locals, so beside a program's `struct T` it reflected on nothing and lowering found no callee; a local or a type parameter of the name now wins. The same collision in `Json.deserialize[T: Deserialize]`'s `T.deserialize(d)` read every type as the program's T, fixed by B-2026-11-09-3. (b) Tuples have no Serialize/Deserialize impl (the language has no impls for tuple types), so the derive now writes a tuple field or payload itself (runtime/stdlib/source/serde.kara serde_write_value / serde_read_value): a sequence of its elements, nested tuples nesting, read back from a sequence of exactly its length ("too few/too many values in a tuple"). `{"pair":[1,true],"deep":["a",[2.5,3]],"n":4}` matches Python json.dumps, and enum tuple and struct variants holding tuples round-trip. A tuple inside another type (`Vec[(A, B)]`, `Option[(A, B)]`) is refused at check naming the field, instead of passing check and failing in MIR; design.md § Serialize and Deserialize says so. Pins: corpus/design/ok_derive_serialize_writes_a_tuple_field_as_an_array and err_derive_serialize_refuses_a_tuple_inside_a_vec_by_name, on interp, llvm and ASan. Remainder: tuples nested in containers need trait impls for tuple types, not filed separately.

title: `Json.deserialize(text)` takes `text: String`, so a `Str` (a line from `text.lines()`, a slice) is refused ("expected 'ref String', found 'Str'") and needs `.to_string()`; `Json.parse(text: Str)` takes the view, and strings.md's reading methods all take `Str`
detail: karac 0.8.1-dev+g27fedd3da. `for line in text.lines() { let r: Result[User, DeserializeError] = Json.deserialize(line); }` -> `expected 'ref String', found 'Str': .to_string() copies the text into a String`. runtime/stdlib/source/serde.kara:1129 `fn deserialize[T: Deserialize](text: String)`. Reading NDJSON line by line is the common case; the parameter only reads its text, so `Str` would accept both a String and a view at no cost.
fix: ef6cd921e9. `Json.deserialize[T: Deserialize](text: Str)` and `JsonDeserializer.new(text: Str)` (runtime/stdlib/source/serde.kara): a line of `text.lines()`, a slice and a String all read; a String argument is only borrowed. Pin: corpus/design/ok_json_deserialize_reads_a_str_and_names_the_renamed_key (interp, llvm, ASan).

title: A missing field in `Json.deserialize` is reported by its Kāra name, not its JSON key: a `#[serde(rename: "userName")] name: String` field absent from the input gives "missing field `name`", though the sender never sees a `name` key
detail: karac 0.8.1-dev+g27fedd3da. In probe-core/js/api.kara, deserializing a User whose input lacks "userName": `err missing field `name``. serde reports the renamed key (`missing field `userName``). The other messages in that run name the wire form correctly (`score: expected a number, found a string at line 1 column 53`, `unknown variant `Frozen` of Status`, `unknown variant `Nope` of Event`, `the value fits no variant of untagged Id`), and the rest of the program (externally, internally and untagged enums, Option, Vec, SortedMap, skip, default: 3, unknown fields ignored, escapes and non-ASCII text, 1e+21) matches a Python json oracle on interp, JIT, the built binary and ASan.
fix: ef6cd921e9. serde_read_fields names a missing field by serde_key(name, args), the key the input should have held: "missing field `userName`" for `#[serde(rename: "userName")] name: String`. Pin: corpus/design/ok_json_deserialize_reads_a_str_and_names_the_renamed_key.

title: `s.chars().last()` walks the whole string: `StrChars` and `StrViewChars` take `Iterator.last`'s default rather than reading from the back, so kata 2030's string arm (its stack kept as a `String`, the top read with `chars().last()`) is quadratic
detail: Kata 2030 (smallest k-length subsequence) keeps one arm's stack as the answer String and reads its top with `out.chars().last()`. Iterator.last (runtime/stdlib/source/iter.kara) walks every item, and neither StrChars nor StrViewChars overrides it, though both implement next_back. 20000 reads of a 20000-char string took over 120 s under __mir-run, against 0.17 s for `chars().rev().next()`; the arm's __mir-run lane ran past 20 minutes on its 50000-letter problems while __mir-llvm-run took 3.5 s. Rust's Chars::last uses next_back.
fix: 89d9feafb3: StrChars and StrViewChars override Iterator.last with next_back, as Rust's Chars::last does, so s.chars().last() is O(1) on a String and a Str view, also after the front was consumed. 20000 reads of a 20000-char string: over 120 s under __mir-run before, 0.3 s after (debug build). Pinned by tests/kata_2030_chars_last.rs (behaviour, and agreement with a full walk over every prefix of a mixed-width text).

title: Map, SortedMap, Set and SortedSet do not implement PartialEq/Eq, and the refusal suggests `#[derive(PartialEq)]` on a std type
detail: karac 0.8.1-dev+g27fedd3da. Ruled at 7908341b95 (docs/library/collections.md, Common traits): Map and SortedMap are PartialEq when V: PartialEq and Eq when V: Eq (equal when they hold the same keys and each key's values are equal); Set and SortedSet are PartialEq and Eq (same elements); comparison is order-independent; no PartialOrd; a struct holding one can derive PartialEq. Measured (probe-core/meq/a.kara): `a == b` on two Map[String, i64] gives `type 'Map[String, i64]' does not implement PartialEq; add #[derive(PartialEq)] to use == or !=`; the same on Set[i64]; and `#[derive(PartialEq)] struct Inv { stock: Map[String, i64] }` is refused with `field 'stock' has non-PartialEq type 'Map[String, i64]'`. Two parts: (1) implement the impls per the ruling across check, the MIR interpreter and the LLVM backend, with corpus pins including a derived struct and maps built in different insertion orders; (2) the `add #[derive(PartialEq)]` hint must not be offered for a std/library type the user cannot annotate.
fix: 68aa472f3f: per docs/library/collections.md § Common traits (7908341b95). The checker's `type_supports_partial_eq` and `type_supports_eq` (src/typechecker/derives.rs) take Map and SortedMap by their value type and Set and SortedSet always, so `==`, `!=`, `assert_eq` and a derived PartialEq/Eq over them check. The MIR builder's `eq_places` (src/mir/lower.rs) calls the library's `map_eq`, `sorted_map_eq`, `set_eq` or `sorted_set_eq` (runtime/stdlib/source/collections.kara): equal lengths, then every key's values (or every element) found in the other, so insertion and iteration order play no part and the interpreter and LLVM share one body. Part 2: a PartialEq or PartialOrd refusal on a type the program does not declare (`program_declares`, src/typechecker/table_keys.rs) now reads "type 'Map[String, Fn(i64) -> i64]' does not implement PartialEq, so == and != do not apply to it" with no derive hint; a program's own type keeps the hint and its fix. No PartialOrd, as ruled. Pins: corpus/core/ok_maps_and_sets_compare_by_content (maps built in different insertion orders, a removal, Set and SortedSet, a SortedMap of Vec values, a derived struct holding a Map, nested Map of Set, assert_eq), byte-identical on interp, llvm, ASan and build under KARAC_HASH_SEED 1, 3, 5 and 99; tests/map_set_equality.rs (the checker cases and both hints). A first ASan run printed wrong set answers: it was stale runtime archives against main's new map runtime (42bfb964f0), gone after a rebuild.

title: A borrow of a `shared` field that stays live across a recursive call makes recursion quadratic in depth: the run-time flag table is a linear list, and every `shared enum` payload binding takes a flag although enum payloads are never `mut`
detail: karac 0.8.1-dev+g27fedd3da. Found in probe-core/ti/ti.kara, a tree-walking interpreter (parser to a `shared enum Expr`, eval, show; output matches the Python oracle on all lanes). On a 100k-term left-deep `1 + 1 + ...` its compiled build took 18.6 s against the oracle's 2.2 s; eval alone took 9.1 s, 59/311/1064/9104 ms at 12.5k/25k/50k/100k nodes. Reduced in probe-core/ti/q/: d.kara walks `shared enum E { Num(i64), Bin(String, E, E) }` with `match e { E.Bin(op, l, r) => { let a = f(l); let b = f(r); a + b + op.len() - 1 } }`. Chain of 100k: 8177 ms; the same function reading `op` BEFORE the calls: 4 ms; a balanced tree of the same size: 6 ms. __mir-run: 8308 ms at 50k against 165 ms for the read-before form. f.kara does the same for a shared struct with a `mut name: String` field held by `let nm = ref n.name;` across the recursive call: 269/1179/8497 ms at 25k/50k/100k against 0-2 ms without the held ref. gdb samples sit in karac_mir_flag_acquire. Two causes: (1) runtime/src/mir_flags.rs keeps the held flags in a Vec searched linearly in acquire, release and check (`fl.iter_mut().find(|f| f.addr == addr)`); its header assumes few flags are held at once, but a recursion over shared data holds one per frame, so each operation costs O(depth). (2) src/mir/flags.rs may_be_written returns true for every field of a `shared enum` (`adt.is_enum || mut_field(..)`), so binding a payload takes a flag even though, as far as I can see, no payload of a shared enum can be written through a handle (§6.2 flags `mut` fields; enum payloads have no `mut`). The ASTs, JSON values and query trees design.md recommends `shared enum` for are walked exactly this way. Fix direction is the owner's: skip flags on enum payloads if they cannot be written, and/or key the table by address (a hash map, or a per-object flag word) so a deep recursion stays linear.
fix: d308599fbb. Two halves. (1) runtime/src/mir_flags.rs keys the borrow-flag table by address in a hash map (a multiply-and-fold hasher) instead of a linear Vec scan, and a check with no flag held returns at once; 5000 live flags stay distinct (`many_flags_are_kept_apart`). (2) src/mir/flags.rs `written_payloads` finds the shared enum variant fields some body writes (assignment, `mut` loan, SetDiscriminant, call destination); a payload nothing writes takes no flag, as a struct field not declared `mut` already did. Pin: corpus/core/panic_shared_enum_payload_alias (a `mut ref` payload write through a second handle still panics, §6.2); unit test `mir_flags_skip_an_enum_payload_nothing_writes`. Full gate green.

title: Index assignment into a `Vec[dyn Trait]` (`xs[i] = v`) leaves a freed block in the slot on the LLVM backend: heap-use-after-free on the next call through it, a segfault or exit 101 in plain builds
detail: karac 0.8.1-dev+g27fedd3da. probe-core/dy/m3.kara: `trait T { fn v(self) -> String; } struct A { s: String }`, `let mut xs: Vec[dyn T] = Vec.new(); xs.push(A { s: "one" }); xs.push(A { s: "two" }); xs[0] = A { s: "three" }; println(f"now {xs[0].v()} {xs[1].v()}");`. __mir-run prints `now three two`, which is right. __mir-llvm-asan reports heap-use-after-free: a READ in clone.String under kara.A.v, reached through dyn_slot.0.0 from main. The block was freed by `drop.dyn` in main and allocated in main. __mir-llvm-run happens to print the right line here. The same shape with the value from a `-> dyn T` function (m4.kara: `xs[0] = mk("three")`) exits 101 with no output under __mir-llvm-run. The full plugin program (p.kara, `ps[0] = make("e", 4)`) segfaults as a `karac build` binary (exit 139), and its buffered stdout is lost, so not even the lines before the crash appear. A concrete type with Drop (m1.kara) shows the same UAF in Echo.drop at the Vec's drop. Not affected, clean under ASan: `Vec[A]` index assignment with Drop (m2); assigning a `dyn T` local, a struct field of type `dyn T`, or an `Option[dyn T]` (m5); and `m[k] = v` on `Map[String, dyn T]` (m6map). Also hit: assigning an existing `dyn T` binding (`xs[0] = n`, m6vec). Replacing it with `ps.remove(0); ps.insert(0, ..)` makes p2.kara match the hand-derived expected.out on all lanes. That covers dyn dispatch, default and overridden methods, `own self` consuming a dyn, `ref dyn` into `[T: Plugin]`, Option[dyn] reassign, Vec drop order, and design.md § `dyn Trait` 'Assign the owned dyn Trait itself, which drops the old value first'.
fix: d308599fbb. `xs[i] = v` on a `Vec[dyn T]` lowers to `Vec.__replace(&mut xs, i, v)` (src/mir/lower.rs `dyn_index_set`): the value is cast to the element's `dyn` type, swapped into the slot, and the old element is dropped by a Drop terminator. Before, the store went into a copy of `index_mut`'s fat view, so the slot kept the freed block. Interpreter (`("Vec", "__replace")`, src/mir/interp.rs) and backend (src/backend/mir/call.rs, bounds-checked) agree. Pin: corpus/core/dyn_vec_index_assign, which prints each drop once and in order. Full gate green (cargo test --all; --features llvm 10907 passed, 0 failed).

title: `sort()` on a Vec of tuples runs about 3.3x Rust's stable `sort`: anything but a plain integer goes to the runtime's byte-wise `merge_sort` with the comparator called through a pointer, so katas 2015 and 2021 (sorted event triples and pairs) bench at 2.07x and 2.46x Rust under overflow checks while a Vec[i64] sort beats Rust
detail: Kata 2015's bench (average height of buildings, events (pos, delta, height) sorted per call) runs 0.841 s against rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on's 0.407 s, and kata 2021's (brightest position, (pos, delta) pairs) 1.136 s against 0.462 s; both beat C's qsort. A probe isolates the sort: 100 rounds of sorting 100000 random (i64, i64) pairs take 1.60 s in Kāra (KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build) against 0.48 s in Rust, and (i64, i64, i64) triples 1.82 s against 0.72 s; a Vec[i64] of the same size sorts in 0.19 s against Rust's 0.25-0.36 s. sort_own_order (src/backend/mir/seq.rs) sends integers, chars and bools to karac_mir_sort_int (ipnsort, monomorphic) and every other element type to karac_mir_sort (runtime/src/mir.rs), a merge sort over bytes of `size` that calls the generated structural cmp through a function pointer on each comparison. Rust monomorphizes driftsort over (i64, i64) and inlines the lexicographic compare. Reproduce with the two katas' bench/ directories.
fix: d308599fbb. A plain `sort()` of anything but integers, chars and bools (tuples among them) runs the emitted merge sort `sort_by` uses (`Shim::PartSort` with the element type standing for its own order, src/backend/mir/seq.rs `sort_own_order`), so the comparison is inlined rather than called per pair through `karac_mir_sort`'s callback. Measured on x86 (callgrind, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build, KARAC_MIR_SORT_SHIM=0 is the old path): kata 2015 5.145G -> 3.747G (Rust 2.923G), kata 587 18.823G -> 15.073G (Rust 12.265G); outputs identical. The remaining gap is outside the sort.

title: A range of bare literals takes `i64` where it is written, so `(1..=5).collect()` (or `.filter(..)`, `.map(..)` first) into a `Vec[i32]` return or binding is refused with "`C: FromIterator[i64]` is not satisfied" and no fix, though design.md § Type inference lets a return or an annotation fix a literal's type
detail: Kata 2032's Rust arm (LeetCode's template: `(1..=100).filter(|x| ..).collect()` as the body of a fn returning `Vec<i32>`) reaches no clean check through karac fix: after the syntax rounds it stops at `trait bound C: FromIterator[i64] is not satisfied; Vec[i32] implements FromIterator[i32]`, plus `implicit coercion from i64 to i32` at each `s.contains(x)` on a `Set[i32]`. Minimal: `fn f() -> Vec[i32] { (1..=5).collect() }`, `fn g() -> Vec[i32] { (1..=5).filter(|x| x % 2 == 1).collect() }`, `let v: Vec[i32] = (1..=5).map(|x| x * 2).collect();` are all refused. In Rust all three infer i32. The range synthesis in src/typechecker/exprs.rs (ExprKind::Range) promotes a literal bound only to the OTHER bound's type, or to an expected Range type (B-2026-11-05-37); with both bounds literal and no expected type it types them i64 at once. design.md § Type inference: an integer literal starts as a type variable a later use may fix (a return, an annotation), and a generic call's literal argument stays open until the result's use fixes it (B-2026-11-08-44). A first try (inferring the start open and checking the end against it) trips the bounds-match check (`range bounds must have same type: 'i64' and 'i64'`), so the element var has to flow through Range[T], the adaptors and the FromIterator bound. No machine fix is offered; `(1..=100i32)` or an `as i32` per item are the workarounds the kata does not take.
fix: 1a8ab6b981. A range whose bounds are both bare literals stays open (exprs.rs Range arm); collect() into a numeric collection fixes the items' literal (collect_fixes_literal_items); a closure checked against a formal naming the callee's own unsolved parameters no longer settles its literals (names_open_callee_param); an operator's right operand unifies with an impl's parameter; a probe's needle fixes its open literal as any argument does (infer_needle), so seen.contains(x) on a Set[i32] in the filter checks. 37b53dade4 carries the generic-call side: a bare collect() handed to a generic callee, an associated-type equality (chain's J.Item, from_iter's I.Item) and Vec.from_iter(0..3) take an open literal item; (0..3).chain(b.iter()) is still refused against ref i64. Pin corpus/design/ok_a_range_of_bare_literals_takes_the_type_its_use_gives_it; kata 1061's test flipped (the range collects as its Vec[usize]).

title: PriorityQueue's sift-to-bottom loop still takes 18 instructions a level against Rust BinaryHeap's 9-12 after B-2026-11-08-10: a swap (2 loads, 2 stores, 2 bounds checks) where Rust moves a hole, and an overflow check on `2 * i + 1` (kata 480: 4.36G instructions against Rust's 3.63G)
detail: The remainder of B-2026-11-08-10 (fixed at 833870bb07, which moved the sift loops onto a `mut Slice[T]` view so the pointer and length stay in registers: 22 -> 18 instructions a level, kata 480 4.92G -> 4.36G). Measured on x86 with callgrind, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build of kara-katas leetcode/401-500/480-sliding-window-median/bench against rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on (3.63G per the parity pass). The down loop in `pq_sift_to_bottom` per level: `c = c + (xs[c] <= xs[c + 1]) as i64` (the index reads' checks fold away under `c + 1 < n`), then `xs.swap(i, c)`: two unsigned bounds checks against the slice length (LLVM does not carry the signed `c + 1 < n` over to them), 2 loads and 2 stores; then `c = 2 * i + 1` with its two overflow compares. Rust's `sift_down_to_bottom` holds the moving element in a `Hole` (ptr::read once, one load and one store a level, no checks) and std is built without overflow checks. Two directions to look at: a library-internal unchecked swap or hole primitive for slices, and whether value ranges (`i < n / 2` from the loop condition) can drop the overflow test on `2 * i + 1`. Wall time on the 4-core container was within noise of Rust's (about 0.62 s each), so this is instructions, not yet a measured wall gap on x86; the M5 rows may differ.
fix: f6dfaaa342. The sifts (runtime/stdlib/source/priority_queue.kara: pq_sift_up, pq_sift_down, pq_sift_to_bottom) move a hole as Rust's BinaryHeap does: the sifted element is read out once through a raw pointer, each element it passes moves one level into the hole (one load and one store a level, where a swap was three moves and, past a word, a stack slot), and a `defer` writes it back where it settles. The defer is the panic guard: a user `cmp` that panics inside an isolating group runs it at teardown (core-semantics 11.12), so the queue still holds each element once. A first try that compared first and rotated the path after (no hole open during user code) helped big elements but cost i64 queues a second loop (480 4.33G -> 4.55G), and swapping through registers was worse than the stack slot (786 9.31G vs 7.93G); both were dropped. On x86 (callgrind, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build of the kara-katas bench, outputs identical to main): 632 2.59G -> 2.16G (Rust 1.72G), 743 2.11G -> 1.86G (1.77G), 480 4.33G -> 3.93G (3.63G), 786 7.93G -> 6.70G (5.85G), 778 5.26G -> 4.54G. The 256 corpus entries that use PriorityQueue give the same results as main on interp, LLVM and ASan. Needed B-2026-11-09-20 (raw pointers to a non-Copy element). Pin: corpus/design/ok_priority_queue_cmp_panic_in_an_isolating_task_drops_each_element_once.

title: A plain list literal's element literal is not fixed by where the binding goes (the remainder of B-2026-11-08-57): `let mut v = [0, 0]; g(mut v)` with `g(a: mut ref Vec[i32])`, and `let v = [0, 7]; g(v)` into a `ref Vec[i32]`, are refused as `Vec[i64]`, with no machine fix
detail: 8da3c36f75 (B-2026-11-08-57) leaves the element literal of an unannotated `let x = [v; n]` / `Vec.filled(n, v)` open, so a return, an argument or an assignment fixes it (design.md §8 Literals). The same for a list literal (`[0, 0]`, every element a number literal) was tried and reverted: it regressed two design pins, corpus/design/ok_a_sequence_search_takes_the_element_view (`let wide = [0, 3, 1, 2]; rows.contains(wide[1..2])` with `rows: Vec[Vec[i64]]`: the element-view lookup `is_elem_view` saw `Slice[?]` and fell through to 'expected Vec[i64], found Slice[i64]') and a check-mode push (`nv.push([18446744073709551615])` on a `Vec[Vec[u64]]`, where the open element was range-checked as i64). So `fn g(a: mut ref Vec[i32]) { a[0] = 1; } fn main() { let mut v = [0, 0]; g(mut v); println(v[0]); }` is still 'expected mut ref Vec[i32], found Vec[i64]: a number held inside a collection ... keeps its type', with no fix. Wanted (design.md §8 decides, as for the fills): the elements open under an unannotated `let`, with consumers that need a concrete type (the element-view lookup) unifying a literal element with their slot rather than comparing; or, failing that, the `: Vec[i32]` annotation as the machine fix. Owner: C (literal-inference rows), per the review thread.
fix: 1a8ab6b981. An unannotated let of a list of bare numbers leaves its elements open (exprs.rs ArrayLiteral), so a later argument fixes them: [0, 0] into mut ref Vec[i32], [0, 7] into Vec[i32]. The two consumers that broke the reverted try are handled: the element-view lookup unifies a literal slice element with the Vec[T] slot (settle_view_literals, called from contains, binary_search and the library-source contains), and is_key_view resolves the slice element. 37b53dade4 fixes the cases the gate found: a collect of the open list handed to a generic callee (largest(w.iter().cloned().collect())), v == [] beside an open list, and a chain of an open list. Pin corpus/design/ok_a_list_literal_s_numbers_take_the_type_its_binding_s_use_gives_them.

title: A tuple comparison (`a >= b` on `(i64, i64, i64)`) lowers through `cmp`'s Ordering: each element takes setg/inc/cmp/cmov (about 7 instructions) where Rust's lexicographic `PartialOrd` is a compare and a branch (kata 632: 2.91G instructions against checked Rust's 1.72G on x86); the 24-byte stack-slot swap it also named is B-2026-11-08-87's
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-09 on x86 (callgrind, karac at 3d45c76221 with B-2026-11-08-10's slice sifts, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build of kara-katas leetcode/601-700/632-smallest-range-covering-elements-from-k-lists/bench/smallest_range.kara against rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on; outputs identical). 2,910,343,067 instructions against 1,721,863,139 (1.69x; the M5 relay measured 3.18G before -10). Everything is inlined into main; the hot loop is PriorityQueue[(i64, i64, i64)]'s `pq_sift_to_bottom`, about 44 instructions a level. Per element of `xs[c] >= xs[c + 1]`: `xor; cmp; setg; inc; cmp; mov 0; cmovge; jne` builds the Ordering (0/1/2) and then compares it with 1 (`cmp r10,1; sbb`), where Rust's derived tuple `ge` is `cmp; jne` per element plus one final setcc. The swap of two 24-byte elements is spilled: `vmovups` + a qword to a stack slot, the second element copied over the first, the slot copied back (12 instructions, 6 memory round trips through the stack); Rust's `Hole` moves one element a level (see B-2026-11-08-87). Two separate improvements: (1) lower `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` on tuples (and derived-Ord structs) as a lexicographic chain of the element operators instead of `cmp(..) op Equal`; (2) swap large elements through registers, or a hole primitive. Owner: drop schedule (src/backend/) and whoever owns the comparison lowering in src/mir/lower.rs.
fix: 6d16b370c8. Part (1): ordered_exprs (src/mir/lower.rs) lowers `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` on a tuple whose elements are all integers, bools or chars as the chain of element compares (scalar_tuple_rel): at the first differing element its strict compare decides, the last takes the operator. Floats keep the Ordering route, whose NaN answers the chain would change. On x86 (callgrind, outputs identical) kata 632 went from 2.91G to 2.62G instructions (Rust 1.72G) and kata 743 (PriorityQueue[(i64, i64)]) from 2.40G to 2.09G (Rust 1.77G). The sift's element compare is now `cmp; jne` per element plus one setcc. Part (2), the 24-byte swap through a stack slot, is the PriorityQueue hole remainder already tracked as B-2026-11-08-87 and is not part of this close. Pin: corpus/design/ok_tuple_comparison_is_lexicographic_under_every_operator, a 6x6 table checked against Python's tuple order (interp, llvm, ASan).

title: A by-value function's `mut ref Vec[i64]` parameter gets no `noalias` (mark_noalias skips by-value signatures), so every store into an element reloads the Vec's data pointer and length and re-checks the bound: kata 695's union-find `join` executes 1.54G instructions against Rust's 0.86G (whole bench 1.28x checked Rust on x86)
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-09 on x86 (callgrind, karac 3d45c76221, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build of kara-katas leetcode/601-700/695-max-area-of-island/bench/max_area_of_island.kara against rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on; outputs identical). Total 3.091G against 2.411G. `kara.join` (with `find` inlined) is 1.54G inclusive against Rust's `join` 0.86G. The IR signature is `define internal void @kara.join(ptr align 8 dereferenceable(24) %0, ptr align 8 dereferenceable(24) %1, i64 %2, i64 %3)`, no `noalias`. `Cx::mark_noalias` (src/backend/mir/mod.rs) skips every function with a by-value signature (`value_sig`). In find's path-compression loop each iteration is `mov [r8],r9` (parent[at] = root) followed by `mov r10,[rdi+8]` (reload len), the bound check against it, `mov r11,[rdi]` (reload data pointer), then the load of parent[next]: LLVM cannot tell the i64 element store left the i64 header fields alone. Rust's `&mut [usize]` arrives as pointer and length in registers. `mut ref` is exclusive under borrowck, so `noalias` on a `mut ref` parameter of a by-value function looks sound where B-2026-11-04-39 and B-2026-11-07-33 left `ref` parameters open (core-semantics 5.9 / 6.2); the same reload shape is what B-2026-11-08-10 removed inside the library by viewing the Vec as a slice. Owner: drop schedule (src/backend/).
fix: d308599fbb. `Cx::mark_deref_params` (src/backend/mir/mod.rs) marks a by-value function's `mut ref T` parameter `noalias` when `T` takes a §6.2 borrow flag (`mir::flags::takes_flag`: not Copy, not a handle or handle aggregate). Through one handle place borrowck rejects a second path; through another handle a flagged `T` panics before it is read or written. A Copy `mut` field of a shared value can be read through another handle while a `mut ref` to it lives (measured: `g(mut node.count, other)` reads 5 through `other`), so a `mut ref` of a Copy or counted type stays unmarked. `KARAC_MIR_NOALIAS_MUTREF=0` turns it off. Kata 695: 3.091G -> 2.578G (Rust 2.427G). Sweep of 1075 benches, off vs on: outputs identical, 106 binaries differ; the wall outliers re-measured by callgrind all execute fewer or equal instructions. IR pin updated: tests/mir_pair_and_sret_calls.rs.

title: A `Vec[(i64, i64)]` is accepted for a `Vec[(i64, u64)]` parameter (a tuple inside a generic argument is compared by the value rule, not the layout rule), and an open literal key lets `Map[?, i64]` pass for a `Map[i64, u64]`; interp prints -9 where the binary prints 18446744073709551607
detail: Found while gating B-2026-11-08-42. `fn second(m: Vec[(i64, u64)]) { println(m[0].1); } fn main() { let nine: i64 = -9; let t: (i64, i64) = (5, nine); let v: Vec[(i64, i64)] = [t]; second(v); }` checks clean at c6016977c7 (and at the 0.8.0 release binary); __mir-run prints -9 and __mir-llvm-run prints 18446744073709551607. Cause: `numeric_args_agree` (typechecker/types.rs), which keeps numeric generic arguments invariant (B-2026-08-05-19), compared only scalar keys, so a tuple or an array inside a generic argument fell to `types_compatible`'s symmetric numeric arm. Second door: `check_assignable`'s literal branch accepted any successful `unify_types`, whose last arm is `types_compatible`, so a type holding any open literal (a map's key `1`) unified i64 with u64 in its other arguments and returned true: `let mut m = Map.new(); let nine: i64 = 9; m.insert(5, nine); f(m)` into `Map[i64, u64]` passed once -42 kept the key open, and a pushed `(5, nine)` into a `Vec[(i64, u64)]` passed before it.
fix: ee2d9fee79. numeric_args_agree (typechecker/types.rs) reaches into tuples and arrays, so a generic argument's tuple keeps its numbers' types, and check_assignable's literal branch re-judges the value once its literals are fixed rather than accepting any unification (whose last arm takes any two numbers). The repro is refused 'expected ref Vec[(i64, u64)], found Vec[(i64, i64)]'; the open-key Map case is refused 'expected Map[i64, u64], found Map[i64, i64]'. Pinned by corpus/design/err_a_tuple_held_in_a_vec_keeps_its_numbers.

title: Inside a generic body, `T.default()` (any `T.f(..)` path call) with `T` a type parameter calls the program's own `struct T`'s `f` at every instance when the program declares a type named `T`: `fn fresh[T: Default]() -> T { T.default() }` with `let u: U = fresh()` builds a `T`
detail: karac 0.8.1-dev at ee55dfa7c7. `struct T { n: i64 }` and `struct U { m: i64 }`, each with `impl Default` (n: 1, m: 2); `fn fresh[T: Default]() -> T { T.default() }`; `let u: U = fresh(); println(u.m); let t: T = fresh(); println(t.n);` prints `1` and `1` on interp (expected 2, 1). The checker resolves the path's head to the type parameter (the resolver records SymbolKind::TypeParam), but the typed-HIR bridge (src/typed_hir.rs, the call loop) finds no callee by path for a `Res::Generic` head and falls back to the name-keyed `T.default` method key, which `method_callee` resolves to the program's `struct T`. Lowering then takes the recorded `Callee::Def` instead of `type_param_call`. With a generic trait the struct implements twice (`impl Mk[i64] for T`, `impl Mk[String] for T`), `T.mk(n)` under `T: Mk[i64]` failed at LLVM with `native T.mk is not lowered yet`. The same collision broke `Json.deserialize[T: Deserialize]` for any program with a `struct T` (it read every type as the program's `T`, B-2026-11-08-78). Found while fixing B-2026-11-08-78.
fix: ef6cd921e9. The typed-HIR bridge (src/typed_hir.rs) gives a path call whose head resolves to a type parameter (Res::Generic) a builtin callee keyed by the checker's `T.f`, never the name-keyed fallback that found the program's `struct T`, so lowering takes type_param_call at the instance type. The checker's multi-impl associated-call and conversion intercepts (src/typechecker/expr_call.rs) skip a type parameter too. `fresh[U]` now gives U's default (2) and `fresh[T]` T's (1); `T.mk(n)` under `T: Mk[i64]`, with struct T implementing Mk twice, gives the instance's (it failed at LLVM). Pin: corpus/design/ok_a_type_parameter_named_like_a_program_type_is_the_instance (interp, llvm, ASan).

title: `T.from(x)` under a `T: From[X]` bound is refused with an internal message ("a type that failed to check is not lowered yet" at the callee `T.from`), so a generic body cannot convert into its parameter; `karac check` reports the same internal message
detail: karac 0.8.1-dev at ee55dfa7c7 (and main df2cb8bef1). `struct W { n: i64 } impl From[i64] for W { fn from(n: i64) -> W { W { n: n } } } fn conv[T: From[i64]](n: i64) -> T { T.from(n) } fn main() { let w: W = conv(5); println(w.n); }` -> `error[typecheck]: 3:38: a type that failed to check is not lowered yet` under `T.from`. A user generic trait in the same shape (`trait Mk[A] { fn mk(a: A) -> Self; }`, `U.mk(n)` under `U: Mk[i64]`) works and prints 5, so the gap is `From`: the library's `trait From { }` (runtime/stdlib/from.kara) declares no `from`, so `try_dispatch_typeparam_assoc_fn` (src/typechecker/expr_method_call.rs) finds no trait method under the bound and the path falls to `resolve_path_type`'s type-parameter arm (src/typechecker/expr_ops.rs, `T.default` only), which types every other member as Error without a diagnostic. Expected: `5`, the instance's `from` (design.md §10 Converting errors writes `E2.from(e)` in exactly this generic position). `TryFrom` is likely the same.
fix: 6d16b370c8. The library's `trait From { }` and `trait TryFrom { type Error; }` declared no method, so try_dispatch_typeparam_assoc_fn found none under a `T: From[X]` bound and resolve_path_type's type-parameter arm typed the callee Error with no diagnostic. runtime/stdlib/from.kara and try_from.kara now declare `trait From[T] { fn from(value: own T) -> Self; }` and `trait TryFrom[T] { type Error; fn try_from(value: own T) -> Result[Self, Self.Error]; }` as design.md § Conversion traits writes them, and the impl conformance check (src/typechecker/items.rs) reads a bare `impl From for Out { fn from(a: A) }` as `From[A]` (9 corpus fixtures use that form). `conv[W](5)` gives 5 and `T.try_from` under `T: TryFrom[i64]` gives Ok 3 / Err `30 is too big`. Any other member no bound declares (`T.build(n)` under `T: Make`) is now refused at check naming the bounds (src/typechecker/expr_ops.rs). Pins: corpus/design/ok_a_type_parameter_converts_through_its_from_bound and err_a_type_parameter_call_no_bound_declares_is_refused (interp, llvm, ASan).

title: A literal table of constants iterated in a hot loop (`for step in [1, 9]`) is slower promoted to a static (src/mir/literal_tables.rs) than built in place: the static is a zero-initialized mutable global filled at startup, so LLVM reloads its pointer and length and bounds-checks each step of a 2-step loop it no longer unrolls (kata 752: 6.38G instructions, 4.61G with KARAC_MIR_LITERAL_TABLES=0, checked Rust 4.85G)
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-09 on x86 (callgrind, karac at ef6cd921e9, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build of kara-katas leetcode/701-800/752-open-the-lock/bench/open_lock.kara against rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on; outputs identical). 6,382,615,496 instructions against 4,847,214,714 (1.32x; the M5 relay measured 1.45x); a Rust mirror rewritten to i64 with the Kara expression is 4,726,949,432, so the type choice is not the gap. 95% is inlined into main; the hot block is the inner `for step in [1, 9]` (116M iterations): `cmp 0x8(%r14),%r13; jae` (the bounds check against the length read from the static's header each step), `mov (%r14),%rax` (the data pointer reloaded), then the element load, around 28 instructions a step. In the IR the table is `@kara.static.table0 = global [24 x i8] zeroinitializer`, written by `kara.static.table0.ptr` at startup, so nothing tells LLVM its contents. The same program with KARAC_MIR_LITERAL_TABLES=0 is 4,611,144,462 (LLVM sees the local Vec of two constants and folds it away), equal to replacing the loop by `for k in 0..2 { let step = 1 + 8 * k; ... }` (4,611,144,462). The pass exists for tables of Strings (kata 804, B-2026-10-19-34), where it removes one allocation per element per call. Remedy, least sure: leave a table whose elements are all scalar constants unpromoted (LLVM already elides it), or emit such a static as a constant global with its buffer in a constant array. Owner: drop schedule (src/mir/literal_tables.rs, src/backend/).
fix: 64f7f708eb. A non-`mut` static `Vec` whose initializer only builds it from an array of integer, bool, char or f32/f64 constants (`Cx::const_table`, src/backend/mir/body.rs) is emitted as a constant global `{ptr, len, 0}` over a private constant buffer, the borrowed-literal form, and its initializer is not run at startup (`init_statics`, src/backend/mir/mod.rs). LLVM then sees the elements and folds a short loop over them. A table of strings keeps its initializer. Kata 752 on x86 (callgrind, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build): 6.38G -> 4.63G instructions, the same as KARAC_MIR_LITERAL_TABLES=0 (checked Rust 4.85G); outputs identical. Pin: tests/mir_const_literal_table.rs (interpreter and compiled agree on index, len, iter, and a clone then grown; the IR holds six constant tables and the one string table zeroed).

title: A counting loop that starts at a local, `for i in low..low + k`, is not presized: `mir::presize` takes only a constant start, so kata 658's window copy grows its vector 4, 8, 16, ... on every query (1.94x checked Rust on x86)
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-09 on x86 (callgrind, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build of the kara-katas bench against rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on; outputs identical). Kata 658 (find k closest elements): 1.966G instructions against Rust's 1.015G; the gap is the `out` vector's doubling growth, a malloc, copy and free per step, in the `for i in low..low + k { out.push(arr[i]) }` that ends each query. `mir::presize` required `i = const k` as the loop's start. A start that is a local `s` with a bound `s + n` runs `n` trips whenever neither `s` nor `n` changes between the add and the loop, so `n` can be reserved.
fix: d308599fbb. `mir::presize` takes a start `i = copy s` from a local when the bound copies `t.0` of `t = s + n` (checked or not, either order) and neither `s` nor `n` is written in the loop or between the add, the start and the reservation (`counted_past`, src/mir/presize.rs); the loop then reserves `n`. Kata 658: 1.966G -> 1.042G (Rust 1.015G), outputs identical. Pin: tests/mir_presize_offset_start.rs (a `moved` start still grows by doubling).

title: `i64.parse` of a negative number calls the runtime: the in-line decimal parse takes only digits, so kata 682's `-` scores each paid a runtime call (1.69x checked Rust on x86)
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-09 on x86 (callgrind, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build of the kara-katas bench against rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on; outputs identical). Kata 682 (baseball game): 4.418G against Rust's 2.613G. `parse_decimal` (src/backend/mir/num.rs) parses up to 18 ASCII digits in line and sends anything else, a leading `-` included, to `karac_mir_parse_int`. For a signed type the sign can be taken in line too: up to 19 characters with the sign, magnitude checked against max + 1 when negative.
fix: d308599fbb. `parse_decimal` (src/backend/mir/num.rs) takes a leading `-` in line for a signed type: up to 19 characters with the sign, the magnitude checked against max + 1 when negative, the result negated by a select. Kata 682: 4.418G -> 2.404G (Rust 2.613G). Pin: tests/mir_parse_negative.rs, whose expected output matches the interpreter on i64 and i8 edge cases (`-9223372036854775808`, `-128`, `-`, `--1`, overflow).

title: A by-value function's `ref Vec` parameter gets no `noalias`, so every store into another vector reloads its header and re-tests its bounds: kata 718's DP loop runs 3.57x checked Rust's instructions on x86
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-09 on x86 (callgrind, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build of the kara-katas bench against rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on; outputs identical). Kata 718 (maximum length of repeated subarray): 15.77G against Rust's 4.41G. Both input `ref Vec[i64]` headers are reloaded, and their bounds re-tested, after every store into the DP row: LLVM cannot tell the i64 store left the headers alone. A shared borrow freezes the pointee's own bytes for the call (core semantics 5.9) when they are numbers, a String/Vec/VecDeque header, a shared handle, or tuples/arrays/options of those; their elements are behind a pointer, which `noalias` does not reach. Sweep of 1075 benches with KARAC_MIR_NOALIAS_REF=0/1: outputs identical, wall geomean 0.983, 718 0.56x; the one wall outlier (662, 1.24x) executes the same instruction count.
fix: d308599fbb. A by-value function's `ref T` parameter is `noalias` when `T` keeps its own bytes while shared-borrowed (`Cx::frozen_inline`: numbers, bool, char, unit, String/Vec/VecDeque headers, shared/weak handles, tuples, arrays and options of those); the elements are behind a pointer, which `noalias` does not reach. `KARAC_MIR_NOALIAS_REF=0` turns it off. Kata 718: 15.772G -> 6.090G (Rust 4.414G); the earlier sweep of 1075 benches with it off vs on: outputs identical, wall geomean 0.983, 718 0.56x, the one wall outlier (662) executes the same instructions. Pins: tests/mir_noalias_frozen_ref.rs; tests/mir_deref_params.rs and tests/mir_pair_and_sret_calls.rs updated.

title: `String.push_str` is a runtime call and a `memcpy` call per append: kata 763's strings built a letter at a time run 1.84x checked Rust on x86
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-09 on x86 (callgrind, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build of the kara-katas bench against rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on; outputs identical). Kata 763 (partition labels): 5.456G against Rust's 2.964G; `karac_mir_string_push_str` is 1.41G and its `memcpy` 0.82G, for 50M one-byte appends. Rust's `push_str` is in line, and a slice whose length is known is copied as that many bytes.
fix: d308599fbb. `String.push_str` appends in line (`Cx::string_append`, src/backend/mir/seq.rs): while `len + n` fits the capacity the bytes are copied straight in with an `llvm.memcpy` LLVM can shorten for a known length; a full buffer or a borrowed literal (capacity 0) goes through the cold `Shim::StrReserve`, which keeps the reserve's header slot out of the append site (300 appends in one function otherwise kept 300 slots past SROA; tests/mir_collections.rs `jit_ir_has_its_stack_slots_replaced`). Kata 763: 5.456G -> 3.196G (Rust 2.964G). Pin: tests/mir_push_str_inline.rs (literal copy-out on an empty append, growth past doubling, multi-byte text).

title: A vector made before its loop's bound is worked out (`let mut seat_of = Vec.new(); for _ in 0..row.len() { seat_of.push(0) }`) is not presized, since the bound is not known where `Vec.new()` is: kata 765 runs 1.27x checked Rust on x86
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-09 on x86 (callgrind, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build of the kara-katas bench against rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on; outputs identical). Kata 765 (couples holding hands): 4.074G against Rust's 3.198G; malloc, free and realloc of `seat_of`'s doubling growth are about 600M of the gap. `mir::presize` reserves right after `Vec.new()`, so a bound computed between it and the loop was refused. The vector can be reserved for the trips at the loop's way in instead, past any seed pushes, as a second fill already is.
fix: d308599fbb. When the bound is not held where `Vec.new()` is, `mir::presize` places the reservation at the loop's way in (the chain block nearest the loop), past any seed pushes, as a second fill already was. Kata 765: 4.074G -> 2.796G (Rust 3.198G). Pin: tests/mir_presize_bound_after_new.rs (10 pushes reserve 10 rather than doubling to 16; a seed and 10 more reserve 11).
