title: A library body's located function (`<fn>.at`, every library body a program calls) gets none of the parameter attributes the plain function gets: no `dereferenceable`, `align` or `noalias`, so `PriorityQueue.push` reloads `self` and its length after every swap (kata 778, 1.31x checked Rust on x86)
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-09 on x86 (callgrind, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build of the kara-katas bench against rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on; outputs identical). Kata 778 (swim in rising water): 6.537G against Rust's 4.999G; `PriorityQueue[(i64, i64)].push.at` is 1.95G. `Cx::located_function` (src/backend/mir/debug.rs) declares the `.at` twin without `mark_deref_params`, so its `mut ref self` carried nothing, and the sift reloaded `self.max` and `self.xs.len` on every level.
fix: d308599fbb. `Cx::located_function` (src/backend/mir/debug.rs) gives the `.at` twin the parameter attributes the plain function gets (`noalias` on the result slot, and `mark_deref_params`: dereferenceable, align, and the `noalias` of B-2026-11-09-8 and B-2026-11-09-2). With `mut ref self` marked, `PriorityQueue.push`'s sift keeps `self.max` and the length in registers. Kata 778: 6.537G -> 6.119G (Rust 4.999G); kata 786 8.959G -> 7.836G. The rest is B-2026-11-09-12 (sifts by swaps).

title: `PriorityQueue`'s sifts swap elements a level at a time where Rust's `BinaryHeap` moves a hole, three element copies a level against one: kata 786 runs 1.34x and kata 778 1.22x checked Rust on x86
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-09 on x86 (callgrind, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build of the kara-katas bench against rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on; outputs identical). Kata 786 (k-th smallest prime fraction): 7.836G against Rust's 5.847G after B-2026-11-09-11, 6.47G of it `PriorityQueue[Fraction].pop.at`, about 35 instructions a level of `sift_down_to_bottom`, a third of them the 32-byte swap through a stack slot; kata 778's `push.at` is 1.58G with 23 a level. `BinaryHeap` keeps the moving element in a hole and copies each child up once. Kāra's library cannot move an element out of a `Vec` slot for an unconstrained `T`, and a hole needs a guard that refills it if a user `cmp` panics, so this wants a library primitive (a `Vec` rotate along the sift path, or a guarded hole) rather than a rewrite in Kāra.
fix: d308599fbb filed this; it is the same defect as B-2026-11-08-87 (PriorityQueue's sift swaps where BinaryHeap moves a hole), which tracks it. Its measurements, for that row: on x86 after B-2026-11-09-11, kata 786 is 7.836G against Rust's 5.847G, 6.47G of it `PriorityQueue[Fraction].pop.at` at about 35 instructions a level (a 32-byte element swapped through a stack slot), and kata 778's `push.at` is 1.58G at 23 a level.

title: `karac fix` turns a plain Rust `BinaryHeap` into a smallest-first `PriorityQueue.new()` whenever any other heap in the program wraps its items in `Reverse`, so a max heap beside a min heap silently becomes a second min heap and the carried program checks clean and prints wrong answers
detail: Found carrying kata 2034's Rust template (Stock Price Fluctuation): `max_heap: BinaryHeap<(i32, i32)>` and `min_heap: BinaryHeap<Reverse<(i32, i32)>>`, both built `BinaryHeap::new()` in a struct literal. After four `karac fix` rounds the program checks clean with `max_heap: PriorityQueue.new()`, so `maximum()` returns the minimum: LeetCode's example prints [5, 5, 3, 2] for [5, 10, 5, 2]. The resolver's `report_rust_binary_heap` chose the side for the whole program (`rust_heaps_pop_smallest`: any Reverse wrap and any heap constructor), and wrote `PriorityQueue.new()` for every constructor. The same holds for two `let`s (`let mut most = BinaryHeap::new(); let mut least = BinaryHeap::new(); most.push(p); least.push(Reverse(p));`). A two-heap program (max beside min) is the standard shape of running-median, stock-price and sliding-window problems.
fix: FIXED by 4899210bd7. The parser now links each `BinaryHeap::new()` constructor to the binding it initializes (a struct-literal field, a `let`, an assignment) and reads that binding's side from its declared item type (`NAME: BinaryHeap[Reverse[..]]` against any other item) and from what is pushed onto it (`NAME.push(Reverse(..))` against a bare item). A heap of `Reverse` items becomes `PriorityQueue.new()` and a heap of bare items `PriorityQueue.max_first()`, each on its own. A constructor whose side cannot be told, in a program that holds both kinds, gets no fix, and then no heap and no `Reverse` in the program does, since a later round would read the program without the `Reverse` evidence. A `let Reverse(x) = ..` pattern is dropped like a `Some(Reverse(x))` payload. Kata 2034's Rust arm now carries to `max_first()` for the maximum heap and `new()` for the minimum, and matches the mirror on every lane. Pinned by tests/kata_2034_heap_sides.rs: struct fields and lets beside a reversed heap each keep their side, and an unnamed heap beside both kinds gets no fix.

title: Rust's `binary_search` taken apart as a `Result` has no fix: `xs.binary_search(&v).unwrap_or_else(|x| x)` is refused with "expected 'OnceFn() -> i64', found 'Fn(?T) -> ?T'" and `match xs.binary_search(&v) { Ok(i) => .., Err(i) => .. }` with a generic pattern error, though Kāra's `binary_search` returns `Option[i64]` and `partition_point(|y| y < v)` is the insertion point
detail: Found carrying kata 2035's Rust template (meet in the middle: `let at = ys.binary_search(&want).unwrap_or_else(|x| x);`), and before it kata 2034's sorted-Vec arm (`match prices.binary_search(&p) { Ok(i) => .., Err(i) => prices.insert(i, p) }`). Rust's `binary_search` returns `Result<usize, usize>`: `Ok` of a matching index, `Err` of the insertion point. Kāra's returns `Option[i64]` (docs/library), so `unwrap_or_else` takes a zero-argument closure and the Rust `|x| x` is refused with a type message that names neither shape; the `Ok`/`Err` match is refused at its patterns. Neither has a machine fix, and every LeetCode Rust template that does an insertion-point search uses one of the two. The translation is mechanical: `unwrap_or_else(|x| x)` on `binary_search(v)` is `partition_point(|y| y < v)` (Rust's Ok index among equal items is unspecified, and the first one is a valid answer); an `Ok(i)`/`Err(i)` match is `let i = xs.partition_point(|y| y < v); if i < xs.len() and xs[i] == v { ..Ok arm.. } else { ..Err arm.. }`. Repro: `fn main() { let v = [1, 3, 5].to_vec(); println(v.binary_search(4).unwrap_or_else(|x| x)); }`. Either a fix for the two shapes, or a diagnostic that says Kāra's `binary_search` is an `Option` and points at `partition_point`.
fix: 182b518950. src/typechecker/rust_binary_search.rs, hooked after a method call (`infer_method_call`) and around every `match`/`if let` (`infer_expr` and `check_expr`): when a check fails inside a Rust shape over `xs.binary_search(v)`, its errors are replaced by one: "Kāra's `binary_search` returns `Option[i64]`, the index of an element equal to the value or `None`, not Rust's `Result` of an index or the insertion point; the insertion point is `partition_point(|y| y < v)`". The mechanical shapes carry a fix. `.unwrap_or_else(|i| i)` becomes `xs.partition_point(|y| y < v)` (the row's cell and kata 2035's line). Any other closure body becomes `{ let i = xs.partition_point(..); if i < xs.len() and xs[i] == v { i } else { body } }`. A `match` over `Ok(i)`/`Err(j)` (either order, `_` allowed) and `if let Ok(i)`/`Err(i)` (with or without `else`) become the same block with the arms as its branches, the other arm's name bound to `i`; it is laid out by the formatter at the expression's column. A shape is not rewritten, and the message says why, when the sequence is not a plain place or the value is not free of effects (the rewrite names each more than once), or for `.unwrap_err()`, `.map_err()`, `.ok()`, `.err()` and the like ("takes Rust's `Result` apart, and the `Option` has no counterpart"). Kata 2035's Rust arm now loses that error; it keeps -15's two. `.is_ok()`/`.is_err()` on the Option are accepted today and behave as `is_some`/`is_none`, so they draw no error to replace: filed as B-2026-11-09-21. Pins: tests/rust_binary_search_result_fixes.rs.

title: A defaulted `i64` literal that reaches a narrower slot through a collection (`let mut a = 0; a += nums[i]; left[k].push(a)`, then `best.min(x + ..)` for `x` in `left[k]`, `best: i32`) is refused at the `min` with no edit; the fix is `a: i32` at the binding, two hops away
detail: Kata 2035's Rust template builds `left = vec![vec![]; n + 1]` and pushes each subset sum `a` (`let mut a = 0; a += nums[i]` over `Vec<i32>`): Rust types `a` and so `left` `i32` from the later uses. In Kāra the literal keeps `i64` (design.md §8: an operator does not fix a literal's type), `Vec.filled(n + 1, Vec.new())` takes `Vec[Vec[i64]]` from the push, and the refusal comes where a loop over `ref left[k]` meets the `i32` receiver: "`min` expects an argument of type `i32`, got `i64`" with nothing to apply. kara (this commit series) gives the annotation when the argument reads the defaulted binding itself (`best.min(a + nums[j])`, `tests/kata_2035_check_gaps.rs`), and an annotated `left: Vec[Vec[i32]]` gets it at the push; the case left is the value read back out of the collection the binding was pushed into. Repro: `fn f(nums: Vec[i32]) -> i32 { let mut left = Vec.filled(2, Vec.new()); let mut a = 0; a += nums[0]; left[0].push(a); let mut best = i32.MAX; for x in ref left[0] { best = best.min(x + nums[1]); } best }`. The fix wanted is the same `a: i32` edit, found through the collection's element type.
fix: 6464505444. A push of an unannotated literal binding into a collection (left[k].push(a)) is remembered against the collection's root binding (note_literal_push), and a for over that collection (left[k], ref left[k], left[k].iter()) binds its loop variable to a's literal_lets entry for the body (note_literal_for_binding), so the refusal at best.min(x + nums[j]) with best: i32 offers a: i32, which karac fix applies; the program then checks clean and prints its answer. Pinned in tests/kata_2035_check_gaps.rs (kata_2035_a_literal_read_back_out_of_a_collection_gets_its_annotation).

title: A move inside a `let … else` else block is reported E0500 "value 'x' moved here, used again here (moved at line L)" against a move of the same binding AFTER the `let … else`, which only runs when the pattern matched: the ownership CFG continued the rest of the block in the block the else branch leaves from
detail: Found writing apps/cli/mini_jsonlogic: `reduce` reads `let init = arg(args, 2); let Val.List(items) = apply(args[0], data)? else { return Ok(init); }; ... let mut acc = init;`. karac check (0.8.1-dev.15070) refused it at the `return Ok(init)` with `value 'init' moved here, used again here (moved at line <the later let>)`, and karac fix applied the suggested `init.clone()` at the later move: a needless copy written into a correct program. Reduced: `fn pick(xs: Option[Vec[i64]], init: String) -> String { let init = init.clone(); let Some(items) = xs else { return init; }; let mut acc = init; ... acc }` gives the same E0500. The else block diverges and the statements after the `let … else` run only when the pattern matched, so the two moves are on different paths and neither reaches the other (core-semantics.md §3.2: a use after move is one a move reaches on some path). Cause: src/cfg.rs lowers `StmtKind::LetElse` by adding an edge from the initializer's block `after` to the else block and then returning `after` itself, so every later statement's uses were recorded in `after` too and the else block became their successor: the later move appeared to flow into the else block's use. The sibling `if c { return x; } let y = x;` is accepted because `if` lowering joins into a fresh block.
fix: 6db1634956. In src/cfg.rs, the ownership CFG's `StmtKind::LetElse` arm now continues the rest of the enclosing block in a fresh block, reached from the initializer's block beside the else branch, instead of carrying on in the block the else branch leaves from. The else block stays a dead end (its `return`/`break` reaches only the exit), so a move after the `let … else` no longer flows into a use inside the else block. Measured: the row's reduced `pick` passes `karac check` and prints `a12` / `b` under `karac run`; a genuine reuse (`let other = init; let again = init;` after the let-else) is still E0500. Pinned by corpus/core/ok_a_let_else_branch_moves_what_the_rest_moves (a `return fallback` and a `let kept = fallback; return kept` else branch, each followed by a move of `fallback`), matching its expected output on __mir-run, __mir-llvm-run, __mir-llvm-asan and karac build; added to `needs_library` in src/mir/borrowck.rs (`Vec.into_iter`). Control: karac 0.8.1-dev at the Nov 4 release build reports both pin moves E0500. apps/cli/mini_jsonlogic's `reduce` now reads `let mut acc = init;` with no clone. Gate: full four legs green on the pre-rebase bases (10719 + 10900 passed), and fmt, both clippy legs and cargo test --all (10735 passed) on the final rebase.

title: `.slice(a, b)` on a `Vec`, an array or a slice (JavaScript's spelling of a run of elements) gets a bare "no method 'slice' on type 'Vec'", with no pointer to the range index `v[a..b]` and nothing for `karac fix` to apply
detail: Kata 1078's differential first wrote its prefix property as `words.slice(0, cut).join(" ")` and `answer.slice(0, part.len()).to_vec()`. `karac check` said only `no method 'slice' on type 'Vec'` at each call. collections.md has no `slice` method: a run of a `Vec`, an array or a slice is the range index `v[a..b]`, a `Slice[T]`, which `.to_vec()` copies out. The kata spells it `words[0..cut].to_vec().join(" ")`. A diagnostic should name the range index, and `karac fix` should write it where it can.
fix: e9cca2f951: `.slice(a, b)` on a `Vec`, an array or a slice is now refused with "a run of elements is the range index `v[a..b]`, a `Slice[T]`; `.to_vec()` copies it out" (reject_slice_method_on_sequence in src/typechecker/method_vec_mutation.rs, called from expr_method_call.rs), and carries a fix-it to `v[a..b]` when both bounds are an integer literal or a name; a computed bound gets the hint alone, since the checker has no source text to write it back. A type with its own `slice` method is left alone. tests/kata_1078_slice_hint.rs pins both.

title: `c as u8` on a `char` (LeetCode's Rust template for 1079, `count[(c as u8 - b'A') as usize]`) is refused with a help naming `c as u32 as u8` but no machine fix, so `karac fix` stops the template there
detail: Kata 1079's Rust arm keeps LeetCode's `for c in tiles.chars() { count[(c as u8 - b'A') as usize] += 1; }`. Kāra refuses `char as u8` (E_CHAR_AS_NARROW_INT: the scalar range does not fit in 8 bits) and the message's help says `c as u32 as u8` for explicit truncation, which is exactly Rust's meaning of `c as u8` (the low 8 bits of the scalar value). The error carried no fix-it, so after three rounds `karac fix` reported no fixable diagnostics and the arm did not check. The cast is checked in `check_cast_pair` (src/typechecker.rs), which sees only the operand's span; for an operand that is itself a cast that span is the innermost operand's, so the insertion point is not known there.
fix: 10ef8e8c7a: E_CHAR_AS_NARROW_INT now carries a fix-it inserting ` as u32` after the operand, giving `c as u32 as u8`, Rust's meaning of `c as u8`. check_cast_pair (src/typechecker.rs) takes the operand text's end from the Cast arm (src/typechecker/exprs.rs), which passes it unless the operand is itself a cast, whose span is its own operand's; such a cast keeps the help alone. tests/kata_1079_char_cast_fix.rs pins the edit on an index expression, a method chain, a Vec[char] index and a dereference, and no edit on `n as char as u8`. Kata 1079's Rust arm now reaches a clean check in three fix rounds.

title: `v.contains(d)` with a float needle on a `Vec[u8]` (`let d = 1.5`) passes `karac check`; the interpreter then stops with "Eq on Int(1) and Float(1.5)" and the binary prints `false`, while `Set[u8].contains(d)` and a `u8` parameter refuse the same float
detail: Found while fixing B-2026-11-08-86's probe needles (37b53dade4 era). Repro: `fn main() { let v: Vec[u8] = [1]; let d = 1.5; println(v.contains(d)); }` checks clean on main and on the 0.8.0-dev release binary; `__mir-run` fails 'in Vec[u8].contains at bb7[0]: Eq on Int(1) and Float(1.5)'; `__mir-llvm-run` prints false. Siblings refuse it: `fn t(a: u8)` called as `t(e)` with `let e = 2.5` gives "expected 'u8', found 'f64'", and `Set[u8].contains(d)` gives "expected 'u8', found 'f64'; a float does not implicitly convert to an integer — use `as u8` to truncate". Vec/VecDeque.contains under library_methods_from_source goes through method_user_impl's library-source path (get_mut_by_key_view returns None for a non-view needle, then the generic `ref T` argument check), which accepts f64 for ref u8; the stdlib_seq arm's check_assignable + coercion checks never run there. Wanted: the same refusal and `as u8` fix as the Set arm (design.md §5: a float does not implicitly convert to an integer).
fix: 2e41a1c552: check_assignable's float-into-integer refusal (design.md: a float does not implicitly convert to an integer) looked only at a bare integer slot; it now looks through `ref` and `mut ref`, so `Vec[u8].contains(d)`, `VecDeque[u8].contains(d)` and a `ref u8` / `mut ref u8` parameter given a float are refused ("use `as u8` to truncate" for a `ref`, "cannot be written through a `mut ref u8`" for a `mut ref`). The -55 view path was not the cause: its probe falls through to the same argument check. Measured on the rebased tree before the change: all five refusals checked clean, including a free fn with a `ref u8` parameter. Pinned by tests/float_into_borrowed_integer.rs, with the element and view needles (Str on Vec[String], Slice on Vec[Vec[i64]], u8, f64) still accepted and run.

title: A raw pointer cannot reach a non-`Copy` element: `ptr.mut(xs[i])` is refused as a move out of the collection, `p.read()` as a move out of a borrowed place, and the MIR interpreter stops at `p.write(v)` over a live value, so a library cannot move a `PriorityQueue` element through a hole
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-09 while writing B-2026-11-08-87's hole sift in runtime/stdlib/source/priority_queue.kara. Over `fn f[T](xs: mut Slice[T])`: (1) `let p: *mut T = ptr.mut(xs[0]);` gave ownership error "cannot move a non-`Copy` value out of a collection element": the use classifier walked the argument of the `ptr.mut` special form as consumed, though design.md calls `ptr.const` / `ptr.mut` place-taking forms. (2) `unsafe { p.offset(i).read() }` gave error[mir] "cannot move a non-`Copy` value out of a borrowed place": raw_ptr_method (src/mir/lower.rs) lowered `read` through use_place, a Move out of `*p`; making it a Copy then failed the MIR validator's "copy of (*_12) whose type String is not Copy". (3) With both past, the interpreter refused `p.write(v)` with "assignment overwrites (*_25), which still owns a value", its check that MIR never overwrites a live place; the compiled backends already stored without a drop. design.md said nothing about read and write on a non-Copy pointee.
fix: f6dfaaa342 (its commit message cites this row as B-2026-11-09-19, an id another session took first). (1) `ptr.mut(place)` / `ptr.const(place)` arguments are borrow positions in the use classifier (is_ptr_place_call, src/ownership.rs). (2) `p.read()` lowers to a bitwise Copy of `*p`, and the MIR validator allows a Copy of any type when the place is a raw pointer's pointee (is_raw_pointee, src/mir/place_ty.rs). (3) The interpreter skips its overwrite check for a raw pointee, so `p.write(v)` replaces without a drop as the compiled backends do. design.md § Raw pointers now says it: read copies the bits, write does not drop, and keeping each value owned once is the unsafe block's promise. Pin: corpus/design/ok_raw_pointer_moves_a_non_copy_element_without_a_drop (a three-way rotation of Drop-bodied elements and Strings, no drop during it, each element dropped once; interp, LLVM, ASan agree).

title: Tracker for the next minor release: `is_ok()`/`is_err()` on an `Option` become a compile error; in 0.8.x they are a `deprecated` warning with a `karac fix` to `is_some()`/`is_none()` (85675b25f1, core-types.md 49ba9850cd)
detail: Found closing B-2026-11-09-14. `let o: Option[i64] = Some(1); println(o.is_ok());` checks and prints `true` on __mir-run; `v.binary_search(4).is_err()` prints `true`. The builtin unwrap family in src/typechecker/method_temp_receiver.rs (the `is_some | is_none | is_ok | is_err` arm, ~line 431 and ~507) and expr_method_call.rs (`is_builtin_unwrap_family`, matched for `Some("Option") | Some("Result")`) types all four predicates on either receiver; `unwrap_err`/`expect_err` on an `Option` are refused elsewhere, so only the two predicates leak. core-types.md's `Option[T]` table has `is_some`/`is_none`/`is_some_and`, its `Result` table `is_ok`. Wanted, a ruling first: either `Option` keeps them as documented aliases, or they are refused with a machine fix to `.is_some()`/`.is_none()` (which is also the binary_search rewrite B-2026-11-09-14's relay asked for). Refusing them changes accepted programs, so it needs the review thread's word and a CHANGELOG "now refused" entry. Ruled 49ba9850cd: deprecated spellings in 0.8.x, an error at the next minor. 85675b25f1 warns (`deprecated`, suppressible with `#[allow(deprecated)]`) with a machine-applicable fix to `is_some()`/`is_none()` (tests/option_result_predicates_deprecated.rs). This row stays open until the warning becomes the error.

title: Kata 404 (sum of left leaves) runs 1.73x checked Rust's time on the M5 against 1.23x its instructions on x86: the arm64 share of the gap is unattributed
detail: The arm64 remainder of B-2026-11-07-33, whose x86 part was measured to a standstill (see its fix). M5 (review thread's 400-426 batch, kara-katas 3d7ad5f1): 1.73x rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on. x86 at e64d8e0c80's parent (callgrind, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0): 2.607G instructions against Rust's 2.113G (1.23x), visit 16.6 against 13.4 instructions a call. Needs an M5 profile of `visit` (the recursive `visit(nodes: Vec[Node], node: i64, is_left: bool)`) against Rust's `visit(&[Node], ..)`: whether the extra cost is the post-call header reload, the second bound check, or the extra saved register on arm64's call path. CROSS-BUILT 2026-11-12 (drop schedule, release karac at 49c3b65d78 for aarch64-apple-darwin at its default CPU, object kept; rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on --target aarch64-apple-darwin --emit asm): the static instruction counts of `visit` are 35 against Rust's 29 on an interior node and 26 against 23 on a leaf, the same ratio as x86's 1.23x. Kāra's extra work is the Vec header: the length and data pointer loaded on entry, and again after the first recursive call with the bound check repeated (B-2026-11-07-33's shape); Rust holds one element pointer. Instruction count therefore does not explain the M5's 1.73x time, which needs the M5's cycle counts, ideally re-run at HEAD (the 1.73x is from kara-katas 3d7ad5f1, 2026-11-07). The same object showed that no function set up its frame record, B-2026-11-12-10; with that fixed, `visit` gains Rust's one `add x29, sp, #0x20`.

title: A `pub fn` in an inherent impl of a type that is not `pub` (LeetCode's `struct Solution; impl Solution { pub fn sufficient_subset(root: Option<Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>>, ..) }` after `karac fix`) is refused with E0221 for naming the private `TreeNode`, though the method is on no public surface
detail: Kata 1080's Rust arm keeps LeetCode's template: `struct Solution;` and `impl Solution { pub fn sufficient_subset(root: Option<Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>>, limit: i32) -> Option<Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>> }`. `karac fix` carries the types to `Option[TreeNode]` over the program's own `shared struct TreeNode`, and the check then stops at E0221 PrivateTypeInPublicSignature, "private type 'TreeNode' leaks through method parameter 'root' of 'sufficient_subset'". Neither `Solution` nor `TreeNode` is `pub`, so nothing outside the package can name `Solution` or reach the method; Rust accepts the same shape (its private_interfaces lint is about reachable items). The leak walk in src/typechecker/items.rs checked every `pub fn` of every inherent impl, whatever the target type's visibility. The only way past it in the kata was to drop `pub` from the template's method or make both types `pub`, either a workaround.
fix: 52b677beea: the leak walk over public signatures in src/typechecker/items.rs skips an inherent impl (no trait) whose target type is not `pub` (names_private_type: a path whose last segment the type-visibility table marks private). Its `pub fn`s are reached only through a type users of the package cannot name, as Rust's private `struct Solution` with a `pub fn` is. A `pub` type's `pub fn` that names a private type is still refused with E0221. Pinned by tests/kata_1080_private_impl_pub_fn.rs; kata 1080's Rust arm now checks clean after `karac fix`.

title: A `char` handed to `replace` or `replacen` (Rust's `rest.replace(c, "")`) is refused with "expects String arguments" and no machine fix, though `find` and `contains` give the same char a `c.to_string()` fix
detail: Kata 1081's greedy arm takes every copy of a placed letter out of the rest of the text with `rest.slice(1, rest.len()).replace(c, "")`, `c: char`, as Rust's `str::replace` takes a char pattern. Kāra's string methods take a `Str` pattern; `s.find(c)` and `s.contains(c)` are refused through char_pattern_for_str (src/typechecker/exprs.rs, B-2026-10-20-22) with "'find' takes a `Str` pattern, found 'char': write it as `c.to_string()`" and a fix-it, and `karac fix` applied it in the same arm. The `replace` and `replacen` arms in src/typechecker/stdlib_seq.rs kept their own check, "'replace' expects String arguments, found 'char'", with no help and no edit, so `karac fix` stopped the arm there.
fix: 5eee63ee71: the `replace` and `replacen` arms in src/typechecker/stdlib_seq.rs send a char argument through char_pattern_for_str, as `find` and `contains` do: "'replace' takes a `Str` pattern, found 'char': write it as `c.to_string()`" with a machine fix (a char literal becomes the string literal), on the pattern and on the replacement alike. Any other non-string type keeps "expects String arguments". Pinned by tests/kata_1081_replace_char_fix.rs; kata 1081's greedy arm now checks clean after `karac fix`.

title: A presized push fill whose trip count is not a constant keeps two exits a trip, its bound and its reservation's reach, so LLVM does not vectorize it: kata 484's `(1..=n).collect()` (n = letters.len() + 1) runs 7 instructions an element where Rust's TrustedLen fill is vectorized, and its `s.chars().collect()` runs 14 a char against Rust's 11 (the chars().collect part is B-2026-11-09-47)
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-09 on x86 at 774d3877a5 (release karac, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build, callgrind --dump-instr against rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on): kata 484 (kara-katas leetcode/401-500/484-find-permutation/bench) 742M instructions against Rust's 551M, after 774d3877a5 lowered `(a..=b).collect()` to a presized counting loop (843M before). Of the rest: the fill loop runs 7 instructions an element on 20M elements (about 140M): `Vec.__push_within` stores below the reach `presize` returned and tests `len == reach` on each trip beside the loop's own `i < bound`; LLVM cannot show reach >= bound (the reservation is clamped to 2^30 bytes), so both exits stay and the loop is not vectorized. The same fill with a constant bound (a test calling `fill(100000 + r)` after inlining) vectorizes at under one instruction an element, so the shape is right and the missing fact is reach >= trips. Rust's `(1..=n).collect()` sizes the vector exactly (TrustedLen) and fills it with no capacity test. Also `s.chars().collect()` into a Vec[char] runs 14 instructions a char (280M) against Rust's 11 (220M): the decode loop tests the reserved length per push too. A possible remedy: version the presized loop on `trips <= reach` at its way in, with an unchecked store fill on the fast side.
fix: 1cbfcd7e92: a presized push fill whose vector is a Vec of Bool, Char, Int or Float, and which nothing indexes, gets a second copy of its loop (src/mir/presize.rs `version`), taken when the vector's length plus the trips fits the reservation. On that copy each push is `Vec.__push_exact`, whose length bump is a no-overflow add (src/backend/mir/seq.rs), and the copy's step is a CheckedAdd split into its own block, so the copy's induction is `add nsw`; LLVM then counts the pushes, drops the grow test and vectorizes. Measured by callgrind (release, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0) against main before the change: kata 484 742,238,883 -> 615,993,796 instructions (-17%; Rust 551M), kata 459 2,761,195,973 -> 2,761,197,237 (unchanged), kata 718 6,090,271,376 unchanged. Across 1075 kara-katas benches, 115 binaries changed and every output is equal; re-counted outliers: 1058 -18%, 60 -7%, 153 -1.5%, 72 +1.8%, 187 +1.2%. Left out on purpose: a vector the loop also indexes (kata 718 ran 1.8x with the copy, because the two copies' lengths join in a phi and later bounds facts are lost), text and struct element fills (459 lost 0.7%), and the auto-par recording build (`presize_pushes(.., copies = false)`). Pinned by tests/mir_presize_version.rs (both copies' edges on the interpreter and the built binary; the fill vectorizes, and does not with KARAC_MIR_PRESIZE_VERSION=0). The `s.chars().collect()` part of this row (14 instructions a char against Rust's 11) is B-2026-11-09-47.

title: `let Json.Array(queries) = row[3] else { … };` with `queries` only read is refused with E0515 "cannot move a non-`Copy` value out of a collection element" and no fix, where a plain `let t = row[3];` already gets the borrow `ref row[3]`
detail: Porting nestedtext's loader (mini_nestedtext), the report loop takes each line of loads.jsonl as `row: ref Vec[Json]` and destructures its queries with `let Json.Array(queries) = row[3] else { continue; };`, then only iterates `queries`. karac check refuses the move out of the element (E0515, ownership pass) with the hint "read the element in place, or take it out with `v.swap(i, j)` / `mem.replace` (this type has no `.clone()`)" and no machine fix. The repair is `= ref row[3] else`, which checks and runs. The read-only analysis behind E_INDEX_MOVE_NON_COPY's `ref` fix (src/ownership/index_let.rs, B-2026-10-24-18, -38 and B-2026-11-04-3) only looked at `StmtKind::Let` with binding, `_` and tuple patterns, so a let-else, or a variant or struct pattern, never reached it. Measured: of the four fixtures in tests/fix_let_else_index_borrow.rs, the three repairs fail on c9e5bdc8b7 and the moved-binding guard passes.
fix: 4e69fdaed4: the read-only analysis behind E_INDEX_MOVE_NON_COPY's `ref` repair (src/ownership/index_let.rs) now takes a `let … else`, and variant and struct patterns, so the ownership pass's E0515 on `let Json.Array(xs) = row[3] else { … };` carries the fix `ref row[3]` when the bindings are only read, saying it borrows the element (or the field, for `v[i].f`); a binding moved on keeps the refusal without it. Pinned by tests/fix_let_else_index_borrow.rs (4 tests; the three repairs fail on c9e5bdc8b7, the moved-binding guard passes). mini_nestedtext (kara-katas dfebba46, corpus/apps/cli/mini_nestedtext) writes the `ref`.

title: Every `karac check` (and every kara-lsp edit) re-parses, re-registers and re-checks the whole standard library: 305M instructions and ~66 ms for a 3-line program; cache the checked library
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-09 (Thread C, callgrind on a release build with line tables at 58ebb8f8ab, `karac check` of a 3-line `fn main`): 305M instructions, about 66 ms, and almost all of it is the standard library, which every check re-does from source. Program-independent: parsing the baked modules (STDLIB_PROGRAMS LazyLock, 41M) and the gated ones (GATED_STDLIB_PROGRAMS, 21M, forced even for a program that imports none, through marks_cross_task_fn and the variance tables). Program-dependent: library_source plus the parse of the program-with-library text (~65M, node ids 12M), library_prune (15M), build_type_env (46M, which clones every baked item, 11M), the library impl signature checks in check_items (29M), resolve (20M), effects (19M), ownership and the MIR borrow check (54M). malloc/free are about 35% of the total. kara-lsp pays everything but the two LazyLocks on every edit, so this is editor latency as well as CLI start-up. WHY THERE IS NO CACHE TODAY: the library is not a separately checked unit. It is text appended to each program (lower::library_source), and five steps make it depend on that program: (1) rename_clashing_library_items renames library names the program also declares; (2) BAKED_SOURCES are appended only for words the program uses; (3) library_prune drops items the program cannot reach; (4) register_baked_stdlib skips baked types the program redefines and impls a library source restates; (5) library spans are offsets after the program's text (`library_start = user_len`). The AST and the TypeEnv derive no serde. The staged cache design (Stages 1-4), the progress on each stage and the measurements are kept in full in review/library-cache-row-09-28.md, review/library-cache-design.md and review/library-cache-stage0.md in the project's shared folder.
fix: 4a462894da (last pre-v1 cut). The pre-v1 cuts that landed on this row are: 7972326d2e (completion reads a library checked once per process, 120-165 ms down to about 32 ms warm); 4c20adca24 and 0e3a67c5ba (the 3-line check went from 282.4M to 240.7M instructions: the prune reuses parser tokens, the library text is reused, there is no free at exit, baked items are borrowed, and node ids are a bitset); 4a462894da (the program is parsed once for the read-only scans, and library_source looks names up in a token set: mini_parsy 2,709M to 2,465M, with `check --output=json` byte-identical on 7,559 corpus programs). Stage 0 (review/library-cache-stage0.md) measured the library at about 220M instructions per check, whatever the program's size. That is all of a tiny check and about 8% of a 4.9k-line one. Stage 1, an in-process library AST memo, would net about 25M instructions (about 6 ms) per LSP request: cloning the parsed library costs 10.5M against its 35M parse. It also needs every consumer that indexes the combined text by library offset (the MIR lowering behind check, the editor, the prune) routed through a fixed span band. Stage 2 saves 12-30M, and 10% of apps would fall back. Review held both, and both fold into Stage 4. Stage 3 (an on-disk cache) and mimalloc wait for the same point. All of this is recorded in docs/deferred.md § Pre-checked Standard Library and Package Interfaces (094bf4bfb2, 891cab9c40, 7cdc0fadd4), together with the step-7 ruling (a library's signatures keep their own types; the cost is io.md's own-Response-with-headers allowance used by http_cache and object_store). RELOCATED there.
tracker: docs/deferred.md § Pre-checked Standard Library and Package Interfaces

title: A program's inherent impl on a library type that redefines a library method is also refused at the library's own impl, past the program's end, under "in the standard library: " six times
detail: design-conformance at 85675b25f1 found design.md:3821 (`impl Option[Ordering] { fn is_lt .. }`, the spec's exhibit of the library's own helpers) newly refused with two errors: the right one at the program's impl (an inherent impl on a type the program does not declare, design.md § Coherence), and `conflicting impl: impl Option[Ordering] redefines methods is_eq, .. already provided by an existing impl Option` placed at line 4411, the library's impl, prefixed `in the standard library: ` six times. The program's impl is registered first, so the library's was the overlapping one; cli.rs prefixed the message on each pass without checking. `impl Option[i64] { fn is_some(self) -> bool { true } }` showed the same.
fix: 8adc0b0e29. A library impl that overlaps a program's own impl now looks for the program's impl first (impl_overlap_conflict takes which registered impls to compare with). An inherent impl on a library type is left to its own coherence error, so `impl Option[Ordering] { fn is_lt .. }` draws exactly one error, at the program's impl; a trait impl that a library restatement overlaps is reported at the program's target. cli.rs no longer prefixes "in the standard library: " to a message that already has it. Pinned by tests/library_impl_overlap_names_the_program.rs (both repros: one error, at 1:1, no library prefix). design.md:3821 is baselined in design-conformance as the library's own exhibit. The baked-impl case, where a program's `impl Clone for String` passes unrefused, is B-2026-11-09-31.

title: JsonError, PoolError, SendError, RecvTimeoutError and SendTimeoutError do not implement `Error`, so `?` cannot convert them into `AnyError`
detail: design.md §10 and error.kara: the standard library's error types implement `Error`. library-conformance at 85675b25f1 found json.md's own example refused: `Json.parse(..)?` in a function returning `Result[_, AnyError]` drew `'?' cannot convert error 'JsonError' to 'AnyError': 'JsonError' does not implement Error`. An audit of every `pub struct/enum *Error` under runtime/stdlib found four more with neither `Display` nor `Error`: PoolError[E] (std_pool.kara), SendError[T] (channel.kara), RecvTimeoutError and SendTimeoutError[T] (source/sync.kara).
fix: 8adc0b0e29. JsonError (both json.kara copies), SendError[T] (channel.kara), RecvTimeoutError and SendTimeoutError[T] (source/sync.kara) implement Display and Error; PoolError[E] does when E: Display (std_pool.kara). The text is documented on each library page: the message for JsonError, `channel full` / `channel closed` / `timed out` for the channel errors, and `timed out waiting for a pooled value` / `too many callers already waiting` / `pool closed` / `could not create a pooled value: <e>` for PoolError. json.md's example now conforms (dropped from the library-conformance baseline). Pinned by corpus/design/ok_std_errors_convert_to_anyerror (`?` from Json.parse, recv_timeout and Pool.acquire into AnyError), passing on mir-interp, mir-llvm and mir-llvm-asan.

title: A program's `impl Clone for String` is accepted and replaces the library's `clone`: an impl overlapping a baked library trait impl is not refused
detail: design.md § Coherence: an application is exempt from the orphan rule, but the overlap rule still applies, and a type implements a trait once. `impl Clone for String { fn clone(self) -> String { "x" } }` checks clean and `"ab".clone()` then prints `x` under __mir-run. `impl Default for Ordering { .. }` is accepted the same way. Cause (read, not bisected): impl_overlap_conflict skips a baked impl when library methods come from source (`!(library_methods_from_source && baked_impls.contains(&i))`), so that a library source can restate a baked impl; a program's impl passes through the same gap. Two impls of one trait on one program type are refused correctly. Found while fixing B-2026-11-09-29, which handles the case where the library's restatement comes after the program's impl.
fix: 0352915c4b. design.md § Coherence exempts the application from the orphan rule, not the overlap rule, so a program's impl of a library trait for a library type is refused exactly when the library already has one, naming the library's impl. Two paths: (1) impl_overlap_conflict skipped every baked impl when library methods come from source, so that a library source could restate one; it now skips them only for the library's own impls (`overlap_from_program`, false during the baked pass via `registering_baked`), and the Duplicate message says "the standard library already implements `T` for `X`". (2) The derive-style builtins (Clone, Copy, Debug, Display, Hash, Eq, PartialEq, Ord, PartialOrd, Default) have no impl-table entry for library types (String's Clone is the compiler's), so a non-generic program impl of one for a type the program does not declare is refused when `type_satisfies_bound` already holds. `impl Clone for String` is now refused at 1:1; `impl Default for Ordering` (which the library lacks) still checks and runs. Pins: tests/library_impl_overlap_and_builtin_ufcs.rs (both cases). 285 corpus, kata and example files with trait impls draw no new refusal.

title: `Clone.clone(s)` on a `String` passes `karac check`, then `__mir-run` refuses it: "a type that failed to check is not lowered yet"
detail: `fn main() { let s = "ab"; println(Clone.clone(s)); }`: `karac check` reports nothing; `karac __mir-run` exits 3 with `error[mir]: build: 1:35 in main: a type that failed to check is not lowered yet`. The method form `s.clone()` runs. A check-versus-run divergence on the trait-qualified call form for a library type's trait method.
fix: 0352915c4b. `Clone` has no declaration, so try_ufcs_method_of found no trait to narrow to and fell through; the call was typed as an error with no diagnostic. `Clone.clone(x)` is now UFCS for the builtin (every `clone` is Clone's): typed as `x.clone()` and recorded in ufcs_calls, so lowering rewrites it to the receiver form. The same silent error hid `Default.default()`, an associated function with no receiver; design.md § Default says code calls it as `T.default()`, so it is refused as naming no type, with a machine-applicable fix from the expected type (`let w: W = Default.default()` becomes `W.default()`; no fix where the expected type is generic or a String annotation). Pins: tests/library_impl_overlap_and_builtin_ufcs.rs (Clone.clone checks and runs; three Default.default() sites fixed and run), corpus/design/ok_clone_qualified_call_on_a_library_type (String, Vec, derived struct) on mir-interp, mir-llvm and mir-llvm-asan.

title: kara-lsp: incremental user-code checking -- a completion re-checks the whole buffer and the unpruned library on every request: 186 ms on a 5-line file, 428 ms mid-file in mini_parsy (4.9k lines), 1.54 s in mini_markdown (14.8k lines)
detail: MEASURED at e1f777ad12 on the 4-core cloud box, release build, medians of 5 in-process calls (`karac::completions_at` at a mid-file `x.` made by deleting a method name after its dot; `karac::check_source` for the didChange diagnostics of the same file unedited). completions_at / check_source: 5-line program 186 / 47 ms; freight_audit (1239 lines) 190 / 134 ms; csv_query (1249) 264 / 156 ms; mini_parsy (4931) 428 / 540 ms; mini_markdown (14776) 1539 / 2307 ms. Each completion offered the deleted name. WHERE THE TIME GOES: completion runs karac check's pipeline once (twice when the buffer needs a `;` after the placeholder) on the buffer with a placeholder at the cursor, against the WHOLE library (Pipeline::whole_library, src/cli/editor_complete.rs) so a receiver's unused methods are offered; that is the 186 ms floor, about 140 ms above the pruned check's 47 ms. Above the floor the cost is the user program: about 0.05 to 0.09 ms per line, so a 5k-line file is past 400 ms and a 15k-line one past 1.5 s, against the ~200 ms an editor completion should take. Every didChange also re-checks the whole buffer (540 ms on mini_parsy, 2.3 s on mini_markdown), so typing in a large file queues diagnostics behind each other. SHAPE (not built): (1) the library share is B-2026-11-09-28's cache; the unpruned library completion needs should be the cached variant (Thread C told). (2) user code: keep the last good check's item signatures (struct_info, impls, fn sigs, the resolver's root scope) per document, and on a request re-check only the function body containing the cursor against them, falling back to a full check when an item signature changed. Completion needs only the receiver's type in that body; diagnostics can do the same per edited function and keep the others' results.
fix: de8310019f. `karac::DocumentChecker` (src/cli/editor_incremental.rs) keeps a document's last check: text, diagnostics, an outline of bodies and declared names, and each function's rendered inferred effects. An edit confined to function bodies is checked with the other bodies emptied in place (offsets kept): bodies the edited ones reach are kept or replaced by a stand-in with the same inferred effects (`loop {}`, `panic("")`, an allocating prefix), recursion partners are kept, the rest become `loop {}`. Cached diagnostics outside the edited items are shifted across the edit; the focused check's diagnostics inside them are taken. Full check on: a change outside bodies, a body naming a different set of the file's items, a comptime or impl-signature body, an edited or stood-in body whose inferred effects differ from the cache, any open or save, and any package member. Completion empties every body but the cursor's (`editor_incremental::focus`). Measured after the rebase onto C's 7972326d2e (release, x86): mini_markdown (14,776 lines) edit 92 ms vs 1650 ms full, completion 132 ms (was 1539); mini_parsy 23 vs 446 ms, completion 62 ms; csv_query 6 vs 147 ms; a 5-line file completion 28 ms. Correctness: lsp/tests/incremental.rs (4 tests: incremental agrees, signature/new-call fall back, a private fn's changed effects fall back, unchanged text cached) and the ignored sweep over corpus/apps: 472 files, 1416 edits (type error, unused let, newline at three statement points each), 1407 incremental, every one and its revert identical to a full check. KARAC_LSP_INCREMENTAL=0 turns both paths off. Gate 10818 + 10994 passed.

title: A program's own `struct Response { status, body, headers }` (io.md § HTTP server) is also what `Client.get`/`send` return, and the compiled client wrote only fields 0 and 1: `headers` stayed unwritten and its drop freed garbage (`free(): invalid pointer` / SIGSEGV; interpreter right)
detail: Building the tus_upload service app: the program declares `struct Response { status: i64, body: String, headers: Vec[(String, String)] }` so its handler can send `Upload-Offset` and `Tus-Resumable` headers, as io.md § HTTP server documents, and its client half matches `c.request("OPTIONS", url).send()` in a `fn show(label: Str, r: Result[Response, HttpError])`. `karac __mir-run` printed the right lines; `karac run` exited 139 and the built binary aborted with `free(): invalid pointer` (rc 134). Minimized (/tmp probes c1/c2): the crash needs the client's result to reach a drop of the Ok payload. Cause: the typechecker gives `Client.get`/`post`/`RequestBuilder.send` the nominal type `Response`, which under the program's declaration IS the program's struct (`fn f(r: Response) -> i64 { r.status }` called with a client response checks clean). The compiled client (`http_native` in src/backend/mir/io.rs) stored the status at field 0 and the body at field 1 of that type and never touched field 2, so the `Vec` drop freed whatever the stack held. The readers `status()` / `body()` / `bytes()` / `header()` / `headers()` used the same fixed indices on both backends, so a declaration in another field order (`is_documented_response` accepts any order) read the status from the body; the interpreter built a 2-field aggregate, so `resp.headers` on a client response had no field.
fix: 76b6fbd33a: the client places a Response's fields by name on both backends. `http_native` (src/backend/mir/io.rs) looks up `status`, `body` and `headers` in the Ok payload's struct (`response_field`), stores the status and body there, and when the program's own `Response` has `headers`, fills it from the runtime's header table keyed by the body's buffer (`karac_runtime_http_client_mir_headers`, the call `headers()` already makes). The readers `status()` / `body()` / `bytes()` / `header()` / `headers()` use the same lookup. The interpreter's `http_send` (src/mir/interp.rs) builds the aggregate in the declared field order with `headers` filled, and `http_method` reads `status`/`body` by name from the receiver's type. io.md § HTTP server now says the declaration is the client's `Response` too. Pinned by tests/client_response_own_struct.rs: a program declaring `struct Response { headers, body, status }` (reordered) gets 200, the body and the server's headers from `get` and `send`, through the field and the methods, interpreted and compiled (it aborted with `free(): invalid pointer` before; the /tmp probe c2 was the control). Found by apps/service/tus_upload.

title: A scalar `ref` handed to a type parameter a closure returns solved it as the `ref`: `m.map_or(x, |k: i64| k + 1)` with `x: ref i64` made `U` a `ref i64` while the closure returned the value, so the interpreter stopped on "deref of non-reference Int(3)" and the build read the value as an address; `v.iter().fold(None, |acc: Option[i64], x| Some(x))` built and printed an address
detail: Found writing kata 2036's fold arm, whose step is `minus.map_or(x, |m: i64| x.max(m + x))` over `nums.iter()` (items `ref i64`). Option.map_or[U](own self, default: own U, f: own OnceFn(own T) -> U) -> U: pass 1 of the generic call check unified `U` with the default's type, `ref i64`; the closure's tail is an `i64`, which the closure check accepted against `ref i64` (the scalar peel), so the closure was typed `Fn(i64) -> i64` while the call's `U` stayed `ref i64`. Repro: `fn pick(m: Option[i64], x: ref i64) -> i64 { m.map_or(x, |k: i64| k + 1) } fn main() { let v = 3; println(pick(Some(2), v)); println(pick(None, v)); }` -- __mir-run: `run: in pick at bb1[0]: deref of non-reference Int(3)`; __mir-llvm-run exits 101 with no output. The same inside a fold closure (`nums.iter().fold(0, |acc, x| { let np = m.map_or(x, |m: i64| x.max(m + x)); acc + np })`) crashed the interpreter alike. `v.iter().fold(None, |acc: Option[i64], x| Some(x))` is the converse: the annotated `acc` and the tail's `Option[ref i64]` disagreed, the call's accumulator became `Option[ref i64]`, and the build printed a pointer for the value. Measured on main c07536519a.
fix: 5a9b370550. A scalar `ref` handed for a callee type parameter that a function argument returns (`Option.map_or`'s `U`, from `map_or(x, |k| k + 1)` with `x: ref i64`) is now solved as the value in pass 2 of the generic call check (src/typechecker/exprs.rs), so the closure's `i64` result and the default agree and both backends read a value. The same commit lets `fold` accumulators that start `None` or hold one in a tuple be solved by the closure's tail. Pinned by tests/kata_2036_fold_inference.rs (8 tests, interpreter and build); kata 2036's fold arm runs as written.

title: `v.iter().fold(None, |acc: Option[i64], x| Some(x))` is refused: the tail `Some(x)` with `x: ref i64` is an `Option[ref i64]`, though `Some(x)` against an `Option[i64]` slot elsewhere reads the scalar as its value (the remainder of the row that stopped it building an address)
detail: Since the fix to the scalar-ref miscompile filed beside this row, the program is refused with "expected 'Fn(Option[ref i64], ref i64) -> Option[ref i64]', found 'Fn(Option[i64], ref i64) -> Option[ref i64]'" rather than built wrong. Refusing is sound, but the annotation says what the accumulator is: `acc: Option[i64]` should solve `fold`'s `B` before the tail is checked, and the tail `Some(x)` then reads `x` as its value, as `let o: Option[i64] = Some(x);` does. Repro: `fn main() { let v = [1, 2, 3].to_vec(); let r = v.iter().fold(None, |acc: Option[i64], x| Some(x)); println(r); }` -- want `Some(3)`. Pinned refused by `kata_2036_annotated_accumulator_against_a_ref_tail_is_refused` (tests/kata_2036_fold_inference.rs), which the fix flips.
fix: 0a401ccd53: the closure pushdown (src/typechecker/exprs.rs) unifies an annotated parameter with an open slot parameter before the body is checked, so `acc: Option[i64]` solves fold's `B`; the body is then checked against the return type as it stands, resolved through that binding, so the tail `Some(x)` with `x: ref i64` reads the scalar as its value, as `let o: Option[i64] = Some(x);` does. Prints Some(3) on the interpreter and the JIT. Flipped kata_2036_annotated_accumulator_against_a_ref_tail_is_refused to kata_2036_annotated_accumulator_against_a_ref_tail_takes_the_value; tests/closure_annotated_param_solves_slot.rs runs match, block and if tails on both executors and keeps `acc: Option[String]` refused.

title: No iterator or slice has `chunk_by`, yet `v.chunk_by(|a, b| a == b)` on a `Vec` is refused as an iterator adaptor with the machine fix `v.iter().chunk_by(..)`, which is refused in turn ("no method 'chunk_by' on type 'VecIter'") beside a stray "cannot compare '?T2' and '?T3'"
detail: Found writing kata 2038's runs arm with Rust's `chunk_by` (slice::chunk_by, stable since 1.77, the natural way to take run lengths: `c.chunk_by(|a, b| a == b).map(|r| r.len())`). `is_iterator_surface_method` (src/typechecker/expr_method_call.rs) lists `chunk_by`, so the Vec receiver gets the "iterator adaptors/terminals require an explicit `.iter()`" error and its fix; the legacy iterator table in src/typechecker/stdlib_iter.rs still types an itertools-style `chunk_by(key_fn)`, but no library iterator source has it, and neither form runs. Repro: `fn main() { let c: Vec[char] = "AAB".chars().collect(); let runs: Vec[Vec[char]] = c.chunk_by(|a, b| a == b).map(|r| r.to_vec()).collect(); println(runs.len()); }` -- after `karac fix`, `no method 'chunk_by' on type 'VecIter'`. Either the method (Rust's slice form, `chunk_by(own self, f: Fn(ref T, ref T) -> bool) -> Vec[Slice[T]]` beside `windows`/`chunks`), or no fix pointing at it and a diagnostic that names the run-length loop.
fix: 7842702532. Built to the review thread's ruling: `Slice.chunk_by(self, same: own MutFn(T, T) -> bool) -> Vec[Slice[T]]` in runtime/stdlib/source/collections.kara, beside `Slice.split`. It cuts the slice between each pair of neighbours `same` refuses and returns the runs as views into it, in order; an empty slice gives no runs. A `Vec` or `Array` receiver reaches it through the slice coercion, so `v.chunk_by(|a, b| a == b)` now resolves and the iterator-adaptor misreading no longer fires. Pinned by tests/kata_2037_slice_chunk_by.rs under the MIR interpreter: runs of equal values, rising runs (`a < b`), the empty `Vec`, `String` elements, and `Vec` and list receivers.

title: A tuple value cannot be assigned to existing places: `(lo, hi) = if c { (lo, mid) } else { (mid + 1, hi) };` (Rust's destructuring assignment) is refused E_ASSIGN_TARGET_NOT_PLACE with advice to drop the parentheses, and `lo, hi = if ..` is then a parse error ("2 target(s) but 1 value(s)"), so the halving step of a binary search carried as a pair has no spelling but a `let` and two assignments
detail: Found writing kata 2040's iterator arm, whose search halves `let mut (lo, hi) = (..)` with `(lo, hi) = if at_most(mid) >= k { (lo, mid) } else { (mid + 1, hi) };`, as Rust 1.59+ writes it. `karac check` gives E_ASSIGN_TARGET_NOT_PLACE ("a parenthesized tuple is a value, not a place; to assign several places at once, drop the parentheses (`a, b = b, a`)"); `karac fix` reports no fixable diagnostics; following the advice by hand gives the parse error, since design.md's MULTI_ASSIGN takes only a literal list of values on the right (`EXPR { "," EXPR }`, the same count as the targets). A tuple-valued expression (a call returning a pair, an `if`, a `match`) has no way into two places at once; `let pair = ..; lo, hi = pair.0, pair.1;` or two `if`s are the only spellings. Repro: `fn main() { let mut (lo, hi) = (0, 10); let c = true; (lo, hi) = if c { (lo, 5) } else { (6, hi) }; println(f"{lo} {hi}"); }` -- want `0 5`. Related fixed rows B-2026-11-01-11 and B-2026-11-03-22 are about the fix's text for a literal right side; this one is the right side that is not a list. Either the destructuring assignment (`(p, q) = e` with `e` a tuple, values before places as MULTI_ASSIGN does), or advice that names the `let` form when the right side is not a literal list. The arm stays blocked on this row (kara-katas leetcode/2001-2100/2040-.../product_iter.kara).
fix: b415f2e55f. Built to the review thread's ruling. The parser now accepts a parallel assignment with one value and several targets, `(lo, hi) = e` and `lo, hi = e`, and src/desugar.rs (`expand_multi_assign`) expands it to `let (__karac_pa_<off>_0, ..) = e;` followed by one assignment per target, so the value is evaluated once and taken apart before any target is written. The machine fix the row asked for: `unparenthesized_multi_assign_fix` (src/typechecker/items.rs), which previously offered only a tuple-literal rewrite, now leaves a non-tuple value alone and rewrites the target list to the joined places. Pinned by tests/kata_2038_tuple_parallel_assign.rs: an `if` of tuples, a function's tuple result, an index place among the targets, `String` targets, a tuple of the wrong arity refused as a type error, and parenthesized targets given the fix; tests/typechecker.rs's parenthesized-tuple test was updated, as `(a, b) = pair` is now accepted.

title: A closure whose body fixes nothing about its parameter, handed to a bounded generic `F: Fn(i64) -> i64`, passes `karac check` but types its parameter and result as `()`: `ap(1, |x| { println("a"); x })` stops every backend with "invalid MIR: ap[Fn(()) -> ()]: argument 0 of a Fn call has the wrong type"
detail: Found while fixing kata 2036's fold inference (tests/generic_fn_value_par_effect.rs passes the expression-bodied form). With `fn ap[F: Fn(i64) -> i64](x: i64, f: F) -> i64 { f(x) }`: `ap(2, |x| x + 1)` and `ap(2, |x| { let y = x * 3; y })` run (3, 6); `ap(1, |x| { println("a"); x })` checks clean ("All checks passed") and then `karac __mir-run` and `__mir-llvm-run` both stop at MIR validation, `ap[Fn(()) -> ()]: bb0[term]: argument 0 of a Fn call has the wrong type` and `the result of a Fn call has the wrong type`; `ap(1, |x| { let y = x; y })` is refused at lowering's typecheck with "cannot infer type parameter 'T'". `|x: i64| { println("a"); x }` runs (a, 1). So the closure's parameter is solved from the bound `F: Fn(i64) -> i64` only when the body itself pins `x` to an integer (`x + 1`, `x * 3`); when the body only passes `x` through, the open variable defaults to `()` for the instantiation `ap[Fn(()) -> ()]` while the checker accepted the call. Reproduced on karac at 991c45adcd and on a karac built before kata 2036's fold change, so it predates that fix. Expected: the bound's `Fn(i64) -> i64` solves the closure's parameter and result before its body is checked, as Rust infers a closure's signature from the `F: Fn(i64) -> i64` bound of the callee.
fix: 3545dc7fee: the row's reading was right about the effect and narrower than the cause. A bare parameter borrows (core-semantics §4.1), so the slot of `f: F` is `ref F`, and pass 2 of a generic call (`typechecker/exprs.rs`) looked up `F`'s function-trait bound only when the slot was a plain `F`. The closure was therefore checked against nothing and synthesised `Fn(?a) -> ?a`: a body that pinned `x` (`x + 1`) defaulted it to i64, one that passed it through (`|x| x`, `|x| { println("a"); x }`) left it to default to `()` in the instance `ap[Fn(()) -> ()]`, and `|x| { let y = x; y }` was refused. The `where F: Fn(i64) -> i64` spelling and either argument order failed the same way. The slot is now peeled to `F` for the lookup (`peel_slot_ref`); the closure is checked against the bound's signature while the borrow context and call-site marker still come from `ref F`. Pass 1's unify of a function value with the bound peels it too, so `app(double, 4)` over `F: Fn(i64) -> U` solves `U` (it failed to lower, "UnknownParam U"), but only for a function whose parameters are known: an unannotated closure held in a binding (`let g = |s| s; twice(mut g, ..)`) keeps its "cannot infer closure parameter type" refusal; peeled, it was solved into `twice[Fn(ref String) -> ref String]`, which does not validate. Pinned by tests/generic_fn_bound_borrowed_slot.rs (both executors, plus the refusal).

title: A closure whose body ends in `collect()` takes its target from nowhere: `let to32 = |v: ref Vec[i64]| v.iter().map(|x| x as i32).collect();` used as `take(to32(a))` with `take(v: Vec[i32])`, or `let r: Vec[i64] = f(a)`, checks clean and then stops at lowering with "an expression whose type does not lower (UnsolvedParam(\"C\")) is not lowered yet"; a Kāra closure cannot declare its return type, so nothing can fix `C`
detail: Found writing kata 2032's Rust-arm adapter, which turned each `Vec[i64]` into the template's `Vec[i32]` with one closure called three times as `Solution.two_out_of_three(to32(nums1), to32(nums2), to32(nums3))`. Minimal: `fn take(v: Vec[i32]) -> i64 { v.len() }` and in main `let to32 = |v: ref Vec[i64]| v.iter().map(|x| x as i32).collect(); println(f"{take(to32(a))}");`. `karac check` (991c45adcd and a karac built before kata 2036's inference change alike) reports "error[typecheck]: 7:34: an expression whose type does not lower (UnsolvedParam(\"C\")) is not lowered yet" at the `v.iter()` receiver; `__mir-run` fails at build with the same message. `let f = |v: ref Vec[i64]| v.iter().map(|x| x + 1).collect(); let r: Vec[i64] = f(a);` fails the same way, so it is the closure's own `collect` and not the i32 cast. Writing the return (`|v| -> Vec[i32] { .. }`) is refused by the parser: "a closure does not declare its return type; the type is inferred from the body". So the only spellings left are an annotated `let` inside the body or outside the closure. Three defects: (1) typed HIR's place_substs finds no solution for `collect`'s `C` (src/typed_hir.rs, `HirError::UnsolvedParam`) though the call through the closure type-checks against the use site; a hypothesis, not traced, is that the closure body's `collect` records its substitution before the closure's result variable is unified with the use; (2) the message is the lowering's internal wording, reported under `typecheck` with no fix; (3) the parser's advice that the type is inferred from the body is not true for a body that ends in `collect()`. Expected: as in Rust, a closure's result type is inferred from its uses within the enclosing function, and `collect`'s target follows.
fix: 86c3102afc. src/typechecker/items.rs open_closure_tail_params: when a let binds a closure whose type leaves a parameter open, the closure body's tail call (walking blocks to the final expression) whose type is that parameter takes the let's variable, in its node type and as its own type argument, so a use of the closure (`take(to32(a))`, `let r: Vec[i64] = inc(a)`) solves what the body's `collect` builds. Defect (1) of the row is fixed; (2) and (3), the message wording and the parser's advice, no longer arise for these spellings since they now check and run. An immediately invoked closure, `(|v| ...collect())(a)` into an annotated `Set[i64]`, still stops at lowering with UnknownParam("C"): filed as its own row. Pinned by tests/collect_target_decided_later.rs a_closure_ending_in_collect_builds_what_its_uses_decide.

title: `PriorityQueue` has no `iter`, `into_iter`, `for`, `Clone` or `Display`, though collections.md says every collection works with `for` and is `Display` when its elements are
detail: Kata 1086 (High Five) keeps five scores per student in a `PriorityQueue[i64]` and sums each queue at the end. `best[id].iter().sum()` was refused with "no method 'iter' on type 'PriorityQueue'", `heap.into_iter()` (LeetCode's Rust template) with "no method 'into_iter'", `for x in pq` with "cannot be iterated by a `for` loop: it implements neither `Iterator` nor `Iterable`", `f"{pq}"` with "does not implement Display", and `best[id].clone()` with "`PriorityQueue` does not derive `Clone`". docs/library/collections.md § Iteration opens "Every collection works with `for`" and § Common traits "Every collection implements `Display` when its elements implement `Display`"; its collection table lists `PriorityQueue[T]` as Rust's `BinaryHeap<T>`, whose `iter`, `into_iter`, `into_vec`, `Clone` and `Debug` are the usual way to read a heap without draining it. The only reading left was `into_sorted_vec`, which drains and sorts.
fix: 2f62c55005: runtime/stdlib/source/priority_queue.kara gives PriorityQueue `iter` (returning the backing vector's `VecIter`) and `into_vec`, the `Iterable` and `IntoIterator` impls, so `for x in pq` and `pq.into_iter()` work, a `Clone` (the vector cloned, the direction copied) and a `Display` that renders the backing vector. All follow the queue's own order, its backing vector's, as Rust's `BinaryHeap::iter` does: fixed by the pushes and pops, the same on every run and backend, but not pop order. `iter` and the `Iterable` impl name `VecIter[T]` rather than `impl Iterator`: a library-source method returning `impl Iterator` ran, but `karac check` refused its call with "an expression whose type does not lower (impl Trait)", so the library names the concrete type as every other collection's `iter` does. collections.md's method table, iteration table, Clone list and Display list name the queue. tests/kata_1086_priority_queue_iter.rs. The 257 corpus entries that mention PriorityQueue run under mir-llvm-asan with no sanitizer report (13 fail on pre-existing expectations: 12 with an empty expected.out, and kata 1500's class-e files_solution).

title: Rust's `heap.into_iter().map(|Reverse(s)| s)` gets no fix for the `Reverse` parameter, and `or_insert_with(BinaryHeap::new)` is not seen as a heap's constructor, so no `Reverse` in the program gets the smallest-first fix
detail: Kata 1086's LeetCode Rust template keeps a `BTreeMap<i32, BinaryHeap<Reverse<i32>>>`, builds each heap with `map.entry(id).or_insert_with(BinaryHeap::new)`, pushes `Reverse(score)` and sums with `heap.into_iter().map(|Reverse(s)| s).sum()`. After `karac fix` the check stopped at three errors with no edit: the closure parameter `|Reverse(s)|` got only "a parameter's pattern must be irrefutable, and `Reverse(..)` matches only some values"; `BinaryHeap.new` named as a value got the largest-first message ("`BinaryHeap.new()` is `PriorityQueue.max_first()`") with no fix, because the parser records a Rust heap constructor (Program::rust_heap_ctor) only where it is called; and with no constructor recorded, rust_heaps_pop_smallest was false, so `Reverse[i32]` in the heap's type and `heap.push(Reverse(..))` got "Kāra has no such wrapper" and no fix either. Meanwhile round 2 renamed the type `BinaryHeap[Reverse[i32]]` to `PriorityQueue[Reverse[i32]]`, after which the type's `Reverse` no longer sits after `BinaryHeap[` and could not be fixed in a later round.
fix: 2f62c55005: a parameter written `Reverse(p)`, in a program that imports `std::cmp::Reverse` or writes `BinaryHeap<Reverse<..>>` / `BinaryHeap[Reverse[..]]` (Parser::uses_rust_reverse), now says Kāra's PriorityQueue holds the value itself and is fixed to `p` (src/parser/items.rs); any other `Reverse(..)` parameter keeps the irrefutable-pattern error. `BinaryHeap::new` / `BinaryHeap.new` named as a value rather than called is recorded as a Rust heap constructor (src/parser/exprs.rs, the uncalled type-path branch), so it gets `PriorityQueue.new` or `max_first` by its heap's side, and the program's `Reverse` wraps get their fix. Kata 1086's LeetCode template reaches a clean check in four `karac fix` rounds. tests/kata_1086_priority_queue_iter.rs.

title: `let t = text?;` on a bare (borrowed) `text: Option[String]` parameter is refused as "'?' operator requires `Result` or `Option`, found 'ref Option[String]'" with no fix, about a value that is one; `??` on the same operand already names the borrow and offers `.clone()`, and a `Copy` payload (`n?` on a bare `Option[i64]`) is refused too
detail: Building the tus_upload service app, the server parses `Upload-Length` and `Upload-Offset` with `fn parse_length(text: Option[String]) -> Option[i64] { let t = text?; ... }`, its argument being `req.header(...)`. `karac check`: `error[typecheck]: '?' operator requires `Result` or `Option`, found 'ref Option[String]'`, no fix-it, so `karac fix` leaves it. Under D5 a bare `Option[String]` parameter reads as `ref Option[String]`, and `resolve_question` (src/typechecker/expr_ops.rs) matched only a `Type::Named` operand, so every borrowed wrapper fell to the generic "requires" message. The same on `Result[String, String]` (`r?`), and on `n: Option[i64]` / `r: Result[i64, i64]`, where nothing moves at all. `??` on the same operands was fixed by B-2026-10-28-32: Copy payloads are read, non-Copy ones refused with "would move its 'String' out of the borrow" and a machine-applicable `.clone()`. design.md (`?` and `??`) treats the two operators together.
fix: b490bc1d36: `infer_question` (src/typechecker/expr_ops.rs) reads a `ref` / `mut ref` `Option` or `Result` operand as the wrapper. When its payload and error are `Copy` (or counted handles, `index_read_part_counts_or_copies`) it goes on to `resolve_question` with the wrapper, so `n?` on a bare `n: Option[i64]` checks and runs on both backends. Otherwise it is refused with "'?' on a borrowed 'Option[String]' would move its payload ('String') out of the borrow: take a copy with `.clone()` first (core-semantics §3.7)" (for `Result`, "its value or error"), with the machine-applicable `.clone()` after the operand that `??` already had; that fix-it code is now one helper, `reject_out_of_borrow_operand`, shared by both operators. Pinned by tests/question_borrowed_wrapper.rs (the refusal, the `karac fix` output and its run for `Option[String]` and `Result[String, String]`; the Copy case interpreted and compiled). The tus_upload app's `text?` is `text.clone()?` after `karac fix`.

title: The HTTP client turns a status of 400 or more into `Err(HttpError)` carrying only a message ("<url>: status code 409"): a program cannot read the status, the headers or the body of an error response, so a tus client cannot take `Upload-Offset` from a 409 and a REST client cannot read a JSON error body
detail: Building the tus_upload service app's client half: tus answers a stale `PATCH` with 409 and the server's `Upload-Offset`, a bad checksum with 460, a missing `Tus-Resumable` with 412 and `Tus-Version`, and an over-size `POST` with 413. io.md § HTTP client says a status outside 2xx is an `Err`, and `impl HttpError` has only `message()`. The runtime (`karac_runtime_http_client_*`, runtime/src/lib.rs ~7136) and the interpreter's `http_fetch` build the message `"{url}: status code {n}"` and drop the response's headers and body. So the only way to branch on the status is to parse the message's tail, and the 409's `Upload-Offset` (the reason the header is sent) is unreachable; the app's client re-reads the offset with a `HEAD` after any failure and prints each error's message. Every mainstream client exposes these (reqwest's `Error::status()` and `Response::error_for_status`, Python's `HTTPError.code`/`.headers`/`.read()`, Go's `resp.StatusCode` without an error). A remedy keeps the documented `Err` and gives `HttpError` `status() -> Option[i64]` (None for a transport failure), `header(name)` / `headers()` and `body()`, read by name like `Response`'s; user providers build `HttpError { message }` literals (tests/mir_network_provider.rs), so a new field needs a default or the readers stay methods over runtime-side state, as `Response.headers()` does. Needs a spec line in io.md first.
fix: 9ca01280c9. An HttpError for a status of 400 or more keeps the response: status(), header(name) (names compared without case) and body() (io.md § HTTP client), None for a failure with no response and for an HttpError a program or a fake provider builds; the message is unchanged. Runtime: http_deliver hands an error status back negated with its message, body and headers, and karac_runtime_http_client_mir_send keeps them by the message buffer's address (MIR_ERROR_RESPONSES, bytes compared at each read); the three karac_runtime_http_error_mir_* readers are in both archives. Interpreter: ureq's Status error is a response, kept by the message's box (http_error_responses). Pinned by tests/mir_io.rs http_error_keeps_the_response_of_an_error_status and http_error_a_program_builds_keeps_no_response, interp and build.

title: A `mut ref` cursor cannot walk to a list's tail: Rust's `let mut tail = &mut list; while tail.is_some() { tail = &mut tail.as_mut().unwrap().next; } *tail = rest;` has no Kāra spelling, since `Option` has no `as_mut`, and the natural `while let Some(n) = tail { tail = mut ref n.next; }` (or the same as a `match` in a `loop`) is refused E0516 by both borrow checks: the rebinding reads as a use of `tail` while `tail` still borrows from itself
detail: Found carrying LeetCode's Rust template for kata 2046 (sort a linked list already sorted by absolute values), whose last step appends the reversed positives behind the negatives with the cursor walk above. Every other step of the template now carries through `karac fix` (Box[T], the parameter's own, the array literal's suffix; same push). Three spellings, all with `list: own Option[N]`, `let mut list = list; let mut tail = mut ref list;` and `*tail = rest; list` after the loop: (1) `while tail.is_some() { tail = mut ref tail.as_mut().unwrap().next; }` -- "no method 'as_mut' on type 'Option'"; with an `as_mut(mut ref self) -> Option[mut ref T]` added to option.kara it is then E_REF_OPERAND_UNSUPPORTED, a `mut ref` of a place reached through a call result (core-semantics.md §5.1). (2) `while let Some(n) = tail { tail = mut ref n.next; }` -- E0516 "cannot read `tail` while `tail` still holds a borrow of it", "cannot write to `tail` while it is still borrowed", "cannot drop `tail` .." at the `*tail = rest`, and the MIR borrow check agrees (read of (*_t) while borrowed mutably). (3) `loop { match tail { Some(n) => tail = mut ref n.next, None => break } }` -- the same three. Repro: `struct N { v: i64, next: Option[N] }` with `fn append(list: own Option[N], rest: own Option[N]) -> Option[N]` as above, `main` appending `Some(N{v:3,..})` to a 1 -> 2 list and printing `1 2 3`. Rust accepts (2) and (3) because the new borrow `&mut n.next` reborrows through `tail`'s referent, not `tail` itself, and the old `tail` is dead once it is overwritten (NLL problem case #4 is the harder variant that Rust also refuses; this one Rust takes). design.md has no ruling on a `mut ref` local rebound to a part of its own referent; `docs/design.md` § Local worklists covers frozen handles only. Untraced hypothesis: the checker keys the loan on the local `tail` rather than on `*tail`, so the reassignment kills nothing. A ruling either way is wanted: the reborrow-through-cursor accepted, or a documented spelling for appending at a tail (a recursive helper is what remains). The template's arm stays blocked on this row (kara-katas leetcode/2001-2100/2046-.../sort_solution.kara).
fix: e82c519a66 implements the review's §5.3 ruling (75f3e1cace, "A borrow through a reference is not a borrow of the reference") in the MIR borrow check, the only checker that refused it (src/mir/borrowck.rs). A forward may-analysis of the loans in scope (`scope_dataflow`) kills, at an assignment to a whole reference local `r`, every loan whose place goes through `*r`; an out-of-scope loan conflicts with nothing. The assignment itself no longer conflicts with such a loan (`conflicts`, beside the existing StorageDead/Drop exception). The old referent stays borrowed because a reborrow already keeps `r`'s own loans. The row's hypothesis was right: the loans were keyed on the place `(*tail)..`, and reassigning `tail` killed nothing. Spellings (2) `while let Some(n) = tail { tail = mut ref n.next; } *tail = rest;` and (3), the same as a `match` in a `loop`, now check and run: the row's repro prints `1 2 3` on the interpreter and under mir-llvm-asan. Spelling (1) still needs an `Option.as_mut`, which is not this row. Pins in corpus/core: ok_mut_ref_cursor_walks_to_tail (E0516 three times on the pre-fix binary) and ok_ref_cursor_rebinds (a `ref` cursor, already accepted before), plus three refusals that still hold: err_cursor_used_while_reborrow_live (writes `*tail` while `n` is used), err_cursor_rebound_to_root_while_reborrow_live (`tail = mut ref list` while `n` is live, the review's case: the live borrow is charged to `list`), and err_cursor_walk_reads_root_while_cursor_live. Every other corpus/core err_ pin is still refused (re-judged at this tree). Gate green before the push: 10965 + 11156.

title: `karac __mir-run` builds an owned (non-`shared`) recursive list in quadratic time: `head = Some(N { v: i, next: head })` n times takes 3.2 s at n = 5000, 13.8 s at 10000 and 56 s at 20000, where the same program with `shared struct N` takes 0.29 s at 20000 and the compiled backend is linear
detail: Found carrying LeetCode's Rust template for kata 2046, whose `ListNode` is a plain struct holding `next: Option[ListNode]` (Rust's `Option<Box<ListNode>>` after the Box fix). With the template's last step written as a recursive append (the cursor walk is blocked, see the kata's other row), `__mir-llvm-run` prints every line of the kata's expected output in 1.8 s, but `__mir-run` passes the 2000 short lists and then runs past 300 s on the first 100000-node list. Repro: `struct N { v: i64, next: Option[N] }` and `fn main() { let mut head: Option[N] = None; for i in 0..20000 { head = Some(N { v: i, next: head }); } let mut count = 0; let mut cur = head; while let Some(node) = cur { count += 1; cur = node.next; } println(f"{count}"); }` -- each doubling of n costs 4x (3.2 s, 13.8 s, 56.1 s at 5000, 10000, 20000, wall time on kara 991c45adcd while a test leg ran beside it, so read the ratio rather than the seconds); `shared struct N` with `mut next` runs 20000 in 0.29 s. Untraced hypothesis: a move of the owned list into the new node's field copies (or walks for drop flags) the whole value already built, so step i costs O(i). A Rust template's linked list is always this shape, so every carried linked-list kata will time out in the interpreter lanes at LeetCode's 10^5 nodes.
fix: 8f5b9afb81. Three interpreter steps each cost the value's depth at every node. drop_adt copied the whole value to read its variant and length; it now reads in place. drop_at found each part by walking its path from the root; a place 16 or more levels deep now moves to a slot of its own and drops there. Every move and return checked the whole value for an uninitialized part; that check now looks at 64 parts. Release: 8000 nodes 19 s -> 0.16 s (build and drop), 400000 nodes build/walk/drop 0.9 s. Pinned by tests/interp_owned_list.rs (50000-node build+drop and build+walk under 120 s on a debug build, 0.9 s measured; a 40-node list with a Drop body drops outermost first past the in-place depth).

title: `s.chars().collect()` into a Vec[char] runs 14 instructions a char against Rust's 11: the UTF-8 decode loop tests the reserved length on each push, and the loop copy B-2026-11-09-26 gives counted fills does not apply because the char count is not known at the way in
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-09 on x86 at 774d3877a5 and again at 1cbfcd7e92 (release karac, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build, callgrind --dump-instr against rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on): kata 484 (kara-katas leetcode/401-500/484-find-permutation/bench) spends about 280M instructions in `s.chars().collect()` on 20M chars, 14 a char, where Rust's `s.chars().collect::<Vec<char>>()` runs 11 (220M). The push in the decode loop is a `Vec.__push_within` against a reservation of the byte length, so each trip tests `len == reach` beside the decode's own end test. 1cbfcd7e92 (B-2026-11-09-26) versions counted fills on `len + trips <= reach`; a chars fill has no trip count before it runs, so it keeps the test.
