The byte length bounds the char count, so a reach of `len + bytes` covers every push; a remedy could take that fact (an exact push when the reservation is the byte length) rather than a loop copy. After 1cbfcd7e92 kata 484 runs 616M against Rust's 551M, and this loop is most of the gap.
fix: 0d3ccaa7cd versions the chars walk on the reservation it already makes. `collect_chars` reserves the text's byte length, a ceiling on its char count; the lowering now asks `presize` for the reach, tests `n <= reach` once, and runs the decode loop in two copies: the covered copy pushes through the new `Vec.__push_reserved` (store, bump len with nsw, no capacity test, no grow call; `vec_push_reserved` in src/backend/mir/seq.rs, the interpreter treats it as push), the other keeps the ordinary push, which is what a reservation clamped below the byte length (2^28 elements) still takes. MEASURED on x86 with callgrind, release karac, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0: a 20M-char micro collect 283,470,693 -> 223,470,694 instructions (14 -> 11 a char, Rust 11); kata 484 (leetcode/401-500/484-find-permutation/bench) 616M after B-2026-11-09-26 -> 555,993,673, against Rust's 551M. Output unchanged on kata 484 and on all 39 kara-katas benches that collect chars (old vs new binary). Pinned by tests/mir_chars_collect_reserved.rs: empty, multi-byte chars of every width, push after the collect, a `for` over chars, on the interpreter and the built binary, plus the IR shape (two walks in `letters`, one grow call).

title: `Json` has no `.clone()`: `Some(v.clone())` on a field of a parsed request body is refused as "no method 'clone' on type 'Json': `Json` does not derive `Clone`; add `#[derive(Clone)]` to its declaration", advice that points at the library's own declaration
detail: Building the webhook_relay service app, the ingress looks a field up in a parsed body with `fn field(doc: Json, name: Str) -> Option[Json] { match doc { Json.Object(fields) => { for (k, v) in fields { if k == name { return Some(v.clone()); } } None } _ => None } }`; `doc` is a borrowed parameter, so the field must be copied out. `karac check`: E0236 "no method 'clone' on type 'Json': `Json` does not derive `Clone`; add `#[derive(Clone)]` to its declaration". `Json` (runtime/stdlib/source/json.kara and runtime/stdlib/json.kara) declared no derives, though json.md presents it as the tree a program checks field by field and passes through, and every JSON library's value type copies (serde_json's `Value: Clone`). The advice comes from `missing_derive_fix_it` (src/typechecker/method_user_impl.rs), which tested only that the type has a declaration span, and std.json's source is spliced into the program, so the library's declaration counted as the program's; the same advice reaches `JsonError` and every other spliced library type.
fix: FIXED by b8b6871a6c. `Json` derives `Clone` (runtime/stdlib/source/json.kara and runtime/stdlib/json.kara), so `Some(v.clone())` on a field of a borrowed parsed body type-checks and runs on every backend. The missing-trait refusal for a type declared in the library (offset at or past `library_start`) now says "the library's `T` does not implement `Tr`" and offers no fix-it, instead of advising `#[derive(...)]` on a declaration the user cannot edit (src/typechecker/method_user_impl.rs `missing_derive_fix_it`). Pinned by tests/json_clone_and_str_to_vec.rs and corpus/apps/service/webhook_relay.

title: `["a", "b"].to_vec()` passed to a `Vec[Str]` parameter, or `[("event", v)].to_vec()` to a `Vec[(Str, Json)]` one, is refused as "expected 'Vec[Str]', found 'Vec[String]'": the string literals default to `String` because the wanted element type does not reach the array literal behind `.to_vec()`
detail: Building the webhook_relay service app, JSON bodies are built with `fn obj(pairs: Vec[(Str, Json)]) -> String` called as `obj([("event", s("push")), ("ref", s("refs/heads/main"))].to_vec())`. `karac check`: "expected 'Vec[(Str, Json)]', found 'Vec[(String, Json)]'" at each of the six calls, no fix. A string literal is a `Str` where a `Str` is expected (design.md § String literals), and `total(["a", "b"].to_vec())` into `fn total(xs: Vec[Str])` fails the same way, though a `Vec[Str]` of literals borrows nothing. `check_expr` passed the expected `Vec[E]` to the method call, but the receiver, the bare array literal, was inferred on its own (synthesis mode types it `Vec[String]`), and nothing carried `E` into its elements.
fix: FIXED by b8b6871a6c. When `[..].to_vec()` is checked against an expected `Vec[E]` (refs peeled) whose element mentions `Str`, check_expr records `E` as a hint for the array literal's node (`array_element_hint`); the ArrayLiteral arm takes the hint and checks each element against `E`, so string literals become `Str` and the call is `Vec[E]` (src/typechecker/exprs.rs `str_elements_to_vec`). Covers a `Vec[Str]` argument and a `Vec[(Str, Json)]` one. The annotated-let form `let v: Vec[Str] = [..].to_vec()` still fails a later view-origin check and is filed as B-2026-11-09-50. Pinned by tests/json_clone_and_str_to_vec.rs.

title: `let v: Vec[Str] = ["a", "b"].to_vec();` is refused as a reference to a temporary that outlives its statement (typecheck §5.5, and E0516 in MIR borrowck once that passes), though the `Vec` holds static literals and borrows nothing from the array
detail: The remainder of B-2026-11-09-49, whose fix makes the literals `Str` when a `Vec[Str]` is wanted. In a `let` with that annotation the typechecker's §5.5 rule (`core_view_temp_origin`, src/typechecker/items.rs) treats a view-typed result of a method call on a temporary receiver as borrowing that receiver, so `[..].to_vec()` borrows the array literal; exempting `to_vec` on an array literal there (the elements' origins, not the array's) passes the check, and MIR borrowck then refuses the same `let` with E0516 "drop of _N while it is borrowed": the call's result is taken to borrow its `ref self` receiver (§5.4 elision). `to_vec` copies the elements, whose own origins are what the `Vec` carries. As a call argument (`total(["a"].to_vec())`) the program checks and runs; only a kept binding is refused. Both the typechecker rule and the MIR borrowck's origin for a `to_vec`/`clone` of a view collection need the element-origin rule; core-semantics §5.4 may want a line for it.
fix: FIXED by a9fc6d3b59. `[..].to_vec()` now carries what the elements borrow, not the array literal. Typechecker: `core_view_temp_origin` (src/typechecker/items.rs) answers a `to_vec` on an array literal with its elements' temporary origins, so a `Str` literal element is static and `[s.as_str(), ..]` keeps `s`'s borrow, while `[String.from(..).as_str(), ..]` is still refused at the temporary element. MIR borrowck: `to_vec` joins the natives whose result is `ResultBorrows::ReceiverValue` in `result_borrows` (src/mir/lower.rs), so the result borrows what the sequence holds, not the `ref` to it; `drop(s)` while such a `Vec` lives is still E0516. Pinned by tests/review_rulings_apps.rs (to_vec_of_a_literal_array_keeps_its_elements_borrows, _compiled, to_vec_still_carries_a_temporary_elements_borrow). A `to_vec` of a non-literal temporary receiver still takes the receiver's origin in the check.

title: Kata 1087's bench (20 million short words cloned into vectors and freed) runs 26% behind `rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on -C target-cpu=x86-64-v3` with the same allocations: 13.65G instructions against 10.45G, the extra in glibc's malloc slow path (14.8M `_int_malloc` calls against 2.7M) and in `malloc_consolidate` (0.72G, none in Rust)
detail:
MEASURED at 521196fb53 (karac built at 2f62c55005 with the runtime of that tree) on the 4-core cloud box, kara-katas leetcode/1001-1100/1087-brace-expansion/bench: 2000 random brace patterns built once, 400 rounds each expanding every pattern by a depth-first walk that pushes and pops letters on one `String` and pushes `word.clone()` into a `Vec[String]`, which is dropped after its length and one byte are folded into a checksum. Medians of 12 interleaved runs: Kāra `KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build` 1.221 s, Rust overflow-checked at x86-64-v3 0.970 s, plain `rustc -O` 0.946 s, C `clang -O3` 0.657 s, Go 1.555 s; output identical (`20187600 words, checksum 95123740`).

SAME WORK: valgrind memcheck reports 27,554,621 allocs / 1,668,217,818 bytes for Kāra and 27,557,679 / 1,667,988,517 for Rust, so the two allocate the same blocks; the gap is not extra allocation. Vec element drop order is front to back in both (checked with a Drop probe).

WHERE IT GOES (callgrind, Ir): total 13.65G Kāra, 10.45G Rust. The walk itself: 3.76G against 2.98G (+0.78G). glibc `malloc` is entered 26.2M times in both, but Kāra's falls to `_int_malloc` 14,763,850 times (2.22G) against Rust's 2,720,916 (0.79G): most of Kāra's small requests miss tcache and the fastbins. `malloc_consolidate` costs Kāra 0.72G (652M of it from 14,804 `_int_free_maybe_consolidate` calls, i.e. frees whose merged chunk reached 64 KiB with fastbins non-empty) and does not appear in Rust's profile, though Rust enters `_int_free_maybe_consolidate` 1.22M times. `karac_mir_string_from` (the clone) 0.55G against Rust's `String::clone` about 0.56G: level. Kāra's `karac_realloc_or_panic` makes 1.18M calls and its `small_realloc` path (runtime/src/alloc.rs, malloc + copy + free for blocks up to 1 KiB) issues 1.18M extra `free`s; Rust's realloc grows in place.

`KARAC_MALLOC_TUNE=0` (the mallopt trim/mmap thresholds off) changes nothing: 1.263 s against 1.278 s median of 6. NOT MEASURED: which Kāra free pattern empties the bins (the small_realloc churn is the first suspect, since it is the one allocator call sequence that differs from Rust's), and whether the walk's +0.78G is the out-of-line `karac_mir_string_push_char` / `karac_mir_char_before_byte` calls for `push(char)` and `pop()` (both appear as calls in the walk's disassembly). A check: rerun the profile with small_realloc routed to `realloc`, and with `pop` and `push` of an ASCII char inlined.
fix:
3305966202 is the tree every number below was measured at (x86 callgrind Ir, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, KARAC_HASH_SEED=1, outputs identical). WONTFIX: the cause is confirmed, and every policy that removes it on 1087 costs more across the corpus than it saves.

CAUSE, CONFIRMED: the row's first suspect. Routing `small_realloc` (runtime/src/alloc.rs, malloc + copy + free up to 1 KiB) to glibc `realloc` for requests above 256 B takes 1087 from 13.65G to 10.94G (Rust 10.45G): `_int_malloc` calls 14.76M -> 2.74M, `malloc_consolidate` 0.72G -> absent. Wall, medians: 0.726 s against Rust's 0.721 s (0.937 s before). The pushes and pops of the walk are already inlined for ASCII (no `karac_mir_string_push_char` / `karac_mir_char_before_byte` calls in the profile), so the walk's remainder is not those calls.

WHY IT DOES NOT SHIP: a random 120 of the frozen-set benches under 0.3 s, each run under four policies against the same binary (a KARAC_SR_MAX knob in an experiment archive). Ratios to today's policy (realloc only above 1 KiB): realloc above 384 B geomean 1.0013, worst 1.061 (combination_sum_ii), best 0.989; above 256 B geomean 1.0055, worst 1.291 (kata 113 path_sum_ii, 2.25G -> 2.91G), 1.160 (three_sum), 1.092, 1.091, best 0.976; realloc for every size geomean 1.0116, 16 programs above 1.02, worst 1.210 (group_shifted), 1.181 (insert_interval), 1.159 (maximum_swap), none below 0.996. Earlier single cuts on 1087: 128 B 11.12G, 192 B 10.96G, 384 B 11.77G. So the malloc + free path wins most programs (its new block comes from tcache; `_int_realloc` never takes tcache when it cannot grow in place) and loses only where the heap layout lets realloc grow in place and the moved blocks' frees, adjacent to top, trigger `malloc_consolidate` with fastbins full. No size cut separates the two.

OTHER LEVERS MEASURED: GLIBC_TUNABLES glibc.malloc.mxfast=0: 1087 14.95G, Rust 14.68G (worse for both); tcache_count=32: Kara 12.92G, Rust 10.12G; tcache_count=64: 12.69G / 10.00G (a tunable a program cannot set for itself after exec). The runtime's own small lists switched on from the start on Linux with small_realloc through them: 1087 13.70G (no change), 113 2.17G, 445 5.13G, the B-2026-08-20-9-style sequential probe 0.80G -> 0.578G. The lever left is a bundled allocator in place of glibc's, a design decision beyond this row. The unshipped cut (POOL_STARTED gating the 256 B split, so auto-par keeps B-2026-08-20-9's fix) is saved at project-files patches/B-2026-11-09-51-unshipped-realloc-cut.diff. 1087 stays at 1.30x Rust wall, inside the perf bars.

title: `karac fmt` writes the 30 soft words as raw identifiers: `let group = 1` comes out as `let r#group = 1`, and so does every binding, field, parameter or function named `seq`, `resource`, `with`, `stable`, `layout`, `alias`, `reads`, `requires` and the rest, though each lexes as a plain identifier
detail:
Found adding kata 1087 (Brace Expansion) to the corpus: its harness builds a brace group with `let group = f"{{{parts.join(",")}}}";`, and `karac fmt` on the file printed `let r#group = ...` and `r#group.len()` / `push_str(r#group)` at each use. `karac check` accepts the bare name, and `tests/contextual_keywords.rs` asserts every one of the 30 soft words lexes as `Token::Identifier`. Probe at 521196fb53 (release karac): a `main` binding `group`, `layout`, `verb`, `seq`, `stable` and `resource` passes check and formats to `r#group` ... `r#resource` everywhere, the f-string holes included.

Cause: src/formatter.rs needs_raw_escape held its own copy of the lexer's keyword table (its comment says it mirrors src/lexer.rs identifier()), and the copy kept every word the 2026-10-07 design review made contextual (union, marker, mod, use, weak, lock, the effect verbs, transparent, stable, seq, par, layout, group, alias, independent, distinct, shared, where, with, effect), plus requires / ensures / invariant (no longer keywords since B-2026-11-06-18), providers and f16 / bf16. The output still parses and means the same, so the round-trip test (tests/fmt_round_trip.rs, fixed point and same diagnostics) never saw it; it shows only as noise: a soft-word name in any file `karac fmt` touches gets an escape its author never wrote, and the redundant `r#union` of corpus/fixtures/contextual_keywords/raw_escape_of_a_soft_word_is_still_accepted is kept rather than dropped.
fix: 7732ad152a: src/formatter.rs needs_raw_escape no longer keeps a list of its own. It lexes the name with crate::lexer::Lexer and escapes it only when the token is not a plain Token::Identifier (and the word is raw-escapable at all), so the formatter and the lexer cannot drift apart again. `let group = 1` and every binding, parameter, field or function spelled like a soft word (union, marker, mod, use, weak, lock, resource, the effect verbs, transparent, stable, seq, par, layout, group, alias, independent, distinct, shared, where, with, effect, requires, ensures, invariant, providers) now format as written, and a redundant `r#union` is dropped; real keywords (`r#match`) and reserved words (`r#async`, `r#try`) keep their escape. Pinned by tests/kata_1087_fmt_soft_words.rs (the 33 words as a field, a parameter, a binding and an f-string hole, unchanged by fmt; the corpus fixture's `r#union` / `r#reads` formatted bare and to a fixed point; three escaped keywords kept). Control on the pre-fix formatter: the first two tests fail, the third passes. tests/fmt_round_trip.rs (every corpus program formats to a fixed point and checks the same) passes with the change.

title: Six Rust-isms were diagnosed with no fix `karac fix` applies: `pub(crate)` (and `pub(super)`, `pub(self)`), an unreachable `_ =>` arm, `?` in a unit `main` over an error that is no `Error` or an `Option` (the fix declared `AnyError`, which did not check), a tuple struct and its `Name(x)` / `.0`, `.collect::<Vec<_>>()` (the binding was left unannotated), and `impl<T: Add<Output = T>>` (the `=` stopped the bracket fix)
detail: Found by scripts/mend/rustism_audit.py, which injects one Rust-ism at a time into corpus apps and katas that check clean and print their expected output, then asks whether `karac check` reports one new diagnostic and whether `karac fix` (up to three passes) leaves a program that checks and prints the same. First run over 34 programs: pub(crate) 0/20 (parse error, no fix), `_ =>` 0/11 (W0237 with no fix), `?` in main 0/5 (the fix wrote `-> Result[(), AnyError]` whatever the operand: a `Result[_, String]` or an `Option` operand then failed), tuple struct 0/9 ("Expected `{` after struct name"), `.collect::<Vec<_>>()` 0/17 (the turbofish was deleted and the binding left with nothing to fix its type: "cannot infer type parameter 'C'"), `impl<T: Copy + Add<Output = T>>` 0/1 (the bracket fix stopped at the `=`). Not a Mend rate: the mistakes are a script's, not a blind model's.
fix: 01d64b96db. Each mistake now has a fix `karac fix` applies, and the audit (scripts/mend/rustism_audit.py, table in scripts/mend/README.md) passes them on every program it injects them into: `pub(crate)`/`pub(super)`/`pub(in ..)` are deleted and `pub(self)` becomes `private` (parser `eat_pub`, at every `pub` site); an unreachable arm's fix deletes from the end of the arm before it, and `karac fix` widens that to the arm's own lines when it has them to itself (cli.rs `widen_unreachable_arm_fixes`); `?` in a unit `main` records each operand's error and whether it converts to `AnyError`, and the fix declares `AnyError` when all do, else the one error they share, and rewrites to `.unwrap()` an `Option` operand or an error that cannot pass up; `struct S(T);` is fixed to named fields (`value`, or `f0`, `f1`, ..), `S(x)` on a program struct to the literal in field order, `.0` on a struct to the field and on a distinct type to `.raw()`; `let v = it.collect();` whose target nothing decides is refused as "cannot infer what this `collect` builds" with `: Vec[T]` from the iterator's item; and the angle-bracket fix scans past an `=` inside a nested list. Pinned by tests/rustism_fixes.rs. The `collect` whose target a later use decides is B-2026-11-09-56.

title: Eleven library error types did not implement `Display` and `Error` though design.md §10 says the library's error types do (Utf8Error, NulError, NetError and its alias TcpError, TlsError, HttpError, RegexError, CliError, ChannelError, SemaphoreError, DiscriminantError, AlreadySetError): `String.from_utf8(b)?` in a function returning `Result[T, AnyError]` was refused, and `f"{e}"` printed the variant's name. A remainder of 8adc0b0e29, which covered JsonError, SendError, the timeout errors and PoolError
detail: The audit's `?`-in-main injection on kata 49 (group anagrams) declared `-> Result[(), AnyError]` over `String.from_utf8(..)?` and was refused: "'Utf8Error' does not implement `Error`, which `AnyError`'s `From` asks of the error it converts". A sweep of every `struct|enum *Error` in runtime/stdlib found the eleven. Their Display had to go in a library source file too: the MIR builder lowers no baked impl, so `Utf8Error.InvalidByte.to_string()` printed `InvalidByte` with the baked impl alone (as io_error.kara's header says of IoError).
fix: 01d64b96db. Each of the eleven implements `Display` and `Error` in the baked file that declares it (what the checker reads), and its `Display` is also in runtime/stdlib/source/library_errors.kara, which the MIR builder lowers, since it lowers no baked impl; NetError's is in source/net.kara with a `Display` for TlsFailure, RegexError's in source/regex.kara, and CliError's in cli.kara, which MIR now appends when a program names `CliError` (it would otherwise load std.cli for every program). Pinned by tests/rustism_fixes.rs (`String.from_utf8(..)?` into AnyError prints "invalid UTF-8 byte"; each type's message).

title: No lint reports a `let mut` binding that is never written: Rust's habit of `let mut` on a binding that is only read draws nothing (the Rust-ism audit's injection was silent in 20 of 20 programs), so Kāra written from Rust habits keeps every one; Rust warns `unused_mut`
detail: The program stays correct, so this is a lint, and design.md § Built-in lints (v1 starter set) has none for it: adding one is a spec change (a lint name in the starter set, tests/lints' registry pin). The ownership checker already has the exact complement: `report_write_to_immutable_binding` (src/ownership.rs) is called at every write to a binding and refuses the ones without `mut`; marking the `let mut` ones it sees written, and reporting the rest at the function's end with a fix deleting `mut `, is the shape. Its warnings would need a channel: ownership emits errors and perf notes, no lint warnings. Validation: every corpus program that checks clean must still check after `karac fix` applies the new lint's edits.
fix: df878ae40f: the ownership pass records each function's `let mut` statements (keyed by offset; a loop body is walked twice) and marks one written at every write the `let mut` rule sees, before that rule's exemptions, plus a call to a local `MutFn` (TypeCheckResult::mut_fn_local_calls), a method call the strict check reads as writing its receiver (receiver_write_calls; the ownership table lacks VecDeque and others, B-2026-11-09-101) and an unmarked `mut ref` method argument (B-2026-11-09-100). A write marks every `let mut` of that name in the function, so shadowing can only under-report. cli.rs report_unused_muts reports the unwritten ones, once the program has no parse, resolve, type, ownership or MIR error (an error's fix can be the write: `add(v)` becomes `add(mut v)`), at the level of a lint attribute on the function or its `impl` (lints::attr_level, shared with unused_effect), else the command line's, else warn, as StyleLint W0295 with a fix deleting `mut` and the space after it; a `let` whose text is not `let mut ..` is skipped. A marked method argument on a non-`mut` binding is now refused like a free-function one. Corpus sweep over the 15,870 clean programs: 340 warnings in 227 programs; applying every fix leaves each checking clean and printing what it printed. tests/unused_mut_lint.rs.

title: `let v = it.collect();` whose `Vec` target a later use decides passes the type checker and is refused by MIR: `fn count(v: Vec[char]) -> i64` and `let cs = text.chars().collect(); count(cs)` draws "the method call `.collect` with no resolved callee is not lowered yet". 6 of 16 audit programs reached it once `karac fix` removed a `.collect::<Vec<_>>()` turbofish
fix: 86c3102afc. Three parts. (1) src/typechecker/exprs.rs settle_binding_lent_to_ref: a binding whose type is still an open variable, lent to a `ref T` / `mut ref T` parameter, is unified with `T` before the argument is checked, so the binding holds the value and not a reference (the borrow is the call's). (2) src/typechecker/items.rs open_unsolved_let_params: a call whose whole type is a parameter it left open (`collect`'s `C`, which the generic path keeps out of its frame) takes the let's variable as that type argument in node_call_subs, so typed HIR places it once a use solves it; this was the missing callee for map/split-based chains (`Vec[1,2].iter().map(..).collect()`). (3) discharge_deferred_call_bounds resolves that variable, so `let ws = "a b".split(" ").collect(); words(ws)` with `words(v: Vec[String])` is the same `FromIterator[Str]` error an annotated binding gets rather than a run that mis-executes. A receiver or index use before the deciding use (`let c = ws[0].clone(); take(ws)`), which Rust also refuses, is now "cannot infer what this `collect` builds where it is first used, at L:C ... name it on the binding" with the `: Vec[T]` fix-it, where it was "a type that failed to check is not lowered yet". The rustism audit's `.collect::<Vec<_>>()` row is 16/16 (was 10/16). Pinned by tests/collect_target_decided_later.rs.

title: Strings have no `match_indices` (nor `char_indices`): kata 2052's text arm wrote Rust's `sentence.match_indices(" ").map(|(at, _)| at + 1)` to find each word's start and was refused "no method 'match_indices' on type 'String'" with no hint at what to write instead
fix: 758eca16fe. Built to the review thread's ruling, in runtime/stdlib/source/collections.kara: `char_indices()` on strings returns `StrCharIndices`, a double-ended iterator of `(i64, char)`, each scalar value with its byte offset; `match_indices(pat)` returns `StrMatchIndices`, each non-overlapping match's byte offset and text as `(i64, Str)`, found with `find_at_byte` from the end of the last match. An empty pattern matches at every char boundary and at the end, as `split` treats it. `String` receivers reach both through `as_str()`; src/desugar.rs lists `match_indices` among the iterator-chain methods. tests/design_md_code_blocks.rs keeps both names in SPEC_AHEAD_STRING_METHODS, because its probe typechecks without the library source and cannot see library methods (as with rfind and split_once). Pinned by tests/kata_2052_char_match_indices.rs. Writing `match_indices`' `next` as `-> Option[(i64, Str)]` met B-2026-11-10-7; the library writes `Option[Self.Item]`.

title: `karac fix`'s `fn main() -> Result[(), AnyError]` for a `?` in `main` left each bare `return;` of `main` as it was, so the fixed program failed to check with "expected return value of type 'Result[(), AnyError]'" at every one
detail: Building the uptime_monitor app: `main` ends its setup with `return;` on a bind or open failure (three sites) and reads the incident log with `println(f"  {line?}")`. The `?` draws B-2026-11-07-43's fix (`offer_unit_main_result_fix`, src/typechecker/items.rs), which declares the return type and appends `Ok(())`; the next `karac check` then refuses each `return;` and nothing fixes them, so a blind Mend loop stalls on errors the fix itself made. Remedy: the same fix also inserts ` Ok(())` after each `return` with no value in `main`'s body, skipping one inside a closure, which returns from the closure.
fix: FIXED by f42a83543c. src/typechecker/items.rs `offer_unit_main_result_fix` collects every `return` with no value in `main`'s body (span_visitor) and appends ` Ok(())` to each that no closure encloses, in the same fix that adds the `Result` return type; a closure's own `return` stays. Pinned by tests/uptime_monitor_gaps.rs `the_main_result_fix_returns_ok_from_a_bare_return` (the fixed program checks).

title: A format spec in Python's spelling, `{x:.1f}` or `{name:>8s}`, is refused as "unsupported type `f` (expected one of x, X, o, b, d)" with no fix, though Kāra's spelling is the same spec without the letter
detail: Building the uptime_monitor app: the uptime line was written `{pct:.1f}%`, as in Python, C's printf, and most LLM-written code. design.md §3 gives floats a precision and no type letter, and a value's text is its `Display`, so `f`/`F` after a precision and `s` anywhere are spellings with an exact Kāra equivalent: delete the letter (and the `:` when nothing else is left, `{name:s}` to `{name}`). The parser validates the spec (src/parser/exprs.rs, the f-string hole) and reported only the general `SpecError::Type` message. Remedy: when the spec minus its last letter parses and the letter is `f`/`F` after a `.` or `s`, report it by name at the letter's own span, with the edit that deletes it. `e`, `g`, `%` and a bare `f` keep the general message: they change the digits.
fix: FIXED by f42a83543c. src/parser/exprs.rs `foreign_spec_letter`: a format spec whose last letter is Python's `f`/`F` (after a precision) or `s`, and whose rest parses as a Kara spec, is reported as "format spec `.2f`: Kāra has no `f` type, a float's precision alone sets its digits after the point; write `.2`" (or the `s` wording, or "drop the `:s`" for a bare `s`), with a machine-applicable edit deleting the letter (and the colon when nothing is left). Other letters keep "unsupported type". Pinned by tests/uptime_monitor_gaps.rs `a_python_float_or_string_format_letter_is_named_and_deleted` and `an_unknown_format_letter_keeps_the_general_message`.

title: An HTTP request past its `timeout` fails in `karac run` with ureq's "Network Error: Network Error: Error encountered in the status line: timed out reading response", without the URL, where the compiled client says "<url>: request timed out after <ms> ms"
detail: Building the uptime_monitor app: its `hang` endpoint sleeps past the check's `timeout(300)` twice. runtime/src/lib.rs `http_fetch_blocking` wraps the whole fetch in `tokio::time::timeout` and reports `{url}: request timed out after {timeout_ms} ms`; the interpreter's `http_exchange` (src/mir/interp.rs) hands ureq the timeout per request and falls through to `Err(e) => e.to_string()`, ureq's doubled kind text with no URL. A program printing the message diverges between backends, and the corpus A/B rule catches it. Remedy: a transport error whose source chain holds an `io::Error` of kind `TimedOut` or `WouldBlock`, when a timeout was set, is reported in the compiled client's words, naming the URL the program asked for. io.md § HTTP client now states the message.
fix: FIXED by f42a83543c. src/mir/interp.rs `http_exchange` takes the request's URL and maps a ureq transport error whose source chain holds an io `TimedOut`/`WouldBlock` (`http_timed_out`), on a request with a timeout, to "<url>: request timed out after <ms> ms", the compiled client's text. docs/library/io.md states the message. Pinned by tests/uptime_monitor_gaps.rs `an_http_timeout_says_so_in_the_interpreter` and `an_http_timeout_says_so_compiled` (a listener that never answers).

title: `File` has no `write_all`: `f.write_all(text.bytes())?` is "no method 'write_all' on type 'File'", though `TcpStream`, `TlsStream`, `BufWriter` and `ChildStdin` have one and `File.write` may write fewer bytes than given
detail: Building the uptime_monitor app's state file (write a temporary file, `sync_all`, rename it over the old one): the natural line is `f.write_all(text.bytes())?`, which Rust users write. io.md's `File` table has `write` only, which returns a count that a correct program must loop on. Remedy: `File.write_all(self, buf: Slice[u8]) -> Result[(), IoError] with writes(self) blocks`, every byte by `write` until none is left, retrying `Interrupted`, a zero-byte write being `Other("failed to write whole buffer")` as in Rust. Written in Kāra (runtime/stdlib/source/file_write_all.kara, appended to a program that names `write_all`, `File` in LIBRARY_SOURCE_TYPES), so it reaches a `FileSystem` fake through `write` like any write.
fix: FIXED by f42a83543c. `File.write_all(buf: Slice[u8]) -> Result[(), IoError]` is library Kara (runtime/stdlib/source/file_write_all.kara, baked in src/mir/lower.rs on the word `write_all`, `File` added to LIBRARY_SOURCE_TYPES): it calls `write` until the buffer is gone, retries `Interrupted`, and fails a zero-length write. It routes through a `FileSystem` fake's `write_handle` as `write` does. docs/library/io.md lists it. Pinned by tests/uptime_monitor_gaps.rs `a_file_writes_all` and `a_file_writes_all_compiled`.

title: Under a `FileSystem` override, a compiled `File.open`, `File.create` or `OpenOptions.open` of a `String` path built at run time hands the fake's `open` a garbage path (the `&String` read as a `Str`; ASan: stack-buffer-overflow in the caller); a literal path works, and the interpreter is right
detail: Building the uptime_monitor app's self-test: `save_state` opens `f"{path}.tmp"` through `File.options()...open(tmp)` under an in-memory fake, writes, and renames it; compiled, the rename was NotFound and the fake's key was `\ufffd`. `providers::route_files` turns the open into `FileSystem.open_file(path, flags)` and `open_via` calls the provider's `open(self, path: Str, opts)` with the path operand as the native took it; the natives read a path behind a reference or as a view (`str_parts`), so a `String` argument arrives as `&String`, 8 bytes, and the provider's body reads 16 from it. `owned_texts` had fixed the same shape for the HTTP client's `__get` / `__post` (B-2026-11-03-18). Remedy: `open_via` views a borrowed or owned `String` path with `String.as_str` before the call (`Spec::path_view`, src/mir/providers.rs). Pinned by tests/uptime_monitor_gaps.rs `a_fake_file_system_opens_string_paths_compiled` (OpenOptions.open and File.create of a `String`).
fix: FIXED by f42a83543c. src/mir/providers.rs `open_via` now passes the path through `path_view`, which turns a borrowed or owned `String` operand into a `Str` view with a `String.as_str` call before the provider's `open(self, path: Str, opts)` is called, so the fake reads the path's bytes rather than the `String`'s header. Pinned by tests/uptime_monitor_gaps.rs `a_fake_file_system_opens_string_paths` and `a_fake_file_system_opens_string_paths_compiled` (`OpenOptions.open` and `File.create` of run-time `String` paths), and by the uptime_monitor app's self-test on every backend.

title: There is no `drop(x)`: ending an owned value early (closing a `BufWriter[File]` before reopening its file) is "undefined name 'drop'" with no hint, and the only spellings are a block around the value's scope or a helper taking `own T`
detail: Building the uptime_monitor app: the incident log's `BufWriter` is closed with `drop(log)` before the program restarts its monitor and reopens the log, as in Rust (`std::mem::drop`, in Rust's prelude). core-semantics §7 says when values drop and §7.11 how a `Drop` body runs, but names no function to end a value's life early, and the resolver's refusal says nothing of the alternatives. The app wraps each writer in a block. Two remedies, a spec call: a prelude `fn drop[T](x: own T) {}` (the value moves in and drops at the callee's end, so it adds no new rule), or keep the language without it and make the diagnostic name the block and an `own` parameter as the ways to end a value early. Either needs a line in core-semantics §7.
fix: FIXED by a9fc6d3b59. Per the review ruling (4d7151c588), `drop` joins the prelude as an ordinary `fn drop[T](x: own T) {}` (runtime/stdlib/mem.kara, registered in src/prelude.rs PRELUDE_FN_ARITY and the names list). The library body is not lowered, so MIR lowers the call in `mem_call` (src/mir/lower.rs): the argument moves into a temporary that a Drop terminator ends at the call, and the call's value is `()`. A BufWriter flushes and a Drop impl runs at the call on the interpreter and compiled; a use after `drop(a)` is "value 'a' moved here"; a program's own `fn drop` still wins. Pinned by tests/review_rulings_apps.rs (drop_ends_a_value_at_the_call, _compiled, a_dropped_value_is_moved, a_programs_own_drop_function_wins). uptime_monitor now calls `drop(log)` as first written (kara-katas d71586fd).

title: `set_read_timeout` on a socket a `Network` fake opened returns `Err(Unsupported)`, so a TCP client that sets a timeout, as io.md tells a client to, cannot be tested against a fake without ignoring the error
detail: Building the uptime_monitor app's self-test: its TCP check connects, calls `s.set_read_timeout(Some(ep.timeout_ms))` and treats an error as a failed check; under the fake `Network` (which serves `+PONG`) the check fails with `set timeout: unsupported` and the self-test prints that. io.md § Sockets under an override says `try_clone`, `local_addr` and `set_read_timeout` on a fake's socket return `Unsupported`, and that a fake's reads run to completion and never wait, so a timeout cannot fire there. Accepting it (`Ok(())`, a timeout below 1 ms still `InvalidInput`) changes no fake's behaviour and lets the code under test be the code that ships; otherwise every timed client needs `let _ =` on the call. A spec call for io.md, then the interpreter's and the runtime's fake-socket paths.
fix: FIXED by a9fc6d3b59. Ruling taken (the review left it to the apps thread): a fake's socket accepts `set_read_timeout` as a no-op `Ok(())`, since a fake's read never waits; a timeout below 1 ms is still `InvalidInput`, and once the override has ended the call is `ProviderUnavailable`. io.md § Sockets under an override and core-semantics §14.12 say so. Interpreter: `fake_socket_method` (src/mir/interp.rs) answers it through `timeout_arg`. Compiled: `karac_mir_net`'s provided-socket branch (runtime/src/mir_io.rs) calls the new `net_provider::other`, which also makes every other op on an ended override's socket `ProviderUnavailable` rather than `Unsupported`, matching the interpreter. `try_clone` and `local_addr` stay `Unsupported`. Pinned by tests/review_rulings_apps.rs (a_fakes_socket_accepts_a_read_timeout, _compiled); uptime_monitor's self-test TCP check now passes (expected.out updated from its mirror).

title: A chain of two literal lists is refused: `v.iter().chain(w.iter())` over `[1, 2]` and `[10, 20, 30]` reports `J.Item = ref i64` is not satisfied by `Item = ref i64`
detail: v1 gate re-check, mir-interp lane: the five fixtures/interpreter/iter_range/test_iter_chain_* entries that chain two literal lists were refused at check. Both items are `ref` of an open literal variable (B-2026-11-07-3); 37b53dade4 paired an open literal with the other side of an associated-type equality only at the top of each type, so `ref ?a` against `ref ?b` compared two distinct variables and failed. Regression from 37b53dade4 (B-2026-11-08-86, -88 follow-up).
fix: 7c40eb7a02. The pairing of open literals in an associated-type equality matches the two sides part by part (pair_open_literals in src/typechecker/exprs.rs: under a borrow, in a tuple, in generic arguments), so two literal lists chained unify their element variables; literals of different kinds settle apart. The five fixtures/interpreter/iter_range/test_iter_chain_* entries run again.

title: `chain` accepts items of another numeric width or kind: `Vec[f64]` chained with `Vec[i64]` builds and prints `[1.5, 5e-324]`; `Vec[i32]` with `Vec[i64]` prints `[7, 705032704]`
detail: Found while fixing -74. `discharge_assoc_type_eq_bounds` compares `J.Item` with `Self.Item` by `types_compatible`, which lets any number answer for any other (the value-level rule). An item type is a layout: the interpreter printed `[1.5, 1]` and `[7, 5000000000]`, the binary reinterpreted the bits. The generic-argument path already refuses this (`numeric_args_agree`, B-2026-08-05-19); the associated-type path did not, under a borrow either. Pinned by corpus/design/err_chained_items_of_another_numeric_width.
fix: 7c40eb7a02. discharge_assoc_type_eq_bounds also requires numeric_args_agree under the borrows (peel_borrows), the rule generic arguments already follow (B-2026-08-05-19): an item is a layout. Both programs are refused at check with E_WHERE_CLAUSE_ASSOC_TYPE_EQ_NOT_SATISFIED; pinned by corpus/design/err_chained_items_of_another_numeric_width.

title: A program declaring its own `struct F64` or `struct F32` fails to build: `typecheck: 3694:5: no associated function 'from' on type 'F64'` from the library's `f64_wrapper_from`
detail: v1 gate re-check, mir-interp lane: fixtures/codegen/control/test_e2e_shadowed_prelude_name_keeps_its_own_comparison refused. Two lines (`struct F64 { x: i64 }` and a `main`) reproduce it: the appended library text's `fn f64_wrapper_from(value: f64) -> F64 { F64.from(value) }` (collections.kara) resolves `F64` to the program's struct. `check` accepts the program with a prelude_shadow warning saying built-in paths keyed on the name no longer apply. Fix shape: rename the program's type apart, as `rename_compiler_name_shadows` does for `Range`, `IoError` and the other names the compiler spells.
fix: 7c40eb7a02. library_source blanks the library's f64_wrapper_from / f32_wrapper_from (blank_float_wrapper_froms in src/mir/lower.rs) when the program declares its own F64 / F32, keeping every offset; renaming the program's type apart was tried and dropped its prelude_shadow warnings (fmt_round_trip caught it). Both shadow fixtures run; the prelude's F64.from as a value still works where nothing shadows it.

title: A hand-rolled `BoundedChannel { handle_id: 0 }` stops the interpreter (`BoundedChannel[i64].send of a channel never made`) instead of failing closed as bounded_channel.kara documents
detail: v1 gate re-check: fixtures/interpreter/concurrency/test_bounded_channel_hand_rolled_zero_handle_fails_closed. The legacy expectation was an E0238 refusal (T not inferred); since literal inference fixes T from `send(1)` the program checks, and runtime/stdlib/bounded_channel.kara says id 0 is reserved for exactly this literal: `send` is `Err(ChannelError.Full)`, `recv` is `None`. The build remainder is its own row (-78).
fix: 7c40eb7a02. The interpreter's channel natives treat a BoundedChannel holding id 0 as hand-rolled: send drops the value and returns Err(Full), recv returns None, drop does nothing (src/mir/interp.rs channel_method). The fixture is pinned to full/none from bounded_channel.kara; the binary's segfault is B-2026-11-09-78.

title: A hand-rolled `BoundedChannel { handle_id: 0 }` segfaults the built binary (exit 139; `__mir-llvm-run` exits 101 with no output) where bounded_channel.kara says send fails closed with `Full` and recv returns `None`
detail: Remainder of -77, which fixed the interpreter. corpus fixtures/interpreter/concurrency/test_bounded_channel_hand_rolled_zero_handle_fails_closed (expected `full` then `none`): `karac build` then running the binary segfaults at 44c2788ade. The runtime's send/recv/drop all accept a null handle and return 0, so the fault is in the lowering of the struct literal or of the compiler_builtin methods on a channel not made by `new`. Routed to the backend owner (src/backend).
fix: a2b8b07dad: the fault was in the MIR runtime, not the lowering. A `BoundedChannel { handle_id: 0 }` written by hand holds a null runtime channel, and `karac_mir_chan_send` (with recv, ready, closed and clone) read through it; only `karac_mir_chan_end` took a null. Each now accepts a null channel and fails closed as bounded_channel.kara says: a send is refused as full (the lowering then drops the value, as for a full channel), a recv finds nothing, readiness answers at once so a task does not wait on it, and clone keeps it null. Pinned by the runtime unit test `null_channel_fails_closed` and the corpus fixture test_bounded_channel_hand_rolled_zero_handle_fails_closed, which passes on mir-interp, mir-llvm and mir-llvm-asan (the built binary printed `full`, `none` against the rebuilt archives). A nonzero hand-rolled handle is still a pointer the runtime trusts; nothing in the corpus writes one.

title: A write through a read-only `Slice` binding is now refused earlier as E0517, not without a code: the fixtures' legacy E0200 expects were stale
detail: v1 gate re-check, mir-interp lane: fixtures/core_strict_check/check_write_through_a_read_only_slice, _2 and _3 (`let mut t = b.bytes(); t[4] = 97;`) fail `refused, but without E0200`. 34d42091dd (B-2026-11-08-64) skips the older typecheck report under the core check so the error prints once; the core check's report it keeps carries no code, so `--output=json` and `karac explain` lose E0200. Either the kept report carries E0200 or the fixtures' expectation changes with a decision. Routed to Thread A (diagnostics).
fix: c0efe0ebfb: the report is not codeless. The core check refuses the write as E0517 (WriteThroughSharedRef: a place reached through a `ref` is written) before the type check's E0200, which 34d42091dd stopped printing a second time. The three fixtures' E0200 expects were recorded from the legacy run; the review thread ruled E0517 right, and they now expect it (expected_from = decision).

title: An escaping closure capturing a borrow is now refused earlier as E0515 (moving out of a borrowed place), not without a code: the fixtures' legacy E0516 expects were stale
detail: v1 gate re-check, mir-interp lane: fixtures/mir_escaping_view/CLOSURE_INTO_SHARED, PIN and PUSHED fail `refused, but without E0516`. The check from 5f1a515ae0 (B-2026-10-25-20) now refuses them first, with no code, before MIR borrowck's E0516. Routed to Thread A (ownership errors).
fix: c0efe0ebfb: the report is not codeless. The ownership check refuses the closure as E0515 (MoveOutOfPlace: an escaping closure captures a place behind a borrow by move, core-semantics §9.3, §3.7) before MIR borrowck's E0516.
