ADR-2 at 5244494204 vs legacy 741fbf08c1: build geomean 0.750x (was 0.851 at 2991314acf, 0.886 at 7b70e3b10f), max 1.348x, size 0.309x, none over 1.5x (review/adr2-dual/frozen-head-5244494204.json). The pinned trait methods (RangeStep x 12 int types) and the word-based keep the row also named still stand; with build time below the 11-02 level they are not filed separately.

title: Rust's `Iterator::eq` is missing: `a.iter().eq(b.iter().rev())` is refused with "`VecIter` does not implement `PartialEq`", and adding `eq` to the library's `Iterator` trait broke every program on every MIR lane, because a trait default copied into an impl kept its bound's `Self.Item` unresolved (not, as first guessed, because `==` found the new `eq`)
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-10 on kara 0909d4aa26 (release, --features llvm). Kata 2081's iterator arm (kara-katas leetcode/2001-2100/2081-sum-of-k-mirror-numbers, kmirror_iter.kara) tested a number's base-k digits as Rust does, `digits.iter().eq(digits.iter().rev())`. `karac check` says `no method 'eq' on type 'VecIter': the library's `VecIter` does not implement `PartialEq``, which reads as if `eq` were the operator's method and the iterator should implement it; Rust's `Iterator::eq` compares the items. TRIED: a default method on `trait Iterator` in runtime/stdlib/source/iter.kara, first `fn eq[J: Iterator](own self, other: own J) -> bool where Self.Item: PartialEq[J.Item]`, then `fn eq[J: Iterator[Item = Self.Item]](own self, other: own J) -> bool where Self.Item: PartialEq` (a `loop` over `a.next()` / `b.next()` returning false at the first `x != y`). `karac check` then accepts the arm, but `__mir-run` and `__mir-llvm-run` refuse every program that compiles the library, the arm and a control that never calls `eq` (the kata's kmirror_next.kara) alike: `error[mir]: typecheck: 573:28: cannot compare 'I.Item' and 'Self.Item'` (and `639:28: cannot compare 'i64' and 'Self.Item'`, `644:28: ... 'I.Item' and 'Self.Item'`); with the `PartialEq[J.Item]` bound, `cannot compare 'Self.Item' and 'J.Item'`. HYPOTHESIS (not traced): the MIR pipeline's library typecheck resolves `==` / `!=` in generic library bodies by looking up a method named `eq`, which now finds the iterator's default method before `PartialEq.eq`. The attempt is kept at /mnt/attach/project-files/kata2001/iter-eq-attempt.patch. Rust also has `ne`, `lt`, `le`, `gt`, `ge`, `cmp` and `partial_cmp` on `Iterator`, with the same name clash. The kata's arm writes `digits.iter().zip(digits.iter().rev()).all(|(a, b)| a == b)`, equal there because both sides have one length.
fix: 36c8731fe3: `Iterator.eq` is a default on `trait Iterator` (runtime/stdlib/source/iter.kara): `fn eq[J: Iterator[Item = Self.Item]](own self, other: own J) -> bool where Self.Item: PartialEq`. The row's hypothesis was wrong. `==` did not find the iterator's `eq`. Trait defaults are copied into every impl, and the copy's bound equation kept `Self.Item` as an unresolved projection, so `x != y` between `Self.Item` and `J.Item` was refused in every copy, and every program that compiled the library failed. lower_assoc_eq (src/typechecker/bounds.rs) resolves `Self.<assoc>` against the impl's self type wherever an associated-type equation is lowered: the bound-receiver dispatch and resolve_enclosing_assoc_eqs (expr_method_call.rs), and normalize_enclosing_assoc_eqs. A program's own trait default with the same bound shape gets the same fix. Cost: `eq` is an operator name in library_prune's ALWAYS_KEPT, and a kept PartialEq impl spells it, so the default was kept and copied into every kept iterator impl (+10-20 ms a __mir-run, +20-30 ms a build on a 3-line program, against a control built without the default). library_prune now keeps `trait Iterator`'s defaults named eq/ne/lt/le/gt/ge/cmp/partial_cmp only when the program's own words name them or kept text writes `.name` (Method.called_only); after that, check/run/build of the program match the control within noise. Kata 2081's `digits.iter().eq(digits.iter().rev())` arm matches its Python mirror on __mir-run and __mir-llvm-run. Fixtures: tests/iterator_eq.rs (both lanes: items equal, unequal and of different lengths, chars, owned Strings, empty; mismatched item types refused with E_WHERE_CLAUSE_ASSOC_TYPE_EQ_NOT_SATISFIED; a user trait default with `J: It[Item = Self.Item]` in a generic impl), and library_prune::tests::iterator_comparisons_are_kept_only_when_called.

title: `SortedMap.insert` of a key smaller than every key present is O(n): the map is one sorted array, so 100000 inserts of falling keys take 1.8 s compiled against 0.018 s for rising ones, where collections.md promises a B-tree with O(log n) operations
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-10 on kara 0909d4aa26 (release, --features llvm; the tree also carries this thread's unpushed kata fixes, none of which touch this path). `let mut m: SortedMap[i64, i64] = SortedMap.new(); for i in 0..100000 { m.insert(100000 - i, i); }` built with KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 runs in 1.82 s; the same loop inserting `i` runs in 0.018 s (about 100x). Kata 2092 (Find All People With Secret, kara-katas leetcode/2001-2100/2092-find-all-people-with-secret/secret_struct.kara) keeps meetings in a `SortedMap` keyed by time; its constraints' largest input gives 99998 meetings in falling times, and that arm runs 5.8 s compiled against 0.4 to 0.6 s for the other arms, 4.7 s of it in that chain, 22 s under __mir-run. runtime/stdlib/source/collections.kara keeps SortedMap as a sorted array (SortedMapIter walks `front`/`back` indices), so an insert at the front moves every entry. docs/library/collections.md: SortedMap/SortedSet are B-trees, 'Every operation is O(log n)'. Expected: an insert anywhere in O(log n), or the doc's complexity corrected.
fix: c5303d91b3. A sorted table stays one array, which compiled code indexes in line, up to 16 KiB of entries (twice a leaf at least), then moves into a counted B+-tree (runtime/src/mir_map/tree.rs): leaves of up to 2 KiB of entries (8 to 512) linked in key order, under inner nodes of 32 children that record each child's entry count and leftmost leaf. A key is found by comparing it with each child's first key, an index by the counts; insert and remove move at most one leaf's entries, so every operation is O(log n). A rising run past the last leaf or a falling run before the first fills leaves whole; a short node takes from or merges with its sibling; a tree down to one leaf goes back to an array. An index walk in order is answered from the last leaf reached, kept as one atomic word (leaf id, start index) so readers sharing a table see a whole cursor or none. Compiled code (src/backend/mir/table.rs `entry_at`) sends an index read to the runtime when `buf` is null, as it does for a hashed table with holes. Node rows abort on a bad index rather than panic, so the table natives still link no panic hook (tests/mir_panic_free_floor.rs). MEASURED on this Emerald Rapids container, both arms the same karac with the archive swapped (KARAC_RUNTIME): 100000 falling inserts 1.63 s -> 0.013 s; rising 0.017 -> 0.015 s; 200000 builds of a 40-entry map 4.05G -> 3.62G instructions (the array bisection no longer passes the holes check); 3M lookups in a 30k-entry tree 1.38G -> 1.26G; 300 walks of that tree level in wall time (0.045 s both) but 179M -> 489M instructions, about 35 more per entry through `karac_mir_map_at` than the in-line array read. The five frozen-set programs that use a sorted table: 0.83x to 1.03x, outputs identical. Pins: runtime unit tests `a_sorted_table_in_a_tree_matches_a_model` (a Vec model through falling, rising and random runs, removal by index and by lookup from both ends, `pick`'s six ops, clear; es 8, 16, 40, 200; every merge and borrow branch was counted as reached) and `a_falling_run_fills_leaves`; corpus/design/ok_sorted_map_past_one_array (25k to 34k entries, Python mirror source.py), passing on mir-interp, mir-llvm, mir-build and mir-llvm-asan. The interpreter still keeps one sorted vector (12.7 s against 0.32 s for the falling loop): remainder B-2026-11-11-4.

title: A tuple of literals was typed `(i64, i64)` where it was written, not left open as design.md §8 leaves a bare literal -- filed as a diagnostics gap (the narrowing refusal not naming the `0`), but the refusal itself was the bug: `heap.push((0, 0))` then `while let Some((d, u)) = heap.pop()` made `d` an `i64`, and `return d` / `dist[v] = d + t` in an `i32` context were refused (kata 2093)
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-10 on kara 0909d4aa26 (release, --features llvm; the tree also carries this thread's unpushed kata fixes, none of which touch this path). A function returning `i32` with `dist: mut ref Vec[i32]`, `let mut heap = PriorityQueue.new(); heap.push((0, 0)); while let Some((d, u)) = heap.pop() { if d > dist[u] { continue; } let nd = d + toll; .. dist[u + 1] = nd; .. return d; }` (toll: i32) gets two errors, 'implicit coercion from i64 to i32 would narrow or change sign ... Write an explicit as i32', at `dist[u + 1] = nd` and `return d`. The cause is the literal `0` in `heap.push((0, 0))`, which kept its default beside an `i32` that widens (design.md §8 Literals, by design). For a plain local the message already says so: `let mut a = 0; a = a.max(3 as i32); a` in an `i32` function is told '`a` is an i64 because its literal kept the default ... declare it `a: i32`'. Kata 2093's Rust template (LeetCode's Dijkstra with `heap.push((0, 0, 0))`) met three of these after `karac fix`, and the by-hand repair was the heap's type, `PriorityQueue[(i32, i64, i64)]`, which no message pointed to. Expected: the explanation names the literal that fixed the tuple slot (here the push's `0`) or the heap's element type, as it does for a local, ideally with a fix.
fix: d70ec4a181. A tuple whose parts are all number literals (unsuffixed ints or floats, their negations, nested tuples of these) is now a tuple of literal variables in a `let`, a pushed element and a heap push, open until a use fixes them, as a bare literal is (`src/typechecker/exprs.rs`, the Tuple arm). A compare of an open literal tuple with a fixed one unifies them (`pair == (n, 5)`, `src/typechecker/expr_ops.rs`). Tuples with a non-number part (`(s, 1)`) stay as before, and a literal tuple passed straight to a generic argument (`id((0, 0))`) is still settled at once: opening it broke the core pin `ok_fold_tuple_reads_a_borrowed_scalar_as_its_value`. The core_strict_check case "tuple-value-into-a-narrower-tuple" now binds its tuple from an `i64` variable, and "tuple-literal-into-a-narrower-tuple" pins the literal form as accepted. Pins: `tests/literal_tuple_stays_open.rs` (let and heap pairs; kata 2093's Dijkstra prints 15). Class changed from diagnostics to false-positive per the review thread. Gate on a6491451e1's tree: 10993 + 11184 passed, 0 failed.

title: Rust's `Reverse` on one part of a heap's tuple item has no Kāra spelling and no fix: `BinaryHeap<(Reverse<i32>, String)>` and `BinaryHeap<(i32, Reverse<String>)>` are refused at every `Reverse`, and the remaining repair is a hand-written `Ord` or a negated number, impossible for a `String`
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-10 on kara 0909d4aa26 (release, --features llvm; the tree also carries this thread's unpushed kata fixes, none of which touch this path). Kata 2102 (Sequentially Ordinal Rank Tracker, kara-katas leetcode/2101-2200/2102-sequentially-ordinal-rank-tracker/rank_tracker_solution.kara) writes LeetCode's Rust template with fields `served: BinaryHeap<(Reverse<i32>, String)>` and `waiting: BinaryHeap<(i32, Reverse<String>)>`, `push((Reverse(score), name))`, `let (Reverse(s), n) = pop().unwrap()` and `let (s, Reverse(n)) = ...`. `karac fix` takes three rounds (22, 1, 4 edits: Rust spellings, the `use` lines, BinaryHeap to PriorityQueue.max_first()) and stops with 7 errors, each '`Reverse` is Rust's std::cmp::Reverse; Kāra has no such wrapper ...'. The existing fix (kata 1057/2008, B-2026-11-08-4) drops a Reverse that wraps the whole heap item; with one tuple part reversed no edit of the tuple keeps the order. The Kāra spellings that work are a struct with hand-written PartialEq/Eq/PartialOrd/Ord (four impls, 20 lines; the kata's ★ arm) or `(-score, name)` for a number (the tuples arm); a reversed String has neither. A mixed-direction key (sort_by_key with Reverse, a heap by score descending then name ascending) is common in real services, so this is a design question rather than a fix-it: a library `Reverse[T]` (std.cmp, Ord by the inner value reversed) would let the fix rewrite each Reverse as itself; otherwise the diagnostic could at least point at the Ord-impl spelling. The kata's Rust arm stays as the fix leaves it.
fix:
3d987fca00. Fixed by the library's `std.cmp.Reverse[T]` (core-types.md § Reverse, review ruling 2026-11-11), runtime/stdlib/std_cmp.kara, a gated module. It is a struct with one field, `value`, ordered by T's order reversed. A generic `a.cmp(b)` at a String lowers now; before, it was "not lowered yet". `karac fix` carries Rust's spelling over:
- `use std::cmp::Reverse;` becomes `import std.cmp.Reverse;` when a use stays. The parser's `rust_reverse_stays`.
- An unimported `Reverse` gets the import from the resolver, through `Program::std_cmp_reverse_import`.
- `Reverse(x)` becomes `Reverse { value: x }` in expressions, through the typechecker's struct-call fix, now allowed for the library's `Reverse`.
- In let and match patterns, `report_struct_spelled_as_tuple_pattern` writes the struct pattern; a program struct gets the same fix.
- In closure parameters, the parser writes the struct pattern.
- `r.0` becomes `r.value`.
The whole-heap-item drop and the whole-sort-key rewrite still apply when every Reverse can go. When one stays, all do, and every heap is `max_first()`: the wraps and the heap sides go empty. Kata 2102's Rust template now mends to a clean program, and the kata's file matches its Python oracle under run and build. Holding a Reverse in a tuple exposed B-2026-11-11-60, fixed in the same commit. Pins are in tests/std_cmp_reverse.rs; kata 1058's old no-fix pin is flipped to `kata_1058_reverse_inside_a_larger_key_takes_std_cmp_reverse`.

title: A bare handle parameter handed to `BufReader.new` / `BufWriter.new` (`fn serve(conn: TcpStream) { BufReader.new(conn) }`, a Rust port's owned parameter) gets E0297 "not a `ref TcpStream`" with no fix, where any other `own` parameter gets the D5 refusal and the fix that writes `own`; before E0297 (d5307a5abd) it passed check and the buffer closed the caller's handle
detail: Porting irc_lite: `fn serve(srv: Server, id: i64, conn: TcpStream) { let reader = BufReader.new(conn); ... }`. In Rust `conn: TcpStream` is owned; in Kāra a bare parameter borrows (core-semantics §4.1), so the call gives a borrow away. A call to a user function's `own` parameter gets E0200 "cannot give away parameter `conn`" with the machine fix `own `; `BufReader.new(inner: own R)` is generic, so the D5 check (d5_give_away) never saw an owned type expected and said nothing, and the only refusal was E0297's "`BufReader` wraps a `File`, `ChildStdout`, `ChildStderr` or `TcpStream` ..., not a `ref TcpStream`", with no fix. Before d5307a5abd the program passed check, and a caller's File then read "BufReader[File].new of a closed file" (interpreter) or was freed twice (ASan bad-free) once the buffer dropped. Repro: `import std.io.{BufReader}; fn first(x: File) -> String { let r = BufReader.new(x); let mut s = String.new(); let _ = r.read_line(mut s); s } fn main() { fs.write("o.txt", "one\n").unwrap(); let f = File.open("o.txt").unwrap(); println(first(f)); }`.
fix: FIXED by 0e5453a321. src/typechecker/expr_call.rs: at `BufReader.new` / `BufWriter.new` (and `with_capacity`) whose argument is an identifier of type `ref H`, H a handle a buffer wraps (File, child pipe, TcpStream, TlsStream), the call runs the D5 check (d5_give_away) against H, so a bare parameter gets E0200 "cannot give away parameter `conn`" and the machine fix that writes `own`; the pending E0297 judgement skips it. Any other borrowed handle (an element of `files.iter()`) is refused by buf_source_refusal (src/typechecker/exprs.rs) by name: "`BufReader` takes the `File` it wraps, and closes it when it drops, but this `File` is borrowed: pass an owned one". Fixture: tests/buffered_io_borrowed_source.rs (karac fix writes `own` on both parameters and the program checks; the iterated borrow is refused by name). irc_lite's `serve(srv, id, conn: TcpStream)` is fixed by karac fix now.

title: `let s: String = pieces.map(|x| f"[{x}]").collect()`, Rust's `FromIterator<String> for String`, is refused with only "`String` implements `FromIterator[char]`, not `FromIterator[String]`", without naming Kāra's spelling (collect a `Vec[String]` and `join("")`)
detail: Porting irc_lite's `show`: `let params: String = m.params.iter().map(|x| format!("[{}]", x)).collect();`. Rust implements FromIterator<String> and FromIterator<&str> for String; Kāra's String gathers chars only (library/iterators.md § collect and FromIterator), which is a deliberate surface. The refusal states the bound but not the way to write it, so a Rust port stalls with no fix and no help. Repro: `fn main() { let v = ["a", "b"].to_vec(); let s: String = v.iter().map(|x| f"[{x}]").collect(); println(s); }`.
fix: FIXED by 0e5453a321, as a help: the refusal stays, since a Kāra `String` gathers `char`s (library/iterators.md § collect and FromIterator), and now ends "; collect the pieces into a `Vec[String]` and join them, `pieces.join("")`" when the target is `String` and the items are text (src/typechecker/exprs.rs, the FromIterator mismatch arm). No machine fix: the rewrite changes the binding's type and its uses. Fixture: tests/collect_string_pieces.rs.

title: `read_exact` on `TcpStream`, `TlsStream`, `File` and the child pipes was missing; Rust's `conn.read_exact(&mut hdr)?` failed "no method 'read_exact' on type 'TcpStream'" (the `BufReader` remainder is B-2026-11-11-63)
detail: Porting socks5_proxy: every step of the SOCKS5 handshake reads a fixed number of bytes (`let mut head = [0u8; 2]; conn.read_exact(&mut head)?;`). docs/library/io.md lists `read` only on TcpStream, TlsStream, File, BufReader and the pipes, so a program loops over `read` itself, and a hand loop is where short reads are mishandled. The app carries a `read_exact(conn, mut buf) -> Result[(), String]` helper that loops until the slice is full and calls a 0-byte read the end. The library method needs an error for an early end (Rust: ErrorKind::UnexpectedEof; NetError and IoError have none today), so this is a library-surface decision. Repro: `fn main() { let l = TcpListener.bind("127.0.0.1:0").unwrap(); let c = TcpStream.connect(l.local_addr().unwrap()).unwrap(); let mut b = [0u8; 2]; let _ = c.read_exact(mut b); }`.
fix: 8279013053. `read_exact(mut buf: Slice[u8])` on `TcpStream`, `TlsStream`, `File`, `ChildStdout` and `ChildStderr`, specified in docs/library/io.md (§ Reading an exact count, review-approved) as Rust's: it reads until `buf` is full, retries `Interrupted`, and an end of stream before then is `Err(UnexpectedEof)`. Bytes read before the early end stay in `buf`, and how many is unspecified. `NetError` gains `UnexpectedEof` as its last variant (native code 12 in the interpreter, the backend's `NET_ERRORS` and the runtime provider), so a program matching every `NetError` variant needs the new arm; `IoError` already had one. The methods are Kāra library code over `read` (runtime/stdlib/source/net.kara, process.kara, read_exact.kara for `File`, baked on the word `read_exact`). REMAINDER: `BufReader` has no `read_exact` yet, because a method on the generic `impl[R] BufReader[R]` trips B-2026-11-11-62 (`self` in a generic impl is typed without its arguments). That is filed as B-2026-11-11-63. PINS: kara-katas 6c56195f ports apps/service/socks5_proxy (each handshake step is `conn.read_exact(mut head)`) and apps/service/mqtt_broker (`read_packet` is the Rust's, with `conn.read_exact(mut body)?`), copied to corpus/apps/service/{socks5_proxy,mqtt_broker}; both match their Python oracles on __mir-run and __mir-llvm-run. tests/read_exact_io.rs covers a fill across several writes and the early end over TCP, File and a child pipe, and a fake `Network` provider's socket, on the interpreter and a built binary alike.

title: `port.to_be_bytes()` / `u16.from_be_bytes(b)` (and the `le` forms) are refused, "did you mean 'to_ne_bytes'" (a different byte order, reported twice), though both backends already implement `to_le_bytes` and `to_be_bytes`
detail: Porting socks5_proxy: a SOCKS5 port is big-endian on the wire, written `port.to_be_bytes()` and read `u16::from_be_bytes(pb)` in Rust. src/typechecker/method_numeric.rs admits only `to_ne_bytes` (its comment: design.md names only the native form), while src/mir/interp.rs (`to_ne_bytes | to_le_bytes | to_be_bytes`) and src/backend/mir/num.rs (bswap for `to_be_bytes`) already lower all three. The refusal suggests `to_ne_bytes`, which is the wrong order on every little-endian target, and is printed twice at the same span, followed by a cascade "no method 'extend_from_slice' on type 'Vec' taking these arguments". `from_be_bytes` / `from_le_bytes` / `from_ne_bytes` do not exist at all. The app writes `((pb[0] as u16) << 8) | pb[1] as u16` and `[(port >> 8) as u8, (port & 0xFF) as u8]`. Repro: `fn main() { let p: u16 = 47762; let b = p.to_be_bytes(); let q = u16.from_be_bytes(b); println(q); }`.
fix: FIXED by 6fe383ed8a. `x.to_le_bytes()` and `x.to_be_bytes()` now check beside `to_ne_bytes()` (src/typechecker/method_numeric.rs; both backends already lowered them), and `<int>.from_ne_bytes(b)` / `from_le_bytes` / `from_be_bytes` take the `Array[u8, N]` of the type's width, refusing any other with "u16.from_be_bytes expects an `Array[u8, 2]`, got ..." (src/typechecker/method_identifier_receiver.rs, `int_from_bytes` in src/mir/interp.rs and src/backend/mir/num.rs). docs/library/core-types.md § Byte order. Pinned by tests/int_byte_order.rs on the interpreter and a compiled build (u8 through i64, signed, a borrowed array parameter). socks5_proxy now writes `u16.from_be_bytes(pb)` and `port.to_be_bytes()`.

title: `Result.unwrap_or_default()` does not exist (`String.from_utf8(v).unwrap_or_default()` fails "no method 'unwrap_or_default' on type 'Result'"), though `Option` has it (library/core-types.md) and Rust has both
detail: Porting socks5_proxy: `let user = String::from_utf8(read_n(conn, ulen)?).unwrap_or_default();`. library/core-types.md lists `unwrap_or_default` on Option only; Result has `unwrap_or` and `unwrap_or_else`. The app writes `.unwrap_or(String.new())`. Repro: `fn main() { let r: Result[String, i64] = Ok("x"); println(r.unwrap_or_default()); }`.
fix: fff48b5d17: `impl[T: Default, E] Result[T, E] { fn unwrap_or_default(own self) -> T }` in runtime/stdlib/source/result.kara, matching `Option.unwrap_or_default`; the error is dropped. library/core-types.md's Result table lists it. Fixtures: tests/result_unwrap_or_default.rs, with `Ok` and `Err` over String, i64 and Vec, and `String.from_utf8` on valid and invalid bytes, on __mir-run, __mir-llvm-run and __mir-llvm-asan. A `T` without `Default` is refused with "trait bound `T: Default` is not satisfied; `P` does not implement `Default`".

title: Rust's `let local = [127u8, 0, 0, 1];` (an array in Rust, a `Vec` by default in Kāra) passed to an `Array[u8, 4]` parameter gets "expected 'Array[u8, 4]', found 'Vec[u8]'" at each use, with no fix to annotate the `let`
detail: Porting socks5_proxy: `let local = [127u8, 0, 0, 1];` then `ipv4_request(1, local, ECHO_PORT)` with `addr: [u8; 4]` (karac fix: `Array[u8, 4]`). design.md § Collection literals makes an unannotated list literal a Vec, so the refusal is right, but each use reports it and none names the fix, `let local: Array[u8, 4] = [..]`, which the literal's length and the parameter make machine-applicable. Repro: `fn f(a: Array[u8, 4]) -> i64 { a.len() } fn main() { let local = [127u8, 0, 0, 1]; println(f(local)); }`.
fix: 662c8ece18. An unannotated `let` of a non-empty list literal is noted (`list_lit_lets`, `src/typechecker.rs`). A use of it refused where an `Array[T, N]` is wanted, with N the literal's length and the element type matching (or still an open literal), now gets ": `local` (bound at L:C) is a `Vec`, because a list literal with no expected type is one (design.md § Collection literals)" at each use. When nothing else is assigned to the binding it also gets "; declare it `local: Array[u8, 4]`", with that annotation as the machine-applicable fix on the first use. A reassigned binding is explained without the fix, and a literal of another length is left as before. socks5_proxy's shape runs after `karac fix` (4, 4 on both lanes). Pins: `tests/list_literal_let_into_array.rs`. Gate: 11029 + 11223 passed, 0 failed.

title: An unknown method in a `let` initializer (`text.trim_end_matches('\n').split("\n").collect()`) is followed by a spurious "a reference to a temporary outlives its statement (core-semantics.md §5.5)" at the same span
detail:
Porting socks5_proxy: `let lines: Vec[Str] = text.trim_end_matches('
').split('
').collect();`. The first error is right and helpful ("no method 'trim_end_matches' on type 'String': Kāra strips a suffix with `strip_suffix(p)` ..."); the second, about a temporary dropped at the `;`, comes from the error-typed receiver and goes away with the fix (`text.strip_suffix("
").unwrap_or(text).split("
")` checks). Repro: `fn main() { let text = String.from("a
b
"); let lines: Vec[Str] = text.trim_end_matches('
').split("
").collect(); println(lines.len()); }`.
fix:
e30304b318. The `let` check for a reference to a temporary outliving its statement (core-semantics.md §5.5, `src/typechecker/items.rs`) now skips a value that already has an error inside its span: an unknown method has no type, so nothing is known to borrow from a temporary. `text.trim_end_matches('
').split("
").collect()` reports only the unknown method and its `strip_suffix` hint. A real temporary in the same shape (`String.from("a
b").split("
").collect()`) is still refused. Pins: `tests/unknown_method_no_temporary_cascade.rs`. Gate: 11029 + 11223 passed, 0 failed, then a re-check after the rebase (11063 passed).

title: A `let` bound to an `if`, `match` or block whose every value is an unsuffixed literal is typed `i64` at once, not as the literal variable design.md §8 ("A join of literals is a literal") says later uses fix: `let x = if c { 1 } else { 0 }; take_i32(x)` and kata 2103's `let bit = match pair[0] { b'R' => 1, b'G' => 2, _ => 4 }; rods[i] |= bit` over a `[u8; 10]` are refused as narrowing (the binding half of B-2026-11-10-6)
fix: a6491451e1. A `let` bound to an `if`, `match` or block whose every value is an unsuffixed literal, and such a join as a list element (`[31, if leap { 29 } else { 28 }, 31]`), is a literal variable now (design.md §8, "A join of literals is a literal", eb38ac12ab): the join's tails are inferred open (`open_literal_join`, the `open_match_arms` flag through `infer_match`), and a later use fixes them. Kata 1118's `let feb = if leap { 29 } else { 28 }` returned from an `i32` function prints 29/30. Kata 2103's `rods[i] |= bit` over `[u8; 10]` stays refused, by the §8 binding-widening rule (beside a type that widens into the default a literal keeps `i64`), exactly as `let bit = 4` is; the refusal now says "`bit` is an 'i64' because its literal kept the default" and `karac fix` writes `let bit: u8 = ...`. Pins: `tests/literal_join_stays_open.rs` (both lanes). Gate: 10993 + 11184 passed, 0 failed.

title: A binary search over an `i32` interface written as Rust writes it, `let mut lo = 0; let mut hi = n - 1;` (n: i32), is refused at every `mid` use with only `as i32` advice and `karac fix` has nothing to apply: a value computed from a defaulted literal binding (`let mid = (lo + hi) / 2`), a tuple `let mut (l, r) = (0, n - 1)` read through `m = l + (r - l) / 2`, and `for (lo, hi, s) in [(0, peak, 1), ..]` get no annotation
detail: FOUND writing kata 1095 (Find in Mountain Array, kara-katas leetcode/1001-1100/1095-find-in-mountain-array), whose arms read LeetCode's `MountainArray` through `get(index: i32) -> i32` and `length() -> i32`. Every arm's binary search starts `let mut lo = 0;` beside `hi = n - 1` with `n: i32`; design.md §8 Literals keeps the literal at `i64` beside a type that widens into it, so `mid = (lo + hi) / 2` is an `i64` and `mountain.get(mid)`, `hi = mid` and `return mid` are each refused "implicit coercion from 'i64' to 'i32' would narrow ... write an explicit 'as i32'". The annotation that fixes the whole function is `lo: i32` (or `0i32` in a tuple), and B-2026-11-08-20 / -62 already offer it when the refused value IS the binding or a plain copy of it; here the refused value is computed from it, so the refusal names nothing and `karac fix` applies nothing. Measured on the five Kāra arms and LeetCode's Rust template (which `karac fix` turns into `let mut (l, r) = (0, n - 1);`): all five arms and the template were refused with no fix. Three shapes: (1) `let mid = (lo + hi) / 2`, an operator tree over one literal binding and narrower integers; (2) the same over a tuple-let literal (`let mut (l, r) = (0, n - 1)`); (3) a `for` tuple pattern over an array of tuples whose position holds a literal (`for (lo, hi, sign) in [(0, peak, 1), (peak + 1, n - 1, -1)]`), where the tuple's literal is settled to i64 when the tuple is built.
fix: 6a4c75838e: A binary search over an i32 interface written as Rust writes it, `let mut lo = 0; let mut hi = n - 1;` with `n: i32`, keeps `lo` at i64 (design.md §8 Literals), so `mid = (lo + hi) / 2` is an i64 and every use of it as an i32 was refused with only `as i32` advice. The refusal now names `lo` and `karac fix` writes `lo: i32` when the refused value is an operator tree over one literal binding and integers narrower than i64; a tuple let `let mut (l, r) = (0, n - 1)` and a `for` tuple pattern over an array of tuples get the literal's suffix, `0i32`. Kata 1095's five arms and LeetCode's Rust template now reach a clean check through karac fix. Pinned by tests/kata_1095_literal_index_annotation.rs.

title: Rust's open range on a `SortedSet`/`SortedMap`, `seen.range(..k - x).next_back()`, is refused with advice naming the end to supply but `karac fix` has nothing to apply, though over an integer element type the missing end is `T.MIN`/`T.MAX`
detail: FOUND writing kata 1099 (Two Sum Less Than K, kara-katas leetcode/1001-1100/1099-two-sum-less-than-k), whose one-pass arm keeps the values seen so far in a `SortedSet[i64]` and takes each value's best partner as Rust writes it, `seen.range(..k - x).next_back()`. Kāra's `range` and `range_inclusive` take both ends (docs/library/collections.md); a closed `a..b` / `a..=b` argument has had the parser's edit to `range(a, b)` / `range_inclusive(a, b)` since kata 2008, and since kata 2070 (c0435987ac) a range open at an end gets advice naming the bound to supply (and `floor`/`ceiling` on a SortedMap), but no edit, so `karac fix` stops on the arm. Over an integer element (or key) type the open end has an exact stand-in, the type's MIN or MAX, which iterates the same elements. REPRO: `let mut seen: SortedSet[i64] = SortedSet.new(); let y = seen.range(..5).next_back();` -> error[typecheck] method 'range' expects 2 argument(s), found 1 with advice only; `karac fix` reports no fixable diagnostics. Same for `m.range(..=5)`, `m.range(3..)` and `m.range(..)` on a `SortedMap[i32, i32]`.
fix: e6bd0300b4: Kata 1099's one-pass arm takes the best partner of each value as Rust writes it, `seen.range(..k - x).next_back()` on a `SortedSet[i64]`. Kāra's `range` and `range_inclusive` take both ends, so the call is refused, and since kata 2070 the refusal names the end to supply, but `karac fix` had nothing to apply. Over an integer element (or key) type the missing end is the type's bound, so the parser now records the edit with a stand-in for it and the typechecker writes `T.MIN` or `T.MAX`: `..b` to `range(T.MIN, b)`, `..=b` to `range_inclusive(T.MIN, b)`, `a..` to `range_inclusive(a, T.MAX)`, and `..` to `iter()` over any type. Any other element type keeps the advice alone. Pinned by tests/kata_1099_open_range_fix.rs.

title: A Rust `scan` closure with a `return None;` guard, `(1..).scan(candies, |left, gift| { if *left <= 0 { return None; } let given = gift.min(*left); *left -= given; Some(given) })`, gets advice alone where the same closure without the guard gets the rewrite to Kāra's `Some((state, item))` shape
detail: FOUND writing kata 1103 (Distribute Candies to People, kara-katas leetcode/1101-1200/1103-distribute-candies-to-people), whose iterator arm hands out gifts of 1, 2, 3, ... candies with Rust's `scan`, ending when the candies run out. Since kata 2012 a Rust `scan` closure that writes its state through `*state` gets the mechanical rewrite to Kāra's shape (`let left = left - given; Some((left, given))`), but `src/typechecker/rust_scan.rs` withheld it whenever the body held any `return`, so this closure got advice alone and `karac fix` stopped on the arm. `return None` ends the iteration and carries no state, so it reads the same in Kāra's shape. Also seen once the rewrite applied: a body too long for one line was inserted with every later line at column 0. REPRO: the closure above in `fn handed_out(candies: i64) -> Vec[i64] { (1..).scan(..).collect() }` -> one diagnostic naming the shape, `karac fix` has nothing to apply.
fix: a54501be77: Kata 1103's iterator arm hands out gifts with Rust's `scan`, ending when the candies run out through `if *left <= 0 { return None; }`. Any `return` in the closure withheld the rewrite to Kāra's `Some((state, item))` shape and left advice alone. `return None` ends the iteration and carries no state, so it now stays as written and the rest of the body is rewritten. A rewrite too long for one line keeps its body's indentation rather than starting each later line at column 0.

title: `format!("{}{}{}", &s[..i], if v { "t" } else { "f" }, &s[j..])` gets advice alone: the f-string rewrite refuses any argument containing `f"`, which a plain `"f"` literal does
detail: FOUND writing kata 1106 (Parsing A Boolean Expression, kara-katas leetcode/1101-1200/1106-parsing-a-boolean-expression), whose reduce arm rebuilds its string with `format!("{}{}{}", &s[..open - 1], if value { "t" } else { "f" }, &s[close + 1..])`. `format_arg_fits_hole` in src/parser.rs refuses an argument containing `f"` so that an f-string never lands inside a hole (B-2026-10-24-12), and the literal `"f"` matched that test, so the macro got the message naming the f-string to write and no edit. An `f"` opens an f-string only when the `f` is not the end of a longer identifier or literal. REPRO: the call above in any function -> `Kāra has no macros; format!(...) is Rust syntax: write an f-string`, `karac fix` has nothing to apply.
fix: d7b33992ad: Kata 1106's reduce arm writes `format!("{}{}{}", .., if value { "t" } else { "f" }, ..)`. The rewrite refused any argument containing `f"`, meant to keep an f-string out of a hole, and so refused the literal `"f"` too. An `f"` opens an f-string only when the `f` does not end a longer word or literal, so the check now looks at the character before.

title: `let top = frames.last_mut().unwrap();` followed by `top.seen_true = true;` gets advice alone: the `last_mut` rewrite (B-2026-11-08-46) covers only `match` and `if let`
detail: FOUND writing kata 1106 (Parsing A Boolean Expression), whose frames arm keeps a stack of open operators as Rust writes it, `let top = frames.last_mut().unwrap(); if v { top.seen_true = true; } else { top.seen_false = true; }`. Kāra has no `last_mut`; B-2026-11-08-46 gave `karac fix` an edit for `match v.last_mut()` and `if let Some(x) = v.last_mut()`, but a `let` binding the unwrapped reference had advice alone. When the rest of the block names neither the vector nor a new binding of the same name, and every use of the binding is the object of a field access, an index or a method call, or the operand of `*`, the `let` can be dropped and each use written `frames[frames.len() - 1]`. REPRO: the two statements above inside a loop over a `Vec[Frame]` -> `no method 'last_mut'` advice, `karac fix` has nothing to apply.
fix: 79dc9537fd: Kata 1106's frames arm writes to the top frame of a stack as Rust does: `let top = frames.last_mut().unwrap();` and then `top.seen_true = true;`. The last_mut rewrite (B-2026-11-08-46) covered only `match` and `if let`, so a `let` had advice alone. When the rest of the block names neither the vector nor a new binding of the same name, and every use of the binding is the object of a field, an index or a method call, or the operand of `*`, the fix drops the `let` and writes each use as `frames[frames.len() - 1]`.

title: Rust's `use std::iter::Peekable; use std::str::Chars;` and `fn read(chars: &mut Peekable<Chars>)` reach `std.iter has no item Peekable` and `unknown module std.str` with no fix, though Kāra has `Peekable` and the type is `Peekable[StrChars, char]`
detail: FOUND writing kata 1106 (Parsing A Boolean Expression), whose tree arm parses by recursive descent over `expression.chars().peekable()`, passed down as Rust writes it, `chars: &mut Peekable<Chars>`. `karac fix` turns the `use` lines into `import std.iter.Peekable; import std.str.Chars;` and the parameter into `mut ref Peekable[Chars]`, then stops: `std.iter has no item Peekable` (it is a prelude type, `struct Peekable[I, T]` in the library), `unknown module std.str, did you mean std.iter?`, and `Chars` is not a Kāra type (a `String`'s `chars()` is `StrChars`). docs/library/iterators.md writes the type as `Peekable[Self]`, one argument, where the library's has two. The arm was finished by hand: the imports deleted and the parameter written `mut ref Peekable[StrChars, char]`. Wanted: the imports of prelude types dropped by the fix, `Chars` named as `StrChars`, `Peekable[X]` given its item type, and the doc's signature corrected. REPRO: the three lines above with `fn main() { let mut c = "ab".chars().peekable(); read(mut c); }`.
fix: 7d95ec9646. `karac fix` now carries kata 1106's Rust shape to a program that runs. (1) `reject_rust_prelude_import` (`src/parser.rs`) also deletes a `use std::iter::..` whose every name is a prelude type (`Peekable`, `Iterator`, `IntoIterator`, `FromIterator`, `DoubleEndedIterator`, `ExactSizeIterator`) and a `use std::str::..` of `Chars` / `CharIndices`; a real item (`use std::iter::repeat;`) still gets the `::` -> `.` fix. (2) `rust_collection_rename` maps `Chars` -> `StrChars` and `CharIndices` -> `StrCharIndices`, so the message names them and the resolver renames the use. (3) `Peekable[X]` with one argument (`src/typechecker/lowering.rs`, `complete_peekable_args`) is refused as "`Peekable` takes two type arguments, the iterator and its item: write `Peekable[StrChars, char]`" with that as the fix, and lowered with the item so its uses check (no cascade). (4) docs/library/iterators.md gives `peekable`'s result as `Peekable[Self, Self.Item]`. The REPRO mends in four rounds to `fn read(chars: mut ref Peekable[StrChars, char])` and prints on both lanes. Pins: `tests/rust_peekable_chars_port.rs`. Gate: 11066 + 11253 passed, 0 failed (the llvm leg's last three targets run alone after the 2 h limit), then a re-check after the rebase over the mpsc import rule (11078 passed).

title: `address.split('.').collect::<Vec<&str>>().join("[.]")` gets advice alone (bind a typed `let` first), though `Vec[Str].from_iter(address.split(".")).join("[.]")` now names the type at the call and runs
detail: FOUND writing kata 1108 (Defanging an IP Address, kara-katas leetcode/1101-1200/1108-defanging-an-ip-address), whose split arm is Rust's one line. B-2026-10-29-8 (0a5d255d8a) took the delete away from a turbofish on a `collect` whose result is the receiver of a further call, since the type cannot then come from the use, and offered no edit because hoisting the chain into a `let` reorders evaluation and `Vec[String].from_iter(..)` did not lower (B-2026-10-29-40). bd4d547c50 fixed that, so the collection's own `from_iter` is an edit that keeps the order: `{T}.from_iter(` before the receiver and `)` for `.collect::<..>()`, with Rust's `&str`, `HashSet`, `HashMap`, `BTreeSet`, `BTreeMap` written as `Str`, `Set`, `Map`, `SortedSet`, `SortedMap`. REPRO: the line above in `fn defang_ip_addr(address: String) -> String` -> one parse error with no edit; `karac fix` stops.
fix: 33ef2a7ad2: Kata 1108's split arm is Rust's one line, `address.split('.').collect::<Vec<&str>>().join("[.]")`. A turbofish on a `collect` whose result is the receiver of a further call had advice alone (B-2026-10-29-8), since the type cannot come from the use and `Vec[T].from_iter(..)` did not lower then. It does now, and it names the type at the call without reordering anything, so the fix writes `Vec[Str].from_iter(address.split(".")).join("[.]")`, with `&str`, `HashSet`, `HashMap`, `BTreeSet` and `BTreeMap` spelled as Kāra's `Str`, `Set`, `Map`, `SortedSet` and `SortedMap`. The pin that held advice alone for two such calls is flipped; `sum` and a type with `_` keep it.

title: `String.from_iter(s.chars().rev())` passes the type checker and stops in the MIR builder: "a call with no resolved callee is not lowered yet"
detail: FOUND writing kata 1108 (Defanging an IP Address) while working out the rewrite for a mid-chain `collect::<String>()` (B-2026-11-10-42). The library has `impl FromIterator[char] for String` and `C.from_iter(it)` with `C` a type parameter instantiated at `String` lowers through it (`generic_fn_by_receiver`'s primitive branch), but the call written with the type's name records no callee in the checker, and `src/mir/lower.rs` handled only `default` for a bare `Type.method` path with none. `Vec[Str].from_iter`, `Set[..]`, `SortedSet[..]`, `Map[..]`, `SortedMap[..]` and `VecDeque[..]` all run. REPRO: `fn main() { let t = String.from_iter("abc".chars().rev()); println(t); }` -> `karac check` and `karac run` both report error[mir] `a call with no resolved callee is not lowered yet`.
fix: 33ef2a7ad2: `String.from_iter(it)`, which that rewrite gives for a `String` target, checked and then stopped in the MIR builder with "a call with no resolved callee": it now reaches the library's `impl FromIterator[char] for String`.

title: The sync HTTP client shared one current-thread tokio runtime across threads: a program calling it from more than one thread raced on tokio's IO driver (TSan, apps/service/http_cache; shipped in 0.8.1)
detail: FOUND by CI's ThreadSanitizer job, red on every run since apps/service/http_cache entered the corpus (e922bfc642; green at 9838a2a944, red from 595f6ff02f). REPRODUCED with the -Zbuild-std TSan archive: `karac __mir-llvm-tsan` on http_cache with KARAC_THREADS=4 reported 2 races in 8 of 12 runs. Both are inside tokio 1.54.1: Driver::turn reading and ScheduledIo::wake writing a ScheduledIo that another work_pool helper thread had just allocated in RegistrationSet::allocate under TcpStream::connect, each thread inside `http_client_runtime().block_on(http_fetch_blocking ...)` on karac_mir_ready_https's pool. The report names no `Mutex M`: the memory is tokio's IO driver state, not a program_state global. CAUSE: runtime/src/lib.rs `http_client_runtime()` was one process-wide current-thread runtime, so whichever thread held its core in block_on drove the IO driver for sockets the other blocked threads had registered. A tokio-only Rust program in the same shape (one shared current-thread runtime, 4 threads x 200 block_on connect/write/read against a local listener, TSan with build-std) reports the same ScheduledIo set_readiness/wake races in 5 of 5 runs; the same program with a thread_local runtime reports none in 5 of 5. Any program that calls Client / http get/post from more than one task can hit it.
fix: b92145453b. runtime/src/lib.rs: `with_http_client_runtime` gives each calling thread its own current-thread runtime (thread_local, `shutdown_background` at thread exit so a thread ending inside another runtime's context cannot panic). Because a thread's runtime now runs only inside a request, `http_exchange_h1` / `http_exchange_h2` drop the request sender and await the spawned connection task (`http_close_conn`) before returning, so no connection is left detached with its socket open on an idle thread's runtime; without that, one TSan run of 16 hung at 300 s. MEASURED on http_cache, 4 workers: TSan 36 of 36 runs with no report and the expected output (was a report in 8 of 12); the plain mir-llvm build matches expected in 40 of 40. Full gate green.

title: B-2026-11-09-97's `karac fix` allocates: `opt != Some(TOKEN)` with `opt: Option[String]` and `TOKEN: Str` became `opt != Some(TOKEN.to_string())`; the review ruling (core-types.md, 8d86d26197) is `.as_deref()` on the owned side, which the library did not have
detail: Review-thread ruling 2026-11-10 on B-2026-11-09-97: no payload comparison across `Option[String]` / `Option[Str]` (comparison looks through each operand, not inside type arguments, design.md); the library gains Rust's `as_deref`, and -97's fix inserts `.as_deref()` on the owned operand instead of `Some(x.to_string())`, which allocates on every comparison. At 18c7e2b429 report_compare_mismatch (src/typechecker/expr_ops.rs, option_str_some_fix) rewrote the `Some` side. The `Option[Vec[T]]` form is its own row (B-2026-11-11-3).
fix: 67ebc5faa6: `impl Option[String] { fn as_deref(ref self) -> Option[Str] }` in runtime/stdlib/source/option.kara. report_compare_mismatch (src/typechecker/expr_ops.rs) now says comparison looks through each operand but not inside type arguments (design.md), and option_str_as_deref_fix replaces option_str_some_fix: `karac fix` inserts `.as_deref()` after the Option[String] operand (`h.as_deref() != Some(PURGE_TOKEN)`, `g.as_deref() == Some(lm)`) instead of writing `Some(x.to_string())`. Fixtures: tests/http_cache_diagnostics.rs an_option_string_against_some_of_a_str_constant_takes_as_deref; tests/option_as_deref.rs (`==` against a `Some` of a Str const, a `match` on string patterns, `unwrap_or`, `map`, both lanes). The Option[Vec[T]] form is B-2026-11-11-3.

title: `Option[Vec[T]].as_deref() -> Option[Slice[T]]` (library/core-types.md) is missing: 0.8 refuses a second specialized inherent impl that defines `as_deref` beside `Option[String]`'s, and the library has no trait that names a type's view
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-10 while landing B-2026-11-11-2. core-types.md (8d86d26197) lists `as_deref` on `Option[String] -> Option[Str]` and on `Option[Vec[T]] -> Option[Slice[T]]`. `impl Option[String] { fn as_deref .. }` lands; adding `impl[T] Option[Vec[T]] { fn as_deref(ref self) -> Option[Slice[T]] { .. } }` to runtime/stdlib/source/option.kara is refused, because two specialized inherent impls of one type may not define the same method name (0.8 has no method specialization). Ways out, each a design call for the review thread: method specialization on disjoint type arguments; a library-internal trait with an associated view type (`String -> Str`, `Vec[T] -> Slice[T]`) and one `impl[T: ..] Option[T] { fn as_deref }` (collections.md says there is no user-facing `Borrow`-like trait, so it would have to stay unnamed to users); or a differently named method for the vector form.
fix: 27a5b91f4b. `Option[Vec[T]].as_deref()` returns `Option[Slice[T]]`, as the review ruled (way 2). The library's `impl Option[String] { fn as_deref }` became `impl[T: DerefView] Option[T] { fn as_deref(ref self) -> Option[T.View] }` (runtime/stdlib/option.kara). `DerefView` is a library-internal trait with `type View` and `fn __view(ref self)`, implemented by String (View = Str) and Vec[T] (View = Slice[T]). The MIR builder normalizes `String.View` (`normalize_proj` HK::Str). `receiver_view` in src/mir/lower.rs makes `as_deref` and `__view` borrow their receiver, as core semantics §5.4 (amended by the review) says, so the view cannot outlive the vector or string. -97's mismatch fix also covers `Option[Vec[T]]` against `Some(<slice>)`. `as_deref` and `__view` are in the prune's ALWAYS_KEPT list, since the borrow rules name them. Pinned by tests/option_as_deref.rs: the Vec view on both backends, three escapes refused, a non-String/Vec Option refused, and the Vec/slice mismatch fix.

title: The MIR interpreter keeps a `SortedMap` / `SortedSet` as one sorted vector of values, so 100000 inserts of falling keys take 12.7 s under `__mir-run` against 0.32 s rising; the compiled backend moved to a B+-tree at c5303d91b3
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-11 on c5303d91b3 (release karac): `let mut m: SortedMap[i64, i64] = SortedMap.new(); while i < 100000 { m.insert(100000 - i, i); }` runs 12.7 s under `karac __mir-run`, the rising loop 0.32 s (about 40x). The remainder of B-2026-11-10-39, whose compiled fix (runtime/src/mir_map/tree.rs) runs the falling loop in 0.013 s. src/mir/interp.rs addresses a table's entries by index in one heap vector (`Addr { root: Root::Heap(id), path: [i] }`, `table_find` bisects `vec_elems`), so a sorted insert shifts every later value. collections.md promises O(log n) for every SortedMap/SortedSet operation; the interpreter is the reference for semantics, so this matters for programs run with `karac __mir-run` on large inputs (kata 2092's largest arm took 22 s there). Expected: inserts and removals near the front in O(log n) amortized, or the interpreter's complexity noted as exempt.
fix: 788a3150a6 (documentation, not a code change). The cost was measured on release karac at the 2026-11-11 tip: 100000 SortedMap inserts under `__mir-run` take 0.36 s with rising keys, 14.2 s falling and 6.7 s pseudo-random. The search is already a binary search; the cost is `Vec<Value>::insert` shifting every later entry. The interpreter addresses a table's entries by index (`get` and `index` return `Addr { root: Heap(id), path: [i, 1] }`, iteration and ranges work by slot), so O(log n) would need either an order-statistic Value variant or chunked entries, a change of several days to the reference lane's addressing. Who pays: `karac run` and `karac test` use the JIT by default; `karac repl`, comptime evaluation and `--interp` run on the interpreter. Corpus: all 459 programs that use SortedMap or SortedSet were timed on __mir-run. The slowest (65-120 s, already in bucket timeout) were sampled with gdb across all threads, 6 samples each, and none had a stack in the sorted-table insert, remove or bound paths, against 6 of 6 for the falling-insert control. Review ruling 2026-11-11 (overriding its own REPL condition on purpose): document rather than rebuild. collections.md now says the O(log n) bounds are compiled code's, and that `karac repl`, comptime evaluation and `--interp` keep a sorted array with O(n) inserts, citing design.md's principle 4 ("The MIR interpreter is not a performance target"). A REPL user's report reopens it as its own row.

title: `format!("'{}'", String::from_utf8_lossy(&payload))` (and `println!`) gets no f-string fix when an argument holds a `::` path: the refusal names the f-string, but `karac fix` leaves the call, so every Rust `format!` over `Type::func(..)` is hand-converted
detail: Porting mqtt_broker: `karac fix` rewrote every `format!`/`println!` but three whose arguments were `String::from_utf8_lossy(&payload)` (show, the retained dump) and a `collect::<..>()` chain. src/parser.rs `format_arg_fits_hole` refuses any `:` outside quotes, since a hole's `:` starts a format spec, so a `::` path argument has no rewrite. `format!("<{}>", f(&p))` is fixed; `format!("<{}>", String::from(p))` is not. Repro: `fn main() { let p: Vec[u8] = Vec.new(); let s = format!("<{}>", String::from(p)); println(s); }` then `karac fix`: 'Kāra has no macros; `format!(...)` is Rust syntax' and no edit. Remedy (hypothesis): treat `::` before an identifier as a path separator, written `.` in the hole, which the `::` fix does anywhere else; keep refusing a turbofish `::<`.
fix: FIXED by 2776b10314. src/parser.rs `format_arg_fits_hole` refused any `:` outside quotes, since a hole's `:` starts a format spec; a path's `::` between identifiers (`is_path_colons`) is now accepted and written as Kāra's `.` in the hole (`path_colons_as_dots`), so `format!("<{}>", String::from_utf8(v.clone()).unwrap_or(String::new()))` becomes `f"<{String.from_utf8(v.clone()).unwrap_or(String.new())}>"` and `println!("{} {}", s, i64::from(v[0]))` becomes `println(f"{s} {i64.from(v[0])}")`. A turbofish `::<` still has no hole form, and a `:` inside a quoted argument still refuses. Pinned by tests/format_fix_path_args.rs (the fixed program checks and runs).

title: `u16.from_be_bytes([a, b])` refuses its list-literal argument as a `Vec[u8]` ("expects an `Array[u8, 2]`, got `Vec[u8]`"), where Rust's `u16::from_be_bytes([a, b])` is the common form: the argument is not checked against the `Array[u8, N]` it must be
detail: Porting mqtt_broker's `Cursor.u16`: `u16::from_be_bytes([self.body[self.at], self.body[self.at + 1]])` after karac fix is refused at src/typechecker/method_identifier_receiver.rs's `from_*_bytes` arm (added by 6fe383ed8a for B-2026-11-10-45), which infers the argument with no expected type, so the literal takes its default `Vec`. An annotated `let b: Array[u8, 2] = [..]` is accepted. Remedy (hypothesis): check the argument against `Array[u8, N]` as an annotated `let` does. The app binds `let b: Array[u8, 2]` first.
fix: FIXED by 6008a2790e. The `from_*_bytes` arm of src/typechecker/method_identifier_receiver.rs checks a list-literal argument against `Array[u8, N]` with `check_expr`, as an annotated `let` does, so `u16.from_be_bytes([v[0], v[1]])` and `u32.from_le_bytes([1, 0, 0, 0])` are accepted and a literal of the wrong length gets "array literal has 3 element(s), expected 2". Pinned in tests/int_byte_order.rs on the interpreter and a compiled build. mqtt_broker's `Cursor.u16` now writes it inline.

title: `String.from_utf8_lossy(bytes)` does not exist ("no associated function 'from_utf8_lossy' on type 'String'"): text from a socket or a file with a bad byte can only be shown by `from_utf8(..).unwrap_or(..)`, which drops all of it
detail: Porting mqtt_broker: payloads and topics are shown with Rust's `String::from_utf8_lossy(&payload)`; strings.md § Building lists only `from_utf8 -> Result[String, Utf8Error]`. A log line, a protocol dump or a terminal printer of untrusted bytes wants each bad sequence replaced by U+FFFD and the rest kept. The app writes `String.from_utf8(payload).unwrap_or(String.new())` (same as socks5_proxy's -46 workaround), which is only right because its payloads are ASCII. Remedy (hypothesis): `fn from_utf8_lossy(bytes: Slice[u8]) -> String` on the interpreter and the runtime, documented in strings.md.
fix:
202af9c0be adds `String.from_utf8_lossy(bytes: Slice[u8]) -> String`, which is Rust's: each invalid sequence becomes U+FFFD. It borrows its bytes the way `from_utf8` does. The pieces are the typechecker signature in env_build.rs, the ownership mode, the lowering's lent argument, the interpreter native beside `from_utf8`, and a `karac_mir_str_from_utf8_lossy` runtime entry called from backend seq.rs. It is documented in library/strings.md with a CHANGELOG entry under Added.

Rust's `String::from_utf8_lossy(&b).into_owned()` also mends now. `into_owned` on a String names its twin, and `karac fix` renames it to `to_string()`, the same rename `to_owned` already had.

tests/mir_from_utf8_lossy.rs pins invalid bytes, a truncated sequence, an emoji, a `bytes()` round trip, empty input and the lent Vec's reuse on the interpreter, a built binary and ASan. It also pins the Rust template's mend loop.

title: `?` on a `TcpStream` read inside `fn read_packet(..) -> Result[Option[Packet], IoError]` is refused "cannot convert error 'NetError' to 'IoError': no `impl From[NetError] for IoError` in scope" with no fix, where the Rust author's `io::Result` meant the socket's error type
detail: Porting mqtt_broker: `fn read_packet(conn: &TcpStream) -> Result<Option<Packet>, IoError>` with `conn.read(&mut head)?` twice. Kāra's sockets return `NetError` (io.md § Networking), files `IoError`, and nothing converts one into the other; Rust has one `io::Error` for both. Every `?` gets the same refusal and no edit. Remedy (hypothesis): when every `?` in the function converts from one error type and the declared one has no `From` for it, offer the fix that writes that type in the return type, or say in the message that sockets fail with `NetError`. The app declares `NetError`.
fix: 8279013053. `impl From[NetError] for IoError` in the library (runtime/stdlib/source/net.kara; docs/library/io.md § Errors, review-approved, following the `From[VarError] for IoError` precedent), so `?` on a socket operation in a function that returns `IoError` converts as Rust's `io::Result` does. Same-named variants keep their name (`Interrupted`, `PermissionDenied`, `InvalidInput`, `UnexpectedEof`, `ProviderUnavailable`, `Unsupported`); every other variant becomes `IoError.Other(e.to_string())`, the error's display, so `NetError.Other(104)` becomes `Other("os error 104")` rather than the system's message for that code. Lowering: `user_from` skipped the whole lookup when it met a baked `From` impl whose item is in the def table but is not lowered (the `VarError` one) and reported "not lowered yet"; it now passes over such an entry and keeps looking. PIN: kara-katas 6c56195f, apps/service/mqtt_broker, whose `fn read_packet(..) -> Result[Option[Packet], IoError]` now uses `conn.read_exact(mut body)?` directly, as in the Rust draft (corpus/apps/service/mqtt_broker; matches mqtt_broker.py on __mir-run and __mir-llvm-run). tests/read_exact_io.rs `question_mark_converts_net_error_into_io_error` checks the conversion of a read, a timeout, an interrupt and an OS code on both backends.

title: `Option[String].as_deref()` does not exist ("no method 'as_deref' on type 'Option'"), so Rust's `proto.as_deref() != Some("MQTT")` has no Kāra spelling short of building a `String` to compare with
detail: Porting mqtt_broker's CONNECT check: `if proto.as_deref() != Some("MQTT") || level != Some(4)`. The app writes `proto != Some("MQTT".to_string())`, which allocates a String to compare. B-2026-11-09-97 (fixed) made the mismatch diagnostic for `Option[String] != Some(<Str>)` point somewhere; `as_deref` itself is still missing. Thread A mentioned `as_deref` in its queue on 11-10; this row records the app's instance.
fix: 67ebc5faa6. `Option[String].as_deref()` was on main before this row was filed (review ruling on B-2026-11-09-97; closed with B-2026-11-11-2). Measured 2026-11-11 on release karac at 3d987fca00's parent tree: `fn check(proto: Option[String], level: Option[i64]) -> bool { proto.as_deref() != Some("MQTT") or level != Some(4) }` checks clean, and `check(Some("MQTT".to_string()), Some(4))`, `check(None, Some(4))` print `false true`. The app's build predated the method. `Option[Vec[T]].as_deref` followed in 27a5b91f4b (B-2026-11-11-3).

title: Rust's `.scan(0, |depth, c| { let g = if c == '(' { *depth += 1; .. } else { *depth -= 1; .. }; Some(g) })` gets no fix: the rewrite to Kāra's `Some((state, item))` is withheld when the state is written below the closure body's own statements
fix: 3402c1954a: a scan closure writing its state below the body's own statements is rewritten with let mut depth = depth; and Some((depth, item)).

title: `.scan(0, ..)` collected into a `Vec[i32]` has no fix: the state's literal `0` takes the default `i64`, its items are computed from it, and the collect is refused with no edit, where the fix is `0i32`
detail: FOUND writing kata 1111: once its scan arm is rewritten to Kāra's `Some((depth, group))`, `.scan(0, ..).collect()` into the function's `Vec[i32]` result is refused as `i64` items for `i32` ones. The state's starting literal took the literal default (design.md §8 Literals) and the items are `depth % 2`. The collect-literal fix already writes a suffix on a `map` closure's literal; a `scan` whose starting value is an unsuffixed literal in the element type's range now takes the suffix on that literal. REPRO: `fn f(s: Str) -> Vec[i32] { s.chars().scan(0, |d, c| { let d = d + 1; Some((d, d % 2)) }).collect() }` -> error, no fix.
fix: 3402c1954a: a scan whose literal start feeds narrower items collected into a Vec[i32] gets the start's suffix, 0i32.

title: `match v.last() { Some(g) => 1 - g, None => 0 }` over a `Vec[i32]` is refused: the `None` arm's literal `0` takes `i64` against the `Some` arm's `ref i32`, though beside an owned `i32` the literal takes `i32`
detail: FOUND writing kata 1111's stack arm, which gives each `(` the group its enclosing pair does not: `let group = match open.last() { Some(g) => 1 - g, None => 0 };` over `open: Vec[i32]`. Variants with the arm being `g` itself (`Some(g) => g`, `if let Some(g) = e.last() { g } else { 0 }`) were refused as `ref i32` against `i64`. On the MIR pipeline a `ref` to a `Copy` number reads as the number (core-semantics.md §5.10), so the sibling literal should take `i32`, as it does beside an owned `i32`. REPRO: `let v: Vec[i32] = [4, 7]; let a = match v.last() { Some(g) => g, None => 0 }; let t: i32 = a;` -> mismatch.
fix: 3402c1954a: a literal arm beside an arm that is a ref to a number takes that number, as beside an owned one.

title: Rust's `Duration::from_millis(n)` / `from_secs(n)` get `no associated function` and no fix, where Kāra's are `Duration.ms(n)` / `Duration.secs(n)`; `from_micros` and the other sub-millisecond constructors are not told what Kāra has
detail: FOUND writing kata 1114 (Print in Order), whose polling arm sleeps between checks; Rust writes that sleep `thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(1))`. After the `::` fix, `Duration.from_millis(1)` is refused with `no associated function 'from_millis' on type 'Duration'` and no edit. `from_millis` and `from_secs` now become `ms` and `secs` (the arguments kept); `from_micros`, `from_nanos` and `from_secs_f64`/`f32` get a message naming the two constructors Kāra's millisecond `Duration` has (docs/library/time-random-env.md). REPRO: `sleep(Duration::from_millis(1));` -> after one fix round, error with no fix.
fix: 3402c1954a: Duration.from_millis / from_secs become Duration.ms / secs, their arguments kept; the sub-millisecond ones say what Kāra has.

title: Rust's `use std::sync::mpsc::{channel, Receiver, Sender};` with `Mutex<Sender<()>>` and `self.tx.lock().unwrap().send(())` leaves an import of a module that does not exist and four errors with no fix; `channel()` with no capacity is told only `expected 1 argument(s), found 0`
detail: FOUND writing kata 1114's Rust arm, two `std::sync::mpsc` channels behind `Mutex`es as Rust writes them. `karac fix` left `use std::sync::mpsc::..` (Kāra's prelude has `channel`, `Sender` and `Receiver`), `.unwrap()` on a `MutexGuard` (a Kāra lock is never poisoned; docs/library/concurrency.md), and a method of the guarded value called on the guard rather than through `.value`. Each now has its fix: the import goes when every name it brings is the prelude's, `.unwrap()` on a guard goes, and `g.send(x)` on a `MutexGuard[Sender[T]]` becomes `g.value.send(x)`. `channel()` has no machine fix, since no capacity can be picked for it, and now says that Kāra's channels are bounded and what `channel(n)` takes. REPRO: kata 1114's `print_in_order_rust.kara` at r0.
fix: 3402c1954a: use std::sync::mpsc::{..} goes (the prelude has the names), .unwrap() on a MutexGuard goes, a method of the guarded value is reached through .value, and channel() says it takes its capacity.

title: `sleep(Duration.ms(0))` never lets another task run: a task that waits on a flag with a zero sleep between reads spins forever on the MIR interpreter, on a one-worker native build, and on the pool once the spinners fill its workers, though core-semantics.md §11.1 names a sleep as a suspension point
fix: 1267e2aa72: Kata 1114's polling arm, and 1115's to 1117's, wait for their turn with a zero sleep between reads of an Atomic. core-semantics.md §11.1 names a sleep as a suspension point, but a pause that had already passed when first asked completed without parking, so the spinner kept its worker and, with as many spinners as workers, the task that sets the flag never ran. Both the interpreter's ready("sleep_ms") and karac_mir_ready_sleep now park once before reporting ready.

title: `Duration` has no unit below the millisecond: `Duration.ms(n)` and `Duration.secs(n)` build it and `as_ms()` reads it, so a pause or an elapsed time under 1 ms (Rust's `from_micros`, `as_micros`, `as_nanos`; Go's `time.Microsecond`) cannot be written or measured
detail: FOUND writing kata 1114, whose polling arm sleeps between checks of an `Atomic`. A Rust spin-wait backs off for microseconds (`Duration::from_micros(50)`); the nearest Kāra is `Duration.ms(0)`, no pause at all, or `Duration.ms(1)`, twenty times the pause. docs/library/time-random-env.md declares `ms`, `secs` and `as_ms` only, and `Instant`'s differences are `Duration`s, so `start.elapsed()` reads only whole milliseconds: timing a function that runs in microseconds, the first thing a benchmark or a latency metric needs, reads 0. Real-world uses: per-request latency histograms, spin-wait backoff, rate limiters at sub-ms granularity, profiling. Every mainstream library's span type carries nanoseconds (Rust `Duration`, Go `time.Duration`, Java `Duration`, C++ `std::chrono`). REPRO: no spelling for a 50 µs sleep; `Instant.now().elapsed().as_ms()` after a microsecond's work is 0.
fix:
86a48f366b adds the library half. `Duration.us(n)` and `Duration.ns(n)` build a span, and `as_us()`, `as_ns()` and `as_secs()` read one, all in runtime/stdlib/std_time.kara. `sleep(d)` parks through the drop schedule's `__sleep_ns` (c4748de3ff), so a 50 µs pause is a real pause instead of rounding down to `sleep_ms(0)`. It is documented in library/time-random-env.md, with a CHANGELOG entry under Added.

Rust's `Duration::from_micros` / `from_nanos` now mend to `us` / `ns`, which flips the kata 1114 pin `kata_1114_a_sub_millisecond_duration_mends_to_us`. `as_millis` / `as_micros` / `as_nanos` rename to `as_ms` / `as_us` / `as_ns` where the library's `Duration` is the receiver (method_mapset.rs); a program's own `Duration` keeps its plain "no method".

tests/duration_sub_millisecond.rs pins the builders, the readers and a 50 µs sleep that measures at least 50 µs. It runs on the interpreter, a built binary and ASan, plus the Rust template's mend loop.

Remainders have their own rows: Duration arithmetic is B-2026-11-11-72, and the `std::thread::sleep` mend is B-2026-11-11-73.

title: The prelude `Semaphore` does not wait under tasks: `acquire(timeout)` on an exhausted semaphore fails at once with `Timeout` though another task will `release` it, and `release` caps the count at the starting permits, so `Semaphore.new(0)` can never be released and cannot signal between tasks
fix: c47fd80f23 makes Semaphore.acquire a suspending native on both backends. In a task an exhausted acquire waits until another task's release frees a permit or its timeout passes; outside a task, where no task can release one, it waits the whole timeout, as Pool.acquire does (B-2026-10-21-44). The compiled __ready (karac_mir_ready_sem) takes the permit for the acquire after it, so another worker cannot take it in between (the race B-2026-11-11-47 records for Pool), and release bumps the executor's progress (mir_task::peer_progressed): without that, the executor napped to the waiter's 60 s deadline in 28 of 40 compiled runs of kata 1115's shape. DECIDED (the row's second half): release is uncapped, as Python's threading.Semaphore, POSIX sem_post and Tokio add_permits are, so Semaphore.new(0) signals; the legacy fixture test_semaphore_release_saturates_at_initial_budget is flipped (expected_from = decision). Pinned by corpus/design/ok_semaphore_waits_under_tasks (Python mirror): kata 1115's FooBar alternates in 200 of 200 random runs, a waiter is released by a later task, a waiter with no releaser times out, one permit and two releases give three acquires; passes on mir-interp, mir-llvm and mir-llvm-asan, and 0 of 60 compiled runs hang. docs/library/concurrency.md gains a Semaphore section. Gate green (all 11075, llvm 11267).

title: LeetCode's `class H2O` as `struct H2O` is refused as a Const-class name with `consider renaming to H2o` and no fix, though the rename is mechanical: the declaration, its `impl`, and every use in the file
detail: FOUND writing kata 1117 (Building H2O), whose statement names the class `H2O`. `struct H2O { .. } impl H2O { fn new() -> H2O { H2O { .. } } }` gets `H2O is Const-class but struct names must be Type-class (PascalCase); consider renaming to H2o` with `replacement: null`, so `karac fix` stops and every site is renamed by hand. Rust accepts `H2O` (its `non_camel_case_types` lint reads digits as word breaks), so a Rust solution carried over meets the error at once, as would any type named for an acronym (`IO`, `URL`, `HTTP`). Either the name is accepted or the rename is a fix over the file's uses of the name, which the resolver knows; the kata's arms are written `H2o` meanwhile. REPRO: the three-line struct above -> error, no fix.
fix: cc0bc927f2. No classifier change: by CN-1 and CN-4 `H2O` is Const class (all capitals and digits), so the refusal stands. The parser now attaches a machine-applicable fix to it: `offer_type_rename` (src/parser.rs) renames every non-raw identifier token naming a private struct or enum to the suggested Type-class name (`H2O` -> `H2o`), across the file, and withholds the fix when a string interpolation names it. `karac fix` turns LeetCode's `class H2O` port into a checking program. Pinned by tests/const_class_type_rename_fix.rs.

title: `String.from_iter(atoms.iter())` over a `Vec[char]` says `.cloned()` but offers no fix: the assoc-eq bound's fix reached only a method whose bound names its receiver, and a path call never recorded its arguments' ends
detail: FOUND writing kata 1117 (Building H2O), whose harness builds a string with `String.from_iter(atoms.iter())`. The error reads `associated-type bound I.Item = char is not satisfied; VecIter[char] has Item = ref char; .cloned() turns an iterator of ref T into one of T`, with no edit. The fix-it in src/typechecker/exprs.rs read the call's argument ends from `method_call_ends`, which only `infer_method_call` pushed, so a path call (`String.from_iter(..)`) found none, or an enclosing method call's. A plain call now pushes its arguments' ends too, and a function's own bound on its one argument puts `.cloned()` after it. REPRO: `let atoms: Vec[char] = ['H']; let s = String.from_iter(atoms.iter());` -> error, no fix.
fix: 3402c1954a: a plain call records its arguments' ends, so String.from_iter(v.iter()) over ref items gets .cloned().

title: `g.value = Molecule { .. }` on a `MutexGuard` is asked for `let mut g` and then writes through the guard, where plain `=` on a `mut ref` local is refused with the `*r = v` fix (design.md § Auto-deref)
detail: FOUND writing kata 1117, whose polling arm resets the molecule under its lock with `let g = m.lock(); g.value = Molecule { hydrogens: 0, oxygens: 0, out: 0 };`. `karac fix` turned `let g` into `let mut g`, after which the assignment wrote through the guard's `mut ref` field. design.md § Auto-deref: plain `=` does not write through a `mut ref`; a local's `r = v` gets the `*r = v` fix. The field now gets the same refusal and the fix `*g.value = v`, and `let g` stays. REPRO: the two lines above -> `let mut g` suggested, then accepted.
fix: 3402c1954a: g.value = v on a guard's mut ref field is refused with the *g.value = v fix, as a mut ref local's is, and asks for no let mut.

title: An `if` or `match` of unsuffixed literals as an element of a list or tuple literal is typed `i64` at once: `let v: Vec[i32] = [1, if b { 2 } else { 3 }];` and `let t: (i32, i32) = (1, if b { 2 } else { 3 });` are refused as a narrowing, with no fix
detail: FOUND writing kata 1118 (Number of Days in a Month), whose cumul arm lists the months' lengths as `[31, if leap { 29 } else { 28 }, 31, 30, ..]`. The bare literals of a list or tuple stay open until a use fixes them (B-2026-11-10-40), and a `let` bound to an `if` of literals does too (B-2026-11-10-49), but an `if` or `match` of literals one level down, as an element, is typed `i64` as it is met, so the list's annotation or its use as `Vec[i32]` meets an `i64` and is refused: `implicit coercion from 'i64' to 'i32' would narrow or change sign`, with no edit. design.md §8 Literals: a literal takes its type from its use. REPROS (each `fn main` alone): `let b = true; let v: Vec[i32] = [1, if b { 2 } else { 3 }];`; `let b = true; let v: Vec[i32] = [if b { 2 } else { 3 }];`; the same with `match b { true => 2, false => 3 }`; `let t: (i32, i32) = (1, if b { 2 } else { 3 });`. All refused on dde373791d, which has -40 and -49.
fix: 3b45dc0f0e. An `if`, `match` or block whose every branch is an unsuffixed literal is a literal (design.md §8, "a join of literals is a literal"), so as an element of a list or tuple literal it now takes its slot's type instead of settling to `i64` first. `check_literal_join_element` (src/typechecker/exprs.rs) checks such an element against its slot's numeric type, peeling a reference; it runs first in the scalar-collection element loop and at the top of `check_tuple_literal_element`. `let v: Vec[i32] = [1, if b { 2 } else { 3 }]` and the tuple form now check as written. Pinned by tests/literal_join_element.rs.

title: `String` has no `retain`: `s.retain(|c| c != ' ')`, Rust's `String::retain`, is refused as `no method 'retain' on type 'String'` though `Vec`, `VecDeque`, `Map` and `Set` have it
detail: FOUND writing kata 1119 (Remove Vowels from a String), whose retain arm copies the text and drops its vowels in place with `out.retain(|c| not is_vowel(c))`, as Rust's `String::retain` does. docs/library/strings.md lists no `retain`; the collections all have one. Added to `impl String` in runtime/stdlib/source/collections.kara: the kept chars in order, the predicate a `MutFn(char) -> bool` as Rust's `FnMut`. REPRO: `let mut s = "abc".to_string(); s.retain(|c| c != 'b');` -> no method.
fix: 3c79788215: Kata 1119's retain arm drops a text's vowels in place with out.retain(|c| ..). Vec, VecDeque, Map and Set had retain; String did not. It keeps the chars the predicate accepts, in order.

title: Rust's `let n = n.borrow();` in an `Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>` walk becomes `let n = n;` when the `RefCell` goes: a binding that only renames, left in the fixed text
detail: FOUND writing kata 1120 (Maximum Average Subtree), whose solution arm is LeetCode's Rust: `Some(n) => { let n = n.borrow(); let (ls, lc) = dfs(&n.left, ans); .. }`. The Rc/RefCell rewrite (src/parser/rust_rc.rs) drops each `.borrow()` and `.borrow_mut()`, which leaves `let n = n;`. It now drops a `let [mut] X = X.borrow[_mut]();` whole, with its line when it stands alone. REPRO: tests/fix_rust_rc_refcell.rs's tree template with that statement -> `let n = n;` after fix.
fix: c80adee665: Kata 1120's solution arm is LeetCode's Rust, with let n = n.borrow(); in its walk. Dropping .borrow() left let n = n;, a binding that only renames. The statement now goes, and its line when it stands alone.

title: A `chain` of literal lists collected into a `Vec[i32]` is refused with no fix: `let v: Vec[i32] = [0].into_iter().chain([1, 2].into_iter()).collect();` says `C: FromIterator[i64]`, and a `scan` over literals chained after a literal head gets a fix for neither literal
detail: FOUND writing kata 1118, whose cumul arm takes the days before each month as a running total: `let starts: Vec[i32] = [0].into_iter().chain(lengths.iter().scan(0, |total, d| { let total = total + d; Some((total, total)) })).collect();`. The collect wants `i32` items; the head `[0]`, the lengths and the scan's state are all unsuffixed literals, and every item is computed from them, but the items are read as `i64`: `trait bound C: FromIterator[i64] is not satisfied; Vec[i32] implements FromIterator[i32]`, no edit. A `map` over a literal list into `Vec[i32]` is accepted, and a `scan` over one alone gets the `0i32` fix, so the gap is the `chain`: B-2026-11-08-86 pairs the open literals of the two sides of `(0..3).chain(b.iter())` with each other, but the pair is not then fixed by the collect. Suffixing one literal by hand moves the error rather than clearing it (`scan(0i32, ..)` alone: the closure's `(i64, i64)` against `(i32, OutV)`; `[0i32]` alone: `J.Item = i32` against the scan's `i64`). REPRO: the one-line `chain` above in `fn main`. Refused on dde373791d.
fix: a65b4dc882, narrowed by c84408b911. A list literal that is the receiver of `into_iter` is inferred with its elements open (`open_collection_let`), so its literals stay open through `chain` and `collect` and take the collected `Vec[i32]`'s element type, as at a generic `T` the call returns (e564bd2acc). c84408b911 limits the open receiver to `into_iter`: an open `iter()` receiver yields `ref` items, which broke mir_library's `sorted_table_bounds_and_ranges`. `discharge_deferred_call_bounds` now refuses a FromIterator item that settled to a concrete mismatch instead of skipping it (`unify_types(i64, i32)` was true), which closes a pre-existing miscompile: a `scan` inside a chain built a `Vec[i32]` from `i64` items. `collect_literal_fix` recurses through both `chain` sides to offer the `0i32` fix. Pinned by tests/literal_list_chain_collect.rs. The remainder, a `scan` state literal that settles to `i64` before the `collect` (kata 1118's Rust shape), is B-2026-11-11-61.

title: On Linux the runtime's per-thread small-chunk lists start only with the auto-par worker pool, and small_realloc bypasses them, so a sequential program's free bursts overflow glibc's seven-deep tcache into the fast bins: lists from the start cost 0.993x the instructions over 120 benches (0.795x on kata 57's bench)
detail: MEASURED at 3305966202 (x86 callgrind Ir, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0, KARAC_HASH_SEED=1) while closing B-2026-11-09-51. An experiment archive that starts runtime/src/alloc.rs `small` lists before main and routes small_realloc's malloc and free through them on Linux (as macOS already does), against the same tree's lean archive, over 120 random frozen-set benches under 0.3 s: geomean 0.9929, best 0.795 (kata 57 insert_interval), 0.835 (strobogrammatic_count), 0.864, 0.884, 0.924; worst 1.022, one above 1.02; outputs identical. Kata 1087's bench: 13.65G -> 13.78G (+0.9%). The lists keep up to 64 chunks a size class against tcache's 7, so a burst of frees (a collection of strings at the end of a scope) stays out of the fast bins, whose chunks `malloc_consolidate` walks when a later free merges into the top chunk.
fix: ba5b881217 starts the lists in karac_mir_run_main on Linux (glibc), still off under a sanitizer or KARAC_ALLOC_CACHE=0, reads that variable through libc getenv so the start links no std::env path, and drops small_realloc's macOS-only cfgs so both halves of a small resize go through the lists. Pinned by the runtime test a_small_resize_keeps_the_old_chunk_on_the_lists (fails without the fix: the old chunk is not on the list). Gate green (all 11060, llvm 11251). Wall, 7 runs each: the B-2026-08-20-9 auto-par probe 0.019-0.026 s -> 0.010-0.011 s; its sequential build 0.040-0.051 s -> 0.030-0.036 s. Instruction counts are the detail's (same change as the experiment archive). Binaries grow by 4 KiB (the sanitizer probe now links in every program). macOS keeps its lists starting with the pool: not measured there.
