57c72847ab: Kata 1121 writes longest * (k as i64) <= nums.len() with k an i32. The cast widens implicitly there, and the lossless_cast fix deleted only the ` as i64`, leaving longest * (k). The parser now records a cast written in parentheses of its own, with the operand's text, and the fix replaces the parentheses and the cast with the operand when it is a single term. A parenthesized operand, ((a - b) as i64), keeps its own, and a call's parentheses, f(k as i64), are not the cast's.
title: The `lossless_cast` fix (W0291) deletes only ` as i64` from a cast written in parentheses of its own and leaves the parentheses: `longest * (k as i64) <= nums.len()`, with `k: i32`, becomes `longest * (k) <= nums.len()`, a single name in parentheses.
detail: Kata 1121 (Divide Array Into Increasing Sequences) compares a run's length times `k` with the array's length in four arms: `longest * (k as i64) <= nums.len()` and `nums.len() / (k as i64)`. An i32 widens implicitly in a binary op with an i64, so W0291 fires, and `karac fix` applied a FixIt whose span is ` as i64` alone. The program still checks clean and runs, but the text it leaves, `(k)`, is not what anyone writes. The cast's parentheses belong to the cast when nothing else claims them: a parenthesized operand `((a - b) as i64)` keeps its own pair, and a call's `twice(k as i64)` parentheses are the call's.

title: `karac fix` turns Rust's `pkt[2..].split(|&b| b == 0).collect()` into `.split(..).iter().collect()`, which the next check refuses with E0516: the `.iter()` lends from the `Vec` that `split` returns, a temporary dropped at the end of the statement
detail: Porting tftp_server's `parse_request`: `let parts: Vec<&[u8]> = pkt[2..].split(|&b| b == 0).collect();`. Kāra's `Slice.split` returns `Vec[Slice[T]]` (collections.md), so `collect` on it is refused "no method 'collect' on type 'Vec': iterator adaptors/terminals require an explicit `.iter()`" with a machine fix that inserts `.iter()` (B-2026-10-29-3's `iter_hint_fix`, src/typechecker/method_user_impl.rs). On a call's result that fix produces `let parts: Vec[Slice[u8]] = pkt[2..].split(|b| b == 0).iter().collect();`, refused with E0516 "cannot drop the temporary value of the expression ... while `parts` still borrows it": the fix loop ends on a program that does not check. `.into_iter()` hands the slices over and checks and runs on interp, llvm and asan. Remedy (hypothesis): insert `.into_iter()` when the `Vec` receiver is a call's result, keep `.iter()` for a place; a `Slice` receiver (`s.bytes()`) keeps `.iter()`.
fix: FIXED by a193908f55. The iterator-surface hint on a Vec/VecDeque receiver that is a call (`pkt[..].split(p).collect()`, `s.to_vec().map(..)`, `mk().map(..)`) now names and inserts `.into_iter()`, which hands the returned collection's items over, instead of `.iter()`, which lent from the temporary the statement drops and was refused with E0516. A place, a Slice and an Array keep `.iter()` (an Array's into_iter on a temporary is not lowered in MIR yet). Pinned by tests/iter_hint_temporary.rs (check names the hop, two `karac fix` passes, then __mir-run prints "3 2 3 6"); tests/typechecker.rs's iterator_methods_on_a_slice_name_the_iter_hop and tests/mend_iter_surface.rs's windows_find cell flip to into_iter. kara-katas apps/service/tftp_server's `.split(..).into_iter().collect()` is now karac fix's own output.

title: A compiled `Pool.acquire` can stall for its whole timeout though a value is free: its `__ready` (karac_mir_ready_pool) sees the pool free and lets the task through, another worker takes the value before the `acquire` runs, and `karac_mir_pool_full`, finding no verdict, sleeps the worker thread for the timeout (2 of 20 runs of two tasks trading one value with a 60 s timeout)
detail: MEASURED at af8a457139 plus the B-2026-11-11-34 change (c47fd80f23) (x86, 4 workers): two tasks in one TaskGroup each loop 100 times over `pool.acquire(Duration.ms(60000))` on a `Pool.new(|| conn(1), 1, 4)`, holding the loan across a `sleep_ms(0)`. 2 of 20 compiled runs (6 of 60 in a second batch) did not finish in 10 s; gdb on a stuck one shows the first worker in `clock_nanosleep` under `karac_mir_pool_full`, under `karac_mir_task_run`, and the other workers napping. The interpreter (one task at a time) finishes every run. The readiness and the acquire are two calls with no hold between them: ready_pool answers `free` without reserving anything, so on a multi-worker executor another task's acquire can take the idle value or the last room in between, and the losing acquire falls to the full branch, whose outside-a-task fallback (`std::thread::sleep(timeout)`) runs inside a task. B-2026-11-11-34's `Semaphore` avoids the same race by having its `__ready` take the permit for the `acquire` after it (`SEM_TAKEN`). Probe: project-files patches/pool_race_probe.kara. Pool returns and closes also do not bump the executor's progress count (`peer_progressed`, added by B-2026-11-11-34 for `release`), so a waiting acquire may only be re-polled at its deadline; not separately measured.
fix: 30b8a505a3 makes Pool.acquire a may-be-not-ready native (src/mir/coroutine.rs): in a task with no verdict, karac_mir_pool_full answers __io_again and the readiness loop asks __ready again, so an acquire that lost the value or room to another worker waits again instead of sleeping its worker for the timeout; outside a task nothing changes. pool_count(0) now counts the value it grants room for and a factory's Err gives it back, so two acquires that both saw room cannot both mint past max (found by reading, not measured). A loan given back, an eviction and a close bump the executor's progress (mir_task::peer_progressed, from B-2026-11-11-34), so a waiting acquire is polled again rather than napping to its deadline. The detail's repro: 8 of 80 runs stalled before; 0 of 200 after. tests/mir_pool_race.rs runs it 40 times with a 10 s cap (about 98% likely to catch a 1-in-10 stall). A lost race restarts the waiter's deadline from its timeout. Gate green (all 11083, llvm 11277). CHANGELOG line under 0.8.2.

title: A tuple, array, `Vec`, `Option` or derived-`Ord` struct holding a value with a hand-written `Ord` sorts and keys sorted tables by its parts' plain order, ignoring that `Ord`: `v.sort_by_key(|x| (Down { v: x }, 0))` under a descending `Down` sorts ascending, on the MIR interpreter and compiled builds alike
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-11 on 879d428d9d plus the std.cmp.Reverse library change (release karac, --features llvm), found while implementing B-2026-11-10-41. With `struct Down { v: i64 }` whose `Ord.cmp` is `other.v.cmp(self.v)`: `a.sort_by_key(|x| Down { v: x })` gives [3, 2, 1], but `b.sort_by_key(|x| (Down { v: x }, 0))` gives [1, 2, 3] on __mir-run and __mir-llvm-run, while `c.sort_by(|x, y| (Down { v: x }, 0).cmp((Down { v: y }, 0)))` and `max_by_key` with the same tuple key are right. With `Reverse` the same: `sort()` of `[(Reverse { value: 1 }, 2), (Reverse { value: 3 }, 1), (Reverse { value: 1 }, 1)]` gave 1/1 1/2 3/1, a `SortedMap[(Reverse[i64], i64), _]` iterated 1 2 3, and `sort()` of `[Some(Reverse { value: 1 }), None, Some(Reverse { value: 3 })]`, of arrays and Vecs of Reverse and of a `#[derive(Ord)] struct Row { r: Reverse[i64], n: i64 }` all came out ascending. Cause, three places: the interpreter's sorts and sorted-table searches (`order_forms`, `sort_by_key`, `sort`, `insert_at`, `sorted_bound`, `table_find`, `binary_search`) asked only whether the key type itself has a user `cmp` (B-2026-10-06-109) and otherwise compared key forms field by field; the compiled key glue's structural `cmp` (src/backend/mir/key.rs `cmp_call`) recursed into parts with the structural op, never the part's own `cmp` body; and `queue_user_cmp` (src/mir/lower.rs) queued only the key type's own `Ord.cmp`, so a part's body was not even built unless something else called it.
fix:
3d987fca00. A part with its own `cmp` now orders what holds it, as the derived `cmp` does, in three places.
- Interpreter: `ord_of(ty, a, b)` calls the user `cmp`, or compares tuples, arrays, Vecs, slices and enum/struct fields part by part where `has_user_cmp` finds one inside. `Option` puts None first. Every site that asked only `user_cmp(key_ty)` now routes through it: `sort`, `sort_by_key`, `is_sorted`, `binary_search`, `order_forms`, and the sorted table's `insert_at`, `sorted_bound` and `table_find`.
- Compiled backend: `cmp_call` in src/backend/mir/key.rs turns the structural op into the part's own body (KeyOp::User) where `user_cmp_body` finds one.
- MIR builder: `queue_user_cmp` walks the key type's parts and builds each part's `Ord.cmp`, which nothing else may call.
Pinned on __mir-run, __mir-llvm-run and __mir-llvm-asan by tests/std_cmp_reverse.rs: `a_hand_written_ord_orders_the_tuple_array_vec_option_and_struct_holding_it` and `a_reversed_part_orders_the_tuple_key_it_is_in`. Both printed ascending orders before the fix.

title: A `scan` whose state starts at an unsuffixed literal settles the state to `i64` before the `collect` that would fix it, so kata 1118's Rust shape `[0].into_iter().chain(lengths.iter().scan(0, |total, d| { let total = total + d; Some((total, total)) })).collect()` into `Vec[i32]` (with `let lengths = [31, 28, ..]`) is refused, and its `0i32` fix moves the error to `total + d` (the remainder of B-2026-11-11-41)
detail: MEASURED 2026-11-11 on kara c84408b911 (release, --features llvm). B-2026-11-11-41's fix (a65b4dc882, c84408b911) keeps a list literal iterated with `into_iter` open for the chain's end to fix, so `[0].into_iter().chain([1, 2].into_iter()).collect()` into `Vec[i32]` checks. With a `scan` on one side the `scan`'s state literal `0` has settled to `i64` by the time the `FromIterator` bound is discharged, so the bound is refused (before a65b4dc882 it was skipped and the program built a `Vec[i32]` from `i64` items: garbage compiled, an AddressSanitizer abort). The refusal offers `0i32` (now also through a `chain`), but with `lengths` a literal `let` the closure's `total + d` then keeps `d`'s literal at the default beside the `i32` state (design.md §8: beside a type that widens into the default a literal keeps `i64`), and the closure is refused as returning `Option[(i64, i64)]` where `Option[(i32, _)]` is wanted, with no fix. The plain `lengths.iter().scan(0, ..).collect()` into `Vec[i32]` behaves the same. Wanted: the state literal stays open through `scan` as a literal at a generic parameter does when the call's result carries it (design.md §8, e564bd2acc, for a `T` the call returns), so the `collect` fixes state, items and `lengths` together; or, failing that, a refusal at the closure that names `lengths` and offers its annotation. May need a ruling: the §8 rule speaks of a call that returns `T`, and `scan` returns `IterScan[I, S, F, OutV]`. REPRO: `fn main() { let lengths = [31, 28, 31]; let starts: Vec[i32] = [0].into_iter().chain(lengths.iter().scan(0, |total, d| { let total = total + d; Some((total, total)) })).collect(); println(starts); }`.
fix: e036c0dfdd. Under the review thread's ruling (design.md §8 Literals, b320dcc291), a literal at a generic parameter stays open when the call's result carries that parameter as a type argument, not only when the call returns it. `check_call_args_with_substitution_full` (src/typechecker/exprs.rs) opens such a literal (`result_carries_param`: `T` itself, or `T` among the result's arguments, as in the `IterScan[I, S, F, OutV]` a `scan` returns) and holds it open (`held_open_literals`) while the call's other arguments, its closure, are checked. A plain read of a held literal no longer settles it to `i64`, and `check_assignable` accepts it against a slot that still names the callee's other parameters (`Option[(StateV, OutV)]`). A method called on it (`m.max(x)`) still decides it, as before. Kata 1118's Rust shape `[0].into_iter().chain(lengths.iter().scan(0, ..)).collect()` into `Vec[i32]`, and the plain `lengths.iter().scan(0, ..)` form, now check and run as written (interp and compiled, ASan clean). Beside items of an already fixed type (`lengths: Vec[i32]`), the state keeps the default by the operator rule and keeps its `0i32` fix. Pinned by tests/scan_state_literal_open.rs. Flipped pins: tests/literal_list_chain_collect.rs (the scan-in-chain refusal now runs) and two in tests/kata_1111_scan_nested_write_fix.rs (no `0i32` is needed).

title: `self` in a generic impl (`impl[R] Wrap[R]`) is typed `Wrap` with no arguments, so handing it to `fn helper[R](w: ref Wrap[R])` is refused "expected 'Wrap[R]', found 'Wrap'", and inside a library generic impl over a baked type (`impl[R] BufReader[R]`) a call of the type's native method on `self` gets no callee
detail: Found adding BufReader.read_exact (B-2026-11-10-44). Repro: `struct Wrap[R] { x: Option[R] }  impl[R] Wrap[R] { fn tag(ref self) -> i64 { 1 }  fn twice(ref self) -> i64 { helper(self) + self.tag() } }  fn helper[R](w: ref Wrap[R]) -> i64 { w.tag() }  fn main() { let w: Wrap[i64] = Wrap { x: None }; println(f"{w.twice()}"); }` fails `typecheck: 5:40: expected 'Wrap[R]', found 'Wrap'` on `karac __mir-run` and check alike, with a phantom `struct Wrap[=R] { }` too; `helper[R](self)` gets past the checker and the MIR builder then refuses `a type that failed to check`. Cause (read, not bisected): check_impl_block_inner (src/typechecker/items.rs, the `self_type` block) deliberately erases a struct/enum/generic target to `Named { name, args: [] }` (its comment says consumers rely on that shape), so `self` never carries the impl's parameters. The second face: runtime/stdlib/source/read_exact.kara with `impl[R] BufReader[R] { fn read_exact(ref self, buf: mut Slice[u8]) -> .. { .. self.read(mut buf[done..]) .. } }` checks, but the MIR builder fails `in BufReader[File].read_exact: the method call .read with no resolved callee is not lowered yet`; a free generic `fn f[R](r: ref BufReader[R], ..) { r.read(..) }` in a program works. This blocks BufReader.read_exact (B-2026-11-11-63).
fix: d763f8b1fa. Both faces were one cause: `check_impl_block_inner` types `self` of a generic `impl[R] Wrap[R]` by the bare name `Wrap`, which carries no arguments. `impl_self_with_args` (src/typechecker/exprs.rs) gives back the impl's full target `Wrap[R]` (through a `ref` or `mut ref`), from `current_impl_target`. Two places use it. A generic call's argument types: `helper(self)` with `fn helper[R](w: ref Wrap[R])` now solves the callee's `R` to the impl's, and so do `mut ref` helpers and helpers whose parameters have other names. A method's receiver in `dispatch_user_impl_method` (src/typechecker/method_user_impl.rs): the callee's `R` is recorded as the caller's, so the typed HIR resolves `self.read(..)` in a library `impl[R] BufReader[R]` instead of refusing it as `UnsolvedParam("R")`, which the MIR builder reported as "the method call `.read` with no resolved callee". The erased shape everywhere else is unchanged. Pinned by tests/generic_impl_self_args.rs: the row's repro, and a two-parameter impl at two instances, in run and interp. The library face was checked with a scratch `impl[R] BufReader[R] { fn read_exact .. self.read(mut buf[done..]) .. }` appended to read_exact.kara: interp, build and ASan read 5 bytes and then reported `UnexpectedEof`. That scratch is not committed. It is C's B-2026-11-11-63, and the source is at /mnt/attach/project-files/thread-b/bufreader-read-exact-scratch.kara.

title: `BufReader` has no `read_exact` (the remainder of B-2026-11-10-44): the sockets, `File` and the child pipes have it, but a library `impl[R] BufReader[R]` cannot call the native `read` on `self` (B-2026-11-11-62)
detail: B-2026-11-10-44 added read_exact to TcpStream, TlsStream, File, ChildStdout and ChildStderr as Kāra over each type's `read` (net.kara, process.kara, read_exact.kara), and io.md names those five. The approved io.md text also put it on BufReader, whose own methods are natives (runtime/stdlib/bufreader.kara). Written the same way in an appended source it fails at the MIR builder (B-2026-11-11-62); routed through a free generic helper `__buf_read_exact[R](self, ..)` it fails the checker `expected 'BufReader[R]', found 'BufReader'`. Two ways on: fix B-2026-11-11-62 and use the Kāra loop, or make `BufReader.read_exact` a native beside `read` (interp `Buf::Reader` arm with `std::io::Read::read_exact` mapping ErrorKind::UnexpectedEof, backend `buf_native` op, runtime, effects.rs and coroutine.rs entries, and a socket-backed buffer's wait that needs N bytes rather than some). Until then `r.read_exact(..)` on a BufReader fails "no method 'read_exact'". Pin to flip: add `BufReader` to tests/read_exact_io.rs and io.md's list.
fix: a267acdbe9: `BufReader.read_exact(buf)` is a baked library method (runtime/stdlib/source/bufreader_read_exact.kara, selected by the word `read_exact` with `BufReader` as its owner). It loops on the reader's own `read`, so it takes the bytes the buffer holds first and then reads what it wraps; `Ok(0)` before the slice is full is `IoError.UnexpectedEof`, `Interrupted` retries, and any other error returns. Over a socket the typechecker types the receiver `BufReader[TcpStream]`, and the effect checker's network seed list now names `BufReader[TcpStream].read_exact`, so a caller's inferred effects keep `receives(Network)` and `blocks` (without the seed they lost both). Pinned by tests/read_exact_io.rs: `bufreader_read_exact_over_a_file_a_socket_and_a_pipe` (a file through a 4-byte buffer, a socket on the main task and in a spawned task, a child's stdout; the short reads report end of file) on the interpreter, and `bufreader_read_exact_over_a_socket_has_the_socket_effects` (`karac query effects`). Clean under `__mir-llvm-asan`, and a read that suspends inside its task at KARAC_THREADS=1 works on both backends. io.md's BufReader table and "Reading an exact count" paragraph, and the CHANGELOG's 0.8.2 entry, name it.

title: A method on a const (`NAME.as_bytes()`, `CODES.map(..).sum()`) gets no fix-it, or one in the wrong place: the path call it parses as becomes a method call whose receiver and `)` both carry the whole call's span
detail: An uppercase receiver parses as a path call, `Call(Path([NAME, method]))`, and `infer_call` routes a value-binding first segment through `infer_method_call` with a synthesized receiver whose span is the callee's (the whole call) and with the call's span standing in for the close-paren span. Fix-its placed from those spans miss. `const NAME: Str`; `NAME.as_bytes()` is refused with a bare "no method 'as_bytes' on type 'Str'", without the `.bytes()` hint or fix a `let` receiver gets, because the fix's offset (`)` minus the method name) is not past the receiver's start. `const CODES: Array[i64, 3]`; `CODES.map(|x| x * 2).sum()` gets the `.iter()` hint, and `karac fix` writes `CODES.map(|x| x * 2).iter().sum()`, inserting at the receiver's end, which is the call's end. Found porting kara-katas apps/service/stun_server (`SOFTWARE_NAME.as_bytes()`).
fix: FIXED by 4e2cef2b9b. `Span::path_call_parts` (src/token.rs) gives a path-parsed method call (`NAME.method(..)` on a value binding) its receiver's span, the first segment's `NAME.len()` bytes from the call's start, and its `)`, the call span's last byte. `infer_call` (src/typechecker/expr_call.rs) passes both to `infer_method_call`, and lowering's `rewrite_path_call_to_method_call` (src/lowering.rs) builds the MethodCall with the same two spans, so a stash keyed on the close paren (a const integer's `count_ones` width) is found where it was recorded. `NAME.as_bytes()` now gets the `.bytes()` hint and fix, also split over lines, and `CODES.map(..).sum()` is fixed to `CODES.iter().map(..).sum()`. A 3+-segment receiver (`CFG.field.method()`) keeps the call's span for its field node, since whitespace makes the field's extent unknowable from the call span alone. Pinned by tests/path_call_receiver_fix.rs (check names the hint, fix, then __mir-run prints "4 12 4 3 3").

title: `concat` of a sequence of `Vec`s is not Rust's flatten: on a `Slice[Vec[u8]]` it is refused with a `T: Display` bound, and on a `Vec[Vec[u8]]` it is the elements' Display text, a `String` ("[1, 2][3]")
detail: Rust's `[Vec<T>]::concat()` returns the `Vec<T>` of every element's items in order (`[S]::concat` for `S: Borrow<[T]>`), and a ported STUN message builder writes `let body: Vec<u8> = attrs.concat();` over `attrs: &[Vec<u8>]`. In Kāra `concat` is only the library's `impl[T: Display] Slice[T]` text join (runtime/stdlib/source/collections.kara: `self.join("")`). On a `Slice[Vec[u8]]` parameter, check refuses it: "method 'concat' is not callable on this `Slice`: trait bound `T: Display` is not satisfied; `Vec[u8]` does not implement `Display`", though a `Vec[u8]` prints in an f-string. On a `Vec[Vec[u8]]` it is accepted (lowering routes a `Vec` receiver's `concat` to the same library method without the bound) and `println(f"{vv.concat()}")` prints `[1, 2][3]`, so `let flat: Vec[u8] = vv.concat()` is a type mismatch rather than the flattened bytes. The Slice and Vec receivers disagree on whether the call is legal at all, and neither gives the flatten a Rust port means. Either `concat` of a sequence of sequences flattens (as Rust's does), or the refusal names the flatten spelling (`v.iter().flat_map(..)` / a loop of `extend_from_slice`). Workaround in kara-katas apps/service/stun_server: a loop of `extend_from_slice`.
fix: FIXED by cbf2b8ae4b. Per the review thread's ruling (eaae42ef07, design.md § Vec): `concat()` on a `Vec[Vec[T]]` or `Slice[Vec[T]]` flattens, giving the `Vec[T]` of every element's items in order, as Rust's does. src/typechecker/method_concat.rs `try_concat_of_sequences` types the call (hooked in expr_method_call.rs after the dyn receiver), and src/mir/lower.rs `concat_of_vecs` calls the library's new free functions `vec_concat_vecs` (ref Vec[Vec[T]]) / `slice_concat_vecs` (Slice[Vec[T]]) in runtime/stdlib/source/collections.kara, named in LIBRARY_NAMES_THE_COMPILER_USES. A sequence of `String`/`Str` keeps the text join; a program's own trait impl on Vec/Slice defining `concat` is left alone. On other `Display` elements the 0.8.0 join now warns `deprecated` with a machine-applicable fix to `join("")`; the next minor release makes it an error, tracked as B-2026-11-11-81. CHANGELOG 0.8.2 (Added, Deprecated) and a `concat` row in docs/library/collections.md. mini_parsy's 27 `.concat()` calls are its own `Parser.concat` method, unaffected. stun_server's hand loop of `extend_from_slice` went back to the Rust draft's `attrs.concat()` (corpus re-extracted; 8 of 8 lanes pass at KARAC_THREADS=1 and 4). Pinned by tests/concat_flattens.rs (flatten on Vec and Slice receivers incl. Vec[String] items and an empty sequence; deprecation + `karac fix` + unchanged output; `#[allow(deprecated)]`). Full gate green before the rebase (test --all, llvm leg 11324 passed 0 failed, both clippy legs).

f6489288db: Kata 1122 sorts by match place.get(x) { Some(i) => (0, i), None => (1, x as i64) }, with i a ref i64. A ref to a Copy value beside the value joins at the value (core semantics 5.10), but two tuples were compared whole, so the arms were refused as (i64, ref i64) against (i64, i64). join_branch_types now joins two tuples element by element when their elements differ in being a ref. A tuple literal already builds at its slot's types; a tuple made elsewhere and stored into the joined slot is now made at its own type and each referenced element read into the slot. A ref String beside a String is still refused.
title: Two tuple match arms, one holding a `ref` to a `Copy` value and the other the value, are refused: `match place.get(x) { Some(i) => (0, i), None => (1, x as i64) }`, with `i: ref i64`, reports "match arms have incompatible types: '(i64, ref i64)' and '(i64, i64)'", though a bare `ref i64` arm beside an `i64` joins at the value (core semantics §5.10).
detail: Kata 1122 (Relative Sort Array) sorts by that key in its key arm: `out.sort_by_key(|x| match place.get(x) { .. })`. join_branch_types (src/typechecker.rs) peels a top-level `ref` to a Copy value but compared two tuples whole, so the join failed in either arm order, in a `match` and in an `if`/`else` alike. An annotation (`let k: (i64, i64) = match ..`) was accepted, which is the shape the arms should join to. A tuple of a `ref String` and one of a `String` must stay refused: that arm would move out of a borrow. The MIR side builds a tuple literal at its slot's element types already (operand_at); a tuple made elsewhere (`{ let t = (0, i); t }`) and stored into the joined slot would keep the reference, which borrow checking refused as a view stored where its borrow is not kept (E0509).

fix: 75af478a7c: Kata 1122's solution arm starts with use std::collections::HashMap; between two blank lines. The fix deleted the line and its newline, and the blank lines either side of it became two in a row. It now takes one of them too when there is a blank line before it, and at the top of a file the blank line after it.
title: `karac fix` deleting a Rust `use std::collections::HashMap;` line between two blank lines leaves the two blank lines in a row.
detail:
Kata 1122's solution arm, written as Rust, begins `// ..fix`.

use std::collections::HashMap;

impl Solution {`. The E0001 fix in src/parser.rs (a Rust std import whose names Kāra has in its prelude) deletes the line and its newline, so the blank lines either side of it remained and the file read `fix`.


impl`. The program checks and runs; the text is what nobody writes, and `karac fmt` is not part of the Mend loop. The fix should also take one blank line when one is on each side, and at the top of a file the blank line after it.

fix:
316e6be03d. The acquire was never the one waiting. The group's join on the root task was. Only the first worker (the main thread) polls the root. gdb at a stall showed the main thread in clock_nanosleep inside the executor's idle_wait, and the other workers napping. block() had seen another worker running. By idle_wait's own read under the lock, that worker had settled its task (no longer counted as running) and had not yet taken the waiter that its release had made worth polling. idle_wait took "none running" to mean nothing could change, and slept to the nearest timed wait's deadline: the waiter's 60 s acquire deadline. The other worker then ran the pair to the end, and the join waited until the main thread woke. The hypothesis in the detail does not hold: under the pool the executor state, including the progress count, is one shared, locked structure, not per thread.

The fix: idle_wait also reads, under the same lock, whether a queued task is worth polling, and returns at once when one is (another worker is about to take it, or this one will).

Measured on a 4-core cloud VM with the built differential. Unfixed: 1 of 60 serial runs took 62 s. A probe with 1 s timeouts that flags any run() slower than 100 ms found 15 stalls in 150 runs. Fixed: 0 of 60 (max 3.0 s, mean 2.52 s against 2.46 s unfixed, excluding the stall) and 0 stalls in 150 runs. tests/mir_sem_idle_wait.rs runs 20000 semaphore-pair groups three times with KARAC_THREADS=4 and fails on any group slower than 1 s. Against the unfixed runtime archive it failed 3 of 3; it passes with the fix. Gate: fmt, both clippy legs, test --all 11111/0, llvm 11313/0. Pool.acquire and any other TaskBy wait shared the same stall.
title: A compiled program's group join sometimes waited out a task's whole acquire timeout after every task had finished: the first worker, which alone polls the root, slept in idle_wait to the nearest TaskBy deadline while another worker briefly counted as not running between tasks. Kata 1115's differential, with its semaphore arm on Semaphore and acquire(60000), took 62 to 63 s instead of 3 s in 6 of 120 runs (3 of 40 built binaries, 2 of 40 __mir-llvm-run, 1 of 40 karac run), with the right output.
detail: Found moving kata 1115's semaphore arm onto Semaphore after c47fd80f23 (B-2026-11-11-34). Repro: /mnt/attach/project-files/kata-thread/sem-stall/differential_1115.kara (the differential; its semaphore section is A1FooBar, foo_sem = Semaphore.new(1), bar_sem = Semaphore.new(0), each method acquiring its own with a 60 s timeout and releasing the other's after it prints). Run it 40 times and time each: a slow run is 60 s longer, the acquire's timeout, and still prints the right log, so the permit was there and the waiter took it only at its deadline. Its `run` helper starts two or four tasks (two FooBar pairs with their own logs when `two` is set), and each print does busy work and takes a Mutex. The interpreter never stalls (30 runs). The previous differential, whose semaphores are channels, never stalled in 30 karac run executions. Instrumenting the acquires (5 s timeout, a line on Err) shows no Timeout in 80 runs, as expected if the waiter wakes at its deadline and finds the permit. A smaller program, two FooBar pairs at once with a 1 s timeout, 1000 runs, saw no slow run on any lane, so the busy work or the other arms' tasks in the same process matter. Hypothesis, not traced: release calls mir_task::peer_progressed, which marks progress on the calling thread's EXEC (a thread-local), so a release on one worker does not wake another worker napping to the waiter's deadline (Wait::TaskBy); channels move a global CHAN_EPOCH instead.

title: An argument's `&&` (Rust's borrow of a borrow, `MONTHS.contains(&&rest[..3])`) is a parse error with no fix, "Expected expression, found `&&`", which also turns the rest of the function into top-level statements
detail: An argument's single `&` is dropped by a machine-applicable edit (B-2026-11-03-27, `parse_call_args`), but `&&x` lexes as one `AmpAmp` token, which the argument check does not look for, and the expression parser has no prefix `&&`. Rust writes `slice.contains(&&s[..3])` whenever the element is itself a reference (`[&str; 12]`). The parse fails with "Expected expression, found `&&`", and the recovery leaves the rest of the function's body at top level, so check adds "file contains both top-level statements and an explicit `fn main()`" three times and `karac fix` stops. Found porting kara-katas apps/service/syslog_collector (`MONTHS.contains(&&rest[..3])`).
fix: FIXED by 37af642c5e. The argument list's borrow-sigil check (`parse_call_args`, src/parser/exprs.rs) now looks for `AmpAmp` as well as `Amp`, so `f(&&x)` gets the same machine-applicable edit that drops the sigil, with the message "`&&` on an argument is Rust syntax -- an argument is borrowed with no sigil, and Kāra has no borrow of a borrow: drop the `&&`". The parse no longer fails, so the top-level-statements cascade is gone and `karac fix` goes on to the rest of the file. A prefix `&&x` outside an argument list is still a parse error. Pinned by tests/double_borrow_arg_fix.rs (`MONTHS.contains(&&s[..3])` mends to `MONTHS.contains(s[..3])` and runs).

title: Rust's `s.into_bytes()` on a String is a bare "no method 'into_bytes' on type 'String'", with no hint or fix toward `s.bytes().to_vec()`
detail: `String::into_bytes` is how Rust turns an owned string into a `Vec<u8>` (`format!("{} ", n).into_bytes()` to start a length-prefixed frame). Kāra has `.bytes()` (a `Slice[u8]`) and `.to_vec()`, and `as_bytes` already gets a hint and a rename to `bytes` (B-2026-10-24-42), but `into_bytes` falls to the generic no-method error with no edit-distance neighbour. Found porting kara-katas apps/service/syslog_collector.
fix: FIXED by 37af642c5e. `into_bytes` joins the Rust string-method twins (`rust_string_method_twin`, src/typechecker/expr_method_call.rs): on a String or Str with no user method of that name, the error says "a string's UTF-8 bytes are `.bytes()`, a `Slice[u8]`, and an owned `Vec[u8]` of them is `.bytes().to_vec()`", and a no-argument call gets a rename of `into_bytes` to `bytes().to_vec`, the same edit shape as `to_owned`/`into_owned` to `to_string`. Pinned by tests/double_borrow_arg_fix.rs (`f"{v} ".to_string().into_bytes()` mends and runs).

title: `Duration` has no arithmetic: `a + b`, `a - b` and `d * n` are refused ("type 'Duration' does not implement trait Add"), where Rust's, Go's and Java's spans add, subtract and scale; `Instant + Duration` works
detail: FOUND closing B-2026-11-11-33. runtime/stdlib/std_time.kara implements `Sub for Instant` and `Add[Duration] for Instant` but nothing for `Duration` itself, so a backoff that doubles (`delay * 2`), a budget that sums phases (`parse + check`) or a remaining time (`deadline - spent`) has to go through `Duration.ns(a.as_ns() + b.as_ns())`. Real-world uses: retry backoff, request budgets, latency accounting. REPRO: `import std.time.{Duration}; fn main() { let d = Duration.ms(1) + Duration.us(5); println(d.as_us()); }` is refused at check with `type 'Duration' does not implement trait Add`; `-` and `* 3` likewise. Remedy hypothesis: `impl Add for Duration`, `impl Sub for Duration`, `impl Mul[i64] for Duration` (and `Div[i64]`) in std_time.kara, documented in library/time-random-env.md, overflow checked as every i64 is.
fix: 5c76d17174: `Duration` implements `Add`, `Sub`, `Mul[i64]` and `Div[i64]` in runtime/stdlib/std_time.kara. That covers `a + b`, `a - b` (negative when `b` is longer), `d * n`, `d / n` rounded toward zero, and the compound assignments (`total += d`). It is documented in library/time-random-env.md, with a CHANGELOG entry under Added. tests/duration_sub_millisecond.rs `a_duration_adds_subtracts_and_scales` pins a doubling backoff, a total, a difference, and a sleep of `Duration.us(20) * 2`, on the interpreter, a built binary and ASan.

title: Rust's `thread::sleep(d)` does not mend: `use std::thread;` becomes `import std.thread;` ("unknown module `std.thread`") and `std::thread::sleep(d)` becomes a bare `sleep(d)` with no `import std.time.sleep;` ("undefined name 'sleep'"), where Kāra's is `std.time.sleep`
detail: FOUND closing B-2026-11-11-33, mending a Rust spin-wait template. After `karac fix` runs to a fixed point on `use std::thread; use std::time::Duration; fn main() { thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(1)); std::thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(1)); }`, the file reads `import std.thread; ... thread.sleep(Duration.ms(1)); sleep(Duration.ms(1));` and check reports `unknown module std.thread` and `undefined name 'sleep'`, neither with a fix. Every Rust program that pauses writes one of the two (kata 1114's polling arm is one). Remedy hypothesis: map Rust's `std::thread::sleep` to `std.time.sleep` as the parser's Rust-path mends do: drop the `use std::thread;` line when `sleep` is all it is used for, rewrite `thread::sleep(` to `sleep(`, and insert `import std.time.sleep;` (or add `sleep` to an existing `std.time` import), as `std_cmp_reverse_import` does for `Reverse`.
fix: 5c76d17174: src/parser/rust_thread.rs `reject_rust_thread_import` rewrites `use std::thread;` (when `sleep` is all the program reaches through it) and `use std::thread::sleep;` to `import std.time.sleep;`. `rewrite_rust_path` drops the module from `thread::sleep(d)` and `std::thread::sleep(d)`. Where no import line of `thread` or `sleep` is there, the path's fix also inserts `import std.time.sleep;` above the first item; identical insertions dedupe, so there is one import however many calls there are. A `use std::thread;` that a `thread::spawn` also goes through stays, for the spawn's own diagnostic. tests/duration_sub_millisecond.rs pins the three Rust shapes mending to a program that checks clean and runs on every lane, and pins the spawn case being left alone.

e70aabada4: The Rc/RefCell `use` fix in src/parser/rust_rc.rs and the prelude-import fix in src/parser.rs now share Parser::rust_use_line_length: the line, its newline, and a blank line after it when a blank line (or the top of the file) is before it. The two `use` lines go in separate rounds, so each round sees the lines the last one left, and kata 1120's solution arm now keeps one blank line after its header comment. tests/kata_1122_use_line_blank.rs pins two `use` lines of each fix between blank lines.
title: `karac fix` deleting a Rust `use std::rc::Rc;` / `use std::cell::RefCell;` line between two blank lines leaves the two blank lines in a row (the remainder of B-2026-11-11-65).

fix: 628eb9974d: The `&T` fix in src/parser/types.rs now drops the `&` of a parameter's `&Rc<RefCell<T>>` or `&Option<Rc<RefCell<T>>>` (Parser::rust_rc_param_borrow in src/parser/rust_rc.rs): the type becomes the shared struct `T`, a handle, and a bare parameter already borrows, so a node matched out of it is a `T` and `Some(n)` returns as `Option[T]`. Not when the file reads `*name` for the parameter, since a bare parameter has nothing to dereference and that error has no fix. Kata 1123's solution arm mends to a clean check in five rounds and matches the Python mirror. tests/kata_1123_rc_param_borrow.rs pins both cases.
title: `karac fix` writes a Rust parameter's `&Option<Rc<RefCell<T>>>` as `ref Option[T]`, so a node matched out of it is a `ref T` and `Some(n)` cannot be returned as `Option[T]`: a type error with no fix (kata 1123's solution arm).
detail: Kata 1123's solution arm, written as LeetCode's Rust users write it, has `fn dfs(node: &Option<Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>>) -> (i32, Option<Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>>)` returning `(ld + 1, Some(Rc::clone(n)))` for the `Some(n)` it matched. After `karac fix` (four rounds, release karac at c57d79254b) the header is `fn dfs(node: ref Option[TreeNode]) -> (i32, Option[TreeNode])` and the arm `(ld + 1, Some(n))`, refused with E0200 `expected '(i32, Option[TreeNode])', found '(i32, Option[ref TreeNode])'` and no fix. The `&T` fix in src/parser/types.rs writes `ref`; `n` bound from a `ref Option[TreeNode]` is a `ref TreeNode`. Kata 1120's solution arm got past the same `ref` because nothing returned the node: the `redundant_ref_param` style lint dropped the `ref` in a later round, but the lint runs only on a program that checks. With the `ref` dropped by hand the arm checks and matches the Python mirror. An `Rc<RefCell<T>>` becomes the shared struct `T`, a handle, and a bare parameter already borrows, so the parameter's `&` should go.

title: Tracker for the next minor release: `concat()` joining the `Display` forms of elements that are neither sequences nor text becomes a compile error; in 0.8.x it is a `deprecated` warning whose `karac fix` writes `join("")` (design.md § Vec)
detail: Split from B-2026-11-11-51 under the review thread's ruling (eaae42ef07, design.md § Vec): `concat()` on a `Vec` or `Slice` of `Vec`s flattens, a sequence of `String` or `Str` joins into one `String`, and on any other `Display` element the 0.8.0 text join is deprecated. src/typechecker/method_concat.rs `try_concat_of_sequences` emits the warning (TypeErrorKind::Deprecated, lint `deprecated`) with a machine-applicable fix replacing `concat()` with `join("")` from the method name to the `)`, then lets the call go on to the existing join typing. Not reported when a program's own trait impl on `Vec`/`Slice` defines `concat`, or when the element is `Str`, `StringSlice`, an unsolved variable or an error. `#[allow(deprecated)]` on the enclosing item silences it. In-tree uses that warn now: corpus/fixtures/core_strict_check/check_join_of_display_elements_2 (`c.concat()` on `Vec[char]`) and the same program in tests/core_strict_check.rs and tests/mir_build.rs. At the next minor: turn the warning into a type error keeping the same fix, migrate those uses with `karac fix`, and flip tests/concat_flattens.rs `concat_of_display_elements_is_deprecated_with_a_join_fix` and `concat_deprecation_is_suppressed_by_allow_deprecated`. Repro: `fn main() { let n: Vec[i64] = [1, 2, 3].to_vec(); println(n.concat()); }` -> warning[deprecated], prints `123`; `karac fix` writes `n.join("")`.

title: An allocator swap (mimalloc as karac's #[global_allocator]) speeds `karac check` by about a quarter at 20-70% more peak RSS; not landed, re-measure once the library cache changes the CLI's allocation profile
detail: Split from B-2026-10-31-8 on 2026-11-11, at the review thread's routing. MEASURED 2026-11-09 (Thread C, release build without LLVM at 2ec5518d64, cloud box, hyperfine -N, 40 runs; /usr/bin/time -v), experiment only: mimalloc 0.1 as #[global_allocator]. Tiny `check` (3-line program) 66 -> 48 ms, peak RSS 45 -> 78 MB (55 MB and 52 ms with MIMALLOC_ARENA_EAGER_COMMIT=0); mini_parsy `check` 575 -> 417 ms, RSS 127 -> 175 MB. malloc/free were about 37% of a tiny check's instructions, almost all of it the standard library's re-parse and re-check (B-2026-11-09-28). REVIEW 2026-11-09: not landed, being a new dependency of the shipped compiler for ~14 ms and ~10 MB more RSS on a small check, most of whose allocation is the library re-check; re-measure after the library cache. That cache's Stages 1 and 2 were folded into Stage 4 (docs/deferred.md 7cdc0fadd4), whose entry says the mimalloc experiment waits for the same point.
