fix: 46ef5d349a: The `&` argument fix in src/parser/exprs.rs (parse_arg_list_inner) now also deletes the argument's parentheses when they wrap the whole argument: Parser::whole_arg_parens finds a `(` right after the `&` whose matching `)` (Parser::matching_paren, now pub(crate) in src/parser/rust_rc.rs) ends the argument, with nothing between them at depth 0 that makes a tuple (a comma) and the pair not empty. `seen.get(&(score - 1))` becomes `seen.get(score - 1)`, and `sum(&(a, 2), &(a + 3))` becomes `sum((a, 2), a + 3)`. Pinned by tests/kata_1124_amp_paren_arg.rs. Kata 1124's solution arm re-mended to `seen.get(score - 1).cloned()` in three rounds; all five arms match the Python mirror in every lane.
title: `karac fix` drops the `&` of a Rust argument `&(expr)` but leaves its parentheses: `seen.get(&(score - 1))` becomes `seen.get((score - 1))` (kata 1124's solution arm).
detail: Kata 1124's solution arm, written as LeetCode's Rust users write it, looks a score up with `if let Some(&j) = seen.get(&(score - 1))`. Rust needs the parentheses so the `&` borrows the whole difference. The `&` argument fix in src/parser/exprs.rs (parse_arg_list_inner) deletes only the sigil, so after `karac fix` (release karac at 628eb9974d) the line reads `seen.get((score - 1)).cloned()`: it checks clean and runs right, but the doubled parentheses are a Rust remnant nobody writes in Kāra, and nothing later removes them. A tuple argument `&(a, 2)` must keep its parentheses, since they make the tuple.

fix: afb930a6c1: A `let mut x = e;` re-binding of a bare `for` element now inherits the element's `.into_iter()` fix (TypeChecker::core_for_into_iter_aliases, recorded in the Let arm of src/typechecker/items.rs), so a move of `x` takes the loop's `.into_iter()` when nothing uses the collection after the loop, as a move of `e` does (B-2026-11-07-30). Otherwise the move's `.clone()` goes on the `let`'s initializer (TypeChecker::core_let_mut_views; the E0200 projection-copy fix in items.rs and the `expected 'T', found 'ref T'` fix in src/typechecker.rs via let_mut_view_init_at), and the write through `x` reports a new Origin::ForElemCopy in src/typechecker/core_ref_write.rs, `Write .clone() where it is bound`, with the same edit in place of the `.iter_mut()` advice, which would change the collection. Pinned by tests/kata_1125_let_mut_for_elem.rs (over a temporary: `.into_iter()`; over a borrowed map used after: `let mut next = team.clone();`; the write's message). Kata 1125's sparse arm mends in one round to `for (m, team) in best.clone().into_iter()`.
title: `karac fix` puts the `.clone()` for a moved `let mut next = team;` re-binding of a `for` element at the move, leaving `next.push(p)` writing through the element's `ref`: an error nothing fixes (kata 1125's sparse arm).
detail: Kata 1125's Map arm grows teams with `for (m, team) in best.clone() { let mut next = team; next.push(p); best[grown] = next; }`, Rust's way to change a copy of an element it owns. A bare `for` borrows the collection (core-semantics.md §4.6), so `next` is a `ref` to the element. `karac check` (release karac at 46ef5d349a) reports only the move, E0200 `cannot move 'next': it borrows its value`, with a `.clone()` at the move: `best[grown] = next.clone()`. After that fix the MIR borrow check refuses `next.push(p)` (E0517, a mutable borrow through a shared reference) with no fix. Over a borrowed map used after the loop the typechecker reports both at once, the move as `expected 'Vec[i64]', found 'ref Vec[i64]'` with a `.clone()` at the move and the write as E0517 with the advice `Iterate with .iter_mut()`, which would change the collection the Rust meant to copy from. A move of `team` itself already takes the loop's `.into_iter()` when nothing uses the collection after it (B-2026-11-07-30), but the `let` re-binding did not inherit it.

title: A call on an ambient module (`fs.write(...)`) in a program that also uses sockets is charged `TcpStream.write`'s `sends(Network) receives(Network)`, so `fn save() with writes(FileSystem) { fs.write("x.txt", "hi").unwrap(); }` is refused
detail: Found while testing B-2026-11-11-63. In a program that also uses `TcpStream`, `fn save() with writes(FileSystem) { fs.write("x.txt", "hi").unwrap(); }` is refused: "function 'save' performs sends(Network) (via call to 'TcpStream.write' at line 2)", and the same for receives(Network). A program with only `TcpListener` is accepted, since the pruned library then has no `TcpStream.write`. Cause, in src/effectchecker/inference.rs's MethodCall arm: the typechecker records no callee for an ambient module's method (`precise` is None), and the alias map routes `fs.write` to `FileSystem.write`, but the two name-keyed fallbacks still run: the method-name index adds every library `write` with a body (`TcpStream.write`), and the stdlib seed map adds the seeded `write`s. `stdin.read_line()` meets the same fallbacks by name (`BufReader[TcpStream].read_line`).
fix: e92c63a596: an ambient module's method that the typechecker left unresolved (`precise` is None and the receiver is `env`, `clock`, `rand`, `stdin`, `stdout`, `stderr` or `fs`) is routed to its own key by the alias map and takes neither name-keyed fallback: it counts as deferred for the method-name index, and the stdlib seed map skips it (src/effectchecker/inference.rs). `fs.write` beside sockets now infers `writes(FileSystem)`, `panics`, `blocks` and no network effect. A receiver the typechecker did resolve, such as a local named `fs`, keeps today's path. Pinned by tests/effects_ambient_module_methods.rs: `ambient_fs_and_stdin_calls_keep_their_own_effects_beside_sockets` (accepted) and `ambient_fs_call_is_still_charged_its_own_effect_beside_sockets` (refused for `writes(FileSystem)` via `FileSystem.write`, with no Network in the message). Control: with the inference change reversed, both fail on the `TcpStream.write` network errors.

5a92d2ae01: A closure checked against a return type its callee leaves open (`map`'s `OutV`, a `TypeParam`, or an unbound variable) now marks the values it gives as open (TypeChecker::open_closure_values, src/typechecker.rs; TypeChecker::closure_value_ids in src/typechecker/exprs.rs collects the body, a block's tail, and each branch of a tail `if` or `match`). `check_expr` and `infer_expr` open a literal at those ids as they open a `let`'s value (`open_literal_expr`, `open_collection_let`), so an unsuffixed number, a list or tuple of them, or a join of those stays a literal variable. Before a body's literals take their defaults, TypeChecker::solve_collect_items_before_defaults (src/typechecker/exprs.rs, called from the fn-body check in src/typechecker/items.rs) runs the body's deferred `FromIterator` bounds whose collection the body fixed, reading `collect`'s `C` from `node_call_subs`, and solves the items' literal variables with solve_collected_item_vars. `(0..n).map(|i| if i % 2 == 0 { [4, 7] } else { [7, 4] }).collect()` into a `Vec[Vec[i32]]` checks, as do `|i| 5`, `{ 5 }`, `5 + 0`, `(1, 0.5)` and `match` arms into their slots; an unfixed one defaults (`.sum()` into `i64`, `5000000000` into `Vec[i64]`); an out-of-range one is still refused (`3000000000` into `Vec[i32]`). `with_provider` commits its call's type from the closure's return only when concrete, and an open literal there had typed the call `Error` (`|| tg.spawn(|| 7)`, and already before this `let x = Some(7); .. || x`): the return's literals now take their defaults there (src/typechecker/expr_call.rs). Tests: tests/kata_1128_closure_literal_collect.rs (a_closure_number_takes_the_collected_item_type, a_later_use_fixes_a_closure_number_and_unfixed_ones_default, a_closure_number_past_the_collected_type_is_refused, a_with_provider_closure_number_takes_its_default). Gate on the same code before a rewrite that changed only the ids in comments: test_all 11136 passed, llvm 11348 passed, 0 failed.
title: A number a closure gives to `map` takes `i64` before `collect` can type it: `(0..n).map(|i| if i % 2 == 0 { [4, 7] } else { [7, 4] }).collect()` into a `Vec[Vec[i32]]` is refused as `FromIterator[Vec[i64]]` (kata 1128's harness)
detail: Kata 1128's harness builds 40,000 alike dominoes with `let same: Vec[Vec[i32]] = (0..40000).map(|i| if i % 2 == 0 { [4, 7] } else { [7, 4] }).collect();`. Release karac at afb930a6c1 refuses it: `trait bound C: FromIterator[Vec[i64]] is not satisfied; Vec[Vec[i32]] implements FromIterator[Vec[i32]], not FromIterator[Vec[i64]]`. The same for a closure giving `5`, `{ 5 }`, `5 + 0`, `[4, 7]` or `(4, 7)` into the matching `Vec[i32]`, `Vec[Vec[i32]]` or `Vec[(i32, i32)]`; a scalar `if c { 4 } else { 7 }` already worked. design.md §8 says an unsuffixed literal nothing types where it is written stays open for a later use to fix, as a `let`'s value does (`let x = [4, 7]; let y: Vec[i32] = x;` works). The closure is checked against `map`'s return parameter `OutV`, which `check_expr` read as a known type, so a lone literal took `i64` on the spot; and once the body's literals took their defaults the `collect`'s `FromIterator` bound, discharged only when the program is checked, found the item `i64`. With `with_provider` the open number exposed an older failure: a closure there whose return held an open literal (`let x = Some(7); with_provider[R](p, || x)`, or `|| tg.spawn(|| 7)`) typed the call `Error` and MIR refused it as `a type that failed to check is not lowered yet`.

fix: 0385ddd3ac: The parser records a `let`'s whole value that is a cast of a parenthesized operand (Parser::note_whole_value_cast in src/parser.rs, called from parse_let_statement in src/parser/stmts.rs) in Program::whole_value_casts (src/ast.rs): the span from the operand's `(` to the end of the type, and the operand's text. lint_unneeded_cast (src/typechecker/exprs.rs) takes it as the fix, so `redundant_cast` and `lossless_cast` replace `(j - i) as i64` with `j - i` there; inside an operator the parentheses stay (`(j - i) as i64 * 2` to `(j - i) * 2`), and a parenthesized argument keeps its own (`index((c - b'a'))`, kata 1061). Kata 1061's fixture pinned `let b: i64 = (( c - b'b' ));` and now expects `let b: i64 = c - b'b';`. Test: tests/kata_1128_closure_literal_collect.rs (a_whole_let_value_cast_takes_its_parentheses_with_it). Gate on the same code before a rewrite that changed only the ids in comments: test_all 11136 passed, llvm 11348 passed, 0 failed.
title: `karac fix` turns `let run = (j - i) as i64;` into `let run = (j - i);`: the redundant cast's fix keeps parentheses that group nothing (kata 1128's sort arm)
detail: Kata 1128's sort arm, written as Rust measures a run of equal keys, has `let run = (j - i) as i64;` with `j` and `i` already `i64`. `karac fix` (release karac at afb930a6c1) applies `redundant_cast` by deleting from the operand's `)` to the end of the type (the kata 1061 rule for a parenthesized operand, `Program::cast_operand_ends`), which leaves `let run = (j - i);`. Inside an operator the parentheses are needed (`(j - i) as i64 * 2` to `(j - i) * 2`), but around a `let`'s whole value nothing binds. The same shape as B-2026-11-11-83, where the `&` of `&(score - 1)` went and its parentheses stayed. Kata 1061's fixture pinned `let b: i64 = (( c - b'b' ));` as the expected text.

fix: 2d47b8e713: `Vec.push`'s slot check (TypeChecker::infer_element_arg, src/typechecker/method_vec_mutation.rs) now infers a tuple argument pushed into a tuple slot open, as it did one pushed into an unknown element type (infer_element_open), and the tuple arm of infer_expr_inner (src/typechecker/exprs.rs) opens a tuple nested inside an open one. TypeChecker::fix_tuple_literal_slots then unifies each open literal variable in the argument's type, or one under a `ref` (a `for` element's), with the number type at the same place in the slot, through nested tuples, and leaves every concrete element to the slot check. `let x = 0; q.push((x, 1))` into a `Vec[(i32, i32)]`, `push_back((x, y, 3))` into a `VecDeque[(i64, i32, u8)]`, `w.push(((z, 5), 0.5))` into a `Vec[((i16, u8), f32)]`, and `for (next, color) in ref graph[0] { q.push_back((next, color)); }` over pairs pushed as `(1, 0)` all type, a `Vec.new()` given `((1, 2), 3)` takes `((u8, i16), i32)` from a later annotation, and an `i64` binding in such a tuple is still refused as a narrowing. Tests: tests/kata_1129_tuple_literal_push.rs (an_open_number_in_a_pushed_tuple_takes_its_slot_type, a_number_read_back_from_a_pushed_tuple_takes_a_later_slot_type, a_fixed_wide_value_in_a_pushed_tuple_is_still_refused). Gate on the same code before a rewrite that changed only the ids in comments: test_all 11139 passed, 0 failed; llvm 11350 passed, 1 failed, the run_v2_jit_units handoff check matching another process's temp file by a pid prefix, which passes alone and is fixed in 45cfa217d0.
title: A number inside a tuple pushed into a tuple slot keeps `i64`: `let x = 0; q.push((x, 1))` into a `Vec[(i32, i32)]` is refused as narrowing `x` (kata 1129)
detail: Found while cutting down kata 1129's solution arm, which reads a colour out of an adjacency list of `(node, colour)` pairs pushed as `(e[1] as i64, 0)` and pushes it on in `q.push_back((next, d + 1, color))`. Release karac at 73ff6fcbfc refuses `let x = 0; let mut q: Vec[(i32, i32)] = []; q.push((x, 1));` with `implicit coercion from 'i64' to 'i32' would narrow or change sign: `x` is an 'i64' because its literal kept the default`, and the same into a `VecDeque[(i64, i32, u8)]` through `push_back`, and `for (a, b) in v.iter() { q.push((a, b)); }` over a `v` whose pairs were pushed as `(1, 0)`. design.md §8 says an argument fixes a literal's type, and `q.push(x)` alone, `q.push(Some(x))`, `q.push([x])`, `m.insert((x, 1), 1)` on a `Map[(i32, i32), i32]` and `let t: (i32, i32) = (x, 1)` all type `x` as `i32`. `Vec.push`'s hand-written slot check (try_vec_mutation_method, infer_element_arg in src/typechecker/method_vec_mutation.rs) infers a tuple argument, and a tuple that is not all literals infers each element closed, so `x` took its default there; the open-literal unify after it looks only at a top-level literal variable. Not this row: `let t = (x, 1); q.push(t)` is refused by the documented rule that a number held in a tuple keeps its type, and the kata's own refusal, where `color != last` with `last: i32` kept `color`'s default first, is B-2026-11-12-2.

title: A number read out of a tuple a literal was pushed into, then kept `i64` by a comparison, narrows into an `i32` slot with no machine fix: kata 1129's solution arm needs a hand `as i32`
detail: Kata 1129's solution arm is a Rust solution as LeetCode's Rust users write it: `graph[e[0] as usize].push((e[1] as usize, 0))` and `(.., 1)` for the blue edges, a `VecDeque` of `(usize, i32, i32)` started with `(0usize, 0i32, -1i32)`, and in the loop `for &(next, color) in &graph[node] { if color != last && !seen[next][color as usize] { ..; q.push_back((next, d + 1, color)); } }`. Rust types the pushed `0` and `1` as `i32` from the comparison. In Kāra a comparison beside an `i32` keeps the literal's default (design.md §8, review-thread rulings 2026-11-08), so `color` is `i64`, and after five `karac fix` rounds (which fix everything else) release karac at 73ff6fcbfc refuses `q.push_back((next, d + 1, color))` with `implicit coercion from 'i64' to 'i32' would narrow or change sign; an out-of-range value is not caught at compile time. Write an explicit 'as i32'` and no replacement. The refusal is right; the gap is the fix. When the narrowed value is a let-bound literal, or one read out of a collection it was pushed into, the message names the binding and `karac fix` declares it (`literal_let_annotation`, B-2026-11-09-15's `literal_pushes`), but an inline literal inside a pushed tuple, read back through a tuple pattern, is neither. The kata keeps the `as i32` the message asks for, written by hand. A remedy: trace the settled literal variable back to the literals that made it and offer their suffix (`0i32`, `1i32`) at the push, the fix that makes the program mean what its author meant; an `as i32` at the use would acknowledge a truncation that never happens.

fix: 73ec8b248f: the parser's Rust-`&` diagnostic (src/parser/exprs.rs) now treats an array, repeat or prefixed collection literal as it treated a number literal or a slice view: the edit drops the `&` and keeps the operand as it is, rather than offering `ref [..]`, which the checker refuses. Kata 1131's solution arm now mends in four rounds; tests/kata_1131_fix_gaps.rs pins `for &(p, q) in &[..]`, `&[1, 2, 3]` and `&[5; 2]`.
title: `karac fix` rewrites Rust's `&[..]` on a list literal to `ref [..]`, which the checker refuses: `for &(p, q) in &[(1, 1), (1, -1)]` (kata 1131)
detail: Kata 1131's solution arm is a Rust solution as LeetCode's Rust users write it, walking the four sign pairs as `for &(p, q) in &[(1, 1), (1, -1), (-1, 1), (-1, -1)]`. The parser's Rust-`&` diagnostic (src/parser/exprs.rs, the `&` prefix operand) offered `ref place` for every operand but a number literal and a slice view, so the machine fix turned `&[..]` into `ref [..]`; the next `karac check` refuses that, since a list literal is a new value and no place to borrow, and offers nothing, leaving the arm stuck after one round. The same holds for a repeat literal `&[0; 4]` and a prefixed collection literal. Measured on the arm itself: round 1 left `for (p, q) in ref [(1, 1), ..]`, then a refusal that `karac fix` had nothing to apply for.

fix: 73ec8b248f: literal_operator_copy (src/typechecker/exprs.rs) keeps the first literal binding's entry when several take part instead of giving up, so the narrowing offers that binding's annotation or suffix, and a later `karac fix` round the next. Kata 1131's solution arm gets `(1i32, 1)` and then `(1i32, 1i32)`; tests/kata_1131_fix_gaps.rs pins two `let` bindings and a walked tuple list.
title: A value made an `i64` by two literal bindings has no machine fix: `let p = 1; let q = 2; m = m.max(p * a + q * a)` with `a: i32` (kata 1131)
detail: Kata 1131's solution arm computes `p * arr1[i] + q * arr2[i] + i as i32` with `p` and `q` bound from a walked list of literal pairs, and folds it into an `i32` maximum. `literal_operator_copy` (src/typechecker/exprs.rs) offers the let annotation or literal suffix that types a literal binding when that binding alone keeps a value at the default `i64`, but returned None as soon as a second, different literal binding took part, so the narrowing was reported with no fix. Measured on the arm with its `&` removed by hand: the narrowing carried no replacement, and `karac fix` had nothing to apply.

fix: d361886e40: `infer_element_arg` (src/typechecker/method_vec_mutation.rs) records the slot's type as a cast argument's expected type when the slot is concrete, and the `Index` arm (src/typechecker/exprs.rs) records `i64` for a cast index into an Array, Slice, Vec or VecDeque (`indexes_by_position`), so `lint_unneeded_cast` says W0291 and offers the deletion as it does for a call argument. tests/kata_1136_element_cast_lint.rs pins five flagged element casts and three index casts with their fixed text and output, and the casts left alone (a narrowing, a float to integer, a Map key); tests/fix_usize_every_use.rs now expects `adj[e[0]].push(e[1] as i64)`.
title: `lossless_cast` misses a widening cast pushed or inserted into a list and one used as a list position, so `karac fix` leaves `graph[r[0] as i64].push(r[1] as i64)` with `r: Vec[i32]` (kata 1136)
detail: Kata 1136's solution arm is a Rust solution as LeetCode's Rust users write it, filling `graph[r[0] as usize].push(r[1] as usize)` and `indegree[r[1] as usize] += 1` with `r: Vec<i32>`. `karac fix` retypes `usize` to `i64` and leaves `graph[r[0] as i64].push(r[1] as i64)` and `indegree[r[1] as i64] += 1`. Both casts widen for nothing: a list position takes any integer and widens it, and an element slot whose type is known widens an argument as a parameter does. `lossless_cast` (W0291) said so for a call argument, a field, a `let` with a type and a return, because those check the value against an expected type that `pending_cast_expected` records; a `push`/`insert`/`push_back`/`push_front` element is inferred and then unified with the slot (`infer_element_arg` in src/typechecker/method_vec_mutation.rs), and an index is inferred, so neither recorded one and nothing was said. A cast that changes the value (`x as u8` from `i64`, `f as i64` from `f64`) and a `Map` key are not widenings and stay. Where the slot is still a type variable at the push (`let mut graph = Vec.filled(n + 1, Vec.new())` before the first push) the cast is what fixes the element type, so it is not flagged; kata 1136's arm keeps that one `as i64`. Validated over every kara-katas file the change newly flags (431 files, 1020 casts, `.orig.kara` drafts aside): after `karac fix`, every program prints what it printed before except six, and each of those six prints the same with only this change's edits applied; their changes come from older fix faults filed beside this row.

fix: 3436c6649a: `join_checked_arms` (src/typechecker/patterns.rs) takes the expectation, and arms that join only through it (each widened to a concrete expected type) give the `if`, `if let` or `match` that type, so the MIR builds the value in the `i64` slot and widens the `u8` arm into it. In the synthesized `if`, `if let` and `match` (src/typechecker/exprs.rs, patterns.rs), a literal or literal tree takes its sibling's numeric type only when `literal_tree_fits`, so a `65533` beside a `u8` keeps its `i64` and, with nothing to widen to, the branches are refused as incompatible. tests/kata_1136_branch_widening.rs pins the call argument, function tail, typed `let` match and an `i8` sibling (65533, 70000, -5 on the interpreter and the compiled backend), the refused `if` and `match`, and a fitting `255` still taking `u8`. mini_piexif after `karac fix` prints its expected output.
title: A literal beside a narrower branch takes that branch's type even when it does not fit: `show(if c < 128 { c } else { 0xFFFD })` with `c: u8` and `show(x: i64)` prints 253, and `let d = if c < 128 { c } else { 65533 }` is accepted as a `u8` (kata 1136)
detail: Found checking kata 1136's lint fix (B-2026-11-12-5) over kara-katas: after `karac fix`, apps/cli/mini_piexif printed `UserComment.load(b'ASCII\x00\x00\x00caf\xe9') = 'cafý'` where its expected output has `'caf\ufffd'`. Its decoder reads `push_cp(mut out, if *c < 128 { *c as i64 } else { 0xFFFD })`; `lossless_cast` called the `as i64` unnecessary, since each branch is checked against the parameter's `i64`, and the fix deleted it. Two faults made the result wrong rather than refused. (1) `check_if_against`, `check_if_let_against` and `check_match_against` (src/typechecker/patterns.rs) checked each arm against the expectation, which widens it, but recorded the `if`'s type as the join of the arms' own types, and with `u8` and `i64` not joining, the first arm's `u8`; the MIR stored 65533 into that `u8` and widened 253 into the argument. (2) In the synthesized `if` (no expectation), `literal_taking_branch_type` let an unsuffixed integer literal take its sibling's type without asking whether the value fits (its doc comment said it did), so `let d = if c < 128 { c } else { 65533 }` checked as a `u8` and printed 253 too, and `let m = match c { 65 => c, _ => 70000 }` printed 112. Both reproduce on the MIR interpreter and the compiled backend; a negated literal was already range-checked (`unsuffixed_num_literal`), and an arithmetic operand has `check_promoted_arith_literal`.

fix: 3436c6649a: `StmtKind::Assign` (src/typechecker/items.rs) drops the first walk's `BranchTypeMismatch` on the value's own span when the value is an `if`/`if let` with an `else` or a `match` and the walk against the place's type added no error, so the assignment accepts what a typed `let` accepts. tests/kata_1136_branch_widening.rs pins a local, a field, a list position and an `if let`, with a `u8` 200 and an `i8` -5 widened, and a `String` branch still refused. mini_prettytable, mini_protobuf and mini_csv check and print their expected output after `karac fix`.
title: An assignment refuses an `if`/`match` whose branches widen to the place: `y = if c { a } else { y }` with `a: u8`, `y: i64` is "if/else branches have incompatible types" where `let y2: i64 = if c { a } else { y }` is accepted, so `karac fix` deleting a flagged `a as i64` breaks the program (kata 1136)
detail: Found checking kata 1136's lint fix over kara-katas: after `karac fix`, apps/cli/mini_prettytable, mini_protobuf and mini_csv no longer checked (`if/else branches have incompatible types: 'i64' and 'u8'` at `dialect.quotechar = if g.quotechar == 0 { b'"' as i64 } else { g.quotechar as i64 }`, and an `f32`/`f64` pair). `StmtKind::Assign` (src/typechecker/items.rs) walks the value twice: `infer_expr` first, for the value-position checks, where the `if` arm joins its branches with nothing to widen to and reports the mismatch, then `check_expr` against the target's type, which goes through `check_if_against` and widens each branch, as a typed `let`, a call argument, a `return` and a function tail do. The second walk's `lossless_cast` told the user each `as i64` was unnecessary, and it is, by design.md's widening rule (a value widens wherever its destination type is known), but the first walk's error stayed. Shapes refused: `y = if ..`, `d.q = if ..` (a field), `v[0] = match ..` (a position), `y = if let ..`, `y = match ..`. Where a branch has two casts and only one has a machine fix (`b'"' as i64` is a byte literal, offered none), `karac fix` applied the other and left the program refused.

fix: 3436c6649a: `StmtKind::Assign` (src/typechecker/items.rs) notes whether the target is a binding whose literal no use has fixed, and when the value is a cast it marks the cast as already linted before the walk against the place, so `lossless_cast` stays silent where the cast fixes the binding's type. tests/kata_1136_branch_widening.rs pins `letter = b[j] as i64` after `let mut letter = -1` unflagged and a cast into a typed `i64` binding still flagged. Kata 664's differential checks and prints the same after `karac fix`.
title: `lossless_cast` calls a cast unnecessary where it fixes an open binding's type: `letter = b[j] as i64` after `let mut letter = -1` with `b: Vec[u8]`, and `karac fix` deleting it leaves `-1` initializing a `u8` (kata 1136)
detail: Found checking kata 1136's lint fix (B-2026-11-12-5) over kara-katas: after `karac fix`, kata 664's differential no longer checked (`negative integer literal -1 cannot initialize unsigned type 'u8'`). It reads `let mut letter = -1;` and later `letter = b[j] as i64;` with `b` a byte list. An assignment to a binding whose literal no use has fixed yet fixes it from the value (`fix_literal_from_assigned`, B-2026-11-07-57), so the cast is what makes `letter` an `i64`; the assignment then checks the value against that `i64`, and `lossless_cast` saw a `u8` cast to the slot's own type and called it unnecessary. Without the cast the binding becomes a `u8`. Same shape as the element slot B-2026-11-12-5 leaves alone, where the slot is still a type variable at the push. The lint predates B-2026-11-12-5 (an older karac flags the same line).

fix: 97dd97098e: a list-literal binding records its literal's shape at every level (`ListShape` in src/typechecker.rs), so a literal whose elements are list literals of one shape matches a nested `Array` of the same lengths (`list_shape_is_array`), and `name = value` keeps the fix when the value is an `Array` (`note_list_lit_assign`, now called after the value is typed, src/typechecker/items.rs). Each use records its error's span with its index, and the explanation is attached only to an error still at that index and span, once. Kata 1137's matrix arm gets the explanation at every use of `result` and `step` and `karac fix` declares both `Array[Array[i64, 3], 3]`. tests/kata_1137_nested_list_literal_array.rs pins the 2 by 2 template, and a ragged literal, a wider one and one reassigned a list literal getting no fix.
title: A nested list literal passed as a nested `Array` is refused with no explanation or fix: `let mut result = [[1, 0, 0], [0, 1, 0], [0, 0, 1]]; result = multiply(result, step)` with `multiply(x: Array[Array[i64, 3], 3], ...)`
detail: Kata 1137's matrix arm (T(n) by squaring a 3 by 3 step matrix) binds `let mut result = [[1, 0, 0], [0, 1, 0], [0, 0, 1]]` and `let mut step = [[1, 1, 1], [1, 0, 0], [0, 1, 0]]` and passes them to `multiply(x: Array[Array[i64, 3], 3], y: Array[Array[i64, 3], 3]) -> Array[Array[i64, 3], 3]`. The literals are `Vec[Vec[i64]]` (design.md § Collection literals), so karac check gave six bare `expected 'Array[Array[i64, 3], 3]', found 'Vec[Vec[i64]]'` errors and karac fix nothing. B-2026-11-10-47 explains and fixes the flat case (`let local = [127u8, 0, 0, 1]` into `Array[u8, 4]`), but it recorded only the outer length, so a nested literal never matched, and any `name = value` cleared the fix although storing an `Array` (here `multiply`'s result) cannot change the lengths the declaration names. Separately, the uses' error indices could go stale when an argument is checked twice, attaching a binding's note to an unrelated error.

title: Programs built for macOS keep no frame records: every function saved x29 (rbp) without pointing it at its own record, against Apple's arm64 and x86_64 ABIs, so sample, Instruments and crash reports walk past every Kāra frame
detail: FOUND 2026-11-12 (drop schedule) while cross-building kata 404's bench for aarch64-apple-darwin to compare its `visit` with rustc's (B-2026-11-09-22). Every function in the object, `_main` and `_kara.main` included, stores x29/x30 (`stp x29, x30, [sp, #0x20]`) and none sets x29 to its record (`add x29, sp, #0x20`), where rustc's `visit` does. Apple's arm64 ABI ("Writing ARM64 code for Apple platforms") requires x29 to always address a valid frame record, leaf functions excepted; x86_64 Darwin keeps rbp frames throughout. The system's backtracers walk that chain without unwind tables, so a sample or crash report through Kāra code shows the nearest non-Kāra caller instead. The cause: LLVM omits the frame pointer unless the function asks for one, and clang and rustc add `"frame-pointer"` per function on Apple triples (arm64 non-leaf, x86_64 all); karac added it only for the ASan build (`all`, src/backend/mir_asan.rs). Linux and Windows output are unaffected.
fix: c5e9a24b82: src/backend/driver.rs mark_frame_pointers, called at the end of compile_mir_with (so karac build, karac run's JIT and the corpus backends all take it), gives every defined function the triple's frame-pointer attribute: aarch64/arm64 Apple non-leaf, x86_64 Apple all, rustc's and clang's defaults; any other triple gets none, and a function that already names one (the ASan build's all) keeps it. KARAC_MIR_FRAME_POINTER=0 leaves them out. Verified on the cross-built aarch64-apple-darwin object of kata 404's bench: _kara.main, _kara.visit and the grow helper now set x29 (add x29, sp, #imm), as rustc's visit does; KARAC_MIR_FRAME_POINTER=0 gives the old object. tests/mir_darwin_frame_pointer.rs checks the attribute on both Apple triples and its absence on x86_64 Linux (control: with the knob at 0 the IR names none). The helper lives in driver.rs because library_prune's test reads every string literal under src/backend/mir as a library method name, and all is one.

032df1a4c2. A fill of fills (`Vec.filled(m + 1, Vec.filled(n + 1, 0))`, or the same with list repeats) is now read to its innermost literal: the literal-let entry records how many indexes deep the element sits (`LiteralLet.depth`), so `g[i][j]` reaches the inner `0` and its `i32` suffix lands at the inner literal's column. A binding that holds an element copied out of the fill (`let k = t[1]`, `let k = max(t[1], t[0])` or `.min(..)`, or the loop variable of a range over an element, `for k in (1..=t[1]).rev()`) is traced back to it (`literal_element_copy`, `element_copy_source`, `literal_range_for_entry`), so its typed use (`let r: i32 = k`, `r = k`) names the fill and offers the suffix there. An assignment whose value is an identifier or an index is inferred open, as a typed `let`'s value is, so `r = t[1]` with `r: i32` is accepted on an open fill as `let r: i32 = t[1]` is. A nested fill whose literal is still open is opened by a typed read as a flat one is. Pinned by tests/kata_1139_fill_element_copy.rs (four copy shapes fixed and run, a fill of fills fixed at its inner literal and accepted open, an assigned element read accepted). Kata 1139's Rust arm now carries to Kāra in five `karac fix` rounds. The order dependence a stored literal leaves is B-2026-11-12-12.
title: A narrowing refused at a binding that holds an element of a fill offers only `as i32`: LeetCode's `let max_k = min(left[i][j], up[i][j]); for k in (1..=max_k).rev() { res = k }` with `left = Vec.filled(m + 1, Vec.filled(n + 1, 0))` and `res: i32` has no machine fix, and `res = t[1]` is refused where `let r: i32 = t[1]` is accepted
detail: Kata 1139's Rust arm keeps two `vec![vec![0; n + 1]; m + 1]` tables of runs; after `karac fix` they are `Vec.filled(m + 1, Vec.filled(n + 1, 0))`, `left[i][j] = left[i][j - 1] + 1` settles the literal to i64 (design.md §8 Literals: an operator does not fix a literal), and `res = k` into `res: i32` was refused with only 'write an explicit as i32'. B-2026-11-08-57 offers the fill's literal suffix (`0i32`) only at a read of a flat fill's element itself: a fill of fills was not read to its literal (`let r: i32 = g[1][1]` of `Vec.filled(2, Vec.filled(3, 0))` was refused even with nothing settling it), and a binding holding an element (`let k = t[1]`, `let m = min(t[1], t[0])`, a range loop variable over one) was not traced to the fill. Separately, an assignment's value was inferred bare before the target's type was known, so `r = t[1]` with `r: i32` settled the open fill literal to i64 and was refused, though `let r: i32 = t[1]` fixes it to i32.

title: A literal stored into an element of an open fill settles the fill's literal: `let mut t = Vec.filled(3, 0); t[1] = 4; let r: i32 = t[1];` is refused (narrowing i64 to i32), though without `t[1] = 4` it is accepted and `t[1] = 4` after the typed read is too
detail: Found pinning B-2026-11-12-11. design.md §8 Literals leaves `Vec.filled(n, 0)`'s literal open for a later use to fix (B-2026-11-08-57), and a stored literal is not such a use, but `t[1] = 4` settles it to i64, so the later `let r: i32 = t[1]` is refused. The refusal offers `0i32` as its machine fix, so the program checks after one `karac fix`; the order dependence is the defect: `let r: i32 = t[1]; t[1] = 4;` is accepted.

fix: d34854564c. An index whose type is a literal variable a generic call holds open (`literal_held_open`, the `fold` seed while its closure is checked) settles it, as a method call on it already did (e036c0dfdd): a position is an `i64`. Kata 2091's differential checks clean again and prints `0 failures`; pinned by tests/check_sweep_fold_seed_and_hashed_items.rs (`a_fold_seed_read_as_an_index_in_its_closure_is_an_index`, a `(0..n)` fold and an `.iter()` fold, checked and run).
title: A `fold` seed read as an index in its closure is refused, `index must be an integer or range, found 'i64'`: the seed is held open while the closure is checked (B-2026-11-11-61) and an index did not decide it, as a method call on it does
detail: Found by a `karac check` sweep over kara-katas after kata 1139: kata 2091's differential, which checked clean on an 11-09 build, is refused at `(0..n).fold(0, |best, k| if nums[k] < nums[best] { k } else { best })`. Any fold whose literal seed indexes in the closure fails the same way: `nums.iter().fold(0, |best, x| .. nums[best] ..)`, `(0..n).fold(0, |best, k| nums[best] + k)`. Bisected (two builds a side, 0e54521e35..HEAD) to e036c0dfdd, which keeps a literal at a generic parameter open while the call's closure is checked, so a scan's state can be fixed by the collect; an identifier read of such a literal no longer settles it, and a method call on it was made to, but an index was not: the index's type stays the literal's variable, which `is_integer` rejects and `type_display` renders as `i64`. A seed with a suffix (`fold(0i64, ..)`) is accepted.

fix: d34854564c. The settled-item FromIterator check compares the item and the impls' arguments with every `Map` / `Set` hasher their display leaves off (the default, or a variable never inferred) dropped at any depth (`types::without_hidden_hashers`), so `Set.new()` and `Map.new()` items collect into a `Vec[Set[i64]]` or `Vec[Map[String, i64]]` again. Kata 2077's three files check clean, `maze.kara` matches `maze.py`, and its differential prints `0 failures`; pinned by tests/check_sweep_fold_seed_and_hashed_items.rs (`hashed_collections_made_in_a_map_closure_collect_into_a_vec_of_them`).
title: `(0..=n).map(|_| Set.new()).collect()` into a `Vec[Set[i64]]` is refused, `Vec[Set[i64]]` implements `FromIterator[Set[i64]]`, not `FromIterator[Set[i64]]`: the settled item is compared with the impls whole, hasher included
detail: Found by a `karac check` sweep over kara-katas after kata 1139: kata 2077's three files, which checked clean on an 11-09 build, are refused at `let mut up: Vec[Set[i64]] = (0..=n).map(|_| Set.new()).collect();`. The same holds for `Map.new()` items into a `Vec[Map[K, V]]` and over `.iter()`; `Vec.new()` items are accepted. Bisected (2fd4cbdc5b good, 62d52e930c bad) to a65b4dc882, which checks a FromIterator bound whose item a default already settled against the impls' arguments by equality. `Set.new()`'s item is `Set[i64, ?H]`, its hasher a variable never inferred, and the impl's is `Set[i64]`; the display leaves both hashers off, so the message names one type twice.

title: `"U".repeat(n)` of a one-byte string is a call into `karac_mir_str_repeat`, an allocation through `karac_alloc_or_panic` and up to three `memcpy` calls where Rust's is inlined: kata 1138's bench runs 7.0G instructions to Rust's 4.6G (0.81 s to 0.59 s)
detail: Found timing kata 1138 (Alphabet Board Path). The bench (`bench/alphabet_board_path.kara`) answers 100,000 targets of 100 letters, each letter writing its moves with four `path.push_str("U".repeat(..))` calls, so 40M repeats of a one-byte string, most of them 0 to 4 long. Rust writes the same `path.push_str(&"U".repeat(..))`. Medians at 87bec305bc: Kāra 0.809 s, Rust 0.589 s, C (one buffer, the runs written in place, no temporaries) 0.210 s. Under callgrind both make the same allocations (malloc 687M and _int_free 882M instructions each), but Kāra spends 1,662M instructions in `karac_mir_str_repeat` (about 41 a call), 555M in `karac_alloc_or_panic` and 1,109M in `memcpy`, against Rust's 522M of `memcpy` and its repeat inlined into `main`: 7.03G instructions in all to 4.57G. The runtime copies the first byte and then doubles (`runtime/src/mir.rs`, `karac_mir_str_repeat`), so a run of 4 is three `memcpy` calls of 1, 1 and 2 bytes; a one-byte string could be a `write_bytes`, and the call itself could be inlined or the repeat fused into the `push_str` that consumes it. Not measured: how much each of the three would take back.

fix: 9049969b63. An array of unsuffixed integer literals bound whole (`let mut res = [0, 0]`) is now noted in `literal_lets` like a fill, one index deep (`literal_array_entry` with `element`, shared with the `for v in [..]` case), so a narrowing read of an element, directly or through a binding copied out of it, offers the first literal's suffix (`[0i32, 0]`) when every literal of the array fits the target; `[0, 5000000000]` is offered nothing. The advice now names the first literal ("write the first of them with the suffix `i32`, which types them all") rather than the largest, which it used to quote for `for v in [..]` too. Tests: tests/kata_1144_array_literal_suffix.rs (four shapes fixed and run, one too wide). A `karac check --output=json` sweep of all 7723 kara-katas .kara files gives byte-identical output under this binary and a control built at 24bc48a66d.
title: A narrowing read of an element of an array of literals offers only `as i32`: LeetCode's `let mut res = [0, 0]; ... res[i % 2] += <i32>; min(res[0], res[1])` returned as `i32` gets no suffix fix, where `Vec.filled(2, 0)` and a lone literal are offered theirs
detail: Kata 1144's Rust arm (Decrease Elements To Make Array Zigzag) counts the moves for each parity in `let mut res = [0, 0]`, adds `max(0, nums[i] - min(left, right) + 1)` with `nums: Vec[i32]`, and returns `min(res[0], res[1])` as the `i32` answer. After `karac fix` carried the rest (`Vec<i32>`, `std::cmp::max`/`min`, `Solution::`, `struct Solution {}`), `karac check` still refused the return twice with "implicit coercion from 'i64' to 'i32' would narrow ... Write an explicit 'as i32'" and no replacement: the array is typed by its first literal, which the `+=` operator leaves at the default `i64` (widening `i32` into it is implicit), and only a fill (`Vec.filled(n, 0)`, `[0; n]`, B-2026-11-08-57, B-2026-11-12-11) or a lone literal binding was recorded in `literal_lets`. Probes at 24bc48a66d: `let mut r = 0; r += v[0]; r` offers `: i32`; `let mut r = Vec.filled(2, 0); r[1] += v[0]; r[1]` offers `0i32`; `let mut r = [0, 0]` with `r[1] += v[0]`, `r[1] = r[1] + v[0]` or `r[1] = v[0]`, then `r[1]` returned as `i32`, offers nothing. `for v in [10, -10, 5]` already offered its first literal's suffix (kata 2046), so the array case was missing only for an array bound whole.

title: `for i in (low..n).step_by(2)` over an `i64` range runs about 1.2x the same loop written `while i < n { ...; i += 2 }`: `IterStepBy[Range].next` takes the generic path (a `first` flag, `advance_by(step - 1)` through `step_forward_within` and an `Option`, then `next`), which Rust's `StepBy<Range>` specializes
detail: Kata 1144's bench (20 arrays of 1000 values, 5000 rounds, the star arm's two passes `for i in (low..n).step_by(2)` lowering every second place) at 9049969b63, KARAC_AUTO_PAR=0 karac build, seven interleaved runs each on a 4-core container: the step_by program 447-503 ms (median 484), the same program with the loop written `let mut i = low; while i < n { ... i += 2; }` 362-432 ms (median 403), `rustc -O -C overflow-checks=on` of the step_by loop 391-453 ms (median 408). So the while loop matches overflow-checked Rust and the step_by loop costs about 1.2x it. MIR (KARAC_MIR_DUMP=elaborated) lowers the loop to `Range[i64].step_by(..)` then a call to `IterStepBy[Range[i64]].next` per item; the stdlib's `impl[I: Iterator] Iterator for IterStepBy[I]` (runtime/stdlib/source/iter.kara) checks and clears `first`, calls `Range.advance_by(step - 1)` (range.kara: `step_forward_within` returning an `Option`) and then `Range.next` (another `Option`), and LLVM does not reduce the loop-carried `first` flag and the two Options to a counted loop. Rust's `StepBy` over a range precomputes and steps by `step` (a `SpecRangeSetup` specialization). Not fixed in the kata (the star arm keeps `step_by(2)`, the natural Rust/Kāra form); the README cites this row for the gap to overflow-checked Rust.

fix: 18ea960272. `copy_item_param` (src/typechecker/exprs.rs) now takes an item that is an unbound literal variable for a copy, as it does an `i64`: the predicate's parameter over `(1..10)` is the literal itself rather than `ref` of it, so `*x` is refused with "drop the `*`" (machine-applicable) exactly as over `(1..n)`, and a bare use still types the literal (`let a: Vec[u8] = (1..10).filter(|x| x % 3 == 0).collect()` prints [3, 6, 9]). Tests: tests/kata_1145_literal_item_copy.rs (filter, position and a variable bound refused then fixed and run; a bare literal item typed by its use). A `karac check --output=json` sweep of 29380 sources (every kara-katas .kara and every corpus source.kara) gives byte-identical output under this binary and a control built at 8abeb07206, so no existing program used the accepted form.
title: `(1..10).filter(|x| *x % 2 == 0)` is accepted while `(1..n).filter(|x| *x % 2 == 0)` is refused with "drop the `*`": over a range of bare literals the predicate's item is a literal no use has typed yet, which `copy_item_param` does not take for a copy, so the parameter keeps the library's `ref`
detail: Kata 1145's differential wrote `(1..n + 1).filter(|v| ... *v ...)` (LeetCode's Rust habit) and `karac check` refused it: "unary '*' requires 'ref T' ... found 'i64'; a 'i64' is copied, so drop the `*`", as core-semantics.md §5.10 and docs/library/iterators.md say (a range's item is lent to the predicate as a bare `Self.Item`, a copy over `Copy` values, B-2026-10-13-32). The kata's harness had `(1..100).filter(|x| not f(Some(big), 99, *x))`, and that was accepted. Probes at 8abeb07206: `let a: Vec[i64] = (1..10).filter(|x| *x % 2 == 0).collect()` checks clean and prints [2, 4, 6, 8]; `let n = 10; (1..n).filter(|x| *x % 2 == 0)` is refused; `(0..5).position(|x| *x == 3)` is accepted. `copy_item_param` (src/typechecker/exprs.rs) strips the predicate parameter's `ref` only when `copied_item` holds for the item, and an unbound integer literal variable is not one of its concrete scalar types, so the parameter stayed `ref ?int` and `*x` read through it. No program's output differs: both forms run alike, only which one `karac check` accepts depended on whether the range's bounds were literals.

title: `String.normalize` and `std.regex` pass `karac check --targets=wasm_wasi` and then fail `karac build --target=wasm_wasi` with a bare wasm-ld `undefined symbol: karac_unicode_normalize_mir` / `karac_regex_mir`
detail: karac 0.8.1-dev+gde5c0dd08. The multilingual text tool, probe-core/uni/tool.kara, uses normalize, to_uppercase and to_lowercase, chars().rev(), split_whitespace and a Map word count over NFC/NFD, Greek final sigma, Turkish dotted I, ß, emoji ZWJ sequences, CJK and compatibility ligatures. Its output matches a Python unicodedata oracle (expected.out, 102 lines) on __mir-run, __mir-llvm-run, __mir-llvm-asan, `karac run` and `karac build`. For wasm_wasi, `karac check --targets=wasm_wasi tool.kara` prints 'All checks passed under target wasm_wasi', and `karac build --target=wasm_wasi` then fails with `error[link]: wasm-ld failed: rust-lld: error: ...: undefined symbol: karac_unicode_normalize_mir`. Minimal cells: nm.kara (`"é".normalize(NormalizationForm.Nfd)`) and rx.kara (`Regex.compile("a+b")`, link error `undefined symbol: karac_regex_mir`). to_uppercase alone builds and runs under node WASI (`STRASSE`). runtime/Cargo.toml says the regex and unicode features are 'never in default / lean / wasm archives', and the driver has no wasm counterpart of the native missing-opt-in-archive message with its recipe. So a program a user was told passes for wasm_wasi dies in the linker with a symbol name. The precedent is B-2026-11-08-37 (Network on wasm_wasi, refused at check with the call chain). The choice belongs to the owner: refuse normalize and regex at `check --targets=wasm_wasi` and at build with a named diagnostic and the call chain, or build wasm32-wasip1 unicode and regex archives and select them as on native. Either way, design.md §16's per-target resource list should say which one.
fix: Owner: review thread to route (target rules; the precedent -37 went to C).

title: A list literal compared with `==` / `!=` against an `Array` is typed `Vec` instead of taking the other operand as its expected type: `m != [75u8, 82u8, 69u8, 67u8]` with `m: Array[u8, 4]` is refused
detail: karac 0.8.1-dev+gde5c0dd08. Ruled at 60cc717ee6 (design.md § Collection literals): the other operand of `==` or `!=` is an expected type for a list literal, as it is for a number literal, so the literal builds an Array[u8, 4]. Measured in probe-core/bin/lit/a.kara with `let m: Array[u8, 4] = [75u8, 82u8, 69u8, 67u8];`: `m == [75, 82, 69, 67]` gives `cannot compare 'Array[u8, 4]' and 'Vec[i64]'`, and `m != [75u8, 82u8, 69u8, 68u8]` gives `cannot compare 'Array[u8, 4]' and 'Vec[u8]'`. The unsuffixed form should also type its elements u8 from the Array's element type. Found writing a magic-number check in a binary record decoder (probe-core/bin/rec.kara; workaround: a typed `let want: Array[u8, 4]`). Pin both spellings, and both operand orders (`[..] == m`).
fix: 16d2756e18. Under the ruling at 60cc717ee6 (design.md § Collection literals), `infer_binary` (src/typechecker/expr_ops.rs) now handles `==` and `!=` where one operand is a non-empty list literal and the other is not. It infers the other operand first. If that operand's type, read through a borrow, is an `Array`, a `Vec[T]` or a `Set[T]`, it checks the literal against that type, in either operand order. So with `m: Array[u8, 4]`, `m != [75, 82, 69, 67]` builds an `Array[u8, 4]` with `u8` elements. `s == [2, 1]` with `s: Set[i64]` builds a `Set`. `v == [1, 2]` with `v: Vec[i32]` builds a `Vec[i32]`, where before it was refused as `Vec[i32]` against `Vec[i64]`. Checked this way, a literal of the wrong length or with an element out of range is now refused for that reason, not as "cannot compare". `SortedSet` is left out because no list literal builds one (`let t: SortedSet[u16] = [5, 6]` is refused). Pinned by tests/list_literal_compare_expected.rs: both spellings, both orders, a borrow, Set, a narrow Vec and the refusals, run under run and interp.

title: A `MutFn` stored in a struct field or a `Vec` can be called through shared access (a non-`mut` binding, a borrowed `self`, a bare parameter), which core-semantics §9.6 forbids; `unused_mut` even tells the user to drop the `mut`
detail: karac 0.8.1-dev+gde5c0dd08. core-semantics.md §9.6 says a `MutFn` 'can be called only through an access that is unique: an owned binding, an `own` parameter or a `mut ref`. A shared borrow of a `MutFn` (a `ref`, or a bare parameter) cannot call it, which rules out a call re-entering the same closure.' For a local, the check works: `let f: MutFn() -> i64 = || { n += 1; n }; f()` is refused with 'calling it needs `let mut f`' (probe-core/bus/e4.kara). Through a container it does not. probe-core/bus/e5.kara: `struct Holder { f: MutFn() -> i64 }` with `fn call_shared(self) -> i64 { (self.f)() }` and `fn via_ref(h: Holder) -> i64 { (h.f)() }` (both shared), and `let fs: Vec[MutFn() -> i64] = [|| { n += 1; n }]; (fs[0])(); (fs[0])();` on a non-`mut` binding. All of this passes `karac check`, and every lane prints `1 2 1 2 3`: the closure's state changes through each shared path. e2.kara/e3.kara: `let mut h = Holder { f: .. }; (h.f)()` draws `warning[unused_mut]: h is never written ... the let needs no mut`, and with the `mut` removed it still compiles and runs. Expected: each shared-path call is an error naming the MutFn and the needed access (`mut ref self`, `h: mut ref Holder`, `let mut fs`), and the field call counts as a write of its base for unused_mut. Found while building an event bus (probe-core/bus/bus.kara, clean with `emit(mut ref self)`); that program and the §9.3 escaping-capture checks (e1.kara, E0500 after a move into a stored closure) behave as the spec says.
fix: Owner: Thread A (ownership / check).

title: A `par for` whose body value is a tuple is refused at check with the internal `an expression with no recorded type is not lowered yet`
detail: karac 0.8.1-dev+gde5c0dd08. probe-core/pwc/r3.kara: `let r = par for i in 0..4 { (i, i * 2) };` fails `karac check` with `error[typecheck]: r3.kara:3:31: an expression with no recorded type is not lowered yet`, pointing at the body's `{`. __mir-run gives the same message as `error[mir]: build: 3:31 in main.c0`. The same happens when the tuple comes from a call (`par for p in paths.iter() { count_file(p) }` where count_file returns `(i64, i64, Map[String, i64], (i64, String))`, the natural map step of a parallel word count) and over `paths.iter()` (r.kara). With the same loop, a body of `p.len()`, `count_file(p).0`, a struct literal, `Some(i)`, `[i, i]` or a String all check and run. A `par { (1, 2), (3, 4) }` block with tuple branches and a `map(|i| (i, i))` closure also work (r5.kara). core-semantics §11 says the value of `par for` is the Vec of the bodies' values, with no restriction on their type. The wording is also an internal message reaching a user, which is the diagnostics half. Workaround: wrap the tuple in a struct (pwc.kara does). Once wrapped, the program (par for map plus a TaskGroup(limit: 4) reduce into a sync struct with Atomic and Mutex[Map]) matches its Python oracle 3/3 times on __mir-run, __mir-llvm-run and ASan.
fix: Owner: Thread B (typed HIR / MIR builder).

title: `div_euclid` and `rem_euclid` exist only on `i64`: `i32`, `u8` and the other integer widths, and `f64`, have neither, although design.md names them as the Euclidean forms of `/` and `%`
detail: karac 0.8.1-dev+gde5c0dd08. design.md § Division, remainder and shifts: 'for Euclidean division call `x.div_euclid(n)`' and 'The always-non-negative remainder is `x.rem_euclid(n)`'. That section covers every integer type, and its examples are i32. probe-core/ints/e.kara: `(-17i64).rem_euclid(5)` and `.div_euclid(5)` work. `let b: i32 = -17; b.rem_euclid(5)` gives `no method 'rem_euclid' on type 'i32'`, and the same for `div_euclid`, for `u8.rem_euclid`, and for `f64.rem_euclid` / `div_euclid` (Rust has both on floats). library/core-types.md lists neither method in the integer or the float tables, so the docs need the entry too. The rest of the integer-width sweep (probe-core/ints/i.kara) agrees on __mir-run, __mir-llvm-run and ASan, checked against Python: u8/i8/u16/i32/u64/i128/u128 wrapping/checked/saturating/overflowing, casts, shifts, bit ops, rotate/swap/reverse, MIN/MAX, parse, saturating float casts and radix formatting.
fix: Owner: review thread to route (library surface).

4341008d1e. `src/typechecker/rust_binary_search.rs` reads a Rust binary search as a receiver and what it searches by: `binary_search(v)` as before, `binary_search_by_key(k, |p| key)` (a Rust `&k` read as `k`) and `binary_search_by(|p| order)`. The match, `if let` and `unwrap_or_else` rewrites build the closure's body into the two searches: `xs.partition_point(|p| key < k)` finds the insertion point, and the index holds `k` when it lies below `xs.partition_point(|p| key <= k)`; an ordering closure reads `order == Ordering.Less` and `order != Ordering.Greater`. The message opens "Kāra has no `binary_search_by_key`" (or `binary_search_by`) and names the two searches; a key value that is not free of effects is explained and not rewritten. Kata 1146's solution arm now reaches a clean check through `karac fix` alone and prints the same output as its mirror. Pinned by tests/kata_1146_binary_search_by_key.rs (by_key matched on Ok/Err, the value missing, `.unwrap_or_else(|i| i)`, `binary_search_by` matched and under `if let Err`, and a call as the key explained), and the B-2026-11-09-14 suite (tests/rust_binary_search_result_fixes.rs) still passes.
title: Rust's `binary_search_by_key` and `binary_search_by` taken apart as a `Result` have no fix: `match h.binary_search_by_key(&snap_id, |&(s, _)| s) { Ok(i) => h[i].1, Err(i) => h[i - 1].1 }` is refused with only "no method 'binary_search_by_key' on type 'Vec'" and "tuple pattern used but type is `?T7`", where the same shapes over `binary_search` are carried through `partition_point` (B-2026-11-09-14)
detail: Kata 1146's Rust arm (LeetCode's Snapshot Array as its Rust users write it) finds a place's value at a snap with `h.binary_search_by_key(&snap_id, |&(s, _)| s)` matched on `Ok(i)` / `Err(i)`. Kāra's library has `binary_search` (returning `Option[i64]`) and `partition_point`, and no `binary_search_by_key` or `binary_search_by` (docs/library/collections.md). B-2026-11-09-14 carried Rust's `binary_search` taken apart as a `Result` (a match or `if let` on `Ok`/`Err`, `.unwrap_or_else(|i| ..)`) to a `partition_point` rewrite, but `src/typechecker/rust_binary_search.rs` recognized only `binary_search` itself, so after `karac fix` had carried every other Rust-ism of the arm the match stayed refused with the bare no-method error and a type-variable message, with no fix and no word of `partition_point`. Measured at 595109dc62 on the arm, and on four shapes: by_key matched, by_key `.unwrap_or_else(|i| i)`, `binary_search_by(|p| p.0.cmp(&5))` matched, and `if let Err(i) = v.binary_search_by(..)`: each ends at "no method 'binary_search_by_key'" / "no method 'binary_search_by'".

fix: 4341008d1e. `check_i64_arg` (src/typechecker/exprs.rs), the check every library `i64` argument goes through after it is inferred (`Vec.filled`, `Vec.with_capacity`, `chunks`, `truncate` and the rest), now reads a cast argument's (from, to) from `operand_casts`, where an expression inferred with no expected type records it, and when it widens an integer losslessly to the slot's `i64` calls `lint_unneeded_cast` with that `i64` expected: "unnecessary cast: 'i32' widens to 'i64' implicitly here", machine-applicable. A `u64` to `i64` cast stays. A sweep of `karac check` against a control at 595109dc62 over the 4007 kara-katas and corpus programs holding `as i64` or `binary_search_by` differed only by this warning, at 12 files: the solution arms and differentials of katas 1514, 2022, 2028 and 2099 (`Vec.filled(n as i64, ..)`, `chunks(n as i64)`, `truncate(k as i64)`) and the corpus copies of 2022 and 2028; `karac fix` dropped each cast with the same output. Pinned by tests/kata_1146_binary_search_by_key.rs (`a_widening_cast_at_a_library_i64_argument_is_dropped`, and a `u64` cast kept).
title: `Vec.filled(n as i64, 0)` with `n: i32` is not linted as a lossless cast, while `let x: i64 = n as i64` and `g(n as i64)` at a user function's `i64` parameter are: a library argument checked through `check_i64_arg` is inferred with no expected type, so `lint_unneeded_cast` never sees the slot's `i64`
detail: Kata 1146's Rust arm writes `vec![vec![(0, 0)]; length as usize]` with `length: i32`; `karac fix` carries it to `Vec.filled(length as usize, ..)`, then `as i64`, and drops the `as i64` the arm's indexing casts became (`self.history[index as i64]` to `self.history[index]`, lossless_cast) but leaves `Vec.filled(length as i64, [(0, 0)])`, since `karac check` says nothing of it. Probe at 595109dc62: `fn f(n: i32) -> i64 { let v: Vec[i64] = Vec.filled(n as i64, 0); let x: i64 = n as i64; v.len() + x + g(n as i64) }` warns "unnecessary cast: 'i32' widens to 'i64' implicitly here" at `x` and at `g(..)` only. `Vec.filled` (src/typechecker/expr_call.rs) infers its count and then calls `check_i64_arg`, like `Vec.with_capacity`, `Vec.from_fn` and the other library `i64` slots; an expression inferred with no expected type records its cast in `operand_casts`, which only the binary-operator lint read.

title: Rust's `dst.copy_from_slice(src)` is "no method 'copy_from_slice' on type 'Slice'" with no fix, and the error type sets off a borrow error at every later use of the buffer
detail: A ported DHCP message builder writes the fixed BOOTP header with `pkt[4..8].copy_from_slice(xid)`, `pkt[236..240].copy_from_slice(&COOKIE)` and the like: Rust's slice copy, the usual way to fill a binary protocol's fixed fields. After `karac fix` (which drops the `&`) each call is `error[typecheck]: no method 'copy_from_slice' on type 'Slice'` with no fix and no hint, and the ownership pass then reports `pkt cannot be borrowed as mut ref T because it is also borrowed as Slice[T]` at each later `pkt.extend_from_slice(..)` / `pkt.push(..)` and `cannot move pkt while a slice borrow into it is still live` at the return: 6 type errors became 19. design.md § Range indexing already names the spelling: `c[a..b] = other` copies the elements of `other` into the range (T: Copy, length mismatch panics), and `clone_from_slice` for other element types. Repro: `fn main() { let mut pkt = Vec.filled(8, 0u8); let xid: Vec[u8] = [1u8, 2].to_vec(); pkt[0..2].copy_from_slice(xid); pkt.push(9); println(pkt); }`. Expected: an error naming the range assignment, with a machine-applicable fix to `pkt[0..2] = xid`, and no borrow errors after it.
fix: FIXED by b4be496812. src/typechecker/method_copy_from_slice.rs `try_copy_from_slice` (hooked in expr_method_call.rs after the concat hook) takes `copy_from_slice` with one argument on a Vec, Array or Slice receiver: an error (NoMethodFound) naming Kāra's spelling per design.md § Range indexing, with a machine-applicable fix that replaces from the receiver's end to the `)` with ` = <src>` when the receiver is a range index of a `Copy` element, and `.clone_from_slice(<src>)` otherwise; the call is typed `()`. A program's own trait impl of `copy_from_slice` on a sequence is left alone. `copy_from_slice` joined SLICE_MUTATING_METHODS, so the range view it writes through lives for the call alone and the later uses of the buffer no longer report borrow errors (19 diagnostics became the 6 real ones). Pinned by tests/copy_from_slice_fix.rs (four receivers: two Copy range views, a non-Copy range view, a `mut Slice` parameter; no borrow errors; `karac fix` output; the fixed program's run). apps/service/dhcp_server needs no hand edits.

title: `s == a` with a `Slice` on the left and an `Array` of the same element type on the right is never equal in compiled code (the array is read as a slice header); the MIR interpreter compares them
detail: A ported DHCP server checks the magic cookie with `pkt[236..240] != COOKIE` (`COOKIE: Array[u8, 4]`). Under __mir-run every message passes; under __mir-llvm-run, __mir-llvm-asan and karac build every one is dropped as `bad cookie`, so every client prints `no reply`. Repro: `fn main() { let v: Vec[u8] = [1u8, 2, 3, 4].to_vec(); let a: Array[u8, 4] = [1, 2, 3, 4]; let s: Slice[u8] = v[0..4]; println(f"{s == a} {s != a}"); }` prints `true false` in the interpreter and `false true` compiled (the same with `i64` elements). Slice == Slice and Vec == Vec agree. Cause: src/mir/lower.rs `eq_exprs` calls `eq_places(.., lt, ..)` with the LEFT operand's type for both places, so `seq_eq` calls `Slice[u8].len` on the array's place and compares against garbage. The checker accepts this direction (the right operand is `eq`'s argument); `Array == Slice` is refused with an `.as_slice()` fix (expr_ops.rs `vec_slice_compare_fix`), which is B-2026-11-13-17.
fix: FIXED by b4be496812. src/mir/lower.rs `eq_exprs`: when the two operands' types differ and both are a Vec, an Array or a Slice of the same element type (`mixed_seq_slice`), each side is viewed as a read-only slice (`seq_as_slice`, through `slice_view_of`'s `{T}.as_slice`) and compared by `eq_places` at that slice type, so `seq_eq` reads each side's own length. Pinned by tests/mir_slice_array_eq.rs (interp and compiled cells, u8 / String / i64 elements, unequal lengths, slice vs Vec; added to ci.yml's llvm list). apps/service/dhcp_server's cookie check passes on all four backends at KARAC_THREADS=1 and 4. The operand-order question is B-2026-11-13-17.

title: Comparing a `Slice` with an `Array` or `Vec` is accepted with the slice on the left and refused with it on the right; design.md § Slices does not say which a comparison is
detail: `s == a` (`s: Slice[u8]`, `a: Array[u8, 4]`) and `s == v` (`v: Vec[u8]`) check clean and run (the right operand is `eq`'s argument, a call boundary), while `a == s` and `v == s` are `cannot compare 'Array[u8, 4]' and 'Slice[u8]': a Vec[T] or Array[T, N] passes as a Slice[T] only at a call boundary (design.md § Slices); .as_slice() views it as one`, with a fix appending `.as_slice()` (src/typechecker/expr_ops.rs `vec_slice_compare_fix`, whose doc says 'a comparison is not one'). design.md § Slices says the conversion happens only at call boundaries, a method receiver included, and that `let` and assignment do not convert; it does not say whether `==` is a call (its right side `eq`'s argument, its left the receiver, which would accept both orders) or not (which would refuse both). Needs a ruling: accept both directions (drop the refusal) or refuse both (add the slice-left case to the refusal, with the same fix). Either way the two orders should agree. Found writing apps/service/dhcp_server, whose `pkt[236..240] != COOKIE` is the accepted order. The compiled answer for the accepted order was wrong (B-2026-11-13-16, fixed separately).
fix: FIXED by 1e72807626. Per the ruling (design.md § Slices, Comparison), `==` and `!=` between a `Slice`, a `Vec` and an `Array` of compatible element types are accepted in either order. The check's Eq/NotEq arm (src/typechecker/expr_ops.rs, `seq_compare`) now admits any such pair, and the `.as_slice()` fix is dropped for equality; an ordering comparison still takes it (tests/kata_1053_check_gaps.rs). MIR lowering already compared mixed sides as slices (b4be496812, B-2026-11-13-16), so both orders give the same answer on every backend. A length mismatch is `false`. Pinned in tests/mir_slice_array_eq.rs (`interp_/compiled_compares_slice_vec_and_array_in_either_order`, every pair in both orders, interpreter and compiled). The dhcp_server README notes both orders are accepted.

title: In a generic fn with `it: own I` and `I: Iterator[Item = T]`, the item of `for x in it` is typed as `I` itself for method calls and annotations: `x.abs()` gets "no method 'abs' on type parameter 'I'" and `let y: i64 = x` gets "expected 'i64', found 'I'"
detail: Relayed by the review thread 2026-11-13 from the probe; reproduced by Thread B on kara 47683e05ce. `fn total[I: Iterator[Item = i64]](it: own I) -> i64 { let mut t = 0; for x in it { t += x.abs(); } t }` is refused with "no method 'abs' on type parameter 'I'", and `let y: i64 = x` with "expected 'i64', found 'I'". The same happens with `Item = Str` and `to_string()`, with `T: Display`, and with the `where` spelling. `t += x` and the `while let Some(x) = it.next()` form work. B-2026-11-04-17 fixed the borrowed `it: I` form, and its message points users to this `own I` form. Read, not bisected: the `for` arm of `infer_expr` (src/typechecker/exprs.rs) takes the item from `element_type_of`, `iterable_item` or `iterable_param_item`. The last of these reads only an `Iterable[Item = T]` equation, and `borrowed_iterator_for` handles only borrowed iterators, so an owned `I: Iterator` parameter keeps `I` as the item. Cells: /mnt/attach/project-files/probe-core/sfz/g1.kara, g3, g7 and g8.
fix: Owner: Thread B.

title: A `par` or `par for` that calls an un-annotated local holding a returned function value is refused as "`unknown (a call through a value)`", even when the function's return type declares `with ()`
detail: Relayed by the review thread 2026-11-13 from the probe (the remainder of B-2026-10-27-8); reproduced by Thread B on kara 47683e05ce's release build. `fn mk() -> Fn() -> i64 + CrossTask with () { || 1 }`, then `let f = mk(); let (a, b) = par { f(), f() };` is refused "branches 1 and 2 of the `par` conflict: `unknown (a call through a value)`". title: `ParseError` variants differ from core-types.md Parsing in two edge cases: `u8.parse("-0")` gives `Invalid` where `InvalidDigit` is specified, and whitespace-only input to `i64.parse` gives `InvalidDigit` where `Empty` is specified
detail: Relayed by the review thread 2026-11-13 from the probe; reproduced by Thread B on kara 47683e05ce's release build, on both lanes. (a) `u8.parse("-0")` and `u8.parse("-00")` return `ParseError.Invalid`. The doc says an integer parse reports `InvalidDigit`, as Rust does for a sign on an unsigned type, and `u8.parse("-5x")` already gives `InvalidDigit`. (b) `i64.parse("   ")` and `i64.parse("\n")` give `InvalidDigit`. Parse ignores surrounding whitespace, so the trimmed input is empty and should give `Empty`. The doc is right in both cases. Repros: /mnt/attach/project-files/probe-core/ffz/iv.kara and ip.kara.
fix: Owner: Thread B.

title: A run-time value as a const generic argument (`Array[i64, n]` with `n` a parameter or local, or `n + 1`) is not reported at the argument as design.md § Const generic parameters specifies; it surfaces later as a type mismatch, an "undefined type", or three cascading errors. The same path leaves a top-level `const` opaque, so `Array[i64, SIZE]` refuses its own `[0; 3]`
detail: A lone name in a type argument is parsed as a type path. lower_array_type and lower_vector_type kept it as an opaque const name unless it was a const generic parameter in scope, so `fn f(n: i64) { let a: Array[i64, n] = [0; 3]; }` failed only as a mismatch between `Array[i64, n]` and `Array[i64, 3]`; an undeclared name failed in the resolver as "undefined type"; `n + 1` gave three errors. A top-level `const SIZE: i64 = 3` took the same opaque path, so `let a: Array[i64, SIZE] = [0; 3]` was refused. design.md § Const generic parameters gives the error: "const generic argument must be a compile-time constant expression".
fix: 2d1651fa5d. lower_array_type and lower_vector_type turn the length argument back into an expression (a lone name the parser routed to a type path becomes an identifier) and take it as a literal, a const generic parameter in scope, or eval_const_expr's value, so a top-level const lowers to its value. Anything else is one error at the argument: "`n` is a run-time value (a length known only at run time needs a `Vec`)" for a local or parameter, "`zzz` is not a `const` or a const generic parameter in scope" otherwise, deduplicated across the signature's two lowerings; the type becomes Type::Error so uses do not cascade. The resolver no longer reports such a length as "undefined type". Pinned by tests/const_arg_runtime_value.rs (3 tests; 3 failed on the old compiler).

title: Assigning into a field of a value moved as a whole (`eat(p); p.a = 1;`) is correctly refused, but the help suggests deriving `Clone` and cloning `p` at the move (with a `karac fix` edit) though nothing reads `p`; it should say a wholly moved value is initialized again only as a whole (core semantics § 3.4)
detail: The use-after-move report treats the field assignment as a use and offers the clone replacement it gives for a read. Core semantics § 3.4: a wholly moved value can be initialized again only as a whole, so the actionable help is to assign all of `p` (`p = ...`) or move out only the fields the callee needs. The clone suggestion compiles but copies a value nothing reads.
fix: 2d1651fa5d. ownership.rs assigns_into_part recognises a use that is an assignment into a field of the moved binding; the report then drops the clone replacement and its karac fix edit and says "'p' was moved as a whole, and a wholly moved value is initialized again only as a whole (core semantics §3.4): assign all of it (`p = ...`), or move out only the fields the callee needs". The refusal itself is unchanged. Pinned by tests/moved_root_part_assign.rs (2 tests).

title: A script inside a package but outside `src/` does not get the package's dependencies: `karac run app/scripts/s.kara` importing a path dependency is "this file belongs to no package"
detail: design.md § 4, Finding the package: `karac run file.kara` walks up from the file's own directory, "so a script inside a package gets that package's dependencies wherever it is run from". With app/kara.toml declaring `util = { path = "../util" }`, `karac run scripts/s.kara` (`import util.hello;`) failed at resolve: "unknown module `util`: this file belongs to no package", from the package root and from outside it alike; `karac check` the same. run_manifest_preamble found the manifest, but project_v2::package_tree built a tree only from the walk of `src/` and returned None when the entry was not in it, so the script ran as a lone file (`with_lone_file`). Found by the probe thread (probe-core/pkg case p26); routed to the apps thread by the review thread.
fix: FIXED by 0e77ed613d. A script inside a package but outside its `src/` now gets the package's dependencies (design.md § 4, Finding the package). project_v2::package_tree builds such a file's tree from walker::walk_script (the script as its only module and entry) beside the dependency walks; with no dependencies it stays a lone file. combine() checks the script's own program (build_cmds::script_check / run_check_cmds::script_check_refusal) rather than the package's src/, and `karac check <script>` routes through cmd_check_package_member with the script. The package's own src/ modules are not part of the script's program, so an error there is not the script's. run, check (text and JSON) and build all work, from the package root and from outside it. Pinned in tests/script_in_package_deps.rs (3 tests).
